practice.stem:
A trainee prepared the statement of changes in equity of Zhob Marble Limited for the year ended 31 December 2026. At 1 January 2026 the company had ordinary share capital $500,000 ($0.50 shares), share premium $25,000 and retained earnings $305,000. The trainee made these entries for the year:
• Profit for the year $142,000 added to retained earnings.
• Land revaluation gain of $50,000 added to retained earnings.
• Final dividend for 2025 paid $36,000 and interim dividend paid $22,000, both deducted from retained earnings.
• Final dividend for 2026 of $40,000, proposed in February 2027, deducted from retained earnings.
• Rights issue of 240,000 shares at $0.75 each: the full $180,000 added to share capital.
The trainee's closing retained earnings were $399,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three errors in the trainee's treatment.
parts.answer: 1 The proposed final dividend has been deducted – it is not a liability at the year end and is only disclosed in a note. 2 The revaluation gain was put in retained earnings – it belongs in a revaluation reserve (capital reserve). 3 The whole rights issue proceeds were put in share capital – $60,000 should be share premium.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the correct closing balances of (i) retained earnings, (ii) share capital, (iii) share premium and (iv) revaluation reserve.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of correcting the errors on total equity at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer: Total equity increases by $40,000 (only the proposed dividend changes the total).

practice.stem:
At 1 January 2026, Swat Orchards Limited had 2,000,000 ordinary shares of $0.25 each, share premium $140,000, revaluation reserve $60,000, general reserve $75,000 and retained earnings $412,000.
During 2026:
• February: paid the final dividend for 2025 of 3 cents per share.
• April: rights issue of 2 shares for every 5 held at $0.70 per share, fully subscribed.
• June: bonus issue of 1 share for every 4 held, using the share premium account.
• September: orchard land revalued upwards by $90,000.
• October: interim dividend of 2 cents per share paid.
• Profit for the year $286,000; $40,000 transferred to general reserve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of shares in issue at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer: 3,500,000 shares

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the statement of changes in equity for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.answer: Closing: share capital $875,000; share premium $325,000; revaluation reserve $150,000; general reserve $115,000; retained earnings $528,000; total $1,993,000.

practice.stem: Quetta Fruits Limited issued 200,000 ordinary shares of $1 each at $1.40 per share. The issue was fully subscribed and all money received by bank transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the share issue. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer:
Debit $    Credit $
Bank                           280,000            
Ordinary share capital                     200,000
Share premium                               80,000
parts.working: Dr Bank 280,000 (1); Cr share capital 200,000 at nominal value (1); Cr share premium 80,000 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one purpose for which the share premium account may be used.
parts.answer: To finance a bonus issue of fully paid shares (also accept: writing off share issue expenses).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Thar Solar Limited issued 500,000 ordinary shares of $0.25 each at $0.90 per share. All the money was received by bank transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amounts to be credited to (i) the ordinary share capital account and (ii) the share premium account.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the issue. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer: Dr Bank 450,000; Cr Ordinary share capital 125,000; Cr Share premium 325,000.
parts.working: 1 mark each line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three differences between a bonus issue and a rights issue of shares.
parts.answer: Bonus issue: no cash is received from shareholders, and the shares are paid for out of reserves / rights issue: shareholders pay cash for the new shares. Bonus issue: total equity is unchanged / rights issue: total equity rises by the cash received. Rights shares are offered to existing holders at a price, usually below market price; bonus shares are issued free to every holder in proportion to their holding.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three clear contrasts (cash; effect on total equity; price paid or not).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why the directors of a company might make a bonus issue.
parts.answer: To reduce the market price per share so that shares are easier for small investors to buy; to show that reserves are permanently kept in the business (capitalising them); to reward shareholders without paying out cash.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: Tharparkar Dairies Limited has ordinary share capital of $900,000 in shares of $0.50 each, share premium $80,000 and retained earnings $510,000. It makes a bonus issue of 1 share for every 4 held, using the share premium account first and then retained earnings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of bonus shares issued and the number of shares in issue after the bonus issue.
parts.answer: 450,000 bonus shares; 2,250,000 shares in issue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry for the bonus issue.
parts.answer: Dr Share premium 80,000; Dr Retained earnings 145,000; Cr Ordinary share capital 225,000.
parts.working: 450,000 × $0.50 = 225,000; share premium used first 80,000, remainder 145,000 from retained earnings. 1 mark debits, 1 mark credit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A shareholder owned 6,000 shares before the issue, when the market price was $2.50. Assuming the total market value of the company is unchanged, calculate the market price per share after the issue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a rights issue is offered to existing shareholders first.
parts.answer: So that each shareholder can keep the same percentage ownership and voting control; offering shares to the public could dilute their control and the value of their holding.
parts.working: 1 mark keep proportion/control; 1 mark avoids dilution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A company makes a rights issue of 1 share for every 3 held at $1.20. Hira owns 4,500 shares. Calculate how many new shares she can buy and how much she must pay.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what Hira could do if she does not want to buy the new shares.
parts.answer: Sell (renounce) her rights to another investor, or let them lapse.

practice.stem: Sukkur Sugar Limited has ordinary share capital of $1,200,000 in $1 shares, share premium $90,000, general reserve $100,000 and retained earnings $340,000. The directors make a bonus issue of 1 share for every 3 held. They use the share premium first, then the general reserve, then retained earnings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of bonus shares issued.
parts.answer: 400,000 shares

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the bonus issue.
parts.answer:
Debit $    Credit $
Share premium                   90,000            
General reserve                100,000            
Retained earnings              210,000            
Ordinary share capital                     400,000
parts.working: Share premium used in full 90,000 (1); general reserve 100,000 (1); retained earnings 210,000 (1); Cr share capital 400,000 (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of the bonus issue on (i) the company's cash and (ii) total equity.
parts.answer: (i) No effect — no cash is received. (ii) No effect — reserves are converted into share capital.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Gwadar Fisheries Limited has ordinary share capital of $450,000 in shares of $0.50 each. The market price of each share is $2.10. The company makes a rights issue of 1 new share for every 5 held at $1.60 per share. All the rights are taken up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash raised by the rights issue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in (i) share capital and (ii) share premium.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a company usually offers rights shares at a price below the current market price.
parts.answer: To encourage existing shareholders to take up the shares so the issue is fully subscribed and the cash is raised; shareholders who do not wish to buy can sell their rights.
parts.working: 1 mark: attractive to shareholders / ensures take-up; 1 mark: development.

practice.stem: Hala Pottery Limited has equity: ordinary shares of $1 each $1,500,000; share premium $120,000; general reserve $200,000; retained earnings $465,000. The directors make a bonus issue of 2 shares for every 5 held. They use reserves in this order: share premium, general reserve, retained earnings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the nominal value of the bonus issue and show how it is financed.
parts.answer: $600,000: share premium $120,000, general reserve $200,000, retained earnings $280,000.
parts.working: 1,500,000 × 2/5 = 600,000 (B1); 120,000 + 200,000 = 320,000 from capital and general reserves (M1); remainder 280,000 from retained earnings (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the equity section of the statement of financial position immediately after the bonus issue.
parts.answer: Ordinary share capital 2,100,000; share premium 0; general reserve 0; retained earnings 185,000; total equity 2,285,000.
parts.working: 1 mark share capital; 1 mark retained earnings; 1 mark total unchanged.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why directors normally use the share premium account first when making a bonus issue.
parts.answer: Share premium is a capital reserve that cannot be used to pay cash dividends, so using it keeps revenue reserves (retained earnings/general reserve) available for future dividends.
parts.working: 1 mark share premium cannot be distributed; 1 mark keeps distributable reserves.

practice.stem: Ravi Paper Mills Limited has 800,000 ordinary shares of $1 each. During the year it will make a rights issue of 1 share for every 4 held at $1.50, and a bonus issue of 1 share for every 5 held. All rights are taken up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of shares in issue at the end of the year if the rights issue takes place before the bonus issue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cash raised by the rights issue (i) if it comes before the bonus issue and (ii) if it comes after the bonus issue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why the order of the issues matters to the company.
parts.answer: If the bonus issue comes first, more rights shares are issued, so more cash is raised (and the bonus shares also earn rights).

parts.label: a
parts.text: For a bonus issue funded from retained earnings, and for a rights issue at a premium, state whether each of the following increases, decreases or has no effect: cash; number of shares; share capital; share premium; retained earnings; total equity.
parts.answer: Bonus issue: cash no effect; shares increase; share capital increase; share premium no effect; retained earnings decrease; total equity no effect. Rights issue at a premium: cash increase; shares increase; share capital increase; share premium increase; retained earnings no effect; total equity increase.
parts.working: 1 mark for each line (cash; number of shares; share capital; share premium; retained earnings; total equity) where both issues are correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a bonus issue does not make shareholders richer.
parts.answer: Each shareholder keeps the same proportion of the company; the company's net assets are unchanged, so the market price per share falls in proportion and the value of each holding stays about the same.
parts.working: 1 mark same proportion/net assets unchanged; 1 mark price per share falls.

practice.stem: Gilgit Hydro Limited has 3,000,000 ordinary shares of $1 each, currently quoted at $2.40. It needs exactly $1,350,000 for a new turbine and plans a rights issue at $1.80 per share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of new shares that must be issued and express the rights issue as a ratio of new shares to existing shares.
parts.answer: 750,000 shares; 1 for every 4 held.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in share capital and in share premium.
parts.answer: Share capital $750,000; share premium $600,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two risks to the company if the rights issue is not fully taken up.
parts.answer: It will not raise the full amount needed for the project; it may signal a lack of shareholder confidence and lower the share price; it may need an underwriter (at a cost) or other finance.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two.

practice.stem:
Shandur Ceramics Limited has 3,000,000 ordinary shares of $1 each in issue, with a market price of $2.40. The directors are considering two options:
Option 1: a bonus issue of 1 share for every 6 held, funded from the share premium account, which has a balance of $650,000.
Option 2: a rights issue of 1 share for every 6 held at $1.80 per share.
Ayesha owns 12,000 shares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash the company would raise under Option 2, and the amount Ayesha would have to pay to take up all her rights.
parts.answer: Company: $900,000; Ayesha: $3,600

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of each option on the company's (i) cash, (ii) share capital and (iii) total equity.
parts.answer: Option 1 (bonus): (i) no change; (ii) increases by $500,000; (iii) no change. Option 2 (rights): (i) increases by $900,000; (ii) increases by $500,000; (iii) increases by $900,000.
parts.working: 1 mark per row (i), (ii), (iii) correct for both options.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The company needs $850,000 to modernise its kiln. Advise the directors which option they should choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Rights issue: raises 900,000, enough for the $850,000 kiln; no interest or repayment; existing holders keep their percentage if they take up rights. But shareholders must find cash, and it may depress the share price; any shortfall in take-up reduces funds. Bonus issue: costs shareholders nothing and may please them, makes shares more marketable, but raises no cash, so it does not meet the need. Decision: choose the rights issue (Option 2), as only it provides the finance required.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for points on both options, using figures; 1 mark for a justified decision.

practice.stem: Imran owns 2,000 ordinary shares in Margalla Cement Limited, quoted at $3.00 each. The company makes a rights issue of 1 new share for every 4 held at $2.20 per share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assuming the total market value of the company rises by exactly the cash raised, calculate the market price per share after the rights issue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of Imran's investment after the issue if he (i) takes up all his rights and (ii) sells all his rights at their value of $0.64 each. Show the cash he pays or receives in each case.
parts.working: New shares 500 (B1). (i) cash paid 1,100, value 7,100 (M1 A1). (ii) value of right = 2.84 − 2.20 = 0.64; cash 320; shares + cash = 6,000 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Imran's wealth before the issue was $6,000. Use your answers to explain why a shareholder who does nothing will lose wealth.
parts.answer: If he lets the rights lapse he keeps 2,000 shares worth 2.84 = $5,680, a loss of $320; by taking up or selling the rights his wealth is preserved (6,000 + cash paid, or 6,000 in shares and cash).
parts.working: 1 mark loss calculated; 1 mark explanation of dilution/price fall.

practice.stem: Hingol Foods Limited has 4,000,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each. Profit after tax is $1,080,000 a year. It plans a new factory costing $1,500,000, to be financed by an issue of new shares at $2.50 each. The factory is expected to increase profit after tax by $260,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the earnings per share (i) before the expansion and (ii) after the expansion, in cents to two decimal places.
parts.answer: (i) 27.00 cents (ii) 29.13 cents

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the share issue, assuming the shares have a nominal value of $0.50.
parts.answer: Dr Bank 1,500,000; Cr Ordinary share capital 300,000; Cr Share premium 1,200,000.
parts.working: 1 mark capital, 1 mark premium.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether the share issue is in the interests of the existing shareholders. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: EPS rises from 27.00c to 29.13c, so shareholders' earnings per share improve; the project's extra profit more than covers the dilution. However: the forecast profit may not be achieved; if the issue is to new investors existing holders' control is diluted (a rights issue avoids this); the share price may fall on issue. Conclusion: yes, if the forecast is reliable and it is offered as a rights issue.
parts.working: 1 mark use of EPS figures; 2 marks other factors; 1 mark justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Sibi Textiles Limited has ordinary share capital of $600,000 in $0.50 shares, share premium $30,000 and retained earnings $390,000. It makes a rights issue of 1 for 3 at $0.80, fully taken up, and then a bonus issue of 1 for 2, using share premium first and then retained earnings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the journal entries to record (i) the rights issue and (ii) the bonus issue. Narratives are not required.
parts.answer: (i) Dr Bank 320,000; Cr Ordinary share capital 200,000; Cr Share premium 120,000. (ii) Dr Share premium 150,000; Dr Retained earnings 250,000; Cr Ordinary share capital 400,000.
parts.working: Rights shares 1,200,000 ÷ 3 = 400,000 (B1); entries (2). Bonus shares 1,600,000 ÷ 2 = 800,000, value 400,000 (B1); entries (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the equity section of the statement of financial position after both issues.
parts.answer: Ordinary share capital $1,200,000; share premium $0; retained earnings $140,000; total $1,340,000.
parts.working: 1 mark each line; total follows.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between ordinary shares and loan notes (debentures).
parts.answer: Any two: ordinary shareholders are owners, loan note holders are lenders (creditors); dividends are paid only if declared and profits allow, interest must be paid at a fixed rate whether or not there is profit; ordinary shareholders usually vote, loan note holders do not; loan notes are repaid on a set date, ordinary shares are not normally repaid; on liquidation loan note holders are repaid before shareholders; interest is an expense in the SOPL, dividends are a distribution in the SOCE.
parts.working: 2 marks per difference, clearly comparing both.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three differences between ordinary shares and preference shares.
parts.answer: Preference shares usually receive a fixed rate of dividend; ordinary dividends vary with profit. Preference dividends are paid before ordinary dividends. On winding up, preference shareholders are repaid before ordinary shareholders. Preference shareholders usually have no vote; ordinary shareholders vote at general meetings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ordinary shares are described as carrying the highest risk.
parts.answer: Ordinary shareholders are paid last – dividends only after interest and preference dividends, and capital only after all other claims on winding up – so they may receive nothing if the company does badly (though they gain most if it does well).
parts.working: 1 mark paid last; 1 mark may receive nothing / variable return.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each item, suggest a suitable source of finance and state whether it is short-term or long-term:
(i) buying extra inventory before the Eid sales season
(ii) building a new warehouse
(iii) paying wages during a month when customers pay late
(iv) buying a fleet of delivery vans
parts.answer: (i) bank overdraft / trade credit – short-term; (ii) loan notes, long-term bank loan or share issue – long-term; (iii) bank overdraft / debt factoring – short-term; (iv) bank loan, leasing or hire purchase – medium/long-term.
parts.working: 1 mark each (source and term).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a business should not use a bank overdraft to pay for a new building.
parts.answer: An overdraft is repayable on demand and is meant for short-term needs; the building produces returns over many years, so the business could be forced to repay before it has earned the money – causing a liquidity crisis; overdraft interest is usually high.
parts.working: 1 mark repayable on demand/short-term; 1 mark mismatch with long-term asset.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages and two disadvantages to a company of using retained profits to finance expansion.
parts.answer: Advantages: no interest or repayment; no dilution of control; no issue costs; quickly available. Disadvantages: less available for dividends, which may upset shareholders; may not be enough for large projects; opportunity cost of keeping cash in the business.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two advantages and two disadvantages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by loan notes (debentures).
parts.answer: Long-term loans made to a company, usually at a fixed rate of interest and repayable on a stated date.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A company issues $250,000 of 7% loan notes on 1 April 2026. Its year ends on 31 December 2026. Calculate the finance cost for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two differences between loan notes and ordinary shares from the point of view of the company.
parts.answer: Loan note interest must be paid whether or not profit is made, dividends are at the directors' discretion; loan notes are repaid on a fixed date, shares are permanent capital; loan note holders have no vote; interest is a charge against profit, dividends an appropriation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Mehran Packaging Limited has 2,000,000 ordinary shares in issue and needs $500,000 for a new production line. Profit before interest and tax next year is expected to be $640,000 under either option. Tax is 25% of profit after interest.
Option A: issue 7% loan notes (2034) of $500,000.
Option B: issue 250,000 ordinary shares at $2.00 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual interest under Option A.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit after tax under each option.
parts.answer: Option A: $453,750; Option B: $480,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit after tax per ordinary share, in cents to two decimal places, under each option.
parts.answer: Option A: 22.69 cents; Option B: 21.33 cents

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the directors which option to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Option A (loan notes): higher return per share (22.69c v 21.33c); no dilution of control; interest is fixed. But interest must be paid even in a bad year and the 500,000 must be repaid; gearing rises; security may be needed. Option B (shares): no compulsory payments or repayment; lower risk. But return per share falls and control is diluted. Decision with reason, e.g. choose loan notes if profits are stable, as the profit before interest is well above the interest cost (640,000 v 35,000).
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for points on both sides (using figures); 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: Thal Agro Limited has equity of $2,400,000 and non-current liabilities of $600,000. It needs $1,000,000 for irrigation equipment. Option A: issue 8% loan notes. Option B: issue ordinary shares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gearing ratio (non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities)) as a percentage to one decimal place: (i) now, (ii) under Option A and (iii) under Option B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to ordinary shareholders of the company becoming more highly geared.
parts.answer: Advantage: if the return on the new investment exceeds the interest rate, the surplus goes to ordinary shareholders, raising EPS; no dilution of control. Disadvantage: interest must be paid even in bad years, so profits available to shareholders become more volatile and the risk of insolvency rises.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Lahore Lighting Limited has profit from operations of $420,000 and finance costs of $36,000. It plans a bank loan of $900,000 at 9% per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest cover (profit from operations ÷ finance costs) before the new loan, and after it if profit from operations rises by $75,000. Give answers to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Before 11.67 times; after 4.23 times.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a bank considering the loan would be interested in the interest cover.
parts.answer: It shows how many times profit can pay the interest, so how safe the interest payments are; a big fall means less margin of safety if profits drop, so the bank may refuse, charge more or demand security.
parts.working: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark link to risk of lending.

practice.stem: Sialkot Sports Goods Limited exports footballs on 90-day credit. It has trade receivables of $240,000. A factoring company offers to pay 80% of the receivables immediately and the balance, less a fee of 2% of the receivables, when customers pay.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash Sialkot Sports Goods Limited receives immediately and the total amount it will receive when the customers have paid, assuming all debts are collected.
parts.answer: Immediately $192,000; in total $235,200.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages and one disadvantage of debt factoring for the company.
parts.answer: Advantages (any two): immediate cash, improving liquidity; saves the cost of credit control; may protect against irrecoverable debts if the factor takes the risk. Disadvantage (any one): the fee reduces profit; customers may see it as a sign of financial weakness; the company loses direct contact with its customers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two advantages and one disadvantage, each explained.

practice.stem: The Qureshi family owns 1,800,000 of the 6,000,000 ordinary shares in Qureshi Rice Mills Limited. The company needs to issue 1,500,000 new shares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the family's percentage holding (i) now and (ii) after a public issue of the new shares.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many shares the family would need to buy in a 1 for 4 rights issue to keep its present percentage holding.
parts.answer: 450,000 shares

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the family whether the company should raise the money by a public issue or a rights issue. Give one reason for and one reason against your choice.
parts.answer: e.g. Rights issue: keeps their 30% holding and influence (for); but they must find cash to buy their shares (against). Public issue: brings in new investors and may raise more (for) but dilutes control to 24% (against). Any justified recommendation.
parts.working: 1 mark recommendation; 1 mark reason for; 1 mark reason against.

practice.stem: Swat Valley Hotels Limited wants $2 million to build a new wing. Its gearing (non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities)) is already 58%. Profits are seasonal and fell in each of the last two years after floods. The directors are considering: (1) a rights issue of ordinary shares; (2) a five-year bank loan at 11% interest secured on the hotel; (3) a sale and leaseback of its existing staff accommodation annex.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each of the three sources of finance for Swat Valley Hotels Limited, and recommend which the directors should use. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Rights issue: no interest or repayment, no security needed, keeps gearing low (already high at 58%); but shareholders may not take up the issue after two poor years; cost of issue; dividends expected later. Bank loan (5 years): quick, interest tax-deductible, owners keep control; but interest and repayments must be met from uncertain seasonal cash flow, raises gearing further, bank may require the hotel as security and may refuse given current gearing. Sale and leaseback of the annex: releases cash from existing assets quickly; leaseback means future lease payments and loss of the asset's future value. Recommendation: a rights issue (or mixed with a smaller loan) because gearing is already high and profits are volatile, so fixed interest increases risk.
parts.working: Level 3 (8–10): balanced discussion of all three sources applied to the hotel (gearing, seasonality, control), clear justified recommendation. Level 2 (4–7): advantages and disadvantages of at least two sources with some application, recommendation given. Level 1 (1–3): generic points about sources of finance, little application.

practice.stem: Karachi Shipyard Services Limited needs $2,400,000 to buy a floating dock. Option 1: 9% loan notes repayable in 2036. Option 2: issue ordinary shares at $2.40; the company pays a dividend of 15 cents per share each year. Interest is allowable against tax at 25%; dividends are not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate (i) the annual interest under Option 1 and its cost after tax relief, and (ii) the extra annual dividends payable under Option 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the two options and recommend which the directors should choose.
parts.answer: Option 1: costs $162,000 a year after tax relief, a little more than the $150,000 of dividends under Option 2; interest is fixed and compulsory; no dilution of control, but increases gearing and risk, must be paid every year and repaid in 2036; needs security. Option 2: no compulsory payment – dividends can be cut in a bad year; no repayment; lowers gearing; but dilutes control and EPS, issue costs, dividends not tax-deductible and expectations of a rising dividend. Recommendation depends on current gearing, stability of profits and attitude of existing shareholders.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each option's advantages/disadvantages applied to the case (max 4); 1 mark comparison of costs using (a); 1 mark justified recommendation.

practice.stem: Faisal Plastics Limited bought new injection-moulding machines last year using its bank overdraft. It now has current assets of $380,000 and current liabilities of $410,000, including the overdraft of $220,000. The bank has offered to convert the overdraft into a five-year loan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio before and after the overdraft is replaced by a five-year bank loan, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Before 0.93 : 1; after 2.00 : 1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the overdraft had grown so large and why the bank is concerned.
parts.answer: The overdraft has been used to pay for long-term assets (the new machines), not just short-term working capital; it is repayable on demand and the company now has more current liabilities than current assets; the bank fears the company could not repay if it demanded the money.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three points linked to the case.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether converting the overdraft into a loan solves the company's problems.
parts.answer: It matches long-term finance to long-term assets and improves the current ratio, removing the risk of repayment on demand; interest may be lower. But it does not create any cash: total borrowing is the same, gearing rises, fixed repayments must be met, and if the business is unprofitable or has poor credit control the overdraft will build up again. Conclusion: a sensible step, but the company must also improve cash flow.
parts.working: 2 marks for benefits, 2 marks for limitations/conclusion.

practice.stem:
Okara Textiles Limited has annual credit sales of $1,460,000 and average trade receivables of $300,000. It finances these with a bank overdraft costing 14% a year.
A factor offers to advance 85% of receivables at 12% interest a year, for a service fee of 1.5% of credit sales. The company would save $7,000 a year in credit control costs. Any receivables not advanced would still be financed by the overdraft.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual cost of financing the receivables (i) by the overdraft and (ii) by factoring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to use the factor. Include one non-financial factor in your answer.
parts.answer: Factoring costs $9,800 more a year, so on cost alone keep the overdraft; however the factor gives more certain finance that grows with sales and may cover bad debts, while the overdraft can be withdrawn. Non-financial: customer relationships may suffer if the factor chases debts aggressively. Recommendation with reason.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison of costs; 1 mark non-financial factor; 1 mark justified advice.

practice.stem: Bright Sun Panels Limited assembles solar panels in Karachi. It has equity of $5,000,000 and non-current liabilities of $3,000,000. It needs $3 million for new automated equipment, which is expected to be out of date in about five years. Competition from imports has reduced profits in the last two years. The founding family owns 60% of the shares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gearing ratio (non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities)) as a percentage to one decimal place if the $3 million is raised (i) by a long-term loan and (ii) by an issue of ordinary shares.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the suitability of a long-term loan, an issue of ordinary shares and leasing the equipment for Bright Sun Panels Limited, and recommend the best source.
parts.answer: Loan: interest tax-deductible, no dilution, but gearing becomes high (54.5%), interest fixed while profits are falling with competition; security needed. Shares: no fixed cost, gearing falls to 27.3%, good for a risky growing business, but family may lose control, issue costs, EPS diluted. Leasing: no large initial outlay, equipment can be upgraded as technology changes quickly, payments spread and matched to use; but total cost higher, asset not owned, lease liability still adds to debt under current standards. Recommendation, e.g. shares or leasing because profits are uncertain and technology changes fast.
parts.working: Level 3 (7–8): all three sources discussed with reference to the case and gearing figures; justified recommendation. Level 2 (4–6): two or three sources with some application; recommendation. Level 1 (1–3): general points about sources.

practice.stem: The bookkeeper of Kaghan Dairy Limited included dividends paid of $40,000 in administrative expenses. The draft profit for the year was $146,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why your correction does not change the retained earnings at the end of the year.
parts.answer: The dividend is now deducted in the statement of changes in equity instead of the statement of profit or loss, so retained earnings are reduced by the same amount either way.
parts.working: 1 mark: dividend deducted in SOCE; 1 mark: same overall effect on retained earnings.

practice.stem: The draft profit for the year ended 31 December 2026 of Bolan Mining Limited is $212,400. The company has had $300,000 of 6.5% loan notes throughout the year. No loan note interest has been paid or recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of the correction on the statement of financial position at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer: Current liabilities (other payables) increase by $19,500; retained earnings decrease by $19,500.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The bookkeeper of Neelum Woodcraft Limited included a transfer to the general reserve of $25,000 in administrative expenses. Draft profit for the year was $158,300.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the transfer should not be charged in the statement of profit or loss, and state where it should be shown.
parts.answer: A transfer to general reserve is an appropriation of profit, not a cost of earning revenue; it simply earmarks part of retained earnings. It is shown in the statement of changes in equity: retained earnings column decreases and general reserve column increases.
parts.working: 1 mark appropriation not expense; 1 mark shown in SOCE; 1 mark RE down / GR up.

practice.stem: The draft statement of profit or loss of Ziarat Apiaries Limited shows a profit of $186,000. The accountant has forgotten to include the estimated tax on profit of $41,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year after correcting this omission.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the tax will appear in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Current liability: tax payable $41,500.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a limited company's statement of profit or loss includes a tax charge but a sole trader's does not.
parts.answer: A company is a separate legal entity and pays corporation (income) tax on its own profits; a sole trader's tax is a personal liability of the owner, so any tax paid by the business is treated as drawings.
parts.working: 1 mark company separate taxable person; 1 mark sole trader's tax is personal/drawings.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each error, state whether correcting it changes (A) the profit for the year, (B) retained earnings only, without changing profit, or (C) neither profit nor retained earnings.
(i) An interim dividend paid was debited to wages.
(ii) The proceeds of a share issue were credited to revenue.
(iii) A bonus issue was debited to retained earnings instead of share premium.
(iv) Closing inventory was overstated.
(v) A transfer to general reserve was not recorded.
parts.answer: (i) A – profit rises (wages fall) and retained earnings are unchanged overall, because the dividend is then deducted in the SOCE; (ii) A – profit falls, and share capital/premium increase; (iii) B – retained earnings increase, share premium decreases; (iv) A – profit falls; (v) B – retained earnings decrease, general reserve increases.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
The draft profit for the year of Pothohar Steel Limited was $284,600. The following errors and omissions were found.
1 Closing inventory was overvalued by $7,800.
2 The company has $300,000 8% loan notes. Interest for the second half of the year has not been paid or recorded.
3 The allowance for irrecoverable debts should be increased by $2,200.
4 A new machine costing $16,000 was debited to repairs. Machinery is depreciated at 25% per year on cost, with a full year's charge in the year of purchase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year.
parts.answer:
Draft profit for the year                          284,600
1 Closing inventory overvalued                     (7,800)
2 Loan note interest owing                        (12,000)
3 Increase in allowance for irrecoverable debts     (2,200)
4 Machine treated as repairs                        16,000
4 Depreciation on machine                          (4,000)
Corrected profit for the year                      274,600
parts.working: 1 mark each for items 1–3 (7,800, 12,000 = 8% × 300,000 × 6/12, 2,200); item 4: add back 16,000 (1), depreciation 4,000 (1); corrected profit 274,600 (1) — max 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of item 4 on the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Non-current assets increase by $12,000 (cost 16,000 less depreciation 4,000); retained earnings increase by the same amount.
parts.working: 1 mark NCA carrying amount; 1 mark retained earnings.

practice.stem:
The draft profit of Malakand Cables Limited for the year ended 31 December 2026 is $345,200. The auditors found:
1 Closing inventory was overvalued by $6,400.
2 Depreciation of $12,000 has been charged on land.
3 Rent receivable of $3,500 for the last month of the year has not been recorded.
4 Insurance of $4,800 paid for the year to 31 March 2027 was all charged to this year (year end 31 December 2026).
5 A customer owing $2,750 has been declared bankrupt; the debt has not been written off.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.working: Draft 345,200; less inventory 6,400; add land depreciation 12,000 (land is not depreciated); add rent receivable 3,500; add insurance prepaid 1,200 (4,800 × 3/12); less irrecoverable debt 2,750 = 352,750. 1 mark each adjustment, 1 mark final.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of correcting the land depreciation on the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: The carrying amount of land increases by $12,000 (accumulated depreciation removed); retained earnings increase by $12,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: 274,800 + dividends 64,000 − revaluation gain 45,000 = 293,800.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the retained earnings and the general reserve at 31 March 2027.
parts.answer: Retained earnings $517,800; general reserve $90,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where the revaluation gain should be shown.
parts.answer: In the revaluation reserve (other comprehensive income / statement of changes in equity), not in profit.

practice.stem:
Errors found in the books of Kalam Valley Resorts Limited:
1 The issue of 120,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each at $0.80 was credited to revenue.
2 An interim dividend paid of $18,000 was debited to the wages account.
3 Office equipment costing $7,500 was debited to repairs. Office equipment is depreciated at 10% per year on cost, with a full year's charge in the year of purchase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare journal entries to correct each error. Narratives are not required.
parts.answer:
1 Dr Revenue 96,000; Cr Ordinary share capital 60,000; Cr Share premium 36,000.
2 Dr Retained earnings (dividends) 18,000; Cr Wages 18,000.
3 Dr Office equipment 7,500; Cr Repairs 7,500; and Dr Depreciation (SOPL) 750; Cr Accumulated depreciation 750.
parts.working: 2 marks per item (1 mark for each correct line pair).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect of correcting all three errors on the draft profit for the year.
parts.working: Revenue −96,000; wages +18,000; repairs +7,500; depreciation −750 → net −71,250 (M1 A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each error, state whether profit for the year, total equity and current assets are overstated, understated or unaffected, giving the amount where there is an effect.
1 Goods costing $3,200 sent to a customer on sale or return were included in revenue at selling price $4,000 and excluded from inventory.
2 A loan of $50,000 received from a bank was credited to share capital.
3 Prepaid advertising of $2,600 was not recorded.
parts.answer: 1: profit overstated $800; total equity overstated $800; current assets overstated $800 (receivables +4,000, inventory −3,200). 2: profit no effect; total equity overstated $50,000; current assets no effect (liabilities understated). 3: profit understated $2,600; total equity understated $2,600; current assets understated $2,600.
parts.working: 2 marks per error (all three effects correct = 2; two correct = 1).

practice.stem:
Draft profit for the year ended 31 March 2027 of Margalla Software Limited was $418,300. Retained earnings at 1 April 2026 were $236,000. Dividends paid in the year were $90,000 and have been correctly recorded.
Errors found:
1 A bonus issue of $25,000, which was to be funded from share premium, was debited to general expenses and credited to share capital.
2 Rent received of $12,000 for April to June 2027 was included in income for the year.
3 Office equipment costing $64,000 was depreciated at 10% per year on cost instead of the company's policy of 15% per year on cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working:
Draft profit                                     418,300
1 Bonus issue wrongly charged as expense          25,000
2 Rent received in advance                      (12,000)
3 Extra depreciation (15% − 10%) × 64,000        (3,200)
Corrected profit                                 428,100
1 mark per adjustment (3), 1 mark corrected profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the retained earnings at 31 March 2027.
parts.working: 236,000 + 428,100 − dividends 90,000 = 574,100. (The bonus issue is funded from share premium, so it does not reduce retained earnings.) M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the correct double entry for the bonus issue.
parts.answer: Dr Share premium $25,000; Cr Ordinary share capital $25,000.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Draft profit of Tarbela Engineering Limited for 2026 is $512,600. At 1 January 2026: share capital $1,000,000 ($1 shares), share premium $150,000, general reserve $80,000, retained earnings $426,000. An interim dividend of $45,000 was paid and correctly deducted in the statement of changes in equity. The following were then discovered:
1 A bonus issue of 1 for 5 was recorded as Dr Administrative expenses, Cr Share capital $200,000. It should have been made from the share premium first and then the general reserve.
2 A final dividend of $70,000, proposed by the directors in March 2027, was charged as an expense and shown as a current liability.
3 A revaluation gain on land of $120,000 was included in revenue.
4 Loan note interest of $9,000 for December 2026 has not been recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: 512,600 + bonus issue 200,000 + proposed dividend 70,000 − revaluation 120,000 − interest 9,000 = 653,600. 1 mark per adjustment (max 4 incl. answer).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the closing balance of each component of equity at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer: Share capital $1,200,000; share premium $0; general reserve $30,000; revaluation reserve $120,000; retained earnings $1,034,600.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the correct treatment of the proposed final dividend in the financial statements for 2026.
parts.answer: Not recognised as a liability or deduction at 31 December 2026; disclosed in a note (IAS 10, non-adjusting event).

practice.stem: While preparing the financial statements of Dera Ghazi Cotton Limited for the year ended 31 December 2026, the accountant finds that closing inventory at 31 December 2025 was overstated by $14,000 because some goods were counted twice. Draft profits are: 2025 $184,000 (already published); 2026 $205,000 (draft, using the overstated opening inventory). The amount is material.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for 2025 and for 2026.
parts.working: Closing inventory 2025 overstated → 2025 profit overstated: 184,000 − 14,000 = 170,000 (B1). The same figure was 2026 opening inventory → 2026 cost of sales overstated, profit understated: 205,000 + 14,000 = 219,000 (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the correction should be presented in the 2026 financial statements, which also show 2025 comparatives.
parts.answer: It is a material prior period error: correct it retrospectively – restate the 2025 comparative figures (profit, inventory, retained earnings) and adjust the opening retained earnings for 2026 in the statement of changes in equity by −$14,000; disclose the nature and amount of the error. It is not put through 2026 profit.
parts.working: 1 mark restate comparatives; 1 mark adjust opening retained earnings in SOCE; 1 mark not through current profit / disclosure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the effect of the error on total retained earnings at 31 December 2026 before correction.
parts.answer: No effect – the overstatement in 2025 and the understatement in 2026 cancel out.

practice.stem: Draft profits of Nagar Valley Foods Limited were $90,800 for Year 1 and $131,300 for Year 2. An investigation finds that closing inventory at the end of Year 1 was understated by $5,600, and closing inventory at the end of Year 2 was overstated by $2,900.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for each of the two years.
parts.working: Year 1: closing inventory understated by 5,600 → profit 90,800 + 5,600 = 96,400 (M1 A1). Year 2: opening inventory understated by 5,600 → profit 131,300 − 5,600 = 125,700; closing inventory overstated by 2,900 → 125,700 − 2,900 = 122,800 (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected retained earnings at the end of Year 2, given the draft figure was $347,500, and explain why only one error affects it.
parts.answer: $344,600. The Year 1 error reverses in Year 2 (its effects cancel), so only the Year 2 closing inventory error of $2,900 remains: 347,500 − 2,900 = 344,600.
parts.working: M1 A1 figure; 1 mark explanation of the reversing error.

practice.stem: Rohtas Hotels Limited revalued its building at the start of the year to $720,000, with a remaining useful life of 36 years. The accountant continued to charge depreciation based on the original cost of $480,000 over 40 years. During the year it also issued shares at a premium; the premium of $90,000 was credited to retained earnings. Draft profit was $238,600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: Correct depreciation 720,000 ÷ 36 = 20,000 (B1); charged 12,000; extra 8,000 (M1); 238,600 − 8,000 = 230,600 (A1). The share premium error does not affect profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the corrections needed to the equity section of the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Share premium increase $90,000 and retained earnings decrease $90,000 (to remove the premium wrongly credited there); retained earnings also decrease by $8,000 for the extra depreciation.
parts.working: 1 mark share premium +90,000; 1 mark retained earnings −90,000; 1 mark retained earnings −8,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the premium on the share issue could never be part of retained earnings.
parts.answer: Share premium is capital paid in by shareholders above nominal value, not profit earned by trading; it is a capital reserve and cannot be distributed as a cash dividend, so recording it in retained earnings would overstate distributable reserves.
parts.working: 1 mark capital contributed, not earned; 1 mark non-distributable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a capital reserve and a revenue reserve.
parts.answer: A capital reserve arises from capital transactions (e.g. share premium, revaluation) and cannot be used to pay cash dividends. A revenue reserve arises from retained profits and can be distributed as dividends.
parts.working: 1 mark each side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of each type of reserve.
parts.answer: Capital: share premium, revaluation reserve (also capital redemption reserve). Revenue: retained earnings, general reserve.
parts.working: 1 mark for two capital, 1 mark for two revenue.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each item as share capital, a capital reserve, a revenue reserve or not part of equity:
(i) share premium
(ii) general reserve
(iii) 8% loan notes
(iv) revaluation reserve
(v) retained earnings
(vi) ordinary shares of $1 each
parts.answer: (i) capital reserve (ii) revenue reserve (iii) not part of equity – non-current liability (iv) capital reserve (v) revenue reserve (vi) share capital
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a share premium arises.
parts.answer: When a company issues shares at a price above their nominal value, the excess over nominal value is credited to the share premium account.
parts.working: 1 mark issue price above nominal; 1 mark excess credited to share premium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one use of the share premium account and one use for which it cannot be used.
parts.answer: Can be used to issue fully paid bonus shares; cannot be used to pay a cash dividend.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A company issues 400,000 shares of $0.20 each at $0.55. Calculate the increase in share premium.

practice.stem: Balances of Kalabagh Salt Limited at 30 June 2027 include: ordinary shares of $0.50 each $750,000; share premium $95,000; revaluation reserve $60,000; general reserve $45,000; retained earnings $183,400; 7% loan notes (2032) $200,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the equity section of the statement of financial position at 30 June 2027.
parts.answer: Ordinary shares of $0.50 each $750,000; share premium $95,000; revaluation reserve $60,000; general reserve $45,000; retained earnings $183,400; total equity $1,133,400.
parts.working: 1 mark share capital and capital reserves; 1 mark revenue reserves; 1 mark total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of ordinary shares in issue and the net assets per share, in cents to one decimal place.
parts.answer: 1,500,000 shares; 75.6 cents.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a company might transfer profits to a general reserve.
parts.answer: To show that the profits are being kept in the business (e.g. for future expansion or replacing assets) and are not intended for distribution, so dividend expectations are kept down.
parts.working: 1 mark earmarking/retaining profits; 1 mark purpose (expansion, prudence, limit dividends).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A shareholder believes the general reserve of $250,000 is money kept in the bank. Explain why this is not correct.
parts.answer: Reserves are part of equity (a claim of shareholders on net assets), not an asset; the profits may have been invested in non-current assets, inventory or receivables, so there may be little cash.
parts.working: 1 mark reserves are not assets/cash; 1 mark represented by net assets of any kind.

practice.stem: Lahore Leather Limited has ordinary share capital of $900,000 ($1 shares), share premium $180,000, general reserve $40,000 and retained earnings $95,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum cash dividend the company could legally pay from its reserves.
parts.working: Only revenue reserves can be distributed: retained earnings 95,000 + general reserve 40,000 = 135,000. Share premium is a capital reserve. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum bonus issue that could be made without reducing revenue reserves, and express it as a ratio of new shares to existing shares.
parts.answer: $180,000, i.e. 1 new share for every 5 held
parts.working: Share premium 180,000 ÷ share capital 900,000 = 1/5 → 1 for 5.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a company might choose to keep profits in a general reserve rather than pay them as dividends.
parts.answer: To retain cash in the business for expansion or replacement of assets; to show shareholders that this profit is not intended for distribution; to strengthen the SOFP for lenders.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid reasons.

practice.stem: Ganga Ram Pharmacy Chain Limited has 1,200,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each, share premium $210,000, revaluation reserve $175,000, general reserve $60,000 and retained earnings $138,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum cash dividend the company could pay from its reserves, and the dividend per share this would represent.
parts.answer: $198,000; 16.5 cents per share.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The company's bank balance is $36,000. Explain two reasons why the directors would not pay the maximum dividend.
parts.answer: There is not enough cash – paying would need borrowing and could cause liquidity problems; profits must be kept for replacing assets and expansion; a stable dividend policy is preferred so future dividends can be maintained; creditors/banks may have loan covenants; reserves already invested in non-current assets.
parts.working: 2 marks per developed reason (point + link to case).

practice.stem: Mangla Boats Limited has total assets of $4,860,000 and total liabilities of $1,740,000. It has 2,400,000 ordinary shares in issue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total equity of the company and the net assets per share.
parts.answer: Total equity $3,120,000; net assets per share $1.30.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The shares are quoted at $2.10. Suggest two reasons why the market price is higher than the net assets per share.
parts.answer: Investors value expected future profits and dividends; assets are shown at historical cost below current value; internally generated goodwill (brand, skilled staff, customer base) is not recorded.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two.

practice.stem: Haripur Bricks Limited bought land for $400,000. At the end of Year 1 it was revalued to $520,000, and at the end of Year 2 to $470,000. Land is not depreciated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the revaluation at the end of Year 1.
parts.answer: Dr Land 120,000; Cr Revaluation reserve 120,000.
parts.working: 1 mark each line.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance on the revaluation reserve at the end of Year 2, and state where the fall in value is recorded.
parts.answer: $70,000; the fall of $50,000 is debited to the revaluation reserve (not to profit) because it does not exceed the earlier surplus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the treatment if, in Year 3, the land fell in value to $350,000.
parts.answer: The remaining reserve of $70,000 is used first (Dr revaluation reserve 70,000) and the rest of the fall, $50,000 (below cost of $400,000), is charged as an expense (impairment) in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.working: 1 mark use reserve 70,000; 1 mark 50,000 to profit or loss.

practice.stem: At 1 January 2026, Pindi Gheb Motors Limited had ordinary shares of $1 each $900,000, general reserve $50,000 and retained earnings $240,000. During 2026: 300,000 shares were issued at $1.25; profit for the year was $115,000; dividends paid $54,000; $20,000 was transferred to the general reserve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the equity section of the statement of financial position at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer: Ordinary shares of $1 $1,200,000; share premium $75,000; general reserve $70,000; retained earnings $281,000; total $1,626,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much of the total equity is distributable as dividends.
parts.working: General reserve + retained earnings.

practice.stem: Saadat Hospitals Limited revalued its property at 31 December 2026. Land cost $260,000 and is now valued at $395,000. Buildings cost $480,000, with accumulated depreciation of $96,000, and are now valued at $520,000. There was no revaluation reserve before.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance on the revaluation reserve after the revaluation.
parts.working: Land 395,000 − 260,000 = 135,000; buildings 520,000 − (480,000 − 96,000) = 136,000; total 271,000. M1 (uses carrying amount for buildings) A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entries to record the revaluation of the buildings.
parts.answer:
Debit $    Credit $
Buildings: accumulated depreciation       96,000            
Buildings: cost/valuation                 40,000            
Revaluation reserve                                  136,000
parts.working: Eliminate accumulated depreciation 96,000 (1); increase buildings to valuation 40,000 (1); credit revaluation reserve 136,000 (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the revaluation reserve cannot be used to pay a cash dividend.
parts.answer: The gain is unrealised — no cash has been received and the assets have not been sold — so distributing it would pay out capital and could harm creditors.
parts.working: 1 mark unrealised/no cash; 1 mark protects capital/creditors.

practice.stem:
Equity and selected balances of Tharpak Cement Limited at 31 March 2027:
                                                 $
Ordinary share capital                   1,500,000
Share premium                              180,000
Revaluation reserve                        300,000
General reserve                            125,000
Retained earnings                          540,000
Current assets (including cash $9,000)     268,000
Current liabilities                        246,000
The company spent $2.1 million on a new kiln last year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the company's total reserves and its net current assets.
parts.answer: Total reserves $1,145,000; net current assets $22,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A group of shareholders demands a special dividend of $400,000 because 'the company has over $1 million in reserves'. Evaluate their argument.
parts.answer: Only revenue reserves (general reserve $125,000 + retained earnings $540,000 = $665,000) are legally distributable, so $400,000 is legally possible. But reserves are not cash: the company has cash of only $9,000 and net current assets of $22,000; the profits have been invested in the new plant. Paying would require borrowing or selling assets, harming liquidity and future growth, and might breach loan covenants. Shareholders may gain in the short term but lose from lower future profits. Conclusion: the dividend should not be paid (or be much smaller) until cash flow allows.
parts.working: 1 mark distributable reserves identified; 1 mark reserves ≠ cash; 2 marks consequences for the company; 1 mark justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Shangrila Resorts Limited's hotel building cost $600,000 and had accumulated depreciation of $150,000 (depreciated over 40 years) when it was revalued at $810,000. Its remaining useful life is 30 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revaluation surplus and prepare the journal entries to record the revaluation.
parts.answer: Surplus $360,000. Dr Accumulated depreciation 150,000; Cr Buildings 150,000. Dr Buildings 360,000; Cr Revaluation reserve 360,000.
parts.working: Carrying amount 600,000 − 150,000 = 450,000 (M1); surplus 810,000 − 450,000 = 360,000 (A1); entries eliminate accumulated depreciation (1) and raise asset to valuation (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual depreciation before and after the revaluation and the effect on profit.
parts.answer: Before $15,000; after $27,000; profit falls by $12,000 a year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the directors might choose to revalue even though profits will fall.
parts.answer: The SOFP shows a more realistic (fair) value of assets, raising net assets and lowering gearing, which helps when borrowing (better security) and resists an undervalued takeover bid.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons.

practice.stem: Summary statement of financial position of Jhelum Ferries Limited at 31 December 2026: non-current assets $1,940,000; current assets $615,000; current liabilities $388,000; non-current liabilities $500,000; ordinary share capital $1,000,000; share premium $120,000; revaluation reserve $210,000; general reserve $90,000; retained earnings – to be found.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the retained earnings at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Profit for 2026 was $164,000, dividends paid were $72,000 and $30,000 was transferred to the general reserve. Calculate the retained earnings at 1 January 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the proportion of total equity that is distributable, as a percentage to one decimal place.

practice.stem:
Equity of two companies in the same industry:
                         Alpha Ltd $   Beta Ltd $
Ordinary share capital       250,000      220,000
Share premium                 90,000       35,000
Revaluation reserve           40,000            0
General reserve                    0       65,000
Retained earnings             60,000      180,000
Total equity                 440,000      500,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for each company the percentage of total equity made up of revenue reserves, to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Alpha 13.6%; Beta 49.0%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the figures, compare the history and policies of the two companies, and explain which is better placed to pay dividends in future.
parts.answer: Alpha: most equity is share capital and premium (raised from shareholders) plus a revaluation reserve – low retained profits suggest recent formation, low profits or a high payout policy; revaluation reserve is not distributable. Beta: almost half its equity is retained profits – it has been profitable and has ploughed back profits, a conservative policy. Beta has far more distributable reserves ($245,000 v $60,000) so is better placed, provided it has the cash. Limitations: reserves are not cash; need profit trends and cash flow.
parts.working: 1 mark Alpha interpretation; 1 mark revaluation reserve non-distributable; 1 mark Beta interpretation; 1 mark conclusion; 1 mark limitation.

practice.stem: Ghotki Rice Limited has ordinary share capital of $450,000 in shares of $0.25 each. It paid a total dividend of $108,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dividend per share in cents.
parts.answer: 6 cents per share

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the dividend paid is shown in the financial statements.
parts.answer: In the statement of changes in equity (deducted from retained earnings) – not in the statement of profit or loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A company with ordinary share capital of $2,000,000 in $0.50 shares declares a dividend of 12% of nominal value. Calculate the total dividend and the dividend per share.
parts.answer: $240,000; 6 cents per share.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a dividend expressed as a percentage of nominal value may be misleading to an investor who paid $2.40 for each share.
parts.answer: The investor's return is based on the price paid, not on nominal value: 6c on $2.40 is only a 2.5% yield, not 12%.
parts.working: 1 mark nominal value ≠ price paid; 1 mark yield 2.5%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an interim dividend and a final dividend.
parts.answer: An interim dividend is paid during the financial year, usually after the half-year results, decided by the directors; a final dividend is proposed by the directors after the year end and approved by shareholders at the annual general meeting, then paid.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A company's year ends on 31 December 2026. A final dividend of $85,000 is proposed on 20 February 2027 and paid on 15 May 2027. State how it is treated in the financial statements for 2026 and for 2027.
parts.answer: 2026: not recognised as a liability – disclosed in a note only. 2027: deducted in the statement of changes in equity (and shown as dividends paid in the statement of cash flows).
parts.working: 1 mark each year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why dividends are not an expense of a limited company.
parts.answer: Dividends are a distribution of profit to the owners (shareholders), not a cost of earning revenue; they are paid out of profit after it has been calculated.
parts.working: 1 mark distribution to owners; 1 mark not a cost of earning revenue / after profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two factors that directors consider when deciding the size of a dividend.
parts.answer: Profit for the year; amount of distributable reserves; cash available; future investment plans; shareholders' expectations / past dividend levels; loan covenants; tax position of shareholders.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: Attock Refining Supplies Limited has 1,500,000 ordinary shares. Profit for the year is $360,000. The directors pay a dividend of 9 cents per share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the earnings per share and the total dividend.
parts.answer: EPS 24 cents; total dividend $135,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the dividend payout ratio (dividend per share ÷ earnings per share) as a percentage, and the amount of profit retained.

practice.stem:
Indus Motors Parts Limited had 1,600,000 ordinary shares of $1 each on 1 July 2026. During the year ended 30 June 2027:
• August 2026: paid the final dividend for the previous year of 6 cents per share.
• January 2027: bonus issue of 1 share for every 4 held. The bonus shares rank for any later dividends.
• April 2027: paid an interim dividend of 3.5 cents per share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total dividends paid during the year ended 30 June 2027.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether a company with a large retained earnings balance but a bank overdraft should pay a dividend.
parts.answer: Legally it may pay, as dividends come from distributable profits (retained earnings). But dividends need cash; paying would increase the overdraft and interest, and could harm liquidity and ability to pay suppliers. It may be better to pay a smaller dividend or keep cash until liquidity improves, while considering shareholders' expectations.
parts.working: 1 mark: legal — distributable reserves; 1 mark: cash/liquidity problem; 1 mark: conclusion/shareholder expectations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total dividends paid during the year ended 31 March 2027.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A shareholder held 9,000 shares on 1 April 2026 and bought none during the year. Calculate the dividends she received.

practice.stem: Murree Hills Bottlers Limited: profit for the year $1,260,000; 4,200,000 ordinary shares in issue; total dividend for the year 12 cents per share; market price per share $2.40.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate (i) earnings per share, (ii) dividend cover and (iii) dividend yield.
parts.answer: (i) 30 cents (ii) 2.5 times (iii) 5.0%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the dividend cover tells a shareholder.
parts.answer: How many times the dividend could be paid out of the year's profit available to ordinary shareholders; a cover of 2.5 means 40% of profit is paid out and 60% retained, so the dividend is reasonably safe even if profits fall.
parts.working: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark interpretation of 2.5.

practice.stem: Retained earnings of Sheikhupura Steel Limited were $486,000 at the start of the year and $550,500 at the end. Profit for the year was $189,500 and $40,000 was transferred to the general reserve. There were 1,700,000 ordinary shares throughout the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total dividends paid during the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The interim dividend was 2 cents per share on the 1,700,000 shares. Calculate the final dividend per share for the previous year, which was paid on the same number of shares.
parts.answer: 3.0 cents

practice.stem: Lyari Shipping Limited has 3,000,000 ordinary shares and $400,000 of 7% preference shares. Profit for the year after tax is $520,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit available to ordinary shareholders and the earnings per ordinary share, in cents to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The directors pay an ordinary dividend of 10 cents per share. Calculate the ordinary dividend cover to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 1.64 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the preference dividend is deducted before calculating ordinary dividend cover.
parts.answer: Preference shareholders must be paid their fixed dividend before any ordinary dividend, so only the remaining profit is available for ordinary shareholders.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a final dividend proposed after the year end is not recorded as a liability at the year end.
parts.answer: At the reporting date there is no obligation to pay: the dividend has not been declared/approved by shareholders, so under IAS 10 it is a non-adjusting event after the reporting period.
parts.working: 1 mark no obligation at the reporting date; 1 mark non-adjusting event / disclosed in notes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A company's directors propose a final dividend of 7 cents per share on 2,600,000 shares after the year end. Retained earnings at the year end are $410,000. Calculate the dividend and the retained earnings that will remain after it is paid (ignoring other movements).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the proposed dividend is shown in the financial statements at the year end.
parts.answer: As a note to the financial statements only.

practice.stem: Okara Dairy Products Limited has retained earnings of $680,000. It has current assets of $312,000 (including cash $48,000) and current liabilities of $214,000. The directors want to pay a dividend of 5 cents on each of its 2,000,000 shares, as last year. They also plan to build a new cold-storage warehouse next year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio before and after paying the proposed dividend, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Before 1.46:1; after 0.99:1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the dividend would be paid given the bank balance.
parts.answer: Cash is only $48,000, so $52,000 would have to come from an overdraft or from collecting receivables/selling inventory.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether the directors should pay the dividend.
parts.answer: For: the company is profitable with enough retained earnings; shareholders expect a dividend and cutting it may lower the share price. Against: paying would need borrowing, and the current ratio falls below 1, risking liquidity problems; the new warehouse is needed; interest cost of overdraft. Alternatives: smaller dividend, delay, or bonus issue instead of cash. Justified conclusion.
parts.working: 2 marks arguments for; 2 marks arguments against / alternatives; 1 mark justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Jacobabad Agro Limited has 5,000,000 ordinary shares and has paid 8 cents per share for several years. It plans a 1 for 5 rights issue. Profit after tax was $1,100,000 last year and is forecast at $1,180,000 next year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total dividend needed to keep the dividend at 8 cents per share after the rights issue, and the increase compared with last year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the dividend cover last year and next year, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Last year 2.75 times; next year 2.46 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether the company should maintain the dividend at 8 cents per share.
parts.answer: For: a stable dividend signals confidence and supports the share price after the rights issue; new shareholders expect it; cover still above 2. Against: cover falls, less profit retained for the expansion the rights issue was raised for; profit growth of the new project may come later. Conclusion with reason.
parts.working: 2 marks for, 2 marks against/conclusion (max 4).

practice.stem:
Information for two listed companies:
                           Indus Cables Ltd   Chenab Fans Ltd
Profit for the year                $840,000        $1,350,000
Ordinary shares in issue          3,500,000         6,000,000
Dividend per share                 12 cents          18 cents
Market price per share                $3.60             $2.70

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for each company: earnings per share (cents), dividend cover (2 d.p.), dividend yield (% to 2 d.p.) and price/earnings ratio (2 d.p.).
parts.answer: Indus Cables: EPS 24c; cover 2.00; yield 3.33%; P/E 15.00. Chenab Fans: EPS 22.5c; cover 1.25; yield 6.67%; P/E 12.00.
parts.working: 1 mark per correct pair of figures (4 measures × 2 companies ⇒ 1 mark for each measure for one company + 2 for method).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fatima is retired and wants a reliable income from her savings. Advise her which company's shares she should buy. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Chenab Fans gives a much higher yield (6.67% v 3.33%), suiting an income investor, but its cover is only 1.25, so the dividend is less safe if profits fall. Indus Cables has a higher cover (2.00) and higher P/E (15.00), showing the market expects growth, but gives less income now. Recommendation with reason (e.g. Chenab for income, if profits are stable; consider spreading between both).
parts.working: 1 mark yield comparison; 1 mark cover/safety; 1 mark P/E interpretation; 1 mark justified advice.

practice.stem: Nowshera Flour Mills Limited has 3,000,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each, retained earnings $260,000 and a bank balance of $70,000. The directors are deciding between a cash dividend of 6 cents per share and a bonus issue of 1 share for every 20 held, made from retained earnings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash dividend proposed and the number of bonus shares under the alternative.
parts.answer: $180,000; 150,000 bonus shares

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of each alternative on (i) cash, (ii) retained earnings and (iii) share capital.
parts.answer: Cash dividend: cash −180,000; retained earnings −180,000; share capital no change. Bonus issue: cash no change; retained earnings −75,000 (if funded from retained earnings); share capital +75,000.
parts.working: 1 mark per measure for both alternatives.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors which alternative to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The cash dividend (180,000) exceeds the bank balance (70,000), so it would need borrowing; the bonus issue rewards shareholders while keeping cash for the business, but some shareholders need income and the share price may fall. Recommend bonus issue (or smaller cash dividend) with reason.
parts.working: 1 mark cash problem; 1 mark shareholder view; 1 mark justified advice.
