parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm in Sialkot makes footballs. The cost card for one ball shows: direct materials $14, direct labour $9, variable overhead $4, fixed overhead absorbed $6. The normal selling price is $45. The firm has spare capacity and is offered a one-off order. What is the lowest price per ball it could accept without reducing its profit?
A $23
B $27
C $33
D $45
parts.working: Only the marginal (variable) cost is extra: 14 + 9 + 4 = $27. Fixed overhead will be paid anyway, so C ($33 full cost) is not the minimum; any price above $27 adds contribution.

practice.stem: A business in Sialkot makes school bags. Costs per bag: materials $8.50, labour $6.00, variable overhead $1.50. Fixed costs are $48,000 per month. Normal monthly output is 12,000 bags, sold at $25 each, and there is spare capacity of 3,000 bags. A charity offers to buy 2,000 bags at $19 each; it would need special delivery costing $1,400 in total.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the marginal cost of one bag.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in monthly profit if the order is accepted.
parts.answer: Contribution per bag 19 − 16 = $3; 2,000 × 3 = 6,000; less delivery 1,400 = increase of $4,600
parts.working: M1 contribution per unit; M1 deduct extra delivery cost; A1. Fixed costs ignored (no change).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two non-financial factors the business should consider before accepting the order.
parts.answer: Any two: existing customers may ask for the lower price; whether the order may lead to repeat business; effect on quality and staff workload; reliability of the new customer; damage to brand image if sold cheaply.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
A company in Gujrat makes three ceiling fans. Its statement for last year shows:
                             Standard $  Deluxe $  Premium $
Revenue                         180,000    95,000    140,000
Variable costs                  110,000    70,000     84,000
Fixed costs (apportioned)        40,000    32,000     36,000
Profit/(loss)                    30,000   (7,000)     20,000
The fixed costs would not change if a product were dropped. The directors want to stop making the Deluxe fan because it makes a loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution earned by each product.
parts.answer: Standard $70,000; Deluxe $25,000; Premium $56,000
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total profit if the Deluxe fan is discontinued.
parts.answer: Current profit 43,000; Deluxe contribution lost 25,000; new profit = $18,000
parts.working: M1 fixed costs unchanged; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether the Deluxe fan should be discontinued.
parts.answer: No: it earns a positive contribution of $25,000 towards the fixed costs, which would still have to be paid; profit would fall by that amount.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark reason based on contribution.

practice.stem: A factory in Karachi makes running shoes, sold at $50 a pair. For each pair: materials $12, labour $8, variable overhead $3, and a sales commission of 5% of the selling price. Fixed costs are $36,000 per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by contribution.
parts.answer: Selling price (or revenue) less variable costs; the amount left to pay the fixed costs and then provide profit.
parts.working: 1 mark definition; 1 mark use towards fixed costs and profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per pair.
parts.answer: Variable cost = 12 + 8 + 3 + 2.50 commission = 25.50; contribution = 50 − 25.50 = $24.50
parts.working: M1 commission included as a variable cost; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit for a month in which 2,400 pairs are sold.
parts.working: M1; A1 OF.

practice.stem: Yasmin runs a kitchen-fitting business in Islamabad and has spare capacity. A one-off contract would need materials costing $2,400 (bought specially), 120 labour hours at $15 per hour and variable overhead of $4 per labour hour. Fixed overheads are normally absorbed at $10 per labour hour; they will not change if the contract is taken.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum price Yasmin could charge for the contract.
parts.answer: Materials 2,400 + labour 120 × 15 = 1,800 + variable overhead 120 × 4 = 480 = $4,680
parts.working: M1 labour; M1 variable overhead; A1 (fixed overhead excluded).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why she might charge more than this minimum price.
parts.answer: Any two: to cover fixed costs; to make a profit; customer can afford more / market price is higher; avoid other customers expecting low prices; risk of cost over-runs.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Material is in short supply. Product X earns contribution of $24 per unit and uses 4 kg of material; product Y earns $30 and uses 6 kg; product Z earns $18 and uses 2 kg. In what order should production be ranked?
A X, Y, Z
B Y, X, Z
C Z, X, Y
D Z, Y, X
parts.answer: C Z, X, Y
parts.working: Contribution per kg: X 24 ÷ 4 = $6, Y 30 ÷ 6 = $5, Z 18 ÷ 2 = $9, so Z, X, Y. B ranks by contribution per unit, which ignores the scarce resource.

practice.stem:
Noor Ceramics makes three products. Material costs $5 per kg and only 13,000 kg is available next month. Fixed costs are $52,000 per month.
Product    Price $  Material kg  Labour $  Var. overhead $  Max demand
Alpha           60            4        15                5       1,500
Beta            85            7        18                6       1,000
Gamma           48            2        16                4       2,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per kg of material for each product and rank the products.
parts.answer: Alpha: contribution 20, per kg 5.00; Beta: contribution 26, per kg 3.71; Gamma: contribution 18, per kg 9.00. Ranking: Gamma 1st, Alpha 2nd, Beta 3rd.
parts.working: M1 contribution per unit (material at $5 per kg); M1 ÷ kg; A1 ranking.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the production plan that maximises profit. Make whole units only.
parts.answer: Gamma 2,000 units (4,000 kg); Alpha 1,500 units (6,000 kg); Beta 3,000 kg ÷ 7 = 428 units (2,996 kg).
parts.working: M1 meet full demand in ranking order; M1 remaining material to Beta; A1 428 units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit from this plan.
parts.working: M1; A1 OF.

practice.stem: Rehman Motors makes 10,000 units a year of component K. Cost per unit: materials $6.40, labour $5.20, variable overhead $1.80, fixed overhead absorbed $4.60. A supplier offers component K at $15.50 per unit. If the company buys it in, the space freed can be rented out for $18,000 per year and a supervisor earning $9,000 per year would no longer be needed. Other fixed overheads would not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relevant annual cost of making the component.
parts.working: M1 variable costs only; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net annual cost of buying the component and state whether the company should make or buy it.
parts.answer: 155,000 − 18,000 rent − 9,000 salary saved = $128,000. Buying is cheaper by $6,000, so buy.
parts.working: M1 purchase cost less rent; M1 less salary saved; A1 decision.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two non-financial factors to consider before buying from the supplier.
parts.answer: Any two: reliability of delivery; quality control; loss of skills/jobs and staff morale; dependence on one supplier who may raise prices; confidentiality of design.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A shop in Doha sells water filters at $50 each. Variable cost is $30 per filter and fixed costs are $90,000 per month. It sells 6,000 filters per month. The manager proposes cutting the price by 10%, which is expected to raise monthly sales by 25%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current monthly profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the monthly profit if the proposal is adopted and state the change in profit.
parts.working: M1 new price and volume; M1 contribution − fixed costs; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one factor, other than profit, the manager should consider.
parts.answer: Any one: market share gained; reaction of competitors; whether capacity can make 7,500 units; effect on brand image; reliability of the 25% estimate.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Hashmi Electronics sells air purifiers at $80 each; variable cost is $44 each. Annual sales are 5,000 units and fixed costs are $130,000, including sales staff salaries of $24,000. It plans to stop paying the salaries and instead pay the sales staff a commission of 6% of the selling price. It expects sales to rise to 5,600 units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current annual profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per unit and the annual profit under the commission plan.
parts.working: M1 commission as a variable cost; M1 fixed costs reduced by 24,000; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point in units under each plan.
parts.working: M1 each method; A1 both, rounded up to whole units.

practice.stem: Ghazi Textiles can make 50,000 towels a year. It currently sells 38,000 towels a year in Pakistan at $22 each; variable cost $13 per towel; fixed costs $250,000 a year. A buyer in Kenya offers to buy 9,000 towels at $16 each. Shipping would cost an extra $0.80 per towel and a one-off export certificate would cost $6,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should accept the export order. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The order adds $13,800 to profit and there is enough spare capacity, so accept unless the risks below are judged too great. Either decision accepted if justified.
parts.working: Calculation (max 2): contribution 9,000 × (16 − 13 − 0.80) = 19,800 less certification 6,000 = 13,800 extra profit. For (max 3): spare capacity of 12,000 units is otherwise unused; covers some fixed costs; may lead to further export orders and a new market; keeps staff employed. Against (max 3): home customers may learn of the lower price and demand the same; uses 9,000 of 12,000 spare units, leaving little room for growth at home; exchange-rate and payment risks; the price is below full cost. Decision (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A component costs $18 per unit in variable costs to make. Fixed overhead of $7 per unit is absorbed, which includes a supervisor's salary of $12,000 per year that would be saved if the component were bought in. 4,000 components are needed each year and a supplier offers them at $20.50 each. What is the effect on annual profit of buying instead of making?
A decrease of $10,000
B increase of $2,000
C increase of $12,000
D increase of $18,000
parts.answer: B increase of $2,000
parts.working: Relevant cost of making = 4,000 × 18 + 12,000 = 84,000. Buying = 4,000 × 20.50 = 82,000. Profit rises by $2,000. A ignores the salary saved; D compares with the full cost of $25, but the rest of the absorbed overhead is not saved.

practice.stem:
A workshop in Gujranwala makes two kinds of pump. Next month only 15,000 skilled labour hours are available. Fixed costs are $150,000 per month.
Pump    Price $  Variable cost $  Labour hours per unit  Maximum demand
P            90               54                      3           4,000
Q           120               78                      2           2,500
The variable cost includes labour at the normal rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per labour hour for each product and state which should be made first.
parts.answer: P: 36 ÷ 3 = $12 per hour; Q: 42 ÷ 2 = $21 per hour. Make Q first.
parts.working: 1 mark both figures; 1 mark ranking.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of each product to make and the profit for the month. Make whole units only.
parts.working: M1 Q at full demand; M1 P with remaining hours; M1 total contribution; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Workers will work overtime at a premium of $6 per hour above the normal rate. Calculate the extra profit if overtime is used to meet the full demand for P.
parts.answer: Extra P = 4,000 − 3,333 = 667 units, contribution 667 × 36 = 24,012. Total hours for 4,000 P = 12,000; normal hours available for P = 10,000, so overtime = 2,000 hours (the 1 spare normal hour is used first). Premium = 2,000 × 6 = 12,000. Extra profit = 24,012 − 12,000 = $12,012
parts.working: M1 extra contribution less overtime premium on the overtime hours only; A1 $12,012 (accept $12,006 if all 2,001 hours are treated as overtime).

practice.stem: A factory in Lahore has 20,000 machine hours a month. It makes one product, selling 8,500 units a month at $40 each; variable cost $22 per unit; 2 machine hours per unit. A customer asks for 2,000 units of a modified version at $30 each. Each needs 2 machine hours and has a variable cost of $21. A one-off design cost of $2,500 would be paid. Demand for the normal product is unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the spare machine hours and the number of units of the normal product that must be given up.
parts.answer: Spare = 3,000 hours; order needs 4,000 hours; 1,000 hours short = 500 normal units.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect on profit of accepting the order.
parts.answer: Order contribution 2,000 × (30 − 21) = 18,000; lost contribution 500 × 18 = 9,000; design cost 2,500; increase in profit = $6,500
parts.working: M1 order contribution; M1 lost contribution; M1 design cost; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the minimum price per unit at which the order would be worth accepting.
parts.working: M1 variable cost + opportunity and specific costs per unit; A1.

practice.stem:
Mirza Ltd makes electric kettles. It sells 8,000 kettles a year at $35 each. Variable cost is $21 per kettle and fixed costs are $80,000 a year. The directors are considering two options for next year:
Option 1: reduce the price to $32; sales are expected to rise to 10,500 kettles.
Option 2: keep the price at $35 and spend $18,000 on advertising; sales are expected to rise to 9,600 kettles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors which option, if either, they should choose. Justify your answer with calculations.
parts.answer: Current profit $32,000; Option 1 profit $35,500; Option 2 profit $36,400. On profit alone Option 2 is better by $900, but the difference is small, so either option can be recommended with justification.
parts.working: Calculations (max 3): current profit 14 × 8,000 − 80,000 = 32,000; Option 1: 11 × 10,500 − 80,000 = 35,500; Option 2: 14 × 9,600 − 98,000 = 36,400. Points (max 3): Option 1 break-even 7,273 units, margin of safety 10,500 − 7,273 = 3,227; Option 2 break-even 7,000 units, margin of safety 2,600; the lower price may start a price war and lower brand image; Option 1 needs extra capacity and workload for 2,500 more units; advertising results are uncertain but could have longer-lasting effects; the sales forecasts are estimates. Decision with reason (1).

practice.stem:
A department store in Lahore has three departments. Fixed costs of $96,000 a year are shared by floor area: clothing 50%, footwear 30%, toys 20%.
                  Clothing $  Footwear $  Toys $
Revenue              240,000     120,000  90,000
Variable costs       150,000      84,000  72,000
If the toy department closed, $5,000 of fixed costs would be saved. Its space would be given to footwear, whose revenue and variable costs would both rise by 30%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss of each department and the total profit.
parts.answer: Clothing 42,000; Footwear 7,200; Toys (1,200); total $48,000
parts.working: Apportioned fixed costs 48,000, 28,800, 19,200 (1); departmental results (1); total (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total profit if the toy department is closed and footwear expanded. State whether the plan should go ahead.
parts.answer: Contribution: clothing 90,000 + footwear 36,000 × 1.3 = 46,800 → 136,800; fixed costs 96,000 − 5,000 = 91,000; profit = $45,800. This is $2,200 lower than now, so the toy department should not be closed.
parts.working: M1 footwear contribution × 1.3; M1 toy contribution removed; M1 fixed costs reduced only by 5,000; A1 with decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A product sells for $18 and has a variable cost of $11 per unit. Fixed costs are $42,000. How many units must be sold to make a profit of $14,000?
A 6,000
B 8,000
C 3,112
D 5,091
parts.working: Required contribution = 42,000 + 14,000 = 56,000; ÷ (18 − 11) = 8,000 units. A covers only the fixed costs (break-even).

practice.stem: A company in Peshawar makes ceramic water coolers, sold at $32 each. Per unit: materials $9, labour $7, variable overhead $2. Fixed costs are $30,000 per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per unit.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the contribution to sales ratio as a percentage, correct to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total contribution and the profit for a month in which 3,000 units are sold.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business has a contribution to sales ratio of 40% and fixed costs of $84,000. What revenue is needed to earn a profit of $36,000?
A $48,000
B $90,000
C $210,000
D $300,000
parts.working: (84,000 + 36,000) ÷ 0.40 = $300,000. C ($210,000) is the break-even revenue: it ignores the target profit.

practice.stem: Fresh Squeeze, a juice bar in Lahore, sold 9,000 glasses of juice in July 2026 at $2.50 each. Variable costs per glass: fruit $0.70, cup and straw $0.10, sugar and ice $0.15. Fixed costs for July: rent $3,500, salaries $6,000, electricity $800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a marginal costing statement for July 2026 showing total contribution and profit.
parts.answer: Revenue 22,500; variable costs 8,550; contribution 13,950; fixed costs 10,300; profit $3,650
parts.working: Revenue B1; variable costs 9,000 × 0.95 B1; contribution B1; profit after fixed costs B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per glass and the contribution to sales ratio.
parts.answer: $1.55 per glass; 62%
parts.working: B1 each

practice.stem: Comfort Linen sells bedsheet sets online from Faisalabad at $40 a set. Costs per set: fabric $14, stitching labour $6, courier delivery to the customer $3. Fixed costs are $25,500 per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'contribution'.
parts.answer: Selling price (or revenue) less variable costs; the amount available to cover fixed costs and then provide profit.
parts.working: 1 mark definition; 1 mark purpose

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per set.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of sets that must be sold in a month to make a profit of $8,500.
parts.answer: 2,000 sets

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the courier charge is treated as a variable cost.
parts.answer: It is paid for every set delivered, so the total rises in direct proportion to the number of sets sold.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: Bright Minds Academy, Islamabad, charges each student a fee of $120 per month. Variable costs (books, worksheets and online platform licence) are $30 per student per month. Fixed costs are $27,000 per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of students needed to make a profit of $9,000 per month.
parts.answer: 400 students

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fee income at that number of students.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit if 450 students enrol.

practice.stem: A bakery in Abu Dhabi sells boxes of pastries at $75 per box. Variable cost is $45 per box and fixed costs are $180,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per unit and the contribution to sales (C/S) ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of units needed to earn a profit of $60,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the revenue needed to earn a profit of $60,000.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the profit if 9,500 units are sold.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business sells 5,000 units at $25 each. Variable cost is $13 per unit and the business makes a profit of $36,000. What are its fixed costs?
A $24,000
B $36,000
C $89,000
D $60,000
parts.working: Contribution 5,000 × ($25 − $13) = $60,000; fixed costs = 60,000 − 36,000 = $24,000. D is the contribution with the profit not deducted; C subtracts the profit from revenue ($125,000 − $36,000) instead of from contribution.

practice.stem: Nova Lights sold 7,000 lamps last year at $60 each. Variable cost is $38 per lamp and fixed costs were $110,000. Next year the price and variable cost per unit will not change, but an advertising campaign will add $22,000 to fixed costs. The owner wants a profit of $50,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate last year's profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of lamps that must be sold next year to make the target profit. Give your answer as a whole number of lamps.
parts.answer: 8,273 lamps

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in sales volume required, to two decimal places.

practice.stem: Saba Crafts sells handmade lamps at $50 each. Variable cost is $30 per lamp and fixed costs are $60,000 a year. Saba wants her profit for the year to be 20% of her revenue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of lamps that must be sold.
parts.answer: 6,000 lamps

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prove your answer by calculating the revenue and the profit at that level of sales.
parts.answer: Revenue $300,000; profit $60,000 = 20% of revenue
parts.working: B1 revenue; B1 profit

practice.stem:
Kohat Ceramics makes plates (P) and bowls (B), always sold in the ratio 2 plates to 1 bowl.
Product   Selling price $   Variable cost $
Plate           30                18
Bowl            50                35
Fixed costs are $117,000 a month and the target profit is $39,000 a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution from one 'batch' of 2 plates and 1 bowl.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of plates and bowls needed to make the target profit.
parts.answer: 8,000 plates and 4,000 bowls
parts.working: 156,000 ÷ 39 = 4,000 batches M1 A1; 8,000 plates, 4,000 bowls A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption made in your calculation.
parts.answer: The sales mix stays at 2 : 1 (and prices, variable costs per unit and fixed costs do not change).
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: A workshop in Ankara makes office chairs. This year it sold 8,000 chairs at $120 each; variable cost was $70 per chair and fixed costs were $300,000. Next year fixed costs will rise by 10% and variable cost per chair by 6%. The owners want a profit of $120,000 next year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate this year's profit.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of units needed next year to earn a profit of $120,000 at the current selling price.
parts.working: M1 new costs; M1 required contribution ÷ unit contribution; A1 rounded up.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the selling price needed to earn $120,000 next year if only 8,500 units can be sold. Give your answer to the nearest cent.
parts.answer: Contribution needed per unit = 450,000 ÷ 8,500 = 52.94; price = 74.20 + 52.94 = $127.14
parts.working: M1 required contribution ÷ 8,500; M1 add variable cost; A1.

practice.stem:
Zenith Helmets expects to sell 12,000 helmets next year. Variable cost is $18 per helmet and fixed costs are $150,000. The directors want a profit of $90,000.
The marketing manager believes that if the price were set at $34 instead, sales would be 14,000 helmets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the selling price needed to make the target profit if 12,000 helmets are sold.
parts.working: Contribution needed 240,000 ÷ 12,000 = 20 M1; price 38 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit if the price is $34 and 14,000 helmets are sold.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many helmets would have to be sold at $34 to make the target profit.
parts.answer: 15,000 helmets

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the directors which price to charge. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: $38 gives the target $90,000 against $74,000 at $34, if forecasts are right. But at $38 demand may be less than 12,000 (price sensitive); $34 may build market share and use capacity; competitors' prices and quality matter; 15,000 helmets needed at $34. Clear decision.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison of profits; up to 2 marks for other factors; 1 mark decision

practice.stem: Pak Fans makes table fans that sell at $40 each with a variable cost of $22. One production shift can make up to 5,000 fans a month, with fixed costs of $80,000 a month. A second shift would allow up to 10,000 fans a month in total, but fixed costs would rise by $30,000 a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum monthly profit with one shift.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of fans needed to make a profit of $40,000 a month. Give your answer as a whole number.
parts.answer: 8,334 fans
parts.working: One shift cannot reach the target (its maximum profit is only $10,000) B1; (110,000 + 40,000) ÷ 18 = 8,333.3 M1; 8,334 fans A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the two break-even points and explain why there are two.
parts.answer: 4,445 fans and 6,112 fans
parts.working: 80,000 ÷ 18 = 4,444.4 → 4,445 B1; 110,000 ÷ 18 = 6,111.1 → 6,112 B1; the extra $30,000 fixed cost of the second shift creates a loss just above 5,000 fans, so sales must rise to cover the step in fixed costs M1 A1

practice.stem: Rehan Products sells 10,000 kettles a year at $80 each. Variable costs per kettle are: materials $30, labour $15, variable overheads $5. Next year materials will cost 10% more and labour 6% more; variable overheads will not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current contribution to sales ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the new variable cost per kettle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the selling price needed to keep the contribution to sales ratio unchanged.

parts.label: d
parts.text: If the price stays at $80, calculate the number of kettles that must be sold to keep total contribution at its current level. Give a whole number.
parts.answer: 11,495 kettles
parts.working: Current contribution 300,000 B1; new contribution per unit 26.10 M1; 300,000 ÷ 26.10 = 11,494.3 → 11,495 A1

practice.stem: A company in Lahore makes solar lamps that sell for $140 each. Variable cost is $84 per lamp and fixed costs are $168,000 per year. Budgeted sales are 4,500 lamps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point in units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety in units and as a percentage of budgeted sales.
parts.working: M1 units; A1; A1 percentage.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A product sells for $45 and has variable costs of $27 per unit. Fixed costs are $63,000. What is the break-even point in units?
A 1,400
B 2,333
C 3,500
D 5,250
parts.working: 63,000 ÷ (45 − 27) = 3,500. B divides by the variable cost instead of the contribution.

practice.stem: Nimra's Bakery, Karachi, sells birthday cakes at $30 each. Ingredients and packaging cost $18 per cake. Rent and other fixed costs are $36,000 a year. Budgeted sales are 4,000 cakes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point in cakes and in revenue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety in cakes and as a percentage of budgeted sales.

practice.stem: Jamal, who runs a small bakery in Peshawar, has been told that his business 'has a margin of safety of 25%'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the break-even point.
parts.answer: The level of sales at which total revenue equals total costs, so there is neither profit nor loss (total contribution equals fixed costs).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what a margin of safety of 25% means for Jamal.
parts.answer: Budgeted (or actual) sales are 25% above break-even sales: sales could fall by a quarter before the bakery starts to make a loss.
parts.working: 1 mark sales above break-even; 1 mark interpretation

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two ways Jamal could increase his margin of safety.
parts.answer: Increase sales volume; raise selling price; reduce variable cost per unit; reduce fixed costs (any change that lowers break-even or raises budgeted sales).
parts.working: 1 mark each

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business budgets to sell 12,000 units at $25 each. Variable cost is $15 per unit and fixed costs are $90,000. What is the margin of safety as a percentage of budgeted sales?
A 25%
B 33⅓%
C 40%
D 75%
parts.working: Break-even = 90,000 ÷ 10 = 9,000 units; margin of safety = 3,000 units; 3,000 ÷ 12,000 = 25%. B divides by break-even sales instead of budgeted sales.

practice.stem: A café in Istanbul sells many different items, so it does not calculate costs per unit. Last year revenue was $480,000, variable costs were $312,000 and fixed costs were $126,000. Assume the sales mix stays the same.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution to sales ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even revenue.
parts.working: M1; A1 OF.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety as a percentage of revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Budgeted sales are 6,000 leaflet packs at $9 each. Variable cost is $5 per pack and fixed costs are $12,000. What is the margin of safety in packs?
A 1,333
B 3,000
C 4,667
D 6,000
parts.working: Contribution 9 − 5 = $4 per pack; break-even 12,000 ÷ 4 = 3,000 packs; margin of safety 6,000 − 3,000 = 3,000 packs. A divides fixed costs by the selling price; C uses the wrong break-even point.

practice.stem: A business sells a product at $20 per unit. Variable cost is $12 per unit and fixed costs are $40,000. A break-even chart is drawn with units sold on the horizontal axis (0 to 10,000 units) and $ on the vertical axis. Budgeted sales are 8,000 units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the coordinates of the points where (i) the total cost line meets the vertical axis and (ii) the total revenue line and total cost line cross.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the vertical distance between the total revenue line and the total cost line at 9,000 units, and state what it represents.
parts.answer: $32,000; the profit at 9,000 units

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the margin of safety at budgeted sales would be shown on the chart and calculate it.
parts.answer: The horizontal distance between the break-even point and budgeted sales: 3,000 units
parts.working: B1 description; B1 3,000 units

practice.stem:
Desert Rose Café, Muscat, does not calculate costs per unit. Its selling prices and cost structure were the same in two months:
Month      Revenue $    Profit $
March       200,000      10,000
April       260,000      31,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution to sales ratio.
parts.working: Change in profit 21,000 ÷ change in revenue 60,000 M1 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the monthly fixed costs.
parts.working: 200,000 × 35% = 70,000 contribution M1; − 10,000 profit A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the break-even revenue, to the nearest cent.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety in April as a percentage of revenue, to two decimal places.

practice.stem: A garment maker in Karachi sells a jacket for $25. Variable cost is $15 per jacket and fixed costs are $90,000 a year. Budgeted sales are 14,000 jackets. The landlord has announced a rent increase of $12,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point and the margin of safety (in units and as a percentage of budgeted sales) before the rent increase.
parts.answer: Break-even 9,000 jackets; margin of safety 5,000 jackets, 35.71%
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point and the margin of safety after the rent increase.
parts.answer: Break-even 10,200 jackets; margin of safety 3,800 jackets, 27.14%
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the effect of the rent increase on the risk faced by the business.
parts.answer: Higher fixed costs raise the break-even point and reduce the margin of safety, so a smaller fall in sales would cause a loss: the business is riskier.
parts.working: 1 mark effect on BE/MOS; 1 mark risk

practice.stem:
A manufacturer of school bags in Multan sells each bag for $18. Total costs in two recent months were:
Month     Output (bags)   Total cost $
August        3,000          52,000
October       5,000          72,000
Budgeted sales for next month are 4,000 bags.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the high–low method to find the variable cost per bag and the monthly fixed costs.
parts.answer: Variable $10; fixed $22,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point in bags.
parts.answer: 2,750 bags

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety as a percentage of budgeted sales.

practice.stem: Okafor Ltd in Lagos makes garden tools. Each tool sells for $60 with a variable cost of $36. Fixed costs are $192,000 a year and budgeted sales are 11,000 tools. A new machine would increase fixed costs by $48,000 a year and reduce variable cost by $4 per tool.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current break-even point and margin of safety in units.
parts.answer: 192,000 ÷ 24 = 8,000 units; margin of safety 11,000 − 8,000 = 3,000 units
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point and margin of safety, in units and as a percentage of budgeted sales, if the machine is bought.
parts.answer: Contribution 60 − 32 = 28; fixed 240,000; break-even = 8,571.4 → 8,572 units; margin of safety = 2,428 units = 22.07%
parts.working: M1 new contribution and fixed costs; A1 break-even; A1 margin of safety.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the level of sales at which profit is the same with or without the machine.
parts.working: M1 equation; A1.

practice.stem:
Indus Valves sells one product at $50. Expected demand is 12,000 units a year. The directors are choosing between two methods of production:
Method        Variable cost per unit $   Fixed costs per year $
Manual                   30                     120,000
Automated                22                     200,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point in units for each method. Round up to whole units.
parts.answer: Manual 6,000; automated 7,143
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety as a percentage of expected demand for each method. Give each answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Manual 50.0%; automated 40.5%
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit at expected demand under each method.
parts.answer: Manual $120,000; automated $136,000
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the level of sales at which both methods give the same profit.
parts.answer: 10,000 units

parts.label: e
parts.text: Advise the directors which method to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Automated gives $16,000 more profit at 12,000 units and is better above 10,000 units, but it has a higher break-even point and lower margin of safety, so it is riskier if demand falls below 10,000. Consider reliability of the demand forecast, cost of finance for the machinery, effect on workers and quality. Decision.
parts.working: 1 mark uses figures; up to 2 marks each side; 1 mark decision (max 5)

practice.stem:
Mughal Tiles sells two products, X and Y. Fixed costs are $72,000 a month.
Product   Selling price $   Variable cost $
X               40                25
Y               30                20
Currently X and Y are sold in the ratio 2 : 3 (by units).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point in units of each product and the break-even revenue.
parts.working: Batch contribution 2 × 15 + 3 × 10 = 60 M1; 1,200 batches A1; 2,400 X and 3,600 Y A1; revenue 204,000 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: The sales mix changes to 1 : 1. Calculate the new break-even revenue.
parts.working: Batch contribution 25 M1; 2,880 batches A1; × 70 = 201,600 A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the break-even revenue changes when the sales mix changes.
parts.answer: X has a higher contribution to sales ratio (37.5%) than Y (33.3%); selling relatively more X raises the average C/S ratio, so less revenue is needed to cover fixed costs.
parts.working: 1 mark different C/S ratios; 1 mark effect of mix

practice.stem: Pine View Hotel, Murree, has 60 rooms and is open 365 nights a year. The average room rate is $80 per night. Variable costs (cleaning, laundry, breakfast and toiletries) are $20 per occupied room-night. Fixed costs are $788,400 a year. Budgeted occupancy is 75%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even number of room-nights and the break-even occupancy percentage.
parts.answer: 13,140 room-nights; 60%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety in room-nights and the budgeted profit.
parts.answer: 3,285 room-nights; profit $197,100

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the average room rate needed to break even if occupancy is only 50%.
parts.working: Room-nights 10,950; contribution needed 72 per night M1; + 20 = 92 A1

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why CVP analysis may be less reliable for a hotel than for a manufacturer.
parts.answer: Room rates vary by season and by booking channel, so a single selling price is unrealistic (or many costs such as staff are stepped/semi-variable).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is NOT an assumption of cost–volume–profit analysis?
A Selling price per unit is constant at all levels of sales.
B Fixed costs stay the same within the relevant range.
C Variable cost per unit is constant.
D Inventory levels rise and fall during the period.
parts.answer: D Inventory levels rise and fall during the period.
parts.working: CVP assumes everything produced is sold, so inventory levels do not change. A, B and C are standard CVP assumptions (linear revenue and cost lines).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a break-even chart, what does the area between the total revenue line and the total cost line, to the right of the break-even point, represent?
A contribution
B fixed costs
C profit
D margin of safety
parts.answer: C profit
parts.working: Beyond break-even, revenue exceeds total cost and the gap is profit. A is wrong: contribution is the gap between revenue and variable cost. D is a horizontal distance, not an area.

practice.stem: The owner of a flour mill in Okara is using CVP analysis. Her accountant tells her that 'fixed costs are only fixed within the relevant range'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the relevant range.
parts.answer: The range of output over which the assumed cost behaviour (fixed costs constant, variable cost per unit constant) holds true.
parts.working: 1 mark range of activity; 1 mark cost behaviour assumptions valid

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of how fixed costs at the mill might change outside the relevant range.
parts.answer: e.g. output above capacity needs a second milling machine, extra rented storage or another supervisor, so fixed costs step up.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two uses of CVP analysis for the owner.
parts.answer: Find break-even output; set sales targets for a target profit; measure margin of safety/risk; assess effect of changes in price, costs or volume; compare alternatives.
parts.working: 1 mark each

practice.stem: Afzal sells mobile phone covers from a stall in Rawalpindi. He has worked out his break-even point but does not understand why his accountant says it 'depends on several assumptions'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three assumptions of CVP analysis.
parts.answer: Selling price per unit is constant; variable cost per unit is constant; fixed costs are constant; costs can be split into fixed and variable; production equals sales (no inventory changes); constant sales mix.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why one of these assumptions may not hold for Afzal's business.
parts.answer: e.g. he may give discounts for bulk buyers or reduce prices to clear old designs, so the selling price is not constant; or suppliers give quantity discounts so variable cost per cover falls.
parts.working: 1 mark identifies assumption; 1 mark applied reason

practice.stem: A business sells a product with a contribution of $15 per unit. Fixed costs are $45,000. A profit–volume chart is drawn, with units sold on the horizontal axis and profit or loss on the vertical axis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the value where the profit line meets the vertical axis.
parts.answer: −$45,000 (a loss equal to fixed costs)
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of units where the profit line crosses the horizontal axis.
parts.answer: 3,000 units (break-even)
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit shown on the chart at 5,000 units.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one advantage of a profit–volume chart compared with a break-even chart.
parts.answer: It shows profit or loss at any level of activity directly, without reading the gap between two lines.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: Zubair runs a hardware store in Mardan that sells several hundred different products.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three assumptions made in cost–volume–profit analysis.
parts.answer: Any three: selling price per unit is constant; variable cost per unit is constant; fixed costs are constant within the relevant range; all costs can be split into fixed and variable; all output is sold (no change in inventory); the sales mix is constant; only volume affects costs and revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of using cost–volume–profit analysis for a business that sells several products.
parts.answer: A constant sales mix must be assumed. If customers buy more low-contribution items than planned, the average contribution falls and the true break-even point is higher than calculated.
parts.working: 1 mark limitation; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about cost–volume–profit analysis are correct?
1 Fixed costs are assumed to be constant within the relevant range.
2 It is assumed that all units produced are sold.
3 It is assumed that the selling price falls as more units are sold.
4 It can be used for several products if the sales mix is constant.
A 1, 2 and 3
B 1, 2 and 4
C 2, 3 and 4
D 1, 3 and 4
parts.answer: B 1, 2 and 4
parts.working: CVP assumes a constant selling price per unit, so statement 3 is false; the other three are standard assumptions or uses. Options A, C and D all include statement 3.

practice.stem: Lahore Garments sells a uniform at $30. Variable cost is $12 per unit for output up to 10,000 units. If output exceeds 10,000 units, a bulk discount on cloth reduces variable cost to $11 per unit on all units. Fixed costs are $150,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit at 12,000 units assuming variable cost is $12 per unit, as basic CVP analysis would.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the actual profit at 12,000 units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain which assumption of CVP analysis is shown to be unrealistic, and why this matters to the managers.
parts.answer: The assumption that variable cost per unit is constant at all levels of output (linear cost line). Bulk discounts make the cost line non-linear, so CVP forecasts become inaccurate outside the relevant range: here profit is understated by $12,000, which could lead to a wrong decision.
parts.working: 1 mark assumption; 1 mark non-linearity/relevant range; 1 mark consequence with figure

practice.stem: Sohni Shoes sells 9,000 pairs of sandals a month at $40 a pair. Variable cost is $24 a pair and fixed costs are $96,000 a month. The sales manager proposes cutting the price by 10%, which she expects to increase sales volume by 20%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current monthly profit and the monthly profit under the proposal.
parts.answer: Current $48,000; proposal $33,600

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how CVP analysis helps the managers decide on this proposal.
parts.answer: It shows quickly that although volume rises, contribution per pair falls from $16 to $12, so profit falls by $14,400; managers can test 'what if' changes in price, cost and volume before acting.
parts.working: 1 mark what-if/sensitivity; 1 mark applied to the figures

practice.stem: The bursar of a private school in Islamabad wants to use break-even analysis to find how many pupils the school needs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two difficulties in applying CVP analysis to the school.
parts.answer: e.g. fees differ by class and some pupils receive scholarships, so there is no single selling price; teacher costs are stepped (a new teacher for every extra class), not fixed or variable; some costs are semi-variable and hard to split; pupil numbers are fixed for the year so 'volume' changes only once a year.
parts.working: 1 mark each difficulty identified (×2), 1 mark each applied explanation (×2)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the bursar could still make use of the analysis.
parts.answer: Use an average fee and average variable cost per pupil, and calculate break-even for each range of class sizes (relevant range); review the results as numbers change.
parts.working: 1 mark each sensible suggestion

practice.stem: A business sells two products. Product A has a contribution to sales ratio of 50% and product B of 25%. Fixed costs are $90,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even revenue if revenue is earned 60% from A and 40% from B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even revenue if revenue is earned 40% from A and 60% from B.
parts.working: Weighted C/S 35% M1; 90,000 ÷ 0.35 A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a single break-even figure for this business can be misleading.
parts.answer: Break-even depends on the sales mix; if customers buy relatively more of the low-margin product B than planned, the business needs more revenue to break even than the single figure suggests.
parts.working: 1 mark depends on mix; 1 mark consequence

practice.stem: The directors of Jinnah Paints have drawn a break-even chart. The total revenue line starts at the origin and rises to $900,000 at 10,000 tins. The fixed cost line is horizontal at $240,000. The total cost line starts at $240,000 and rises to $690,000 at 10,000 tins. The lines cross at 5,333 tins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways the directors could use cost–volume–profit analysis when planning next year's production.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: find the break-even output, so they know the minimum sales needed to avoid a loss; set the sales level needed for a target profit; measure risk through the margin of safety; test the effect of changes in price, costs or volume (what-if analysis) before deciding.
parts.working: 1 mark use; 1 mark explanation, × 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the actual profit at 10,000 units might differ from the profit shown by the break-even chart.
parts.answer: Any two: bulk discounts or overtime make variable cost per unit change; prices may have to be cut to sell more; fixed costs may step up when output rises; inventory may be built up instead of sold.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Indus Mats sells mats at $20 each. Variable production cost is $12.50 per mat and fixed production overheads are $30,000 a month. There are no other costs. In March it produced 5,000 mats but sold only 4,000. There was no opening inventory. The company values inventory using absorption costing, with overheads absorbed on actual production.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point in mats using CVP analysis.
parts.answer: 4,000 mats

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for March using (i) marginal costing and (ii) absorption costing.
parts.working: Marginal: contribution 30,000 − fixed 30,000 = 0 M1 A1; absorption: overhead $6 per mat M1; 1,000 × 6 carried forward = 6,000 A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the absorption costing statement shows a profit at the break-even level of sales, and what this shows about the assumptions of CVP analysis.
parts.answer: Under absorption costing $6,000 of the fixed overhead is carried forward in closing inventory, so not all fixed costs are charged in March. CVP assumes production equals sales (no change in inventory) and treats all fixed costs as period costs, so the break-even point is only consistent with marginal costing.
parts.working: 1 mark overhead deferred in inventory; 1 mark CVP assumes production = sales; 1 mark CVP matches marginal costing

practice.stem: Pearl Water Pumps budgets to sell 10,000 pumps at $60 each. Variable cost is $35 per pump and fixed costs are $200,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which each of the following could change, on its own, before the business makes a loss: (i) selling price; (ii) variable cost per unit; (iii) fixed costs; (iv) sales volume. Give answers to two decimal places.
parts.answer: (i) 8.33% fall; (ii) 14.29% rise; (iii) 25.00% rise; (iv) 20.00% fall
parts.working: Each: profit ÷ the relevant total. (i) 50,000 ÷ 600,000 M1 A1; (ii) 50,000 ÷ 350,000 M1 A1; (iii) 50,000 ÷ 200,000 B1; (iv) margin of safety 2,000 ÷ 10,000 B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the managers which factor they should monitor most closely. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Selling price: a fall of only 8.33% eliminates profit, the smallest margin of the four. They should monitor competitors' prices and avoid discounting; variable cost (14.29%) is next most sensitive.
parts.working: 1 mark identifies selling price; 1 mark uses figure; 1 mark sensible action/comparison

practice.stem:
Sabz Organic Foods is launching a new jar of honey priced at $45. Variable cost is $27 a jar and annual fixed costs are $180,000. The marketing team gives three sales forecasts for the first year:
Forecast       Jars
Pessimistic    8,000
Most likely   12,000
Optimistic    15,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss for each forecast.
parts.answer: Pessimistic loss $36,000; most likely profit $36,000; optimistic profit $90,000
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point and the margin of safety at the most likely forecast as a percentage.
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to launch the product, discussing the usefulness and limitations of CVP analysis in this decision.
parts.answer: CVP shows the product is profitable at the most likely level but the margin of safety is small (16.67%) and the pessimistic case gives a $36,000 loss. Limitations: forecasts are estimates; price may need to change; costs may not be linear (bulk buying, step costs); single-product assumption ignores effect on existing products; non-financial factors (brand, customer demand for organic food). Decision justified.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks use of results; up to 3 marks limitations/other factors; 1 mark justified decision

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Under marginal costing, how is closing inventory of finished goods valued?
A at prime cost
B at variable production cost
C at variable production cost plus variable selling cost
D at full production cost including fixed overheads
parts.answer: B at variable production cost
parts.working: Marginal costing includes only variable production costs in inventory; fixed production overheads are period costs. C is wrong because selling costs are never part of inventory value; D describes absorption costing.

practice.stem:
The cost card for one unit of a product made by Al-Hamd Industries shows:
                                     $
Direct materials                      9
Direct labour                         6
Variable production overhead          3
Fixed production overhead absorbed    5
Variable selling cost                 2
At the end of the month there are 1,200 units in closing inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory using (i) marginal costing and (ii) absorption costing.
parts.working: Marginal 18 per unit M1 A1; absorption 23 per unit M1 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference between the two values and explain why it arises.
parts.answer: $6,000: absorption costing includes $5 of fixed production overhead in each unit of inventory, which marginal costing charges as a period cost.
parts.working: 1 mark figure; 1 mark explanation

practice.stem: The managers of Swat Woollens produce internal reports using marginal costing, but the published financial statements use absorption costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the two methods can give different profits for the same period.
parts.answer: They value inventory differently: absorption includes fixed production overhead in inventory, so part of the period's fixed overhead is carried forward (or brought forward) when inventory levels change; marginal costing charges all fixed overhead in the period.
parts.working: 1 mark inventory valuation; 1 mark change in inventory levels

parts.label: b
parts.text: State when the two methods give the same profit.
parts.answer: When there is no change in inventory levels (production equals sales, and the overhead rate per unit is the same).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why absorption costing must be used for the published financial statements.
parts.answer: IAS 2 requires inventory to include all production costs, including a share of fixed production overheads, so that costs are matched with the revenue when the goods are sold (accruals concept).
parts.working: 1 mark IAS 2 requirement; 1 mark matching

practice.stem: Chitral Crafts made and sold 6,000 wooden boxes in May. There was no opening or closing inventory. Selling price $15; variable cost $8 per box; fixed production overheads $18,000; administration costs $10,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for May using (i) marginal costing and (ii) absorption costing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the two profits are the same.
parts.answer: All production was sold, so no fixed overhead is carried forward in inventory; all $18,000 is charged in May under both methods.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company produced 10,000 units and sold 8,500 units in its first month. Fixed production overhead was $60,000, absorbed on units produced. How will profit under absorption costing compare with profit under marginal costing?
A Absorption profit is $9,000 higher.
B Marginal profit is $9,000 higher.
C Absorption profit is $10,588 higher.
D The two profits are the same.
parts.answer: A Absorption profit is $9,000 higher.
parts.working: Fixed overhead per unit = 60,000 ÷ 10,000 = $6. Closing inventory 1,500 units carries 1,500 × 6 = $9,000 of fixed overhead into next month under absorption costing, so absorption profit is $9,000 higher. C wrongly divides the overhead by units sold.

practice.stem: Khyber Foods began making jars of pickle on 1 June. June data: production 5,000 jars, sales 4,200 jars at $30 each. Variable production cost $12 per jar; fixed production overhead $35,000 (absorbed on the normal output of 5,000 jars, so $7 per jar); variable selling cost $1 per jar sold; fixed administration $18,000. There was no opening inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement of profit for June using marginal costing.
parts.answer:
Marginal costing statement
                                                   $         $
Revenue (4,200 × 30)                                   126,000
Variable cost of production (5,000 × 12)      60,000
Less closing inventory (800 × 12)            (9,600)
Variable cost of sales                                (50,400)
Variable selling costs                                 (4,200)
Contribution                                            71,400
Fixed production overhead                             (35,000)
Fixed administration                                  (18,000)
Profit                                                  18,400
parts.working: Closing inventory at 12 (1); contribution 71,400 (1); profit 18,400 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement of profit for June using absorption costing.
parts.answer:
Absorption costing statement
                                            $         $
Revenue                                         126,000
Cost of production (5,000 × 19)        95,000
Less closing inventory (800 × 19)    (15,200)
Cost of sales                                  (79,800)
Gross profit                                     46,200
Variable selling costs                          (4,200)
Fixed administration                           (18,000)
Profit                                           24,000
parts.working: Full cost 12 + 7 = 19 per unit (1); closing inventory 15,200 (1); profit 24,000 (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two profit figures are different.
parts.answer: Absorption profit is $5,600 higher because 800 units of closing inventory carry 800 × $7 = $5,600 of fixed production overhead into July, whereas marginal costing charges all the fixed overhead in June.
parts.working: 1 mark figure; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
During a period, a company's inventory of finished goods fell by 600 units. Fixed production overhead is absorbed at $8 per unit. Which statement is correct?
A absorption costing profit is $4,800 higher than marginal costing profit
B marginal costing profit is $4,800 higher than absorption costing profit
C both methods give the same profit
D marginal costing profit is $600 higher than absorption costing profit
parts.answer: B marginal costing profit is $4,800 higher than absorption costing profit
parts.working: When inventory falls, absorption costing releases fixed overhead carried forward from the previous period into this period's costs, so absorption profit is lower by 600 × 8 = $4,800. A applies when inventory rises.

practice.stem: Thar Coal Briquettes uses marginal costing for internal reports. For June the marginal costing profit was $46,500. Inventory of finished briquettes was 800 tonnes at 1 June and 2,300 tonnes at 30 June. Fixed production overhead is absorbed at $7 per tonne (the same rate as in May).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for June using absorption costing.
parts.working: Increase in inventory 1,500 tonnes M1; × 7 = 10,500 M1; 46,500 + 10,500 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement reconciling the two profits.
parts.answer: Marginal costing profit 46,500; add fixed overhead in closing inventory 16,100; less fixed overhead in opening inventory 5,600; absorption costing profit 57,000
parts.working: 1 mark each adjustment with correct sign

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the absorption costing profit is higher.
parts.answer: Inventory rose, so some of June's fixed overhead is carried forward to July in closing inventory instead of being charged in June.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for each year using marginal costing.
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for each year using absorption costing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total profit for the two years under each method and explain the difference.
parts.answer: Marginal $258,000; absorption $266,000; difference $8,000 = 2,000 cartons in closing inventory at 31 December 2026 × $4
parts.working: 1 mark totals; 1 mark explanation

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for April using marginal costing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for April using absorption costing.
parts.working: Full production cost 24 per unit M1; gross profit 7,000 × 16 = 112,000 M1; less 14,000 and 30,000 = $68,000 A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the variable selling cost is treated the same way under both methods.
parts.answer: It is not a production cost, so it is never included in inventory; under both methods it is charged for units sold in the period.
parts.working: 1 mark not a production cost; 1 mark charged in the period

practice.stem:
Ravi Plastics in Chennai absorbs fixed production overhead at $9 per unit, based on a normal output of 6,000 units a month. Actual fixed overhead is $54,000 each month. There was no inventory at the start of month 1.
                                 Month 1  Month 2
Production (units)                 6,000    5,500
Sales (units)                      5,000    6,300
Profit under marginal costing    $42,000  $55,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the closing inventory in units at the end of each month.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for each month under absorption costing.
parts.answer: Month 1: 42,000 + 1,000 × 9 = $51,000. Month 2: inventory falls by 800 units, so 55,000 − 800 × 9 = $47,800. Month 2 production is 500 units below normal, so 500 × $9 = $4,500 of overhead is under-absorbed and charged as an expense; the difference between the two profits is still fully explained by the change in inventory × $9.
parts.working: M1 inventory change × $9; A1 month 1; M1 decrease deducted; A1 month 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the absorption profit is higher than the marginal profit in month 1 but lower in month 2.
parts.answer: Month 1: inventory rises, so some fixed overhead is carried forward in closing inventory. Month 2: inventory falls, so fixed overhead carried forward from month 1 is released into cost of sales, reducing absorption profit.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorption rate and the under- or over-absorption of fixed production overhead.
parts.answer: $5 per pair; under-absorbed $8,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement of profit for the year using absorption costing.
parts.answer: Revenue 600,000; production cost 22,000 × 19 = 418,000 less closing inventory 2,000 × 19 = 38,000; cost of sales 380,000; add under-absorption 8,000; gross profit 212,000; less variable selling 20,000 and administration 40,000; profit $152,000
parts.working: B1 revenue; B1 production at $19; B1 closing inventory; B1 under-absorption added; B1 non-production costs; B1 profit

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare a statement of profit using marginal costing.
parts.answer: Revenue 600,000; variable cost of sales 280,000; variable selling 20,000; contribution 300,000; fixed production 118,000; administration 40,000; profit $142,000
parts.working: B1 variable costs; B1 contribution; B1 fixed costs; B1 profit

parts.label: d
parts.text: Reconcile the two profits.
parts.answer: Difference $10,000 = 2,000 pairs × $5 fixed overhead in closing inventory
parts.working: M1 A1

practice.stem: Ravi Engineering reported a marginal costing profit of $60,000 for the year. Opening inventory was 1,500 units, valued under absorption costing with fixed production overhead of $6.00 per unit. Closing inventory was 2,500 units; this year's fixed overhead absorption rate is $7.20 per unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the absorption costing profit for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why both the opening and closing inventory figures are needed for the reconciliation.
parts.answer: Absorption profit is reduced by fixed overhead brought forward in opening inventory (charged this year) and increased by fixed overhead carried forward in closing inventory; the net change, not just the closing figure, is the difference.
parts.working: 1 mark opening charged; 1 mark closing deferred

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the change in the absorption rate affects the comparison of profits between years.
parts.answer: Even with constant inventory volumes, a higher rate puts more overhead into closing inventory than came out of opening inventory, so absorption profit can rise without any improvement in trading.
parts.working: 1 mark effect of rate; 1 mark misleading comparison

practice.stem: The production manager of Neelum Furniture receives a bonus of 5% of the annual profit calculated using absorption costing. Demand is 10,000 chairs a year at $50 each. Variable cost is $30 per chair and fixed production overheads are $120,000 a year, absorbed on a normal output of 10,000 chairs. The factory can make up to 14,000 chairs. There was no opening inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the absorption costing profit if (i) 10,000 chairs and (ii) 14,000 chairs are produced, with 10,000 sold in each case.
parts.working: Rate $12 per chair B1; (i) 80,000 A1; (ii) closing inventory 4,000 × $42; over-absorption 48,000 M1; 128,000 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the manager's bonus in each case.
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the marginal costing profit in each case.
parts.answer: $80,000 in both cases
parts.working: Contribution 200,000 − 120,000 B1

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the directors how the bonus scheme should be changed. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Producing for inventory raises absorption profit by $48,000 with no extra sales, so the manager earns $2,400 more bonus while the company bears extra holding, storage and obsolescence costs and ties up cash in 4,000 chairs. Base the bonus on marginal costing profit, or on sales/contribution, or penalise inventory build-up; absorption is still needed for published accounts. Decision.
parts.working: 1 mark identifies incentive to overproduce; up to 2 marks costs/risks to company; up to 2 marks for suitable change with justification

practice.stem: Hunza Dry Fruits produces 10,000 packs in each of three quarters. Selling price $20 per pack; variable production cost $12 per pack; fixed production overheads $30,000 per quarter, absorbed at $3 per pack. Sales: quarter 1 8,000 packs; quarter 2 10,000 packs; quarter 3 12,000 packs. There was no inventory at the start of quarter 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for each quarter using marginal costing.
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for each quarter using absorption costing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that total profit over the three quarters is the same under both methods, and explain why.
parts.answer: Both total $150,000; over the three quarters production equals sales (30,000 packs) and inventory returns to zero, so all fixed overhead incurred has been charged under both methods.
parts.working: 1 mark totals; 1 mark explanation

parts.label: d
parts.text: State which method gives a profit trend that better follows sales, giving a reason.
parts.answer: Marginal costing: profit changes only with sales volume, not with production levels.
parts.working: B1

topics.name: Analysis and communication of accounting information

practice.stem:
Kiran owns a clothing boutique in Hyderabad (Sindh). Her ratios are:
                                2024      2025
Gross margin                     38%       41%
Profit margin                    14%       10%
Return on capital employed       22%       17%
Current ratio                1.9 : 1   1.8 : 1
Trade receivables turnover   34 days   29 days

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ratios that show an improvement in 2025.
parts.answer: Gross margin (rose from 38% to 41%) and the trade receivables turnover (fell from 34 to 29 days).
parts.working: 1 mark each with direction stated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the profit margin fell although the gross margin rose.
parts.answer: Operating expenses (such as rent, wages or advertising) rose faster than gross profit, so a smaller share of revenue was left as profit.
parts.working: 1 mark expenses rose; 1 mark faster than gross profit / as % of revenue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions Kiran could take to improve her profit margin.
parts.answer: Cut operating expenses such as advertising or energy; move to cheaper premises or renegotiate rent.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible expense-control or revenue actions.

practice.stem: Esi runs a homeware shop in Kumasi. For 2025: cost of sales $384,000; inventory 1 January 2025 $40,000; inventory 31 December 2025 $56,000. In 2024 the rate of inventory turnover was 12 times.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inventory turnover for 2025.
parts.answer: 8.00 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two possible reasons why the rate of inventory turnover has fallen from 12 times.
parts.answer: Sales have slowed (fewer customers); Esi bought too much inventory or some lines are out of fashion.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: lower demand/sales; overbuying/bulk purchases; slow-moving or obsolete lines; higher selling prices reduced sales; new competitor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Esi whether she should sell her slow-moving inventory at reduced prices. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Selling at a discount releases cash and storage space and avoids obsolescence, but lowers the gross margin and may train customers to wait for sales; a justified decision.
parts.working: For: cash released, less risk of obsolescence/damage, lower storage cost, turnover improves. Against: lower gross margin, damages brand image, customers wait for discounts. 1 mark per point (max 3), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Mehwish owns a bakery in Quetta. Her ratios and the industry averages for 2025 are:
                             Mehwish  Industry
Gross margin                     42%       38%
Profit margin                     9%       12%
Current ratio                1.4 : 1   1.8 : 1
Trade receivables (days)          12        10
Inventory turnover (days)          3         4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ratios in which Mehwish's bakery performs better than the industry average and two in which it performs worse.
parts.answer:
Better: gross margin (42% compared with 38%); inventory turnover (3 days compared with 4 days — inventory sells faster, important for fresh bread).
Worse: profit margin (9% compared with 12%); current ratio (1.4 : 1 compared with 1.8 : 1, weaker liquidity); trade receivables (12 days compared with 10 days, customers pay more slowly).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two better and two worse ratios, with figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the profit margin is below the industry average even though the gross margin is above it.
parts.answer: Expenses are a larger share of revenue (42 − 9 = 33% compared with 38 − 12 = 26%), e.g. higher rent, wages or energy costs.
parts.working: 1 mark expenses higher; 1 mark figures.

practice.stem: Ibrahim's grocery shop in Jhelum has capital employed of $250,000 and made a profit of $32,000 last year. He works full time in the shop and takes no salary. A supermarket has offered him a job as a manager at $24,000 a year. He could sell the shop for $250,000 and invest the money at 6% a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed for Ibrahim's shop, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total annual income Ibrahim would receive if he sold the shop for $250,000, invested the money and took the job.
parts.working: 1 mark interest; 1 mark total.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Ibrahim whether to sell the shop. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Financially, selling gives $39,000 compared with $32,000 profit — $7,000 more, with less risk and fixed hours. But he would lose independence; the shop's profit could grow; the price may not be achieved; the bank rate could fall; job security is not certain. Decision with reason.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison using figures; 2 marks non-financial / other factors; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Liang owns a bicycle shop in Kunming and has asked a bank for a five-year loan. At 31 December 2025: inventory $64,000; trade receivables $41,000; cash $3,000; current liabilities $72,000. Other information:
                               Liang   Industry average
Return on capital employed       21%                15%
Interest cover               6 times            5 times
Current ratio                      ?           1.80 : 1
Liquid ratio                       ?           1.00 : 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate, to two decimal places, Liang's (i) current ratio and (ii) liquid (acid test) ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the bank whether it should grant the loan. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Profitability is strong (ROCE 21% v 15%), but liquidity is weak (0.61 v 1.00), so the bank may lend only with security or conditions.
parts.working: For: ROCE above the industry; interest cover 6 times. Against: both liquidity ratios below the industry average; may struggle to meet repayments in cash. Other: security available, purpose of loan, owner's record. 1 mark per point (max 3, both sides), 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: Tendai sells farm supplies in Harare. In 2025 he increased the credit period for customers from 30 to 60 days to win more business; his trade receivables turnover in 2024 was 38 days and the business now has a bank overdraft. For 2025: credit sales $730,000; credit purchases $511,000; trade receivables $122,000; trade payables $42,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for 2025, to the nearest whole day: (i) the trade receivables turnover, (ii) the trade payables turnover.
parts.answer: (i) 61 days (ii) 30 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Tendai whether to continue offering 60 days' credit. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Longer credit raised sales but customers now pay 31 days after Tendai pays suppliers, which has caused the overdraft; he should probably return to shorter credit or offer cash discounts.
parts.working: For keeping: sales grew; competitive; customer loyalty. Against: receivables days 38 → 61 while payables 30, overdraft interest, higher risk of irrecoverable debts. 1 mark per point (max 3, both sides), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Yusuf owns a restaurant in Dubai. At the start of 2025 he introduced a premium menu.
                        2024 $      2025 $
Revenue              1,250,000   1,400,000
Cost of sales          500,000     616,000
Operating expenses     450,000     560,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin for each year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit margin for each year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Yusuf whether he should keep the new premium menu. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The menu raised revenue by 12% but profit fell from $300,000 to $224,000 because food and staff costs rose faster; he should change it unless prices can rise or costs be cut.
parts.working: For: revenue up 150,000; new customers/reputation; may take time to pay off. Against: GM down 4 points, PM down 8 points, profit down 76,000; expenses up 110,000. 1 mark per point (max 3), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Directors of Dune Solar Ltd review the last three years. For 2025: profit from operations $840,000; equity $4,200,000; non-current liabilities $1,400,000.
                                2023      2024      2025
Return on capital employed       19%       17%         ?
Gearing                          10%       18%       25%
Current ratio                1.9 : 1   1.6 : 1   1.3 : 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed for 2025, to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether the company's financial position has improved over the three years.
parts.answer: No: profitability has fallen (ROCE 19% → 15%), borrowing has risen (gearing 10% → 25%) and liquidity has weakened (current ratio 1.9 → 1.3), although gearing is still low and the borrowing may be funding growth.
parts.working: ROCE falling each year: less return per $ invested (1–2 marks). Gearing up: more risk, more interest, but still below 50% (1–2). Current ratio down: possible liquidity pressure, still above 1 (1–2). Balanced point: new investment may not yet have produced profit (1). Conclusion (1). Max 6.

practice.stem:
Amara wants to buy a pharmacy in Lagos, Nigeria. Two are for sale:
                                Shop P      Shop Q
Asking price ($)               300,000     220,000
Profit 2023 ($)                 52,000      24,600
Profit 2024 ($)                 49,000      27,500
Profit 2025 ($)                 45,000      30,800
Current assets ($)              58,000      51,000
Current liabilities ($)         40,000      25,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for each shop: (i) the return on the asking price (profit ÷ price × 100) (ii) the current ratio, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Amara which shop she should buy. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Shop P: higher return now (15% vs 14%) and higher absolute profit, but profits have fallen for three years and liquidity is weaker; costs $80,000 more.
Shop Q: slightly lower return, but profits are rising and liquidity is stronger; cheaper, leaving her $80,000 for other uses; if the trend continues Q's return will soon exceed P's.
Decision, e.g. Shop Q because its trend and liquidity are better and it is cheaper.
parts.working: 2 marks points for P; 2 marks points for Q; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Blue Mosque Carpets Ltd, Istanbul, has profit from operations of $360,000 and capital employed of $2,000,000. It is considering a new branch that would cost $250,000, financed by a bank loan at 10% a year. The branch is expected to have revenue of $400,000 a year at a gross margin of 30%, and operating expenses of $85,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected annual profit from operations of the new branch.
parts.working: 1 mark gross profit; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed of the branch, and of the whole company after the expansion, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark branch; 1 mark each for company figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to open the branch. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The branch returns 14% — above the 10% loan interest, so it adds $10,000 to profit after interest, but below the present 18%, so company ROCE falls. Gearing rises. First-year forecasts may be optimistic, but a new branch may grow and build the brand. Decision with reason.
parts.working: 1 mark financial comparison; 1 mark other factor; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Meridian Furniture plc has two divisions. The directors can invest in only one of them.
                           North $     South $
Revenue                  2,400,000   1,500,000
Profit from operations     288,000     270,000
Capital employed         1,600,000   1,800,000
Profit margin               12.00%      18.00%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for each division, to two decimal places: (i) the asset turnover (revenue ÷ capital employed), (ii) the return on capital employed.
parts.answer: North: asset turnover 1.50 times, ROCE 18.00%. South: asset turnover 0.83 times, ROCE 15.00%.

parts.label: b
