parts.text: Advise the directors which division should receive the investment. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: North earns the higher ROCE through efficient use of assets, though South has the better margin; a justified choice, usually North.
parts.working: North: higher ROCE 18% v 15%; uses assets more intensively (1.50 v 0.83). South: higher profit margin 18% v 12% – if extra capital raises its sales, it may gain more. Non-financial: market growth, competition, capacity. 1 mark per point (max 3, both sides), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Omar holds shares in Granite Peak Cement plc, which has 7,000,000 ordinary shares in issue.
                                2024         2025
Profit for the year       $2,100,000   $1,260,000
Ordinary dividends paid   $1,050,000   $1,050,000
Market price per share         $3.00        $2.40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dividend cover for each year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the dividend yield for each year, to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Omar whether to keep his shares. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The higher yield is only because the share price fell; with cover of 1.20 the dividend is at risk, so Omar should consider selling unless he expects profits to recover.
parts.working: For keeping: yield up to 6.25%; dividend maintained; price may recover. Against: EPS fell 30c → 18c; cover 1.20 – dividend barely covered, may be cut; falling price shows market concern. 1 mark per point (max 3, both sides), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Divya runs an electrical wholesaler in Chennai. Her current assets are inventory $60,000, trade receivables $80,000 and cash $10,000. Current liabilities are trade payables $40,000 and a bank overdraft $60,000 (current ratio 1.50 : 1; liquid ratio 0.90 : 1). A debt factor offers to buy all her trade receivables for $76,000 cash. Divya would use the cash to repay the overdraft in full.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate, to two decimal places, the current ratio and the liquid ratio after the proposal.
parts.answer: Current ratio 2.15 : 1; liquid ratio 0.65 : 1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Divya whether to accept the factor's offer. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The overdraft disappears and the current ratio rises, but the liquid ratio falls and the business loses $4,000 and control of debt collection; a justified decision.
parts.working: For: overdraft repaid, no overdraft interest, immediate cash, no irrecoverable debt risk. Against: cost 4,000 (5%); liquid ratio falls 0.90 → 0.65; customers dealt with by a third party; one-off – future receivables still slow. 1 mark per point (max 3), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Andean Textiles, Arequipa, Peru, asks its bank to increase its overdraft limit. The bank has these ratios:
                                      2023        2024
Return on capital employed          18.50%      15.20%
Current ratio                     1.90 : 1    1.50 : 1
Trade receivables (days)                38          46
For 2025: profit from operations $84,000; capital employed $700,000; current assets $210,000; current liabilities $175,000; trade receivables $79,000; credit sales $497,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for 2025: (i) the return on capital employed (ii) the current ratio, to two decimal places (iii) the trade receivables turnover, to the nearest whole day.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the bank whether to increase the overdraft limit from $40,000 to $90,000. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Against: ROCE has fallen each year (18.5% → 15.2% → 12.0%); the current ratio has fallen from 1.90 to 1.20; customers now take 58 days instead of 38, suggesting weak credit control or customers in difficulty; the request may be to cover poor cash management rather than growth; risk of non-repayment.
For: the business is still profitable; ROCE of 12% is above typical overdraft rates; a larger overdraft may help it through a temporary problem; assets may give security.
Conditions: ask for a cash budget, security over property, a plan to collect receivables faster, a lower increase.
Decision: e.g. refuse the full increase; offer a smaller increase with security and conditions.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks against, up to 2 marks for, 1 mark conditions/other information, 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Faisal holds shares in Golden Crescent plc, which has 10,000,000 ordinary shares in issue.
                                      2024        2025
Profit for the year ($)          4,200,000   3,600,000
Ordinary dividends paid ($)      2,000,000   2,400,000
Share price at year end ($)           5.04        4.20
Gearing                                22%         41%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for each year: (i) earnings per share (ii) dividend per share (iii) dividend cover (iv) dividend yield, to two decimal places (v) price earnings ratio, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for each ratio for both years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Faisal whether to buy more shares in Golden Crescent plc. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For: higher dividend (24c) and yield (5.71%) — attractive for income; share price has fallen, so shares are cheaper.
Against: EPS has fallen 14%; dividend was raised while profit fell, so it is now covered only 1.5 times and two-thirds of profit is paid out; it may not be sustainable; gearing has nearly doubled to 41%, increasing risk; falling share price shows the market's concern; P/E fell slightly.
Other: compare with other companies, find reasons for falling profit, Faisal's attitude to risk.
Decision, e.g. do not buy more until profits recover and gearing falls.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for, up to 3 marks against, 1 mark other information, 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Kilimanjaro Tea Ltd: at 31 December 2024 long-term loans were $800,000 and equity was $1,200,000 (gearing 40.00%). At 31 December 2025 long-term loans were $500,000 and equity was $1,500,000. Gearing = non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities) × 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gearing ratio at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the company is high or low geared in 2025 and give one advantage to ordinary shareholders of the change since 2024.
parts.answer: Low geared (below 50%). Less interest has to be paid, so more profit is available for dividends and the risk of not paying a dividend is lower.
parts.working: 1 mark low geared; 1 mark advantage (less interest/lower risk/more profit for dividends).

practice.stem: Mehran Cables plc has 2,500,000 ordinary shares and 5% preference shares. For 2025: profit for the year $860,000; preference dividend paid $60,000; ordinary dividend paid 10 cents per share. The market price of an ordinary share is $4.80.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the earnings per share.
parts.working: 1 mark deducting preference dividend; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the dividend cover.
parts.working: 1 mark dividend total; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the price earnings ratio and the dividend yield (to two decimal places).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the preference dividend is deducted when calculating earnings per share.
parts.answer: Preference dividends must be paid before ordinary shareholders receive anything, so they are not part of the earnings available to ordinary shareholders.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Kalahari Freight Ltd, Gaborone, Botswana, had profit from operations of $285,000 for 2025. Interest on its long-term bank loan was $38,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest cover, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what interest cover shows to the providers of the company's loan.
parts.answer: How many times the profit before interest could pay the interest due; a high cover means interest is safe even if profits fall.
parts.working: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark safety/risk.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why ordinary shareholders would be concerned if the interest cover fell sharply.
parts.answer: Interest is paid before dividends, so less profit is left for dividends / risk of default could threaten the company.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company has 1,200,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each. Its profit for the year was $540,000 and it has no preference shares. What is its earnings per share?
A 45 cents
B 90 cents
C 22.5 cents
D 4.5 cents
parts.answer: A 45 cents
parts.working: 540,000 ÷ 1,200,000 shares = $0.45 = 45 cents. 90 cents wrongly divides by the nominal value of the share capital ($600,000) instead of the number of shares.

practice.stem: Andes Coffee plc has 4,000,000 issued ordinary shares of $1 each and no preference shares. For the year: profit for the year $1,320,000; ordinary dividends paid $480,000. The market price of one share is $4.62.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the earnings per share.
parts.answer: 33 cents

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price earnings ratio.
parts.answer: 14.00 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the dividend cover.
parts.answer: 2.75 times

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the dividend yield, to two decimal places.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain what the price earnings ratio shows an investor.
parts.answer: It shows how many years of current earnings the share price represents; a high P/E means the market expects profits to grow (or sees the share as low risk).
parts.working: 1 mark price paid per $1 of earnings / years to recover price; 1 mark high = confidence/expected growth.

practice.stem:
Extract from the statement of financial position of Baltic Fisheries Ltd at 31 March 2026:
                                 $
Ordinary share capital   2,000,000
Share premium              400,000
Retained earnings        1,100,000
8% debentures (2032)     1,500,000
Profit from operations for the year was $690,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gearing ratio, to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the interest cover, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 5.75 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why both lenders and ordinary shareholders are interested in the gearing ratio.
parts.answer: Lenders: a high gearing means more risk that interest and capital will not be repaid. Shareholders: high gearing means fixed interest is paid before dividends, so dividends are more volatile, although returns can be higher when profits rise.
parts.working: 1 mark lenders' risk of non-payment/security; 1 mark shareholders: interest paid first, dividends at risk; 1 mark development (higher gearing magnifies returns in good years / ability to borrow more).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company has issued ordinary shares of $500,000, reserves of $400,000 and 6% loan notes of $300,000. It has no preference shares. What is its gearing ratio?
A 20.00%
B 25.00%
C 33.33%
D 75.00%
parts.working: Gearing = non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities) × 100 = 300,000 ÷ 1,200,000 = 25.00%. C compares the loan notes with equity only (300 ÷ 900).

practice.stem: Taurus Engineering plc has 8% loan notes of $2,000,000 and profit from operations of $720,000. It plans to borrow a further $1,500,000 at 9% a year, which is expected to increase profit from operations by $150,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the present interest cover and income gearing (interest as a percentage of profit from operations), to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate both ratios, to two decimal places, if the new loan is taken.
parts.working: 1 mark interest; 1 mark each ratio.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the change from the point of view of the existing lenders.
parts.answer: Their interest is covered fewer times (4.50 → 2.95) and a third of operating profit now goes on interest, so the risk of default rises if profits fall; they may ask for security or covenants.
parts.working: 1 mark using figures; 1 mark risk.

practice.stem:
Xenon Software plc: earnings per share 42 cents; share price $8.40.
Yarrow Brick plc: earnings per share 65 cents; share price $5.85.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price earnings ratio for each company.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the difference in the price earnings ratios suggests about how investors view the two companies.
parts.answer: Investors pay $20 for each $1 of Xenon's earnings but only $9 for Yarrow's, so they expect Xenon's earnings to grow faster or consider it lower risk; Yarrow may be seen as having poor prospects or high risk, or may be undervalued.
parts.working: 1 mark meaning of P/E; 1 mark Xenon expectations; 1 mark Yarrow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one limitation of using the price earnings ratio to choose between the two companies.
parts.answer: Share prices change daily / EPS is based on past profit / the companies are in different industries with different typical P/E ratios.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company's equity is $600,000 and its only non-current liability is a loan of $200,000. It issues a further $100,000 of debentures to buy machinery. Gearing = non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities) × 100. What is the gearing ratio after the issue?
A 33.33%
B 25.00%
C 50.00%
D 42.86%
parts.working: 300,000 ÷ (600,000 + 300,000) × 100 = 33.33%. 25.00% is the gearing before the issue; 50.00% divides debt by equity only (300,000 ÷ 600,000).

practice.stem:
Ayesha, a retired teacher in Lahore, wants regular income from shares. She is choosing between two companies:
                           Crescent Foods plc   Delta Tech plc
Profit for the year                  $900,000       $1,560,000
Ordinary shares in issue            3,000,000        6,000,000
Ordinary dividends paid              $450,000         $312,000
Market price per share                  $3.60            $3.90
Dividend cover                      2.0 times        5.0 times
Gearing                                   45%              15%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dividend yield for each company, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Crescent 4.17%; Delta 1.33%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price earnings ratio for each company.
parts.answer: Crescent 12.00; Delta 15.00

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Ayesha which company's shares she should buy. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Crescent suits her need for regular income (higher yield), but its high gearing makes the dividend less safe; a justified decision either way.
parts.working: Crescent: yield 4.17% v 1.33%; pays out half its profit. Against Crescent: gearing 45% – interest comes first, dividend cover only 2.0. Delta: low gearing 15%, cover 5.0 so dividend is safe, higher P/E suggests market expects growth – but low income now. 1 mark per point to 3 (both sides needed for 3), 1 mark decision linked to her need for income.

practice.stem:
Pacifica Bottling plc has 5,000,000 ordinary shares of $1 each, equity of $7,500,000 and no borrowings. It needs $2,000,000 for a new production line, after which profit from operations is expected to be $1,400,000 a year. Ignore taxation.
Option 1: issue 1,000,000 ordinary shares at $2 each.
Option 2: borrow $2,000,000 with a 7% long-term loan.
Gearing = non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities) × 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected earnings per share under each option, to two decimal places (in cents).
parts.answer: Option 1 23.33 cents; option 2 25.20 cents

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gearing ratio under option 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors which option to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Option 2 gives higher EPS and keeps control with existing shareholders; gearing of 21.05% is still low, so the loan is affordable unless profits are uncertain.
parts.working: For loan: EPS 25.20c v 23.33c; no dilution of control; interest cover 10 times. Against: fixed interest must be paid even if profit falls; capital must be repaid; gearing rises. 1 mark per point (max 2), 1 mark decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company's earnings per share are 48 cents and its dividend cover is 3 times. Its share price is $6.00. What is the dividend yield?
A 0.89%
B 2.67%
C 8.00%
D 37.50%
parts.working: Dividend per share = 48 ÷ 3 = 16 cents; yield = 0.16 ÷ 6.00 × 100 = 2.67%. C (8.00%) is the earnings yield (48 ÷ 600).

practice.stem: Orchid Pharma plc has 6,000,000 ordinary shares of $1 each. Profit attributable to ordinary shareholders is $1,500,000 a year and is expected to stay the same. The share price is $3.50. The directors make a bonus issue of 1 new share for every 4 held.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the earnings per share before and after the bonus issue.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected share price after the bonus issue and show that the price earnings ratio is unchanged.
parts.working: 1 mark price; 1 mark P/E both.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The directors intend to keep the dividend at 10 cents per share. Calculate the dividend cover before and after the bonus issue and comment.
parts.answer: Before: dividends 600,000; cover 1,500,000 ÷ 600,000 = 2.50. After: dividends 750,000; cover 2.00. Shareholders receive 25% more dividend in total, but less profit is retained and cover falls, so the dividend is less safe if profits fall.
parts.working: 1 mark each cover; 1 mark comment.

practice.stem: Cedar Bay Resorts plc has 4,000,000 ordinary shares; equity of $3,200,000; 10% loan notes of $1,200,000; and surplus cash of $1,500,000 that earns no interest. Profit from operations is $640,000 a year. Tax is 25% of profit after interest. The directors propose to use $1,200,000 of the cash to repay the loan notes now. Capital employed = equity + loan notes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate, before and after the repayment: (i) the gearing ratio (ii) the interest cover (iii) the return on capital employed (iv) the earnings per share (in cents). Give answers to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each pair; 2 marks for EPS (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to repay the loan notes now. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For: EPS rises by 2.25 cents, ROCE rises, no gearing so lower financial risk, saves $120,000 interest a year.
Against: uses $1.2m of the $1.5m cash, leaving little for emergencies or investment; cheaper to keep the loan if the cash could earn more than 10% in the business; may need to borrow again later at a higher rate.
Decision, e.g. repay because the cash is idle and the loan costs 10%.
parts.working: 1 mark each for points for and against (max 3); 1 mark for decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business had total revenue of $520,000, of which $438,000 was on credit. Trade receivables at the year end were $54,000. What is the trade receivables turnover in days (to the nearest day)?
A 45 days
B 38 days
C 8 days
D 60 days
parts.answer: A 45 days
parts.working: 54,000 ÷ 438,000 × 365 = 45 days. 38 days wrongly uses total revenue instead of credit sales.

practice.stem: Blue Lagoon Laundry, Colombo, had revenue of $1,260,000 for 2025. The carrying amount of its non-current assets at 31 December 2025 was $420,000. Its non-current asset turnover for 2024 was 2.40 times.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the non-current asset turnover for 2025, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 3.00 times
parts.working: Revenue 1,260,000 ÷ non-current assets 420,000 (M1) = 3.00 times (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the change from 2.40 times in 2024 shows.
parts.answer: Each $1 of non-current assets generated $3.00 of revenue instead of $2.40, so the assets are being used more efficiently (or the assets are older with lower carrying amounts).
parts.working: 1 mark improved/more revenue per $1 of assets; 1 mark more efficient use (or credit the effect of depreciation lowering carrying amounts).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business made credit purchases of $365,000 and cash purchases of $73,000 in the year. Trade payables at the year end were $42,000. What is the trade payables turnover?
A 9 days
B 35 days
C 42 days
D 50 days
parts.answer: C 42 days
parts.working: Use credit purchases only: 42,000 ÷ 365,000 × 365 = 42 days. B (35 days) wrongly uses total purchases of $438,000; A is the number of times (8.69) misread as days.

practice.stem: Chenab Textiles, Faisalabad, had revenue of $960,000 for the year, of which $240,000 was cash sales. Credit purchases were $540,000. At the year end trade receivables were $88,000 and trade payables were $51,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate, to the nearest whole day: (i) the trade receivables turnover (ii) the trade payables turnover.
parts.working: (i) 1 mark credit sales, 1 mark answer; (ii) 1 mark method, 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the relationship between the two results.
parts.answer: Customers take about 45 days to pay but suppliers are paid in about 34 days, so cash leaves the business 11 days before it comes in; the business must finance the gap (overdraft) and may have cash flow problems.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison with figures; 1 mark consequence for cash.

practice.stem:
Two hotels in Zanzibar, Tanzania, report for 2025:
                              Palm Court  Harbour View
Revenue ($)                    2,400,000     1,950,000
Non-current assets ($)         6,000,000     3,900,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the non-current asset turnover for each hotel, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the results show.
parts.answer: Harbour View generates $0.50 of revenue for every $1 of non-current assets compared with $0.40 at Palm Court, so it uses its non-current assets more efficiently.
parts.working: 1 mark interpretation; 1 mark comparison.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why Palm Court's non-current asset turnover is lower.
parts.answer: Its buildings may have been revalued recently or are newer (higher carrying amount); lower occupancy; expensive facilities (pool, spa) that add assets but little revenue; it may have bought land for future expansion.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Opening inventory was $34,000, closing inventory was $46,000 and cost of sales was $360,000. What was the rate of inventory turnover?
A 9.00 times
B 7.83 times
C 10.59 times
D 4.50 times
parts.answer: A 9.00 times
parts.working: Average inventory = (34,000 + 46,000) ÷ 2 = 40,000; 360,000 ÷ 40,000 = 9.00 times. 7.83 times uses closing inventory only; 4.50 times divides by the total of the two inventories.

practice.stem:
Ivan Petrov owns a wholesale stationery business in Almaty. For the year ended 30 June 2026:
                                                   $
Revenue (including cash sales of $120,000)   900,000
Purchases (all on credit)                    640,000
Inventory 1 July 2025                         70,000
Inventory 30 June 2026                        80,000
Trade receivables 30 June 2026                96,000
Trade payables 30 June 2026                   70,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate: (i) the rate of inventory turnover (to two decimal places), (ii) the trade receivables turnover in days, (iii) the trade payables turnover in days. Give (ii) and (iii) to the nearest whole day.
parts.answer: (i) 8.40 times (ii) 45 days (iii) 40 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the relationship between the trade receivables and trade payables periods.
parts.answer: Customers take about 45 days to pay but Ivan pays suppliers in about 40 days, so cash goes out before it comes in, which puts pressure on liquidity.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison with figures; 1 mark consequence for cash flow/working capital.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader's revenue for the year was $365,000. All goods are sold at a mark-up of 25% on cost. Opening inventory was $28,000 and closing inventory was $36,000. What is the rate of inventory turnover in days, based on average inventory?
A 32 days
B 40 days
C 43 days
D 45 days
parts.answer: B 40 days
parts.working: Cost of sales = 365,000 × 100/125 = 292,000. Average inventory = (28,000 + 36,000) ÷ 2 = 32,000; 32,000 ÷ 292,000 × 365 = 40 days. A divides by revenue instead of cost of sales; C treats 25% as a margin (cost of sales 273,750, giving 42.7 days); D uses closing inventory only.

practice.stem: Sahara Tiles, Marrakech, Morocco. For the year ended 31 December 2025: inventory at 1 January $46,500; purchases $371,000; inventory at 31 December $53,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inventory turnover for 2025 (i) in times, to two decimal places (ii) in days, to the nearest whole day.
parts.working: 1 mark cost of sales; 1 mark average inventory; 1 mark each answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In 2024 inventory turned over 9.10 times. Suggest two reasons for the change and one consequence for the business.
parts.answer: Reasons: buying in larger quantities (bulk discounts); slower sales or a fall in demand; holding a wider range; obsolete items not cleared. Consequence: more cash tied up, higher storage and insurance costs, risk of damage or obsolescence.
parts.working: 1 mark each reason (two); 1 mark consequence.

practice.stem: Eduardo's building supplies business in Manila, Philippines, has annual credit sales of $730,000 and customers take on average 60 days to pay. He is considering offering a 2% cash discount for payment within 10 days. He expects customers accounting for half of credit sales to take the discount; the rest would still pay in 60 days. The business has a bank overdraft costing 12% a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the trade receivables at present and the expected trade receivables if the discount is offered.
parts.working: 1 mark present; 1 mark 35 days; 1 mark $70,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual cost of the discount and the annual saving in overdraft interest.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Eduardo whether to offer the discount. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: On these figures the discount costs $1,300 a year more than it saves. But faster collection may reduce irrecoverable debts and administration, and improve liquidity. Decision, e.g. do not offer 2% — try 1% or tighter credit control instead.
parts.working: 1 mark net cost $1,300; 1 mark non-financial/other point; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Green Thumb Garden Centre, York, England, has a 31 December year end. Cost of sales was $512,000. Inventory was $22,000 on 1 January and $18,000 on 31 December. The average of the inventory figures at the end of each month was $64,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inventory turnover in times using (i) the average of opening and closing inventory (ii) the average of the monthly inventory figures. Give answers to one decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark average 20,000; 1 mark each answer (max 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the two results are so different and which is more useful to the owner.
parts.answer: A garden centre is seasonal: inventory is low in December (winter) and high in spring and summer. Year-end figures are not typical, so (i) overstates how fast inventory sells. The monthly average (8 times) better reflects the real position and is more useful.
parts.working: 1 mark seasonal business; 1 mark year-end not representative; 1 mark choice with reason.

practice.stem:
Kofi Distributors provides these figures for the year (all purchases are on credit and the business buys goods only for resale; purchases equal cost of sales):
                          $
Cost of sales       474,500
Average inventory    52,000
Credit sales        584,000
Trade receivables    64,000
Trade payables       39,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate: (i) the inventory turnover in days, (ii) the trade receivables turnover in days, (iii) the trade payables turnover in days.
parts.answer: (i) 40 days (ii) 40 days (iii) 30 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the working capital (cash) cycle in days.
parts.answer: 50 days

parts.label: c
parts.text: The business plans to reduce the trade receivables period to 30 days with the same credit sales. Calculate the cash released.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one risk of shortening the credit period offered to customers.
parts.answer: Customers may move to competitors that give longer credit, so sales fall.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Shifa Pharmacy, Rawalpindi, has an annual cost of sales of Rs 1,095,000 and holds average inventory of Rs 150,000. The owner wants to reduce inventory turnover to 35 days with no change in cost of sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current inventory turnover in days.
parts.answer: 50 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the reduction in average inventory needed to reach 35 days.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Holding inventory costs 12% of its value per year. Calculate the annual saving.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two risks to the pharmacy of holding less inventory.
parts.answer: Running out of medicines that patients need, losing customers to other pharmacies; losing bulk-buying discounts.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: stock-outs/lost sales; loss of customer goodwill (patients need medicines urgently); loss of bulk discounts; more frequent ordering costs; supplier delays.

practice.stem:
Baobab Traders, Dar es Salaam, makes all sales and purchases on credit. For the year ended 30 June 2026:
- trade receivables at 30 June 2026 were $54,000 and the trade receivables turnover was 45 days
- the gross margin was 30%
- the rate of inventory turnover was 8 times, based on average inventory; opening inventory was $36,000
- trade payables at 30 June 2026 were $42,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the credit sales for the year.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the closing inventory.
parts.working: 1 mark average; 1 mark closing.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the credit purchases.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Calculate the trade payables turnover, to the nearest whole day.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark answer.

practice.stem: Saffron Motors Components, Pune, India, uses raw materials costing $1,440,000 a year and holds average raw materials inventory of $180,000. A supplier offers a just-in-time (JIT) service that would reduce average inventory to 5 days' usage, but would charge 2% more for all materials. Holding inventory costs 15% of its value a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the present raw materials inventory turnover in days, to one decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average inventory under JIT and the annual saving in holding costs, to the nearest $.
parts.working: 1 mark average inventory; 1 mark reduction; 1 mark saving.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the extra annual cost of materials under JIT and the net financial effect.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to introduce JIT. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Financially JIT costs about $4,759 more each year, and there is a risk of production stopping if a delivery is late. But there may be other savings (less space, less waste, obsolescence) and a better inventory turnover. Decision, e.g. do not adopt unless the supplier lowers the price or other savings are proven.
parts.working: 1 mark financial/non-financial point; 1 mark justified decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A shop had revenue of $250,000 and cost of sales of $175,000. What was its gross margin?
A 30.00%
B 42.86%
C 70.00%
D 25.00%
parts.working: Gross profit = 75,000; 75,000 ÷ 250,000 × 100 = 30.00%. 42.86% is the mark-up (gross profit ÷ cost of sales); 70.00% is cost of sales as a percentage of revenue.

practice.stem:
Tariq Electronics, Gujranwala, provides this information:
                          2024 $    2025 $
Revenue                  480,000   560,000
Gross profit             168,000   179,200
Profit from operations    57,600    50,400
Capital employed         320,000   360,000
Ratios for 2024: gross margin 35.00%, profit margin 12.00%, return on capital employed 18.00%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for 2025, to two decimal places: (i) the gross margin, (ii) the profit margin, (iii) the return on capital employed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two possible reasons for the change in the gross margin.
parts.answer: Selling prices were cut to raise sales volume; the cost of buying goods rose and was not passed on.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: lower selling prices/discounts to customers; higher purchase prices; change in sales mix towards lower-margin goods; loss of trade discounts; more inventory losses/theft.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the change in the return on capital employed.
parts.answer: ROCE fell from 18.00% to 14.00%: each $1 invested earned less profit, because profit fell while extra capital of $40,000 was invested.
parts.working: 1 mark identifies fall (with figures); 1 mark explains (lower profit and higher capital employed / less efficient use of resources).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sole trader's profit for the year was $36,000 after charging loan interest of $4,000. At the year end her capital was $180,000 and she had a long-term loan of $50,000. What is the return on capital employed?
A 15.65%
B 17.39%
C 20.00%
D 22.22%
parts.working: ROCE = (profit for the year + loan interest) ÷ (capital + non-current liabilities) × 100 = 40,000 ÷ 230,000 × 100 = 17.39%. C uses profit ÷ capital only; A forgets to add back the interest.

practice.stem: Mwangi Shoes, Nakuru, Kenya, had revenue of $248,000, cost of sales of $161,200 and operating expenses of $59,520 for the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate: (i) the gross margin (ii) the profit margin (iii) operating expenses as a percentage of revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark each (gross profit 248,000 − 161,200 = 86,800).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the profit margin is lower than the gross margin.
parts.answer: Gross profit is before operating expenses; the profit margin is after deducting expenses (rent, wages, etc.), which take 24% of revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark expenses deducted; 1 mark link to 24%.

practice.stem: Lin's gift shop in Ipoh, Malaysia, adds a mark-up of 40% to the cost of all goods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between mark-up and gross margin.
parts.answer: Mark-up is gross profit as a percentage of cost of sales; gross margin is gross profit as a percentage of revenue (selling price).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Cost of sales for the year was $140,000. Calculate the revenue and gross profit.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Extract from the financial statements of Galle Fort Hotels Ltd for 2025: profit from operations $456,000; finance costs $48,000; equity $2,400,000; 8% loan notes $600,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark capital employed 3,000,000; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why profit from operations, rather than profit for the year, is used to calculate the return on capital employed.
parts.answer: Capital employed includes the loan notes; profit before interest (and tax) is the return earned for all providers of that capital, lenders as well as shareholders.
parts.working: 1 mark profit before interest; 1 mark matches capital including loans.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business sells all its goods at a mark-up of 25% on cost. Its operating expenses are 12% of revenue and it has no other income. What is its profit margin?
A 8%
B 10.67%
C 13%
D 20%
parts.working: A mark-up of 25% gives a gross margin of 25 ÷ 125 = 20%. Profit margin = 20% − 12% = 8%. C (13%) wrongly subtracts 12% from the mark-up; D is the gross margin.

practice.stem:
Kestrel Packaging Ltd, Durban, South Africa:
                                2024 $      2025 $
Revenue                      1,500,000   2,100,000
Profit from operations         180,000     210,000
Capital employed             1,200,000   1,750,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for each year: (i) the profit from operations margin (ii) the asset turnover (revenue ÷ capital employed), to two decimal places (iii) the return on capital employed.
parts.working: 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show how the margin and asset turnover combine to give the return on capital employed, and explain why ROCE fell although profit rose.
parts.answer: ROCE = margin × asset turnover: 12% × 1.25 = 15%; 10% × 1.20 = 12%. Profit rose by $30,000 but capital employed rose by $550,000 and each $ of revenue earned less profit, so the return on the extra capital was low.
parts.working: 1 mark relationship shown; 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem:
Farhan sells mobile phone accessories in Rawalpindi.
                          2024 $      2025 $
Revenue                  820,000     910,000
Gross profit             295,200     291,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin for each year.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit Farhan would have made in 2025 if the 2024 gross margin had been maintained, and the shortfall.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest three possible reasons for the fall in gross margin.
parts.answer: Higher purchase prices not passed on; price cuts or discounts to increase sales (revenue rose 11%); change in sales mix towards lower-margin goods; loss or theft of inventory; loss of bulk discounts; closing inventory written down.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three reasons.

practice.stem:
Café Saigon, Ho Chi Minh City:
                            2024 $      2025 $
Revenue                    600,000     640,000
Gross profit               210,000     224,000
Wages                       90,000     115,200
Rent                        36,000      38,400
Advertising                 12,000      25,600
Other expenses              30,000      32,000
Profit for the year         42,000      12,800

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin, each expense as a percentage of revenue and the profit margin for both years.
parts.answer:
Gross margin: 35% both years.
Wages: 15% → 18%
Rent: 6% → 6%
Advertising: 2% → 4%
Other expenses: 5% → 5%
Profit margin: 42,000 ÷ 600,000 = 7% → 12,800 ÷ 640,000 = 2%
parts.working: 1 mark gross margin; 1 mark each expense ratio pair; 1 mark profit margins.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the main causes of the fall in the profit margin and comment on whether the extra advertising was worthwhile.
parts.answer: Gross margin is unchanged, so the fall is in expenses: wages up from 15% to 18% and advertising doubled from 2% to 4% of revenue. Revenue rose only $40,000, adding $14,000 of gross profit, but advertising rose by $13,600 — it barely paid for itself.
parts.working: 1 mark identifies wages and advertising; 1 mark judgement on advertising with figures.

practice.stem: Sapphire Glass plc, for the year ended 31 March 2026: revenue $3,200,000; gross profit $1,120,000; distribution costs $310,000; administrative expenses $266,000; finance costs $96,000; tax $112,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate: (i) the gross margin (ii) the profit from operations margin (iii) the margin based on profit for the year.
parts.working: 1 mark (i); 1 mark profit from operations and (ii); 1 mark profit for the year; 1 mark (iii).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a potential lender would focus on the profit from operations margin rather than the profit for the year margin.
parts.answer: Profit from operations is before interest and tax, so it shows the profit available to pay interest; the profit for the year depends on how the company is financed (existing interest) and on tax.
parts.working: 1 mark before interest; 1 mark independent of financing/ability to pay interest.

practice.stem: Noor Cosmetics, Islamabad, had a gross margin of 40% and a profit from operations margin of 15% for the year. Its operating expenses were Rs 72,000. There was no other income.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revenue for the year.
parts.working: Gross profit − expenses = profit from operations: 0.40R − 72,000 = 0.15R (M1); 0.25R = 72,000 (M1); R = Rs 288,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mark-up, to two decimal places.
parts.working: Gross profit 115,200 ÷ cost of sales 172,800 × 100 (M1) = 66.67% (A1).

practice.stem: Ruta Furniture, Vilnius, Lithuania, has capital employed of $850,000. The owner wants a return on capital employed of 18% next year. Operating expenses are fixed at $197,000 and the gross margin is 35%. This year's revenue was $880,000. The business has no loans.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit from operations needed to achieve the target return.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revenue needed to achieve this profit.
parts.working: 1 mark adding expenses; 1 mark dividing by 35%; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in revenue needed, to two decimal places, and comment on whether the target is realistic.
parts.answer: (1,000,000 − 880,000) ÷ 880,000 × 100 = 13.64%. A 13.64% rise in one year needs strong demand or price rises; price rises may reduce the margin; costs are unlikely to stay fixed. Possible only with a clear sales plan.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark answer; 1 mark comment.

practice.stem:
Hira makes and sells handmade notebooks in Lahore at $15 each; each costs $9 to make. She sells 24,000 a year and her operating expenses are $96,000.
Option A: cut the price to $13.50; sales would rise to 34,000; delivery costs would add $6,000 to expenses.
Option B: keep the price; spend an extra $18,000 on advertising; sales would rise to 28,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revenue, gross profit, gross margin, profit and profit margin (to two decimal places) at present and under each option.
parts.answer:
Current: revenue 360,000; gross profit 144,000 (40.00%); profit 48,000 (13.33%)
A: revenue 459,000; gross profit 153,000 (33.33%); profit 51,000 (11.11%)
B: revenue 420,000; gross profit 168,000 (40.00%); profit 54,000 (12.86%)
parts.working: 2 marks for each column (deduct 1 per error).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Hira which option to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Option B gives the highest profit ($54,000) and keeps the 40% gross margin; Option A raises revenue most but the price cut lowers gross margin to 33.33% and profit to $51,000. Both beat the present $48,000. Risks: B depends on advertising working; A may start a price war. Decision: B.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison of profits; 1 mark risk/other factor; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Two similar companies run warehouses near Jebel Ali, Dubai.
Alpha Logistics Ltd: profit from operations $420,000; capital employed $3,500,000. During the year Alpha revalued its property upwards by $1,000,000, which increased the year's depreciation by $25,000.
Beta Storage Ltd: profit from operations $380,000; capital employed $2,000,000. Its property is at historical cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed for each company, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recalculate Alpha's return on capital employed as if the property had not been revalued.
parts.working: 1 mark capital employed; 1 mark profit; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether Beta is really more profitable than Alpha.
parts.answer: Most of the gap is caused by the revaluation, which raises capital employed and depreciation. On a like-for-like basis Alpha earns 17.80% against Beta's 19.00%, so Beta is still slightly better, but the difference is small. Beta's assets at old historical cost may also flatter its ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark revaluation distorts; 1 mark comparison of adjusted figures; 1 mark conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which user of a business's financial statements is most interested in its liquid (acid test) ratio?
A A supplier deciding whether to offer 30 days' credit
B A shareholder comparing dividend yields
C The tax authority checking the profit figure
D A competitor comparing gross margins
parts.answer: A A supplier deciding whether to offer 30 days' credit
parts.working: A trade supplier wants to know whether the business can pay its short-term debts on time, which the liquid ratio measures. Shareholders are more interested in returns and dividends.

practice.stem: Bilal owns Sunrise Poultry Farm near Sheikhupura. He employs a farm manager and twelve workers and wants to borrow money from a bank to build a new shed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two internal users of the financial statements of Sunrise Poultry Farm.
parts.answer: The owner (Bilal) and the farm manager/employees.
parts.working: 1 mark each: owner; managers; employees (internal).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the bank would look for in the financial statements before lending to the farm.
parts.answer: Whether the farm makes enough profit and cash to pay interest and repay the loan, and what assets could be offered as security.
parts.working: 1 mark profitability/cash flow to repay; 1 mark security/gearing/existing debts.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the farm's employees are interested in its financial statements.
parts.answer: To judge job security and whether the farm can afford pay rises.
parts.working: 1 mark job security/continuity; 1 mark ability to pay wages/pay rises/bonuses.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which user of a business's financial statements is likely to be most interested in how long the business takes to pay for goods bought on credit?
A a supplier deciding whether to offer credit
B an employee asking for a pay rise
C the tax authority
D a bank deciding on a ten-year mortgage on the premises
parts.answer: A a supplier deciding whether to offer credit
parts.working: The trade payables payment period shows how quickly suppliers are paid, which matters most to a supplier offering credit. A bank lending for ten years is more concerned with long-term profitability, gearing and security.

practice.stem: Rahim runs a builders' merchant in Multan as a sole trader. He has a bank loan, buys from 30 suppliers on credit and employs a manager and six staff.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two external users of the financial statements of Rahim Builders' Merchants and explain what information each would want.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. Bank – ability to repay loan and interest (profit, cash, security of assets, gearing). Suppliers – ability to pay on time (liquidity, payables period). Tax authority – profit to calculate tax. Customers – continuity of supply. Potential partner/investor – profitability and return.
parts.working: 1 mark each user; 1 mark each for relevant information linked to that user's purpose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one internal user and explain one way in which this user would use the financial statements.
parts.answer: The owner (Rahim) – to measure profit and decide whether to expand, cut costs or change prices; or the manager – to control costs against budgets.
parts.working: 1 mark user; 1 mark use.

practice.stem: Lyallpur Spinning Ltd is a private limited company in Faisalabad with 450 employees.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the employees of Lyallpur Spinning Ltd are interested in the company's financial statements.
parts.answer: To judge job security (is the company profitable and able to pay its debts?) and to judge whether the company can afford pay rises or bonuses.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the government (tax authority) is interested in the company's financial statements.
parts.answer: To calculate the corporation tax due on the company's profits and to check that the tax returns are accurate; also for national statistics.
parts.working: 1 mark for tax assessment; 1 mark for check/statistics.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a potential investor would find the latest statement of financial position on its own insufficient.
parts.answer: It shows the position at one date only and historical values; the investor also needs profit trends, cash flows, dividends and future prospects.
parts.working: 1 mark one date/historical; 1 mark needs other information.

practice.stem: Maria owns a café in Lima, Peru, employs a manager and rents the premises.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between internal users and external users of financial statements.
parts.answer: Internal users work within the business and run it (owners who manage it, managers); external users are outside the business (lenders, suppliers, customers, government, investors).
parts.working: 1 mark each definition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of each type of user for a café owned by a sole trader.
parts.answer: Internal: the owner, the café manager. External: the bank, suppliers of food and drink, the tax authority, the landlord, customers.
parts.working: 1 mark each, two internal and two external.

practice.stem: A large hospital in Kampala, Uganda, is choosing a supplier of surgical gloves for a five-year contract. One possible supplier is Delta Medical Supplies Ltd.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the hospital is interested in the financial statements of Delta Medical Supplies.
parts.answer: A five-year contract relies on Delta continuing to trade; if Delta fails, supplies of essential items stop and the hospital must find a new supplier at short notice.
parts.working: 1 mark continuity of supply; 1 mark consequence for the hospital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two ratios the hospital should examine and explain why each is relevant.
parts.answer: Current/liquid ratio – can Delta pay its debts and keep trading? Profit margin/ROCE – is Delta profitable enough to survive? Gearing – is it at risk from high borrowing? Trade payables days – is Delta paying its own suppliers late (sign of cash problems)?
parts.working: 1 mark each ratio; 1 mark each explanation (two ratios).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about users of financial statements are correct?
1 A bank considering an overdraft will examine the liquid (acid test) ratio.
2 An employee concerned about job security will be interested in the business's profitability.
3 The tax authority uses the financial statements when assessing tax due on profits.
4 A competitor has a legal right to inspect a sole trader's ledger accounts.
A 1 and 2 only
B 1, 2 and 3 only
C 2 and 4 only
D 1, 2, 3 and 4
parts.answer: B 1, 2 and 3 only
parts.working: Statements 1–3 are correct. A sole trader's records are private; a competitor has no right to inspect them, so statement 4 is wrong and options C and D are wrong.

practice.stem: Indus Ceramics plc is a public limited company with 12,000 shareholders, most of whom take no part in running the business.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the information needs of the shareholders and the directors of Indus Ceramics plc.
parts.answer: Shareholders want returns: dividends, EPS, share price, and evidence that directors are managing the company well (stewardship). Directors need detailed information for planning and control: costs by product, budgets, cash forecasts, performance of departments, to make decisions.
parts.working: 2 marks shareholders' needs explained; 2 marks directors' needs explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the directors have access to more detailed information than the shareholders.
parts.answer: Directors run the company and receive internal management accounts; published accounts are summarised and some information is commercially sensitive, so it is not released to outsiders (including competitors).
parts.working: 1 mark internal management information; 1 mark summarised/confidential published accounts.

practice.stem: Users of financial statements need information that is useful to them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the meaning of relevance, reliability (faithful representation), comparability and understandability as qualities of useful financial information.
parts.answer: Relevance: information that can affect users' decisions (timely, helps predict/confirm). Reliability: free from material error and bias, complete, a faithful picture. Comparability: prepared consistently so it can be compared over time and with other businesses. Understandability: presented clearly so that a user with reasonable knowledge can understand it.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how relevance and reliability may conflict when a business prepares its financial statements.
parts.answer: Information is most relevant when it is up to date, but producing it quickly may mean using estimates that are less reliable; waiting to check figures improves reliability but makes them less timely.
parts.working: 1 mark timeliness vs accuracy; 1 mark example/explanation.

practice.stem: Thar Coal Mining Ltd operates a large open-cast mine in Sindh and is the main employer in the area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the local community is interested in the financial statements of Thar Coal Mining Ltd.
parts.answer: Employment and income in the area depend on the mine continuing; the community also wants to know whether the company can pay for land restoration and environmental damage (provisions).
parts.working: 1 mark jobs/local economy; 1 mark environmental obligations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the government is interested in the financial statements of Thar Coal Mining Ltd, other than for taxation.
parts.answer: To monitor a strategically important industry (energy supply), to decide on grants or subsidies, to check compliance with regulations and licence conditions, for national statistics.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two limitations of the published financial statements for these users.
parts.answer: They show financial information only, not environmental or social effects; they are historical and summarised; they do not show the company's future plans in detail.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Ravi Foods, a supermarket chain in Lahore, has asked a supplier, Sunflower Oils Ltd, to increase its credit period from 30 to 60 days and to double its credit limit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Sunflower Oils Ltd would want to see the financial statements of Ravi Foods before agreeing to the request.
parts.answer: Sunflower Oils will be owed money for 60 days; it needs evidence that Ravi Foods can pay (liquidity, cash) and is profitable enough to continue trading, otherwise it risks an irrecoverable debt.
parts.working: 1 mark risk of non-payment; 1 mark need to judge ability to pay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other sources of information Sunflower Oils could use before deciding.
parts.answer: Trade references from other suppliers; bank reference; credit rating agency report; Ravi's payment record with Sunflower so far; visits to the premises.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one limitation of using Ravi Foods' financial statements for this decision.
parts.answer: They may be out of date (prepared months after the year end) and show the position on one day, which may have been window dressed; they do not show what will happen in the next 60 days.
parts.working: 1 mark limitation; 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem: Atlas Shipping plc is financed by equity of $120 million and 7% loan notes of $60 million. The directors plan to borrow a further $40 million to buy two new ships, which are expected to earn a return of 11% a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss why the shareholders and the loan note holders of Atlas Shipping plc may take different views of the company's plan to borrow a further $40 million.
parts.answer:
Shareholders: higher gearing can raise EPS and returns if the return on the new investment exceeds the interest rate; no dilution of control. But more risk: interest must be paid before dividends, profits become more volatile.
Loan note holders: their security falls as more debt ranks alongside or ahead of them; interest cover falls; higher risk of default; they may want covenants or higher interest. They do not share in extra profits.
Conclusion: shareholders may welcome it if expected returns are high; lenders are likely to oppose it.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for shareholders' view (both sides); up to 3 marks for lenders' view; maximum 6. A conclusion or comparison is needed for full marks.

practice.stem:
The workers' union at Kohinoor Footwear Ltd, Sialkot, is studying the company's published statements:
                                  2024        2025
Revenue ($)                  4,200,000   4,800,000
Wages ($)                    1,020,000   1,080,000
Number of employees                125         120
Profit for the year ($)        504,000     640,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for each year: (i) profit for the year per employee (ii) wages as a percentage of revenue, to two decimal places (iii) average wage per employee.
parts.working: 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The union asks for an 8% pay rise for all employees for 2026. Evaluate whether the financial statements support this claim.
parts.answer:
For: profit up 27% (504,000 → 640,000) and profit per employee up from $4,032 to $5,333; wages fell from 24.29% to 22.50% of revenue. Cost of an 8% rise = 1,080,000 × 8% = $86,400, well within the profit increase of $136,000.
Against: average wage already rose 10.3%; past profit does not guarantee future profit; the company may need profit for investment, loan repayment or dividends; liquidity not shown.
Judgement: the figures broadly support a rise, perhaps linked to productivity.
parts.working: 1 mark use of figures for; 1 mark cost of rise calculated ($86,400); 1 mark point against; 1 mark judgement.

practice.stem: A finance student in Singapore is preparing for a debate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: "Published financial statements meet the needs of all users." Discuss this statement.
parts.answer:
Support: statements follow IFRS, are audited, consistent and comparable; they give useful common information — profit, assets, liabilities, cash flows — that most users need; notes add detail.
Against: they are general-purpose and cannot meet every user's specific need; historical, published months after the year end; summarised (no product or branch detail for managers); based on historical cost so may not show current values; ignore non-financial factors (staff skills, customer loyalty, environmental impact); some users (e.g. employees, local community) want information not given; complex to understand for non-specialists; may be window dressed.
Conclusion: they meet the basic needs of investors and lenders reasonably well, but other users need extra information (management accounts, forecasts, reports).
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for points in support; up to 4 marks for limitations linked to particular users; 1 mark for reasoned conclusion. Maximum 8.

practice.stem:
Kandy Spice Traders, Sri Lanka, provides the following at 31 March 2026:
                                           $
Inventory                             38,600
Trade receivables                     24,150
Other receivables (prepayments)        1,250
Cash in hand                             830
Trade payables                        29,400
Other payables (accruals)              2,100
Bank overdraft                         6,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate, to two decimal places: (i) the current ratio (ii) the liquid (acid test) ratio.
parts.working: Each ratio: 1 mark correct totals/method, 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the liquidity of the business.
parts.answer: The current ratio is below the commonly quoted 2 : 1 and the liquid ratio is well below 1 : 1, so the business could not pay its current liabilities from liquid assets if they fell due now; it relies on selling inventory and on the overdraft.
parts.working: 1 mark comment on each ratio with figure.

practice.stem: Hassan is studying two liquidity ratios for his clothing business in Bahawalpur.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the current ratio and the liquid (acid test) ratio.
parts.answer: The current ratio compares all current assets with current liabilities. The liquid ratio leaves out inventory, comparing only assets that are cash or quickly turned into cash with current liabilities.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why inventory is excluded from the liquid ratio.
parts.answer: Inventory must first be sold (often on credit) and the money collected before it can pay debts; this takes time and its value may be uncertain (obsolete or slow-moving goods).
parts.working: 1 mark not immediately convertible; 1 mark uncertainty of value/time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a liquid ratio well above 1 : 1 is not necessarily a good sign.
parts.answer: Too much money is tied up in cash and receivables that earn little return; large receivables may mean poor credit control and risk of irrecoverable debts.
parts.working: 1 mark idle funds/low return; 1 mark poor credit control.

practice.stem: Al-Hamra Furniture, Muscat, Oman, has these current assets and liabilities at 31 December 2025: inventory $84,000; trade receivables $61,500; bank $22,500; trade payables $41,000; other payables $3,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the working capital and the current ratio (to two decimal places).
parts.working: 1 mark current assets total; 1 mark working capital; 1 mark ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages to the business of holding this level of working capital.
parts.answer: Money tied up in inventory and receivables earns no return and could be invested or used to repay borrowing; large inventory risks obsolescence, damage and storage costs; high receivables increase the risk of irrecoverable debts; cash held idle loses value through inflation.
parts.working: 2 marks per disadvantage explained (identify + consequence).

practice.stem: Zarina Pharmacy, Tashkent, Uzbekistan, sells mainly for cash. At 30 September 2026: inventory $52,000; trade receivables $9,800; bank $3,400; trade payables $31,600; other payables $1,400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the liquid (acid test) ratio, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what this ratio shows and whether the pharmacy is necessarily at risk.
parts.answer: For every $1 of current liabilities there is only $0.40 of liquid assets, so the pharmacy cannot meet its short-term debts without selling inventory. Not necessarily at risk: most of its sales are for cash and its inventory sells quickly, so cash comes in daily before suppliers must be paid.
parts.working: 1 mark interpretation with figure; 1 mark risk; 1 mark cash sales / fast-moving inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business has current assets of $80,000 and current liabilities of $40,000. It then pays a trade payable $10,000 by cheque from a positive bank balance. What is the new current ratio?
A 2.33 : 1
B 2.00 : 1
C 1.75 : 1
D 1.67 : 1
parts.working: Both current assets and current liabilities fall by 10,000: 70,000 : 30,000 = 2.33 : 1. 1.75 : 1 reduces only the current assets.

practice.stem:
Grace runs a hardware store in Accra. At 31 December 2025:
                         $
Inventory           46,000
Trade receivables   31,500
Prepayments          2,500
Cash in hand         1,200
Trade payables      38,600
Accrued expenses     2,800
Bank overdraft       8,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate, to two decimal places: (i) the current ratio, (ii) the liquid (acid test) ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the liquidity of the business and suggest two ways to improve the liquid ratio.
parts.answer: The liquid ratio is well below 1 : 1, so Grace cannot pay her current liabilities without selling inventory; she relies on an overdraft. She could collect debts faster, reduce inventory purchases, introduce capital or replace the overdraft with a long-term loan.
parts.working: Comment: 1 mark current ratio below a typical 2 : 1 / heavy reliance on inventory; 1 mark liquid ratio below 1 : 1 so difficulty paying debts as they fall due. Ways: 1 mark each for any two of: chase receivables/offer cash discounts; sell surplus inventory for cash; owner introduces cash; convert overdraft to long-term loan; sell unused non-current assets.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business has a current ratio of 1.5 : 1 and a liquid (acid test) ratio of 1.0 : 1. It buys inventory on credit. What is the effect on the two ratios?
A current ratio increases; liquid ratio no change
B current ratio decreases; liquid ratio decreases
C current ratio no change; liquid ratio decreases
D current ratio decreases; liquid ratio no change
parts.answer: B current ratio decreases; liquid ratio decreases
parts.working: Current assets and current liabilities rise by the same amount; because the current ratio is above 1 it moves towards 1, so it falls. Liquid assets are unchanged but current liabilities rise, so the liquid ratio falls. D forgets that current liabilities rise in the liquid ratio.

practice.stem:
Fietsen van Dijk, a bicycle retailer in Utrecht, Netherlands:
At 31 December                2024 $      2025 $
Inventory                     40,000      62,000
Trade receivables             35,000      41,000
Bank                           8,000           –
Trade payables                30,000      44,000
Other payables                 2,000       3,000
Bank overdraft                     –       7,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and the liquid (acid test) ratio for each year, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the change in liquidity between 2024 and 2025.
parts.answer: Both ratios have fallen. The liquid ratio has dropped below 1 : 1, so liquid assets no longer cover current liabilities. The bank balance has turned into an overdraft and trade payables have risen by $14,000, while inventory has risen by $22,000 — money is tied up in inventory. The business may struggle to pay suppliers on time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three relevant points using figures.

practice.stem:
Nile Office Supplies, Cairo, Egypt, has current assets of $60,000 (including inventory of $25,000) and current liabilities of $30,000. Four possible transactions are:
(i) inventory costing $4,000 is sold for $6,000 cash
(ii) $5,000 is paid to trade payables
(iii) a computer is bought for $8,000, paid from the bank
(iv) a five-year bank loan of $10,000 is received.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and the liquid (acid test) ratio before any of the transactions, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate both ratios, to two decimal places, after transaction (i) and after transaction (ii). Treat each transaction separately.
parts.working: (i) CA 60,000 − 4,000 + 6,000 = 62,000, inventory 21,000; (ii) CA and CL both fall by 5,000. 1 mark each ratio.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate both ratios, to two decimal places, after transaction (iii) and after transaction (iv). Treat each transaction separately.
parts.working: (iii) CA falls by 8,000 (the computer is a non-current asset); (iv) CA rises by 10,000, CL unchanged (the loan is non-current). 1 mark each ratio.

practice.stem:
Extracts from the statements of financial position of two companies ($000):
                           FreshMart     Karakoram
                        supermarkets   Engineering
Inventory                      1,800           900
Trade receivables                100         1,600
Cash and bank                    400           200
Trade payables                 3,100         1,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and the liquid (acid test) ratio for each business, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why FreshMart can operate safely with much lower liquidity ratios than Karakoram Engineering.
parts.answer: FreshMart sells for cash, so it has almost no receivables and cash comes in every day. Its inventory sells within days. It buys on credit and pays suppliers after it has sold the goods. Karakoram sells on credit, holds raw materials and work in progress for long periods and must wait for customers to pay, so it needs a larger cushion.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four points; must compare the two businesses for full marks.

practice.stem:
Kwame's printing business in Accra has current assets of $48,000 (including inventory $30,000) and current liabilities of $40,000 (including a bank overdraft of $15,000). He is considering:
A converting the overdraft into a five-year bank loan
B selling a spare delivery van for $9,000 cash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and the liquid (acid test) ratio at present, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate both ratios, to two decimal places, under each proposal.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Kwame which proposal will do more to improve liquidity. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Proposal A improves both ratios more, and removes the risk of the bank demanding repayment of the overdraft; but it adds a long-term commitment with interest. Proposal B brings in real cash but is a one-off and the van may be needed. Decision with reason, e.g. A.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison using figures; 1 mark justified decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business has a current ratio of 2.4 : 1 and a liquid (acid test) ratio of 1.5 : 1. Its current liabilities are $36,000. What is the value of its inventory?
A $32,400
B $54,000
C $86,400
D $18,000
parts.working: Current assets = 2.4 × 36,000 = 86,400; liquid assets = 1.5 × 36,000 = 54,000; inventory = 86,400 − 54,000 = $32,400. B is the liquid assets and C the total current assets.

practice.stem: Lotus Garden Centre, Hanoi, Vietnam, has a current ratio of 1.8 : 1 and a liquid (acid test) ratio of 0.9 : 1. Its inventory is $45,000. Its only liquid assets are trade receivables and cash, and trade receivables are four times the cash balance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current liabilities and the total current assets.
parts.answer: Inventory = (1.8 − 0.9) × current liabilities, so current liabilities = 45,000 ÷ 0.9 = $50,000. Current assets = 1.8 × 50,000 = $90,000.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cash balance and the trade receivables.
parts.answer: Liquid assets = 0.9 × 50,000 = 45,000 = receivables + cash = 5 × cash, so cash = $9,000 and trade receivables = $36,000.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Credit sales for the year were $292,000. Calculate the trade receivables turnover in days.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The owner plans to use all the cash to pay trade payables. Calculate both ratios after the payment and comment on the result.
parts.answer: Current 81,000 : 41,000 = 1.98 : 1; liquid 36,000 : 41,000 = 0.88 : 1. The current ratio improves but the liquid ratio falls and there is no cash left to pay day-to-day expenses.
parts.working: 1 mark each ratio; 1 mark comment.

practice.stem:
Hilal Steel Ltd has been asked by a new customer, Orion Hardware, Ankara, Turkey, for 60 days' credit. Orion's ratios for the last two years were:
                                2023        2024
Current ratio               2.10 : 1    1.60 : 1
Liquid ratio                1.20 : 1    0.80 : 1
Trade payables (days)             34          48
Orion's statement of financial position at 31 December 2025 showed: inventory $96,000; trade receivables $41,000; cash $2,000; trade payables $112,000; bank overdraft $14,000. Credit purchases for 2025 were $576,000. Revenue has grown each year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for 2025: (i) the current ratio (ii) the liquid (acid test) ratio, both to two decimal places (iii) the trade payables turnover, to the nearest whole day.
parts.working: 1 mark each for (i) and (ii); 2 marks for (iii) (method, answer).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Hilal Steel whether to give Orion Hardware a 60-day credit period. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Against: both ratios have fallen every year (current 2.10 → 1.10, liquid 1.20 → 0.34); Orion now has an overdraft and very little cash; it is taking 71 days to pay suppliers compared with 34 days in 2023, so it already pays late — a 60-day term may become 90+ days; risk of irrecoverable debt.
For: revenue is growing, so it may become a valuable customer; inventory is high and could be sold; new sales for Hilal Steel.
Other: obtain trade references, set a low credit limit, ask for security, offer shorter terms or cash on delivery.
Decision: do not give 60 days' credit at present, or give a small credit limit on 30 days with close monitoring.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for points against using figures; up to 2 marks for points for; 1 mark for other factors/conditions; 1 mark for clear decision.

practice.stem:
Sadia's online kitchenware business in Islamabad has grown quickly:
                            2024 $      2025 $
Revenue                    400,000     640,000
Inventory                   50,000      98,000
Trade receivables           40,000      92,000
Bank (overdraft)            12,000    (38,000)
Trade payables              35,000      71,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and the liquid (acid test) ratio for each year, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by overtrading and why Sadia's business shows signs of it.
parts.answer: Overtrading is expanding sales faster than the working capital available can support. Revenue rose by 60% but inventory almost doubled and receivables more than doubled, the bank balance became an overdraft and payables doubled; liquidity ratios have fallen sharply.
parts.working: 1 mark definition; 2 marks evidence from figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions Sadia could take to improve liquidity without stopping growth.
parts.answer: Introduce long-term finance (bank loan or new capital) to fund working capital; tighten credit control or offer cash discounts; reduce inventory levels; use factoring.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Grace is using ratio analysis to review her grocery business in Kingston, Jamaica.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three limitations of ratio analysis.
parts.answer: Any three of: based on historical information; ignores inflation; different accounting policies between businesses; year-end figures may not be typical (seasonal, window dressing); ignores non-financial factors; ratios show symptoms not causes; different definitions of ratios; businesses of different size or industry are hard to compare.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one of the limitations you have stated.
parts.answer: e.g. Ratios use past figures; conditions such as competition or costs may change, so past ratios may not predict future performance.
parts.working: 1 mark statement; 1 mark consequence for users.

practice.stem: A student is comparing the financial statements of businesses in Doha, Qatar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why comparing the ratios of a jeweller with those of a supermarket is of limited use.
parts.answer: Businesses in different industries have very different typical ratios: a jeweller has a high gross margin and slow inventory turnover, a supermarket a low margin and fast turnover; differences reflect the industry, not efficiency.
parts.working: 1 mark different industries have different norms; 1 mark example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the use of historical cost can make ratios misleading.
parts.answer: Assets bought long ago are shown at old cost less depreciation, so capital employed is understated and ROCE overstated compared with a business with new assets; values do not reflect current prices.
parts.working: 1 mark old values; 1 mark effect on ratio.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why ratios on their own do not explain why performance has changed.
parts.answer: Ratios show what has changed (e.g. margin fell) but not the cause; further investigation of the underlying records and business events is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark symptoms not causes; 1 mark need for further investigation.

practice.stem: On 30 June 2026 Diaz Auto Parts, Santiago, Chile, had current assets of $90,000 (including bank $34,000) and current liabilities of $60,000. On 30 June, the last day of its financial year, it paid $30,000 to suppliers from the bank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by window dressing.
parts.answer: Arranging transactions just before the year end so that the financial statements look better than the normal position, e.g. paying suppliers or delaying purchases to improve ratios.
parts.working: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio before and after the payment.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the ratio after the payment may mislead a lender.
parts.answer: The improvement is temporary; the business has the same net working capital ($30,000) and less cash; in the new year it will buy on credit again and the ratio will fall back.
parts.working: 1 mark same working capital/less cash; 1 mark temporary.

practice.stem: Tomasz calculates that his bakery in Kraków, Poland, had a gross margin of 46% in 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a single year's ratio is of limited use on its own.
parts.answer: A ratio has no meaning unless it is compared with something: one figure cannot show whether performance is good or bad, improving or getting worse.
parts.working: 1 mark need comparison; 1 mark cannot judge trend/standard.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three bases with which Tomasz could compare his ratios.
parts.answer: Previous years of the same business (trends); other businesses in the same industry; industry averages; budgeted or target ratios.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Ali & Sons, Peshawar, had profit from operations of $96,000 for 2025. Capital employed was $520,000 at the start of the year and $680,000 at the end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed using (i) closing capital employed (ii) average capital employed. Give answers to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark (i); 1 mark average; 1 mark (ii).

parts.label: b
