parts.text: Explain why ratios must be calculated in the same way when businesses or years are compared.
parts.answer: Different definitions give different results (here 14.12% vs 16.00%), so differences could come from the method rather than real performance.
parts.working: 1 mark different results; 1 mark misleading comparison.

practice.stem: Hira owns a shoe retailer with two shops in Karachi. She compares her ratios with those of a large shoe retailer in Madrid that publishes its financial statements online, to decide whether her business is doing well.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three limitations of using ratio analysis to compare the two businesses.
parts.answer: Different accounting policies (e.g. depreciation methods, inventory valuation) make ratios not comparable; historical cost and different inflation and currency conditions in Pakistan and Spain distort figures; ratios ignore non-financial factors such as location, brand and staff skills.
parts.working: For each of three limitations: 1 mark identifying, 1 mark explaining in context. Accept: different policies; different year ends/seasonal timing; historical cost/inflation; different sizes and markets; ratios are based on past data; window dressing at the year end; non-financial factors ignored; no single 'correct' ratio.

practice.stem: Mint Ltd and Sage Ltd, two identical courier companies in Kuala Lumpur, each bought delivery equipment costing $200,000 at the start of the year. Each made a profit before depreciation of $150,000 and has other net assets of $300,000. Mint uses straight-line depreciation at 20% a year; Sage uses reducing balance at 30% a year. Capital employed = other net assets + carrying amount of the equipment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge, profit from operations and return on capital employed (to two decimal places) for each business for the first year.
parts.working: 1 mark each depreciation; 1 mark each profit; 1 mark each ROCE.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what this shows about comparing ratios of different businesses.
parts.answer: The businesses are identical but Mint appears more profitable only because of its depreciation policy; differences in accounting policies distort comparisons, so users must read the notes.
parts.working: 1 mark difference caused by policy; 1 mark need to check policies.

practice.stem: The owner of a shoe shop in Colombo says sales are growing: revenue was $500,000 in 2024 and $540,000 in 2025. General prices rose by 10% over the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in revenue in money terms.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the 2025 revenue in 2024 prices, to the nearest $, and the real percentage change, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark revenue in 2024 prices; 1 mark real change (a fall).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the owner's claim may be misleading.
parts.answer: Prices rose by 10%, so the 8% rise in money revenue is a real fall of about 1.82% — fewer goods were sold. Financial statements and ratios are not adjusted for inflation.
parts.working: 1 mark real fall; 1 mark statements not adjusted for inflation.

practice.stem:
Rana Opticians, Lahore, has two branches. For 2025:
                          Mall $  Old Town $
Revenue                  600,000     400,000
Gross profit             240,000      60,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin of each branch and of the business as a whole.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how ratios calculated from the totals for the whole business could mislead the owner.
parts.answer: The overall 30% looks acceptable but hides a very weak Old Town branch earning only 15%; totals combine different activities, so the owner may not see where the problem is and fail to act (e.g. investigate pricing or theft at Old Town).
parts.working: 1 mark averages hide differences; 1 mark using figures; 1 mark consequence for decisions.

practice.stem: An investor in Mauritius is considering buying a beach hotel. The hotel's ratios for the last three years are strong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify four non-financial factors that ratio analysis would not reveal about the hotel.
parts.answer: Any four: customer satisfaction and online reviews; quality and morale of staff; location and access; reputation/brand; condition of the building beyond its carrying amount; environmental and safety record; new competitors opening nearby; quality of management.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these factors are important to the buyer.
parts.answer: They affect future revenue and costs; for example poor reviews or a new competitor could reduce future occupancy and profit even though current ratios look good.
parts.working: 1 mark link to future performance; 1 mark example.

practice.stem: Ocean Fresh Seafoods, Gwadar, had revenue of $1,250,000 in 2025 and a profit for the year of $145,000. This profit included a profit of $60,000 on the sale of a plot of land.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit margin for 2025 (i) as reported (ii) excluding the profit on disposal. Give answers to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the trend in the profit margin, given that it was 7.50% in 2024.
parts.answer: The reported margin suggests a rise from 7.50% to 11.60%, but the underlying margin fell to 6.80%; the improvement comes from a one-off gain that will not be repeated.
parts.working: 1 mark underlying fall; 1 mark one-off item explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why one-off items limit the usefulness of ratio analysis.
parts.answer: They distort the year's figures, so trends and comparisons are misleading unless the item is identified and removed; users may not find them if the statements are summarised.
parts.working: 1 mark distort trends; 1 mark need adjustment.

practice.stem: An investor in Johannesburg is reading the published financial statements of a company listed on the stock exchange.

parts.label: a
parts.text: "Ratio analysis tells a potential investor everything she needs to know before buying shares in a company." Discuss this statement.
parts.answer:
Usefulness: ratios summarise large amounts of data; allow comparison over time and with other companies; investment ratios (EPS, P/E, dividend yield and cover) and gearing give direct information about returns and risk; profitability and liquidity show strength.
Limitations: historical; affected by accounting policies, window dressing and one-off items; ignore inflation; year-end may be unrepresentative; differences in size and industry; ignore non-financial factors (management quality, market position, innovation, economic and political conditions); share price reflects expectations not in the statements; ratios show symptoms not causes.
Conclusion: useful starting point, but the investor also needs forecasts, directors' reports, market information and non-financial factors.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for uses; up to 4 marks for limitations explained; 1 mark for conclusion. Maximum 8.

practice.stem:
Two supermarket companies in Nairobi each have revenue of $1,500,000 and profit of $300,000 before premises costs.
Leaseway Ltd rents its premises for $90,000 a year; its capital employed is $800,000.
Ownhome Ltd owns its premises (carrying amount $1,200,000, depreciation $30,000 a year); its capital employed is $2,000,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit from operations, the profit from operations margin and the return on capital employed for each company, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each profit; 1 mark each pair of ratios.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the ratios give a misleading picture of which company is better managed.
parts.answer: The trading performance is identical; the difference arises only because Leaseway rents premises (rent expense, no asset) while Ownhome owns them (depreciation, large asset in capital employed). Leaseway looks better on ROCE, Ownhome on margin. Different ways of financing and holding assets distort comparisons; Ownhome also gains from any rise in property value, which the ratios ignore.
parts.working: 1 mark identical trading; 1 mark explanation of rent vs ownership; 1 mark each ratio affected differently; 1 mark further point.

practice.stem: Bilal runs an electrical shop in Sukkur as a sole trader. Revenue $900,000; profit for the year $108,000. He takes no salary. A competitor, Zest Electricals Ltd, had revenue of $950,000 and profit from operations of $76,000 after paying its managing director a salary of $40,000. Bilal says his business is more profitable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit margin of each business, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recalculate Bilal's profit margin after charging a notional salary equal to that paid to Zest's director.
parts.working: 1 mark adjusted profit; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate Bilal's claim that his business is more profitable than Zest Ltd.
parts.answer: On reported figures Bilal's margin is 4 points higher, but a sole trader's profit includes the reward for the owner's work; after a $40,000 salary his margin falls to 7.56%, below Zest's 8.00%. His claim is not supported; other differences (rent, size, accounting policies) should also be checked.
parts.working: 1 mark reported comparison; 1 mark adjusted comparison; 1 mark judgement.

practice.stem: Pearl River Bakeries Ltd, Guangzhou, China, had revenue of $2,000,000 in 2025 and a profit from operations margin of 12%. Capital employed is $1,500,000. A large competitor has opened nearby; the directors forecast that in 2026 revenue will fall by 15% and the margin will fall to 10%. Capital employed will not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit from operations and the return on capital employed for 2025 and for the 2026 forecast, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the limitations of using last year's ratios to judge the company's future performance.
parts.answer: Ratios are based on past results; the new competitor will change revenue and margins (forecast ROCE falls by 4.67 points). External factors (economy, exchange rates, costs) change; the forecast itself is an estimate. Ratios ignore management plans to respond. Use with forecasts and market information.
parts.working: 1 mark historical; 1 mark use of figures; 1 mark external changes; 1 mark conclusion.

practice.stem: Rehan sells sports equipment in Sialkot. Budgeted sales are: January $40,000; February $45,000; March $50,000. 20% of sales are for cash. Credit customers pay 60% in the month after the sale and 40% two months after the sale.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total budgeted cash receipts from sales for March.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the receipts for March are different from the sales for March.
parts.answer: Most sales are on credit, so cash from March credit sales arrives in April and May, while March receipts include cash from January and February credit sales.
parts.working: 1 mark: timing difference due to credit terms. 1 mark: receipts include earlier months' sales / exclude part of current month's sales.

practice.stem: A grocery wholesaler in Hyderabad buys all goods on credit. Budgeted purchases: April $30,000; May $36,000; June $42,000. Half of each month's purchases are paid in the following month, taking a 2% cash discount. The other half is paid two months after purchase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted payments to suppliers in June.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage to the wholesaler of taking the cash discount.
parts.answer: Advantage: reduces the cost of purchases / increases profit. Disadvantage: cash leaves the business sooner, reducing liquidity.
parts.working: 1 mark for each.

practice.stem: Hina is opening a small café in Lahore and her bank has asked for a cash budget for the first six months.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a cash budget will be useful to Hina.
parts.answer: It shows in advance any months with a cash shortage, so she can arrange an overdraft or delay spending. It shows months with surplus cash, which can be used to repay debt or invest. (Also: supports the loan application; lets actual cash flows be compared with plan.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per reason (identify 1, explain 1): plan for shortages/arrange finance; plan use of surpluses; support for bank/loan application; control by comparing actual with budget.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items that appear in a budgeted statement of profit or loss but not in a cash budget.
parts.answer: Depreciation; provision for doubtful debts (also: irrecoverable debts, profit or loss on disposal, accruals not yet paid).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two non-cash items.

practice.stem: A furniture showroom in Karachi has budgeted sales of $80,000 in June and $90,000 in July. Wages earned are $24,000 in June and $28,000 in July. Three-quarters of each month's wages are paid in that month and the rest in the next month. Sales staff earn commission of 5% of sales, paid in the month after the sale.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wages paid in July.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the commission paid in July.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The showroom also charges depreciation of $1,800 a month on its vans. Explain how this affects the cash budget.
parts.answer: It does not appear, because depreciation is not a payment of cash; the cash outflow happened when the vans were bought.
parts.working: 1 mark: excluded / no effect. 1 mark: non-cash expense; cash paid when asset bought.

practice.stem:
Bilal owns a stationery shop in Quetta. His bank balance on 1 February is $3,000. Budgeted figures:
                                 Feb $   Mar $
Cash sales                      18,000  20,000
Receipts from credit customers  22,000  25,000
Payments to suppliers           28,000  30,000
Expenses paid                    9,000   9,500
Drawings                         2,000   2,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare Bilal's cash budget for February and March.
parts.answer:
Cash budget                     February   March
Receipts
Cash sales                        18,000  20,000
Receipts from credit customers    22,000  25,000
Total receipts                    40,000  45,000
Payments
Payments to suppliers             28,000  30,000
Expenses                           9,000   9,500

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two actions a business could take if a cash budget showed a deficit.
parts.answer: Arrange a bank overdraft; reduce or delay drawings (also: delay purchases of non-current assets, chase receivables, ask suppliers for more time).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Zara Textiles, Faisalabad, provides the following budgeted information.
Month      Sales $
May         60,000
June        64,000
July        70,000
August      75,000
September   72,000
1 All sales are on credit: 30% of customers pay in the month after sale and 70% two months after sale.
2 Purchases each month are 60% of that month's sales and are paid in the following month.
3 Wages of $9,000 are paid each month.
4 Rent of $18,000 for the quarter is paid in July.
5 Depreciation of $2,000 a month is charged on equipment.
6 A new machine costing $25,000 will be paid for in August.
7 The bank balance on 1 July is $8,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a cash budget for each of the three months July to September, showing the closing balance each month.
parts.answer:
Cash budget                        July    August  September
Receipts
Receipts from credit customers   61,200    65,800     71,500
Total receipts                   61,200    65,800     71,500
Payments

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why depreciation is not included in the cash budget.
parts.answer: Depreciation is a non-cash expense; no money is paid out.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one action the business could take because of the August balance.
parts.answer: Arrange an overdraft for August in advance, or delay the machine payment until September.

practice.stem:
Shifa Clinic, Peshawar, budgets fees of: January $50,000; February $54,000; March $58,000; April $60,000.
1 70% of fees are received in cash in the month of treatment; the rest are paid by insurance companies two months later.
2 Salaries are $30,000 a month.
3 Medical supplies cost 20% of each month's fees and are paid for in the following month.
4 The clinic has an equipment loan of $120,000 on 1 March. It repays $2,500 at the end of each month, plus interest of 1% of the balance outstanding at the start of that month.
5 The bank balance on 1 March is $4,000.

parts.text: Calculate the fees received in March and in April.

parts.label: b

practice.stem:
Sindhri Exports, Multan, sells mangoes overseas. The business is seasonal. Budgeted figures:
                                       May $  June $   July $
Sales receipts                        30,000  95,000  140,000
Purchases of mangoes (paid in month)  60,000  70,000   50,000
Packing and transport                  3,000   9,500   14,000
1 Fixed expenses are $8,000 a month.
2 A bank loan of $50,000 will be received on 1 May and repaid in full on 1 August. Interest at 1.5% per month on the loan is paid at the end of each month.
3 The bank balance on 1 May is an overdraft of $2,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the cash budget for May, June and July.
parts.answer:
Cash budget                May    June     July
Receipts

Bank loan               50,000       –        –
Total receipts          80,000  95,000  140,000
Payments
Purchases of mangoes    60,000  70,000   50,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the bank balance immediately after the loan is repaid on 1 August.

parts.label: c

practice.stem:
Kohistan Ltd expects a bank balance of $15,000 on 1 October 2026. Budgeted information:
                      Oct $    Nov $    Dec $
Operating receipts  120,000  110,000  135,000
Operating payments   95,000  118,000  101,000
1 In October a vehicle with a carrying amount of $6,000 will be sold for $7,500 cash.
2 A dividend of $30,000 will be paid in November.
3 New shares will be issued in December, raising $50,000 in cash.
4 Tax of $22,000 will be paid in December.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the cash budget for October to December.
parts.answer:
Cash budget         October  November  December
Receipts
Operating receipts  120,000   110,000   135,000
Sale of vehicle       7,500         –         –
Share issue               –         –    50,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the profit on disposal of the vehicle does not appear in the cash budget.

practice.stem:
Gul Fans makes table fans. Budgeted sales in units: January 1,200; February 1,400; March 1,500; April 1,800; May 2,000.
1 The selling price is $25 a fan until February and $27 from 1 March. All sales are on credit; customers pay in the month after sale.
2 Each month the business produces the number of fans it will sell in the following month.
3 Materials cost $8 a fan and are paid for in the month after production.
4 Labour costs $6 a fan and is paid in the month of production.
5 Fixed costs paid are $6,000 a month.
6 The bank balance on 1 March is $5,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the receipts from customers for March and April.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the payments for materials and labour in March and April.
parts.answer: Materials: March $12,000, April $14,400. Labour: March $10,800, April $12,000.
parts.working: Materials Mar = Feb production (1,500) × 8 = 12,000; Apr = Mar production (1,800) × 8 = 14,400 (B1 B1). Labour Mar 1,800 × 6 = 10,800; Apr 2,000 × 6 = 12,000 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the closing bank balance for March and for April.

practice.stem:
Karim Electronics, Dubai, has these budgets:
                 Oct $    Nov $    Dec $    Jan $
Sales           80,000   90,000  120,000   70,000
Purchases            –   60,000   50,000        –
Wages earned         –   20,000   24,000   18,000
1 10% of sales are for cash. Of credit sales, 50% are received in the month after sale, after a 2% cash discount; 45% are received two months after sale; 5% become irrecoverable.
2 Purchases are paid in the month after purchase.
3 75% of each month's wages are paid in that month and 25% in the following month.
4 Other expenses are $7,500 a month, including depreciation of $1,500. All other expenses are paid in the month incurred.
5 The bank balance on 1 December is an overdraft of $3,200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted receipts from sales for December and for January.

parts.label: b

parts.answer:

Receipts

Payments

Other expenses (excluding depreciation)     6,000    6,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the business offers a cash discount even though it reduces the amount received.
parts.answer: It encourages customers to pay sooner, improving cash flow and reducing the risk of irrecoverable debts.

practice.stem:
Noor Interiors, Islamabad, has an agreed overdraft limit of $12,000. The bank balance on 1 January 2027 is expected to be $6,000. Budgeted totals are:
                 Jan $   Feb $   Mar $   Apr $
Total receipts  42,000  38,000  51,000  60,000
Total payments  47,500  55,000  49,000  44,000
February payments include $15,000 for new display equipment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted closing bank balance for each month.
parts.answer: January $500; February $(16,500); March $(14,500); April $1,500.
parts.working: M1 running balance; A1 all four correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the months in which the overdraft limit would be exceeded.
parts.answer: February and March.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The owner proposes to delay the equipment payment from February to April. Calculate the revised closing balances.
parts.answer: January $500; February $(1,500); March $500; April $1,500.
parts.working: M1 moving 15,000 to April; A1 balances.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the owner whether delaying the equipment payment solves the cash problem. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Yes, on these figures: the balance never goes beyond a $1,500 overdraft, well inside the $12,000 limit, and April still ends $1,500 in credit. However, the supplier must agree to the later payment, the display may arrive later and delay any extra sales, and the margin is small in February and March if customers pay late. Decision: delay the payment, but agree it in writing with the supplier and keep the overdraft facility available.
parts.working: 1 mark: all months now within limit (with figures). 1 mark: a risk or condition (supplier agreement, lost sales, late receipts, April end-balance same). 1 mark: clear justified decision.

practice.stem: All sales of Indus Tiles Ltd are on credit. Customers pay 40% in the month after sale and 60% two months after sale. There are no irrecoverable debts. March sales were $48,000 and budgeted receipts from customers in May are $57,600. Budgeted sales for May are $66,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted sales for April.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted receipts from customers in June.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted trade receivables at 31 May.
parts.working: Unpaid 60% of April 43,200 + all of May 66,000 (M1) = 109,200 (A1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one reason why the directors would monitor the trade receivables figure.
parts.answer: A rising balance may show customers taking longer to pay, which harms cash flow.
parts.working: B1 any valid reason (credit control, liquidity, risk of irrecoverable debts).

practice.stem:
The cash budget of Saeed Packaging Ltd shows a cash deficit of $40,000 for the next three months, after which the balance becomes positive. The directors are considering two options:
Option 1: an overdraft of $40,000 for three months at an interest rate of 12% per annum.
Option 2: offer customers a 2.5% cash discount to pay one month earlier. The directors expect customers owing $64,000 to accept, which would remove the deficit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of Option 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of Option 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors which option they should choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Option 1 is cheaper by $400 and does not depend on customers' behaviour; the bank may withdraw an overdraft at short notice, and it adds to interest costs. Option 2 is more expensive, customers may not all accept, and once offered the discount may be expected permanently, reducing future profit; but it lowers the risk of irrecoverable debts and needs no bank approval. Decision: choose the overdraft because it is cheaper and more certain, provided the bank agrees.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for Option 1 (cheaper by 400; certain amount; temporary). Up to 2 marks for points for/against Option 2 (uncertain take-up; permanent expectation; fewer bad debts; no security needed). 1 mark for use of figures. 1 mark for a clear decision consistent with the argument.

practice.stem:
Budgeted information for Ravi Traders, Lahore, for August:
1 credit sales $50,000; receipts from credit customers $42,000
2 credit purchases $30,000; payments to suppliers $28,000 (inventory levels do not change)
3 depreciation of equipment $3,000
4 insurance of $6,000 paid on 1 August for six months
5 repayment of a bank loan $5,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted profit for August.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted net cash flow for August.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain three reasons why the profit and the net cash flow are different.
parts.answer: Depreciation reduces profit but is not a cash payment; insurance paid for six months is a cash outflow of $6,000 but only $1,000 is an expense of August; the loan repayment is a cash outflow but not an expense. (Also: receipts and payments differ from sales and purchases because of credit.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason, with reference to the figures (max 3).

practice.stem: Sahara Solar Lamps plans to sell: January 4,000 units; February 5,000 units; March 6,000 units; April 5,500 units. Inventory of finished goods at the end of each month is to be 20% of the next month's sales. Inventory on 1 January will be 800 units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the production budget in units for January, February and March.
parts.answer:
Production budget (units)    Jan      Feb      Mar
Sales                      4,000    5,000    6,000
Add closing inventory      1,000    1,200    1,100
Less opening inventory     (800)  (1,000)  (1,200)
Production                 4,200    5,200    5,900
parts.working: B1 closing inventory 1,000, 1,200, 1,100; B1 opening inventory 800, 1,000, 1,200; B1 method; B1 production 4,200, 5,200, 5,900.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the sales budget is usually prepared before the production budget.
parts.answer: Sales demand is usually the principal budget factor; the number of units to produce depends on how many can be sold, so the other budgets are built from the sales budget.
parts.working: 1 mark: sales is the limiting/principal budget factor. 1 mark: production depends on forecast sales (plus inventory changes).

practice.stem:
Gujrat Fans Ltd makes two ceiling fans. Budgeted sales:
                    Quarter 1  Quarter 2
Deluxe – units          1,500      1,800
Deluxe – price $           60         60
Standard – units        3,200      3,000
Standard – price $         35         36

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the sales budget in $ for each quarter.
parts.answer:
Sales budget  Quarter 1 $  Quarter 2 $
Deluxe             90,000      108,000
Standard          112,000      108,000
Total             202,000      216,000
parts.working: B1 Deluxe; B1 Standard; B1 totals 202,000 and 216,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two factors the sales manager should consider when forecasting sales.
parts.answer: Past sales trends; expected competitor prices (also: economic conditions, advertising plans, seasonal demand, market research).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A manufacturing business prepares a full set of budgets each year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'master budget'.
parts.answer: The summary budget that brings together all the functional budgets as a budgeted statement of profit or loss, budgeted statement of financial position and cash budget.
parts.working: 1 mark: combines functional budgets. 1 mark: shown as budgeted financial statements/cash budget.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two functional budgets, other than the sales budget.
parts.answer: Production budget; materials purchases budget (also labour, overheads, receivables, payables budgets).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the term 'principal budget factor' and give an example.
parts.answer: The factor that limits the activity of the business, so it must be budgeted first; for example, sales demand or a shortage of skilled labour.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition. 1 mark: valid example.

practice.stem: Neelam Ceramics Ltd budgets to sell 18,000 tea sets in the quarter ending 31 March 2027. Inventory of finished tea sets is expected to be 2,500 at the start of the quarter and 3,200 at the end. Each tea set uses 0.8 kg of special glaze costing $3.50 per kg. Inventory of glaze will be 2,000 kg at the start and 2,600 kg at the end of the quarter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted production in units for the quarter.
parts.answer: 18,700 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted usage of material in kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted purchases of material in kg and in $.

practice.stem: Indus Pumps Ltd is starting a formal budgeting process for the first time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List, in a suitable order, five functional budgets that a manufacturer prepares before its master budget.
parts.answer: Sales budget → production budget → materials usage budget → materials purchases budget → labour budget (also: production overheads, selling and administration budgets, then the cash budget).
parts.working: B2 five correct budgets; B1 sensible order (sales first, production before materials/labour).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the three statements that make up the master budget.
parts.answer: Budgeted statement of profit or loss; budgeted statement of financial position; cash budget.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Ravi Chemicals plans production of: April 3,000 units; May 3,600 units; June 4,000 units; July 4,400 units. Each unit uses 2.5 kg of material costing $4 per kg. The inventory of material at the end of each month must equal 30% of the next month's production requirements. The inventory at 1 April will meet this policy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the materials purchases budget, in kg and in $, for April, May and June.
parts.answer:
Materials purchases budget      April      May     June
Material for production (kg)    7,500    9,000   10,000
Add closing inventory (kg)      2,700    3,000    3,300
Less opening inventory (kg)   (2,250)  (2,700)  (3,000)
Purchases (kg)                  7,950    9,300   10,300
Purchases at $4 per kg ($)     31,800   37,200   41,200

parts.label: b
parts.text: Material is paid for in the month after purchase. State the payment to suppliers in June.
parts.working: May purchases 37,200 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why the business holds an inventory of material.
parts.answer: To avoid production stopping if a delivery is late.
parts.working: B1 any valid reason (buffer against supplier delays, bulk discounts, demand changes).

practice.stem: For the quarter ending 31 March 2027, Lyari Traders budgets: trade receivables on 1 January $46,000; credit sales $180,000; receipts from credit customers $171,500; discounts allowed $2,300; irrecoverable debts written off $1,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the trade receivables budget for the quarter.
parts.answer:
Trade receivables budget          $
Balance 1 January            46,000
Credit sales                180,000
                            226,000
Less receipts             (171,500)
Less discounts allowed      (2,300)
Less irrecoverable debts    (1,800)
Balance 31 March             50,400
parts.working: B1 opening + credit sales; B1 receipts; B1 discounts and irrecoverable debts; B1 closing 50,400.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted trade receivables collection period in days, using closing receivables and a 90-day quarter. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: 25.2 days

practice.stem: Khyber Hardware budgets for the year: cost of sales $150,000; inventory at start $24,000 and at end $30,000; all purchases on credit; trade payables at start $18,000; payments to suppliers $149,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted purchases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the trade payables budget for the year.
parts.answer:
Trade payables budget          $
Balance at start          18,000
Credit purchases         156,000
                         174,000
Less payments          (149,000)
Balance at end            25,000
parts.working: B1 opening; B1 purchases and payments; B1 closing 25,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a just-in-time (JIT) system would change the inventory figures in these budgets.
parts.answer: Goods would be delivered only as needed, so closing inventory would be close to zero and purchases would nearly equal cost of sales.
parts.working: 1 mark: minimal inventory. 1 mark: purchases ≈ cost of sales / less cash tied up.

practice.stem: Swat Woodworks Ltd plans to make 1,200 chairs and 800 cabinets in June. Each chair needs 2 direct labour hours and each cabinet needs 3.5 direct labour hours. It employs 30 workers, each available for 160 hours in June at $14 an hour. Any extra hours are worked as overtime, paid at time and a half.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted direct labour hours required for the month.
parts.answer: 5,200 hours

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overtime hours needed.
parts.answer: 400 hours

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare the direct labour cost budget for the month.
parts.working: Basic pay 5,200 × 14 = 72,800 (B1); overtime premium 400 × 7 = 2,800 (B1); total 75,600 (B1).

practice.stem: Karakoram Cycles Ltd sells on average 10,000 bicycles a quarter, but sales are seasonal. The seasonal factors are: Q1 0.8, Q2 1.1, Q3 1.3, Q4 0.8. The selling price is $25 per bicycle in Q1 and Q2, rising by 4% from the start of Q3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the sales budget, in units and $, for each quarter and for the year.
parts.working: B1 units using seasonal factors; B1 price 25 × 1.04 = 26 from Q3; B1 Q1 and Q2 revenue; B1 Q3 and Q4 revenue; B1 total 1,021,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the sales budget is usually prepared before the other functional budgets.
parts.answer: Sales is normally the principal budget factor – it limits the level of activity, so production, materials, labour and overhead budgets all depend on the planned sales volume.
parts.working: B1 principal budget factor/limiting; B1 other budgets based on it.

practice.stem: A garment factory in Karachi plans to produce 2,400 shirts next month. Each shirt needs 1.5 productive labour hours. Idle time is expected to be 10% of hours paid. Workers are paid $12 an hour. The normal capacity is 3,800 paid hours; any extra hours are paid as overtime at time and a half.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total labour hours that must be paid.
parts.answer: 4,000 hours

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total budgeted labour cost.
parts.working: Basic 4,000 × 12 = 48,000 (M1); overtime 200 hours × premium 6 = 1,200 (M1); total 49,200 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways the factory could avoid paying overtime.
parts.answer: Recruit extra workers or temporary staff; reduce idle time through better scheduling/maintenance (also: spread production over earlier months, subcontract).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Margalla Ltd prepares budgets for the six months ending 30 June 2027:
1 sales 9,000 units at $50 each
2 production 9,500 units; variable production cost $22 per unit
3 fixed production overheads of $57,000 are absorbed on budgeted production
4 opening inventory 600 units valued at $28 each; inventories are valued at full production cost
5 administration expenses $48,000; selling expenses 5% of revenue; depreciation of office equipment $6,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the budgeted statement of profit or loss for the six months ending 30 June 2027.
parts.answer:
Budgeted statement of profit or loss         $          $
Revenue (9,000 × $50)                             450,000
Opening inventory (600 × $28)           16,800
Production cost (9,500 × $28)          266,000
Less closing inventory (1,100 × $28)  (30,800)
Cost of sales                                   (252,000)
Gross profit                                      198,000
Administration                          48,000
Selling (5% × 450,000)                  22,500
Depreciation                             6,000   (76,500)
Budgeted profit                                   121,500
parts.working: B1 revenue; B1 absorption rate 57,000 ÷ 9,500 = $6, full cost $28; B1 closing inventory 600 + 9,500 − 9,000 = 1,100 units; B1 cost of sales 252,000; B1 expenses 76,500; B1 profit 121,500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the budgeted profit will not equal the budgeted increase in the bank balance.
parts.answer: Profit includes non-cash items such as depreciation and inventory changes, and sales or purchases on credit are counted before cash moves; capital spending and loan repayments affect cash but not profit.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reason; 1 mark for a relevant example.

practice.stem:
Ravi Foods Ltd is preparing its master budget for the year ending 31 December 2027. Figures from the functional budgets:
1 non-current assets at 1 January 2027: cost $260,000, accumulated depreciation $60,000
2 new equipment costing $40,000 will be bought in 2027
3 depreciation is 10% per annum on the cost of all non-current assets held at the year end
4 closing inventory $32,000; trade receivables (December sales) $48,000; trade payables (December purchases) $27,000
5 the cash budget shows a closing bank balance of $14,500
6 share capital $150,000; retained earnings at 1 January 2027 $83,500; budgeted profit for the year $64,000; dividends paid $20,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the budgeted statement of financial position at 31 December 2027.
parts.answer:
Budgeted statement of financial position                $        $
Non-current assets: cost (260,000 + 40,000)       300,000
Less accumulated depreciation (60,000 + 30,000)  (90,000)  210,000
Inventory                                          32,000
Trade receivables                                  48,000
Bank                                               14,500   94,500
Total assets                                               304,500
Share capital                                              150,000
Retained earnings (83,500 + 64,000 − 20,000)               127,500
                                                           277,500
Trade payables                                              27,000
Total equity and liabilities                               304,500
parts.working: B1 cost 300,000; B1 depreciation 30,000, carrying amount 210,000; B1 current assets 94,500; B1 retained earnings 127,500; B1 payables as current liability; B1 totals 304,500 balancing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the directors can use the master budget.
parts.answer: It brings all functional budgets together to show whether the plans give an acceptable profit and financial position; later, actual results can be compared with it to control performance.
parts.working: 1 mark: coordination/overall plan (check plans are consistent, profitable, liquid). 1 mark: control – compare actual with budget.

practice.stem: Lahore Kitchenware Ltd expects demand of 13,500 food processors next year. Each needs 2.5 kg of a special plastic, and only 30,000 kg can be bought in the year. Finished goods inventory will be 800 units at the start of the year, and the directors want 1,000 units at the end. Each unit earns a contribution of $14.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum production possible and the budgeted sales in units.
parts.answer: Production 12,000 units; sales 11,800 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the contribution lost because demand cannot be met.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the principal budget factor and identify it for the company.
parts.answer: The factor that limits the activity of the business and so must be budgeted for first. Here it is the supply of material (30,000 kg), not sales demand.
parts.working: B1 definition; B1 material supply.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two actions the company could take to reduce the lost contribution.
parts.answer: Any two: find another supplier of the material (even at a higher price); reduce planned closing inventory of finished goods; redesign to use less material per unit/reduce waste; raise the selling price to match the lower volume.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Sadiq Electricals Ltd is preparing its budgeted statement of financial position at 31 December 2027. Budget data for 2027:
• credit sales $1,200,000; customers are expected to take 1.5 months to pay
• cost of sales $840,000; closing inventory will equal one month's cost of sales
• credit purchases $720,000; suppliers are paid after 2 months
• budgeted bank balance at 31 December 2027 $35,000; accrued expenses $15,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted trade receivables, inventory and trade payables at 31 December 2027.
parts.answer: Receivables $150,000; inventory $70,000; payables $120,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted working capital and current ratio at 31 December 2027. Give the ratio to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Working capital $120,000; current ratio 1.89 : 1

parts.label: c
parts.text: The bank requires a current ratio of at least 2 : 1. Calculate the extra cash the company would need at 31 December 2027, with no change to current liabilities.

practice.stem: The owner of a chain of three pharmacies in Lahore is thinking about introducing a system of budgets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three purposes of budgeting for the business.
parts.answer: Planning: forces managers to think ahead about sales, staff and stock. Coordination: makes sure the three pharmacies and departments work to the same plan. Control: actual results can be compared with budget and variances investigated. (Also motivation and communication.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each purpose: 1 mark naming it, 1 mark applying/explaining it (max 6).

practice.stem: Hamdam Herbal Ltd's owner says, 'We already forecast our sales, so why do we need a budget?'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a budget.
parts.answer: A detailed plan for a future period, expressed in money (and/or quantities), agreed by management, setting out how resources will be obtained and used to achieve the organisation's objectives.
parts.working: B1 plan for a future period; B1 in financial/quantitative terms, used to achieve objectives.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between a budget and a forecast.
parts.answer: A forecast is a prediction of what is likely to happen (e.g. expected demand); a budget is a plan of what management intends to achieve, a target used for control.
parts.working: B1 forecast – prediction; B1 budget – plan/target for control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the principal budget factor.
parts.answer: The factor that limits the activities of the organisation for the budget period, so it determines the level of all other budgets and must be identified first.
parts.working: B1 limiting factor on activity; B1 determines other budgets/prepared first.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a likely principal budget factor for (i) a new private hospital in Islamabad, and (ii) a cement factory running at full capacity.
parts.answer: (i) e.g. number of qualified doctors/nurses or beds available (or patient demand); (ii) production capacity (machine hours/kiln capacity).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A restaurant group in Karachi uses an annual budget for each of its outlets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three limitations of budgeting.
parts.answer: Any three of: budgets are based on estimates that may be wrong; time-consuming and costly to prepare; may become out of date if conditions change; can cause inflexibility (managers stick to the budget even when a change is better); may encourage budgetary slack or short-term behaviour; imposed budgets may demotivate.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Zarkhez Fertiliser Distributors Ltd has separate sales, production and purchasing managers who seldom meet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how budgeting helps to co-ordinate the activities of the sales and production departments. Use an example.
parts.answer: Budgets are prepared from the same plan, so the production budget is based on the sales budget: e.g. if the sales department plans to sell 10,000 units in March, production plans output (and inventory) to meet this, avoiding shortages or excess inventory. Departments work towards common targets.
parts.working: B1 budgets linked to one overall plan; B1 example of sales → production; B1 avoids conflict/shortages/overproduction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a budget helps communication within the business.
parts.answer: The budget tells each manager what is expected of them (targets and resources) and passes senior management's plans down the organisation.
parts.working: B1 managers know targets; B1 plans communicated.

practice.stem: Al-Shifa Hospital, Karachi, currently sets departmental budgets centrally. The new finance director suggests participative budgeting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'participative budgeting'.
parts.answer: Budget holders (department managers) are involved in setting their own budgets with senior management, rather than having budgets imposed.
parts.working: 1 mark: managers take part. 1 mark: contrast with imposed/top-down.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of participative budgeting for the hospital.
parts.answer: Advantages: department heads know their patient numbers and costs, so budgets are more realistic; managers feel ownership and are more motivated to meet them; better communication between departments. Disadvantages: takes longer; managers may build in budgetary slack; targets may not match the hospital's overall goals; senior managers may still override them, causing demotivation.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for advantages and up to 3 for disadvantages, each developed in the hospital context.

practice.stem: The board of Rehan Snacks Ltd sets every department's budget itself and sends it to the department managers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages of an imposed (top-down) budget.
parts.answer: 1 Quicker and cheaper to prepare, because only senior managers are involved. 2 Targets match the overall strategy of the business; senior managers can prevent budgetary slack. Also: senior management has a wider view of the whole business.
parts.working: B1 + B1 each advantage stated and explained (2 × 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages of an imposed budget.
parts.answer: 1 Managers may feel no ownership and become demotivated, so they do not try to meet the targets. 2 Targets may be unrealistic because they ignore the local knowledge of operational managers. Also: may cause resentment or poor communication.
parts.working: B1 + B1 each disadvantage stated and explained (2 × 2).

practice.stem: The head office of Bank Al-Shams sets each branch a target for new deposits. This year head office has increased all targets by 20%, although several branch managers say the local economy is weak.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how budgets can motivate the branch managers.
parts.answer: A clear, achievable target gives managers something to aim for; achieving it gives a sense of success and may be linked to rewards; if managers took part in setting it, they feel committed to it.
parts.working: B1 each point explained (up to 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the new targets may instead demotivate the managers.
parts.answer: If targets are set too high (20% growth in a falling market) managers believe they cannot be achieved and stop trying; they may be blamed for factors they cannot control; pressure may lead to short-term actions (cutting service quality).
parts.working: B1 each point explained (up to 3).

practice.stem: The factory manager of Gulnar Prints Ltd receives a monthly report comparing all factory costs, including a share of head-office costs, with the budget.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by responsibility accounting.
parts.answer: A system in which costs and revenues are traced to the managers responsible for them (cost/profit centres), and each manager reports on and is judged on the items they control.
parts.working: B1 costs/revenues assigned to responsible managers; B1 judged on these.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the factory manager should be judged only on controllable costs. Give one example of a cost she can control and one she cannot.
parts.answer: It is unfair and demotivating to hold a manager accountable for costs she cannot influence, and it would not improve decisions. Controllable: e.g. overtime, material wastage, maintenance. Uncontrollable: e.g. head-office charges, factory rent set by the board, depreciation on equipment bought by directors.
parts.working: B1 fairness/motivation; B1 meaningful control; B1 controllable example; B1 uncontrollable example.

practice.stem: Noor Hospital, Lahore, receives monthly reports with more than 200 lines of costs for each ward.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'management by exception'.
parts.answer: Managers concentrate on significant variances (large differences between budget and actual) and investigate them, rather than spending time on items that are going to plan.
parts.working: B1 focus on significant variances; B1 saves time/attention.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two steps in the budgetary control cycle after the budget has been agreed.
parts.answer: Record actual results and compare with the (flexed) budget to find variances; investigate the causes of significant variances; take corrective action (or revise the plan) and feed information into next period's budget.
parts.working: B1 + B1 for each of two steps explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of the budget committee and the budget manual in Faiz Foods Ltd.
parts.answer: Budget committee: senior managers who co-ordinate the preparation of budgets, set timetables, resolve conflicts between departments and approve the final master budget. Budget manual: a document setting out the procedures, timetable, responsibilities, forms and policies for budgeting, so that everyone prepares budgets in the same way.
parts.working: B1 + B1 committee role; B1 + B1 manual role.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the committee should include the sales director and the production director.
parts.answer: Their departments' budgets depend on each other; having both on the committee makes sure plans are consistent (e.g. production capacity can meet planned sales) and that they accept the budget.
parts.working: B1 co-ordination; B1 commitment/ownership.

practice.stem: The directors of Shah Logistics Ltd plan to pay each depot manager a bonus if the depot's actual costs are below its budget.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'budgetary slack'.
parts.answer: Deliberately overstating budgeted costs (or understating revenue) so the target is easier to achieve.
parts.working: 1 mark: deliberate overstatement/understatement. 1 mark: to make the target easy to meet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should link the bonus to the budget. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: gives managers a clear target and incentive to control costs; aligns their goals with the company's. Against: encourages budgetary slack in the budget-setting stage; managers may cut essential spending (maintenance, training) to earn the bonus; ignores factors outside their control such as fuel prices; may harm service quality. Decision: link bonuses only if budgets are reviewed for slack and include non-financial targets, or use a flexed budget; otherwise do not.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for; up to 3 marks for points against (slack, short-termism, uncontrollable costs, quality); 1 mark for a justified decision.

practice.stem: The cafeteria budget at a university in Islamabad is set by the finance office each year by adding 5% to last year's actual spending. Student numbers have risen by 25% this year, and the cafeteria has extended its opening hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the weaknesses of the current method of setting the cafeteria budget and advise the university on how the budget should be set.
parts.answer: Weaknesses: adding 5% to last year's figure carries forward past inefficiencies and waste; ignores changes in activity (student numbers, opening hours, menu) and in prices; manager may spend the full budget to avoid future cuts; no link to objectives; does not motivate cost control. Advice: build the budget from expected activity (meals served × cost per meal), with fixed and variable costs identified and flexed for actual activity; involve the manager in setting it (participation) while senior staff check for slack; review each cost line and its need; compare actual with flexed budget monthly. Conclusion: use activity-based, participative budgeting with flexible budgets for control.
parts.working: Level 3 (7–8): several weaknesses explained in context and well-justified advice with a conclusion. Level 2 (4–6): weaknesses and advice stated with some explanation. Level 1 (1–3): simple points.

practice.stem: The maintenance manager of Sonmiani Power Generation Ltd earns a bonus if annual maintenance costs are below budget. This year he postponed servicing on two turbines and came in $40,000 under budget. In January one turbine broke down and repairs cost $120,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the behavioural problems that the bonus scheme may cause, and advise the directors how to improve it.
parts.answer: Problems: managers cut necessary spending (maintenance) to stay under budget, causing breakdowns and higher future costs; they may build slack into budgets so they are easy to beat; they may delay spending to next year; focus only on cost, ignoring quality and customer service; conflict with other departments. Advice: link bonuses to several measures (quality, output, breakdowns, customer complaints); use flexed budgets; set budgets through participation but review them for slack; judge managers only on controllable costs; consider longer-term targets. Conclusion with justification.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): problems explained in context with balanced, justified advice. Level 2 (3–4): problems and some advice. Level 1 (1–2): simple points.

practice.stem: Bushra runs a family bakery in Rawalpindi and keeps everything 'in her head'. She plans to open a second shop next year, to buy a new oven with a bank overdraft, and to employ a shop supervisor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Bushra should introduce a formal system of budgeting for her bakery.
parts.answer: For: planning sales and production avoids waste of perishable goods; a cash budget would show the overdraft needed for the new oven and when it can be repaid; comparing actual with budget helps control rising flour and energy costs; she can delegate to the new shop supervisor with clear targets; the bank may require budgets. Against: time and cost for a small business; she has little accounting knowledge (may need software or an accountant); estimates may be inaccurate because sales depend on weather/festivals; she already knows the business well. Conclusion: benefits outweigh costs because she is expanding and borrowing; a simple sales, purchases and cash budget, reviewed monthly, would be suitable.
parts.working: Level 3 (7–8): balanced evaluation in context with justified conclusion. Level 2 (4–6): points on both sides, weak conclusion. Level 1 (1–3): simple points.

practice.stem: A bottling plant in Hub records electricity costs of $9,200 when output is 4,000 crates and $13,700 when output is 7,000 crates. The cost is semi-variable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the high–low method to calculate the variable cost per crate and the fixed cost.
parts.answer: Variable $1.50 per crate; fixed $3,200.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the flexed budget cost of electricity for an output of 5,800 crates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Actual electricity cost at 5,800 crates was $12,400. Calculate the variance and state whether it is favourable or adverse.
parts.answer: $500 adverse

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one possible cause of this variance.
parts.answer: An increase in the electricity tariff (or machines left running when idle).
parts.working: B1 any valid cause.

practice.stem: Pearl Bay Laundry Services planned to wash 50,000 kg of hotel linen in March but actually washed 42,000 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a fixed budget and a flexible budget.
parts.answer: A fixed budget is prepared for one planned level of activity and is not changed. A flexible budget recognises cost behaviour and is adjusted (flexed) to the actual level of activity, with variable costs changing and fixed costs unchanged.
parts.working: B1 fixed – one level of activity; B1 flexible – adjusted to actual activity using cost behaviour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why comparing actual costs with the fixed budget may mislead managers when output is lower than planned.
parts.answer: Variable costs would naturally be lower at lower output, so the comparison shows 'favourable' variances that are due only to volume, hiding inefficiency.
parts.working: B1 lower output → lower variable costs; B1 favourable variances misleading.

practice.stem: Hareem Juice Packs has a variable cost of $6.40 per carton and fixed costs of $18,000 a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted total cost at output levels of (i) 7,500 units and (ii) 9,000 units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted cost per unit at each level, and explain why it is lower at the higher output.
parts.answer: $8.80 at 7,500 units; $8.40 at 9,000 units. The fixed cost of $18,000 is spread over more units.
parts.working: B1 8.80; B1 8.40; B1 explanation.

practice.stem:
A hotel in Murree has these costs.
1 Cleaning materials used in each room each night.
2 The general manager's salary.
3 Electricity: a standing charge of $400 a month plus a charge per unit used.
4 Housekeeping supervisors: one supervisor is needed for every 20 rooms occupied.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each cost as variable, fixed, semi-variable or stepped.
parts.answer:
1 Variable
2 Fixed
3 Semi-variable
4 Stepped
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Zaiqa Spices budgeted to sell 12,000 boxes for $180,000. It actually sold 10,500 boxes for $162,750.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the flexed revenue and the sales revenue variance, stating whether it is favourable or adverse.
parts.answer: Flexed revenue $157,500; variance $5,250 favourable

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the actual selling price per unit.

practice.stem:
Bolan Biscuits budgeted to make and sell 10,000 cartons. Actual output and sales were 11,500 cartons.
                    Original budget $  Actual $
Revenue                       300,000   339,250
Direct materials               80,000    94,300
Direct labour                  60,000    67,850
Variable overheads             20,000    24,150
Fixed overheads                50,000    52,000
Profit                         90,000   100,950

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a flexed budget for 11,500 cartons.
parts.answer:
Flexed budget (11,500 cartons)         $

practice.stem: Cholistan Sugar Mills crushed 20% less sugar cane than budgeted because of a poor harvest. The flexed budget shows adverse cost variances of $85,000. The production manager says, 'These variances are only there because we crushed less cane.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the limitations of flexible budgeting for Cholistan Sugar Mills and advise the board whether the production manager's explanation should be accepted.
parts.answer: Limitations: costs must be classified as fixed or variable, but many are semi-variable or stepped and the split is an estimate; cost behaviour may not be linear (bulk discounts, overtime); the flexed budget shows that a variance exists but not why; a single activity measure (tonnes) may not drive all costs (e.g. cane quality affects processing time). On the manager's claim: the flexed budget already removes the effect of lower volume, so remaining adverse variances are not explained by volume; however, if some costs were wrongly treated as variable (e.g. fixed staff), the flexed figure would be too low and the variance unfair. Advice: check the cost classification, investigate the main variances with the manager, and only then judge; do not accept the explanation without evidence.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): limitations explained and applied, judgement on the manager's claim with justified advice. Level 2 (3–4): limitations listed with some application. Level 1 (1–2): simple points.

practice.stem: Farid is a sole trader whose business has made an average profit of $46,000 a year. Zenith Ltd offers to buy his business for 200,000 ordinary shares of $1 each, valued at $1.50 per share. Farid would be employed by Zenith Ltd as branch manager at a salary of $30,000 a year. parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Farid whether he should accept the offer. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For: expected income $48,000 is $2,000 more than now; a fixed salary is less risky than trading profit; shares are worth $300,000 and can be sold; limited liability; fewer working hours and responsibilities.
Against: dividends are not guaranteed and may fall; the share price may fall; he loses control and becomes an employee who can be dismissed; he is a small minority shareholder with little say; the gain of $2,000 is small.
Decision: e.g. accept, because income rises and risk falls, provided he is satisfied with the dividend record and a service contract.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for points for, up to 3 marks for points against (max 5 for points); 1 mark for a justified decision.

parts.working: B1 assets at book value; B1 expenses; B1 payables and Gull Ltd credited; B1 loss 7,600; B1 shared 4,560 : 3,040 on the credit side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the loss on realisation shows.
parts.answer: The business has been sold for less than the book value of its net assets; the assets were overvalued in the books (or there is no goodwill), and the partners bear the shortfall by reducing their capitals in the profit-sharing ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: consideration below book value of net assets; 1 mark: borne by partners/reduces capital.

practice.subtopic: Partnership or sole trader acquired by a company
practice.stem:
On 1 May 2025 Quail Ltd bought the business of Nadia and Omar, partners trading in Islamabad. Quail Ltd took over these assets and liabilities at the agreed values shown:
                                  $
Premises                    140,000
Fixtures and fittings        22,000
Inventory                    18,600
Trade receivables            12,400
Trade payables               (9,800)
Bank loan                   (25,000)
The purchase consideration was settled by: $30,000 paid from Quail Ltd's bank account; 80,000 ordinary shares of $1 each issued at $1.25 per share; and $40,000 of 6% debentures issued to the partners.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the business purchase account in the books of Quail Ltd.
parts.answer:
Business purchase account
Dr: Premises 140,000; Fixtures and fittings 22,000; Inventory 18,600; Trade receivables 12,400; Goodwill 11,800 = 204,800
Cr: Trade payables 9,800; Bank loan 25,000; Vendors – Nadia and Omar 170,000 = 204,800
parts.working: Purchase consideration = 30,000 + (80,000 × 1.25) 100,000 + 40,000 = 170,000 (B1). Net assets = 158,200 (M1). Goodwill = 170,000 − 158,200 = 11,800 (A1). Assets debited (B1), liabilities and vendors credited (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the vendors' account in the books of Quail Ltd to show how the consideration was settled.
parts.answer:
Vendors (Nadia and Omar) account
Dr: Bank 30,000; Ordinary share capital 80,000; Share premium 20,000; 6% debentures 40,000 = 170,000
Cr: Business purchase 170,000
parts.working: B1 bank; B1 share capital 80,000 and share premium 20,000 shown separately; B1 debentures and totals agree.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the annual debenture interest Quail Ltd must now pay, and explain one effect of the debenture issue on Quail Ltd's gearing.
parts.answer: 40,000 × 6% = $2,400 a year. Gearing rises because long-term borrowing (debentures) increases relative to equity, so fixed interest must be paid before any dividend.
parts.working: B1 interest 2,400; B1 explanation of higher gearing.

practice.subtopic: Partnership or sole trader acquired by a company
practice.stem:
Mehwish and Naveed are partners sharing profits 3:2. Their statement of financial position at 31 March 2027 was:

practice.subtopic: Partnership or sole trader acquired by a company
practice.stem:
Willow Ltd bought the business of Hamid and Imran on 1 August 2026.
                       Book value $ Agreed value $
Premises                     90,000        125,000
Machinery                    40,000         31,000
Inventory                    26,000         23,500
Trade receivables            18,000       see note
Trade payables               15,600         15,600
Note: a provision for doubtful debts of 5% is to be made on the trade receivables taken over.
The purchase consideration was: 80,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each issued at $1.20 per share; $50,000 of 6% debentures; and $40,000 in cash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net assets acquired at agreed values.
parts.working: B1 receivables 17,100; M1 sum of agreed assets less payables; A1 181,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the increase in Willow Ltd's ordinary share capital and share premium.
parts.answer: Share capital $40,000; share premium $56,000

parts.label: d
parts.text: Willow Ltd had a bank balance of $28,000 before the purchase. State the effect of the purchase on the bank balance and suggest one way the company could have avoided this.
