parts.working: B1 overdraft 12,000; B1 valid suggestion.

practice.subtopic: Partnership or sole trader acquired by a company
practice.stem: Rafiq and Sohail share partnership profits equally. The partnership has made a profit of $84,000 a year. Tern Ltd offers to buy the business. Each partner would receive 60,000 ordinary shares of $1 each and $25,000 of 7% debentures. Rafiq would be employed by Tern Ltd as manager at $28,000 a year; Sohail would retire. Tern Ltd expects to pay a dividend of 12% on its ordinary shares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's annual income before and after the sale.
parts.answer:
Before: each $42,000
After: Rafiq $36,950 (salary 28,000 + dividend 7,200 + interest 1,750); Sohail $8,950 (dividend 7,200 + interest 1,750)
parts.working: B1 before 42,000 each; B1 dividend 7,200; B1 interest 1,750; B1 Rafiq 36,950 and Sohail 8,950.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Sohail whether he should accept the offer. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: his income falls from $42,000 to $8,950. For: he will no longer work, so the comparison is with retirement income; he receives an asset (shares and debentures) that can be sold; debenture interest is secure and repaid at maturity; liability is limited and he is free of business risk. Decision: accept if he wishes to retire and the capital value is fair; otherwise negotiate more debentures or cash.
parts.working: 1 mark: income falls with figures; 1 mark each for up to two other relevant points; 1 mark: justified decision.

practice.subtopic: Partnership or sole trader acquired by a company
practice.stem: Kingfisher Ltd bought a partnership business. The fair value of the net assets acquired was $186,000 and goodwill of $14,000 was recorded. Kingfisher Ltd paid $40,000 in cash and issued 100,000 ordinary shares of $1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the purchase consideration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the issue price of each share.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Before the purchase the share premium account had a balance of $25,000. Costs of $3,000 for issuing the shares were written off against share premium. Calculate the new balance on the share premium account.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A year later an impairment review shows that the goodwill should be reduced by $3,500. State how this is recorded in the financial statements.
parts.answer: An impairment loss of $3,500 is charged as an expense in the statement of profit or loss; goodwill is shown at $10,500 in the statement of financial position (an impairment of goodwill is never reversed).
parts.working: 1 mark: expense in profit or loss; 1 mark: goodwill reduced to 10,500.

practice.subtopic: Partnership or sole trader acquired by a company
practice.stem:
Maple Ltd's statement of financial position at 30 June 2027 showed: non-current assets $255,000; bank $18,000; other net current assets $42,000; ordinary shares of $1 each $200,000; share premium $20,000; retained earnings $95,000.
On that date Maple Ltd bought a sole trader's business, taking over non-current assets $70,000, inventory $12,000 and trade payables $9,000 (agreed values). It issued 40,000 ordinary shares at $1.75 each and paid $30,000 in cash. The cash was raised on the same day by a bank loan repayable in 2032.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Maple Ltd's total equity after the purchase.
parts.working: B1 share capital 240,000 and premium 50,000; B1 total 385,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate Maple Ltd's net current assets after the purchase.
parts.working: B1 60,000 + 12,000 − 9,000; B1 loan received and cash paid cancel: 63,000.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate total non-current assets, including goodwill, and show that net assets equal equity.
parts.answer: Non-current assets $352,000; net assets 352,000 + 63,000 − loan 30,000 = 385,000 = equity.
parts.working: B1 352,000; B1 reconciliation.

practice.subtopic: Partnership or sole trader acquired by a company
practice.stem:
Heron Ltd's equity on 1 October 2026 was: ordinary shares of $1 each $400,000; share premium $60,000; retained earnings $210,000.
On 1 October 2026 it made a rights issue of 1 new share for every 5 held at $1.30 per share; all rights were taken up.
On 15 October 2026 it bought a partnership business with net assets at fair value of $148,000. It paid $90,000 in cash and issued 50,000 ordinary shares at $1.50 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash raised by the rights issue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill on the purchase of the partnership.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare the equity section of Heron Ltd's statement of financial position after both transactions.
parts.answer:
Equity
                                       $
Ordinary shares of $1 each       530,000
Share premium                    109,000
Retained earnings                210,000
Total equity                     849,000
parts.working: B1 share capital 530,000; B1 premium on rights 24,000; B1 premium on purchase 25,000 (total 109,000); B1 total 849,000.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the net effect of the two transactions on Heron Ltd's bank balance.
parts.answer: Increase of $14,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define purchased goodwill.
parts.answer: The amount by which the purchase consideration for a business exceeds the fair value of its identifiable net assets.
parts.working: 1 mark: consideration paid; 1 mark: in excess of fair value of identifiable net assets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A company pays $260,000 for a business whose identifiable net assets have a fair value of $231,500. Calculate the goodwill.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the seller of a business expects to be paid for goodwill.
parts.answer: Any two: the business has loyal customers and a good reputation; a good location; skilled and experienced staff; established supplier relationships; brand names – all of which will earn the buyer future profits.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A sole trader's profits for the last four years were $42,000, $47,500, $39,000 and $51,500. A buyer agrees to value goodwill at two years' purchase of the average annual profit. The net assets of the business at fair value are $310,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average annual profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of goodwill.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total purchase price.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain one limitation of valuing goodwill on past profits.
parts.answer: Past profits may not continue: the owner's personal skills or customers may leave with the owner, market conditions may change, and profits may include one-off items.
parts.working: 1 mark: future profits may differ; 1 mark: a reason.

practice.stem: A pharmacy in Hyderabad, Sindh, is for sale. Its average annual profit is $72,000 and its net assets have a fair value of $520,000. A normal rate of return for a pharmacy business is 10% of net assets. The buyer agrees to value goodwill at three years' purchase of the super profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the normal profit expected on the net assets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the super profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the value of goodwill and the total price for the pharmacy.
parts.answer: Goodwill $60,000; price $580,000

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why goodwill is based on super profit rather than total profit in this method.
parts.answer: The buyer could earn the normal return just by investing the same amount in similar net assets; only profit above that normal return is due to the business's reputation, location and customers, so only that excess is paid for as goodwill.
parts.working: 1 mark normal return available anyway; 1 mark goodwill = earnings above normal.

practice.stem: Lotus Ltd, Dubai, bought the business of a sole trader. The fair value of the net assets taken over was $160,000. Lotus Ltd paid: $45,000 in cash; 120,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each, issued at $0.80 per share; and $30,000 of 8% debentures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total purchase consideration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in Lotus Ltd's ordinary share capital and in its share premium account.
parts.answer: Share capital $60,000; share premium $36,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill arising on the purchase.

practice.stem: Mango Ltd, Multan, bought the business of a sole trader who wished to retire quickly. Mango Ltd paid $210,000 in cash. The fair value of the identifiable net assets taken over was $224,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the purchase consideration and the fair value of the net assets, and state what this difference is called.
parts.answer: $14,000; negative goodwill (a gain on a bargain purchase)
parts.working: 224,000 − 210,000 = 14,000 (B1); named as negative goodwill / bargain purchase (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how Mango Ltd should treat this amount in its financial statements.
parts.answer: Mango Ltd first re-checks that the fair values of the assets and liabilities are correct; any remaining amount is recognised immediately as a gain in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.working: 1 mark reassess fair values; 1 mark gain in profit or loss immediately (not shown as an asset).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the sole trader accepted less than the fair value of the net assets.
parts.answer: Any two: wanted a quick sale to retire; saves time and cost of selling assets one by one; poor recent profits; ill health; no family member to take over; needs cash now.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Neem Ltd is buying a garment business in Sialkot. The directors list the following things that make the business valuable:
1 a registered trademark for the business's school uniforms
2 a loyal group of regular customers who return every year
3 a highly skilled and experienced workforce
4 a patent for a stain-resistant fabric treatment
5 a convenient location close to several large schools

parts.label: a
parts.text: State, for each item 1 to 5, whether Neem Ltd would record it as a separate identifiable asset or whether it forms part of goodwill.
parts.answer: 1 separate identifiable (intangible) asset; 2 part of goodwill; 3 part of goodwill; 4 separate identifiable (intangible) asset; 5 part of goodwill
parts.working: 1 mark each. Trademarks and patents are legal rights that can be separately identified and valued; customer loyalty, the workforce and location cannot be separated from the business, so they are part of goodwill.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define goodwill.
parts.answer: The amount by which the value of a business as a whole exceeds the fair value of its identifiable net assets.

practice.stem: On 1 January 2023 Olive Ltd recorded purchased goodwill of $60,000 when it bought a bakery in Lahore. Annual impairment reviews found impairment losses of $7,500 at 31 December 2023 and $4,000 at 31 December 2024. At 31 December 2025 the recoverable amount of the bakery had risen and was well above its carrying amount.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of goodwill at 31 December 2024.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of the 2024 impairment loss on the profit for 2024.
parts.answer: Profit for the year is reduced by $4,000 (an expense in the statement of profit or loss).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State, with a reason, whether Olive Ltd may reverse the earlier impairment losses at 31 December 2025.
parts.answer: No. An impairment loss on goodwill can never be reversed, because any rise in value would be internally generated goodwill, which may not be recognised.
parts.working: B1 no; B1 reason (internally generated goodwill not recognised).

practice.stem:
Two partners are negotiating the sale of their business. Recent profits were:
Year ended 31 December      Profit $
2024                          38,000
2025                          44,000
2026                          55,000
The 2026 profit includes a one-off gain of $4,000 on the sale of land. Goodwill is to be valued at two years' purchase of the weighted average profit, using weights of 1, 2 and 3 for 2024, 2025 and 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the adjusted profit for 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the weighted average profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the value of goodwill.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why a weighted average and the adjustment for the gain on land are used.
parts.answer: Weighting gives more importance to recent profits, which are a better guide to future profits. The gain on land is a one-off, non-trading item that will not recur, so it is removed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: On 1 January 2026 Cedar Ltd bought a business and recorded goodwill of $48,000. At 31 December 2026 an impairment review of the business found that its recoverable amount was $412,000. The carrying amount of its net assets, excluding goodwill, was $381,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the impairment loss.
parts.working: M1 carrying amount 429,000 compared with 412,000; A1 17,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of goodwill at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the impairment loss is treated in the financial statements.
parts.answer: It is charged as an expense in the statement of profit or loss for 2026 and deducted from goodwill in the statement of financial position. It cannot be reversed in later years.
parts.working: 1 mark: expense in profit or loss; 1 mark: reduces goodwill / not reversed.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why purchased goodwill is tested for impairment each year rather than written off on a fixed schedule.
parts.answer: Goodwill has no fixed useful life, so an annual impairment review (IAS 36) shows it at no more than its recoverable amount instead of using an arbitrary amortisation period.

practice.stem:
Rehana runs a hardware business in Quetta. Her statement of financial position at 31 August 2025 showed:
                                  $
Premises                    110,000
Equipment                    26,000
Inventory                    19,500
Trade receivables            16,000
Bank                          7,200
Trade payables              (11,400)
Bank loan                   (30,000)
On that date Saffron Ltd bought the business. Rehana kept the bank balance and repaid the bank loan herself. The remaining assets and liabilities were taken over, with these adjustments:
• premises revalued at $134,000 and equipment at $21,500
• inventory costing $2,300 was found to be damaged and worthless
• an allowance for irrecoverable debts of 5% is to be made on trade receivables
Saffron Ltd paid by issuing 150,000 ordinary shares of $1 each at $1.40 per share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of the net assets taken over by Saffron Ltd.
parts.working: Premises 134,000 + equipment 21,500 (B1) + inventory 17,200 (B1) + receivables 16,000 × 95% = 15,200 (B1) − payables 11,400 = 176,500 (A1). Bank and loan excluded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill on the purchase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the increase in Saffron Ltd's share capital and share premium.
parts.answer: Share capital $150,000; share premium $60,000
parts.working: B1 each.

practice.stem:
Daniyal is selling his printing business in Karachi. He has two offers:
Offer A: $250,000 in cash. Daniyal would deposit the cash in a bank account paying 5% interest a year.
Offer B: from Falcon Ltd, 160,000 ordinary shares of $1 each valued at $1.50 per share, plus $40,000 of 9% debentures. Falcon Ltd has paid a dividend of $0.12 per share for each of the last three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total value of Offer B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Daniyal's expected annual income from each offer.
parts.answer: Offer A $12,500; Offer B $22,800

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Daniyal which offer he should accept. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For B: higher value ($30,000 more) and higher income ($10,300 more); shares may rise in value; debenture interest is secure. Against B: dividends are not guaranteed and share price may fall; shares may be hard to sell if Falcon is a private company; risk concentrated in one company; cash gives certainty and flexibility. Decision with reason, e.g. accept B if he can accept the risk and does not need cash now.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for B, up to 2 for points against/for A (using figures), 1 mark for a justified decision.

practice.stem: Ivy Ltd plans to buy a sole trader's café in Kuala Lumpur. The café's average annual profit is $66,000, but the owner has never charged a salary for his own work. Ivy Ltd would have to employ a manager at $18,000 a year. Ivy Ltd expects a return of 12% a year on businesses of this kind. The fair value of the café's net assets is $345,000. Goodwill is to be valued by capitalising the maintainable profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maintainable profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of the whole business by capitalising the maintainable profit at 12%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the value of goodwill.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the manager's salary is deducted before valuing the business.
parts.answer: Ivy Ltd will have to pay a manager, so the profit it will actually earn is lower; using the owner's profit without a salary would overstate the profit and the price.
parts.working: 1 mark cost the buyer will bear; 1 mark otherwise value overstated.

practice.stem: Hazel Ltd agreed a purchase consideration of $288,000 for a partnership business in Peshawar. $48,000 was paid by cheque and the rest by issuing ordinary shares of $0.50 each at $1.60 per share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of shares issued.
parts.answer: 150,000 shares

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amounts credited to the share capital and share premium accounts.
parts.answer: Share capital $75,000; share premium $165,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry in Hazel Ltd's books to record the settlement of the consideration. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer: Dr Vendors (partnership) 288,000; Cr Bank 48,000; Cr Ordinary share capital 75,000; Cr Share premium 165,000
parts.working: B1 debit vendors; B1 credit bank; B1 credits to share capital and share premium.

practice.stem: Jasmine Ltd's profit from operations is $180,000 a year on capital employed of $1,200,000. It is considering buying a sole trader's business for $300,000 (net assets $240,000 and goodwill $60,000), paid by issuing shares. The business is expected to add $39,000 a year to Jasmine Ltd's profit from operations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Jasmine Ltd's return on capital employed before the purchase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected return on capital employed after the purchase, and the return on the purchase price of the new business.
parts.answer: After: 14.60%; on the new business: 13.00%

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should buy the business. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: return on the purchase (13%) is below the existing 15%, so overall ROCE falls to 14.60%; goodwill of $60,000 may be impaired; new shares dilute control. For: profit rises by $39,000; possible synergies or cost savings not in forecast; removes a competitor; growth and market share. Decision justified.
parts.working: 1 mark each side using figures, 1 mark non-financial point, 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem:
Juniper Ltd is buying the business of a sole trader. The sole trader's statement of financial position shows:
                               $
Land                      60,000
Equipment                 34,000
Inventory                 17,000
Trade receivables         11,000
Bank                       4,000
Trade payables           (9,500)
Loan                    (20,000)
Capital                   96,500
Juniper Ltd will take over all assets and liabilities except the bank balance. Agreed values: land $85,000; equipment $28,000; inventory to be reduced by $1,500; a provision for doubtful debts of 3% on trade receivables. The loan and trade payables are taken over at book value.
Consideration: 50,000 ordinary shares of $1 each issued at $1.80; $10,000 of 6% debentures; and $15,000 cash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net assets acquired at agreed values.
parts.working: B1 land and equipment at agreed values; B1 inventory 15,500; B1 receivables 10,670; B1 less payables and loan: 109,670.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the share premium arising.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain the effect on goodwill if the shares had been valued at $2.00 each instead of $1.80.
parts.answer: The consideration would rise by 50,000 × $0.20 = $10,000, so goodwill would also rise by $10,000 to $15,330 (net assets are unchanged).
parts.working: 1 mark: consideration +10,000; 1 mark: goodwill 15,330.

practice.stem: Larch Ltd is considering buying a sole trader's business. The business has made a steady profit of $58,000 a year, before any payment for the owner's work. After the purchase Larch Ltd would have to employ a manager at $22,000 a year. Larch Ltd requires a return of 12.5% a year on any investment. The fair value of the net assets is $247,000. The owner is asking $300,000 for the business.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum price Larch Ltd should pay to earn its required return.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum goodwill Larch Ltd should accept.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Larch Ltd whether to buy the business at the owner's asking price. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: At $300,000 the return is 36,000 ÷ 300,000 = 12%, below the 12.5% required, and goodwill of $53,000 exceeds the $41,000 justified. However, the business may grow, give synergies or remove a competitor, and the profit record is steady. Decision: do not buy at $300,000; offer up to $288,000, or buy only if future profits are expected to rise.
parts.working: 1 mark: return at asking price 12% / goodwill too high; 1 mark: non-financial or future factor; 1 mark: further relevant point; 1 mark: justified decision.

practice.stem:
Larkspur Ltd is negotiating to buy the business of Waleed, a sole trader in Rawalpindi. Waleed's reported profits were:
Year ended 30 June      Profit $
2023                      61,000
2024                      54,500
2025                      70,000
Further information:
1 Waleed has never charged himself a salary. Larkspur Ltd will employ a manager at $20,000 a year.
2 The 2024 profit is after a one-off loss of $7,500 caused by a flood; this will not happen again.
3 The 2025 profit includes rent received of $4,000 from sub-letting part of the premises; the sub-letting ends when the business is sold.
Goodwill is to be valued at 2.5 years' purchase of the average adjusted profit. The agreed value of the net assets is $292,500. The consideration is to be paid 25% in cash and the rest in ordinary shares of $1 each issued at $2.50 per share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the adjusted profit for each year and the average adjusted profit.
parts.working: Deduct 20,000 each year (B1); add back 7,500 in 2024 (B1); deduct 4,000 in 2025 (B1); average 129,000 ÷ 3 = 43,000 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill and the total purchase consideration.
parts.answer: Goodwill $107,500; consideration $400,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of shares issued and the share premium created.
parts.answer: 120,000 shares; share premium $180,000

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the rent received is removed from the 2025 profit.
parts.answer: Goodwill should reflect profits the buyer can expect to keep earning (maintainable profit). The rent will stop, so including it would overstate future profit and the price.
parts.working: 1 mark maintainable/future profit; 1 mark overstatement.

practice.stem:
On 1 March 2025 Banyan Ltd, Colombo, bought a partnership business. It paid $34,000 in cash and issued 90,000 ordinary shares of $1 each; the market price of a Banyan Ltd share on that date was $2.40. The fair value of the identifiable net assets acquired was $228,500.
Banyan Ltd also paid legal and due-diligence fees of $6,500 for the purchase, and $2,800 of costs for issuing the new shares. Before the purchase the share premium account had a balance of $40,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill arising on the purchase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance on the share premium account after the purchase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the legal and due-diligence fees are treated, and their effect on profit for the year.
parts.answer: They are acquisition costs, charged as an expense in the statement of profit or loss (not added to goodwill); profit for the year falls by $6,500.
parts.working: B1 expense, not goodwill; B1 profit reduced by 6,500.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the directors might have preferred to add the fees to goodwill.
parts.answer: Adding them to goodwill would avoid reducing this year's profit (and EPS); the cost would only reach profit later if goodwill were impaired. This is not allowed because the fees are not part of the value of the business acquired.
parts.working: 1 mark higher reported profit; 1 mark reason not allowed.

practice.stem:
Cypress Ltd expects a return of at least 12% a year on the price it pays for any business. It is choosing between two businesses for sale in Faisalabad:
                                 Business X    Business Y
                                          $             $
Asking price                       380,000       300,000
Fair value of net assets           320,000       290,000
Expected annual profit              52,000        33,000
Business X has a well-known brand and a long-term supply contract with a supermarket chain. Business Y owns modern machinery but its two largest customers are reviewing their contracts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill included in each asking price.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected return on the asking price for each business, to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors which business, if either, they should buy. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: X: return 13.68% exceeds the 12% target; brand and supermarket contract support future profit; but goodwill of $60,000 is high and may be impaired. Y: return 11.00% is below target; goodwill is low and price is mostly backed by tangible assets (lower risk of loss); but risk of losing key customers could cut profit further. Other factors: finance available, fit with existing business, reliability of forecasts. Decision: buy X (meets target, stronger future prospects) – or a justified alternative.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks on X, up to 2 marks on Y using figures, 1 mark other factor, 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem:
The owner of a private school in Abbottabad is selling the business to Elm Education Ltd. The school's profits, after charging a fair salary for the head teacher, were:
Year      Profit $   Weight
2023        50,000        1
2024        56,000        2
2025        62,000        3
The agreed value of the net assets is $400,000. A normal return for this kind of business is 11% a year. Elm Education Ltd proposes to value goodwill at 2.5 years' purchase of the super profit, based on the weighted average profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the weighted average profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the super profit and the goodwill proposed by Elm Education Ltd.
parts.answer: Super profit $14,000; goodwill $35,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: The owner is asking $460,000 for the school. Calculate how many years' purchase of super profit this price implies, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 4.29 years
parts.working: Goodwill in asking price 460,000 − 400,000 = 60,000 (M1); ÷ 14,000 = 4.29 years (A1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why a weighted average is used, and one reason why the owner may argue for a higher number of years' purchase.
parts.answer: Weighting gives more importance to recent profits, which better predict future profit when profits are rising. Owner's argument: e.g. strong reputation and waiting list mean super profits are likely to last longer than 2.5 years.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: On 1 April 2027 Ayesha and Bilal combined their sole-trader businesses to form a partnership. The agreed value of the net assets brought in was Ayesha $84,000 and Bilal $62,000. Goodwill was valued at $16,000 for Ayesha's business and $10,000 for Bilal's, and is to be kept in the partnership books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's opening capital.
parts.answer: Ayesha $100,000; Bilal $72,000
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total net assets of the partnership, including goodwill.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the assets of each business are revalued before the merger.
parts.answer: Book values may not reflect current worth; revaluing at agreed fair values means each partner is credited with the true value of what they bring in, so neither partner gains at the other's expense.
parts.working: 1 mark: book values out of date; 1 mark: fairness between partners/correct capital.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages and two disadvantages for two sole traders of merging their businesses to form a partnership.
parts.answer:
Advantages (any two): more capital; shared workload and skills; economies of scale (bulk buying); losses and risks shared; cover for holidays and illness.
Disadvantages (any two): profits shared; decisions must be agreed and disputes may arise; unlimited liability for the other partner's actions; loss of independence.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two advantages and two disadvantages.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the two owners must agree a value for goodwill before merging.
parts.answer: Each business may have built up goodwill of different value. If it is not valued and credited to the owner who created it, the other partner would share in it without paying, so capitals would be unfair.
parts.working: 1 mark: goodwill differs between businesses; 1 mark: fairness of capital/profit sharing.

practice.stem:
Kamran, a sole trader in Hyderabad, India, is merging his business with that of Lakshmi to form a partnership. His statement of financial position before the merger showed: premises $85,000; vehicle $14,000; inventory $12,600; trade receivables $9,000; bank $3,400; trade payables $6,800.
For the merger it was agreed that: premises are valued at $98,000; the vehicle at $11,500; inventory at $11,900; and an allowance for irrecoverable debts of 4% is made on trade receivables. Other items are taken over at book value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Kamran's capital according to his statement of financial position before the merger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Kamran's opening capital in the partnership.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net gain on revaluation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why an allowance for irrecoverable debts is made before the receivables are transferred.
parts.answer: Prudence: some customers may not pay, so receivables should not be overstated; otherwise Kamran would be credited with capital for amounts the partnership may never collect, which would be unfair to Lakshmi.
parts.working: 1 mark prudence/not overstated; 1 mark fairness between partners.

practice.stem: Lina and Musa, two sole traders selling mobile phone accessories in Amman, merged their businesses on 1 January 2025. Lina brought in net assets of $90,000 and Musa $60,000. Their partnership agreement says profits and losses are shared in the ratio of their opening capitals. The profit for the first year was $72,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit-sharing ratio in its simplest form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's share of the profit for the first year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how profits would be shared if the partners had no partnership agreement, and give one reason why sharing in the capital ratio may be unfair to Musa.
parts.answer: Equally (Partnership Act 1890). Musa may work longer hours or bring more skill/customers, but receives a smaller share because he brought less capital.
parts.working: B1 equally; B1 reason.

practice.stem: On 1 April 2025 Nida brought the following into a new partnership formed by merging her business with that of Parveen: premises $120,000; equipment $15,000; inventory $8,000; and her trade payables of $5,000, which the partnership took over.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Nida's opening capital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry in the partnership's books to record the assets and liabilities brought in by Nida. A narrative is required.
parts.answer: Dr Premises 120,000; Dr Equipment 15,000; Dr Inventory 8,000; Cr Trade payables 5,000; Cr Capital – Nida 138,000. Narrative: assets and liabilities introduced by Nida on the merger of her business into the partnership.
parts.working: B1 assets debited; B1 payables credited; B1 capital credited 138,000; B1 narrative.

practice.stem: Two sole traders who run neighbouring shoe shops in Mardan are planning to merge their businesses into a partnership.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three matters that their partnership agreement should cover because of the merger.
parts.answer: Any three: agreed values of each trader's assets and liabilities; value and treatment of goodwill (kept or written off); which liabilities the partnership takes over; profit-sharing ratio; interest on capital and drawings; partners' salaries; amount of capital each must keep in the business.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the agreed values of the assets may differ from their book values.
parts.answer: Book values are based on historical cost less depreciation, which may not reflect current market values (e.g. property prices rise, inventory becomes obsolete); fair values are needed so each trader's capital is fair.
parts.working: 1 mark historical cost; 1 mark fairness/current value.

practice.stem:
Owais and Pervez merged their tailoring businesses in Lahore on 1 July 2025. Goodwill of each business is valued at 1.5 times the average profit of its last two years, and goodwill is to be kept in the partnership books.
                       Owais $    Pervez $
Profit 2023/24          28,000      21,000
Profit 2024/25          32,000      25,000
Agreed net assets       70,000      58,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill of each business.
parts.answer: Owais $45,000; Pervez $34,500
parts.working: Averages 30,000 and 23,000; × 1.5 (B1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's opening capital.
parts.answer: Owais $115,000; Pervez $92,500
parts.working: Net assets + goodwill (B1 each).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total of the partnership's opening statement of financial position (net assets including goodwill).

practice.stem:
On 1 July 2026 Carla and Diego merged their businesses to form a partnership. Their statements of financial position on that date were:
                         Carla $   Diego $
Premises                  70,000         –
Equipment                 12,000    18,000
Vehicle                        –    11,000
Inventory                  9,000     7,500
Trade receivables          6,500     4,000
Bank                       3,500     2,600
Trade payables           (5,000)   (4,100)
It was agreed that: Carla's premises are revalued at $82,000; Diego's vehicle is valued at $9,500; a provision for doubtful debts of 5% is made on Diego's trade receivables; no goodwill is recorded. All other items are taken over at book value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's opening capital.
parts.working: B1 Carla's premises 82,000; B1 Carla 108,000; B1 Diego's vehicle and receivables 9,500 and 3,800; B1 Diego 37,300.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the opening statement of financial position of the partnership.
parts.answer:
Carla and Diego – Statement of financial position at 1 July 2026
                                           $         $
Non-current assets
Premises                              82,000
Equipment                             30,000
Vehicle                                9,500   121,500
Current assets
Inventory                             16,500
Trade receivables                     10,300
Bank                                   6,100    32,900
Total assets                                   154,400
Current liabilities: trade payables             (9,100)
Net assets                                     145,300
Capital: Carla                                 108,000
Capital: Diego                                  37,300
                                               145,300
parts.working: B1 non-current assets 121,500; B1 receivables 10,300 and other current assets; B1 payables 9,100; B1 capitals totalling 145,300.

practice.stem: Ellie and Faisal merged their businesses. Ellie brought in net assets of $55,000 and goodwill valued at $20,000; Faisal brought in net assets of $40,000 and goodwill valued at $8,000. They will share profits Ellie 3 : Faisal 2. Goodwill is not to be kept in the books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's capital after goodwill has been written off.
parts.answer: Ellie $58,200; Faisal $36,800
parts.working: B1 capitals credited 75,000 and 48,000; B1 goodwill 28,000 written off in 3:2; B1 debits 16,800 and 11,200; B1 Ellie 58,200 and Faisal 36,800.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether Faisal gains or loses from this treatment of goodwill.
parts.answer: Faisal loses $3,200: he was credited with $8,000 of goodwill but is debited with $11,200 (2/5 of $28,000). Ellie gains $3,200: credited with $20,000 but debited with only $16,800. Writing goodwill off in the new ratio, which differs from the ratio in which it was contributed, transfers value from Faisal to Ellie.
parts.working: 1 mark: loses 3,200 with figures; 1 mark: reason – goodwill written off in new ratio differs from contribution.

practice.stem:
Qadir, Rubina and Sana each ran a small courier business in Karachi. On 1 October 2025 they merged to form a partnership sharing profits equally. Agreed values were:
                       Qadir $   Rubina $    Sana $
Net assets              64,000     51,000    47,000
Goodwill                30,000     18,000    12,000
Goodwill is to be credited to each partner and then written off in the profit-sharing ratio; it is not kept in the books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's opening capital after goodwill has been written off.
parts.working: Total goodwill 60,000 written off 20,000 each (B1); Qadir 94,000 − 20,000 (B1); Rubina 69,000 − 20,000 (B1); Sana 59,000 − 20,000 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each partner, calculate the gain or loss caused by this treatment of goodwill compared with their net assets brought in.
parts.answer: Qadir gains $10,000; Rubina loses $2,000; Sana loses $8,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Qadir gains even though goodwill is not shown in the books.
parts.answer: He brought in the most goodwill but bears only one third of the write-off, so his capital is credited with the excess.

practice.stem:
Tariq, a sole trader in Riyadh, is about to merge his business with that of Umar. Before the merger he adjusts his own books to the agreed values. His capital balance before any adjustment is $88,000. Agreed changes:
• premises: book value $60,000, agreed value $75,000
• machinery: book value $22,000, agreed value $17,500
• inventory: book value $9,800, agreed value $9,100
• goodwill of $12,000 is to be recognised

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the revaluation account in Tariq's books.
parts.answer:
Revaluation account
Dr: Machinery 4,500; Inventory 700; Capital – Tariq (gain) 21,800 = 27,000
Cr: Premises 15,000; Goodwill 12,000 = 27,000
parts.working: B1 premises 15,000 credit; B1 goodwill 12,000 credit; B1 machinery and inventory debits; B1 gain 21,800 to capital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the capital Tariq will transfer to the partnership.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a decrease in the value of machinery is debited to the revaluation account.
parts.answer: A fall in an asset's value is a loss, which reduces the owner's capital; the asset account is credited and the loss debited.

practice.stem:
Uzair and Vania merged their businesses in Nairobi on 1 June 2025, taking over all assets and liabilities at book value. On that date:
                              Uzair $     Vania $
Premises                            –      75,000
Equipment                      30,000           –
Inventory                      14,000       9,500
Trade receivables              11,500       7,800
Bank                            6,000     (2,600) overdraft
Trade payables                 (8,200)    (10,400)
Uzair's trade receivables include $3,000 owed by Vania's business, and Vania's trade payables include the same $3,000 owed to Uzair. The partnership will keep one bank account and the overdraft is cleared from Uzair's bank balance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's opening capital.
parts.answer: Uzair $53,300; Vania $79,300
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the opening statement of financial position of the partnership at 1 June 2025.
parts.answer:
Non-current assets: premises 75,000; equipment 30,000 = 105,000
Current assets: inventory 23,500; trade receivables 16,300; bank 3,400 = 43,200
Current liabilities: trade payables 15,600
Net assets 132,600
Capital: Uzair 53,300; Vania 79,300 = 132,600
parts.working: B1 non-current assets; B1 receivables 16,300 (inter-business debt removed); B1 payables 15,600; B1 bank 3,400; B1 capitals and balancing totals.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the $3,000 is removed from both receivables and payables.
parts.answer: After the merger it is a debt the partnership owes to itself, so it is no longer an asset or a liability.

practice.stem: Wasim and Yasmin, sole traders in Islamabad, agreed to merge their businesses into a new private limited company, WY Foods Ltd. Agreed values: Wasim – net assets $140,000 and goodwill $20,000; Yasmin – net assets $96,000 and goodwill $4,000. Each receives ordinary shares of $1 each, issued at par, equal to the total value of the business brought in.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of shares issued to each owner.
parts.answer: Wasim 160,000; Yasmin 100,000
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the voting shares held by each owner, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Wasim 61.54%; Yasmin 38.46%

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for Yasmin of merging into a limited company rather than a partnership.
parts.answer: Advantage: limited liability – she can lose only her investment. Disadvantage: as a minority shareholder Wasim can outvote her on ordinary resolutions; or more regulation and published accounts.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Zain owns a software repair business in Lahore that earns a profit of $40,000 a year. Ahsan, who runs a similar business, suggests merging into a partnership. The forecast profit of the merged business is $115,000 a year. The proposed agreement is:
• capitals: Zain $120,000, Ahsan $80,000
• interest on capital at 5% a year
• salaries: Zain $15,000, Ahsan $10,000
• remaining profit shared equally

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the residual profit to be shared equally.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Zain's total expected income from the partnership.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Zain whether he should agree to the merger. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: income rises from $40,000 to $61,000 (+$21,000); shared workload, skills and customers; more capital for growth. Against: forecast may be optimistic; profits must be shared and decisions agreed with Ahsan; unlimited liability for Ahsan's actions (joint and several); he puts in more capital but residual profit is shared equally; disputes may arise. Decision justified.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for, up to 2 against, 1 mark use of figures, 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: Gul and Hira merged their sole-trader businesses on 1 January 2027 to form a partnership sharing profits Gul 3 : Hira 2. Agreed values: Gul net assets $71,000 and goodwill $15,000; Hira net assets $52,500 and goodwill $6,000. Goodwill is to be written off in the new profit-sharing ratio. The partners agree that total capital will be $150,000, held in their profit-sharing ratio, and each partner will pay in cash to achieve this.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's capital before goodwill is written off.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's capital after goodwill is written off.
parts.working: B1 write-off 12,600 : 8,400; B1 both capitals.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the cash each partner must pay in.
parts.working: B1 target 90,000 : 60,000; B1 both amounts.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the net assets of the partnership after the cash has been paid in.

practice.stem: Akbar and Bano are partners in a printing business in Gujranwala, sharing profits 3 : 2. Their capitals are Akbar $80,000 and Bano $60,000. On 1 January 2025 their partnership merged with the business of Chen, a sole trader, who brought in net assets of $45,000. Goodwill was valued at $40,000 for the partnership and $15,000 for Chen's business. In the new partnership Akbar, Bano and Chen will share profits 2 : 2 : 1. Goodwill is not to be kept in the books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of goodwill credited to and debited to each partner's capital account.
parts.answer: Credited: Akbar $24,000; Bano $16,000; Chen $15,000. Debited (written off 2 : 2 : 1): Akbar $22,000; Bano $22,000; Chen $11,000
parts.working: B1 partnership goodwill 3 : 2; B1 Chen 15,000; B1 total 55,000; B1 write-off 2 : 2 : 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's capital after the merger.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Bano's capital falls even though her business had goodwill of $40,000.
parts.answer: She is credited with $16,000 (2/5 of her old firm's goodwill) but debited with $22,000 (2/5 of the total goodwill of $55,000). The extra $6,000 is her payment for a 2/5 share of Chen's goodwill ($15,000 × 2/5), which she now shares in.
parts.working: 1 mark debit 22,000 exceeds credit 16,000; 1 mark she is paying for a share of the goodwill owned by others.

practice.stem:
Daud and Erum, sole traders in Peshawar, merged their businesses on 1 September 2025 to form Dera Supplies Ltd.
• Daud's business: assets less current liabilities $150,000, but it also has a $30,000 loan from a relative. The company takes over the loan by issuing $30,000 of 7% debentures to the relative. Daud's goodwill is valued at $25,000.
• Erum's business: net assets $95,000; goodwill $5,000.
Each owner receives ordinary shares of $1 each, issued at $1.25 per share, equal to the value of his or her net assets plus goodwill.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of the business brought in by each owner.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of shares issued to each owner.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the company's ordinary share capital, share premium and total equity on 1 September 2025.
parts.answer: Share capital $196,000; share premium $49,000; total equity $245,000
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the ordinary shares held by Daud, to two decimal places, and explain one reason why Erum may be concerned.
parts.answer: 59.18%; Daud holds a majority so can control ordinary resolutions and the board.
parts.working: B1 percentage; B1 explanation.

practice.stem:
Two partnerships of architects in Karachi merged on 1 March 2025.
• Faraz and Gohar shared profits 3 : 2; capitals Faraz $70,000, Gohar $50,000; goodwill of their firm valued at $50,000.
• Hania and Irfan shared profits equally; capitals Hania $65,000, Irfan $45,000; goodwill of their firm valued at $30,000.
In the merged partnership Faraz, Gohar, Hania and Irfan will share profits 3 : 2 : 3 : 2. Goodwill is to be credited to the old partners in their old ratios and written off in the new ratio; it is not kept in the books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net adjustment to each partner's capital for goodwill, stating whether it is an increase or a decrease.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's capital in the merged partnership.
parts.working: B2 all four correct; B1 two correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Hania and Irfan might still agree to these terms.
parts.answer: Their share of a larger firm's profit (50% in total, the same as Faraz and Gohar) may give them a higher income than before, even though their firm had less goodwill; access to bigger clients, shared costs.
parts.working: 1 mark profit share/higher income; 1 mark other benefit.

practice.stem:
Jamal and Kiran merged their sole-trader businesses on 1 January 2025 to form a partnership. Their opening capitals, based on the agreed values of the net assets they brought in, were Jamal $84,000 and Kiran $56,000. The partnership agreement provides for:
• interest on capital at 6% a year
• a salary for Kiran of $12,000 a year
• interest on drawings: Jamal $500, Kiran $375
• remaining profit shared in the ratio of opening capitals
Profit for the year ended 31 December 2025 was $68,000. Before the merger Kiran's own business made a profit of $30,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the appropriation account for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer: Profit for the year 68,000; add interest on drawings Jamal 500, Kiran 375 = 68,875; less interest on capital Jamal 5,040, Kiran 3,360; salary Kiran 12,000; residual profit 48,475 shared Jamal 29,085 (3/5), Kiran 19,390 (2/5).
parts.working: B1 interest on drawings added; B1 interest on capital; B1 salary; B1 residual 48,475; B1 shares in 3 : 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Kiran's total income from the partnership for the year, net of interest on drawings, and compare it with her profit before the merger.
parts.answer: $34,375; $4,375 more than the $30,000 she earned alone

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the partners chose to share residual profit in the ratio of opening capitals and how Kiran's salary balances this.
parts.answer: Capital ratio rewards Jamal for bringing more net assets (3 : 2). Kiran's salary rewards her for the extra work she does, so the agreement rewards both capital and effort.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Laila and Moin are merging their stationery businesses in Lahore into a partnership that will share profits equally. Laila's draft statement of financial position shows net assets of $92,000. Before the merger the following are discovered in Laila's books:
1 electricity of $1,400 owing has not been recorded
2 inventory is overstated by $2,600 because damaged items were valued at cost
3 a customer owing $1,800 has become bankrupt and will pay nothing
Moin's net assets are agreed at $70,000. Goodwill is valued at $18,000 for Laila's business and $12,000 for Moin's. Goodwill is to be credited to each partner and then written off equally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Laila's agreed net assets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's opening capital.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Laila argues that the goodwill should be kept in the books rather than written off. Discuss whether this would be better for her.
parts.answer: If goodwill were kept, capitals would be Laila $104,200 and Moin $82,000. The difference between them is $22,200 either way (89,200 − 67,000 = 104,200 − 82,000), so her position relative to Moin is the same. Keeping it would only help if interest on capital is paid (higher capital, more interest – but Moin gains too). Kept goodwill may later be impaired, and any loss would be shared equally. Conclusion: not clearly better for her; writing it off is more prudent.
parts.working: 1 mark figures/same difference; 1 mark impairment or interest point; 1 mark reasoned conclusion.
