parts.label: a
parts.text:
A product uses direct materials of $14 and 2.5 direct labour hours at $12 per hour. Production overheads are absorbed at $8 per direct labour hour. The selling price is full production cost plus a mark-up of 25%. What is the selling price?
A $85.33
B $80.00
C $64.00
D $55.00
parts.working: Full cost = 14 + 30 + 20 = 64; price = 64 × 1.25 = 80.00. A applies 25% as a margin on selling price (64 ÷ 0.75); C is full cost with no mark-up; D applies the mark-up to prime cost only (44 × 1.25).

practice.stem: A company in Multan packs olive-oil gift boxes. Each box uses direct materials of $8.40 and 0.5 direct labour hours at $14 per hour. Production overheads are absorbed at $18 per direct labour hour. Administration overheads are absorbed at 10% of production cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the production cost of one box.
parts.working: B1 labour 7.00; B1 overhead 9.00; B1 total 24.40.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of one box.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The company wants a profit margin of 20% on the selling price. Calculate the selling price of one box.

practice.stem: A printing firm in Rawalpindi has completed a job printing school yearbooks. Direct materials cost $1,240. Direct labour was 36 hours at $13 per hour. Production overheads are absorbed at $21 per direct labour hour. The price quoted to the school was $3,080.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the job.
parts.working: B1 labour 468 and overhead 756; B1 total 2,464.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the job.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit as (i) a mark-up on cost and (ii) a margin on the price.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The full cost of a product is $72 per unit. The business wants a profit margin of 25% of the selling price.
What is the selling price per unit?
A $54.00
B $90.00
C $96.00
D $108.00
parts.working: Margin of 25% means cost = 75% of price: 72 ÷ 0.75 = $96. $90 is a 25% mark-up on cost (72 × 1.25), which confuses mark-up with margin.

practice.stem:
A sportswear maker in Sialkot makes football shirts. For each shirt:
Fabric $3.80
Trims and labels $0.70
Direct labour 0.4 hours at $9 per hour
Production overheads are absorbed at $6.50 per direct labour hour. Administration and selling overheads are added at 15% of production cost. The selling price is total cost plus a mark-up of 25%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the prime cost of one shirt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the production cost of one shirt.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of one shirt.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of one shirt, correct to the nearest cent.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Calculate the profit as a percentage of the selling price.

practice.stem:
A furniture workshop in Faisalabad is quoting for Job 417, a set of tables for a hotel.
                                  Machining        Finishing
Direct labour hours                      12               30
Machine hours                            18                –
Labour rate per hour                    $11               $9
Overhead absorption rate    $24 per mach hr   $15 per lab hr
Direct materials for the job cost $2,860. The workshop adds a mark-up of 30% to total cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of Job 417.
parts.working: B1 labour 132 + 270 = 402; B1 machining overhead 18 × 24 = 432; B1 finishing overhead 30 × 15 = 450; B1 total 4,144.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price quoted for the job.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The hotel offers $5,000 for the job. Calculate the profit as a percentage of total cost at this price. Give your answer to two decimal places.

practice.stem: Rehman Ltd prices its products at full cost plus a mark-up of 40%. Product K has a full cost of $65 per unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of product K.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit margin (profit as a percentage of selling price). Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A competitor sells a similar product for $84. Calculate the mark-up Rehman Ltd would earn if it matched this price. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of cost-plus pricing.
parts.answer: Advantage: simple, and every unit sold covers its full cost / gives a profit if budgeted volume is achieved. Disadvantage: ignores competitors' prices and customer demand; if output falls, cost per unit rises and the price may be uncompetitive.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid advantage; 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.

practice.stem: Nexa Ltd has capital employed of $600,000 and wants a return on capital employed of 15% a year. It plans to make and sell 24,000 units of its only product. The full absorption cost is $32 per unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit required for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the selling price per unit needed to earn this return.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mark-up percentage on full cost. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain two limitations of setting the price in this way.
parts.answer: Any two: the return is achieved only if 24,000 units are actually sold; the price ignores what customers will pay and competitors' prices; the full cost depends on the absorption basis chosen, which is arbitrary; a higher price may reduce demand, raising cost per unit.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid limitations.

practice.stem:
Nadia Fashions, Karachi, makes a quilted jacket. A competitor sells a very similar jacket for $48, and Nadia's sales manager believes Nadia must charge the same price. The company requires a profit margin of 20% of the selling price.
Current full cost of one jacket:
                                     $
Direct materials                 18.50
Direct labour                    12.00
Production overheads              7.20
Non-production overheads          3.50
Full cost                        41.20

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum full cost per jacket that allows the required margin at a price of $48.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost reduction needed per jacket, in dollars and as a percentage of the current full cost. Give the percentage to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which Nadia Fashions could reduce the cost of a jacket.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. negotiate bulk discounts or cheaper fabric suppliers; reduce fabric waste in cutting; train staff to raise labour productivity; cut factory overheads such as energy use.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible, specific ways.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain one limitation of setting prices by adding a mark-up to full cost.
parts.answer: It ignores what customers will pay and competitors' prices, so the price may be too high to sell (or lower than the market would bear); also the full cost depends on the budgeted volume and on arbitrary apportionment of overheads.
parts.working: 1 mark for the limitation; 1 mark for the explanation/consequence.

practice.stem:
Falcon Data Services, Dubai, prices client jobs at full cost plus a mark-up of 20%. Staff time is costed at $40 per hour, and overheads are absorbed at 75% of staff cost. Travel costs are passed on to the client at cost, with no mark-up.
A client has asked for a quote for a job needing 120 staff hours and travel costing $900.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price Falcon Data Services would quote for the job.
parts.working: B1 staff cost 4,800; B1 overheads 3,600; M1 full cost 8,400 × 1.2 = 10,080; A1 + travel 900 = 10,980.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The client offers to pay $9,000 in total, including travel. Calculate the profit or loss on the job using full cost.
parts.answer: Loss of $300

parts.label: c
parts.text: Staff are paid fixed monthly salaries and currently have idle time. Overheads will not change if the job is accepted. Advise Falcon Data Services whether to accept the client's offer. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Accept: the only extra cost is travel of $900, so profit rises by $8,100 even though full-cost accounting shows a $300 loss. But the low price may become expected by this and other clients, and staff may be needed for full-price work later.
parts.working: B1 relevant cost is travel only; B1 increase in profit 8,100; B1 one risk (precedent/other clients/capacity); B1 decision consistent with reasoning.

practice.stem:
Product T has a variable production cost of $26 per unit. Fixed production overheads of $180,000 a year are absorbed on budgeted production of 20,000 units. The selling price is full production cost plus a mark-up of 40%. There are no non-production costs.
In the year, only 16,000 units were made and sold at the budgeted price. Fixed production overheads were $180,000 as budgeted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the full production cost and the selling price of one unit.
parts.answer: Full cost $35; price $49

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted profit and the actual profit for the year.
parts.answer: Budgeted $280,000; actual $188,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the under-absorbed fixed production overhead for the year.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why profit fell by more than the mark-up on the 4,000 units not sold.
parts.answer: Mark-up lost = 4,000 × $14 = $56,000, but profit fell by $92,000: the fixed overheads of $36,000 meant to be recovered in the price of the lost 4,000 units were not recovered (under-absorbed), so they reduce profit too.
parts.working: B1 identifies the under-absorbed $36,000; B1 links 56,000 + 36,000 = 92,000.

practice.stem:
Indus Tiles Ltd makes floor tiles. Budgeted production is 40,000 boxes a year; the factory can make 50,000 boxes. The cost of one box at the budgeted output is:
                                       $
Direct materials                    6.00
Direct labour                       4.50
Variable production overhead        1.50
Fixed production overhead           3.00
The normal selling price is $20 per box. An overseas customer offers to buy 8,000 boxes at $13.50 per box. Special packaging costing $0.40 per box would be needed. Fixed costs will not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the full production cost of one box.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect on profit of accepting the order.
parts.answer: Profit increases by $8,800
parts.working: B1 relevant cost per box 12.40 (fixed overhead excluded, packaging included); B1 contribution 1.10 per box; B1 total 8,800 increase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should accept the order. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Accept, on the figures: there is spare capacity of 10,000 boxes, fixed overheads are already covered by normal sales, so the order adds $8,800 to profit even though $13.50 is below full cost of $15.00. Against: existing customers may learn of the low price and demand a reduction; the margin is very thin (1.10 per box), so a small cost rise wipes it out; currency and payment risk on an overseas customer; capacity may be needed if domestic demand grows. Decision: accept as a one-off order if it can be kept separate from the home market.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points in favour (spare capacity, positive contribution, fixed costs unchanged, possible future orders); up to 2 marks for points against (effect on regular prices, low margin, risk, capacity); 1 mark for a clear decision consistent with the points.

practice.stem:
A factory has budgeted production overheads of $180,000 for the year. Budgeted activity is 30,000 direct labour hours and 12,000 machine hours. It makes two products:
                                Product P  Product Q
Prime cost per unit                   $30        $28
Direct labour hours per unit            2          1
Machine hours per unit                0.5        1.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate an overhead absorption rate per direct labour hour and per machine hour.
parts.answer: $6.00 per labour hour; $15.00 per machine hour
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the full production cost of each product using each absorption rate.
parts.answer:
Labour hour basis: P $42.00, Q $34.00
Machine hour basis: P $37.50, Q $50.50
parts.working: 1 mark for each cost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The factory is highly automated. Explain which absorption rate should be used and the effect on pricing if the other rate were used.
parts.answer: Machine hours, because most overheads (power, depreciation, maintenance) are caused by machine running time. With the labour hour rate Q would be under-costed (34.00 instead of 50.50) and could be priced below its true cost, while P would be over-costed and priced uncompetitively.
parts.working: 1 mark: machine hour rate with reason; 1 mark: Q undercosted/underpriced and P overcosted.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A product has a variable production cost of $11 per unit. Fixed production overheads of $240,000 are absorbed on budgeted output of 60,000 units. The selling price is full production cost plus 30%. Budgeted output is then revised to 48,000 units, with no change in costs.
What is the revised selling price per unit?
A $19.30
B $19.50
C $20.80
D $22.10
parts.working: New fixed overhead per unit = 240,000 ÷ 48,000 = $5; full cost 11 + 5 = 16; price 16 × 1.3 = $20.80. $19.50 is the old price (11 + 4) × 1.3, ignoring the revised volume. The rise shows a weakness of absorption cost-plus pricing: lower volume pushes the price up.

practice.stem:
Ravi Plastics Ltd can make up to 50,000 crates a year. It expects to sell 44,000 crates at $30 each. Each crate has a variable cost of $15. Fixed production overheads are absorbed at $9 per crate, based on full capacity of 50,000 crates; actual fixed overheads equal the amount budgeted.
A supermarket chain offers to buy 10,000 crates at $22 each this year. If accepted, Ravi Plastics would lose sales of 4,000 crates to its normal customers because of the capacity limit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total fixed production overheads.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in Ravi Plastics' profit if the order is accepted.
parts.answer: Increase of $10,000
parts.working: B1 contribution from order 10,000 × 7 = 70,000; B1 lost sales 4,000; B1 lost contribution 4,000 × 15 = 60,000; A1 +10,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The production manager says: 'The price of $22 is below the full cost of $24, so we will lose $20,000.' Explain why this view is wrong.
parts.answer: The $9 fixed overhead per crate is not an extra cost: total fixed overheads stay $450,000 whether or not the order is taken, so only variable costs and lost contribution are relevant.
parts.working: B1 fixed costs unchanged by the decision; B1 relevant costs are variable costs and lost contribution.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to accept the order. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Financially accept: profit rises by $10,000. Against: the gain is small; turning away 4,000 crates of regular orders may lose loyal customers permanently; the supermarket may expect $22 again; other customers may learn of the low price. For: large new customer, possible future orders, uses full capacity. A decision with reasons (e.g. accept only if the 4,000 lost crates can be scheduled later or the supermarket accepts fewer crates).
parts.working: B1 uses the +10,000; up to 2 marks for points against; up to 2 marks for points for (incl. non-financial); B1 justified decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Factory rent of $72,000 is apportioned on floor area. Machining occupies 2,400 m², Assembly 1,800 m² and Stores 600 m². How much rent is apportioned to Machining?
A $24,000
B $27,000
C $36,000
D $41,143
parts.working: 72,000 × 2,400 ÷ 4,800 = 36,000. D leaves the Stores area out of the total; the service department must also take its share of rent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between allocation and apportionment of overheads.
parts.answer: Allocation charges a whole overhead to one cost centre because it was incurred wholly by that centre (e.g. a supervisor who works only in assembly). Apportionment shares an overhead between several cost centres on a fair basis because it is shared (e.g. factory rent).
parts.working: 1 mark allocation – whole cost to one centre; 1 mark apportionment – shared cost split on a suitable basis.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Suggest a suitable basis of apportionment for each of the following overheads.
(i) Factory rent
(ii) Depreciation of machinery
(iii) Canteen costs
(iv) Insurance of buildings
parts.answer: (i) Floor area (ii) Cost or carrying amount of machinery (iii) Number of employees (iv) Floor area or value of buildings occupied
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A factory has three departments: Cutting, Packing and Stores. Which overhead should be allocated to the Packing department rather than apportioned?
A factory rent
B the salary of the packing department supervisor
C insurance of the factory building
D the cost of running the staff canteen
parts.answer: B the salary of the packing department supervisor
parts.working: Allocation is used when the whole cost is caused by one cost centre: the packing supervisor works only in Packing. Rent, building insurance and canteen costs are shared by all departments, so they must be apportioned on a fair basis.

practice.stem:
A bakery in Peshawar has three production departments: Mixing, Baking and Packing.
                        Mixing    Baking   Packing
Floor area (m²)            300       500       400
Power used (kWh)        12,000    33,000     9,000
Factory rent is $36,000 a year and power costs $27,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Apportion the factory rent to the three departments.
parts.answer: Mixing $9,000; Baking $15,000; Packing $12,000
parts.working: M1 $30 per m²; A1 two correct; A1 all three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Apportion the power cost to the three departments.
parts.answer: Mixing $6,000; Baking $16,500; Packing $4,500
parts.working: M1 $0.50 per kWh; A1 two correct; A1 all three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a suitable basis for apportioning the cost of the staff first-aid room. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Number of employees in each department, because the service is used by people, so more staff means more use.
parts.working: B1 basis; B1 reason.

practice.stem: A furniture factory has two production departments (Machining and Assembly) and two service departments (Stores and Maintenance).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the overheads of the service departments must be reapportioned to the production departments.
parts.answer: Products pass only through production departments, so overhead absorption rates are set only for them; service department costs must therefore be added to the production departments, or they would never be included in product costs.
parts.working: B1 products do not pass through service departments; B1 so their costs would not be absorbed into product cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a suitable basis for reapportioning (i) Stores overheads and (ii) Maintenance overheads.
parts.answer: (i) number (or value) of material requisitions; (ii) maintenance hours worked for each department.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the difference between a cost centre and a cost unit.
parts.answer: A cost centre is a location, department or function for which costs are collected (e.g. Machining); a cost unit is a unit of product or service to which costs are charged (e.g. one chair).
parts.working: B1 each, with example or clear meaning.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Canteen overheads of $28,000 are reapportioned to the two production departments on the number of employees. Department X has 45 employees, Department Y has 25 and the canteen has 10. How much is reapportioned to Department X?
A $15,750
B $18,000
C $14,000
D $10,000
parts.working: A service department's costs are shared only between the departments it serves: 28,000 × 45 ÷ 70 = 18,000. A wrongly includes the canteen's own 10 employees in the total.

practice.stem:
A garment factory in Sialkot has two production departments, Cutting and Stitching, and one service department, Maintenance. Budgeted overheads for the year are:
Indirect materials $9,800, allocated: Cutting $4,200; Stitching $3,100; Maintenance $2,500
Rent and rates $48,000, apportioned on floor area
Depreciation of machinery $30,000, apportioned on cost of machinery
Supervisors' salaries $21,000, apportioned on number of employees
Power $16,000, apportioned on kilowatt hours
                             Cutting   Stitching Maintenance
Floor area (m²)                1,500       2,000         500
Cost of machinery ($)         90,000      50,000      10,000
Number of employees               12          24           4
Kilowatt hours                50,000      25,000       5,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare an overhead analysis sheet showing the total overheads of each department.
parts.answer:
Total   Cutting Stitching    Maint.
                                     $         $         $         $
Indirect materials               9,800     4,200     3,100     2,500
Rent and rates                  48,000    18,000    24,000     6,000
Depreciation of machinery       30,000    18,000    10,000     2,000
Supervisors' salaries           21,000     6,300    12,600     2,100
Power                           16,000    10,000     5,000     1,000
Total                          124,800    56,500    54,700    13,600
parts.working: B1 allocation; B1 rent; B1 depreciation; B1 salaries; B1 power; B1 totals 56,500, 54,700 and 13,600.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Maintenance spends 60% of its time on Cutting and 40% on Stitching. Calculate the total overheads of each production department after reapportionment.
parts.answer: Cutting $64,660; Stitching $60,140
parts.working: B1 8,160 and 5,440 reapportioned; B1 totals 64,660 and 60,140.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Machinery insurance of $45,000 is apportioned on the carrying amount of machinery: Moulding $270,000, Finishing $180,000, Stores $150,000.
How much is apportioned to Moulding?
A $15,000
B $18,000
C $20,250
D $27,000
parts.working: 45,000 × 270,000 ÷ 600,000 = $20,250. $15,000 is an equal three-way split, which ignores the chosen basis.

practice.stem:
Gulberg Print Works, Lahore, has three production departments. Budgeted overheads for next year:
Indirect labour: Pre-press $18,400; Printing $42,600; Binding $21,000
Rent and rates $64,000
Depreciation of machinery $48,000
Electricity $30,000
Staff welfare $13,500
                          Pre-press   Printing    Binding
Floor area (m²)                 500      1,100        900
Cost of machinery ($)        60,000    220,000    120,000
Electricity (kWh)             5,000     17,000      8,000
Number of employees               6          9         12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare an overhead analysis sheet showing the budgeted overheads of each department. State the basis used for each apportioned overhead.
parts.answer:
Basis: rent – floor area; depreciation – cost of machinery; electricity – kWh; welfare – employees.
                    Pre-press   Printing    Binding
Indirect labour        18,400     42,600     21,000
Rent and rates         12,800     28,160     23,040
Depreciation            7,200     26,400     14,400
Electricity             5,000     17,000      8,000
Staff welfare           3,000      4,500      6,000
Total                  46,400    118,660     72,440
parts.working: B1 bases; B1 rent; B1 depreciation; B1 electricity; B1 welfare; B1 totals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why depreciation of machinery is apportioned on the cost of machinery rather than on floor area.
parts.answer: Depreciation arises from the machines themselves; a department with more expensive machines causes more depreciation, which is unrelated to the space it occupies.
parts.working: B1 cause of the cost; B1 link to fairness.

practice.stem: A factory's annual rent of $90,000 is apportioned on floor area. Department A occupies 1,800 m² and is charged $27,000. Department B occupies 2,600 m². Department C occupies the rest of the factory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rent per m² and the total floor area of the factory.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the floor area of Department C and the rent apportioned to Departments B and C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The business rents an extra store of 1,000 m² for $20,000 a year, used only by Department C. State whether this rent should be allocated or apportioned, and calculate Department C's total rent charge.
parts.answer: Allocated to C; total $44,000
parts.working: B1 allocated (used only by C); B1 44,000.

practice.stem:
After primary apportionment the budgeted overheads of a plastics factory are: Moulding $84,000; Packing $52,000; Stores $18,000; Maintenance $24,000.
Stores serves Moulding 50%, Packing 30% and Maintenance 20%. Maintenance serves Moulding 70% and Packing 30%; it does no work for Stores.
Budgeted activity: Moulding 7,200 machine hours; Packing 8,000 direct labour hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Reapportion the service department overheads to the production departments.
parts.answer:
Moulding   Packing    Stores    Maint.
                                   $         $         $         $
Primary totals                84,000    52,000    18,000    24,000
Stores reapportioned           9,000     5,400  (18,000)     3,600
                                                            27,600
Maintenance reapportioned     19,320     8,280            (27,600)
Totals                       112,320    65,680         –         –
parts.working: B1 stores split 9,000/5,400/3,600; B1 maintenance total 27,600; B1 split 19,320/8,280; B1 totals 112,320 and 65,680.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate an overhead absorption rate for each production department. Give your answers to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Moulding $15.60 per machine hour; Packing $8.21 per direct labour hour
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Stores must be reapportioned before Maintenance.
parts.answer: Stores provides services to Maintenance, so part of Stores' cost must first be added to Maintenance; Maintenance does not serve Stores, so once Stores is cleared nothing comes back to it and every cost ends up in a production department.
parts.working: 1 mark: Stores serves Maintenance; 1 mark: otherwise Maintenance's share of stores cost would be missed / reapportioned twice.

practice.stem:
Heating costs of $60,000 in a factory are at present apportioned on floor area. The production manager says volume would be fairer.
                               Assembly        Finishing
Floor area (m²)                   1,200              800
Ceiling height (m)                    8                3
Other overheads ($)              90,000           50,000
Budgeted activity       10,000 mach hrs    8,000 lab hrs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the heating cost apportioned to each department on (i) floor area and (ii) volume.
parts.answer:
(i) Assembly $36,000, Finishing $24,000
(ii) Assembly $48,000, Finishing $12,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorption rate of each department under each method.
parts.answer:
Floor area: Assembly $12.60/mach hr, Finishing $9.25/lab hr
Volume: Assembly $13.80/mach hr, Finishing $7.75/lab hr
parts.working: B1 each pair.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Job 52 needs 5 machine hours in Assembly and 6 labour hours in Finishing. Calculate the overhead charged to the job under each method.
parts.answer: Floor area $118.50; volume $115.50
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain which basis is more appropriate for heating costs.
parts.answer: Volume, because heating warms the air in a room; Assembly has a much higher ceiling and needs more heat per square metre, so floor area under-charges Assembly and over-charges Finishing.
parts.working: 1 mark: volume; 1 mark: reason linked to ceiling height / space heated.

practice.stem:
Before any service costs are reapportioned, the budgeted overheads of a factory are:
Assembly $132,000; Finishing $96,000; Stores $24,000; Maintenance $40,000.
Stores provides services: Assembly 50%, Finishing 30%, Maintenance 20%.
Maintenance provides services: Assembly 60%, Finishing 40%. Maintenance does no work for Stores.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Reapportion the service department overheads, and calculate the total overheads of Assembly and Finishing.
parts.answer: Stores: Assembly 12,000; Finishing 7,200; Maintenance 4,800. Maintenance total 44,800: Assembly 26,880; Finishing 17,920. Totals: Assembly $170,880; Finishing $121,120.
parts.working: B1 stores split; B1 maintenance total 44,800; B1 maintenance split; A1 Assembly 170,880; A1 Finishing 121,120.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Stores overheads were reapportioned before the Maintenance overheads.
parts.answer: Stores serves Maintenance but Maintenance does not serve Stores; reapportioning Stores first lets its share be added to Maintenance, so all service costs end up in production departments without going back.
parts.working: B1 one-way service; B1 consequence.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assembly has 42,720 budgeted direct labour hours. Calculate its overhead absorption rate.
parts.answer: $4.00 per direct labour hour

practice.stem:
A factory has two production departments, P1 and P2, and two service departments, S1 and S2, which serve each other. Overheads after primary apportionment: P1 $210,000; P2 $150,000; S1 $60,000; S2 $36,000.
Share of service        P1      P2      S1      S2
S1's work              50%     30%       –     20%
S2's work              40%     40%     20%       –

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using simultaneous equations, calculate the total overheads of S1 and S2 after their services to each other are included.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total overheads of P1 and P2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: P1 is machine-intensive with 26,500 budgeted machine hours; P2 is labour-intensive with 38,200 budgeted direct labour hours. Calculate an overhead absorption rate for each department.
parts.answer: P1 $10.00 per machine hour; P2 $5.00 per direct labour hour
parts.working: B1 each.

practice.stem:
A garment factory has two production departments, Cutting and Sewing. Canteen overheads of $48,000 were reapportioned on the number of machines. The finance manager says they should have been reapportioned on the number of employees.
                                 Cutting    Sewing
Overheads before canteen ($)     216,000   180,000
Number of machines                    30        10
Number of employees                   20        60
Budgeted machine hours            24,000         –
Budgeted direct labour hours           –    48,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorption rate for each department (i) as currently calculated and (ii) using number of employees.
parts.answer: (i) Cutting $10.50 per machine hour, Sewing $4.00 per labour hour; (ii) Cutting $9.50, Sewing $4.50
parts.working: B1 canteen split 36,000/12,000; B1 rates (i); B1 canteen split 12,000/36,000; B1 rates (ii).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Job 615 uses 6 machine hours in Cutting and 20 direct labour hours in Sewing. Calculate the overhead charged to the job under each method, and state by how much it is under-costed by the current method.
parts.answer: Current $143.00; employees basis $147.00; under-costed by $4.00

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why number of employees is the more suitable basis for canteen costs.
parts.answer: Canteen costs are caused by the people who use it; Sewing has three times as many staff and so uses the canteen far more, whereas machines do not eat.
parts.working: B1 cause–effect; B1 applied to the data.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one consequence for the business of continuing to use the current basis.
parts.answer: Sewing-heavy jobs are under-costed and may be underpriced (and Cutting-heavy jobs overpriced and lost to competitors).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A labour-intensive department has budgeted overheads of $96,000, budgeted direct labour hours of 16,000 and budgeted machine hours of 6,400. What is the most appropriate overhead absorption rate?
A $6.00 per direct labour hour
B $15.00 per machine hour
C $4.29 per hour
D $0.17 per direct labour hour
parts.answer: A $6.00 per direct labour hour
parts.working: In a labour-intensive department overheads are driven mainly by labour time: 96,000 ÷ 16,000 = $6.00 per direct labour hour. B uses machine hours, which suit a machine-intensive department; D inverts the calculation.

practice.stem:
Budgeted figures for two production departments:
                        Machining   Assembly
Overheads ($)             148,500     86,400
Machine hours              13,500      2,100
Direct labour hours         3,200     19,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate a machine hour rate for Machining and a direct labour hour rate for Assembly.
parts.answer: Machining $11.00; Assembly $4.50
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Justify the choice of basis for each department.
parts.answer: Machining uses far more machine hours than labour hours, so overheads are mainly caused by machine time; Assembly is labour intensive, so labour hours best reflect how overheads are incurred.
parts.working: 1 mark each department.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A unit of product uses 1.5 machine hours in Machining and 2 direct labour hours in Assembly. Calculate the production overhead absorbed by one unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A department makes one standard product. Budgeted overheads are $84,000, budgeted output is 12,000 units and budgeted direct labour hours are 21,000.
What is the overhead absorption rate per unit?
A $0.14
B $4.00
C $7.00
D $11.00
parts.working: 84,000 ÷ 12,000 units = $7 per unit. $4 is the rate per direct labour hour (84,000 ÷ 21,000), not per unit.

practice.stem: The Moulding department of a factory makes one product. Budget for next year: overheads $126,000; output 18,000 units; direct labour hours 9,000; machine hours 31,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate an overhead absorption rate (i) per unit, (ii) per direct labour hour and (iii) per machine hour.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which rate is most suitable for this department. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Machine hour rate: the department uses 3.5 times as many machine hours as labour hours, so it is machine-intensive and overheads are mainly caused by running the machines.
parts.working: B1 machine hour; B1 reason linked to data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a rate per unit would be unsuitable if the department began making several different products.
parts.answer: Different products take different amounts of time and resources; a per-unit rate charges every unit the same overhead, so complex products would be under-costed and simple ones over-costed.
parts.working: B1 products differ in time used; B1 consequence.

practice.stem: Overhead absorption rates are usually calculated at the start of the year from budgeted figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the formula for a direct labour hour absorption rate.
parts.answer: Budgeted overheads ÷ budgeted direct labour hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain three reasons why budgeted figures are used rather than actual figures.
parts.answer: Actual overheads and hours are not known until the end of the year; jobs must be costed and priced as they are done during the year; inventory must be valued at interim dates; one annual rate smooths seasonal changes in costs and activity so similar jobs carry similar overheads.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one disadvantage of using budgeted figures.
parts.answer: Actual overheads or activity will differ from budget, causing under- or over-absorption.

practice.stem:
An engineering workshop in Nairobi has the following budgets: Fabrication overheads $210,000 and 14,000 machine hours; Assembly overheads $127,500 and 25,000 direct labour hours.
Job J88 used direct materials of $1,960; 20 labour hours in Fabrication at $16 per hour; 34 labour hours in Assembly at $12 per hour; and 26 machine hours in Fabrication.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate a suitable overhead absorption rate for each department.
parts.answer: Fabrication $15.00 per machine hour; Assembly $5.10 per labour hour
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total production cost of Job J88.
parts.working: B1 labour 320 + 408 = 728; B1 Fabrication overhead 26 × 15 = 390; B1 Assembly overhead 34 × 5.10 = 173.40; B1 total 3,251.40.

practice.stem: A department's budget shows overheads of $75,000, direct labour cost of $150,000 and 12,500 direct labour hours. Job K uses 40 hours of senior staff paid $18 per hour; Job L uses 40 hours of trainees paid $8 per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorption rate as (i) a percentage of direct labour cost and (ii) a rate per direct labour hour.
parts.answer: (i) 50% of direct labour cost (ii) $6.00 per direct labour hour
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overheads charged to Job K and Job L using each rate.
parts.answer:
Percentage of labour cost: K $360, L $160
Labour hour rate: K $240, L $240
parts.working: 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain which rate gives a fairer charge.
parts.answer: The labour hour rate: both jobs occupy the department for the same 40 hours, so they use the same amount of time-related overheads. The percentage method charges K more only because its workers are paid more.
parts.working: 1 mark: labour hour rate; 1 mark: overheads relate to time, not wage rates.

practice.stem:
A factory has two production departments.
                                Machining   Assembly
Budgeted overheads ($)            180,000     90,000
Budgeted machine hours             20,000      1,500
Budgeted direct labour hours        6,000     30,000
At present the factory uses a single blanket rate per direct labour hour for the whole factory.
Job Q needs 12 machine hours and 3 direct labour hours in Machining, and 10 direct labour hours in Assembly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the blanket rate.
parts.answer: $7.50 per direct labour hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate a suitable departmental rate for each department.
parts.answer: Machining $9.00 per machine hour; Assembly $3.00 per direct labour hour
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the overhead charged to Job Q using (i) the blanket rate and (ii) departmental rates.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the departmental rates give a more accurate cost for Job Q.
parts.answer: Job Q uses a lot of machine time in the high-cost Machining department but few labour hours; the blanket labour-hour rate ignores this, so it under-costs the job by $40.50.
parts.working: B1 departments differ in cost and activity; B1 applied to Job Q.

practice.stem:
A company has two production departments. Cutting absorbs overheads at $18 per machine hour; Finishing absorbs overheads at $11 per direct labour hour. Direct labour is paid $14 per hour in Cutting and $12 per hour in Finishing.
Per unit                       Alpha      Beta
Direct materials ($)           24.00     40.00
Cutting machine hours            1.5       0.6
Cutting labour hours             0.5       0.4
Finishing labour hours           2.0       3.5
Selling prices are set at production cost plus 30%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the production cost of one unit of each product.
parts.working: B1 labour Alpha 31.00, Beta 47.60; B1 overheads Alpha 49.00, Beta 49.30; A1 Alpha 104.00; A1 Beta 136.90.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of each product.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Cutting uses a machine hour rate but Finishing uses a direct labour hour rate.
parts.answer: Cutting is machine-intensive (overheads such as power and depreciation depend on machine running time); Finishing is labour-intensive, so labour time best reflects overhead use.
parts.working: B1 each department.

practice.stem: A hotel in Swat has 40 rooms and is open 300 nights a year. It expects an average occupancy of 75%. Budgeted overheads (staff salaries, heating, depreciation, marketing) are $486,000. Overheads are absorbed per occupied room-night. Direct costs (cleaning, laundry, toiletries) are $16 per occupied room-night. Room prices are set at full cost plus 50%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted number of occupied room-nights and the overhead absorption rate.
parts.answer: 9,000 room-nights; $54.00 per room-night

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price per room-night.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Occupancy falls to 60% with overheads unchanged. Calculate the overhead cost per occupied room-night actually incurred, and explain what this means for the hotel's profit.
parts.answer: $67.50 per room-night; each room-night now carries $13.50 more overhead than was charged in the price, so overheads are under-absorbed and profit is lower than planned.
parts.working: B1 7,200 room-nights; B1 67.50; B1 explanation (under-absorption reduces profit).

practice.stem:
Budgeted data for next year:
                                    Product A  Product B
Production (units)                      4,000      2,500
Machine hours per unit – Dept X             3          2
Labour hours per unit – Dept Y           1.50          4
Budgeted overheads: Dept X $289,000 (absorbed on machine hours); Dept Y $168,000 (absorbed on labour hours).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted machine hours in Dept X and the budgeted labour hours in Dept Y.
parts.answer: Dept X 17,000 machine hours; Dept Y 16,000 labour hours
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorption rate for each department.
parts.answer: Dept X $17.00 per machine hour; Dept Y $10.50 per labour hour
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorbed by one unit of each product.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain two reasons why absorption rates are calculated from budgeted figures rather than actual figures.
parts.answer: Any two: actual overheads and hours are not known until the end of the period, but costs are needed now for pricing and quotations; actual monthly rates would fluctuate with seasonal costs and activity, giving different costs for identical jobs; budgeted rates allow inventory to be valued during the year; differences can be controlled as under/over-absorption.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A jobbing firm absorbs overheads as a percentage of prime cost. Budgeted overheads are $156,000, budgeted direct materials $310,000 and budgeted direct labour $210,000. Job 74 uses direct materials of $1,500 and direct labour of $900.
What overhead is charged to Job 74?
A $668.57
B $720.00
C $754.84
D $960.00
parts.working: Rate = 156,000 ÷ (310,000 + 210,000) = 30% of prime cost; 30% × (1,500 + 900) = $720. $668.57 uses a percentage of direct labour cost (74.29% × 900) and $754.84 a percentage of materials cost, not prime cost.

practice.stem:
A machining department makes three products. Its budgeted overheads are $297,000.
                                  X        Y        Z
Budgeted output (units)       3,000    5,000    2,000
Machine hours per unit          2.0      0.5      4.0
Labour hours per unit           1.0      1.5      1.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted machine hours and a machine hour rate.
parts.answer: 16,500 machine hours; $18.00 per machine hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead per unit of each product using the machine hour rate.
parts.working: B1 two correct; B1 all three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The production director suggests charging the same overhead to every unit. Calculate this rate per unit and the amount by which Y would be over-costed and Z under-costed.
parts.answer: $29.70 per unit; Y over-costed by $20.70; Z under-costed by $42.30

parts.label: d
parts.text: Discuss the effect on pricing and sales if the director's suggestion is adopted.
parts.answer: Y would be priced too high and may lose sales to competitors; Z would be priced too low, so it may sell well but earn little or make a loss; overall profit could fall and the product mix would shift towards the under-costed product.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three developed points.

practice.stem: A packaging factory's fixed production overheads are budgeted at $600,000 for next year. The factory's practical capacity is 50,000 machine hours, but expected activity next year is only 40,000 machine hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the machine hour absorption rate based on (i) practical capacity and (ii) expected activity.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The capacity-based rate is used and actual activity is 40,000 hours, with overheads as budgeted. Calculate the under- or over-absorption.
parts.answer: Under-absorbed $120,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss which rate the factory should use for pricing its products.
parts.answer: Expected activity rate: recovers all overheads if the forecast is right, avoiding under-absorption, but raises the cost per unit and so prices, which may lose sales and create a downward spiral. Capacity rate: keeps prices competitive and shows the cost of idle capacity separately as under-absorption, but prices may not cover all overheads. Reasoned conclusion.
parts.working: B1 point for each rate (×2); B1 consequence/spiral or idle capacity point; B1 justified conclusion.

practice.stem:
A metal-fabrication workshop absorbs overheads as a percentage of direct materials cost. Budget: overheads $240,000; direct materials $480,000; machine hours 30,000.
Job A: direct materials $6,000; 40 machine hours.
Job B: direct materials $800; 260 machine hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead charged to each job using the current basis.
parts.answer: Job A $3,000; Job B $400
parts.working: B1 50%; B1 both jobs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead charged to each job using a machine hour rate.
parts.answer: Rate $8 per machine hour; Job A $320; Job B $2,080

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the machine hour rate is more suitable for this workshop, and the effect of the current basis on the prices of Jobs A and B.
parts.answer: Overheads such as power, depreciation and maintenance arise from machine running time, not from the value of materials. The current basis over-costs Job A (expensive material, little machine time) so it may be overpriced and lost, and under-costs Job B so it may be underpriced and make a loss.
parts.working: B1 cause of overheads; B1 Job A effect; B1 Job B effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Overheads are absorbed at $9 per machine hour, based on budgeted overheads of $108,000 and 12,000 machine hours. Actual overheads were $104,000 and actual machine hours were 11,200. What was the under- or over-absorption?
A Under-absorbed $3,200
B Over-absorbed $3,200
C Over-absorbed $4,000
D Under-absorbed $7,200
parts.answer: A Under-absorbed $3,200
parts.working: Absorbed = 11,200 × 9 = 100,800; actual 104,000; actual exceeds absorbed by 3,200, so under-absorbed. C compares actual with budgeted overheads, which is not the absorption test.

practice.stem:
Dept 1           Dept 2
Absorption rate         $14 per mach hr $7.20 per lab hr
Actual hours                      6,300            9,800
Actual overheads ($)             86,500           72,400

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the under- or over-absorption in each department.
parts.answer:
Dept 1: absorbed 88,200, over-absorbed $1,700
Dept 2: absorbed 70,560, under-absorbed $1,840
parts.working: B1 each absorbed figure; B1 each conclusion with amount.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the net amount and how it is treated in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: Net under-absorption $140; it is added to cost of sales (reduces profit).
parts.working: B1 140 under-absorbed; B1 added to cost of sales / reduces profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Budgeted overheads were $120,000 and budgeted direct labour hours 10,000. Actual overheads were $115,000 and actual direct labour hours 9,800.
What was the under- or over-absorption?
A under-absorbed $2,600
B over-absorbed $2,600
C over-absorbed $5,000
D under-absorbed $2,400
parts.answer: B over-absorbed $2,600
parts.working: Rate $12 per hour; absorbed 9,800 × 12 = 117,600; actual 115,000; absorbed exceeds actual, so over-absorbed $2,600. $5,000 compares budgeted with actual overheads, and $2,400 only reflects the shortfall in hours.

practice.stem: The Moulding department of a plastics factory in Faisalabad budgeted overheads of $165,000 and 15,000 machine hours for the year. Actual overheads were $171,300 and 15,800 machine hours were worked.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorption rate.
parts.answer: $11.00 per machine hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overheads absorbed and the under- or over-absorption.
parts.answer: Absorbed $173,800; over-absorbed $2,500
parts.working: B1 173,800; M1 compare with 171,300; A1 2,500 over.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how this amount is treated in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: Over-absorption is added to profit (deducted from cost of sales).

practice.stem: A factory absorbs production overheads using a predetermined rate per direct labour hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term under-absorption of overheads.
parts.answer: Overheads absorbed into products (actual hours × predetermined rate) are less than the overheads actually incurred.
parts.working: B1 absorbed vs actual; B1 absorbed is lower.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two different causes of under-absorption.
parts.answer: Actual overheads higher than budget (e.g. rent or energy price rises); actual activity lower than budget (fewer labour hours worked, e.g. lower demand or strikes), so less overhead is absorbed.
parts.working: B1 + B1 for each cause (cause plus explanation).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of under-absorption on the profit shown by the cost accounts.
parts.answer: Profit must be reduced by the under-absorbed amount.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Budgeted overheads were $250,000 and budgeted direct labour hours 20,000. Actual overheads were $262,000 and actual direct labour hours 21,500. Which statement is correct?
A Under-absorbed $12,000; profit is reduced
B Under-absorbed $6,750; profit is reduced
C Over-absorbed $6,750; profit is increased
D Over-absorbed $6,750; profit is reduced
parts.answer: C Over-absorbed $6,750; profit is increased
parts.working: Rate 12.50; absorbed 21,500 × 12.50 = 268,750, more than actual 262,000, so over-absorbed by 6,750. Too much overhead was charged to production, so the adjustment increases profit. A compares actual with budget.

practice.stem: A factory budgeted overheads of $192,000 and 16,000 machine hours for the year. Actual overheads were $201,300 and actual machine hours were 16,450.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorption rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the under- or over-absorption of overheads.
parts.answer: Under-absorbed $3,900
parts.working: B1 absorbed 16,450 × 12 = 197,400; M1 compare with 201,300; A1 under-absorbed 3,900.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that this amount is made up of a difference in spending and a difference in activity.
parts.answer: Spending: 201,300 − 192,000 = $9,300 more than budget (under). Activity: 450 extra hours × 12 = $5,400 extra absorbed (over). Net 9,300 − 5,400 = 3,900 under-absorbed.
parts.working: B1 spending 9,300; B1 activity 5,400 and net 3,900.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons for the overspending on overheads.
parts.answer: Any two: price rises (e.g. electricity tariffs) not foreseen in the budget; unplanned machine breakdown and repairs; extra supervision or overtime premium; poor control of indirect materials; an unrealistic budget.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Overheads are absorbed at $5 per machine hour. Actual overheads were $96,000 and overheads were over-absorbed by $4,000.
How many machine hours were worked?
A 18,400
B 19,200
C 20,000
D 20,800
parts.working: Over-absorbed means absorbed = actual + 4,000 = 100,000; hours = 100,000 ÷ 5 = 20,000. 18,400 treats the $4,000 as under-absorption (92,000 ÷ 5); 19,200 ignores it.

practice.stem: A factory absorbs production overheads at $16 per direct labour hour. In the year to 31 March 2027, 19,000 direct labour hours were worked. Actual production overheads were: indirect materials $48,600; indirect labour $121,800; other production overheads $142,000.

parts.answer: Decreases profit (under-absorbed).

practice.stem:

                                     Dept A         Dept B         Dept C
Absorption basis                $22/mach hr      $9/lab hr        140% of DL cost
Actual machine hours                  4,200              –              –

practice.stem:
A canning factory sets one annual overhead absorption rate. Budget: overheads $480,000; machine hours 60,000. Actual results:
                        Q1        Q2        Q3        Q4
Machine hours       13,500    16,200    14,000    17,100
Overheads ($)      118,000   123,500   117,600   124,300

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the under- or over-absorption for each quarter.

parts.working: B1 rate $8; B1 Q1 and Q2; B1 Q3; B1 Q4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the under- or over-absorption for the year.

parts.label: c

parts.working: B1 seasonal fluctuation; B1 stable costs / differences cancel.

practice.stem: Overheads are absorbed at $8.50 per direct labour hour, based on budgeted overheads of $340,000. Actual overheads for the year were $352,600 and overheads were over-absorbed by $4,060.

parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the overheads absorbed.

practice.stem: A factory budgeted 25,000 direct labour hours for the year. Actual direct labour hours were 23,500 and actual overheads $197,000. Overheads were under-absorbed by $9,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overheads absorbed and the absorption rate.
parts.answer: Absorbed $188,000; rate $8.00 per hour

parts.label: b

practice.subtopic: Purpose and features of absorption costing

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by absorption costing.
parts.answer: A costing method in which all production costs – direct costs plus a share of fixed and variable production overheads – are charged to each unit, using overhead absorption rates.
parts.working: 1 mark: all production costs including fixed overheads; 1 mark: charged to units / cost units via absorption rates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why a business uses absorption costing.
parts.answer: Any two: IAS 2 requires inventory in the financial statements to include production overheads; it helps set prices that cover all costs; it recognises that fixed overheads are needed to produce output; it shows the full cost of jobs for quotations.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two differences between absorption costing and marginal costing.
parts.answer: Any two: absorption costing includes fixed production overheads in unit cost, marginal costing charges them as period costs; inventory is valued higher under absorption costing; profits differ when inventory levels change; marginal costing shows contribution, absorption costing does not.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Purpose and features of absorption costing
practice.stem: A manufacturer of ceiling fans uses absorption costing.

parts.answer: A costing method in which all production costs, fixed and variable, are charged to cost units.

practice.subtopic: Purpose and features of absorption costing
practice.stem: Indus Fabrics Ltd uses absorption costing for its published financial statements and for pricing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why absorption costing must be used to value inventory in the published financial statements.
parts.answer: IAS 2 requires inventory cost to include all costs of bringing it to its present condition, including a share of fixed production overheads (based on normal capacity); this also matches costs with the revenue when the goods are sold.
parts.working: B1 IAS 2 / includes production overheads; B1 matching.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages to managers of using absorption costing.
parts.answer: Prices based on full cost ensure all production costs are recovered in the long run; it shows the full cost of each product/job; consistent with financial reporting so one set of figures; overhead analysis makes departments aware of the costs they cause.
parts.working: B1 + B1 for each of two developed advantages.

practice.stem: A company makes one product. Variable production cost is $14 per unit. Fixed production overheads of $96,000 are absorbed on budgeted output of 24,000 units. At the year end, 1,200 units are in closing inventory.

practice.subtopic: Purpose and features of absorption costing
practice.stem: Some managers argue that absorption costing gives misleading information.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two limitations of absorption costing.
parts.answer: Apportionment bases are arbitrary; unit costs depend on the activity level used; profit can be raised by producing for inventory; fixed costs per unit are not relevant for short-term decisions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the apportionment of overheads is described as arbitrary.
parts.answer: Shared costs such as rent or insurance cannot be traced exactly to departments; a basis such as floor area is chosen by judgement and a different basis would give a different product cost.
parts.working: B1 shared costs cannot be traced; B1 choice of basis changes the result.

practice.subtopic: Purpose and features of absorption costing
practice.stem: The managing director of a manufacturing company says: 'Absorption costing gives the full cost of every product, so we should use it for all our decisions, including whether to accept special orders and which products to drop.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the managing director's statement.
parts.answer: Agree: full cost shows the long-run cost that prices must cover; useful for routine pricing and for inventory valuation (IAS 2); consistent with published accounts. Disagree: fixed overheads per unit are not relevant to short-term decisions because they do not change; apportionment is arbitrary, so a product can look loss-making when it makes a positive contribution; a special order below full cost can still add profit if there is spare capacity; unit cost changes with volume; marginal costing/contribution is better for special orders, make-or-buy, limiting factors and dropping products. Conclusion: use absorption costing for pricing and reporting, marginal costing for short-term decisions.
parts.working: Level 3 (7–8): balanced, applied discussion with both sides and a justified conclusion. Level 2 (4–6): some developed points, mostly one-sided or no clear conclusion. Level 1 (1–3): simple points listed.

practice.subtopic: Purpose and features of absorption costing
practice.stem:
Orbit Ltd sells one product at $30. Variable production cost is $12 per unit. Fixed production overheads are $90,000 each period, absorbed at $6 per unit (normal output 15,000 units). There are no other costs and no opening inventory in Period 1.
                      Period 1  Period 2  Period 3
Production (units)      15,000    16,000    12,000
Sales (units)           13,000    15,000    15,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for each period using absorption costing.
parts.working: B1 profit per unit sold $12; B1 P1; B1 P2 including 6,000 over-absorbed; B1 P3 including 18,000 under-absorbed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for each period using marginal costing.
parts.working: B1 contribution $18; B1 all three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Reconcile the profits for Period 3 and comment on the totals for the three periods.
parts.answer: Inventory fell from 3,000 to 0 units: 3,000 × $6 = $18,000 of fixed overhead brought forward is charged in P3, so absorption profit is $18,000 lower. Over the three periods both total $504,000, because all inventory is sold: the difference is only one of timing.
parts.working: B1 inventory change 3,000; B1 × 6 = 18,000; B1 totals equal/timing.

practice.subtopic: Purpose and features of absorption costing
practice.stem:
A company makes three products. Fixed overheads of $153,000 are apportioned on sales value. Its statement for the year:
                             K         L         M     Total
Sales ($)              240,000   180,000    90,000   510,000
Variable costs ($)     132,000    99,000    66,000   297,000
Fixed overheads ($)     72,000    54,000    27,000   153,000
Profit/(loss) ($)       36,000    27,000   (3,000)    60,000
A director proposes dropping Product M. Fixed overheads would not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution of Product M.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total profit if Product M is dropped.
parts.working: M1 contributions of K and L 189,000 − 153,000; A1 36,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the absorption costing statement is misleading for this decision.
parts.answer: M's $27,000 share of fixed overheads is not saved if M is dropped; it is spread over K and L. M covers its variable costs and contributes $24,000 to fixed costs.
parts.working: B1 fixed costs unavoidable; B1 contribution of M.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the director. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Keep M: dropping it reduces profit by $24,000 (from $60,000 to $36,000). Consider: whether resources freed could make something more profitable; whether M supports sales of K and L; whether M's price can be raised or costs cut. Decision with reasons.
parts.working: B1 financial effect; B2 two other factors; B1 justified decision.

practice.subtopic: Purpose and features of absorption costing
practice.stem: Saif Appliances Ltd has always used marginal costing for internal reports. Its marginal costing profit for the year is $210,000. Closing inventory is 6,000 units and there was no opening inventory. Fixed production overheads would be absorbed at $8 per unit. The finance director proposes switching to absorption costing for internal reports this year because 'it will raise profit and please the shareholders'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit under absorption costing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Next year inventory is expected to fall to 1,000 units. Calculate the difference between the two profits next year and state which method gives the lower profit.
parts.answer: $40,000; absorption costing gives the lower profit.
parts.working: B1 5,000 × 8 = 40,000; B1 absorption lower.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate the finance director's proposal.
parts.answer: The change creates no extra cash or sales; it only moves fixed overhead into next year, which then reverses. Changing method to boost profit breaks the consistency concept and could mislead users; it raises ethical concerns. Absorption costing is acceptable (and required for published accounts), so if adopted it should be for good reasons, applied consistently and disclosed. Conclusion: reject the reason given.
parts.working: B1 timing difference/no cash; B1 reversal next year; B1 consistency; B1 ethics/misleading users; B1 justified conclusion.

practice.stem: The new treasurer of Al-Huda Community Sports Club, Quetta, has prepared only a receipts and payments account. Members have asked for an income and expenditure account instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three differences between a receipts and payments account and an income and expenditure account.
parts.answer: R&P is a summary of the cash book; I&E follows the accruals basis. R&P includes capital items such as buying equipment; I&E has revenue items only. R&P ends with a cash/bank balance (an asset); I&E ends with a surplus or deficit. I&E includes non-cash items such as depreciation.
parts.working: For each of three differences: 1 mark identifying, 1 mark developing. Accept: cash v accruals basis; capital and revenue items v revenue only; closing balance v surplus/deficit; no depreciation/accruals in R&P; R&P covers all years' amounts received (e.g. arrears) v I&E for the current year only.

parts.answer: It should not be shown as general income in the income and expenditure account. parts.working: 1 mark for saying it is not general income; 1 mark for identifying a separate restricted fund within the accumulated fund; 1 mark for noting it does not change the surplus for the year.

parts.answer: The library is a non-current asset used over several years, so its cost is spread over its useful life (matching). The depreciation charge is an expense in the income and expenditure account each year, which reduces the surplus.
parts.working: 1 mark for matching cost to the years of use; 1 mark for the depreciation expense reducing the surplus in the I&E account.
