parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the ticket income should be kept out of the refreshment trading account.
parts.answer: Ticket income is not from selling refreshments, so it is not part of the cost of sales or gross profit on refreshments. It is shown as a separate income of the event in the income and expenditure account.
parts.working: 1 mark for saying it does not arise from selling refreshments; 1 mark for identifying the I&E account as the place for it.

practice.stem: Silverbirch Croquet Club sells teas and cakes in its pavilion. For the year ended 31 December 2025 its sales were $9,600. The committee reports a gross margin of 40% on sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales of the tea room for the year, when the gross margin is 40% of sales.
parts.working: Cost of sales = 60% of sales (because the gross margin is 40%): 9,600 × 0.6 = 5,760.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mark-up on cost that this gross profit represents, correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: Mark-up = gross profit ÷ cost of sales = 3,840 ÷ 5,760 = 66.7%. 1 mark for the formula; 1 for the answer.

practice.stem: The canteen at Ashgrove Table Tennis Club, Dubai, buys tea in at a cost of $3.60 per cup. The treasurer wants to set a price that gives a 50% mark-up on cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of one cup of tea that gives a mark-up of 50% on cost of $3.60.
parts.working: Selling price = cost × 1.5 = 3.60 × 1.5 = 5.40. 1 mark for the method; 1 for the price.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit if 2,800 cups are sold in the year at this price.

practice.stem: Kingfisher Fishing Club sells drinks at a mark-up of 60% on cost. For the year: bar inventory at the start $2,700 and at the end $4,200; bar purchases $37,500. Bar takings banked were $55,350. The committee suspects that some takings have been stolen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales of the bar.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected bar sales.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amount of cash that appears to be missing.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two controls the club could introduce to prevent this happening again.
parts.answer: Use a till that records every sale and reconcile it daily; have two people count and bank takings (also: regular inventory counts, CCTV, rotate staff).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid controls.

practice.stem: Jasmine Netball Club holds an annual dinner. 180 tickets were sold at $45 each. The caterer charged $28 per guest. The band cost $900 and hall hire $600. Raffle tickets raised $1,260 (prizes were donated).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net income from the dinner.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ignoring the raffle, calculate the minimum number of tickets that must be sold for the dinner to cover its costs.
parts.answer: 89 tickets
parts.working: Fixed costs 900 + 600 = 1,500 (M1); contribution per ticket 45 − 28 = 17 (M1); 1,500 ÷ 17 = 88.2, so 89 tickets (A1, must round up).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the dinner is shown in the club's income and expenditure account.
parts.answer: As a single net figure: 'Net income from annual dinner $2,820' under income.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Thunder Valley Football Club, Peshawar, sells club kit to members from a small shop in the clubhouse. For the year: kit sales $12,480; kit purchases $9,060; kit inventory at the start $1,950 and at the end $2,310.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the trading account for the kit shop.
parts.answer:
$        $
Sales                         12,480
Opening inventory     1,950
Purchases             9,060
Closing inventory   (2,310)
Cost of sales                  8,700
Gross profit                   3,780
parts.working: B1 sales; B1 opening + purchases; B1 closing inventory deducted; B1 gross profit 3,780.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit of the shop after charging 10% of the club's rent of $9,600.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the committee may want a share of the rent charged to the shop.
parts.answer: The shop uses part of the clubhouse, so charging a share of the rent shows the true profit of the shop and helps the committee decide whether running it is worthwhile.
parts.working: 1 mark shop uses club resources/space; 1 mark true profit for decision-making.

practice.stem: Redwood Archery Club runs a bar. For 2025: bar sales $27,450; bar purchases $18,600; opening bar inventory $3,800; the stocktake valued closing bar inventory at $4,250, but this figure includes bottles costing $380 that were broken and must be written off. During the year $500 of bar goods was taken to pay for the club's members' party.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how the $500 of goods taken for the members' party should be treated, and explain why.
parts.answer: The goods are not for resale, so they should be removed from purchases and charged as a club expense in the income and expenditure account (or treated as a member benefit), not in cost of sales.
parts.working: 1 mark for removing the $500 from purchases / charging it to the I&E account; 1 mark for the reason: not sold, so it is not a cost of the goods sold.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the closing inventory after the stock loss is adjusted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales for the bar for 2025.
parts.working: Opening 3,800 + purchases (18,600 − 500 = 18,100) − closing 3,870 = 18,030. 1 mark for the purchases adjustment; 1 for the answer.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit on bar sales.

practice.stem: The canteen at Highgate Sports Club sold food and drink worth $46,000 in 2025. The club's gross profit is 35% of sales. Opening inventory was $2,400 and closing inventory $3,150.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales for the year.
parts.working: Cost of sales = 65% of sales = 46,000 × 0.65 = 29,900.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the purchases for the year.
parts.working: Purchases = cost of sales + closing inventory − opening inventory = 29,900 + 3,150 − 2,400 = 30,650.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how an overstated closing inventory would affect the reported gross profit.
parts.answer: An overstated closing inventory reduces cost of sales, so gross profit is overstated (too high) by the same amount.
parts.working: 1 mark for reduced cost of sales; 1 mark for gross profit overstated.

practice.stem: Crestwood Golf Club runs a small tea stall beside the first tee. For 2025: sales $4,100; cost of sales $2,900; wages of the stall attendant $1,800. The stall is run by a paid attendant on weekends. The committee is considering whether to continue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net result of the tea stall after wages for the year.
parts.answer: Loss of $600
parts.working: Sales 4,100 − cost of sales 2,900 − wages 1,800 = −600.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether the committee should close the tea stall.
parts.answer: Content points (any sensible discussion): for closing: the stall makes a net loss after wages of $600, wages are a fixed cost that would continue to rise, the volunteers' time could be used elsewhere, and members may not use it enough to justify it. Against closing: it makes a gross profit of $1,200, it is a service to members and visitors, a loss may fall if prices are raised or waste is cut, and closing could lose members or other income. A good answer weighs both sides and reaches a supported conclusion, such as a trial period with clear targets.
parts.working: Band 1 (1–2): identifies the loss and at least one point. Band 2 (3–4): explains the financial effect and considers the gross profit and fixed wages. Band 3 (5–6): balances the arguments with other factors (members, alternatives) and reaches a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A group of residents in Abbottabad are forming a hiking club and ask how its accounts will differ from those of a business.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a non-profit-making organisation.
parts.answer: An organisation run to provide a service or facilities for its members, not to make profit for owners; any surplus is used for the members' benefit.
parts.working: 1 mark purpose is to provide a service to members; 1 mark surplus not distributed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the terms a club uses instead of (i) profit and (ii) capital.
parts.answer: (i) surplus (excess of income over expenditure) (ii) accumulated fund.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a club still needs to keep proper accounting records.
parts.answer: To show members how their money has been used (stewardship) and to plan subscriptions and spending; also to control cash and prevent fraud.
parts.working: 1 mark accountability/stewardship to members; 1 mark planning/control.

practice.stem: Members of Sapphire Drama Society, Colombo, will discuss the year's accounts at their annual general meeting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the stewardship role of a club treasurer.
parts.answer: The treasurer looks after the club's money and assets on behalf of the members and reports how they have been used.
parts.working: 1 mark looks after funds for members; 1 mark accounts/reports to members (e.g. at the AGM).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why members find an income and expenditure account more useful than a receipts and payments account.
parts.answer: It shows whether the year's income covered the year's running costs (surplus or deficit), which helps members decide on subscription levels.
parts.working: 1 mark shows surplus/deficit on accruals basis; 1 mark helps decide subscriptions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two items in a club's statement of financial position that would not appear in a receipts and payments account.
parts.answer: Subscriptions in arrears (or in advance); accumulated depreciation of equipment.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: subscriptions in arrears/advance; accruals/prepayments; depreciation; accumulated fund; life membership balance; non-current assets at carrying amount.

practice.stem: The treasurer of Hillview Rambling Club is preparing the club's annual accounts for the first time with a professional advisor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two users of a club's accounts other than its members, and state one need of each.
parts.answer: Any two users, each with a need: e.g. a bank (to judge whether it can repay a loan or the club can pay its debts); a potential sponsor or donor (to see how funds are used); the local council (for grants or tax status); prospective members (to see the club's financial health); the national sports association (to check it is complying with its rules).
parts.working: 1 mark for each user identified; 1 mark for each matching need (up to 4 marks).

practice.stem: Hollow Oak Sailing Club has a surplus of $20,000 that the committee decides to put on deposit at 4% a year for 2 years. Interest is added to the deposit at the end of each year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest earned in year 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of the deposit after 2 years if interest is reinvested each year, correct to the nearest dollar.
parts.working: 20,000 × 1.04 × 1.04 = 21,632. 1 mark for compounding; 1 for the answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where the deposit appears in the statement of financial position of the club.
parts.answer: As a current asset (short-term investment or deposit)
parts.working: It is a short-term deposit that the club can withdraw, so it is a current asset.

practice.stem: Blue Ridge Golf Club's bar, run by volunteers, made a profit of $9,800 last year; profits have varied between $4,000 and $11,000 over five years and two volunteers have resigned. A catering company offers to run the bar for 3 years and pay the club a fixed fee of $8,500 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in annual income to the club between running the bar itself and accepting the franchise.
parts.answer: The club would receive $1,300 a year less from the franchise.
parts.working: Current bar profit 9,800 − franchise fee 8,500 (M1) = $1,300 less (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the committee whether to accept the franchise offer. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Although the club loses $1,300 a year, the franchise gives a guaranteed income and removes risks and the workload on volunteers; a justified decision.
parts.working: For franchise: fixed, certain income; no inventory, theft or wage risk; volunteers freed; professional service. Against: $1,300 less; club loses control of prices and opening hours; profit could grow if run well; tied for 3 years. 1 mark per point (max 4, both sides), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Palm Grove Gymnasium Club, Jeddah, has 300 members and needs $18,000 for new fitness equipment.
Option 1: increase the annual subscription for 3 years and buy the equipment when enough is collected.
Option 2: a one-off levy of $60 per member now.
Option 3: a bank loan of $18,000 at 8% simple interest per annum, repaid after 3 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate: (i) the extra amount per member per year under option 1, (ii) the total interest under option 3, (iii) the interest cost per member.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the committee which option to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Option 1 or 2 avoids interest of $4,320; option 1 spreads the cost so members are less likely to leave; the loan gives the equipment now but costs more; a justified decision.
parts.working: Option 1: no interest, affordable $20 a year, but equipment not bought for 3 years unless cash saved first. Option 2: fastest, no interest, but $60 at once may make some members leave. Option 3: equipment now, members not asked for money, but interest $4,320, repayments are a commitment, risk if membership falls. 1 mark per point (max 4), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Willowbank Bridge Club's membership has fallen from 150 to 100 in three years. The treasurer's draft surplus of $5,750 includes $2,400 of subscriptions in arrears for the current year, and many of these members have stopped attending.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the going concern concept applies to the club.
parts.answer: Accounts assume the club will continue; with membership falling by a third, if the club might close, assets would need to be shown at what they would sell for instead of their carrying amounts.
parts.working: 1 mark assumption of continuing; 1 mark consequence for asset valuation if in doubt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the surplus if the treasurer follows the prudence concept for subscriptions in arrears.
parts.working: 5,750 − 2,400 arrears not yet received (M1) = $3,350 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the club should apply its policy on subscriptions in arrears consistently.
parts.answer: So that surpluses can be compared fairly from year to year; changing the policy could make the club look better or worse without any real change.
parts.working: 1 mark comparability; 1 mark avoids manipulation/misleading members.

practice.stem: Crescent Ridge Fencing Club, Madrid, has fixed costs for hall rental, coach fees and insurance totalling $36,000 a year. These do not change with the number of members. Each member pays a subscription of $150 a year. The club has no other income.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of members needed to cover the fixed costs exactly.
parts.answer: 240 members
parts.working: Break-even members = fixed costs ÷ subscription per member = 36,000 ÷ 150 = 240.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The club has 210 members. Calculate the subscription per member that would cover the fixed costs exactly, correct to 2 decimal places, and the increase needed on $150.
parts.answer: $171.43 per member; an increase of $21.43
parts.working: 36,000 ÷ 210 = 171.43; 171.43 − 150 = 21.43. 1 mark for dividing by 210; 1 for the subscription; 1 for the increase.

practice.stem: Whitfield Cycling Club, Bristol, needs extra money for new racks. Option A: increase every member's annual subscription by $12, with 150 members. Option B: run a raffle selling 800 tickets at $5 each; prizes cost $1,100 and printing and admin cost $260.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the extra income from option A.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net gain from option B, the raffle.
parts.working: Ticket sales 800 × 5 = 4,000; less prizes 1,100 and costs 260 = 2,640. 1 mark for ticket income; 1 for the net gain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why the committee might still prefer option A.
parts.answer: Any one reason with explanation: option A is certain and does not depend on selling tickets; the raffle needs effort, may not sell out, and may need a licence; subscription income is predictable for budgeting.
parts.working: 1 mark for the reason; 1 mark for explaining why it matters for the committee.

practice.stem: Oakridge Walking Club, Kochi, had 300 members at the end of this year. The treasurer expects 10% of members to leave next year, and 45 new members to join. The subscription is $180 a year for every member.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number of members at the end of next year.
parts.answer: 315 members
parts.working: 300 × 0.9 = 270 members remaining; 270 + 45 new = 315.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected subscription income for next year.
parts.working: 315 members × $180 = 56,700. 1 mark for applying the subscription; 1 for the answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the treasurer should use prudent estimates in the budget.
parts.answer: A budget that overstates income can lead the club to commit to spending it does not receive, so estimates should be cautious and use the lower expected numbers. Prudence reduces the risk of a deficit.
parts.working: 1 mark for the risk of overcommitting spending; 1 mark for prudence reducing the risk of a deficit.

practice.stem: Sunset Tennis Club charges an annual subscription of $200. To raise cash for new courts, the committee proposes a life membership fee of $2,400. Life membership fees would be transferred to the income and expenditure account over 10 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of years of annual subscriptions that the life membership fee represents.
parts.answer: 12 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount credited to the income and expenditure account each year for one life member, and compare it with the annual subscription.
parts.answer: $240 a year, which is $40 more than the annual subscription of $200.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the committee whether to introduce life membership. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Life membership brings in cash now for the new courts and secures members, but the club loses income from long-serving members (after 12 years they pay nothing) and must still provide services; a justified decision.
parts.working: For: immediate cash; loyal members; less collection effort/arrears; income spread $240 a year for 10 years. Against: members staying more than 12 years cost the club income; costs rise with inflation but the fee is fixed; club still serves them after the fee has been fully transferred. 1 mark per point (max 4), 1 decision.

practice.stem: Crescent Moon Cricket Club's café had takings of $18,000, food costs of $9,500 and wages of $7,200. The treasurer also charged the café $2,400 as its share of the clubhouse rent and insurance, which the club will pay whether or not the café stays open.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss of the café after charging its share of general overheads.
parts.answer: Loss $1,100

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect on the club's surplus if the café is closed.
parts.answer: The surplus would fall by $1,300.
parts.working: The 2,400 overheads would still be paid (M1); the club would lose the café's $1,300 surplus over its own costs (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the committee whether to close the café. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Keep the café: it covers its own costs and contributes $1,300 towards overheads, and it attracts members; but look at raising prices or cutting wages.
parts.working: For keeping: contributes 1,300; service to members helps retain them; may raise prices. For closing: shown as a loss; volunteer/staff effort; could use space for something more profitable (e.g. rent to a caterer). 1 mark per point (max 3), 1 mark decision consistent with (b).

practice.stem: Riverbend Athletic Club, Adelaide, borrows $60,000 at 9% a year to build a second pitch. Interest is charged on the balance outstanding at the start of each year. The club repays $22,000 at the end of each year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest for year 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance owed to the bank at the end of year 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the interest charge falls each year even though the club repays the same amount annually.
parts.answer: Interest is charged on the balance outstanding at the start of each year. As the loan is repaid, the balance falls, so the interest falls.
parts.working: 1 mark for interest on the reducing (opening) balance; 1 mark for the reduction in the balance from repayments.

practice.stem: Westmoor Rifle Club's accumulated fund at 31 December 2025 is $62,400. It includes a donation of $15,000 that the donor has restricted to new shooting equipment and not for general use. The club's clubhouse has a net book value of $22,000 and is financed from the fund.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the free reserves available for general use.
parts.working: Accumulated fund 62,400 − restricted donation 15,000 − net book value of the clubhouse 22,000 = 25,400.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the restricted donation should be shown separately from the general fund.
parts.answer: It can be used only for its stated purpose, so showing it separately tells members and donors that it is not available to fund ordinary running costs; this is a fair way to show stewardship of the donor's money.
parts.working: 1 mark for the restriction on use; 1 mark for the stewardship or transparency reason.

practice.stem: Goldcrest Rugby League Club, Hull, has been offered three years of sponsorship at $25,000 a year by a company that makes sweetened drinks. The sponsor requires its logo on the players' shirts and at the entrance to the ground. A survey of members shows that about 30% of them object to the sponsor's products.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the club should accept the sponsorship.
parts.answer: Content points: financial case for (the $25,000 a year is a useful amount, is income for the I&E account, and a sponsor can help the club's finances); against (reputation and member relations, a possible split in membership, and the conditions on the kit may be hard to accept); accounting points (sponsorship income is recognised as income when the conditions are met, and it should be disclosed if it is material); governance (the committee should consult members, for example at a general meeting, before deciding). A strong answer balances these and reaches a supported conclusion.
parts.working: Band 1 (1–2): identifies the financial benefit and at least one concern. Band 2 (3–4): weighs the financial and member concerns with accounting or governance points. Band 3 (5–6): balances the case and reaches a justified conclusion, showing awareness of the members' views.

practice.stem:
The treasurer of Riverside Tennis Club provides these balances at 1 January 2025:
                                 $
Clubhouse                  180,000
Equipment                   24,500
Bar inventory                3,800
Subscriptions in arrears     1,200
Subscriptions in advance       900
Bank                         6,700
Electricity accrued            450
Bar suppliers (payables)     2,100

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the accumulated fund of the club at 1 January 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the meaning of the term 'accumulated fund'.
parts.answer: It is the club's capital: the excess of its assets over its liabilities, built up from past surpluses (and capital receipts) that belong to the members.
parts.working: 1 mark equivalent of capital / assets − liabilities; 1 mark built up from accumulated surpluses.

practice.stem: Cedar Hill Chess Club started on 1 January 2025 with 240 members. The annual subscription is $150. By 31 December 2025, 12 members had not paid their 2025 subscription and 9 members had already paid their 2026 subscription.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the subscriptions income for 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cash received for subscriptions during 2025.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the subscriptions in arrears and in advance are shown in the statement of financial position at 31 December 2025.
parts.answer: Arrears $1,800: current asset. In advance $1,350: current liability.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The statement of financial position of Pinecrest Hockey Club at 31 December 2025 shows: non-current assets $42,000; inventory of kit $3,500; subscriptions in arrears $900; cash at bank $2,200; subscriptions received in advance $1,400; creditors $2,650.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the accumulated fund at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the accumulated fund appears in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: In the equity section, as the accumulated fund
parts.working: The accumulated fund is the club's equivalent of capital and is shown within equity.

practice.stem: A member of Hartfield Sailing Club asks why the club's statement of financial position shows a liability for subscriptions received before the year started.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why subscriptions received in advance are shown as a current liability and not as income of the year in which they were received.
parts.answer: They relate to a future year. The club owes members membership for that future year, so it is a liability until the service is provided; income is recognised as the membership year passes.
parts.working: 1 mark for the obligation to provide membership in a future period; 1 mark for income being recognised in the period it relates to.

practice.stem:
Five items affect Lowmoor Bowls Club in 2026:
(i) subscriptions for 2027 received in cash in December 2026
(ii) a new mower bought for cash
(iii) an old mower sold at less than its carrying amount
(iv) a donation received for general use
(v) insurance for 2027 paid in advance in December 2026

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each item, state whether it increases, decreases or has no effect on the accumulated fund.
parts.answer: (i) No effect: the cash received for next year is matched by a liability, so the fund is unchanged. (ii) No effect: cash is exchanged for an asset. (iii) Decreases: a loss on disposal is charged to the income and expenditure account. (iv) Increases: a donation for general use is income. (v) No effect: the prepaid insurance is an asset that is matched by the payment.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct classification with the reason.

practice.stem:
Moonlight Badminton Club, Kuala Lumpur, provides this information for 2025:
at 1 January 2025: subscriptions in arrears $1,400; subscriptions in advance $600
subscriptions received during 2025: $38,250 (including $1,250 of the 2024 arrears)
at 31 December 2025: subscriptions in arrears for 2025 $1,100; subscriptions received in advance for 2026 $1,350
The rest of the 2024 arrears will never be received and are to be written off.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the subscriptions account for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Subscriptions income transferred to the income and expenditure account: $37,350.
Subscriptions account
Dr                                                                                                   Cr
Date         Details                             $  |  Date         Details                             $
2025 Jan 1   Balance b/d (arrears)           1,400  |  2025 Jan 1   Balance b/d (advance)             600
2025 Dec 31  Income and expenditure         37,350  |  2025         Bank                           38,250
2025 Dec 31  Balance c/d (advance)           1,350  |  2025 Dec 31  Income and exp. (written off)     150
                                                    |  2025 Dec 31  Balance c/d (arrears)           1,100
                                            40,100  |                                              40,100
parts.working: B1 opening arrears debit and advance credit; B1 bank; B1 write-off 150 credited (debited to I&E as an expense); B1 closing balances c/d on correct sides; B1 income 37,350 (balancing figure).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why some clubs do not include subscriptions in arrears as income until they are received.
parts.answer: Prudence: members who have not paid may leave the club and never pay, so the income is uncertain and should not be recognised (nor shown as an asset) until cash is received.
parts.working: 1 mark prudence; 1 mark uncertainty of collection/members may leave.

practice.stem: Crystal Lake Swim Club's treasurer records 84 new members who joined during 2025. Each new member paid an entrance fee of $75 in cash, in addition to their annual subscription. The entrance fee is not refundable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total entrance fee income for 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the entrance fees should be treated in the 2025 accounts, and explain why.
parts.answer: The entrance fees are recorded as income in the income and expenditure account for 2025. They are non-refundable payments for joining the club in that year, so they are income of that year rather than capital or a liability.
parts.working: 1 mark for income in the I&E account; 1 mark for non-refundable / paid for joining in the year; 1 mark for not treating them as capital or a liability.

practice.stem: Ridgeway Pottery Society, Kandy, had an accumulated fund of $82,400 at 1 January 2026. Its surplus for 2026 was $6,100. In December 2026 the committee transferred $5,000 of the fund to a building reserve to pay for a future kiln.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the general accumulated fund at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: Opening fund 82,400 + surplus 6,100 − transfer to building reserve 5,000 = 83,500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the transfer does not change the club's total equity.
parts.answer: The transfer moves an amount from the general accumulated fund to a building reserve; both are within equity, so total equity stays at 88,500.
parts.working: 1 mark for both being equity; 1 mark for the transfer moving money within equity rather than adding or removing it.

practice.stem: Lakeridge Rally Club sold an old minibus during 2026. Its carrying amount was $7,800 and it was sold for $6,250. The surplus before the sale was $14,200. The accumulated fund at 1 January 2026 was $61,900.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the surplus for the year after the loss on disposal.
parts.working: Loss on disposal = carrying amount 7,800 − proceeds 6,250 = 1,550. Surplus = 14,200 − 1,550 = 12,650.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the accumulated fund at 31 December 2026.

practice.stem: Shelter Hill Tennis Club has 120 full members paying $200 a year, 45 junior members paying half the full subscription and 8 honorary members who pay nothing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the subscriptions income from the membership.
parts.working: Full members 120 × $200 = 24,000; junior members 45 × $100 = 4,500; total 28,500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why honorary members, who pay nothing, do not create income for the club.
parts.answer: No amount is due or received from them, so no income is recognised. Unless the club bears a cost for them, there is no expense or entry in the accounts either.
parts.working: 1 mark for no amount due or received; 1 mark for no entry unless the club incurs costs for them.

practice.stem: Highland Golf Society was formed on 1 January 2022. Life membership fees are credited to a life membership account and transferred to the income and expenditure account in equal amounts over 10 years, starting in the year the fee is received. Life membership fees received were: 2022 $9,000; 2023 $6,000; 2024 $12,000; 2025 $7,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount transferred from the life membership account to the income and expenditure account for 2025.
parts.working: All fees received 2022–2025 are still within their 10 years: 10% × (9,000 + 6,000 + 12,000 + 7,500) (M1) = $3,450 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance on the life membership account at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why life membership fees are not treated as income in full in the year they are received.
parts.answer: Matching: the fee pays for membership over many years, so it is spread over the years in which members use the club; taking it all at once would overstate the surplus in one year.
parts.working: 1 mark matching/accruals; 1 mark fee covers future years / avoids distorting one year's surplus.

practice.stem: Lakeside Rowing Club's year ends on 31 March. At 31 March 2026 its accumulated fund was $158,400. The surplus for the year was $12,600. During the year the club received a legacy (a gift in a former member's will) of $20,000, which was credited directly to the accumulated fund.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the accumulated fund at 1 April 2025.
parts.working: Closing fund = opening fund + surplus + legacy (M1). Opening = 158,400 − 12,600 − 20,000 (M1) = $125,800 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the legacy was credited directly to the accumulated fund rather than to the income and expenditure account.
parts.answer: It is a one-off capital receipt, not a regular revenue income; including it would overstate the surplus from normal activities and mislead members about whether subscriptions cover running costs.
parts.working: 1 mark capital/non-recurring receipt; 1 mark would distort the year's surplus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one item, other than a deficit, that would reduce the accumulated fund.
parts.answer: A decrease in the value of assets with no change in liabilities, e.g. a downward revaluation of the clubhouse charged to the fund.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid item (e.g. downward revaluation; loss of an uninsured asset).

practice.stem: Crestview Hiking Club, 2025: subscriptions in arrears at 1 January 2025 (for 2024) $1,800; subscriptions received in advance at 1 January 2025 (for 2025) $600. Cash received during 2025 was $46,900, of which $1,800 was the 2024 arrears and $2,000 was for 2026. At 31 December 2025 subscriptions in arrears were $1,250 before writing off $450 of debts the committee has decided are irrecoverable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the subscriptions income for 2025 before the irrecoverable debt is written off.
parts.working: Income = cash received − opening arrears + closing arrears − closing advance + opening advance = 46,900 − 1,800 + 1,250 − 2,000 + 600 = 44,950. 1 mark for each direction of the adjustments; 1 for the total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net subscriptions income after the write-off.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the $450 written off is deducted from subscriptions income rather than from the accumulated fund.
parts.answer: The debt was part of this year's income, so the write-off is a reduction in this year's income and surplus. Charging it through the accumulated fund would bypass the income and expenditure account.
parts.working: 1 mark for the write-off reducing the income for the year; 1 mark for the fact that it belongs in the I&E account, not the fund directly.

practice.stem: The statement of financial position of Lakeside Tennis and Squash Club at 31 December 2026 shows: clubhouse $60,000 and equipment $28,000; cash $4,500; bar inventory $1,200; subscriptions in arrears $800; creditors $2,100; subscriptions received in advance $1,300; a bank loan of $40,000 of which $6,000 is repayable within one year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total current assets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total current liabilities.
parts.working: 2,100 + 1,300 + 6,000 = 9,400. 1 mark for the loan due within one year; 1 for the total.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the accumulated fund at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: Net assets = non-current assets 88,000 + current assets 6,500 − current liabilities 9,400 − non-current loan 34,000 = 51,100.

practice.stem: The draft accumulated fund of Glenview Scuba Club at 31 December 2025 was $42,000. Two items were overlooked: electricity of $3,600 used in December was not accrued, and insurance of $1,200 paid for 2026 was not treated as a prepayment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected accumulated fund.
parts.working: Draft fund 42,000 − omitted accrual 3,600 + overlooked prepayment 1,200 = 39,600.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how omitting the accrued electricity affected the reported surplus for the year.
parts.answer: The expense was understated by $3,600, so the surplus was overstated by $3,600. The accrual should have been added to expenses.
parts.working: 1 mark for the expense being understated; 1 mark for the surplus being overstated by the same amount.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item is recorded on the credit side of a sales ledger control account?
A credit sales for the month
B a customer's cheque that has been dishonoured
C an irrecoverable debt written off
D interest charged to a customer on an overdue account
parts.answer: C an irrecoverable debt written off
parts.working: Irrecoverable debts reduce the amount owed by customers, so they are credited. A dishonoured cheque (B) is debited because the customer owes the money again.

practice.stem:
Rehman Hardware, Sialkot, provides the following information for the year ended 30 September 2026.
                                                             $
Purchases ledger balance 1 October 2025 (credit)        21,500
Purchases ledger balance 30 September 2026 (credit)     24,800
Payments to credit suppliers                           143,200
Discounts received                                       2,600
Returns outwards                                         3,900
Contra with sales ledger                                 1,100

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the purchases ledger control account for the year ended 30 September 2026, showing the credit purchases as the balancing figure.
parts.answer:
Purchases ledger control account
Dr                              $ | Cr                              $
Bank                      143,200 | Balance b/d                21,500
Discounts received          2,600 | Purchases (credit)        154,100
Purchases returns           3,900 |
Sales ledger control        1,100 |
Balance c/d                24,800 |
                          175,600 |                           175,600
Credit purchases = $154,100
parts.working: B1 each side's items correctly placed (payments, discounts, returns, contra on the debit side; opening balance on the credit side) ×3; A1 credit purchases $154,100.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a contra entry between the sales ledger and the purchases ledger.
parts.answer: A business that both buys from and sells to the same firm sets off the amount it owes against the amount owed to it, so only the net balance is settled in cash.
parts.working: 1 mark: same firm is both customer and supplier. 1 mark: balances are set off/cancelled; recorded Dr purchases ledger control, Cr sales ledger control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two benefits to a business of keeping a sales ledger control account.
parts.answer: Any two explained: it gives a quick total of trade receivables for the statement of financial position; it helps to locate errors to the sales ledger; it acts as a check on the work of the sales ledger clerk / helps detect fraud; it allows a trial balance to be drawn up without listing every customer.
parts.working: 1 mark for each benefit identified, 1 mark for each development (2 × 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why agreement between the control account and the list of sales ledger balances does not prove that the sales ledger is free from errors.
parts.answer: Some errors, such as posting an invoice to the wrong customer's account (error of commission) or omitting a transaction completely, affect neither total.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid reason with an example.

practice.stem:
Al-Noor Textiles, Faisalabad, provides the following information for March 2026.
                                                         $
Sales ledger balances 1 March: debit                56,300
Sales ledger balances 1 March: credit                  740
Credit sales                                       148,900
Cash sales                                          32,000
Cheques received from credit customers             131,250
Discounts allowed                                    2,980
Sales returns                                        4,460
Irrecoverable debts written off                      1,370
Customer's cheque dishonoured                        2,100
Set off against purchases ledger                     1,850
Refund paid to customer with a credit balance          740
Sales ledger credit balances 31 March                  520

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the sales ledger control account for March 2026. Balance the account and bring down the balances on 1 April 2026.
parts.answer:
Sales ledger control account
Dr                                $ | Cr                                $
Balance b/d                  56,300 | Balance b/d                     740
Sales                       148,900 | Bank                        131,250
Bank (dishonoured cheque)     2,100 | Discounts allowed             2,980
Bank (refund)                   740 | Sales returns                 4,460
Balance c/d                     520 | Irrecoverable debts           1,370
                                    | Purchases ledger control      1,850
                                    | Balance c/d                  65,910
                            208,560 |                             208,560
Balance b/d                  65,910 | Balance b/d                     520
parts.working: Closing debit balance $65,910 = (56,300 + 148,900 + 2,100 + 740 + 520) − (740 + 131,250 + 2,980 + 4,460 + 1,370 + 1,850). 1 mark each: opening balances both sides; sales and dishonoured cheque; refund; receipts, discounts and returns; irrecoverable debts and contra; closing balances c/d and b/d.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the cash sales are not recorded in the sales ledger control account.
parts.answer: The control account records only amounts owed by credit customers. Cash sales are paid for immediately, so no receivable is created.
parts.working: 1 mark: control account summarises credit customers/receivables. 1 mark: cash sales create no debt.

practice.stem: Chenab Rice Mills provides the following for May 2026: sales ledger control account balance 1 May $18,250 debit; credit sales $64,300; sales returns $2,150; cheques received from credit customers $59,800; irrecoverable debts written off $900.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the book of prime entry from which each of the following totals in the sales ledger control account is taken:
(1) credit sales
(2) sales returns
(3) cheques received from credit customers
(4) irrecoverable debts written off
parts.answer: (1) sales journal (sales day book); (2) sales returns journal; (3) cash book; (4) general journal (the journal)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the closing balance on the sales ledger control account on 31 May 2026.
parts.answer: $19,700 debit

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item is recorded on the debit side of a purchases ledger control account?
A credit purchases for the month
B goods returned to a supplier
C a refund received from a supplier who had been overpaid
D interest charged by a supplier on an overdue account
parts.answer: B goods returned to a supplier
parts.working: Returns outwards reduce the amount owed to suppliers, so the control account is debited (Cr purchases returns). Credit purchases and interest charged by a supplier increase the liability (credit). A refund received from a supplier is Dr bank, Cr control account, cancelling a debit balance.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The following information is available for the sales ledger of Pak Fasteners for April.
                                                 $
Balance 1 April (debit)                     38,400
Credit sales                               212,600
Cheques received from credit customers     196,300
Discounts allowed                            4,100
Sales returns                                5,800
Irrecoverable debts written off              1,900
Contra with purchases ledger                 2,300
Customer's cheque dishonoured                1,250
What is the closing debit balance on the sales ledger control account on 30 April?
A $39,350
B $41,850
C $44,150
D $46,450
parts.working: 38,400 + 212,600 + 1,250 − 196,300 − 4,100 − 5,800 − 1,900 − 2,300 = 41,850. A treats the dishonoured cheque as a credit; C leaves out the contra; D debits the contra instead of crediting it.

practice.stem:
Asante Cocoa Traders, Kumasi, Ghana, provides the following information for the year ended 31 December 2025.
                                                               $
Purchases ledger balances 1 January 2025: credit          47,200
Purchases ledger balances 1 January 2025: debit              390
Credit purchases                                         186,400
Returns outwards                                           5,120
Payments to suppliers                                    171,600
Discounts received                                         3,240
Contra with sales ledger                                   2,750
Interest charged by a supplier on an overdue account         180
Purchases ledger debit balances 31 December 2025             460

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the purchases ledger control account for the year ended 31 December 2025. Balance the account and bring down the balances.
parts.answer:
Purchases ledger control account
Dr                              $ | Cr                              $
Balance b/d                   390 | Balance b/d                47,200
Purchases returns           5,120 | Purchases                 186,400
Bank                      171,600 | Interest charged              180
Discounts received          3,240 | Balance c/d                   460
Sales ledger control        2,750 |
Balance c/d                51,140 |
                          234,240 |                           234,240
Balance b/d                   460 | Balance b/d                51,140
parts.working: Closing credit balance = (47,200 + 186,400 + 180 + 460) − (390 + 5,120 + 171,600 + 3,240 + 2,750) = 51,140. 1 mark each: opening balances; purchases and interest; returns and payments; discounts and contra; debit balance c/d/b/d; credit balance 51,140 c/d/b/d.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a supplier's account in the purchases ledger can have a debit balance.
parts.answer: The business has paid the supplier more than it owes, for example by paying an invoice twice or returning goods after paying for them, so the supplier owes the business money.
parts.working: 1 mark: overpayment/returns after payment; 1 mark: supplier now owes the business (shown as a receivable).

practice.stem:
At 31 August 2026 the sales ledger control account of Margalla Office Supplies showed a debit balance of $84,620. The total of the list of balances extracted from the sales ledger was $82,585. The following errors were found.
1 The sales journal was undercast by $900.
2 A credit note for $340 was entered in the customer's account but was omitted from the sales returns journal.
3 A discount allowed of $125 was credited to a customer's account twice.
4 An irrecoverable debt of $760 was written off in the customer's account but not in the control account.
5 A customer's balance of $1,280 was omitted from the list of balances.
6 A contra of $430 was recorded in the customer's account but not in the control account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected sales ledger control account balance.
parts.answer:
Balance per control account                            84,620
Add (1) sales journal undercast                           900
Less (2) credit note omitted from returns journal       (340)
Less (4) irrecoverable debt not entered                 (760)
Less (6) contra not entered                             (430)
Corrected balance                                      83,990
parts.working: 1 mark each for items 1, 2, 4 and 6 correctly adjusted; own figure total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected total of the list of sales ledger balances.
parts.answer:
Total of list                                          82,585
Add (3) discount credited twice                           125
Add (5) balance omitted                                 1,280
Corrected total                                        83,990
The corrected totals agree.
parts.working: 1 mark each for items 3 and 5; 1 mark corrected total $83,990 agreeing with (a).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one type of error that would not be revealed by comparing the control account with the list of balances.
parts.answer: For example an error of commission: an invoice posted to the wrong customer's account.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid error.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The following information relates to the sales ledger of a business for the year.
                                           $
Opening debit balances                42,300
Opening credit balances                  650
Credit sales                         186,400
Receipts from credit customers       171,250
Discounts allowed                      3,180
Sales returns                          4,920
Customer's cheque dishonoured          1,400
Contra with purchases ledger           2,600
Irrecoverable debts written off        1,150
Closing credit balances                  820
What is the closing debit balance on the sales ledger control account?
A $44,370
B $47,000
C $47,170
D $52,370
parts.working: Dr: 42,300 + 186,400 + 1,400 + 820 (closing credit balances) = 230,920. Cr: 650 + 171,250 + 3,180 + 4,920 + 2,600 + 1,150 = 183,750. Closing debit balance = 47,170. A ($44,370) treats the dishonoured cheque as a credit; B ignores both credit balances; D puts the contra on the debit side.

practice.stem:
Tan Wei Furniture, Penang, Malaysia, keeps a sales ledger control account. For the year ended 31 December 2025:
                                                     $
Balances 1 January 2025: debit                  28,640
                     credit                        310
Receipts from credit customers                 214,580
Customers' cheques dishonoured                   1,260
Discounts allowed                                2,940
Sales returns                                    5,470
Irrecoverable debts written off                  1,830
Contra with purchases ledger                     3,150
Refund paid to a customer who had overpaid         410
Interest charged on overdue accounts               220
Balances 31 December 2025: debit                31,960
                       credit                      540
The figure for credit sales has been lost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the sales ledger control account for the year ended 31 December 2025, showing the credit sales as the balancing figure.
parts.answer:
Sales ledger control account
Dr                                  $   Cr                                  $
Balance b/d (debit)           28,640   Balance b/d (credit)              310
Credit sales                 229,170   Bank (receipts)               214,580
Bank – dishonoured cheques     1,260   Discounts allowed               2,940
Bank – refund to customer        410   Sales returns                   5,470
Interest on overdue accounts     220   Irrecoverable debts             1,830
Balance c/d (credit)             540   Purchases ledger control (contra) 3,150
                                       Balance c/d (debit)            31,960
                             260,240                              260,240
Credit sales = $229,170
parts.working: Debit-side items correctly placed (1 for dishonoured cheques, refund and interest together; 1 for credit balance c/d); credit-side items (1 for receipts, discounts, returns; 1 for irrecoverable debts and contra); closing balances c/d (1); credit sales $229,170 (1 own figure).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a customer's account in the sales ledger can come to have a credit balance.
parts.answer: The customer has paid more than they owe, for example by paying twice, or by paying for goods that were later returned, or by paying in advance.
parts.working: 1 mark for the idea that the business owes the customer; 1 mark for a valid example (overpayment, returns after payment, payment in advance).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how keeping a sales ledger control account can help the owner to discover fraud by a sales ledger clerk.
parts.answer: The control account is prepared from totals in the books of prime entry by a different person. If the clerk alters customers' accounts (for example to hide stolen receipts), the list of balances will no longer agree with the control account, so the difference is investigated.
parts.working: 1 mark independent preparation from totals; 1 mark disagreement reveals tampering / limits the clerk's opportunity.

practice.stem:
At 30 June 2026 the purchases ledger control account of Lagos Fresh Foods showed a credit balance of $63,410. The total of the list of purchases ledger balances was $65,435. The following errors were discovered.
1 The purchases journal was overcast by $1,000.
2 Goods returned to a supplier, $560, were debited to the supplier's account as $650.
3 Discounts received of $215 were recorded in the suppliers' accounts but not in the control account.
4 A supplier's credit balance of $2,140 was entered in the list as $1,240.
5 A payment of $1,780 to a supplier was entered on the credit side of the supplier's account.
6 A contra of $670 was entered in the control account twice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected purchases ledger control account balance.
parts.answer:
Balance per control account (credit)                   63,410
Less (1) purchases journal overcast                   (1,000)
Less (3) discounts received not entered                 (215)
Add (6) contra debited twice                              670
Corrected balance                                      62,865
parts.working: 1 mark each for items 1, 3 and 6 (direction must be right: a credit balance is reduced by debits); 1 mark own figure total. Items 2, 4 and 5 do not affect the control account.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected total of the list of purchases ledger balances.
parts.answer:
Total of list                                                65,435
Add (2) returns overstated by $90                                90
Add (4) balance listed as $1,240 instead of $2,140              900
Less (5) payment credited instead of debited (2 × $1,780)    (3,560)
Corrected total                                              62,865
parts.working: 1 mark each for items 2, 4 and 5 (item 5 must be doubled); 1 mark total agreeing with (a).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader finds two errors in her sales ledger records.
1 The sales journal was overcast by $500.
2 An invoice for $120 was credited to the customer's account instead of being debited.
What adjustments are needed to the sales ledger control account balance and to the total of the list of customers' balances?
A control account: decrease $500; list: increase $240
B control account: decrease $500; list: increase $120
C control account: increase $500; list: decrease $240
D control account: no change; list: increase $740
parts.answer: A control account: decrease $500; list: increase $240
parts.working: The overcast journal total is posted only to the control account, so its debit balance is $500 too high. The individual invoices were posted correctly except the $120 invoice, which was credited instead of debited, so the customer's balance is understated by 2 × $120 = $240. B forgets to double the reversal.

practice.stem:
Kilimanjaro Coffee Exporters, Mombasa, Kenya, provides the following for the year ended 31 March 2026.
                                                         $
Sales ledger balances 1 April 2025: debit           92,400
Sales ledger balances 1 April 2025: credit           1,150
Credit sales                                       418,700
Receipts from credit customers                     389,600
Discounts allowed                                    6,240
Sales returns                                        9,830
Irrecoverable debts written off                      3,560
Interest charged on overdue accounts                   420
Dishonoured cheques                                  2,890
Contra with purchases ledger                         4,150
Sales ledger credit balances 31 March 2026             980
The business keeps an allowance for doubtful debts of 5% of the closing debit balances.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the sales ledger control account for the year ended 31 March 2026, bringing down the balances on 1 April 2026.
parts.answer:
Sales ledger control account
Dr                                $ | Cr                                $
Balance b/d                  92,400 | Balance b/d                   1,150
Sales                       418,700 | Bank                        389,600
Interest charged                420 | Discounts allowed             6,240
Bank (dishonoured cheques)    2,890 | Sales returns                 9,830
Balance c/d                     980 | Irrecoverable debts           3,560
                                    | Purchases ledger control      4,150
                                    | Balance c/d                 100,860
                            515,390 |                             515,390
Balance b/d                 100,860 | Balance b/d                     980
parts.working: Debit balance c/d $100,860. 1 mark each: opening balances; sales, interest and dishonoured cheques; receipts, discounts, returns; irrecoverable debts and contra; both closing balances. The allowance for doubtful debts is not entered.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the trade receivables figure to be shown in the statement of financial position at 31 March 2026.
parts.working: M1 5% × 100,860 = 5,043.00; A1 95,817.00. (The $980 credit balances are shown separately as a current liability.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the allowance for doubtful debts is not recorded in the sales ledger control account.
parts.answer: The control account must agree with the total of the individual customer accounts. The allowance is only an estimate and is not posted to any customer's account, so it is kept in a separate account.
parts.working: 1 mark: the control account must agree with the customer accounts, and the allowance is an estimate not posted to any customer's account.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
At the year end a purchases ledger control account had a credit balance of $38,450. The total of the list of suppliers' balances was $37,910. These errors were found:
1 The purchases journal was overcast by $400.
2 Discounts received of $90 were entered in a supplier's account but not in the control account.
3 A supplier's credit balance of $50 was left out of the list of balances.
What is the corrected balance of the control account and does it now agree with the list?
A $37,960, which agrees with the corrected list
B $38,760, which does not agree with the corrected list
C $38,140, which does not agree with the corrected list
D $37,910, which agrees with the corrected list
parts.answer: A $37,960, which agrees with the corrected list
parts.working: Control: 38,450 − 400 (overcast purchases credited in error) − 90 (discount received debited) = 37,960. List: 37,910 + 50 = 37,960, so they agree. C adds the discount instead of deducting it; D wrongly adjusts the control account for an error that affects only the list.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bank statement shows a credit balance of $4,200. Cheques of $1,350 paid to suppliers have not yet been presented and a lodgement of $900 has not yet been credited by the bank. The cash book has been fully updated. What is the bank balance in the cash book?
A $1,950 debit
B $3,750 debit
C $4,650 debit
D $6,450 debit
parts.answer: B $3,750 debit
parts.working: Cash book = bank statement − unpresented cheques + outstanding lodgement = 4,200 − 1,350 + 900 = 3,750. C adds the cheques and deducts the lodgement, reversing both adjustments.

practice.stem:
The bank columns of the cash book of Swat Valley Honey showed a debit balance of $6,820 on 30 June 2026. A comparison with the bank statement showed:
1 bank charges of $64 and a standing order for insurance of $350 had not been entered in the cash book
2 a credit transfer of $1,200 from a customer and a dividend of $275 paid directly into the bank had not been entered in the cash book
3 cheques no. 1043 for $1,180 and no. 1045 for $1,235 had not been presented
4 cash and cheques of $1,960 paid in on 30 June did not appear on the bank statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the updated cash book (bank columns) at 30 June 2026.
parts.answer:
Cash book (bank columns)
Dr                                $ | Cr                                $
Balance b/d                   6,820 | Bank charges                     64
Credit transfer: customer     1,200 | Insurance (standing order)      350
Dividend received               275 | Balance c/d                   7,881
                              8,295 |                               8,295
Balance b/d                   7,881 |
parts.working: 1 mark: bank charges and standing order; 1 mark: credit transfer; 1 mark: dividend; 1 mark: balance $7,881.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the bank reconciliation statement at 30 June 2026, starting with the balance shown on the bank statement.
parts.answer:
Balance per bank statement                        8,336
Less unpresented cheques (1,180 + 1,235)        (2,415)
Add lodgement not yet credited                    1,960
Balance per updated cash book                     7,881

practice.stem: Farah runs a dressmaking business in Multan. She records all receipts and payments in a cash book.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the balance on the bank statement may differ from the bank balance in the cash book.
parts.answer: Any two explained: timing differences such as unpresented cheques (entered in the cash book but not yet paid by the bank) or lodgements not yet credited; items the bank has entered that the business does not yet know about, such as bank charges, interest, standing orders, direct debits, credit transfers or dishonoured cheques; errors in the cash book or by the bank.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason, 1 mark for each explanation (2 × 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two benefits of preparing a bank reconciliation statement regularly.
parts.answer: Any two: errors in the cash book or by the bank are found quickly; the cash book is brought up to date; fraud is more likely to be detected; stale (old unpresented) cheques can be identified; it confirms the bank balance shown in the statement of financial position.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
When a bank statement is compared with the cash book, which item requires an entry in the cash book rather than in the bank reconciliation statement?
A a cheque paid to a supplier that has not yet been presented
B cash paid into the bank on the last day of the month that is not yet on the statement
C a direct debit for insurance shown only on the bank statement
D a cheque paid by another customer of the bank, credited to the business's account in error
parts.answer: C a direct debit for insurance shown only on the bank statement
parts.working: The direct debit is a genuine payment the business has not yet recorded, so the cash book must be updated. Unpresented cheques and outstanding lodgements are timing differences and the bank's error is corrected by the bank; all three go in the reconciliation statement.

3 Bank charges of $140 had not been entered in the cash book.

parts.text: Calculate the cash book balance before the corrections were made.
