3 Discount received of $430 was credited to the discount allowed account.
4 An electricity bill of $680 for April 2026 had not been accrued.
5 Goods costing $1,100 taken by Kamran for his own use had not been recorded.
6 Insurance of $360 paid in advance had not been adjusted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 30 April 2026.
parts.answer:
Draft profit for the year                          48,360
Less inventory overvalued                         (1,250)
Add van wrongly charged to motor expenses           9,500
Less depreciation on van (20% × 9,500)            (1,900)
Discount error                                          0
Less electricity accrued                            (680)
Add goods taken by owner                            1,100
Add insurance prepaid                                 360
Corrected profit for the year                      55,490
parts.working: 1 mark each: inventory; van; depreciation; accrual; drawings of goods (reduce cost of sales); prepayment. Own figure total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect on profit of error 3.
parts.answer: None. Discount allowed (an expense) was reduced by $430 instead of discount received (an income) being increased by $430; either way profit is $430 higher, so the profit figure is correct even though both accounts are wrong.
parts.working: 1 mark: no effect on profit; 1 mark: explanation.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense account

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Rent received of $600 from a tenant was correctly debited to the bank account but was credited to the rent payable account (an expense account). What is the effect on the profit for the year of correcting this error?
A profit increases by $600
B profit decreases by $600
C profit decreases by $1,200
D no effect on profit
parts.answer: D no effect on profit
parts.working: Before correction the expense was $600 too low (profit +600). After correction rent payable rises by $600 (profit −600) and rent received rises by $600 (profit +600), so profit is unchanged. A and B look at only one side of the correcting entry.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense account
practice.stem:
Kemal Textiles, Izmir, Turkey. The trial balance at 30 September 2026 did not agree and the difference was entered in a suspense account. These errors were then found:
1 the total of the sales returns journal, $1,340, was posted to the sales returns account as $1,430
2 loan interest paid of $750 was entered in the cash book only
3 the proceeds of $1,600 from selling old equipment were credited to the sales account
4 discount received of $215 was debited to the discount received account
5 a payment of $380 to a supplier was correctly credited in the cash book but debited to the purchases ledger control account as $830.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare journal entries to correct errors 1 to 5. Narratives are not required.
parts.answer:
Dr $     Cr $
1 Suspense                               90
    Sales returns                                90
2 Loan interest                         750
    Suspense                                    750
3 Sales                               1,600
    Disposal of equipment                     1,600
4 Suspense                              430
    Discount received                           430
5 Suspense                              450
    Purchases ledger control                    450
parts.working: 1 mark per correct journal (both sides and amounts).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the suspense account, showing the balance entered when the trial balance was drawn up.
parts.answer:
Suspense account
Dr                                $   Cr                                $
Sales returns                     90   Balance (difference in TB)      220
Discount received                430   Loan interest                   750
Purchases ledger control         450
                                 970                                   970
parts.working: Correct entries for errors 1, 2, 4, 5 (2: deduct 1 per wrong item); opening credit balance $220 (1).

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense account
practice.stem:
The draft profit of Coral Reef Electronics, Colombo, Sri Lanka, for the year ended 31 July 2026 was $72,900. The trial balance did not agree, and a suspense account was opened with a debit balance of $1,340. The following errors were found.
1 Returns inwards of $680 were posted to the credit side of the returns outwards account.
2 Commission received of $450 was entered in the bank account but not posted to the commission received account.
3 Machinery bought for $3,200 was debited to the machinery repairs account. (No depreciation is charged in the year of purchase.)
4 The wages account was undercast by $430.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the suspense account.
parts.answer:
Suspense account
Dr                                  $ | Cr                                  $
Difference in trial balance     1,340 | Returns inwards                   680
Commission received               450 | Returns outwards                  680
                                      | Wages                             430
                                1,790 |                                 1,790
parts.working: 1 mark opening debit balance; 1 mark returns entries (680 + 680); 1 mark commission and wages.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 31 July 2026.
parts.answer:
Draft profit                                     72,900
Less returns inwards understated                  (680)
Less returns outwards overstated                  (680)
Add commission received                             450
Add machinery charged to repairs                  3,200
Less wages undercast                              (430)
Corrected profit                                 74,760
parts.working: 1 mark returns (−1,360 in total); 1 mark commission; 1 mark machinery; 1 mark wages and total $74,760.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of correcting error 3 on the non-current assets in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Non-current assets (machinery) increase by $3,200.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense account
practice.stem:
The trial balance of Hunza Apricot Traders at 31 December 2025 did not agree, and a suspense account was opened with a credit balance of $2,460. The draft profit was $31,250. Three errors were found, after which the suspense account was closed.
1 Insurance paid of $760 was credited to the insurance account.
2 Interest received of $290 was entered in the bank account but not posted to the interest received account.
3 The sales account was undercast by an amount not yet known.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the suspense account, showing the amount by which the sales account was undercast as the balancing figure.
parts.answer:
Suspense account
Dr                                  $ | Cr                                  $
Interest received                 290 | Difference in trial balance     2,460
Sales                           3,690 | Insurance                       1,520
                                3,980 |                                 3,980
parts.working: 1 mark opening credit balance; 1 mark insurance 2 × 760 = 1,520 credit; 1 mark interest 290 debit; 1 mark sales undercast $3,690.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: 31,250 − 1,520 + 290 + 3,690 = 33,710. 1 mark insurance; 1 mark interest and sales; 1 mark answer.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense account
practice.stem:
Diego Ramos owns a hardware shop in Cebu, Philippines. His draft profit for the year ended 31 March 2026 was $54,200. These errors were found:
1 a machine bought on 1 April 2025 for $8,000 was debited to the purchases account. Machinery is depreciated at 25% a year on cost
2 closing inventory included goods at their cost of $2,600; their net realisable value is $1,900
3 goods costing $520 taken by Diego for his own use have not been recorded
4 discount allowed of $340 was credited to the discount received account
5 rent of $900 for April 2026, paid in March 2026, was charged as an expense for the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 31 March 2026.
parts.answer:
$
Draft profit                                 54,200
Add machine wrongly charged to purchases      8,000
Less depreciation on machine (25% × 8,000)   (2,000)
Less inventory written down to NRV             (700)
Add goods taken by owner                        520
Less discount allowed error (2 × 340)          (680)
Add rent prepaid for April 2026                 900
Corrected profit                             60,240
parts.working: 1 mark each: +8,000 and −2,000; −700; +520; −680; +900; corrected profit $60,240 (own figure).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Diego's capital on 1 April 2025 was $72,000 and his recorded drawings for the year were $31,500. Calculate his corrected capital at 31 March 2026.
parts.working: 1 mark drawings increased by $520; 1 mark answer (own profit figure).

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense account
practice.stem:
The trial balance of Coastal Kayaks, Mombasa, did not agree. A suspense account was opened with a credit balance of $1,725. The draft profit for the year was $38,410. After these three errors were corrected the suspense account was cleared:
1 the sales account was undercast by $1,000
2 repairs of $2,450 were correctly credited in the cash book but debited to the repairs account as $2,540
3 the total of discounts received for the year was debited to the purchases ledger control account but not posted to the discount received account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the suspense account and calculate the total of discounts received omitted in error 3.
parts.answer:
Suspense account
Dr                                $   Cr                                $
Sales                         1,000   Balance (difference in TB)    1,725
Repairs                          90
Discount received               635
                              1,725                                 1,725
Discounts received = 1,725 − 1,000 − 90 = $635.
parts.working: Sales 1,000 debited (1); repairs 90 debited (1); opening credit 1,725 (1); discount received $635 as balancing figure (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: 1 mark for all three adjustments added; 1 mark answer (own figure for discounts).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a suspense account balance should not appear in the final statement of financial position.
parts.answer: It is not a real asset or liability; it only shows that errors remain uncorrected, so the statements would be unreliable. All errors should be found and corrected first.
parts.working: 1 mark not a genuine asset/liability; 1 mark statements unreliable / errors must be corrected.

practice.stem: Pooja has just taken over her father's stationery shop in Kathmandu, Nepal. She wants to be sure the ledger balances are correct before the year-end statements are prepared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by verifying the balances in a business's ledger.
parts.answer: Checking the ledger balances against independent evidence or an independent calculation, so that errors are found and corrected before the financial statements are prepared.
parts.working: 1 mark check/compare against another source; 1 mark purpose: find errors / reliable statements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three methods a sole trader can use to verify the accuracy of the ledger balances.
parts.answer: Any three of: trial balance; sales and purchases ledger control accounts; bank reconciliation statement; reconciling suppliers' statements; physical inventory count; checking the non-current asset register against the assets held.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem: Rosa runs a flower shop in Valencia, Spain. Her accountant suggests she should reconcile her cash book with the bank statement every month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three purposes of preparing a bank reconciliation statement each month.
parts.answer: Identifies items not yet entered in the cash book (charges, direct debits, credit transfers) so it can be updated; finds errors in the cash book or by the bank; confirms the correct bank balance for the statement of financial position; can reveal fraud or missing money (e.g. receipts recorded but not banked); identifies old unpresented cheques.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three explained points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two limitations of a bank reconciliation statement as a check on the accuracy of the cash book.
parts.answer: It does not detect an amount that is wrong in both the cash book and the bank (e.g. a cheque written for the wrong amount); it cannot show that a payment was posted to the correct ledger account; it does not check cash transactions that never pass through the bank.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Chukwu Electronics, Enugu, Nigeria, made these errors during May 2026:
1 bank charges of $42 shown on the bank statement were not entered in the cash book
2 a sales invoice was posted to the account of the wrong customer in the sales ledger
3 a purchase invoice of $560, correctly entered in the purchases journal, was posted to the supplier's account as $650
4 the debit side of the rent account was added up as $100 too much.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each error, state which one of the following checks would reveal it: trial balance; sales or purchases ledger control account; bank reconciliation; none of these.
parts.answer:
1 Bank reconciliation.
2 None of these.
3 Purchases ledger control account.
4 Trial balance.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how error 2 is most likely to be discovered.
parts.answer: When monthly statements are sent to customers, the customer who was wrongly charged (or the one whose balance is too low) will query the statement; customer complaints reveal it.
parts.working: 1 mark statements sent to customers; 1 mark customer queries the balance.

practice.stem: Nadia owns a wholesale crockery business in Karachi with 140 credit customers. She keeps a sales ledger control account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why the balance on the sales ledger control account may not agree with the total of the list of customers' balances.
parts.answer: Any two of: a transaction posted to a customer's account but not included in the totals used for the control account (or vice versa); a casting error in a book of prime entry; a balance omitted from the list or copied wrongly; an item posted to the wrong side of a customer's account; a contra or irrecoverable debt entered in only one place.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two limitations of control accounts as a method of checking the accuracy of the sales ledger.
parts.answer: Errors of original entry (wrong amount in the sales journal) are carried to both the control account and the customer's account, so they still agree. Posting to the wrong customer's account (commission) does not change the total. Compensating errors and complete omissions are not revealed. The control account itself may be wrong if the totals are miscast.
parts.working: 2 marks for each limitation explained (1 identify, 1 why it is not revealed), maximum two.

practice.stem: The trial balance of Zafar Builders' Merchants, Sargodha, at 30 June 2026 has debit totals of $248,615 and credit totals of $249,425.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance entered in the suspense account and state whether it is a debit or a credit balance.
parts.answer: 249,425 − 248,615 = $810. The debit side is smaller, so the suspense account has a debit balance of $810.
parts.working: 1 mark amount; 1 mark debit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the business opens a suspense account.
parts.answer: It allows a trial balance (and draft statements) to be prepared on time while the errors are being found; the difference is held temporarily until it can be cleared.
parts.working: 1 mark temporary account; 1 mark allows work to continue while errors are investigated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why clearing the suspense account does not prove that the accounts are free from errors.
parts.answer: The suspense account only deals with errors that make the totals disagree. Errors of omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal and compensating errors leave the totals equal and are still undetected.
parts.working: 1 mark only errors affecting agreement; 1 mark examples of undetected errors.

practice.stem: Ayesha has just started work as an accounts assistant at a pharmacy chain in Islamabad. She believes that because her trial balance agrees, her ledger accounts must be correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two purposes of preparing a trial balance.
parts.answer: Any two: to check the arithmetical accuracy of double entry (debits = credits); to provide a summary of balances from which the financial statements are prepared; to help locate errors.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain three types of error that a trial balance will not reveal. Give an example of each.
parts.answer: Any three with an example: omission (a transaction not recorded at all); commission (posted to the wrong account of the same type); principle (posted to the wrong class of account, e.g. capital expenditure as revenue); original entry (wrong amount in the book of prime entry); complete reversal; compensating errors.
parts.working: 1 mark per error type with a correct example.

practice.stem:
Sana, a pharmacist in Peshawar, says: "My trial balance agrees, so my draft profit of $45,600 must be correct." Her accountant then finds:
1 a credit sale of $1,800 was omitted from the books completely
2 wages of $2,400 paid to the shop assistant were debited to the drawings account
3 electricity of $310 was debited to the rent account
4 a purchase invoice for $920 was entered in the purchases journal as $290.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the trial balance did not reveal any of these errors.
parts.answer: In each case the debit entry and the credit entry are for the same amount (or both omitted), so total debits still equal total credits.
parts.working: 1 mark equal debit and credit / double entry complete; 1 mark applied (e.g. the wrong amount in the purchases journal is posted to both sides).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.answer:
$
Draft profit                              45,600
Add sale omitted                           1,800
Less wages charged to drawings            (2,400)
Less purchase understated (920 − 290)       (630)
Electricity charged to rent                    –
Corrected profit                          44,370
parts.working: 1 mark each: +1,800; −2,400; −630 with no adjustment for error 3; final answer $44,370.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the pharmacist's belief.
parts.answer: She is wrong: a balancing trial balance proves only arithmetical agreement of debits and credits; profit was misstated by $1,230 even though the TB agreed.
parts.working: 1 mark TB only checks arithmetic; 1 mark use of figures.

practice.stem:
Leila Interiors, Muscat, Oman. At 30 November 2026 the account of Gulf Fabrics in Leila's purchases ledger shows a credit balance of $4,355. The statement received from Gulf Fabrics shows $8,280 owing. These differences were found:
1 an invoice for $1,725 dated 29 November is in the post and has not reached Leila
2 Leila's payment of $2,100 sent on 30 November had not reached Gulf Fabrics
3 goods of $460 returned by Leila have not yet been credited by Gulf Fabrics
4 a cash discount of $90 taken by Leila has been disallowed by Gulf Fabrics because the payment was late
5 an invoice for $1,380 was entered in Leila's books as $1,830.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement reconciling the balance on Gulf Fabrics' account in Leila's purchases ledger with the balance on the supplier's statement.
parts.answer:
$
Balance per purchases ledger                       4,355
Less invoice over-recorded (1,830 − 1,380)          (450)
Corrected ledger balance                           3,905
Add invoice in transit                             1,725
Add payment not yet received by supplier           2,100
Add returns not yet credited by supplier             460
Add discount disallowed by supplier                   90
Balance per supplier's statement                   8,280
parts.working: 1 mark each: correction of 450; invoice in transit; payment in transit; returns and discount; final $8,280 agrees.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of the differences require an entry in Leila's own books.
parts.answer: Item 5 (reduce the supplier's balance by $450). Item 4 if Leila accepts that the discount was disallowed (Dr discount received, Cr Gulf Fabrics $90). Items 1–3 are timing differences.
parts.working: 1 mark item 5; 1 mark item 4 with reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why reconciling suppliers' statements is a useful check on the purchases ledger.
parts.answer: The supplier's statement is independent evidence prepared by an outside party, so it reveals errors in posting to the supplier's account (which a control account may not) and prevents paying the wrong amount.
parts.working: 1 mark independent/external evidence; 1 mark finds posting errors / avoids over- or under-payment.

practice.stem:
Haddad Printing, Amman, Jordan. At 31 December 2025 the equipment (cost) account in the ledger had a balance of $186,500. A check against the non-current asset register found:
1 a printer bought for $9,400 was recorded in the ledger but had not been entered in the register
2 a laminator that cost $4,600 was sold during the year; it had been removed from the register but the cost account had not been updated
3 repairs of $2,400 to a printer were debited to the equipment account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected balance on the equipment (cost) account.
parts.working: 1 mark each adjustment; 1 mark answer (max 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The non-current asset register showed total cost of $170,100. Show that, once error 1 is corrected, the register agrees with the corrected ledger balance.
parts.answer: 170,100 + 9,400 = $179,500, the same as the corrected ledger.
parts.working: 1 mark adding 9,400; 1 mark agreement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two benefits of keeping a non-current asset register in addition to the ledger accounts.
parts.answer: It records each asset's details (location, serial number, cost, depreciation), so assets can be physically checked and losses or theft found; it allows depreciation and disposals to be calculated for each asset; it provides an independent check on the ledger total.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two benefits.

practice.stem: Green Valley Dairy, Abbottabad, has replaced its manual ledgers with accounting software. The owner says that the business no longer needs to check its records because "the computer cannot make mistakes".

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the trial balance produced by the new computerised system will always agree.
parts.answer: Every transaction is entered once and the software automatically posts equal debit and credit entries, so arithmetical and one-sided posting errors cannot happen.
parts.working: 1 mark automatic double entry; 1 mark no casting/single-entry errors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the business must still verify its accounting records after changing to the computerised system.
parts.answer: Input errors still occur: wrong amounts (original entry), wrong account codes (commission/principle) and omissions are processed faithfully. Bank charges, direct debits and dishonoured cheques are still found only by bank reconciliation. Inventory and non-current assets must still be physically checked. Fraud or unauthorised entries need independent checks.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four relevant points (or 2 points developed).

practice.stem: At Kibo Builders' Supplies, Arusha, Tanzania, one clerk opens the post, records receipts from customers in the cash book, banks the money, posts the sales ledger and approves irrecoverable debts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the same clerk doing all of these tasks creates a risk of fraud.
parts.answer: The clerk could keep a customer's payment and hide it by delaying the posting, using later receipts from other customers to cover it (teeming and lading), or by writing the debt off as irrecoverable or issuing a false credit note. Nobody independent checks the records.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three points (lack of segregation, example method of concealment, no independent check).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the sales ledger control account and the monthly bank reconciliation, prepared by the owner, would reduce this risk.
parts.answer: The owner prepares the control account from totals of the cash book, sales journal and journal, independent of the clerk; differences with the list of balances must be explained. Unusual write-offs or credit notes appear in the totals. The bank reconciliation checks that receipts recorded were actually banked and in the right amounts.
parts.working: 1 mark independent preparation; 1 mark comparison with list / investigation of write-offs; 1 mark bank reconciliation confirms receipts banked.

practice.stem: The owner of a car-rental business in Dubai makes this statement to her new bookkeeper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: "If my trial balance agrees, my financial statements must be correct." Discuss this statement.
parts.answer:
Agree: a TB that agrees shows debits equal credits, so arithmetical and single-entry errors are unlikely; it is a quick check and the basis for the statements.
Disagree: six types of error do not affect agreement — omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal and compensating errors (examples). Errors of principle and original entry change profit and asset values. The TB says nothing about whether adjustments (accruals, depreciation, irrecoverable debts, inventory valuation) are correct, or whether estimates are reasonable. Fraud can be concealed by balanced entries.
Conclusion: the TB is a necessary but limited check; other verification (control accounts, bank reconciliation, supplier statements, physical counts) and review of adjustments are needed.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for points supporting the statement / purposes of the TB; up to 5 marks for limitations explained with examples (1 per type named with example, 1 per further developed point); 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion within the total. Maximum 8.

practice.stem: Amina owns three shoe shops in Rawalpindi. A clerk spends 20 hours a week on manual sales and purchases ledgers and control accounts and is paid $9 an hour. Accounting software would cost $6,500 a year and would remove this work completely. Assume 52 working weeks a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net annual saving from introducing the software.
parts.answer: Saving in clerk time 20 × 52 × $9 = $9,360; net saving 9,360 − 6,500 = $2,860.
parts.working: 1 mark gross saving; 1 mark net saving.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Amina whether she should replace her manual control accounts and ledgers with the software. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For: net saving of $2,860 a year; automatic posting means control accounts always agree with ledgers and the TB always balances; faster, up-to-date information on customers and suppliers; reports for credit control.
Against: input errors (wrong amount, wrong account) are not detected and a manual control account would no longer act as an independent check; staff training and changeover costs; risk of data loss, viruses or hacking — backups and passwords needed; dependence on one supplier; the clerk's time saved may not be a real saving unless used elsewhere.
Decision: e.g. buy the software because it saves money and gives better information, but keep independent checks such as monthly bank reconciliations and supplier statement reconciliations, with access controls.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for points for (including use of the $2,860); up to 3 marks for points against; 1 mark for a clear decision consistent with the argument.

practice.stem:
Zambezi Hardware, Lusaka, Zambia, found two errors at 31 October 2026:
1 a cheque for $1,460 received from R. Banda was entered correctly in the cash book but was not posted to Banda's account in the sales ledger
2 a cheque for $2,750 paid to a supplier was entered in the cash book as $2,570 and posted from there.
Before correction the sales ledger control account showed $46,280 and the list of sales ledger balances totalled $47,740. The cash book showed a debit balance of $5,630.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each error, state which check revealed it, and explain why the other check did not.
parts.answer:
Error 1 is revealed by the sales ledger control account: the cash book total posted to the control account included $1,460 but Banda's account was not credited, so the list exceeds the control account by $1,460. The bank reconciliation does not reveal it because the cash book and bank both show the $1,460 correctly.
Error 2 is revealed by the bank reconciliation: the bank paid $2,750 but the cash book shows $2,570. The purchases ledger control account does not reveal it because the wrong amount was posted from the cash book to both the control account and the supplier's account.
parts.working: 1 mark each: correct check for error 1; why bank rec misses it; correct check for error 2; why control account misses it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected total of the list of sales ledger balances and the corrected cash book balance.
parts.answer: List: 47,740 − 1,460 = $46,280 (agrees with the control account). Cash book: 5,630 − (2,750 − 2,570) = $5,450.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a business should use more than one method of verification.
parts.answer: Each method checks only certain records and misses certain errors, as shown here; using several methods together covers more types of error and fraud.
parts.working: 1 mark each method has blind spots; 1 mark combination gives wider coverage, with reference to the example.

practice.stem: Ming's Tea House, Kuala Lumpur, recorded sales of $240,000 for the year. After the trial balance had agreed and draft statements were prepared, the auditor found that the sales account had been overcast by $800 and that the wages account had also been overcast by $800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the trial balance agreed.
parts.answer: The two errors are of equal amount on opposite sides: the sales (credit) total and the wages (debit) total are each $800 too high, so they cancel out — compensating errors.
parts.working: 1 mark compensating errors; 1 mark equal amounts on opposite sides.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of the two errors on (i) gross profit and (ii) profit for the year.
parts.answer: (i) Gross profit is overstated by $800 (sales too high). (ii) Profit for the year is unaffected: sales $800 too high and wages $800 too high cancel.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess how far the trial balance can be relied on as a check before the owner uses the gross margin to set next year's prices.
parts.answer: The TB proved only that debits equalled credits; here the gross margin was overstated (sales of $240,000 should have been $239,200), which could lead the owner to think pricing is adequate. Profit for the year is right only by chance. The owner should not rely on the TB alone: control accounts, checking day book casts and analytical review of margins compared with previous years would reveal the error. Conclusion: limited reliance.
parts.working: 1 mark TB checks arithmetic only; 1 mark consequence for gross margin/pricing decisions; 1 mark other checks needed; 1 mark judgement.

topics.name: Company financial statements and IAS adjustments

practice.stem:
The draft profit for the year ended 31 December 2025 of Ravi Valley Cement plc was $286,400. The following matters have not been dealt with correctly.
1 Inventory with a cost of $24,000 has a net realisable value of $17,500.
2 Machinery bought on 1 January 2025 for $60,000 has not been depreciated. The policy is 10% per annum straight-line.
3 The company has $200,000 6% debentures. Interest for the second half of the year has not been paid or accrued.
4 An interim dividend of $15,000 was debited to administrative expenses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Draft profit for the year                                   286,400
Less inventory written down to NRV (24,000 − 17,500)        (6,500)
Less depreciation on new machinery (10% × 60,000)           (6,000)
Less debenture interest accrued (200,000 × 6% × 6/12)       (6,000)
Add interim dividend wrongly charged as an expense           15,000
Corrected profit for the year                               282,900
parts.working: 1 mark each adjustment, total own figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an interim dividend paid must not be included in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: A dividend is a distribution (appropriation) of profit to the owners, not an expense of earning profit. It is deducted from retained earnings in the statement of changes in equity.
parts.working: 1 mark: appropriation/distribution to shareholders; 1 mark: shown in the SOCE / retained earnings.

practice.stem:
Lyallpur Fabrics plc had the following equity at 1 January 2025: ordinary shares of $1 each $500,000; share premium $80,000; retained earnings $214,000.
During the year ended 31 December 2025:
• in March a final dividend for 2024 of $0.06 per share was paid
• in May 100,000 ordinary shares were issued at $1.60 each, fully paid
• in August land was revalued upwards by $45,000
• in October an interim dividend of $0.04 per share was paid on all shares then in issue
• the profit for the year was $96,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the statement of changes in equity for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Statement of changes in equity for the year ended 31 December 2025
                            Share cap    Sh prem  Reval res   Ret earn      Total
Balance 1 January 2025        500,000     80,000          0    214,000    794,000
Share issue                   100,000     60,000                          160,000
Revaluation of land                                  45,000                45,000
Profit for the year                                             96,500     96,500
Dividends paid                                                (54,000)   (54,000)
Balance 31 December 2025      600,000    140,000     45,000    256,500  1,041,500
parts.working: Dividends: final 500,000 × 0.06 = 30,000; interim 600,000 × 0.04 = 24,000. 1 mark opening balances; 1 mark share capital 100,000; 1 mark premium 60,000; 1 mark revaluation; 1 mark profit and dividends 54,000; 1 mark closing balances.

practice.stem: Kohat Builders plc issued $250,000 9% debentures on 1 July 2025. It also had a 7% bank loan of $80,000 outstanding for the whole of the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why debenture interest is charged in the statement of profit or loss but ordinary dividends are not.
parts.answer: Debenture holders are lenders: interest is a contractual cost of borrowing that must be paid whether or not profits are made, so it is an expense. Dividends are a distribution of profit to the owners and are shown in the statement of changes in equity.
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the finance costs for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.working: Debentures 250,000 × 9% × 6/12 = 11,250; loan 80,000 × 7% = 5,600; total 16,850. M1 time-apportioning; M1 loan interest; A1.

practice.stem: Jhelum Packaging plc is preparing its financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each transaction state its effect on (i) the profit for the year and (ii) the statement of financial position.
1 a bonus issue of shares using the share premium account
2 accruing debenture interest owing at the year end
3 an upward revaluation of land
4 paying an ordinary dividend
parts.answer:
1 Profit: no effect; SOFP: share capital up, share premium down, total equity unchanged.
2 Profit: decreases; SOFP: current liabilities up, retained earnings down.
3 Profit: no effect; SOFP: non-current assets up, revaluation reserve up.
4 Profit: no effect; SOFP: cash down, retained earnings down.
parts.working: 1 mark per transaction, both effects correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the gain on revaluation of land is reported in the statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income.
parts.answer: Under other comprehensive income (not in the profit for the year).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Oasis Hotels plc, Dubai, has a draft profit of $418,700 for the year ended 30 September 2026. The following items need attention.
1 The company has an 8% bank loan of $150,000, outstanding all year. Only $7,500 of the interest has been paid and recorded.
2 An ordinary dividend paid of $42,000 was debited to finance costs.
3 A customer's debt of $3,800 is irrecoverable and must be written off.
4 Trade receivables before the write-off were $193,800. The allowance for doubtful debts, currently $2,900, is to be 2% of trade receivables after the write-off.
5 Insurance of $2,600 paid for October 2026 was charged as an expense.
6 Kitchen equipment (cost $24,000, accumulated depreciation $20,500) was sold for $5,000 cash. The proceeds were credited to revenue and no other entries were made.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 30 September 2026.
parts.answer:
Draft profit                                          418,700
Less loan interest accrued (12,000 − 7,500)           (4,500)
Add dividend wrongly charged to finance costs          42,000
Less irrecoverable debt                               (3,800)
Less increase in allowance (3,800 − 2,900)              (900)
Add insurance prepaid                                   2,600
Less disposal proceeds wrongly in revenue             (5,000)
Add gain on disposal (5,000 − 3,500)                    1,500
Corrected profit                                      450,600
parts.working: 1 mark each: interest (12,000 − 7,500 = 4,500); dividend; irrecoverable debt; allowance (2% × 190,000 = 3,800, increase 900); prepayment; disposal (remove 5,000 from revenue, add gain 5,000 − 3,500 = 1,500: net −3,500). Corrected profit $450,600.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the gain on disposal of the equipment is shown in the financial statements.
parts.answer: In the statement of profit or loss, as other income (or deducted from expenses).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
On 1 April 2025 the equity of Bolan Minerals plc was: ordinary shares of $0.50 each $400,000; share premium $120,000; general reserve $50,000; retained earnings $310,000.
During the year ended 31 March 2026:
1 a rights issue of 1 share for every 4 held was made at $0.90 per share, fully taken up
2 after the rights issue, a bonus issue of 1 share for every 5 held was made, using the share premium account
3 profit for the year was $128,000
4 $20,000 was transferred to the general reserve
5 a dividend of $0.05 per share was paid on all shares in issue after the bonus issue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of ordinary shares in issue at 31 March 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the equity section of the statement of financial position at 31 March 2026.
parts.answer:
Equity
Ordinary shares of $0.50 each (1,200,000 shares)    600,000
Share premium                                       100,000
General reserve (50,000 + 20,000)                    70,000
Retained earnings                                   358,000
Total equity                                      1,128,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the bonus issue does not change the total equity of the company.
parts.answer: A bonus issue only transfers an amount from a reserve (share premium) to share capital. No cash is received, so total equity is unchanged; only its make-up changes.
parts.working: 1 mark: transfer between equity accounts; 1 mark: no cash/resources received.

practice.stem:
Coastal Fisheries plc, Gwadar, has a draft profit of $164,000 for the year ended 30 June 2026. The following errors have been found.
1 Closing inventory of frozen fish was included at cost, $12,400; its net realisable value is $9,100.
2 Proceeds of $50,000 from an issue of ordinary shares at par were credited to revenue.
3 A new boat engine costing $18,000, bought at the start of the year, was charged to repairs. Engines are depreciated at 25% per annum reducing balance.
4 Debenture interest of $3,600 owing at the year end has not been recorded.
5 The final dividend for the previous year, $25,000, was charged to administrative expenses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete a table showing the effect (increase, decrease or no effect, with the amount) of correcting each item on (i) the profit for the year and (ii) the net assets.
parts.answer:
Item     Profit for the year          Net assets
1            decrease $3,300     decrease $3,300
2           decrease $50,000           no effect
3           increase $13,500    increase $13,500
4            decrease $3,600     decrease $3,600
5           increase $25,000           no effect
parts.working: 1 mark per item, both columns correct. Item 3: capitalise 18,000 less depreciation 25% × 18,000 = 4,500. Item 2: share issue proceeds move from profit to share capital; net assets unchanged. Item 5: dividend moves to retained earnings; net assets unchanged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

practice.stem: Mirpur Ceramics plc had a profit before tax of $340,000 for the year ended 31 March 2026. Income tax on this year's profit is estimated at $78,000. Last year's financial statements included a tax liability of $61,000, but $64,500 was paid in settlement during this year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the income tax expense for the year ended 31 March 2026.
parts.working: Current estimate 78,000 + under-provision for the previous year (64,500 − 61,000) 3,500. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the amount of the current tax liability in the statement of financial position at 31 March 2026.
parts.working: 1 mark. The previous year's liability has been settled.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an under-provision for tax and how it is treated.
parts.answer: The tax actually agreed and paid for the previous year was more than the amount estimated in last year's financial statements. The shortfall is added to this year's tax expense.
parts.working: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark treatment.

practice.stem:
Nile Valley Textiles plc, Egypt, has a draft profit of $127,800 for the year ended 31 December 2025. These errors have been found.
1 A rights issue of 40,000 ordinary shares of $1 each at $1.75 per share was recorded as Dr Bank $70,000, Cr Share capital $70,000.
2 Repairs to the factory roof of $8,600 were debited to the buildings account. (Ignore depreciation.)
3 Rent of $2,400 owed by a tenant at the year end has not been recorded.
4 Goods sent to a customer on sale or return at a selling price of $6,000 (cost $4,500) were recorded as a credit sale. The customer has not yet accepted the goods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare journal entries to correct items 1–4. Narratives are not required.
parts.answer:
Dr $     Cr $
1 Share capital                  30,000
   Share premium                          30,000
2 Repairs (profit or loss)        8,600
   Buildings                               8,600
3 Other receivables               2,400
   Rent receivable (income)                2,400
4 Revenue                         6,000
   Trade receivables                       6,000
  Inventory                       4,500
   Cost of sales                           4,500
parts.working: 1 mark each for 1–3; 2 marks for 4. Item 1: premium 40,000 × 0.75 = 30,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revised profit for the year.
parts.working: 127,800 − 8,600 + 2,400 − 6,000 + 4,500 = 120,100. 1 mark repairs; 1 mark rent; 1 mark sale or return (net −1,500) and answer.

practice.stem:
Extracts from the equity of Thar Coal Services plc (ordinary shares of $1 each):
                            1 Jan 2025 $ 31 Dec 2025 $
Ordinary share capital           400,000       520,000
Share premium                     60,000       132,000
Retained earnings                233,000       301,400
During the year there was one issue of shares for cash. A final dividend of $0.07 per share for 2024 was paid before the share issue, and an interim dividend of $0.05 per share was paid after it. There were no other changes in equity apart from the profit for the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of shares issued during the year and the issue price per share.
parts.answer: 120,000 shares at $1.60

parts.label: b

practice.stem:
Kestrel Logistics plc, Singapore, has a draft profit of $512,600 for the year ended 30 September 2026. The following matters have been found.
1 A gain of $45,000 on the revaluation of its warehouse was credited to the statement of profit or loss.
2 The final dividend for the previous year, $60,000, paid in January 2026, was debited to administrative expenses.
3 $400,000 6% loan notes were issued on 1 April 2026. No interest has been paid or recorded.
4 Development costs of $28,000, which meet all the IAS 38 recognition criteria, were written off as an expense.
5 A delivery van bought on 1 October 2025 for $36,000 has not been depreciated. Vans are depreciated at 25% per annum using the reducing balance method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 30 September 2026.
parts.answer:
$
Draft profit                           512,600
1 Revaluation gain removed            (45,000)
2 Dividend paid added back              60,000
3 Loan note interest accrued          (12,000)
4 Development costs capitalised         28,000
5 Depreciation on van                  (9,000)
Corrected profit for the year          534,600
parts.working: B1 each adjustment with correct sign (×5); B1 corrected profit 534,600. Interest = 400,000 × 6% × 6/12 = 12,000. Depreciation = 36,000 × 25% = 9,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the revaluation gain in item 1 should be shown in the financial statements.
parts.answer: As other comprehensive income (a revaluation surplus) and in the revaluation reserve in equity, shown in the statement of changes in equity – not in the profit for the year.
parts.working: B1 other comprehensive income / not profit; B1 revaluation reserve in equity (statement of changes in equity).

practice.stem:
The draft statement of financial position of Shalimar Paper plc at 31 March 2026 showed: ordinary shares of $1 each $300,000; share premium $40,000; retained earnings $406,000 (opening balance $94,000 plus draft profit for the year $312,000); trade payables $48,000. There were no other equity or liability balances. The following have been found.
1 On 1 October 2025 the company issued $120,000 7% debentures 2032 at par. The cash received was credited to revenue. No interest has been paid.
2 On 31 March 2026 a building with a carrying amount of $410,000 was revalued at $520,000. The gain was credited to the statement of profit or loss.
3 Inventory costing $15,600 has a net realisable value of $11,200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 31 March 2026.
parts.answer:
Draft profit                                                312,000
Less debenture proceeds wrongly credited to revenue       (120,000)
Less debenture interest accrued (120,000 × 7% × 6/12)       (4,200)
Less revaluation gain wrongly credited to profit          (110,000)
Less inventory written down (15,600 − 11,200)               (4,400)
Corrected profit for the year                                73,400
parts.working: 1 mark each adjustment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the equity and liabilities section of the statement of financial position at 31 March 2026, after the corrections.
parts.answer:
Equity and liabilities
Ordinary shares of $1 each                            300,000
Share premium                                          40,000
Revaluation reserve                                   110,000
Retained earnings (94,000 + 73,400)                   167,400
Total equity                                          617,400
Non-current liabilities: 7% debentures 2032           120,000
Current liabilities: trade payables                    48,000
                    other payables (interest)           4,200
Total equity and liabilities                          789,600
parts.working: 1 mark revaluation reserve; 1 mark retained earnings; 1 mark debentures as non-current liability; 1 mark accrued interest as current liability with correct total.

practice.stem:
The following balances were extracted from the books of Saffron Foods plc at 30 June 2026.
                                                    $
Revenue                                     1,840,000
Cost of sales                               1,104,000
Distribution costs                            186,000
Administrative expenses                       212,000
Debenture interest paid                         9,000
6% debentures                                 300,000
Delivery vans at cost                         160,000
Delivery vans: accumulated depreciation        40,000
Office equipment at cost                       90,000
Additional information
1 Administrative expenses include ordinary dividends paid of $60,000.
2 Depreciation for the year has not been charged: delivery vans 25% reducing balance (distribution costs); office equipment 10% on cost (administrative expenses).
3 Inventory included in cost of sales must be written down by a further $7,000.
4 The debentures were in issue all year.
5 Tax for the year is estimated at $82,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distribution costs and the administrative expenses for the year.
parts.answer: Distribution costs $216,000; administrative expenses $161,000
parts.working: Vans 25% × (160,000 − 40,000) = 30,000 added to distribution (1); dividend 60,000 removed from admin (1); office equipment 10% × 90,000 = 9,000 added (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the statement of profit or loss for the year ended 30 June 2026.
parts.answer:
Saffron Foods plc — Statement of profit or loss for the year ended 30 June 2026
Revenue                                                 1,840,000
Cost of sales (1,104,000 + 7,000)                     (1,111,000)
Gross profit                                              729,000
Distribution costs (186,000 + 30,000)                   (216,000)
Administrative expenses (212,000 − 60,000 + 9,000)      (161,000)
Profit from operations                                    352,000
Finance costs                                            (18,000)
Profit before tax                                         334,000
Tax                                                      (82,000)
Profit for the year                                       252,000
parts.working: 1 cost of sales and gross profit; 1 expenses (own figures from (a)) and profit from operations; 1 finance costs 18,000 (full year, not 9,000 paid); 1 tax; 1 profit for the year.

practice.stem:
The draft statement of financial position of Highland Tea plc, Kandy, at 30 June 2026 shows current assets of inventory $84,000, trade receivables $66,000 and cash $12,000, and current liabilities of trade payables $58,000, accruals $4,000 and tax payable $28,000. The draft profit for the year is $98,000. The following matters have been found.
1 Damaged inventory costing $9,000 has a net realisable value of $3,500.
2 A customer owing $4,800 went into liquidation before the year end; the debt should be written off.
3 An electricity accrual of $1,700 was omitted.
4 A payment of $6,000 to a supplier was entered in the cash book but not in the trade payables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revised profit for the year.
parts.working: 98,000 − 5,500 − 4,800 − 1,700 = 86,000. Item 4 does not affect profit. 1 mark each adjustment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio before and after the corrections. Give your answers to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Before 1.80 : 1; after 1.77 : 1
parts.working: Before 162,000 ÷ 90,000 = 1.80. After: current assets 162,000 − 5,500 − 4,800 = 151,700; current liabilities 90,000 + 1,700 − 6,000 = 85,700; ratio 1.77. 1 mark before; 1 mark CA; 1 mark CL; 1 mark after.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the change in the current ratio.
parts.answer: The ratio has fallen only slightly and remains comfortably above 1, so liquidity is still adequate; the draft figures overstated liquidity.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Pamir Outdoor Gear plc has a draft profit of $205,300 for the year ended 31 December 2025. Retained earnings at 1 January 2025 were $142,000.
1 An interim dividend of $18,000 paid in July 2025 was debited to administrative expenses.
2 A final dividend of $32,000 for 2025, proposed by the directors in February 2026, was charged as an expense and shown as a current liability.
3 Goods sent on sale or return at a selling price of $9,000 were included in revenue; the customer has not accepted them. The company sells at cost plus 50%.
4 Development costs of $14,000 meeting all the IAS 38 criteria for recognition were written off. Production of the new product starts in 2026.
5 The final dividend for 2024, $25,000, was paid in April 2025 and correctly recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Draft profit                                        205,300
Add interim dividend charged as an expense           18,000
Add proposed final dividend wrongly accrued          32,000
Less sale or return goods in revenue                (9,000)
Add those goods returned to inventory at cost         6,000
Add development costs to be capitalised              14,000
Corrected profit                                    266,300
parts.working: 1 mark interim dividend; 1 mark final dividend (IAS 10: proposed after the year end, so not a liability); 1 mark revenue; 1 mark inventory at cost 9,000 ÷ 1.5 = 6,000; 1 mark development costs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the retained earnings at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: 142,000 + 266,300 − interim 18,000 − previous year's final 25,000 = 365,300. 1 mark profit; 1 mark both dividends; 1 mark answer.

practice.stem: At 31 December 2025 a printing machine owned by Urdu Press plc has a carrying amount of $84,000. Because of falling demand, its fair value less costs to sell is estimated at $61,000 and its value in use at $69,500. The machine has never been revalued.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the recoverable amount of the machine.
parts.working: Recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs to sell (61,000) and value in use (69,500). M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the impairment loss.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the impairment loss is treated in the financial statements.
parts.answer: The machine's carrying amount is reduced to its recoverable amount. The loss is charged as an expense in the statement of profit or loss (because the asset has not been revalued, so there is no revaluation reserve to set it against).
parts.working: 1 mark carrying amount reduced; 1 mark expense in profit or loss.

practice.stem:
Zarghun Juices plc bought a bottling machine. The costs were:
                                                         $
List price                                         145,000
Trade discount on list price                            5%
Sales tax (recoverable from the tax authority)      12,000
Import duty                                          9,200
Delivery to the factory                              2,400
Installation                                         6,300
Testing before use                                   1,800
Training staff to operate the machine                3,000
One-year maintenance contract                        4,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the machine to be recognised as a non-current asset under IAS 16.
parts.working: List price less 5% trade discount 137,750; add import duty 9,200, delivery 2,400, installation 6,300, testing 1,800. Exclude recoverable sales tax, staff training and the maintenance contract. 1 mark discount; 1 mark duty and delivery; 1 mark installation and testing; 1 mark exclusions and total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the staff training and the maintenance contract are treated.
parts.answer: Both are revenue expenditure: they do not bring the asset to working condition, so they are charged as expenses in the statement of profit or loss (the maintenance contract over the year it covers).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Mehran Fruit Packers plc has 2,000 tins of mango pulp in inventory at its year end. The costs per tin are:
                                             $
Purchase price                            3.10
Carriage inwards                          0.20
Labelling the tins                        0.15
Advertising (share per tin)               0.40
Storage of finished tins                  0.05
The tins normally sell for $4.00 each, and the sales agent receives commission of $0.30 per tin sold.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost per tin to be used for inventory valuation in accordance with IAS 2.
parts.answer: $3.45 per tin
parts.working: Include purchase price 3.10 + carriage inwards 0.20 + labelling 0.15 = 3.45 (B1). Exclude advertising and storage after completion (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of the 2,000 tins in the statement of financial position, assuming all the tins are in good condition.
parts.working: NRV 4.00 − 0.30 = 3.70 is above cost, so use cost: 2,000 × 3.45 = 6,900.

parts.label: c
parts.text: After the inventory count it was found that 300 tins have damaged labels. They can be sold for $2.80 each after relabelling at $0.25 per tin (the $0.30 commission still applies). Calculate the revised value of the inventory.
parts.working: NRV of damaged tins 2.80 − 0.25 − 0.30 = 2.25, below cost 3.45, so they are written down (B1); 1,700 × 3.45 = 5,865 (M1); 300 × 2.25 = 675; total 6,540 (A1).

practice.stem: Sabz Express Lines plc, Lahore, owns a fleet of intercity buses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'recoverable amount' as used in IAS 36 Impairment of Assets.
parts.answer: The higher of an asset's fair value less costs of disposal (costs to sell) and its value in use.
parts.working: B1 higher of; B1 both measures named (fair value less costs to sell; value in use).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State when an asset is impaired.
parts.answer: When its carrying amount is higher than its recoverable amount.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify two external and one internal indicator that one of the company's buses may be impaired.
parts.answer: External: a significant fall in the market value of used buses; new laws or technology (e.g. a ban on older diesel buses in the city) that reduce the use of the bus; a rise in interest rates. Internal: physical damage to the bus; the route it serves is being closed / the bus is idle; performance worse than expected (higher running costs).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two external indicators and one internal indicator.

practice.stem: Ravi Riverside Developers plc bought a plot of land for $450,000 in 2021. On 31 December 2025 the directors had the land revalued at $620,000 by a professional valuer. Land is not depreciated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the revaluation. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer: Dr Land 170,000; Cr Revaluation reserve 170,000
parts.working: B1 debit land 170,000; B1 credit revaluation reserve 170,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the revaluation is shown in the statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income.
parts.answer: As other comprehensive income (gain on revaluation of property) – it is not included in the profit for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other requirement of IAS 16 that applies when a company chooses to revalue land.
parts.answer: The whole class of assets (all land) must be revalued, and revaluations must be kept up to date / made regularly so that the carrying amount is not materially different from fair value.
parts.working: B1 either point.

practice.stem: Bukhara Carpets plc bought a building on 1 January 2016 for $600,000. It is depreciated at 2.5% per annum on cost (a 40-year life, no residual value). On 31 December 2025, after the depreciation for 2025 had been charged, the building was revalued at $690,000. The useful life is unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revaluation gain.
parts.working: Accumulated depreciation 600,000 × 2.5% × 10 = 150,000; carrying amount 450,000; gain 690,000 − 450,000 = 240,000. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the revaluation. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer:
Dr $      Cr $
Accumulated depreciation: buildings      150,000
Buildings (690,000 − 600,000)             90,000
   Revaluation reserve                             240,000
parts.working: 1 mark eliminating accumulated depreciation; 1 mark building increased by 90,000; 1 mark revaluation reserve.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge on the building for the year ending 31 December 2026.
parts.working: 690,000 ÷ remaining life 30 years = 23,000. M1 A1.

practice.stem:
Arabian Spice Traders plc holds four product lines at 31 May 2026.
Line     Cost $Notes
A        12,000Net realisable value $15,400
B         8,600Expected selling price $8,300; selling costs $1,200
C        21,000Net realisable value $26,500
D         5,400Selling price $4,800 after repackaging costing $600; selling costs $300

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of inventory at 31 May 2026 in accordance with IAS 2.
parts.working: Lower of cost and NRV for each item: A 12,000; B NRV 8,300 − 1,200 = 7,100; C 21,000; D NRV 4,800 − 600 − 300 = 3,900. Total 44,000. 1 mark each item.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the comparison of cost and net realisable value is made item by item rather than for the inventory as a whole.
parts.answer: Comparing totals would let the profit expected on some items hide the losses on others (here total cost 47,000 is below total NRV 52,900, so no write-down would be made). Prudence requires each foreseeable loss to be recognised.
parts.working: 1 mark losses hidden/offset; 1 mark prudence.

practice.stem: On 31 March 2026 the carrying amount of the Clifton showroom owned by Sea Breeze Motors plc, Karachi, was $820,000. The building had been revalued upwards in an earlier year, and the revaluation reserve contains a surplus of $70,000 relating to this building. An impairment review at 31 March 2026 found that the recoverable amount of the building is $700,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the impairment loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the impairment loss should be treated in the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026.
parts.answer: $70,000 is debited to the revaluation reserve (reducing the surplus on this building to nil) and shown as other comprehensive income; the remaining $50,000 is charged as an expense in the statement of profit or loss. The building is shown at $700,000.
parts.working: B1 loss first set against revaluation surplus for the same asset; B1 70,000 to revaluation reserve; B1 50,000 to profit or loss; B1 carrying amount 700,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one possible cause of the fall in value of the building.
parts.answer: E.g. a fall in property prices in the area; flood damage; a new road diverting customers; change of use/planning restrictions.
parts.working: B1 any sensible cause.

practice.stem: Hunza Valley Cold Stores plc bought refrigeration equipment for $200,000 on 1 January 2022. It was depreciated straight-line over 10 years with no residual value. On 1 January 2026 the equipment was revalued at $150,000. Its remaining useful life was then estimated at 6 years, with no residual value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revaluation surplus on 1 January 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.working: 150,000 ÷ 6 remaining years = 25,000 (M1 A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The company transfers the excess depreciation each year from the revaluation reserve to retained earnings. Calculate the amount transferred for 2026 and state where the transfer is shown.
parts.answer: $5,000, shown in the statement of changes in equity (revaluation reserve column reduced, retained earnings column increased).
parts.working: M1 25,000 − 20,000 (depreciation on original cost); A1 5,000; B1 statement of changes in equity, not profit or loss.

practice.stem:
Karakoram Tyres Ltd had the following inventory movements of one type of tyre during the six months to 30 September:
                           UnitsCost per unit $
1 April balance              400       12.00
May purchase                 600       13.00
June issue                   700
July purchase                500       14.50
August issue                 450

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory at 30 September using the first in, first out (FIFO) method.
parts.working: Closing inventory 400 + 600 − 700 + 500 − 450 = 350 units (M1); all from the July purchase: 350 × 14.50 = 5,075 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory using the weighted average cost (AVCO) method, recalculating the average after each purchase. Give your answer to the nearest cent.
parts.working: After May purchase: 1,000 units, 4,800 + 7,800 = 12,600, average 12.60 (M1). After June issue: 300 units × 12.60 = 3,780 (A1). After July purchase: 800 units, 3,780 + 7,250 = 11,030, average 13.7875 (M1). Closing: 350 × 13.7875 = 4,825.63 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which other inventory valuation method is NOT allowed by IAS 2.
parts.answer: Last in, first out (LIFO).

practice.stem: Gilgit Hotels plc bought land for $300,000 in 2020. Land is not depreciated. In December 2023 the land was revalued to $380,000 and a revaluation reserve was created. At 31 December 2026 the land is revalued at $270,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how much of the fall in value is charged against the revaluation reserve and how much is charged in the statement of profit or loss for 2026.
parts.answer: Revaluation reserve $80,000; profit or loss $30,000
parts.working: Total fall 380,000 − 270,000 = 110,000. The reserve for this asset is used first (80,000); the remaining 30,000 is an impairment loss in profit or loss. 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry for the fall in value. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer:
Dr $      Cr $
Revaluation reserve                   80,000
Impairment loss (profit or loss)      30,000
   Land                                        110,000
parts.working: 1 mark each line.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the carrying amount of the land at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Hala Ajrak Printers plc bought a machine on 1 January 2022 for $240,000. It was depreciated straight-line over 10 years with a residual value of $20,000. On 1 January 2026 the directors decided that the machine has only 4 more years of useful life and a residual value of $12,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the machine at 1 January 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for the year ended 31 December 2026 and the carrying amount at that date.
parts.answer: Depreciation $35,000; carrying amount $117,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the change is not applied to the depreciation charged in earlier years.
parts.answer: It is a change in an accounting estimate (IAS 8), not an error or a change of policy. It is applied prospectively, to the current and future years only; past figures were based on the best information available at the time.
parts.working: 1 mark change in estimate; 1 mark prospective treatment.

practice.stem:
At 31 December 2025 a specialised glass-moulding machine owned by Hyderabad Bangles plc had a carrying amount of $96,000 after charging depreciation for 2025. Demand for its products has fallen. The directors estimate:
• the machine could be sold for $78,000, with dismantling and selling costs of $1,500
• the net cash inflows from using the machine will be:
Year           Net cash inflow $     Discount factor at 10%
2026                      40,000                 0.909
2027                      35,000                 0.826
2028                      20,000                 0.751

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value in use of the machine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the impairment loss, if any, at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: Fair value less costs of disposal 78,000 − 1,500 = 76,500 (B1); recoverable amount is the higher, 80,290 (M1); loss 96,000 − 80,290 = 15,710 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for 2026, assuming straight-line depreciation over the remaining 3 years with no residual value. Give your answer to the nearest dollar.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the machine should not be shown at its carrying amount of $96,000.
parts.answer: An asset must not be carried at more than the amount the business expects to recover from using or selling it; showing $96,000 would overstate assets and profit (prudence) and mislead users.
parts.working: B1 carrying amount above recoverable amount overstates assets; B1 prudence / faithful representation.

practice.stem: Murree Heights Resorts plc bought land for $500,000 in 2019. Land is not depreciated and the company uses the revaluation model. On 31 December 2022 the land was revalued at $420,000. On 31 December 2025 it was revalued at $560,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the revaluation in 2022 was recorded.
parts.answer: The fall of $80,000 (500,000 − 420,000) was charged as an expense in the statement of profit or loss, because there was no revaluation surplus on this land to set it against.
parts.working: B1 80,000; B1 to profit or loss (no previous surplus).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amounts to be recognised in (i) profit or loss and (ii) other comprehensive income for the revaluation on 31 December 2025.
parts.answer: (i) $80,000 credited to profit or loss; (ii) $140,000 − $80,000 = $60,000 to the revaluation reserve (other comprehensive income).
parts.working: B1 increase 560,000 − 420,000 = 140,000; M1 reversal of previous loss goes to profit or loss; A1 80,000; A1 60,000 to OCI/revaluation reserve.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the balance on the revaluation reserve for this land at 31 December 2025.

practice.stem: Faisal Mosque Road Offices plc bought an office building on 1 January 2016 for $300,000. It was depreciated straight-line over 50 years, with no residual value. On 1 January 2021 the building was revalued at $405,000 with a remaining life of 45 years. The company does not make annual transfers of excess depreciation. On 31 December 2025, after charging depreciation for 2025, the building was sold for $390,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revaluation surplus on 1 January 2021 and the annual depreciation charge from 2021.
parts.answer: Surplus $135,000; depreciation $9,000 a year

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss on disposal recognised in the statement of profit or loss for 2025.
parts.answer: Profit $30,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the balance on the revaluation reserve for the building is dealt with on disposal.
parts.answer: The $135,000 is transferred directly from the revaluation reserve to retained earnings in the statement of changes in equity; it is not credited to the statement of profit or loss.
parts.working: B1 transfer to retained earnings 135,000; B1 through equity/SOCE, not profit or loss.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem: The directors of Kalash Mountain Resorts plc are preparing the financial statements and are unsure how to deal with a number of uncertain items.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the following terms as used in IAS 37: (i) a provision, (ii) a contingent liability.
parts.answer: (i) A liability of uncertain timing or amount. (ii) A possible obligation whose existence depends on uncertain future events, or a present obligation that is not probable or cannot be measured reliably.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the three conditions that must be met before a provision is recognised.
parts.answer: There is a present obligation (legal or constructive) from a past event; an outflow of resources to settle it is probable; a reliable estimate of the amount can be made.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how a probable contingent asset is treated.
parts.answer: It is disclosed in a note but not recognised in the statement of financial position.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem: Kaghan Furniture plc is finalising its financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026. They will be authorised for issue on 30 June 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an adjusting event and a non-adjusting event after the reporting period.
parts.answer: An adjusting event gives further evidence of conditions that existed at the end of the reporting period, so the figures are changed. A non-adjusting event relates to conditions that arose after the end of the reporting period, so the figures are not changed (it is disclosed in a note if material).
parts.working: B1 adjusting – conditions existing at the reporting date, figures adjusted; B1 non-adjusting – conditions arising after, disclosed only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of each type of event for a company whose year ended on 31 March 2026.
parts.answer: Adjusting: e.g. in April a customer who owed money at 31 March is declared bankrupt; inventory held at 31 March is sold below cost in May. Non-adjusting: e.g. a fire in May destroys a warehouse; a share issue in June.
parts.working: B1 each valid example.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem:
Jinnah Cables plc has the following matters at 31 December 2025.
1 A rival is suing the company for copying a cable design. The lawyers think there is a 30% chance that the company will lose and have to pay about $60,000.
2 The company has guaranteed a bank overdraft of a supplier. The supplier is financially strong and the chance of the guarantee being called is remote.
3 Under new environmental law that came into force in 2025, the company must clean up chemical waste it dumped during 2025. The cost is estimated reliably at $42,000 and the work will be done in 2026.
4 The directors plan to overhaul all factory machines in 2026 at an expected cost of $75,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each item, state whether the company should recognise a provision, disclose a contingent liability, or neither. Give a reason in each case.
parts.answer:
1 Disclose a contingent liability – a possible obligation, outflow not probable but not remote.
2 Neither – the chance of having to pay is remote.
3 Recognise a provision – present legal obligation from a past event, outflow probable, reliable estimate ($42,000).
4 Neither – no present obligation from a past event; the company could avoid the cost (e.g. by selling the machines).
parts.working: 1 mark for each treatment and 1 mark for each reason (4 × 2).

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem: Swat Valley Orchards plc is claiming $25,000 from a supplier whose faulty fertiliser damaged its apple crop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a contingent asset.
parts.answer: A possible asset that arises from past events and whose existence will be confirmed only by uncertain future events not wholly within the control of the company.
parts.working: B1 possible asset from past events; B1 confirmed by uncertain future events outside the company's control.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the claim should be treated in the financial statements for the year ended 30 June 2026 if (i) the lawyers say it is probable that the company will win; (ii) the court has already ruled in the company's favour and the supplier has agreed to pay.
parts.answer: (i) Disclose it in a note as a contingent asset; do not recognise it. (ii) Recognise it as an asset (receivable) and income, because receipt is virtually certain.
parts.working: B1 each.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem:
The financial statements of Port Qasim Traders plc for the year ended 31 December 2025 were authorised for issue on 20 March 2026. The following events happened in early 2026.
1 10 January: a fire destroyed a warehouse and the inventory in it.
2 25 January: goods that were in inventory at 31 December 2025 at a cost of $14,000 were sold for $9,500.
3 4 February: a court case that started in 2025 was settled, and the company agreed to pay damages.
4 1 March: the company issued 500,000 new ordinary shares.
5 12 March: it was discovered that one warehouse had been left out of the inventory count at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each event, state whether it is an adjusting or a non-adjusting event.
parts.answer:
1 Non-adjusting
2 Adjusting
3 Adjusting
4 Non-adjusting
5 Adjusting
parts.working: 1 mark each. 2: sale below cost gives evidence of NRV at year end. 3: the case existed at the year end. 5: the error existed at the year end.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how event 1 should be dealt with in the financial statements.
parts.answer: Disclose the nature of the event and an estimate of its financial effect in a note (no change to the figures).

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem:
Indus Ferries plc has the following matters at 31 March 2026.
1 A passenger is suing the company for injuries suffered on one of its ferries in January 2026. The lawyers say the company will probably lose, and estimate damages of $85,000.
