2 The company has guaranteed a $200,000 bank loan of a supplier. The supplier has had some cash-flow difficulties; the company's advisers consider a default possible but not probable.
3 The company is claiming $40,000 compensation from a shipyard for late delivery of a ferry. The lawyers think the claim will probably succeed, but the shipyard has not agreed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each matter, state how it should be treated in the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026. Give reasons.
parts.answer:
1 Recognise a provision of $85,000: present obligation from a past event, outflow probable, reliable estimate. Charge to profit or loss; show as a liability.
2 Disclose as a contingent liability in a note only: an outflow is possible, not probable.
3 Do not recognise; disclose as a contingent asset in a note because the inflow is probable but not virtually certain.
parts.working: 1 mark treatment and 1 mark reason for each matter.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The draft profit before dealing with these matters was $520,000. Calculate the revised profit.
parts.working: Only the provision affects profit.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem:
The draft profit of Saddar Electronics plc for the year ended 31 March 2026 is $310,000. The financial statements will be authorised for issue on 30 June 2026. These events occurred after the year end.
1 20 April 2026: a customer who owed $18,000 at 31 March 2026 was declared bankrupt; nothing will be received.
2 5 May 2026: a fire destroyed inventory worth $60,000 in the warehouse.
3 12 May 2026: goods held in inventory at 31 March 2026 at a cost of $25,000 were sold for $19,000, with selling costs of $1,000.
4 1 June 2026: the directors proposed a final dividend of $40,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each event as adjusting or non-adjusting and state how each should be treated.
parts.answer:
1 Adjusting: confirms the customer could not pay at the year end; write off $18,000.
2 Non-adjusting: the condition (fire) arose after the year end; disclose in a note if material.
3 Adjusting: gives evidence of NRV at the year end; write inventory down to 18,000.
4 Non-adjusting: no obligation existed at the year end; disclose in a note, no liability.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revised profit for the year ended 31 March 2026.
parts.working: 310,000 − 18,000 − (25,000 − 18,000) = 285,000. 1 mark each adjustment, 1 mark answer (non-adjusting events ignored).

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem: At 31 December 2025, Sindh Bus Services plc recognised a provision of $75,000 for a claim by a passenger injured on one of its buses. In August 2026 the claim was settled for $68,000, which was paid in cash. In November 2026 a second passenger started a claim. The lawyers say it is probable that the company will lose, and estimate damages of $40,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the effect of the settlement of the first claim on the profit for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.answer: Profit increases by $7,000
parts.working: Provision 75,000 − amount paid 68,000 = 7,000 released (credit to profit) (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the provision at 31 December 2026 and the net charge to the statement of profit or loss for 2026 for legal claims.
parts.answer: Provision $40,000; net charge $33,000
parts.working: B1 provision for the new claim 40,000 (probable, reliable estimate); M1 40,000 − 7,000; A1 33,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the provision for the second claim is not discounted to a lower amount just because the directors hope to settle out of court.
parts.answer: A provision must be the best estimate of the amount needed to settle the obligation; hopes of a lower settlement are not evidence, so reducing it would understate liabilities and break prudence/faithful representation.
parts.working: B1 best estimate; B1 prudence/not understating liabilities.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem:
The draft profit of Blue Lagoon Hotels plc, Maldives, for the year ended 30 April 2026 is $640,000. The financial statements are not yet authorised for issue.
1 A provision of $50,000 for operating losses expected at a new branch in the next year was charged as an expense.
2 A guest's claim for $35,000 damages, shown as a contingent liability in the draft, was lost in court in May 2026. The claim relates to an accident in February 2026.
3 Income of $20,000 has been recognised for an insurance claim that the company's lawyers describe as 'probable' but which has not yet been agreed.
4 The warranty provision for refurbishment work sold to other hotels should be $24,000. It is $18,000 in the draft.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 30 April 2026.
parts.answer:
$
Draft profit                           640,000
1 Provision for future losses removed      50,000
2 Provision for damages               (35,000)
3 Contingent asset removed            (20,000)
4 Increase in warranty provision       (6,000)
Corrected profit                       629,000
parts.working: B1 each adjustment (×4); B1 corrected profit 629,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why item 1 is not allowed by IAS 37.
parts.answer: Future operating losses do not arise from a past event, so there is no present obligation; the company can avoid them (e.g. by closing the branch). Creating the provision would also allow profit smoothing.
parts.working: B1 no present obligation from a past event; B1 avoidable / not a liability.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem: Bolan Pharma plc's year ended on 31 March 2026. In April 2026 the directors proposed a final dividend of $0.08 per share. In May 2026 the market value of the company's short-term investments fell by 20% because of a stock market crash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the information that must be disclosed in the notes for a material non-adjusting event.
parts.answer: The nature of the event and an estimate of its financial effect (or a statement that an estimate cannot be made).
parts.working: B1 nature; B1 estimate of financial effect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the final dividend proposed by the directors in April 2026 is not shown as a liability at 31 March 2026.
parts.answer: At 31 March there was no obligation to pay it – the dividend was declared after the reporting period (and still needs shareholders' approval), so it is a non-adjusting event; it is disclosed in a note.
parts.working: B1 no present obligation at the reporting date; B1 declared after year end – disclosed only.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the financial statements are not adjusted when the market value of investments falls after the year end.
parts.answer: The fall reflects conditions that arose after the reporting date (market changes after year end), not conditions at the year end; it is non-adjusting and disclosed if material.
parts.working: B1 conditions arose after year end; B1 disclose if material.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem: In May 2026 Rawal Home Appliances plc discovered a fault in 5,000 gas heaters it had sold during the year. On 20 June 2026 it announced publicly that it would repair every faulty heater free of charge. The company's year end is 30 June 2026. Repairs cost $18 per heater, and the company expects 70% of the heaters to be returned.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the provision to be recognised at 30 June 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a provision should be recognised even though no customer has yet returned a heater.
parts.answer: Announcing the recall before the year end created a constructive obligation (a past event that customers rely on); it is probable that money will be spent on repairs; and the amount can be estimated reliably from past experience. So all IAS 37 conditions are met.
parts.working: B1 present (constructive) obligation from the announcement; B1 probable outflow; B1 reliable estimate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the provision. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer: Dr Product recall expense (profit or loss) 63,000; Cr Provision for product recall 63,000
parts.working: B1 debit; B1 credit.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem:
Crescent Appliances plc sold 12,000 washing machines in 2025 with a one-year warranty. Past experience shows that 80% need no repairs, 15% need minor repairs costing $40 each and 5% need major repairs costing $250 each. The warranty provision brought forward from 2024 is $180,000. At 31 December 2025 the provision should equal the expected cost of repairs on the machines sold in 2025. The draft profit is $960,000. In addition:
• a former employee is suing the company for $70,000; lawyers believe the claim will possibly, but not probably, succeed
• the company's insurer has confirmed in writing that it will pay $15,000 for flood damage costs already charged as an expense in 2025; nothing has been recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the warranty provision required at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: 12,000 × (15% × 40 + 5% × 250) = 12,000 × 18.50. M1 expected value; M1 both outcomes; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the amount to be charged in the statement of profit or loss for the warranty provision.
parts.answer: $42,000 (increase in the provision)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the lawsuit and the insurance claim should be treated.
parts.answer: Lawsuit: an outflow is only possible, so it is disclosed as a contingent liability, not provided for. Insurance: the inflow is virtually certain (written confirmation), so it is no longer contingent and is recognised as a receivable and income of $15,000.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the revised profit for the year.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem:
Highway Logistics plc, Peshawar, has a draft profit of $412,000 for the year ended 31 December 2025, and draft current liabilities of $486,000. The financial statements will be authorised in April 2026. The accountant has dealt with these items as shown.
1 A customer who owed $24,000 at 31 December 2025 went into liquidation on 20 January 2026. The liquidator expects to pay 25% of the debt. No entry has been made.
2 A former employee is suing for unfair dismissal in 2025. The lawyers say it is probable the company will lose and the damages will be about $45,000. No entry has been made.
3 A final dividend of $80,000 proposed in February 2026 was debited to retained earnings and included in current liabilities.
4 A warehouse was destroyed by flood on 15 February 2026. The uninsured loss of $150,000 was charged as an expense and included in current liabilities.
5 A provision of $30,000 was created for staff training planned for 2026; it was charged as an expense and included in current liabilities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.working: Draft 412,000 − irrecoverable debt 18,000 (B1) − provision for claim 45,000 (B1) + flood loss reversed 150,000 (B1) + training provision reversed 30,000 (B1); dividend has no effect on profit; corrected 529,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected total of current liabilities at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: 486,000 + 45,000 provision (B1) − 80,000 dividend (B1) − 150,000 flood (B1) − 30,000 training (B1) = 271,000. Item 1 affects receivables, not liabilities.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what disclosure is needed for item 4.
parts.answer: A note giving the nature of the flood (non-adjusting event) and an estimate of the financial effect, $150,000.
parts.working: B1 nature; B1 estimated effect.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem: Lahore Solar Systems plc gives a two-year warranty on all solar inverters sold. The warranty provision at 1 January 2025 was $36,000. During 2025 warranty claims costing $29,500 were paid and debited to the provision. The directors estimate that the provision required at 31 December 2025 is 2% of 2025 revenue. Revenue for 2025 was $2,150,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge to the statement of profit or loss for warranty costs for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.working: Required closing provision 2,150,000 × 2% = 43,000 (B1); provision remaining after claims 36,000 − 29,500 = 6,500 (B1); charge 43,000 − 6,500 = 36,500 (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show the provision for warranty costs account for the year.
parts.answer:
Provision for warranty costs
Debit: Bank – claims paid 29,500; Balance c/d 43,000; total 72,500
Credit: Balance b/d 36,000; Profit or loss 36,500; total 72,500
parts.working: B1 opening balance and claims; B1 P/L charge 36,500; B1 closing balance 43,000 and totals 72,500.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the provision is reviewed at the end of every reporting period.
parts.answer: Provisions are estimates; IAS 37 requires them to be adjusted to the current best estimate at each reporting date, so that liabilities and profit are not misstated as conditions (sales volume, claim rates) change.
parts.working: B1 best estimate at each reporting date; B1 avoids misstatement / reflects new information.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem: Shaheen Textiles plc made a record profit in 2025. The managing director wants to create a 'general provision for future uncertainties' of $500,000, charged as an expense, so that it can be released in a future year when profits are lower. He says this is 'just being prudent'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the directors should create the general provision. Refer to IAS 37 and accounting concepts in your answer.
parts.answer: No. A general provision for 'future uncertainties' does not meet IAS 37: there is no present obligation from a past event, no probable outflow linked to it and no reliable estimate. Creating it in good years and releasing it in bad years would smooth profits, which breaks neutrality and faithful representation; prudence does not allow deliberate understatement of profit. Users (shareholders, lenders) would be misled about performance and trend. The directors can instead disclose risks in the annual report, keep cash/retained earnings, or transfer to a general reserve (an appropriation of retained earnings, not an expense). Advice: do not create it.
parts.working: Level 3 (7–8): clear use of IAS 37 recognition criteria, explains profit smoothing/neutrality, considers alternatives (reserve transfer/disclosure) and gives a justified conclusion. Level 2 (4–6): some correct points on both sides, conclusion weakly supported. Level 1 (1–3): simple statements, little reference to IAS 37.

practice.stem: Thar Ceramics plc has 4,000,000 ordinary shares of $0.25 each. Its profit for the year after tax was $900,000 and total ordinary dividends for the year were $360,000. The market price of one share is $1.80.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dividend per share.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the dividend cover.
parts.answer: 2.5 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the dividend yield.

practice.stem: Mangla Agro Products plc pays an interim dividend in October and a final dividend in May each year. Its year end is 31 December.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an interim dividend and a final dividend.
parts.answer: An interim dividend is paid during the financial year, usually after the half-year results, on the directors' decision. A final dividend is proposed by the directors after the year end and paid once approved by shareholders at the annual general meeting.
parts.working: B1 interim – during the year; B1 final – after year end, approved at AGM.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where a final dividend proposed after the year end is shown in the financial statements for that year.
parts.answer: Only in a note to the financial statements (it is not a liability and does not appear in the statement of changes in equity until paid/approved).

practice.stem: The directors of Gwadar Seafoods plc are meeting to decide the final dividend for the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three factors the directors should consider before deciding the size of the dividend.
parts.answer: Any three of: the profit for the year and retained earnings available; the cash/bank balance; plans for future investment needing cash; shareholders' expectations / past dividend levels; loan agreements limiting dividends; the level of gearing; tax or economic outlook.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a company with a high profit may still decide to pay a low dividend.
parts.answer: Profit is not the same as cash; the company may lack cash or may want to retain profits to finance expansion without borrowing or issuing shares.
parts.working: B1 profit ≠ cash; B1 retention for investment.

practice.stem:
Attock Engineering plc had 2,400,000 ordinary shares in issue on 1 January 2025. During the year ended 31 December 2025:
• in April it paid the final dividend for 2024 of $0.05 per share
• in July a rights issue increased the number of shares to 3,000,000
• in September it paid an interim dividend of $0.03 per share.
In February 2026 the directors proposed a final dividend for 2025 of $0.06 per share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total dividends shown in the statement of changes in equity for the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the final dividend for 2025 and state how it is treated in the 2025 financial statements.
parts.answer: $180,000 (3,000,000 × 0.06); disclosed in a note only, not recorded as a liability at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: B1 180,000; B1 note only.

practice.stem:
Extract from the statement of financial position of Mohenjo Tiles plc at 31 December 2025:
                                             $
Ordinary share capital               1,000,000
Share premium                          300,000
Revaluation reserve                    150,000
General reserve                         80,000
Retained earnings                       95,000
The directors would like to pay a dividend of $200,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum dividend the company is legally allowed to pay. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: $175,000. Only distributable (revenue) reserves can be used: retained earnings $95,000 + general reserve $80,000. Share premium and revaluation reserve are capital reserves and cannot be used for cash dividends.
parts.working: B1 retained earnings; B1 general reserve is a revenue reserve; B1 share premium and revaluation reserve not distributable; A1 175,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the directors can pay the proposed dividend of $200,000.
parts.answer: No – it exceeds the distributable reserves of $175,000.

practice.stem: Neelum Mineral Water plc has 2,000,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each. Profit for the year ended 31 December 2025 was $380,000 and retained earnings at that date are $1,150,000. An interim dividend of $0.04 per share has been paid. The directors propose a final dividend of $0.12 per share. The company has cash of $90,000 and plans to extend its factory next year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the proposed final dividend.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the dividend cover for the year if the final dividend is paid. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 1.19 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should pay the proposed final dividend. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For: retained earnings of $1,150,000 mean the dividend is legally possible; shareholders expect a return and the share price may fall if it is cut; a stable dividend signals confidence.
Against: cash is only $90,000, so the company would need to borrow about $150,000, adding interest; dividend cover of 1.19 is low, so most of this year's profit is paid out; the factory extension planned for next year needs funds.
Decision: pay a reduced final dividend (for example $0.05 per share, $100,000) or delay payment until cash allows.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for, up to 2 marks for points against (using figures), 1 mark for a justified decision.

practice.stem: Sialkot Sports Goods plc has 6,000,000 ordinary shares in issue. Its profit for the year attributable to ordinary shareholders was $1,260,000 and total ordinary dividends were $504,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for Sialkot Sports Goods plc: (i) earnings per share; (ii) dividend per share; (iii) the dividend payout ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A competitor pays out 65% of its earnings. Explain one reason why each company might choose its payout policy.
parts.answer: Sialkot (40%): retains 60% of earnings to finance expansion (e.g. new factory/machinery) without borrowing; keeps a cash buffer. Competitor (65%): mature business with few investment projects; shareholders want income; high payout supports share price.
parts.working: B1 + B1 explained reason for low payout; B1 + B1 explained reason for high payout.

practice.stem: Before paying a dividend of $100,000, Karachi Port Cargo plc had current assets of $520,000 (including cash of $140,000), current liabilities of $260,000, equity of $1,400,000 and a long-term bank loan of $600,000. The dividend is paid in cash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio before and after the dividend payment. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Before 2.00 : 1; after 1.62 : 1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gearing ratio (non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities) × 100) before and after the dividend payment. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Before 30.0%; after 31.6%

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the effect of the dividend on the company's financial position.
parts.answer: Liquidity is weaker (less cash, current ratio falls) and gearing rises slightly, so the company is a little more risky for lenders, though both ratios remain at reasonable levels.
parts.working: B1 liquidity reduced; B1 gearing up/risk – sensible judgement.

practice.stem: Chitral Mineral Water plc has 1,300,000 ordinary shares. Its bank loan agreement says that (1) total dividends for a year must not exceed 50% of that year's profit, and (2) the bank balance must not fall below $50,000 after any dividend. The profit for the year was $340,000 and the bank balance is $180,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum total dividend that may be paid under the loan agreement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum dividend per share.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the bank included these conditions in the loan agreement.
parts.answer: To make sure the company keeps enough profit and cash in the business to pay interest and repay the loan, so the bank's money is protected.
parts.working: B1 protect lender/ability to repay; B1 cash retained in business.

practice.stem:
Mrs Zubair, a retired teacher in Quetta, wants to invest for a regular income. She is considering two listed companies:
                               Alpha plc    Beta plc
Dividend per share $                0.12        0.09
Earnings per share $                0.36        0.10
Market price per share $            2.40        1.20

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for each company: (i) dividend yield; (ii) dividend cover. Give answers to 2 decimal places where needed.
parts.answer: Alpha: yield 5.00%, cover 3.00 times. Beta: yield 7.50%, cover 1.11 times.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Mrs Zubair which company better suits her need for a steady income. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Beta gives the higher yield now, but its dividend is barely covered by earnings (1.11 times), so a small fall in profit would force a cut. Alpha's dividend is well covered (3 times), so it is more secure and may grow. For a steady, reliable income Alpha is better, even though its yield is lower.
parts.working: B1 Beta higher yield; B1 Beta cover low – risk of cut; B1 Alpha secure; B1 justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Hala Handicrafts plc has 4,000,000 ordinary shares. Profit for the year is $1,500,000 and retained earnings brought forward are $400,000. The directors' policy is to keep dividend cover at a minimum of 2.5 times, and they also plan to transfer $150,000 to a general reserve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum total dividend and the maximum dividend per share for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the retained earnings at the year end if the maximum dividend is paid and the transfer to general reserve is made.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the directors might want to keep the dividend cover at 2.5 times or more.
parts.answer: A high cover means much of the profit is retained to finance growth, and the dividend is secure – it can be maintained even if profit falls, which reassures shareholders.
parts.working: B1 retention for investment; B1 security/stability of dividend.

practice.stem:
Tarbela Engineering plc has 1,500,000 ordinary shares of $1 each, share premium of $400,000, retained earnings of $900,000 and cash of $260,000. The directors are considering two options.
Option A: pay a cash dividend of $0.15 per share.
Option B: make a bonus issue of 1 share for every 5 held, using the share premium account, and pay no cash dividend.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show the effect of each option on share capital, share premium, retained earnings, total equity and cash.
parts.answer:
Cash dividend   Bonus issue
Ordinary share capital        no change     +$300,000
Share premium                 no change     −$300,000
Retained earnings             −$225,000     no change
Total equity                  −$225,000     no change
Cash                          −$225,000     no change
parts.working: Option A: 1,500,000 × 0.15 = 225,000. Option B: 1,500,000 ÷ 5 = 300,000 shares × $1 = $300,000 from share premium. 1 mark each correct column pair (share capital/premium; retained earnings; total equity; cash).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors which option they should choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Cash dividend: rewards shareholders with cash and meets their income expectations, but leaves only $35,000 cash, which may cause liquidity problems. Bonus issue: no cash leaves the company and reserves are kept for growth; shareholders receive more shares, but the share price will fall in proportion, so they gain no real wealth and may be disappointed. Decision: e.g. a bonus issue (or a smaller cash dividend) because cash is needed for operations.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two relevant points, 1 mark use of figures, 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem:
Rohtas Cement plc has 3,000,000 ordinary shares. It has paid the same total dividend of $240,000 for three years.
Year        Profit after tax $
2023                   600,000
2024                   520,000
2025                   380,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dividend cover and the dividend per share for each year. Give dividend cover to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Dividend per share $0.08 each year. Cover: 2023 2.50 times; 2024 2.17 times; 2025 1.58 times.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The directors want to keep the dividend at $0.08 per share for 2025 even though profit has fallen. Discuss whether they should do so.
parts.answer: For: steady dividends signal confidence and support the share price; shareholders who rely on income are kept happy; cover is still above 1, so it is paid from the year's profit; retained earnings may allow it. Against: cover has fallen from 2.5 to 1.58, leaving less profit to reinvest; if the fall continues the dividend would become uncovered; cash may be needed to reverse the decline (new products, marketing); lenders may be concerned. Conclusion: maintain only if cash is sufficient and the fall is temporary; otherwise reduce the dividend and explain the reasons to shareholders.
parts.working: Level 3 (7–8): uses the cover trend, arguments for and against, justified conclusion. Level 2 (4–6): arguments mostly one-sided or conclusion weak. Level 1 (1–3): simple points.

practice.stem:
On 1 January 2026 the equity of Kirthar Glass plc was: ordinary shares of $0.50 each $800,000; share premium $120,000; retained earnings $460,000. During the year ended 31 December 2026:
1 31 March: paid the final dividend for 2025 of $0.05 per share
2 1 July: made a rights issue of 1 new share for every 4 held, at $0.80 per share, fully taken up
3 30 September: paid an interim dividend of $0.03 per share
4 31 December: land was revalued upwards by $90,000
5 profit for the year was $310,000.
In February 2027 the directors proposed a final dividend of $0.07 per share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the statement of changes in equity for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.answer:
Share capital Share premium   Revaluation      Retained         Total
                                   $             $     reserve $    earnings $             $
At 1 January 2026            800,000       120,000             –       460,000     1,380,000
Rights issue                 200,000       120,000                                   320,000
Revaluation of land                                       90,000                      90,000
Profit for the year                                                    310,000       310,000
Dividends paid                                                       (140,000)     (140,000)
At 31 December 2026        1,000,000       240,000        90,000       630,000     1,960,000
parts.working: B1 opening balances; B1 rights issue shares 400,000 × 0.50 = 200,000; B1 premium 400,000 × 0.30 = 120,000; B1 revaluation 90,000; B1 profit 310,000; B1 final 2025 dividend 1,600,000 × 0.05 = 80,000; B1 interim 2,000,000 × 0.03 = 60,000; B1 retained earnings 630,000; B1 total 1,960,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the final dividend for 2026 and state how it is treated in the 2026 financial statements.
parts.working: B1 140,000; B1 note, not a liability.

practice.stem: Lyallpur Spinning plc expects the following cash flows for 2026: cash at 1 January $250,000; net cash inflow from operations $420,000; purchase of new spinning machines $380,000; repayment of a bank loan $100,000; tax payment $60,000. The directors want a minimum bank balance of $50,000 at all times. The company has 2,500,000 ordinary shares and has paid a dividend of $0.06 per share every year for five years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash available for dividends in 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the shortfall if the company pays its usual dividend.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors on their dividend decision for 2026. Consider at least two options.
parts.answer: Options: (1) cut the dividend to $0.032 per share ($80,000) and explain that cash is going into new machinery – keeps minimum cash, no new debt, but shareholders may sell and the share price may fall; (2) pay the usual $0.06 by borrowing or delaying part of the capital expenditure – keeps shareholders happy but raises gearing/interest or slows growth; (3) offer a bonus (scrip) issue instead of part of the cash dividend. A justified recommendation, e.g. reduce the dividend this year while explaining the investment plan, since profit and cash should rise once the machinery is working.
parts.working: B1 each option explained with consequence (up to 4); B2 justified recommendation.

practice.stem: The auditors of Khewra Salt Products plc have found a material error in last year's financial statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a prior period error.
parts.answer: An omission or misstatement in a previous period's financial statements caused by failing to use, or misusing, reliable information that was available when those statements were prepared (e.g. mistakes in calculation, misapplying policies, oversights, fraud).
parts.working: B1 omission/misstatement in earlier period's statements; B1 information was available at the time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a material prior period error is corrected under IAS 8.
parts.answer: It is corrected retrospectively: the comparative figures for the prior period are restated as if the error had never happened, and the opening balance of retained earnings (and any other affected balances) for the earliest period presented is adjusted. The adjustment is shown in the statement of changes in equity, not in the current year's profit.
parts.working: B1 retrospective; B1 restate comparatives/opening retained earnings; B1 shown in SOCE not current profit.

practice.stem:
Al-Noor Textiles plc made these changes when preparing its 2025 financial statements.
1 The useful life of delivery vehicles was changed from 5 years to 4 years.
2 Inventory is now valued using weighted average cost instead of FIFO.
3 It was found that 2024 revenue included $40,000 of goods sent to customers on sale or return that had not been accepted.
4 The allowance for irrecoverable debts was changed from 3% to 4% of trade receivables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each item, state whether it is a change in accounting policy, a change in accounting estimate, or the correction of a prior period error.
parts.answer:
1 Change in accounting estimate
2 Change in accounting policy
3 Correction of a prior period error
4 Change in accounting estimate
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how a change in accounting estimate is applied.
parts.answer: Prospectively – in the current and future periods only; earlier periods are not restated.

practice.stem: The retained earnings of Margalla Paints plc at 1 January 2025 were $380,000 as previously reported. In 2025 it was discovered that depreciation for 2024 had been understated by $12,000, a material error. The profit for 2025 (correctly calculated) was $145,000 and dividends paid in 2025 were $50,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the restated retained earnings at 1 January 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the retained earnings column of the statement of changes in equity for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Retained earnings $
At 1 January 2025 as previously reported               380,000
Prior period adjustment                               (12,000)
At 1 January 2025 restated                             368,000
Profit for the year                                    145,000
Dividends paid                                        (50,000)
At 31 December 2025                                    463,000
parts.working: B1 as previously reported and adjustment; B1 restated 368,000; B1 profit and dividends; B1 closing 463,000.

practice.stem: Bahawalpur Dates plc discovered a material error in its 2024 financial statements while preparing those for 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two items of information that must be disclosed in the notes about a material prior period error.
parts.answer: Any two of: the nature of the error; the amount of the correction for each line item affected in each prior period presented; the amount of the correction at the beginning of the earliest period presented.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why comparative figures are restated rather than the whole correction being put through the current year's profit.
parts.answer: So that each year's profit shows the results of that year only; users can then compare the current year with the prior year on the same basis (comparability), and the current year profit is not distorted.
parts.working: B1 current profit not distorted; B1 comparability between years.

practice.stem: While preparing the financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2025, the accountant of Kirthar Foods plc discovered that closing inventory at 31 December 2024 had been overstated by $36,000 because of a counting error. This is a material error. Retained earnings at 1 January 2025, as previously reported, were $512,000. The draft profit for 2025, calculated using the incorrect opening inventory, is $148,000. Dividends of $50,000 were paid in 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the restated retained earnings at 1 January 2025.
parts.working: 512,000 − 36,000: the 2024 profit was overstated by the overstatement of closing inventory. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for 2025.
parts.working: Opening inventory for 2025 was overstated, so cost of sales was too high: 148,000 + 36,000. M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the retained earnings at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: 476,000 + 184,000 − 50,000 = 610,000. The error has reversed itself by the end of 2025. M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how IAS 8 requires a material prior period error to be corrected.
parts.answer: It is corrected retrospectively: the comparative figures for the prior period are restated and the opening balance of retained earnings is adjusted in the statement of changes in equity, rather than putting the correction through the current year's profit.
parts.working: 1 mark retrospective/restate comparatives; 1 mark adjust opening retained earnings.

practice.stem: Shahrah Couriers plc bought motor vans on 1 January 2023 for $80,000. They were depreciated at 20% per annum straight-line on cost, with no residual value. On 1 January 2026 the directors decided that the reducing balance method at 30% per annum better reflects how the vans are used, and changed the method from that date.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the depreciation charged in 2023 to 2025 is not restated.
parts.answer: A change in depreciation method is a change in accounting estimate (how the asset's benefits are used up), so IAS 8 requires it to be applied prospectively from the date of change; the earlier charges were based on the best estimate at the time, not an error.
parts.working: B1 change in estimate; B1 prospective.

practice.stem: Clifton Electronics plc's year ends on 31 December. In 2025 the auditors found that goods with a selling price of $50,000 had been invoiced and recorded as sales on 30 December 2024, but were not delivered to the customer until 6 January 2025. The goods (cost $32,000) had been left out of the inventory count at 31 December 2024 as though they had been sold. The error is material. Retained earnings at 1 January 2025 were reported as $612,000. The draft profit for 2025 is $218,000; no sale has been recorded in 2025 for these goods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the effect of the error on the profit for the year ended 31 December 2024.
parts.answer: 2024 profit overstated by $18,000
parts.working: Revenue overstated 50,000; cost of sales overstated 32,000 (goods left out of closing inventory); net 18,000 overstated (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect of the error on the draft profit for 2025, and the corrected 2025 profit.
parts.answer: 2025 draft profit understated by $18,000; corrected profit $236,000
parts.working: B1 2025 revenue understated by 50,000 (sale not recorded); B1 2025 opening inventory understated by 32,000, so cost of sales is understated and profit overstated by 32,000; A1 218,000 + 50,000 − 32,000 = 236,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the restated retained earnings at 1 January 2025.

practice.stem: Sukkur Rice Mills plc found in 2026 that its closing inventory at 30 June 2025 had been overstated by $45,000 because one batch of rice was counted twice. This is a material error. Retained earnings at 1 July 2025 were reported as $720,000. The profit for the year ended 30 June 2026, correctly calculated, was $260,000, and dividends of $90,000 were paid during the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the statement of changes in equity for the year ended 30 June 2026 (retained earnings and total only).
parts.answer:
Retained earnings $
At 1 July 2025 as previously reported                720,000
Correction of prior period error                    (45,000)
At 1 July 2025 restated                              675,000
Profit for the year                                  260,000
Dividends paid                                      (90,000)
At 30 June 2026                                      845,000
parts.working: B1 previously reported; B1 adjustment shown separately; B1 restated 675,000; B1 profit and dividends; B1 845,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the comparative statement of financial position at 30 June 2025 will be changed.
parts.answer: Inventory at 30 June 2025 is reduced by $45,000 and retained earnings at 30 June 2025 are reduced by $45,000 (restated).
parts.working: B1 inventory; B1 retained earnings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why IAS 8 treats a change in accounting estimate differently from a prior period error.
parts.answer: An estimate is a judgement based on the latest information; revising it reflects new information or experience, so the earlier figures were not wrong and only current and future periods are affected (prospective). An error means the earlier statements were wrong when published, using information that was available, so they are corrected retrospectively to give a faithful, comparable record.
parts.working: B1 estimate based on information at the time; B1 revision = new information → prospective; B1 error = misuse of available information; B1 retrospective restatement for faithful representation/comparability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a change in accounting estimate for a hotel company.
parts.answer: E.g. changing the useful life or residual value of furniture; changing the allowance for irrecoverable debts; revising a warranty or legal provision.

practice.stem: Kohsar Cold Storage plc bought a building on 1 January 2021 for $500,000. It should be depreciated at 2% per annum on cost. Depreciation was charged correctly in 2021 and 2022, but by mistake none was charged in 2023, 2024 or in the draft for 2025. The draft profit for 2025 is $265,000 and retained earnings at 1 January 2025 were reported as $1,150,000. The errors for 2023 and 2024 are material.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the restated retained earnings at 1 January 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for 2025.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the building at 31 December 2025.

practice.stem: In 2026 the auditors of Swat Marble plc found that a machine bought on 1 July 2024 for $80,000 had been debited to repairs in 2024. The company depreciates machinery at 20% per annum straight-line, with a time apportionment in the year of purchase. The error is material. The year end is 31 December. Retained earnings at 1 January 2026, as previously reported, were $645,000. The draft profit for 2026 is $210,000 (no depreciation has been charged on the machine).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the restated retained earnings at 1 January 2026.
parts.working: 2024: profit understated by 80,000 − depreciation 8,000 (6 months) = 72,000; 2025: depreciation 16,000 omitted. 645,000 + 72,000 − 16,000 = 701,000. 1 mark each step.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the machine at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the correction for 2024 and 2025 is not included in the profit for 2026.
parts.answer: Including it would distort the 2026 profit and make comparison with earlier years misleading. IAS 8 requires material prior period errors to be corrected retrospectively through opening retained earnings, with comparatives restated.
parts.working: 1 mark distortion/comparability; 1 mark IAS 8 retrospective treatment.

practice.stem:
On 1 January 2025 Indus Spare Parts plc changed its inventory policy from FIFO to weighted average cost (AVCO). Inventory values were:
                          FIFO $      AVCO $
31 December 2024         145,000     138,000
31 December 2025         162,000     153,500
The draft profit for 2025, prepared using FIFO, was $210,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the effect of the change in policy on (i) retained earnings at 1 January 2025 and (ii) the profit for 2025. Calculate the restated profit for 2025.
parts.answer: (i) reduced by $7,000; (ii) reduced by $1,500; restated profit $208,500
parts.working: B1 opening adjustment 145,000 − 138,000 = 7,000 decrease; B1 lower opening inventory reduces 2025 cost of sales by 7,000; B1 lower closing inventory increases cost of sales by 162,000 − 153,500 = 8,500; M1 net −1,500; A1 208,500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why IAS 8 requires a change in accounting policy to be applied retrospectively.
parts.answer: So that the statements for all periods shown use the same policy, keeping them comparable (consistency); otherwise a change in reported profit could be caused by the change of method rather than performance.
parts.working: B1 comparability/consistency; B1 effect of method change not shown as performance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one condition under which a company may change an accounting policy.
parts.answer: When required by an accounting standard, or when the change gives reliable and more relevant information.

practice.stem:
During 2025 the accountant of Jhang Dairy plc found two material errors in the 2024 financial statements.
1 Closing inventory at 31 December 2024 was understated by $22,000.
2 Rent of $9,000 for December 2024 was not accrued at 31 December 2024; it was paid in January 2025 and charged as an expense in the 2025 draft.
Retained earnings at 1 January 2025 were reported as $540,000. The draft profit for 2025 is $300,000. Dividends paid in 2025 were $70,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the restated retained earnings at 1 January 2025.
parts.working: +22,000 inventory understatement (B1); −9,000 unaccrued rent (B1); 540,000 + 22,000 − 9,000 = 553,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for 2025.
parts.working: Opening inventory understated, so 2025 cost of sales too low: −22,000 (B1); 2024 rent wrongly charged in 2025: +9,000 (B1); 300,000 − 22,000 + 9,000 = 287,000 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate retained earnings at 31 December 2025, and explain why the errors do not change this figure.
parts.answer: $770,000 (553,000 + 287,000 − 70,000). Both errors reverse in the following year: the effect on 2024 profit is cancelled by an equal and opposite effect on 2025 profit, so by 31 December 2025 the total of retained earnings is correct; only the split between the years was wrong.
parts.working: B1 770,000; B2 explanation of self-reversing errors.

practice.stem:
The 2024 comparative figures of Gilgit Trekking Supplies plc (as originally published) were: revenue $940,000; cost of sales $560,000; expenses $210,000; profit for the year $170,000. In 2025 these errors in the 2024 figures were found.
1 A credit sale of $30,000 was recorded twice in the sales journal.
2 Depreciation of $8,000 on new shop fittings was omitted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the restated statement of profit or loss extract for 2024 (from revenue to profit for the year).
parts.answer:
2024 restated $
Revenue                            910,000
Cost of sales                    (560,000)
Gross profit                       350,000
Expenses                         (218,000)
Profit for the year                132,000
parts.working: B1 revenue 940,000 − 30,000; B1 gross profit 350,000; B1 expenses 210,000 + 8,000; B1 profit 132,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of the corrections on the statement of financial position at 31 December 2024.
parts.answer: Trade receivables reduced by $30,000; carrying amount of non-current assets reduced by $8,000; retained earnings reduced by $38,000.
parts.working: B1 receivables and non-current assets; B1 retained earnings −38,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the 2024 profit for the year caused by the corrections, to 1 decimal place, and comment on whether the errors are material.
parts.answer: Fall of 22.4%; this is clearly material because it would change users' view of the company's performance.

practice.stem:
Sialkot Surgical Instruments plc made a profit of $2,100,000 in 2024. In 2025 two errors in the 2024 statements were found.
1 A $4,000 electricity invoice for December 2024 was not accrued.
2 A sales manager had recorded fictitious sales of $380,000 in 2024 to earn a bonus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether each error should be treated as a prior period adjustment. Advise the finance director.
parts.answer: IAS 8 requires retrospective correction only for material prior period errors. Error 1 ($4,000 on profit of $2.1 million, about 0.2%) is not material – it would not change users' decisions – so it can simply be corrected in the 2025 statement of profit or loss. Error 2 ($380,000 of revenue that was never earned, about 18% of profit) is material, and was fraud using information available at the time, so the 2024 comparatives must be restated and opening retained earnings adjusted, with disclosure of its nature and amount. Materiality depends on size and nature: even a small error might be material if it hid fraud or turned a profit into a loss. Advice: correct error 1 in the current year; treat error 2 as a prior period adjustment.
parts.working: B1 IAS 8 – material errors only; B1 error 1 immaterial with reason; B1 corrected in current year; B1 error 2 material; B1 restate comparatives/opening retained earnings and disclose; B1 justified advice (nature as well as size).

practice.stem:
Solaris Devices plc, Islamabad, spent the following in the year ended 30 June 2026.
1 Salaries of scientists investigating new battery materials, with no particular product in view: $42,000
2 Testing a prototype of a new solar phone charger (all IAS 38 development criteria are met): $68,000
3 Market research carried out before the charger project was approved: $9,000
4 Designing tools for production of the new charger (criteria met): $25,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount to be charged as an expense and the amount to be recognised as an intangible asset for the year.
parts.answer: Expense $51,000; intangible asset $93,000
parts.working: Research (1) and market research before approval (3) are expensed: 51,000. Development meeting all criteria (2) and (4) is capitalised: 93,000. 1 mark per item correctly treated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two of the criteria that development expenditure must meet before it can be recognised as an asset under IAS 38.
parts.answer: Any two: technically feasible to complete; intention to complete and use or sell; ability to use or sell; probable future economic benefits (a market exists); adequate technical, financial and other resources to complete; expenditure can be measured reliably.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Pak Agritech plc employs scientists who study drought-resistant wheat, and engineers who design new irrigation equipment based on the scientists' findings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between research and development as defined in IAS 38.
parts.answer: Research is original, planned investigation to gain new scientific or technical knowledge. Development is applying research findings to a plan or design for new or substantially improved products or processes before commercial production starts.
parts.working: B1 research; B1 development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how research expenditure and development expenditure are treated in the financial statements.
parts.answer: Research: always written off as an expense in the statement of profit or loss. Development: capitalised as an intangible non-current asset when all IAS 38 criteria are met (otherwise expensed), and amortised once production/use begins.
parts.working: B1 research expensed; B1 development capitalised when criteria met.

practice.stem: Zarai Drones plc is developing a crop-spraying drone for farmers in Punjab.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four conditions that must all be met before development expenditure may be capitalised under IAS 38.
parts.answer: Any four of: technical feasibility of completing the product; intention to complete and use or sell it; ability to use or sell it; probable future economic benefits (a market exists or it is useful internally); adequate technical, financial and other resources to complete it; expenditure can be measured reliably.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

practice.stem: Shifa Chemists plc has built a strong reputation over 30 years. In 2025 it bought the business of Patel Pharmacy for more than the fair value of Patel's net assets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the goodwill bought from Patel Pharmacy is recognised as an asset but the goodwill built up by Shifa Chemists plc itself is not.
parts.answer: Purchased goodwill has a cost that can be measured reliably – the price paid above the fair value of the net assets acquired – so it is recognised (and tested each year for impairment). Internally generated goodwill has no transaction to measure it; its value is subjective and changes all the time, so IAS 38 does not allow it to be recognised.
parts.working: B1 purchased – measured by a transaction; B1 recognised and tested for impairment; B1 internally generated – no reliable measure; B1 not allowed by IAS 38.

practice.stem: Murree Hills Foods plc has capitalised development costs of $240,000 for a new range of fruit juices. Commercial production began on 1 July 2025. Development costs are amortised straight-line over 4 years from the start of production, with time apportionment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amortisation charge for the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of development costs at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amortisation charge for 2026.
parts.working: Full year: 60,000.

practice.stem:
Arabian Sea Fisheries plc has the following items.
1 A patent for a fish-processing machine bought from an inventor for $90,000.
2 $25,000 spent training new staff in food hygiene.
3 A list of 3,000 regular customers built up over many years, valued by a consultant at $120,000.
4 A 10-year fishing licence bought from the government for $200,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each item, state whether it can be recognised as an intangible asset in the statement of financial position. Give a reason for each.
parts.answer:
1 Yes – purchased, separately identifiable, cost measured reliably.
2 No – training does not give control over the benefits (staff can leave); it is an expense.
3 No – internally generated customer lists cannot be recognised (cost cannot be separated from developing the business).
4 Yes – purchased licence with a reliable cost, controlled by the company for 10 years.
parts.working: 1 mark each for treatment and 1 mark each for reason (4 × 2).

practice.stem:
Hilal Labs plc spent the following during the year ended 31 December 2025.
1 $85,000 testing chemical compounds to find out whether any of them might lead to a new antibiotic.
2 $160,000 on trials of a new cough syrup. All IAS 38 criteria for capitalisation were met from 1 May 2025; $40,000 of the cost was spent before that date.
3 $25,000 on marketing to launch an existing product in a new city.
4 $60,000 on laboratory equipment bought on 1 January 2025 and used only for research. Equipment is depreciated at 20% per annum straight-line.
No product has yet reached commercial production.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate (i) the total amount charged to the statement of profit or loss for the year, and (ii) the amount shown as an intangible asset at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: B1 research 85,000 expensed; B1 pre-criteria trial costs 40,000 expensed; B1 launch marketing 25,000 expensed; B1 depreciation of lab equipment 60,000 × 20% = 12,000; A1 total 162,000; B1 intangible 120,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the laboratory equipment is shown in the statement of financial position at 31 December 2025.
parts.answer: As property, plant and equipment (tangible), not an intangible: cost $60,000 less depreciation $12,000 = carrying amount $48,000.
parts.working: B1 PPE not intangible; B1 48,000.

practice.stem: On 1 April 2025 Tarang Digital Media plc bought a 5-year licence to stream a television series for $150,000. Its year end is 31 December. The company's own brand name, built up over 15 years, has been valued by consultants at $500,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amortisation charge for the year ended 31 December 2025 and the carrying amount of the licence at that date.
parts.answer: Amortisation $22,500; carrying amount $127,500

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether the brand valuation should be recognised in the financial statements.
parts.answer: No – the brand was internally generated; IAS 38 does not allow internally generated brands to be recognised because their cost cannot be distinguished from the cost of developing the business as a whole. A valuation is not a reliable cost.
parts.working: B1 not recognised; B1 internally generated – IAS 38 prohibition/no reliable cost.

practice.stem: On 1 January 2025 Chenab Foods plc bought the business of a frozen-food distributor for $850,000. The fair value of the net assets acquired was $690,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill arising on the purchase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the goodwill is treated in the financial statements after it has been recognised.
parts.answer: It is not amortised. It is tested for impairment every year (and when there is any sign of impairment). Any impairment loss is charged to the statement of profit or loss and can never be reversed.
parts.working: B1 not amortised; B1 annual impairment review; B1 loss to P/L, not reversed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: One year later the goodwill is found to be impaired by $25,000. State the carrying amount of goodwill after the impairment.

practice.stem: Before accounting for its development costs, Darya Robotics plc has profit of $900,000 and capital employed of $4,200,000. During the year it spent $300,000 in cash on development of a new warehouse robot. The directors believe all IAS 38 criteria are met. Amortisation will not start until next year. (If capitalised, the asset of $300,000 is included in capital employed.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed (profit ÷ capital employed × 100) if the development costs are (i) capitalised; (ii) written off as an expense. Give answers to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why users should be careful when comparing the ROCE of two companies that treat development costs differently.
parts.answer: Capitalising increases both profit and assets in the year of spending, so ratios differ because of accounting treatment, not performance; users should adjust or read the accounting policies notes.
parts.working: B1 treatment affects profit and capital employed; B1 ratios not comparable/like-for-like.

practice.stem: Kasur Leather Tech plc bought a patent for a tanning process on 1 January 2023 for $96,000. It was amortised straight-line over its legal life of 8 years. On 1 January 2026, because a competitor has developed a better process, the directors estimate that the patent will be useful for only 3 more years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amortisation charge for 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the amortisation for 2023 to 2025 should be restated. Give a reason.
parts.answer: No – the change in useful life is a change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively from 2026.
parts.working: B1 no; B1 change in estimate – prospective.

practice.stem: Medisonic plc capitalised development costs of $180,000 for a new ultrasound scanner in 2024. Commercial production began on 1 January 2025 and the costs are amortised straight-line over the expected sales life of 5 years. At 31 December 2026 a competitor launched a cheaper scanner, and the recoverable amount of the development costs was estimated at $90,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amortisation charge for 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the development costs at 31 December 2026 before any impairment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the impairment loss at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: 108,000 − recoverable amount 90,000. M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the total charge in the statement of profit or loss for 2026 relating to the development costs.
parts.working: Amortisation plus impairment.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain why capitalised development costs are amortised.
parts.answer: Matching: the costs are spread over the periods that benefit from sales of the product; the asset has a limited useful life, so its carrying amount should fall as the benefits are used up.
parts.working: 1 mark matching; 1 mark finite life/benefits consumed.

practice.stem:
Roshan Smart Meters plc began a project to create a new electricity meter in 2025.
• January–March 2025: $45,000 on research into new sensor materials.
• April–June 2025: $60,000 on designing a prototype; technical feasibility had not yet been shown.
• July–December 2025: $150,000 on development; all IAS 38 criteria were met from 1 July 2025.
Commercial production began on 1 January 2026; the development asset is amortised straight-line over 5 years. At 31 December 2026, after a competitor launched a cheaper meter, the recoverable amount of the development asset was estimated at $95,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total amount charged to the statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 2025 for this project.
parts.working: Research Jan–Mar 45,000 + development before criteria met Apr–Jun 60,000 = 105,000 (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the development asset at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: Costs from 1 July when all criteria met.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate (i) the amortisation for 2026, (ii) the impairment loss at 31 December 2026, and (iii) the total charge to the statement of profit or loss for 2026.
parts.working: B1 150,000 ÷ 5 = 30,000; M1 carrying amount 120,000 compared with recoverable amount 95,000; A1 25,000; B1 55,000.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The directors suggest that the $60,000 spent from April to June 2025 should now be added to the asset because the project has succeeded. Explain whether this is allowed.
parts.answer: No – IAS 38 does not allow expenditure that was recognised as an expense to be capitalised later; only costs after all criteria were met can be capitalised.
parts.working: B1 no; B1 reason.

practice.stem:
The draft statement of financial position of Bilal Biotech plc at 31 December 2025 shows intangible assets of $420,000, made up of:
• an internally generated brand, valued at $150,000; the gain was credited to the statement of profit or loss
• research costs of $70,000, debited to intangible assets
• development costs of $200,000, correctly capitalised. Commercial production began on 1 October 2025, but no amortisation has been charged. The policy is straight-line amortisation over 4 years with time apportionment.
The draft profit for the year is $560,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected carrying amount of intangible assets at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the effect of the errors on users' view of the company.
parts.answer: Profit was overstated by $232,500 (about 71%) and assets by $232,500, making the company look more profitable and stronger than it is; investors could overvalue its shares and lenders could underestimate risk.
parts.working: B1 profit and assets overstated (quantified); B1 consequence for a user.

practice.stem: Asman Medical Devices plc plans to issue new shares next year. It spent $1.2 million on research and development this year: $500,000 on research into new materials and $700,000 on developing a heart monitor, of which $450,000 meets all IAS 38 criteria. The directors propose to capitalise the whole $1.2 million 'to show investors how much we invest in the future'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the directors' proposal. Advise them whether they should capitalise all the research and development spending.
parts.answer: IAS 38 does not allow research to be capitalised under any circumstances, and development only when all criteria (technical feasibility, intention and ability to complete and use/sell, probable economic benefits, adequate resources, reliable measurement) are met. Capitalising everything would overstate assets and profit, break prudence and faithful representation, and could mislead investors in the share issue; auditors would qualify their report, damaging credibility and possibly causing legal problems. Capitalising qualifying development costs is required (not optional) and does raise profit legitimately. Advice: capitalise only the development spending that meets the criteria, expense the rest, and explain the R&D programme in the narrative report to attract investors.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): applies IAS 38 rules to both research and development, discusses effect on investors/auditors, justified advice. Level 2 (3–4): correct rules with limited discussion. Level 1 (1–2): simple statements.

practice.stem: A rice mill in Larkana is thinking of replacing an old husking machine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two non-financial factors a business should consider before replacing a machine.
parts.answer: Any two: effect on employees (training, job losses, morale); quality of output; environmental impact; reliability and after-sales service of the supplier; flexibility of the new machine.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of net present value over the payback method.
parts.answer: NPV considers all cash flows over the project's life and the time value of money, whereas payback ignores cash flows after the payback point.
parts.working: 1 mark advantage; 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem: The manager of a cinema in Karachi has been told that a new projector has a positive net present value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a positive net present value.
parts.answer: The present value of the future net cash inflows is greater than the initial cost; the project earns more than the cost of capital and increases the value of the business.
parts.working: 1 mark PV of inflows > cost; 1 mark return above cost of capital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two limitations of the net present value method.
parts.answer: Any two: cash flows are hard to forecast; choosing the right discount rate is difficult; ignores non-financial factors; harder to understand than payback; assumes the cost of capital stays the same.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The finance director of a cement company is appraising a new kiln.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a business uses its cost of capital as the discount rate.
parts.answer: It is the return the business must pay to its providers of finance; a project must earn at least this return to add value.
parts.working: 1 mark cost of finance; 1 mark minimum required return.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by sensitivity analysis.
parts.answer: Testing how much one estimate (e.g. sales volume, cost, discount rate) can change before the NPV becomes zero, to show which estimates the decision depends on most.
parts.working: 1 mark change one variable; 1 mark effect on NPV/decision.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one limitation of sensitivity analysis.
parts.answer: Changes one variable at a time, whereas in reality several change together / gives no probability of the change happening.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A food court operator in Riyadh plans to refit a site for $140,000. Net cash inflows are $41,000 a year for five years. The cost of capital is 10% and the cumulative discount factor for years 1–5 at 10% is 3.791.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the NPV of the project.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum initial cost the company could pay for the refit for the NPV to be zero.
parts.answer: 41,000 × 3.791 = $155,431 (the present value of the inflows), so the cost must be no more than $155,431.
parts.working: M1 present value of the inflows; A1 $155,431.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the answer to (b) helps the managers when they negotiate the refit price.
parts.answer: It sets a ceiling: any price above $155,431 makes the NPV negative, so the managers should not agree a higher price without better cash-flow forecasts.
parts.working: B1 ceiling on price with figure; B1 reason for caution about the forecast.

practice.stem:
Khan Engineering can afford only one of two projects. Its cost of capital is 10%. Results:
                             Project Canal  Project Bridge
Net present value                  $24,000         $19,500
Payback period                   3.2 years       2.1 years
Accounting rate of return              18%             22%
Internal rate of return                15%             17%
The company has a large bank overdraft.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors which project they should choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Either project may be recommended with justification; a strong answer recommends Project Canal on NPV (it adds the most value) unless liquidity is a priority.
parts.working: Canal (max 3): higher NPV ($24,000 v $19,500) so adds more to shareholder value; NPV is the most reliable method; both IRRs exceed the 10% cost of capital. Bridge (max 3): faster payback (2.1 v 3.2 years), less risk and better for cash flow; higher ARR and IRR; later cash flows of Canal are harder to forecast. Other points: non-financial factors such as staff, customers, environment; forecasts are estimates. Clear decision (1).

practice.stem: A project costing $100,000 is expected to give net cash inflows of $32,000 a year for five years. The cost of capital is 12% and the sum of the discount factors for years 1–5 at 12% is 3.605.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the annual cash inflow could fall before the project became unprofitable, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 NPV ÷ PV of the inflows; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what your answer to (b) shows.
parts.answer: If annual inflows fall by more than 13.31% (below about $27,739), the NPV becomes negative; a small margin means the project is risky.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Saba Textiles may install a dyeing plant costing $180,000. Net cash inflows are forecast at $55,000, $65,000, $70,000 and $45,000 in years 1–4. The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value.
parts.working: M1 discounting; M1 less cost; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the initial cost that would make the NPV zero, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1; A1 OF.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on your answer to (b).
parts.answer: The project is very sensitive to the initial cost: an overspend of under 4% would make it unprofitable, so cost control/fixed-price quotes are important.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Zainab runs a packaging factory in Lahore. Her old machine breaks down often and three customers complained about late orders last month. A new machine would cost $95,000, financed by a bank loan at 9% interest. Its NPV at the 10% cost of capital is $8,400 and its payback period is 3.8 years over a 5-year life. It uses 15% less electricity. Staff would need two weeks of training, during which output would fall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise Zainab whether she should buy the new machine. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A justified recommendation, e.g. buy: positive NPV, solves the reliability problem and saves energy, but she should plan the training and loan carefully.
parts.working: For (max 4): NPV positive ($8,400) at the 10% cost of capital; breakdowns of the old machine have caused late orders and lost customers; 15% energy saving and lower emissions; better quality may win new contracts. Against (max 4): payback of 3.8 years in a 5-year life leaves little margin; NPV small compared with $95,000 cost so sensitive to forecasts; staff need two weeks of training and output will fall; loan increases gearing and interest at 9%. Decision (1).

practice.stem:
A manufacturer in Sialkot may produce a new football. Equipment costs $90,000 with a four-year life and no residual value. It expects to sell 3,000 balls a year at $48 with variable cost $30 per ball. Extra fixed cash costs are $21,000 a year. Cost of capital 13%.
Discount factors at 13%: year 1 0.885; year 2 0.783; year 3 0.693; year 4 0.613

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the NPV of the project.
parts.working: B1 contribution 18; M1; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum annual sales volume for the NPV to be zero (to the nearest unit) and the percentage fall in volume this represents (to two decimal places).
parts.working: M1 annual flow; M1 add fixed; A1 units; A1 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two limitations of sensitivity analysis.
parts.answer: Changes one variable at a time while others often change together; does not give the probability of the change; does not tell managers what decision to make.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A company may launch a water pump. It needs a machine costing $110,000 with a four-year life and no residual value. It expects to sell 5,000 pumps a year at a contribution of $12 each. Extra fixed cash costs are $20,000 a year. The cost of capital is 10%; the sum of the discount factors for years 1–4 is 3.169.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which sales volume could fall before the NPV becomes zero, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 only contribution varies with volume; M1 NPV ÷ PV of contribution; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the minimum annual sales volume needed, in whole units.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Hassan Foods has $300,000 to invest and a cost of capital of 12%. It is considering two projects:
                                              Project Tulip  Project Lotus
Initial cost                                       $300,000       $150,000
Life                                                6 years        4 years
Net present value                                   $42,000        $31,000
Internal rate of return                                 18%            21%
Payback period                                    3.5 years      2.4 years
Fall in annual inflows that makes NPV zero               7%            16%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors which project, if either, they should invest in. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Either may be chosen with justification; e.g. Lotus: lower risk, faster payback and higher IRR, and leaves $150,000 for other uses, although Tulip has the higher NPV.
parts.working: Tulip (max 3): higher NPV $42,000 adds most value; uses all available funds productively; longer life gives returns for six years. Lotus (max 3): higher IRR 21% v 18%; payback 2.4 v 3.5 years; NPV only falls to zero if inflows drop 16% (Tulip only 7%) so far less risky; half the investment, leaving $150,000 for another project, which could make total NPV higher. Other: forecasts over six years less reliable; non-financial factors. Decision (1).

practice.stem:
An engineering firm in Sialkot appraised a project costing $160,000 with net cash inflows of $45,000 a year for five years and no residual value. The finance manager now believes the inflows will be 10% lower, but the equipment could be sold for $12,000 at the end of year 5. The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683; year 5 0.621

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the original net present value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revised net present value.
parts.working: M1 inflows reduced by 10%; M1 residual at year 5; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on what the revision shows about the project.
parts.answer: The NPV falls to only $947: the project is still just acceptable but is very sensitive to the sales forecast.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A school in Abbottabad may install solar panels costing $85,000. Electricity savings are expected to be $23,500 a year for five years, with no residual value. The cost of capital is 8%.
Discount factors at 8%: year 1 0.926; year 2 0.857; year 3 0.794; year 4 0.735; year 5 0.681

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sum of the discount factors for years 1 to 5.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum annual net cash inflow needed for the project to be worthwhile, to the nearest dollar.
parts.working: M1 NPV = 0; M1 cost ÷ annuity factor; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the expected inflow of $23,500 could fall before the project is rejected, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1; A1 OF.

practice.stem:
The directors of a chain of pharmacies plan a new branch in Multan. Fit-out costs $260,000; the fittings will be worth $30,000 at the end of year 4. Net cash inflows are forecast at $72,000, $85,000, $90,000 and $70,000 in years 1 to 4, arising evenly. The cost of capital is 12%, the company's payback target is 3 years and its ARR target is 12% on average investment. A rival chain is also considering a branch in the same area.
Discount factors at 12%: year 1 0.893; year 2 0.797; year 3 0.712; year 4 0.636

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value at 12%.
parts.working: M1 A1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the payback period (years, two decimal places) and the ARR on average investment (two decimal places).
parts.working: M1 A1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to open the new branch. Justify your answer, considering both financial and non-financial factors.
parts.answer: Do not open on these figures as they stand. NPV is slightly negative ($(279)) at 12%, so the branch does not earn the 12% cost of capital, and payback of 3.19 years misses the 3-year target. For: the ARR of 15.00% beats the 12% ARR target and local demand looks strong. Against: value depends heavily on year 4 flows and the $30,000 residual; a rival chain may reduce demand; staffing a new city is a risk.
