Decision: reject unless the fit-out cost can be reduced by about $279 or the demand forecasts are supported by evidence (for example, a local demand survey).
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for points for (with figures); up to 3 marks for points against, financial or non-financial; 1 mark for a clear decision consistent with the negative NPV.

practice.stem:
A diagnostics laboratory in Lahore plans to buy a DNA sequencer for $150,000. Revenue from tests is $64,000 a year and running costs $22,000 a year for five years, with no residual value. The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683; year 5 0.621

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the NPV on the original forecast.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the NPV if running costs are 20% higher than forecast.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the NPV if the equipment lasts only four years.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the laboratory which of the two risks matters more and whether to go ahead.
parts.answer: The NPV is small and very sensitive: either change makes it negative ($(7,496) and $(16,902)). Losing one year of life is the bigger risk (NPV falls by $26,082 compared with $16,676). The laboratory should check the supplier's evidence on life and running costs, seek a warranty or fixed-price service contract, and go ahead only if these can be secured; otherwise reject or renegotiate the price.
parts.working: 1 mark both negative/sensitive; 1 mark identify life as bigger risk with figures; 1 mark action to reduce risk; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
A dairy in Okara is considering a new bottling machine costing $80,000. It would give net cash inflows of $26,000 at the end of each of the next four years. The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of the machine.
parts.working: M1 present values of inflows; M1 less cost; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the machine should be bought, based on your answer to (a).
parts.answer: Yes: the NPV of $2,394 is positive.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem:
A private school in Islamabad plans to build a science laboratory costing $150,000. Extra fee income less extra running costs is expected to be $40,000, $55,000, $60,000 and $35,000 in years 1 to 4. The cost of capital is 12%.
Discount factors at 12%: year 1 0.893; year 2 0.797; year 3 0.712; year 4 0.636

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of the project.
parts.working: M1 each year discounted; M1 total present value; M1 less cost; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what your answer to (a) shows.
parts.answer: The NPV is negative (−$5,465): the project does not earn the 12% cost of capital, so on financial grounds it should not go ahead.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem:
A courier firm in Peshawar may buy an electric van for $36,000. Fuel and repair savings are expected to be $11,000, $12,000, $12,000 and $9,000 in years 1 to 4, and the van will be sold for $4,000 at the end of year 4. The cost of capital is 14%.
Discount factors at 14%: year 1 0.877; year 2 0.769; year 3 0.675; year 4 0.592

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of buying the van.
parts.working: M1 cash flow for year 4 includes sale proceeds; M1 discounting; M1 total; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State, with a reason, whether the van should be bought on financial grounds.
parts.answer: No: the NPV is negative (−$1,329), so the savings do not cover the cost at a 14% cost of capital.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem:
A fitness centre in Doha may install new rowing machines costing $78,000. Extra membership income less running costs will be $23,000 a year at the end of each of the next five years, with no residual value. The cost of capital is 12%.
Discount factors at 12%: year 1 0.893; year 2 0.797; year 3 0.712; year 4 0.636; year 5 0.567

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cumulative discount factor for years 1 to 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of the project.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the project is financially worthwhile and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Yes. The NPV is positive, so the present value of the inflows exceeds the cost; the project earns more than the 12% cost of capital.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark reason.

practice.stem:
A water-testing laboratory in Karachi tests samples for industrial clients. It may buy an automated analyser for $145,000. Net cash inflows from extra tests are expected to be $38,000, $46,000, $52,000 and $40,000 in years 1 to 4. The analyser can be sold for $12,000 at the end of year 4. The cost of capital is 9%.
Discount factors at 9%: year 1 0.917; year 2 0.842; year 3 0.772; year 4 0.708

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of the analyser.
parts.working: B1 year 4 includes residual (52,000); M1 discounting; A1 PVs; A1 NPV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the laboratory whether to buy the analyser.
parts.answer: Buy – NPV is positive ($5,538), so the analyser returns more than 9%. Should also consider reliability of the forecast number of tests.
parts.working: 1 mark decision on own figure; 1 mark supporting point.

practice.stem:
A food processor in Multan is considering a new production line costing $200,000. It needs extra working capital of $25,000 at the start, which will be released at the end of year 5. Net operating cash inflows will be $52,000 a year for five years and the line will be sold for $30,000 at the end of year 5. The cost of capital is 8%.
Discount factors at 8%: year 1 0.926; year 2 0.857; year 3 0.794; year 4 0.735; year 5 0.681

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for year 0 and for year 5.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of the project.
parts.working: M1 years 1–4 discounted; M1 year 5 discounted; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the working capital is shown as an inflow in year 5.
parts.answer: The extra inventory and receivables are no longer needed when the project ends, so the cash tied up is released.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A transport company in Karachi may buy a bus for $120,000. It will be used for four years and then sold for $20,000. Depreciation is straight-line. Forecast profits after depreciation are: year 1 $18,000; year 2 $22,000; year 3 $27,000; year 4 $15,000. The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for each of years 1 to 4.
parts.working: M1 add back depreciation; A1 including residual value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value.
parts.working: M1 discounting; M1 less cost; A1 OF.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the project should be accepted.
parts.answer: Accept: NPV is positive.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem:
A company in Hyderabad can afford only one of two projects, each costing $60,000 now. Net cash inflows:
Year    Project Indus $  Project Ravi $
1                25,000          10,000
2                25,000          20,000
3                20,000          30,000
4                10,000          35,000
The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of each project.
parts.working: M1 discounting A; A1; M1 discounting B; A1; 1 mark presentation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which project should be chosen on financial grounds and give one reason why the result may be less certain for the other project.
parts.answer: Project Ravi (higher NPV). Ravi's cash flows come later, so they are harder to forecast and riskier.
parts.working: 1 mark for both points.

practice.stem:
An agricultural company in Faisalabad can afford one of two projects, each costing $120,000 now. Cost of capital 11%.
Year       Mango $     Guava $
1           20,000      60,000
2           35,000      45,000
3           50,000      30,000
4           65,000      20,000
Discount factors at 11%: year 1 0.901; year 2 0.812; year 3 0.731; year 4 0.659

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of each project.
parts.working: M1 A1 A1 for each project.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend which project should be chosen. Give two reasons, one of which is not based on NPV.
parts.answer: Choose Guava. Its NPV is slightly lower ($5,710 against $5,825), but the gap is only $115, so the choice rests on risk. Guava returns its cash sooner (payback about 2.5 years, against about 3.2 years for Mango), so less of its value depends on forecasts several years ahead.
parts.working: 1 mark choice with the NPV figures; 1 mark: the NPV gap is small, so NPV does not decide the choice on its own; 1 mark: earlier cash return and shorter payback, so less exposure to forecast risk.

practice.stem:
A cold-storage company in Quetta may build a new chamber costing $210,000 on land it already owns. The land could be sold now for $30,000; if the chamber is built, the land will instead be sold for $30,000 at the end of year 5. Net cash inflows from the chamber are $58,000 a year for five years. A compressor overhaul costing $25,000 is needed at the end of year 3. The chamber equipment will be sold for $20,000 at the end of year 5. Cost of capital 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683; year 5 0.621

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a table of net cash flows for years 0 to 5.
parts.working: B1 opportunity cost of land at year 0; B1 overhaul in year 3; B1 year 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value at 10%.
parts.working: M1 A1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the estimate of the value of the land in year 5 is uncertain.
parts.answer: Land prices may change with the local economy/demand; the valuation is only a forecast.

practice.stem:
A boat-hire company in Muscat plans to buy three electric boats for $164,000. They will last six years with no residual value. The cost of capital is 8%.
Discount factors at 8%: year 1 0.926; year 2 0.857; year 3 0.794; year 4 0.735; year 5 0.681; year 6 0.630

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value if the annual inflow is $37,500.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum annual net cash inflow needed for the project to break even in present value terms. Give your answer to the nearest $.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the annual inflow of $37,500 could fall before the project should be rejected. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1 own figure.

practice.stem:
Sharif Ltd may make a new juicer. A machine costing $190,000 and a launch campaign costing $15,000 would both be paid now. The juicer would sell 6,000 units a year for five years at $45 each, with a variable cost of $27 per unit. Extra fixed cash costs would be $48,000 a year. The machine would be scrapped for $10,000 at the end of year 5. The cost of capital is 12%.
Discount factors at 12%: year 1 0.893; year 2 0.797; year 3 0.712; year 4 0.636; year 5 0.567

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual net cash flow from operating the machine.
parts.working: M1 contribution less fixed cash costs; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of the project.
parts.working: Year 0 includes launch costs: 190,000 + 15,000 (1); scrap in year 5 (1); discounting (1); A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why the net present value may not be reliable.
parts.answer: Any one: sales volume, price or costs are estimates; the cost of capital may change; the machine's life or scrap value may differ.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A private hospital in Lahore may buy a scanner costing $250,000. It would bring net cash inflows of $70,000 a year for six years. A major overhaul costing $40,000 would be needed at the end of year 3, and the scanner could be sold for $15,000 at the end of year 6. The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683; year 5 0.621; year 6 0.564

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the present value of the annual cash inflows, using the sum of the discount factors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of the project.
parts.working: M1 overhaul discounted at year 3; M1 residual at year 6; M1 less cost; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one non-financial factor the hospital board should consider.
parts.answer: Any one: patient waiting times/quality of care; staff training; reliability of the supplier; space needed.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A printing firm in Accra may launch a label-printing service. The equipment costs $90,000 and the service gives net cash inflows of $30,000 a year for four years, with no residual value. The owners are thinking of waiting one year before starting; all cash flows would then happen one year later. Cost of capital 12%.
Discount factors at 12%: year 1 0.893; year 2 0.797; year 3 0.712; year 4 0.636; year 5 0.567

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the NPV if the project starts now.
parts.working: M1 A1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the NPV, valued today, if the start is delayed by one year.
parts.working: M1 shift by one year; A1 PVs; A1 NPV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the owners whether to start now or wait. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Starting now gives NPV $1,140, higher than waiting ($990) – value falls because the inflows are received later. Waiting may be justified only if the delay brings better information or a lower machine price; on figures alone start now.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison; 1 mark reason; 1 mark decision with balance.

practice.stem:
A sugar-cane farm in Sindh is negotiating the price of a mechanical harvester. Net cash inflows are expected to be $44,000, $52,000, $52,000 and $36,000 in years 1 to 4, and the harvester could be sold for $15,000 at the end of year 4. Staff training costing $18,000 would be paid now. The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the present value of the net cash inflows, including the residual value.
parts.working: M1 A1; B1 residual in year 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum price the company should pay for the harvester.
parts.answer: Maximum price = PV of inflows − PV of training cost paid now = 156,833 − 18,000 = $138,833
parts.working: M1 deduct training; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The dealer's price is $140,000. Calculate the NPV and state one non-financial factor the company should consider.
parts.answer: NPV = 138,833 − 140,000 = $(1,167). Factor: reliability/after-sales service of the dealer; effect on farm workers' jobs; environmental impact.
parts.working: B1 NPV; B1 sign/decision; B1 factor.

practice.stem:
A printing firm in Faisalabad forecasts for a new press:
Year    Revenue $  Total costs $
1          90,000         67,000
2         105,000         73,000
3         120,000         81,000
Total costs include depreciation of $15,000 a year on the press.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for each year.
parts.working: M1 depreciation removed from costs; A1 A1 (all three for 2 marks).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why depreciation is not included in the net cash flows.
parts.answer: Depreciation is not a payment of cash; the cash outflow is the purchase cost at the start.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A photocopying shop in Rawalpindi is buying a high-speed printer for $48,000. It will be depreciated at 25% per annum using the reducing balance method. Forecast profits after depreciation for the next three years are: year 1 $9,500; year 2 $11,200; year 3 $12,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for each of the three years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for each year.
parts.working: Profit + depreciation (non-cash expense added back). 1 mark per year, own figure rule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why depreciation is added back to profit when net cash flows are prepared for investment appraisal.
parts.answer: Depreciation is a non-cash expense; the cash outflow for the asset is the purchase price shown at year 0, so deducting depreciation as well would count the cost twice.
parts.working: 1 mark non-cash; 1 mark double counting / cost already shown at year 0.

practice.stem:
Karachi Spice Mills is deciding whether to start packing ground spices in sachets. The finance clerk has listed these items:
1 $4,500 already paid to a consultant for a market survey
2 A storage unit the company owns would be used for the project; it is currently rented to another firm for $9,000 a year
3 $12,000 a year of head office administration costs would be charged to the project
4 Interest of $6,000 a year on a bank loan taken to buy the packing machine
5 Two new machine operators at $15,000 a year each

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each item 1 to 5, state whether it should be included in the net cash flows of the project. Give a reason for each answer.
parts.answer:
1 Excluded – sunk cost, already paid whatever is decided.
2 Included – an opportunity cost: the rent of $9,000 a year is lost if the unit is used.
3 Excluded – apportioned fixed cost that does not change as a result of the project.
4 Excluded – financing cost; the cost of capital already allows for the cost of finance through discounting.
5 Included – an extra (incremental) cash outflow caused by the project.
parts.working: 1 mark for each item with correct decision and reason.

practice.stem: A juice bar in Colombo plans to sell bottled cold-pressed juice. Each bottle sells for $14.00 and has variable costs of $8.50. Expected sales are 8,000 bottles in year 1, 9,500 in year 2 and 11,000 in year 3. Extra fixed cash costs will be $21,000 a year. (Depreciation of the juicing equipment, $6,000 a year, is not included in the fixed cash costs.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per bottle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for each of years 1 to 3.
parts.working: 1 mark each; own figure rule on contribution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the depreciation of $6,000 a year has been left out of the fixed costs above.
parts.answer: Depreciation is not a cash flow.

practice.stem: A frozen-food distributor in Dhaka plans to buy a refrigerated van. The van will generate extra revenue of $180,000 a year. Fuel and other variable costs are 45% of revenue. A driver will be paid $38,000 a year and insurance and servicing will cost $12,000 a year. The van will be depreciated at $15,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual net cash flow from the new van.
parts.working: B1 variable costs 81,000; B1 deduct driver and running costs only; B1 answer (depreciation excluded).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other cash flows that would appear in an appraisal of the van.
parts.answer: The purchase price at year 0; the residual (sale) value at the end of its life; (also any working capital or major repairs).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Fatima Foods is considering a new snack line for four years. Information:
1 Market research already paid: $8,000
2 New machine, paid now: $70,000 (no residual value)
3 Extra supervisor: $14,000 a year
4 Share of head office costs charged to the line: $6,000 a year
5 Contribution from sales: $40,000 a year

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of the items 1 to 5, state whether it is a relevant cash flow for the decision and give a reason for items 1 and 4.
parts.answer: 1 not relevant: market research is a sunk cost (already paid). 2 relevant. 3 relevant. 4 not relevant: apportioned head office cost will be paid whether or not the project goes ahead. 5 relevant.
parts.working: 1 mark for all five classifications; 1 mark each reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for year 0 and for each of years 1 to 4.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Amir runs a car-wash in Sukkur. New equipment would cost $66,000, last three years and be sold for $6,000. Forecast profits after straight-line depreciation are $14,000, $19,000 and $11,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why profit is not used directly in net present value calculations.
parts.answer: Profit includes non-cash items such as depreciation and is based on accruals; NPV discounts the timing of actual cash receipts and payments.
parts.working: 1 mark non-cash/accruals; 1 mark timing of cash.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for each of years 1 to 3.
parts.working: M1 depreciation; M1 added back; A1 including residual.

practice.stem: A brick works near Gujranwala may replace its old kiln with an energy-efficient kiln costing $95,000, payable now. The old kiln would be sold now for $7,000. The new kiln would increase revenue by $62,000 a year and extra cash operating costs would be $24,500 a year for four years. The kiln needs part of a yard that is now rented to a neighbour for $5,000 a year; this rent would be lost. The new kiln's residual value after four years is $10,000. An engineer's report costing $3,000 has already been paid for.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the net cash flow for year 0 and for each of years 1 to 4.
parts.answer:
Year                    Item           $
0                   New kiln    (95,000)
0           Sale of old kiln       7,000
0              Net cash flow    (88,000)
1–4                  Revenue      62,000
1–4         Extra cash costs    (24,500)
1–4        Lost rent of yard     (5,000)
1–4            Net cash flow      32,500
4             Residual value      10,000
4               Total year 4      42,500
Years 1–3: $32,500; year 4: $42,500
parts.working: B1 year 0 net 88,000 outflow; B1 lost rent as outflow; B1 annual 32,500; B1 residual in year 4; B1 sunk survey ignored.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the $3,000 already spent on the engineer's report is not included.
parts.answer: It is a sunk cost: it has already been paid and will not change whichever decision is made, so it is not relevant.
parts.working: 1 mark sunk / past; 1 mark not affected by the decision.

practice.stem: A pharmaceutical wholesaler in Lahore will stock a new range of vitamins for three years. The range needs working capital (inventory plus trade receivables) of $20,000 at the start (year 0), rising to $26,000 at the start of year 2 (treated as end of year 1) and $30,000 at the start of year 3 (end of year 2). All working capital is recovered at the end of year 3. Operating net cash inflows are year 1 $41,000, year 2 $48,000, year 3 $52,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash flow arising from working capital in each of years 0 to 3.
parts.working: B1 increases only, not totals; B1 year 2; B1 full release year 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a table of net cash flows for years 0 to 3, ignoring the cost of the equipment.
parts.working: 1 mark per two years correct; own figure rule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why working capital released at the end of a project is treated as a cash inflow.
parts.answer: Inventory is sold and receivables collected without being replaced, so the cash tied up comes back to the business at the end.
parts.working: 1 mark idea of cash tied up; 1 mark recovered when project ends.

practice.stem: A tile manufacturer in Nairobi is considering a new glazing machine costing $150,000. 60% is paid on delivery (year 0) and 40% one year later. Sales from the machine will be $120,000 a year for three years. Customers pay two months after the sale, so in each year only the sales of the first ten months are received; sales are spread evenly. Cash operating costs of $70,000 a year are paid in the year incurred.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash received from customers in each of years 1 to 4.
parts.working: B1 year 1 (10/12); B1 years 2–3; B1 year 4 (2/12).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a table showing the net cash flow for each of years 0 to 4.

practice.stem: A soap factory in Hyderabad may replace an old mixing machine. If the old machine is kept it has five more years of life, running costs of $31,000 a year and no value at the end. A new machine would cost $64,000 now; the old machine could then be sold now for $9,000. The new machine has running costs of $17,500 a year, would allow extra sales giving contribution of $4,000 a year, and would be worth $6,000 after five years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the incremental net cash flow at year 0.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the incremental annual net cash flow for years 1 to 5.
parts.answer: Running-cost saving 31,000 − 17,500 = 13,500, plus extra contribution 4,000 = $17,500
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total incremental net cash flow in year 5.
parts.working: B1. (The old machine would be worth nothing in 5 years.)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain the term 'incremental cash flow'.
parts.answer: The difference in cash flows between doing the project and not doing it; only cash flows that change because of the decision are included.
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

practice.stem: A laundry in Dubai plans to buy machinery for $120,000, to be used for four years and then sold for $12,000. Extra working capital of $18,000 is needed at the start and will be recovered at the end of year 4. Revenue is forecast at $100,000, $110,000, $95,000 and $80,000 in years 1–4. Variable costs are 40% of revenue. Fixed cash costs are $22,000 a year, and depreciation will be $27,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for year 0.
parts.answer: Machine 120,000 + working capital 18,000 = ($138,000)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for each of years 1 to 4.
parts.working: M1 contribution = 60% of revenue; M1 fixed cash costs deducted; M1 depreciation (27,000) not deducted; M1 working capital released year 4; A1 residual value year 4.

practice.stem: A ceramics studio in Barcelona plans to produce 5,000 hand-painted bowls a year for three years. At today's prices each bowl sells for $60 and has variable costs of $34; fixed cash costs are $40,000 a year. Selling prices are expected to rise by 5% a year and all costs by 3% a year, starting in year 1 (so year 1 price = 60 × 1.05). Contribution and fixed costs are calculated on exact figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for each of years 1 to 3. Give answers to the nearest $.
parts.working: B1 prices; B1 variable costs; B1 fixed costs; M1 contribution × 5,000; A1 A1 net cash flows (exact rates, not rounded prices).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the business should include expected price changes in its forecast cash flows.
parts.answer: Cash flows will be received/paid at future prices; ignoring the fact that selling prices rise faster than costs would understate the cash flows and could lead to a wrong decision.
parts.working: 1 mark actual cash amounts; 1 mark different rates change the net figure.

practice.stem:
An engineering workshop in Sialkot may make steel gym frames for three years.
1 A bending machine costs $72,000 now and will be worth $8,000 at the end of year 3.
2 Steel already in inventory, bought last year for $11,000, would be used at the start. It has no other use but could be sold now as scrap for $2,500.
3 4,000 frames will be sold each year at $21 each. Bought-in parts cost $6 per frame.
4 The existing supervisor, paid $20,000 a year, would oversee the work; she has spare time and her pay will not change.
5 A new operator would be hired at $14,000 a year.
6 Other extra cash costs are $9,000 a year.
7 The machine will be depreciated at $21,333 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for year 0 and for each of years 1 to 3.
parts.answer:
Year 0: −72,000 − 2,500 (lost scrap value of steel) = $(74,500)
Years 1–2: 84,000 − 24,000 − 9,000 − 14,000 = $37,000
Year 3: 37,000 + 8,000 = $45,000
Excluded: the steel's original cost $11,000 (sunk), the existing supervisor (no extra cost), depreciation (non-cash).
parts.working: B1 steel at scrap value (opportunity cost) not 11,000; B1 supervisor excluded; B1 new operator included; B1 annual 37,000; B1 year 3 with residual.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value at a cost of capital of 10%. Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751.
parts.working: M1 discounting; A1 PVs; A1 NPV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State, with a reason, whether the project should go ahead.
parts.answer: Yes – the NPV is positive (23,490), so the project adds value.
parts.working: B1 own figure.

practice.stem:
A dairy cooperative in Okara forecasts the following profits for a new cheese-making unit costing $130,000, which will have a residual value of $10,000 after four years:
Year 1 $18,000; year 2 $25,000; year 3 $31,000; year 4 $22,000.
The profits are after straight-line depreciation and after a charge of $8,000 a year for head office overheads apportioned to the unit; head office costs will not change if the unit is opened.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual straight-line depreciation charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for each of years 1 to 4, including the residual value.
parts.answer:
Profit + depreciation + apportioned overhead:
Year 1 $56,000; year 2 $63,000; year 3 $69,000; year 4 60,000 + 10,000 = $70,000
parts.working: B1 add back depreciation; B1 add back apportioned overhead; B1 years 1–3; B1 year 4 with residual.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The project manager says: 'The total profit is only $96,000, so the project hardly covers its cost.' Comment on this statement.
parts.answer: Total profit is after depreciation of $120,000, which already recovers the net cost of the machine, and after $32,000 of overheads that are not extra costs. Total net cash flow is $258,000 against an outlay of $130,000, so the project more than recovers its cost before allowing for the time value of money.
parts.working: 1 mark depreciation already recovers cost; 1 mark overheads not incremental; 1 mark cash comparison with figure.

practice.stem: A solar-panel project has an NPV of $4,500 at 8% and −$3,000 at 12%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the internal rate of return.
parts.answer: The discount rate at which the net present value of a project is zero; the project should be accepted if it is higher than the cost of capital.
parts.working: 1 mark NPV = 0; 1 mark decision rule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the internal rate of return.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the answer to (b) is only an estimate.
parts.answer: Interpolation assumes NPV changes in a straight line between the two rates, but the real relationship is curved.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A bus operator in Lagos has calculated the net present value of a new route as $21,600 at a discount rate of 9% and $(7,900) at 15%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the internal rate of return, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The cost of capital is 13%. State, with a reason, whether the project should be accepted.
parts.answer: Accept: IRR 13.39% is above the 13% cost of capital.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark reason.

practice.stem: A logistics group in Dubai uses a cost of capital of 12%. Its three independent projects have these internal rates of return: Delta 14.2%; Echo 17.5%; Foxtrot 10.8%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the internal rate of return.
parts.answer: The discount rate at which the net present value of a project is zero; it shows the project's own percentage return.
parts.working: 1 mark NPV = 0; 1 mark rate/return.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify which of the projects should be accepted. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Accept Delta (14.2%) and Echo (17.5%): their IRR exceeds the 12% cost of capital. Reject Foxtrot (10.8%), which earns less than the cost of the finance.
parts.working: 1 mark each project correctly classified with reason.

practice.stem:
A dental clinic in Peshawar may buy a digital X-ray unit for $68,000. It will save $19,000 a year for five years and have no residual value.
Cumulative discount factors for years 1–5: at 10% 3.791; at 16% 3.274.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value at 10% and at 16%.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the internal rate of return, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1 own figure.

practice.stem: The owner of a chain of pharmacies in Lahore is used to judging projects by payback only. Her accountant recommends the internal rate of return.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of the internal rate of return method.
parts.answer: Takes account of the time value of money; uses all cash flows over the project's life; gives a percentage that is easy to compare with the cost of capital; the cost of capital is not needed to calculate it.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two limitations of the internal rate of return method.
parts.answer: The interpolated figure is only an estimate; ignores the size of the project; can rank mutually exclusive projects wrongly; may give more than one IRR when cash flows change sign more than once; more complex to calculate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A project has a net present value of $18,400 at a discount rate of 10% and −$6,200 at 18%. The company's cost of capital is 14%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the internal rate of return, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 interpolation formula; M1 correct substitution; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the project should be accepted.
parts.answer: Accept: the IRR of 15.98% is above the 14% cost of capital.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem:
A greenhouse research company in Nairobi grows disease-free seedlings for farmers. A climate-control system costs $84,000 and gives net cash inflows of $26,000, $30,000, $32,000 and $24,000 in years 1 to 4.
Discount factors at 8%: year 1 0.926; year 2 0.857; year 3 0.794; year 4 0.735
Discount factors at 16%: year 1 0.862; year 2 0.743; year 3 0.641; year 4 0.552

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value at 8%.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value at 16%.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the internal rate of return, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1.

practice.stem:
A cycle-hire scheme in Amsterdam would cost $56,000. Net cash inflows are $22,000 a year for three years and $9,000 in year 4. The NPV at 10% has already been calculated as $4,839.
Discount factors at 20%: year 1 0.833; year 2 0.694; year 3 0.579; year 4 0.482

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value at 20%.
parts.working: M1 A1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the internal rate of return, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the answer in (b) is only an approximation of the true IRR.
parts.answer: Interpolation assumes NPV changes in a straight line with the discount rate, but the NPV–rate relationship is a curve; the wide gap between 10% and 20% increases the error.
parts.working: 1 mark straight line vs curve; 1 mark width of range.

practice.stem:
A boat-builder in Karachi can choose only one of two projects. The cost of capital is 11%.
                        Kite        Sail
Initial cost         $50,000    $200,000
NPV at 11%           $26,000     $41,000
IRR                      29%         18%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the two methods rank the projects differently.
parts.answer: Project Kite is smaller, so it earns a high percentage on a small outlay (high IRR), but Project Sail's larger investment creates more absolute wealth (higher NPV). IRR ignores the size of the project; timing of cash flows also differs.
parts.working: 1 mark scale/size; 1 mark IRR is relative %; 1 mark NPV is absolute $ / timing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors which project to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Choose Sail: the projects are mutually exclusive and NPV measures the increase in shareholders' wealth ($41,000 v $26,000). Both IRRs exceed 11%, so both are acceptable, but Sail adds more value; Kite would be preferred only under capital rationing: if the $150,000 not spent on Kite could earn a positive NPV elsewhere, Kite plus that investment may add more value than Sail.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark NPV reason; 1 mark capital/other consideration.

practice.stem:
A textile mill in Faisalabad may buy a weaving loom for $115,000. Net cash inflows are $34,000, $38,000, $38,000 and $30,000 in years 1 to 4 and the loom can be sold for $15,000 at the end of year 4.
Discount factors at 12%: year 1 0.893; year 2 0.797; year 3 0.712; year 4 0.636
Discount factors at 18%: year 1 0.847; year 2 0.718; year 3 0.609; year 4 0.516

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value at 12% and at 18%.
parts.working: B1 residual in year 4; M1 A1 at 12%; A1 at 18%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the internal rate of return, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The company's cost of capital is 14%. State whether the project should go ahead.
parts.answer: No – IRR 12.57% is below the 14% cost of capital, so the NPV at 14% is negative; on these figures the project should not go ahead.
parts.working: B1 decision (no); B1 reason: IRR below cost of capital.

practice.stem:
A clinic in Karachi may buy dental equipment for $90,000. Net cash inflows are expected to be $25,000, $35,000, $40,000 and $30,000 in years 1–4.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683
Discount factors at 16%: year 1 0.862; year 2 0.743; year 3 0.641; year 4 0.552

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value at 10%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value at 16%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the internal rate of return, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1; A1 OF.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The cost of capital is 12%. State whether the project should go ahead and give one advantage of the IRR method.
parts.answer: Go ahead: IRR 15.88% exceeds 12%. Advantage: a percentage is easy to compare with the cost of capital / takes account of the time value of money.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark advantage.

practice.stem: An analyst at a mobile-network company in Islamabad calculated the NPV of a new tower project as $14,200 at 10% and $3,800 at 14%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the two NPVs to estimate the internal rate of return, correct to two decimal places.
parts.answer: NPV falls by 14,200 − 3,800 = 10,400 for a 4% rise in rate. Extrapolate: 10 + 4 × 14,200 ÷ 10,400 = 15.46%
parts.working: M1 fall per 4%; M1 extrapolation; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this estimate is less reliable than one found by interpolation.
parts.answer: Both rates give positive NPVs, so the IRR lies outside the range used; the straight-line assumption is applied beyond the known points and the curve's shape makes the error larger.
parts.working: 1 mark outside range; 1 mark curve/straight line.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a discount rate the analyst should use for a further trial and explain why.
parts.answer: About 16% (just above the estimate): it should give a negative NPV, so the IRR can be found by interpolating between a positive and a negative value.
parts.working: 1 mark sensible rate above 15.46%; 1 mark reason.

practice.stem: A hospital trust in Cairo is considering a solar water-heating plant costing $250,000 with a life of six years and no residual value. The cumulative discount factor for years 1–6 at 12% is 4.111.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equal annual net cash inflow that would give the project an internal rate of return of exactly 12%. Give your answer to the nearest $.
parts.answer: At the IRR, NPV = 0: annual inflow × 4.111 = 250,000 → $60,812
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The forecast annual inflow is $55,000. Without further calculation of IRR, state whether the IRR is above or below 12% and explain why.
parts.answer: Below 12%: inflows of $55,000 are less than the $60,812 needed, so the NPV at 12% is negative ($(23,895)) and a lower discount rate is needed to bring the NPV to zero.
parts.working: 1 mark below 12%; 1 mark reason (inflow below the break-even inflow, so NPV negative at 12%).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the NPV at 12% using the forecast inflow.
parts.working: M1 A1.

practice.stem:
A dairy farm in Punjab plans to build a biogas digester for $160,000. Sales of electricity and savings on fuel will give net cash inflows of $48,000 a year for five years, with no residual value.
Cumulative discount factors for years 1–5: at 8% 3.993; at 15% 3.352.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the NPV at 8% and at 15%.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the internal rate of return, correct to two decimal places, using the NPVs from (a).
parts.answer: Both NPVs are positive, so the IRR is above 15%. Using the straight line through the two NPVs: 8 + 7 × 31,664 ÷ (31,664 − 896) = 15.20%.
parts.working: M1 correct formula with the two NPVs; A1 15.20% (an estimate, since the IRR lies just above 15%).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The cost of capital is 8%. Calculate the percentage fall in annual inflows that would reduce the NPV at 8% to zero. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the farm whether to build the digester. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: IRR 15.20% is well above 8%; NPV positive $31,664; also reduces waste and fertiliser costs (environmental benefit). Against: inflows can fall only 16.52% before NPV is negative; gas-price and output forecasts over five years are uncertain. Decision: build, as returns exceed cost of capital, but monitor output closely.
parts.working: 1 mark each side with figures; 1 mark non-financial; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
A pilot plant at a chemicals company in Karachi would cost $100,000 and produce net cash inflows of $40,000 at the end of each of the next three years.
Discount factors at 8%: year 1 0.926; year 2 0.857; year 3 0.794
Discount factors at 12%: year 1 0.893; year 2 0.797; year 3 0.712
Discount factors at 16%: year 1 0.862; year 2 0.743; year 3 0.641
Discount factors at 20%: year 1 0.833; year 2 0.694; year 3 0.579

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the NPV at each of 8%, 12%, 16% and 20%.
parts.working: 1 mark each (40,000 × sum of factors − 100,000).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the IRR, to two decimal places, by interpolating (i) between 8% and 20% and (ii) between the two rates in (a) that are closest either side of the IRR.
parts.working: M1 A1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain which estimate is more accurate.
parts.answer: (ii) (8% and 12%): the closer the two rates, the less the straight-line interpolation differs from the curved NPV profile, so the error is smaller (wide range overstates the IRR here).
parts.working: 1 mark (ii); 1 mark reason.

practice.stem: A furniture maker in Chiniot may buy a CNC router for $60,000. It will last five years with no residual value. Total profit after depreciation over the five years is forecast at $45,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average annual profit.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the accounting rate of return based on the average investment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the project meets the target return of 25%.
parts.answer: Yes: 30% is above 25%.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem: A furniture polisher in Karachi may buy a spray booth for $90,000 with a four-year life and no residual value. Total profit after depreciation over the four years is forecast at $54,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average annual profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the accounting rate of return on the initial investment, to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The company's target return is 12%. State whether the machine meets the target.
parts.answer: Yes – 15.00% exceeds 12%.
parts.working: B1 own figure.

practice.stem: A recording studio in Toronto plans to buy a mixing console for $120,000. It will be sold for $20,000 after four years. Profits after depreciation are forecast at $31,000, $27,000, $24,000 and $18,000 in years 1 to 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average investment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average annual profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the accounting rate of return on the average investment, to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1.

practice.stem: A bakery in Gilgit expects a new oven costing $150,000 (no residual value) to earn total profits of $66,000 over its three-year life.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the accounting rate of return on the initial investment, to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two limitations of the accounting rate of return.
parts.answer: Ignores the time value of money; uses profit (affected by accounting policies such as depreciation) rather than cash; ignores timing of profits within the life; different definitions of investment give different answers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
A shipping agent in Chittagong is considering two six-year projects.
                             Pelican       Heron
Cost                        $100,000     $70,000
Residual value               $16,000         nil
Total profit (6 years)       $84,000     $54,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the accounting rate of return on the average investment for each project, to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The company's target ARR is 25%. State which project(s) meet the target.
parts.answer: Heron only (25.71%); Pelican (24.14%) is below 25%.
parts.working: B1 own figures.

practice.stem: A road-haulage firm in Multan is buying a truck for $200,000 that will be sold for $20,000 at the end of its life. Average annual profit after depreciation is $27,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the formula for the accounting rate of return on average investment.
parts.answer: Average annual profit ÷ average investment × 100, where average investment = (initial cost + residual value) ÷ 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ARR, to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one advantage of ARR.
parts.answer: Simple to calculate and understand; uses the whole life of the project; expressed as a percentage like ROCE.

practice.stem: Haroon Builders may buy a crane for $140,000. It will produce net cash inflows of $50,000 a year for four years and then be sold for $20,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average annual profit.
parts.answer: Total cash inflows 200,000 − depreciation 120,000 = 80,000; ÷ 4 = $20,000
parts.working: M1 depreciation deducted; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the accounting rate of return on (i) the average investment and (ii) the initial investment, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one limitation of the accounting rate of return.
parts.answer: Any one: ignores the time value of money; uses profit not cash flow; different formulas give different answers; ignores the timing of profits.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A car-repair workshop in Sharjah may buy diagnostic equipment for $75,000, with a residual value of $5,000 after five years. Net cash inflows are $24,000, $26,000, $28,000, $22,000 and $20,000 in years 1 to 5. Depreciation is straight-line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total profit over the life of the equipment.
parts.answer: Total cash inflows 120,000 − total depreciation (75,000 − 5,000) 70,000 = $50,000
parts.working: B1 inflows; B1 depreciation 70,000; B1 profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the accounting rate of return on the average investment, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Average profit 50,000 ÷ 5 = 10,000; average investment (75,000 + 5,000) ÷ 2 = 40,000; ARR = 25.00%
parts.working: B1 average profit; B1 average investment; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why ARR is calculated using profit rather than net cash flow.
parts.answer: ARR is an accounting measure that compares profit with capital employed, like ROCE in the financial statements; it therefore deducts depreciation to reflect the using up of the asset.
parts.working: 1 mark link to ROCE/accounting profit; 1 mark depreciation.

practice.stem: A hotel in Swat is planning a new spa costing $260,000 with a residual value of $40,000 after five years. The owners require an accounting rate of return of 16% on average investment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum average annual profit needed to meet the target.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum total profit over the five years.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Forecast total profit is $112,000. Calculate the ARR and comment.
parts.answer: 112,000 ÷ 5 = 22,400; 22,400 ÷ 150,000 = 14.93%; below the 16% target, so reject on this measure.
parts.working: M1 A1 with comment.

practice.stem: A clothing retailer in Johannesburg will open a new store. Fittings cost $180,000 and will be worth $30,000 after five years. Inventory (working capital) of $25,000 is needed for the whole five years and will be recovered at the end. Total net cash inflows over five years from trading are $220,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average annual profit.
parts.answer: Total profit = 220,000 − depreciation 150,000 = 70,000; ÷ 5 = $14,000
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average investment, including working capital.
parts.working: M1 A1 (working capital held throughout, so added in full).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the ARR on average investment, to two decimal places.
parts.working: B1 own figures.

practice.stem:
A software company in Bengaluru must choose between two projects, each costing $100,000 with a five-year life and no residual value. Cash inflows arise evenly during each year.
Year      Lark $    Wren $
1         30,000    50,000
2         30,000    40,000
3         30,000    20,000
4         30,000     5,000
5         30,000     5,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the accounting rate of return on average investment for each project.
parts.working: M1 A1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the payback period of each project, in years to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two methods rank the projects differently and advise which should be chosen.
parts.answer: ARR prefers Lark because it earns more profit over the whole life; payback prefers Wren because its cash comes early. Neither uses discounting. Advise Lark if the business can accept the longer wait (higher overall return); Wren if liquidity or risk is the main concern – an NPV calculation should decide.
parts.working: 1 mark ARR reason; 1 mark payback reason; 1 mark advice.

practice.stem: A company in Kenya sells weather data to farmers from a network of sensors costing $48,000. The sensors will last three years and be sold for $6,000. Net cash inflows are $14,500, $16,000 and $17,500. Depreciation is straight-line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average annual profit.
parts.answer: Average cash inflow 16,000 − depreciation 14,000 = $2,000
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ARR on (i) the initial investment and (ii) the average investment, each to two decimal places.
parts.working: B1 (i); B1 average investment 27,000; B1 (ii).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a business must state which basis it has used when comparing ARRs.
parts.answer: The same project gives a much higher ARR on average investment, so comparisons are only valid on the same basis.

practice.stem: A private hospital group in Lahore wants a new sterilisation unit. It will give total net cash inflows of $260,000 over five years and will have a residual value of $10,000. The group requires an accounting rate of return of 20% on average investment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that, if the cost is $C, the ARR on average investment is [(270,000 − C) ÷ 5] ÷ [(C + 10,000) ÷ 2].
parts.answer: Total profit = inflows 260,000 − depreciation (C − 10,000) = 270,000 − C; average profit (270,000 − C) ÷ 5; average investment (C + 10,000) ÷ 2.
parts.working: 1 mark profit expression; 1 mark average investment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum price the hospital group should pay to achieve its 20% target. Give your answer to the nearest $.
parts.working: M1 equation; M1 rearrangement; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Verify your answer by calculating the ARR at that price.

practice.stem: A drone-survey company in Perth buys a drone for $64,000. It will last four years and be sold for $4,000. Net cash inflows are $36,000, $34,000, $30,000 and $28,000 in years 1 to 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for each year using (i) straight-line depreciation and (ii) the reducing balance method at 50%, (the carrying amount at the end of year 4 equals the residual value).
parts.working: M1 A1 each method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ARR on average investment, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Total profit is 68,000 under both methods; average 17,000 ÷ average investment 34,000 = 50.00%
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the choice of depreciation method does not affect the ARR calculated in (b), and state one way in which it could affect a manager's view of the project.
parts.answer: Total depreciation over the life is always cost less residual value, so total and average profit are unchanged. But year-by-year profits differ: reducing balance shows a very low profit in year 1, which could make a manager judged on annual profit reluctant to invest.
parts.working: 1 mark same total; 1 mark yearly effect.

practice.stem: A quarry in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa may buy a stone crusher for $240,000 with a six-year life. Total net cash inflows are forecast at $310,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ARR on average investment assuming no residual value.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ARR on average investment if the residual value is $36,000.
parts.working: B1 profit; B1 investment; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a higher residual value increases both the numerator and the denominator of the ARR, and state which effect is greater here.
parts.answer: Higher residual value lowers total depreciation, so average profit rises; it also raises the average investment. Here the profit effect is greater, so ARR rises from 9.72% to 12.80%.
parts.working: 1 mark both effects; 1 mark conclusion.

practice.stem: A school in Lahore must choose between two projects, each costing $48,000. Project X returns $12,000 a year for six years. Project Y returns $20,000, $18,000, $15,000 and $10,000 in years 1–4. Cash flows arise evenly through each year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the payback period for Project X.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the payback period for Project Y in years and months.
parts.answer: After 2 years 38,000 recovered; 10,000 of year 3's 15,000 needed = 0.67 of a year ≈ 8 months. Payback = 2 years 8 months.
parts.working: M1 cumulative; M1 fraction; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one disadvantage of the payback method.
parts.answer: Ignores cash flows after payback / ignores the time value of money (unless discounted).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A car-wash in Islamabad may buy a water-recycling system for $57,000. It will save $15,000 a year, arising evenly through each year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the payback period in years, to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express the payback period in years and months (to the nearest month).
parts.answer: 3 years 10 months

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why a business might use payback as its main method.
parts.answer: Simple to calculate/understand; favours quick return of cash, so suits a business with liquidity problems or in a fast-changing market; reduces risk.

practice.stem: A print shop in Lusaka is investing $96,000 in a large-format printer. Net cash inflows, arising evenly, are $22,000, $31,000, $29,000, $28,000 and $20,000 in years 1 to 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cumulative net cash flow at the end of each of years 1 to 3.
parts.working: 1 mark for years 1–2; 1 mark year 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the payback period in years and months.
parts.answer: 3 years + 14,000 ÷ 28,000 × 12 = 3 years 6 months
parts.working: M1 A1.

practice.stem: The owners of a mobile-phone accessories business in Karachi say they will accept only projects that pay back within two years because their products go out of fashion quickly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of the payback method.
parts.answer: Simple; uses cash rather than profit; emphasises early cash flows, which are more certain; helps liquidity planning.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of the payback method.
parts.answer: Ignores cash flows after the payback period; ignores the time value of money (simple payback); does not measure profitability; target period is arbitrary.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A small hotel in Hunza installs solar water heaters costing $4,320. They save $240 a month in electricity and $120 a month in gas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the monthly saving.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the payback period in months.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one risk that could make the actual payback period longer.
parts.answer: Electricity prices fall; panels underperform in cloudy weather/dust; repair costs.

practice.stem: A cold-chain logistics firm in Multan is buying a refrigerated trailer for $60,000. Net cash inflows arise evenly within each year: $22,000 in year 1, $24,000 in year 2, $21,000 in year 3 and $18,000 in year 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cumulative net cash flow at the end of each of years 1 to 3, and the payback period in years and months (to the nearest month).
parts.answer: Year 1 (38,000); year 2 (14,000); year 3 7,000. Payback = 2 + 14,000 ÷ 21,000 = 2.67 years = 2 years 8 months.
parts.working: 1 mark cumulative figures for years 1 and 2; 1 mark year 3 and the payback point within year 3 (2 years plus part-year); 1 mark payback 2 years 8 months.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the payback method ignores the $18,000 inflow in year 4, and why this may lead to a wrong decision.
parts.answer: Payback stops counting once the $60,000 is recovered, so inflows after that point (year 4 here) are ignored; a project with strong later inflows may be rejected or undervalued.
parts.working: 1 mark: the calculation stops at the payback point; 1 mark: later inflows may make the project more valuable than payback suggests.

practice.stem:
A cosmetics firm in Dhaka can choose one of two projects each costing $120,000. Cash flows arise evenly. Target payback is 3 years.
Year     Orchid $     Iris $
1          45,000     25,000
2          40,000     30,000
3          42,000     35,000
4          10,000     40,000
5               –     60,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the payback period of each project in years and months (to the nearest month).
parts.answer:
Orchid: 2 + 35,000 ÷ 42,000 = 2.83 years = 2 years 10 months
Iris: 3 + 30,000 ÷ 40,000 = 3.75 years = 3 years 9 months
parts.working: M1 A1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which project meets the company's 3-year target and give one reason why the company should not rely on payback alone.
parts.answer: Orchid only. Payback ignores the inflows after payback (Iris has a large year-5 inflow of $60,000) and ignores the time value of money.
parts.working: 1 mark Orchid; 1 mark reason.

practice.stem: A garment exporter in Lahore may buy an embroidery machine for $84,000 with a four-year life and residual value of $4,000. Forecast profits after straight-line depreciation are $6,000, $9,000, $12,000 and $8,000 in years 1 to 4. Cash flows arise evenly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual net cash flows.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the payback period in years and months.
parts.answer: 2 years + 29,000 ÷ 32,000 × 12 = 2 years 11 months (2.91 years)
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why using profit instead of cash flow would give a wrong payback period.
parts.answer: Profit is after depreciation, a non-cash charge, so the inflows would be understated and payback overstated.

practice.stem: A fruit-processing firm in Swat may buy a pulping machine for $65,000. Net cash inflows are $18,000, $27,000, $30,000 and $24,000 in years 1 to 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the payback period assuming the cash flows arise evenly through each year.
parts.answer: 2 + 20,000 ÷ 30,000 = 2.67 years (2 years 8 months)
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the payback period if the cash flows are received only at the end of each year, and explain the difference.
parts.answer: 3 years: the year-3 inflow arrives only at the end of year 3, so the outlay is not recovered until then. The 'even' assumption allows recovery part-way through the year.
parts.working: 1 mark 3 years; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest which assumption is more realistic for a fruit-processing business whose sales are concentrated in the harvest season.
parts.answer: Neither exactly: cash arrives in a few months of each year; if harvest is late in the year, the end-of-year assumption is closer and the even assumption overstates how quickly the money is recovered.
parts.working: 1 mark seasonality; 1 mark conclusion.

practice.stem: An online grocery start-up in Karachi will spend $85,000 on a delivery app and warehouse fittings. Net cash inflows are $20,000 in year 1 and are expected to grow by 10% a year. Cash flows arise evenly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash inflow for each of years 1 to 4.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the payback period, to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the payback period if there is no growth (inflows stay at $20,000).

practice.stem:
A bakery chain in Islamabad may open a new outlet costing $75,000. Net cash inflows are $28,000, $30,000, $26,000 and $20,000 in years 1–4, arising evenly through each year. The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the simple payback period, correct to two decimal places of a year.
parts.answer: After 2 years 58,000; 17,000 ÷ 26,000 = 0.65; payback = 2.65 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the discounted payback period, correct to two decimal places of a year.
parts.answer: Present values: 25,452, 24,780, 19,526, 13,660. Cumulative after year 3: 69,758; still to recover 5,242; 5,242 ÷ 13,660 = 0.38. Discounted payback = 3.38 years
parts.working: M1 present values; M1 cumulative; M1 fraction of year 4; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the discounted payback period is longer than the simple payback period.
parts.answer: Discounting reduces the value of each future inflow, so it takes longer to recover the cost.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: An electronics assembler in Shenzhen requires payback within 2½ years. New test equipment would give net cash inflows, arising evenly, of $38,000, $41,000, $44,000, $35,000 and $30,000 in years 1 to 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum cost of the equipment if it must pay back within 2½ years.
parts.working: M1 half of year 3; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The supplier quotes $108,000. Calculate the payback period in years and months.
parts.answer: 2 + 29,000 ÷ 44,000 = 2.66 years ≈ 2 years 8 months
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether the company should reject the equipment because it misses the 2½-year target.
parts.answer: The target is arbitrary; payback ignores inflows after year 3 (years 4–5 still bring cash) and profitability; a short delay of about 2 months is small. Should also look at NPV/IRR; if NPV positive, accept or negotiate price down to $101,000.
parts.working: 1 mark limitation; 1 mark later inflows; 1 mark judgement.

practice.stem:
A wind-turbine maintenance firm in Hyderabad (Sindh) may buy a specialist crane for $150,000. Net cash inflows are $50,000 a year for five years, arising evenly. The cost of capital is 14%.
Discount factors at 14%: year 1 0.877; year 2 0.769; year 3 0.675; year 4 0.592; year 5 0.519

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the simple payback period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the discounted payback period, to two decimal places.
parts.answer:
Cumulative PV: year 1 (106,150); year 2 (67,700); year 3 (33,950); year 4 (4,350); year 5 21,600
Discounted payback = 4 + 4,350 ÷ 25,950 = 4.17 years
parts.working: M1 PVs; M1 cumulative; A1 cumulative; A1 period.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the difference between the two answers shows about the project and its risk.
parts.answer: Allowing for the 14% cost of capital, the project takes much longer (4.17 v 3 years) to recover its cost and only just pays back within its 5-year life (NPV $21,600). Any fall in later inflows or shortening of the life would make it unprofitable, so it is riskier than simple payback suggests.
parts.working: 1 mark longer recovery; 1 mark near end of life/small NPV; 1 mark risk conclusion.

practice.stem: A private school in Abbottabad is building a sports complex in two stages. Stage 1 costs $80,000 now. Stage 2 costs $25,000 and is paid at the end of year 2. Net cash inflows from fees are $30,000, $35,000, $36,000 and $34,000 in years 1 to 4, arising evenly. (The year-2 inflow arrives before the stage 2 payment.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cumulative net cash flow at the end of each of years 1 to 4.
parts.working: B1 net year 2; B1 years 1–2; B1 years 3–4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the payback period in years and months (to the nearest month).
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the extra investment in year 2 makes payback a less suitable measure on its own.
parts.answer: A large outflow after the start means cumulative cash goes up and then down; payback does not show the size or timing of later commitments, and a project could 'pay back' before a later big outflow.
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

practice.stem: A tour operator in Skardu may buy two four-wheel-drive vehicles for $117,000. Forecast net cash inflows are $45,000 a year for five years, arising evenly. The operator's payback target is 3 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the payback period on the forecast figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum annual inflow needed to meet the 3-year payback target.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the annual inflow can fall before the target is missed, to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Comment on the result.
parts.answer: A fall of over 13% is a reasonable margin of safety, but the inflows depend on tourist numbers, which can drop sharply (security, weather), so the risk should be considered.
parts.working: 1 mark interpretation; 1 mark context.

practice.stem: A bakery in Lahore makes cakes. The standard is 3 kg of flour mix per batch at $4 per kg. In March it made 2,000 batches, using 6,300 kg that cost $24,570.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the material price variance.
parts.working: M1 AQ × SP − actual cost; A1 with F/A.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the material usage variance.
parts.answer: Standard quantity 2,000 × 3 = 6,000 kg; (6,000 − 6,300) × 4 = $1,200 adverse
parts.working: M1 (SQ − AQ) × SP; A1 with F/A.

practice.stem: A garment factory in Faisalabad sets a standard of 1.5 labour hours per shirt at $12 per hour. Last month 4,000 shirts were made using 5,800 hours, and wages paid were $72,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate variance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour efficiency variance.

practice.stem: A company in Karachi budgeted to sell 5,000 electric irons at $40 each, giving a standard profit of $9 per iron. It actually sold 4,600 irons at $42 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sales price variance.
parts.working: M1 actual units × price difference; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sales volume variance, using standard profit.

practice.stem: A furniture company in Chiniot budgeted to sell 2,000 dining tables at $250 each. The standard cost of a table is $190. It actually sold 2,150 tables at $240 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sales price variance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sales volume variance, using standard profit.
parts.answer: Standard profit 250 − 190 = 60; (2,150 − 2,000) × 60 = $9,000 favourable

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the net effect of the two variances on profit.
parts.answer: Net $12,500 adverse
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem: A workshop in Jaipur makes brass lamps. Each lamp needs 2.5 kg of brass at $8 per kg and 45 minutes of labour at $16 per hour. Variable overhead is absorbed at $4 per labour hour and fixed overhead at $20 per labour hour. Each lamp sells for $65.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the standard cost card for one lamp.
parts.answer:
Standard cost card: one lamp
                                                              $
Direct materials (2.5 kg × $8)                            20.00
Direct labour (45 minutes × $16 per hour)                 12.00
Variable overhead (0.75 hours × $4)                        3.00
Fixed overhead (0.75 hours × $20)                         15.00
Standard cost per unit                                    50.00
parts.working: Labour time converted to 0.75 hours (1); overheads on labour hours (1); total $50.00 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard profit per lamp.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem: A detergent maker in Dhaka uses a standard of 3 kg of powder base per carton at a standard price of $2.20 per kg. It calculates the material price variance when material is purchased. In September it bought 12,000 kg of powder base for $25,800 and used 11,200 kg to make 3,700 cartons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual price paid per kg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the material price variance, stating whether it is favourable or adverse.
parts.answer: $600 favourable

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the material usage variance, stating whether it is favourable or adverse.
parts.answer: $220 adverse

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the price variance is based on the 12,000 kg bought, not the 11,200 kg used.
parts.answer: The variance is identified when the purchase is made, so the buyer is held responsible at once and inventory can be held at standard price.

practice.stem: A hospital laundry in Kuala Lumpur sets a standard of 12 minutes of labour per load washed, at $15 per hour. In March it washed 9,000 loads. Staff worked and were paid for 1,850 hours at a total cost of $28,490.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard hours allowed for the loads washed.
parts.answer: 1,800 hours

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate variance.
parts.answer: $740 adverse
parts.working: Actual hours at standard rate 1,850 × 15 = 27,750 (M1); 27,750 − 28,490 = 740 A (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the labour efficiency variance.
parts.answer: $750 adverse

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the total labour variance and show that it equals the sum of the rate and efficiency variances.
parts.answer: $1,490 adverse

practice.stem: A shoe-polish maker in Lagos has a standard material cost of $18 per tin (6 kg at $3 per kg). In July it made 2,400 tins, using 15,000 kg of material that cost $43,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total material cost variance.
parts.answer: $300 adverse

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the material price variance and the material usage variance.
parts.answer: Price $1,500 favourable; usage $1,800 adverse

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why a favourable price variance might be linked to an adverse usage variance.
parts.answer: Cheaper, lower-quality material may cause more waste.

practice.stem: A print shop in Nairobi produces packs of printed leaflets. Standard variable cost per pack: materials $7.50; labour $12.00; variable overhead $3.00. In May it produced 5,200 packs. Actual costs were: materials $38,900; labour $63,100; variable overhead $15,950.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard cost of the actual output for each element of cost.
parts.answer: Materials $39,000; labour $62,400; variable overhead $15,600
parts.working: 5,200 × each standard (B1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the variance for each element and the total variable cost variance, stating whether each is favourable or adverse.
parts.answer: Materials $100 F; labour $700 A; variable overhead $350 A; total $950 A
parts.working: B1 each element; B1 total.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which manager is most likely to be asked to explain the labour variance.
parts.answer: The production (print room) supervisor/manager responsible for staff.

practice.stem: A manufacturer of steel kettles in Gujranwala budgeted to sell 6,000 kettles in a quarter at $50 each. Standard variable cost is $30 per kettle and standard fixed overhead is $8 per kettle. It actually sold 5,700 kettles at $51.50 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sales price variance.
parts.answer: $8,550 favourable

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sales volume variance using (i) standard profit (absorption costing) and (ii) standard contribution (marginal costing).
parts.answer: (i) $3,600 adverse; (ii) $6,000 adverse
parts.working: Standard profit 50 − 38 = 12 (B1); 300 × 12 = 3,600 A (B1). Standard contribution 20 (B1); 300 × 20 = 6,000 A (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two sales volume variances are different.
parts.answer: Under marginal costing fixed overhead is not charged per unit, so each lost sale loses the full contribution of $20 rather than the profit of $12.

practice.stem: Each valve made by a factory in Gujranwala should take 2 machine hours; variable overhead is absorbed at $3 per machine hour. The standard material cost is $15 per valve. In June 3,500 valves were made. Machine hours were 7,400, variable overhead was $21,460 and material cost $54,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the variable overhead expenditure and efficiency variances.
parts.working: M1 A1 for each variance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total material cost variance.
parts.working: M1 standard cost of actual output − actual cost; A1.

practice.stem: A firm in Sialkot budgeted fixed production overhead of $96,000 for an output of 12,000 cricket bats. Actual output was 11,400 bats and actual fixed overhead was $98,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fixed overhead absorption rate per unit.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fixed overhead expenditure variance and the fixed overhead volume variance.
parts.working: M1 A1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total under- or over-absorbed fixed overhead.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A paint maker in Rawalpindi uses 0.8 litres of resin per tin at a standard price of $6.50 per litre. In May it made 9,000 tins and bought and used 7,050 litres of resin costing $47,235.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual price paid per litre.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the material price variance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the material usage variance.

practice.stem: A call-centre in Islamabad measures output in 'cases handled'. The standard is 30 minutes per case at $16 per hour. In April 8,400 cases were handled; staff worked and were paid for 4,350 hours at $15.60 per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard hours for the actual output.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate variance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the labour efficiency variance and the total labour variance.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A company in Peshawar budgeted to make 10,000 units. Budgeted costs: materials $80,000; labour $60,000; variable overhead $20,000; fixed overhead $45,000. Actual output was 9,000 units. Actual costs: materials $73,500; labour $52,900; variable overhead $18,600; fixed overhead $46,200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a flexed budget for an output of 9,000 units.
parts.answer: Materials $72,000; Labour $54,000; Variable overhead $18,000; Fixed overhead $45,000
parts.working: 1 mark variable costs × 90%; 1 mark fixed overhead unchanged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the variance for each cost and the total cost variance.
parts.answer: Materials $1,500 adverse; Labour $1,100 favourable; Variable overhead $600 adverse; Fixed overhead $1,200 adverse; total $2,200 adverse
parts.working: 2 marks all four (1 mark for two or three); 1 mark total.

practice.stem: Budgeted fixed overhead for a pharmaceutical packaging plant was $180,000, based on 36,000 standard labour hours. Each pack has a standard time of 1.5 labour hours. Actual output was 23,000 packs and actual fixed overhead was $176,400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fixed overhead absorption rate per labour hour.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fixed overhead absorbed and the amount under- or over-absorbed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the fixed overhead expenditure and volume variances.
parts.answer: Expenditure 180,000 − 176,400 = $3,600 favourable; volume (34,500 − 36,000) × 5 = $7,500 adverse
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Marigold Ltd, Chennai, uses standard absorption costing. Its budgeted profit for April was $84,000. The variances for April were:
Variance                             $
Sales price                      6,200 F
Sales volume                     9,600 A
Material price                   2,150 A
Material usage                   1,300 F
Labour rate                        900 F
Labour efficiency                3,400 A
Variable overhead expenditure      450 A
