Variable overhead efficiency       680 A
Fixed overhead expenditure       1,500 F
Fixed overhead volume            2,400 A

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement reconciling the budgeted profit with the actual profit for April.
parts.answer: Budgeted profit 84,000; total favourable variances 9,900; total adverse variances 18,680; net adverse 8,780; actual profit 75,220
parts.working: B1 budgeted profit; B1 favourable total 9,900; B1 adverse total 18,680; M1 adjust; A1 actual profit 75,220.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two variances in the list that may have the same cause, and explain the link.
parts.answer: E.g. labour efficiency adverse and variable overhead efficiency adverse – both depend on hours worked, so slow working raises both; or sales price favourable and sales volume adverse – higher price reduced demand.
parts.working: 1 mark pair; 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem: A paint factory in Lahore has a standard of 2.5 kg of pigment per drum at $5.15 per kg. In June it made 3,000 drums. All pigment bought was used. The material price variance was $1,240 adverse and the actual price paid was $5.31 per kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the quantity of pigment used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the material usage variance.
parts.answer: $1,287.50 adverse

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total material cost variance and check it against the actual cost of pigment.
parts.answer: $2,527.50 adverse

practice.stem: An air-cooler assembler in Multan uses two grades of labour. Standard per cooler: skilled 2 hours at $20 per hour; semi-skilled 3 hours at $12 per hour. In August 1,500 coolers were made. Actual labour: skilled 3,100 hours costing $63,550; semi-skilled 4,350 hours costing $50,460.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate and efficiency variances for skilled labour.
parts.answer: Rate $1,550 adverse; efficiency $2,000 adverse

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate and efficiency variances for semi-skilled labour.
parts.answer: Rate $1,740 favourable; efficiency $1,800 favourable

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total labour variance and comment on what the four variances suggest.
parts.answer: $10 adverse in total. Almost nil overall, but skilled staff were paid more and took longer, while semi-skilled staff were cheaper and quicker – possibly semi-skilled work was done by skilled staff, or overtime was paid to skilled staff.
parts.working: B1 total; B1 comment.

practice.stem: A candle maker in Colombo uses two materials. Standard per candle: wax 0.4 kg at $3.50 per kg; fragrance oil 0.02 litres at $40 per litre. In November 25,000 candles were made. Actual usage: wax 10,300 kg costing $35,535; fragrance oil 480 litres costing $20,160.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price and usage variances for wax.
parts.answer: Price $515 favourable; usage $1,050 adverse

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price and usage variances for fragrance oil.
parts.answer: Price $960 adverse; usage $800 favourable

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total material cost variance.
parts.answer: $695 adverse

practice.stem: A plastics factory in Faisalabad absorbs fixed overhead per unit of output. Budgeted fixed overhead for the year was $150,000 and budgeted output was 25,000 units. At the year end the fixed overhead volume variance was $9,000 adverse and the fixed overhead expenditure variance was $3,200 favourable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fixed overhead absorption rate per unit.
parts.answer: $6 per unit

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the actual output.
parts.answer: 23,500 units

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the actual fixed overhead.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the fixed overhead absorbed and the under- or over-absorption, and show that it equals the net of the two variances.
parts.answer: Absorbed $141,000; under-absorbed $5,800

practice.stem:
Shah Appliances makes one model of water heater. Standard cost card per heater: materials 4 kg × $5 = $20; labour 2 hours × $14 = $28; variable overhead 2 hours × $3 = $6; fixed overhead 2 hours × $10 = $20. Standard cost $74; selling price $100; standard profit $26. Budgeted output and sales: 3,000 heaters (budgeted fixed overhead $60,000).
Actual results for the month: 3,200 heaters made and sold at $97 each; materials 13,100 kg costing $64,190; labour 6,250 hours costing $89,375; variable overhead $19,500; fixed overhead $61,800.
The following variances have already been calculated: material price $1,310 favourable; material usage $1,500 adverse; labour rate $1,875 adverse; labour efficiency $2,100 favourable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sales price and sales volume variances.
parts.answer: Price: 3,200 × (97 − 100) = $9,600 adverse. Volume: 200 × 26 = $5,200 favourable.

parts.label: b

practice.stem: A soap factory in Karachi has a standard of 5 kg of oil per carton at $2.40 per kg. Last month it made 1,800 cartons. The material usage variance was $1,080 adverse and the material price variance was $920 favourable. All material bought was used.

parts.working: M1 SQ; M1 variance ÷ standard price; A1 (adverse, so add).

parts.label: b

parts.working: M1 AQ × SP; M1 less favourable variance; A1.

practice.stem:
Rizvi Garden Products uses standard marginal costing. Standard per planter: price $60; materials 5 kg × $4 = $20; labour 1 hour × $12 = $12; variable overhead 1 hour × $6 = $6; standard contribution $22. Budget: 10,000 planters; fixed costs $150,000.
Actual: 9,400 planters made and sold at $62; materials 48,000 kg costing $187,200; labour 9,700 hours costing $119,310; variable overhead $56,000; fixed costs $153,000.

parts.text: Calculate the sales price variance and the sales volume variance based on standard contribution.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the material price, material usage, labour rate and labour efficiency variances.
parts.answer: Material price 48,000 × 4 − 187,200 = $4,800 favourable; usage (47,000 − 48,000) × 4 = $4,000 adverse; labour rate 9,700 × 12 − 119,310 = $2,910 adverse; efficiency (9,400 − 9,700) × 12 = $3,600 adverse.

practice.stem: A shoe factory in Kasur has a standard of 3 labour hours per pair of boots at $11 per hour. In May it made 2,500 pairs. The labour efficiency variance was $1,650 favourable and the labour rate variance was $2,205 adverse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual labour hours worked.
parts.answer: Standard hours 2,500 × 3 = 7,500; hours saved = 1,650 ÷ 11 = 150; actual = 7,350 hours
parts.working: M1 SH; M1 favourable so fewer hours; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the actual rate paid per hour, correct to two decimal places.
parts.answer: AH × SR = 7,350 × 11 = 80,850; adverse rate variance so actual cost = 80,850 + 2,205 = 83,055; rate = $11.30
parts.working: M1; M1 add adverse variance; A1.

practice.stem: Standard variable cost of one bicycle frame made in Lahore: materials 6 kg × $3.50 = $21.00; labour 1.25 hours × $18 = $22.50; variable overhead 1.25 hours × $4 = $5.00. In July 4,000 frames were made. Actual costs: materials 24,600 kg costing $84,870; labour 4,900 hours costing $90,650; variable overhead $20,090.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the material price and usage variances.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate and efficiency variances.

parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the variable overhead expenditure and efficiency variances.

practice.stem:
Penang Solar Frames Sdn Bhd makes aluminium frames for solar panels and uses standard absorption costing. Standard cost card per frame:
                                          $
Materials       3 kg × $6.00           18.00

Selling price                          95.00

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted profit and the actual profit.

practice.stem: A furniture workshop in Chiniot pays a standard labour rate of $14 per hour. In October it made 4,120 chairs. Labour worked 12,600 hours. The total labour variance was $2,100 adverse and the labour rate variance was $1,260 favourable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual rate paid per hour and the actual labour cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour efficiency variance.
parts.answer: $3,360 adverse
parts.working: Total = rate + efficiency, so efficiency = 2,100 A + 1,260 = 3,360 A (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the standard hours allowed for actual output, and the standard hours per chair.
parts.answer: 12,360 hours; 3 hours per chair

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the standard labour cost per chair.

practice.stem: A company in Ipoh makes one product. Budgeted production and sales were 10,000 units at a standard price of $30. Standard variable cost is $18 per unit and budgeted fixed overhead is $50,000, absorbed per unit of budgeted output. Actual production and sales were 9,200 units. All actual prices, costs and fixed overhead were exactly as standard.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted profit under absorption costing and under marginal costing.
parts.answer: $70,000 under both

parts.label: b
parts.text: Under absorption costing, calculate the sales volume variance and the fixed overhead volume variance.
parts.answer: Sales volume $5,600 A; fixed overhead volume $4,000 A

parts.label: c
parts.text: Under marginal costing, calculate the sales volume variance.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the actual profit and explain why both systems give the same actual profit in this case.
parts.answer: $60,400. Production equals sales, so no fixed overhead is carried forward in inventory; the absorption sales volume variance plus the fixed overhead volume variance (5,600 + 4,000) equals the marginal sales volume variance (9,600).
parts.working: B1 profit 9,200 × 12 − 50,000; B1 no inventory change; B1 variances reconcile.

practice.stem: A courier company in Nairobi uses standard costing for each delivery. Standard per delivery: fuel 0.6 litres at $1.80 per litre; driver time 0.25 hours at $10 per hour. In January it made 48,000 deliveries. Fuel used was 30,400 litres costing $53,200. Drivers worked 12,500 hours and were paid $122,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fuel price and fuel usage variances.
parts.answer: Price $1,520 F; usage $2,880 A

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the driver rate and driver efficiency variances.
parts.answer: Rate $2,500 F; efficiency $5,000 A

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare a statement reconciling the standard cost of the actual deliveries with the actual cost.
parts.answer: Standard cost of 48,000 deliveries 171,840; add adverse: fuel usage 2,880, driver efficiency 5,000; less favourable: fuel price 1,520, driver rate 2,500; actual cost 175,700
parts.working: B1 standard cost 171,840; B1 variances correctly signed; B1 actual 175,700.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one cause that could explain both adverse usage/efficiency variances.
parts.answer: Heavy traffic or road works: longer journeys use more fuel and take more driver time.

practice.stem: A furniture factory in Karachi reports an adverse material price variance and a favourable material usage variance for timber last month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two possible reasons for an adverse material price variance.
parts.answer: Any two: supplier raised prices / inflation; higher-quality material bought; loss of bulk discount; urgent purchase from a dearer supplier; exchange-rate changes on imports; standard set unrealistically low.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two possible reasons for a favourable material usage variance.
parts.answer: Any two: better-quality material with less waste; more skilled or careful workers; new or better-maintained machinery; improved production methods; standard set too loosely.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A clothing factory in Faisalabad bought cheaper fabric from a new supplier. Its variance report shows a favourable material price variance, an adverse material usage variance and an adverse labour efficiency variance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the decision to buy cheaper fabric could cause each of these three variances.
parts.answer: Cheaper fabric lowers the price paid → favourable material price variance (1). Lower quality causes more cutting waste and rejects → adverse material usage variance (1). Workers take longer handling poor fabric and re-cutting → adverse labour efficiency variance (1). The variances are interrelated, so the purchasing decision should be judged on the net effect (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

practice.stem: The owner of a biscuit factory in Lahore is considering introducing standard costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two benefits to a business of using standard costing.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: it gives targets for planning and budgeting; variances show where performance differs from plan so managers can act (management by exception); it helps control costs and motivate staff; it makes inventory valuation and pricing easier.
parts.working: 1 mark benefit; 1 mark explanation, × 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two limitations of standard costing.
parts.answer: Any two: standards are costly and time-consuming to set; they quickly become out of date; less suitable for one-off or service work; may demotivate if unrealistic; focus on cost may harm quality.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The production manager of a shoe factory in Sialkot is setting new labour standards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an ideal standard and an attainable standard.
parts.answer: An ideal standard assumes perfect conditions with no waste, idle time or breakdowns; an attainable standard allows for normal waste and inefficiency and can be achieved with reasonable effort.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which type of standard is more likely to motivate employees.
parts.answer: Attainable: workers can reach it with effort, so it is a realistic target; ideal standards are almost never met, so constant adverse variances demotivate.
parts.working: 1 mark choice; 1 mark reason.

practice.stem: A manager in a printing company in Lahore is pleased that his department has a large favourable labour rate variance because cheaper trainee staff were used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a favourable variance is not always good for the business.
parts.answer: A favourable variance may result from poor decisions elsewhere, e.g. cheaper materials (favourable price) causing waste and returns (1); it may mean the standard was set too loosely, hiding inefficiency (1); cost savings such as cutting maintenance or training may harm quality or future performance (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each point, max 3.

practice.stem: A furniture maker in Peshawar reports a favourable labour rate variance and an adverse labour efficiency variance for the same month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how one decision could have caused both variances.
parts.answer: Using less-skilled or trainee workers paid a lower rate gives a favourable rate variance (B1), but they work more slowly or need supervision (B1), so more hours are taken than standard, giving an adverse efficiency variance (B1).
parts.working: B1 cheaper labour; B1 slower working; B1 link to each variance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other possible cause of an adverse labour efficiency variance that is not linked to the rate paid.
parts.answer: Any one: machine breakdowns; poor-quality material; poor supervision; low morale; new product/learning time.

practice.stem: A company selling solar lanterns in Karachi reports a favourable sales volume variance and an adverse sales price variance for the quarter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two possible reasons for the adverse sales price variance.
parts.answer: Any two: price cut to win market share; discounts for bulk orders; competitors lowered prices; seasonal promotion.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two possible reasons for the favourable sales volume variance, other than a price change.
parts.answer: Any two: successful advertising; competitor left the market; higher demand due to power cuts; new retailer/distribution channel; better product quality.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A garment factory in Faisalabad has an adverse fixed overhead expenditure variance for the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two possible reasons for an adverse fixed overhead expenditure variance.
parts.answer: Any two: rent or rates increased; higher insurance premium; unexpected repairs; electricity standing charges rose; extra supervisory salaries.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the production manager may not be responsible for this variance.
parts.answer: Many fixed costs (rent, insurance, rates) are set by contracts or outside bodies and decided by senior management, so they are outside the production manager's control.
parts.working: 1 mark costs set externally/by others; 1 mark not controllable.

practice.stem: Hassan is setting up standard costing in his bicycle-parts workshop in Lahore.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'standard cost'.
parts.answer: A predetermined (planned) cost of producing one unit under expected efficient conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two sources of information Hassan could use to set the standard price of materials.
parts.answer: Any two: suppliers' price lists or quotations; past purchase invoices adjusted for inflation; trade discounts negotiated; forecasts of market prices.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two sources of information he could use to set the standard labour time per part.
parts.answer: Any two: time-and-motion (work) studies; past production records; trial runs; engineers' estimates; industry benchmarks.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The finance director of a soft-drinks bottler in Lahore says the business uses 'management by exception' with its monthly variance reports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by management by exception.
parts.answer: Managers compare actual results with standards and spend their time only on significant variances (exceptions), not on items that are close to standard.
parts.working: 1 mark compare with standard; 1 mark focus on significant variances.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two benefits of management by exception.
parts.answer: Any two: saves managers' time; focuses attention on problems; quicker corrective action; reduces information overload.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A packaging factory in Dubai has a favourable labour efficiency variance and an adverse labour rate variance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two possible reasons for the favourable labour efficiency variance.
parts.answer: Any two: more skilled/experienced workers; better machinery; good-quality materials; bonus scheme motivating faster work; better supervision.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two possible reasons for the adverse labour rate variance.
parts.answer: Any two: pay rise not built into the standard; overtime premium paid; higher-grade workers used; shortage of labour forcing higher wages.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Three months ago Ahmed Electricals switched to a cheaper supplier of copper wire. Quarterly variances since the change: material price $6,400 favourable; material usage $4,100 adverse; labour efficiency $3,200 adverse. Customer returns of faulty cables have risen from 1% to 4% of sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the production director whether the company should continue to buy from the new supplier. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Net effect of the three variances = 6,400 − 4,100 − 3,200 = $900 adverse each quarter, plus higher returns, so the company should probably return to the old supplier or renegotiate quality. Either decision accepted if justified.
parts.working: Calculation (max 2): net variance 6,400 F − 4,100 A − 3,200 A = 900 adverse. Continue (max 3): lower price saves $6,400; waste may fall as workers get used to the material; supplier might improve quality; standards could be revised. Return (max 3): extra waste and labour time outweigh the saving; customer returns up from 1% to 4% damage reputation and future sales; overtime and morale problems. Decision (1).

practice.stem: A company selling school shoes in Quetta raised its price from the standard $40 to $45. Its variance report shows a favourable sales price variance of $27,000 and an adverse sales volume variance of $33,600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the sales price variance and the sales volume variance might be linked.
parts.answer: Raising the price to $45 gives a favourable price variance on each unit sold (1). Customers are price-sensitive, so fewer units are sold than budgeted (1), causing an adverse sales volume variance (1). Other reasons for the volume fall, e.g. a competitor's new product, should also be considered before judging the sales manager (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

practice.stem: A company that makes ceiling fans in Gujrat uses standard costing and wants to hold managers responsible only for costs they control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of these variances, state the manager most likely to be responsible and give a reason: material price, material usage, labour rate, sales volume.
parts.answer: Material price – purchasing manager (chooses suppliers and negotiates prices). Material usage – production manager (controls waste in the factory). Labour rate – HR/personnel manager (sets pay and grades of staff). Sales volume – sales/marketing manager (responsible for the number of units sold).
parts.working: 1 mark each (manager with reason).

practice.stem: A juice factory in Multan had delays in fruit deliveries in August. Its variance report shows an adverse labour efficiency variance and an adverse fixed overhead volume variance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a problem with materials could cause an adverse labour efficiency variance.
parts.answer: Poor-quality or late material (1) means workers waste time waiting, re-working or handling rejects (1), so more hours are worked than the standard allows for the output (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each step.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what an adverse fixed overhead volume variance shows.
parts.answer: Actual output was lower than budgeted output (1), so less fixed overhead was absorbed than budgeted — the fixed costs were spread over fewer units (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A textile mill in Karachi had an adverse labour rate variance of $1,800 last month; the standard labour cost of actual output was $45,000. The new manager wants employees to help set next year's standards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate variance as a percentage of the standard labour cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which involving employees in setting standards may affect their behaviour.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: staff feel ownership so are more motivated to meet the standard; standards are more realistic because staff know the work; but staff may build in slack (easy standards) to earn bonuses; discussions take time and may cause conflict.
parts.working: 1 mark point; 1 mark explanation, × 2.

practice.stem: A shoe factory in Kasur introduced a bonus for production workers: every worker who makes more pairs than the standard in a week receives a bonus of 10% of their weekly wage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the likely effect of the bonus scheme on (i) the labour rate variance, (ii) the labour efficiency variance and (iii) the material usage variance.
parts.answer: (i) Adverse: bonus payments increase the actual rate per hour above standard (B1) unless the bonus is in the standard (B1). (ii) Favourable: workers work faster to earn the bonus, fewer hours per pair (B1 B1). (iii) Possibly adverse: rushing causes more mistakes and wasted leather (B1), so more material is used per pair (B1).
parts.working: 2 marks for each of (i), (ii), (iii): direction + reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the factory could stop the bonus scheme from harming quality.
parts.answer: Pay the bonus only on pairs that pass quality inspection (or deduct for rejects).

practice.stem:
Rose Textiles, Karachi, investigates a variance when it is more than 5% of the related standard cost. The material usage variance for dyed cotton over four months was:
Month       Variance $   Standard material cost $
January        900 A                    30,000
February     1,240 A                    31,000
March        1,680 A                    32,000
April        2,170 A                    31,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the variance as a percentage of standard material cost for each month, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: January 3.00%; February 4.00%; March 5.25%; April 7.00%
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The policy would first investigate the variance in March. Advise the management accountant whether it should have been investigated earlier. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The variance is adverse every month and rising steadily (3% → 7%), which shows a persistent trend rather than random fluctuation; small adverse variances that grow suggest a developing problem (e.g. machine wear, poor material). It should have been investigated in February when the trend became clear, even though below 5%; the cost of investigating early is small compared with continued losses. A rule based only on size ignores trends.
parts.working: 1 mark trend; 1 mark persistent vs random; 1 mark cost/benefit; 1 mark justified advice.

practice.stem:
The management accountant of a dairy in Multan must decide whether to investigate two adverse variances. Each investigation costs $1,200.
Variance            Chance the cause can be corrected   Saving if corrected
Material usage                    40%                        $4,500
Labour efficiency                 25%                        $3,600

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected benefit of investigating each variance and the expected net benefit after the cost of investigation.
parts.answer: Material usage: expected saving $1,800, net benefit $600. Labour efficiency: expected saving $900, net cost $300.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the management accountant which variance(s) to investigate. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Investigate material usage: expected net benefit $600. On these figures do not investigate labour efficiency (expected net cost $300), unless the probability or savings are underestimated, the variance is recurring (savings in future months too) or it links to quality/safety problems.
parts.working: 1 mark each decision with figures; 1 mark qualification (recurring savings/non-financial).

practice.stem: A soap manufacturer in Lahore set a standard price of $8.00 per kg for palm oil 18 months ago. Since then the market price of palm oil has risen by 8%. Last month the purchasing manager bought 21,000 kg at $8.75 per kg. The directors want to reduce the purchasing manager's bonus because of the large adverse price variance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the material price variance using the original standard.
parts.answer: $15,750 adverse

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard price updated for the 8% market rise, and the price variance against this updated standard.
parts.answer: $8.64 per kg; $2,310 adverse

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should reduce the purchasing manager's bonus. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Most of the variance ($13,440 of $15,750) is caused by the out-of-date standard and market prices outside the manager's control, so it would be unfair to penalise for it; only $2,310 is controllable, which is about 1.3% of cost and may reflect urgent purchases or quality. Standards should be revised. A small reduction might be justified only if the $2,310 was due to poor buying. Decision with reason.
parts.working: 1 mark uncontrollable portion with figure; 1 mark controllable portion; 1 mark need to revise standards/motivation; 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem:
Atlas Engineering, Rawalpindi, pays a bonus to the department manager whose controllable variances are best. Material prices are the responsibility of the central purchasing department. Last month's variances:
Variance              Machining dept $   Assembly dept $
Material price             3,000 A             1,100 A
Material usage             1,800 F             1,500 A
Labour rate                  400 A             2,600 F
Labour efficiency          2,400 F             3,900 A
Labour rates are set by each department manager, who chooses which grade of worker to use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net total variance for each department, and the net controllable variance for each department manager.
parts.answer: Totals: Machining $800 F; Assembly $3,900 A. Controllable (excluding material price): Machining $3,800 F; Assembly $2,800 A.
parts.working: B1 each figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors which manager should receive the bonus. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Machining: its controllable variances are $3,800 F, and the adverse price variance is the purchasing department's responsibility. Assembly saved on wages by using cheaper staff (2,600 F) but lost more through slower work and waste (5,400 A). The machining manager should receive the bonus; check that favourable variances were not achieved by cutting quality.
parts.working: 1 mark controllability; 1 mark analysis of assembly trade-off; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Siddiqui Tools makes 10,000 drills a year. Skilled workers are paid $18 per hour and take 2 hours per drill. Semi-skilled workers would be paid $14 per hour but would take 2.4 hours per drill, and material waste would rise by 3% of the $30 standard material cost per drill.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should replace the skilled workers with semi-skilled workers. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Relevant cost per drill (labour plus extra material): skilled 2 × 18 = $36.00; semi-skilled 2.4 × 14 = $33.60 plus extra material 3% × 30 = $0.90 = $34.50. Saving $1.50 per drill, $15,000 a year. A justified decision either way.
parts.working: Calculations (max 3): skilled 36.00; semi-skilled 34.50; annual saving 15,000. For (max 2): lower costs improve profit; trained over time the semi-skilled workers may reach the standard time. Against (max 3): 20% more labour hours are needed per drill (2.4 v 2), so the same hours give about 17% less output (an extra 4,000 hours a year for 10,000 drills) – may not meet demand; quality and reputation risk; redundancy costs and staff morale; adverse labour efficiency and material usage variances against the current standards. Decision (1).

practice.stem: A factory in Gujrat makes 12,000 ceramic sinks a year. Each sink currently uses 4 kg of clay at $6.00 per kg and 1.5 labour hours at $15 per hour. A cheaper clay costs $5.20 per kg, but each sink would need 4.5 kg and 1.6 labour hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the material and labour cost per unit using (i) the current material and (ii) the cheaper material.
parts.working: M1 current; M1 new; A1 both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: If the standards are not changed, calculate the material price, material usage and labour efficiency variances that the cheaper material would cause for 12,000 units.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State, with a reason, whether the company should change to the cheaper material.
parts.answer: No: the net effect is $10,800 adverse a year (= 12,000 × $0.90), so costs rise despite the lower price.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark reason using figures.

practice.stem:
Yousaf Plastics investigates any variance greater than 5% of the standard cost to which it relates. Last month's variances:
Variance                      Amount $  F/A  Standard cost $
Material price                   2,300    F           40,000
Material usage                     900    A           40,000
Labour rate                      3,100    A           62,000
Labour efficiency                4,400    A           62,000
Fixed overhead expenditure       1,200    F           30,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the management accountant which variances should be investigated. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Percentages of standard cost: Material price 5.75%; Material usage 2.25%; Labour rate 5.00%; Labour efficiency 7.10%; Fixed overhead expenditure 4.00%. Under the 5% rule investigate material price (5.75%) and labour efficiency (7.10%); labour rate is exactly 5% so borderline.
parts.working: Calculations (max 3): percentages as shown. Points (max 3): material price is favourable but large — may be linked to cheaper material, and to the adverse labour efficiency (poor material slows workers); labour rate at 5% and adverse — check if it is a trend; small variances such as material usage cost more to investigate than they would save; consider trends over several months, controllability and cost of investigation versus benefit. Clear conclusion (1).

practice.stem: Malik Packaging installed a new cutting machine seven months ago. Since then the material usage variance has been adverse by about 8% of standard material cost every month. Production staff say the machine design wastes more card than the old one and complain that their bonus, which depends on meeting the standard, is never paid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether the material usage standard should be revised. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A justified recommendation, e.g. revise the standard to an attainable level, because the adverse variance is permanent (caused by the new machine) and is demotivating staff, while keeping a target that encourages improvement.
parts.working: Revise (max 4): adverse usage variance of about 8% every month for six months shows the standard is out of date; the cause (new machine design) is outside workers' control; unrealistic standards demotivate and make variance reports useless; budgets and prices based on the old standard understate costs. Do not revise (max 3): the machine may be adjusted or staff trained to reduce waste; revising too easily builds in inefficiency; cost and time of setting new standards; supplier may be responsible. Decision (1).

practice.stem: A kitchenware factory in Gujrat received a rush order for 800 cooking pots at $70 each. Standard variable cost per pot: materials $20; labour 2 hours × $12 = $24; variable overhead $4. To finish on time all 1,600 labour hours had to be worked as overtime, paid at time-and-a-half. All other costs were at standard. The production manager is now being criticised for a large adverse labour rate variance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate variance caused by the order.
parts.answer: $9,600 adverse

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard contribution from the order and the actual contribution after the overtime premium.
parts.answer: Standard contribution $17,600; actual contribution $8,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether the production manager should be blamed for the variance. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The order still added $8,000 of contribution, so accepting it was profitable; the overtime was a planned consequence of the sales decision, not inefficiency. The variance should be reported separately or charged to the sales department that accepted the deadline. However, if overtime could have been avoided by better scheduling, part of the cost is controllable. Possible goodwill with the customer. Decision: do not blame the production manager.
parts.working: 1 mark contribution still positive; 1 mark controllability/responsibility; 1 mark other factor; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: To reduce costs, the managers of a bottling plant in Karachi cut the machine maintenance budget for the quarter, which gave a favourable fixed overhead expenditure variance of $6,000. During the quarter machine breakdowns caused 420 extra labour hours (standard rate $15 per hour; variable overhead absorbed at $5 per labour hour) and 650 kg of extra material scrap (standard price $4 per kg).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the adverse variances caused by the breakdowns, naming each variance.
parts.answer: Labour efficiency $6,300 A; variable overhead efficiency $2,100 A; material usage $2,600 A
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net effect on profit of the decision to cut maintenance.
parts.answer: $5,000 worse (adverse)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the managers whether they should keep the reduced maintenance budget. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: No: the $6,000 saving is outweighed by $11,000 of extra costs, giving a net loss of $5,000; further risks include late deliveries, lost customers, safety hazards and shorter machine life. Variances should be read together, not individually; a favourable variance is not always good. Possibly reinstate planned preventive maintenance.
parts.working: 1 mark net figure; 1 mark interrelated variances; 1 mark non-financial; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: A maker of electric fans in Gujrat uses standard marginal costing. The budget is 6,000 fans a quarter at $80, with a standard variable cost of $50 per fan. The sales director proposes cutting the price to $74 and expects sales to rise to 7,200 fans. Fixed costs would not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sales price variance and the sales volume variance that would arise if the forecast is achieved.
parts.answer: Sales price $43,200 adverse; sales volume $36,000 favourable

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in total contribution, and the number of fans that must be sold at $74 to earn the same contribution as the budget.
parts.answer: Contribution falls by $7,200; 7,500 fans needed

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the sales director whether to cut the price. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: On the forecast, contribution falls by $7,200, so the cut should not go ahead unless at least 7,500 fans can be sold; higher volume also needs more production capacity, working capital and labour. For: may gain market share long-term and win repeat customers; competitors may also cut prices. Decision justified.
parts.working: 1 mark use of figures; 1 mark break-even volume; 1 mark other factor; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: TechCase Ltd, Shenzhen, makes phone cases. Most production is done by automated machines, labour is a small part of cost, and each design is sold for only about six months before being replaced. The company uses total quality management and buys materials just in time. A director suggests stopping standard costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether TechCase Ltd should continue to use standard costing. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: standards take time to set and quickly go out of date with short product lives; labour variances matter little when machines do the work; TQM aims at continuous improvement, not just meeting a standard; JIT means price variances from bulk buying are less relevant; variance reports may come too late. For: still useful for material cost control, pricing new designs, budgeting and spotting problems; standards can be updated more often or combined with non-financial measures (defect rates, delivery times). Decision justified, e.g. keep a simplified, regularly updated system.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks against, up to 2 for, 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: A tile factory in Gujranwala is choosing between two labour standards for laying a batch of tiles: an ideal standard of 2.0 hours per batch (no breaks, no machine stoppages) and an attainable standard of 2.2 hours per batch. Last month 10,000 batches took 22,500 hours, paid at the standard rate of $15 per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour efficiency variance using each standard.
parts.answer: Ideal $37,500 adverse; attainable $7,500 adverse

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the factory which standard it should use. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Attainable: a variance of $7,500 A (about 2.3%) shows workers were close to a realistic target, so it is useful for control and motivation. Ideal: permanent large adverse variances ($37,500) may demotivate staff and make it hard to see real problems; but it shows the maximum possible improvement. Decision: attainable standard, perhaps reviewing it regularly towards the ideal.
parts.working: 1 mark each standard with figure; 1 mark motivation; 1 mark decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The partners of Hilltop Traders, Quetta, agree to value goodwill at two years' purchase of the average profit of the last three years. Profits were: year 1 $84,000; year 2 $96,000; year 3 $105,000.
What is the value of goodwill?
A $95,000
B $190,000
C $210,000
D $285,000
parts.working: Average profit = (84,000 + 96,000 + 105,000) ÷ 3 = $95,000; × 2 years = $190,000. A is the average only; C uses the latest year; D is the total of three years.

practice.stem:
Jabbar and Sons, a partnership of opticians in Peshawar, made these profits:
Year  Profit $  Weight
2023    72,000       1
2024    81,000       2
2025    90,000       3
The partners agree to value goodwill at three years' purchase of the weighted average profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the weighted average profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of goodwill.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two factors that may give a business goodwill.
parts.answer: For example: a good reputation; a loyal customer base.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: reputation; loyal customers; good location; skilled staff; brand name; good supplier relationships.

practice.stem: Usman, Vania and Waleed are partners sharing profits 2:2:1. Waleed retires on 30 June 2026. Goodwill is valued at $45,000. The partners decide that a goodwill account will be opened and kept in the books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the goodwill. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer:
Dr $    Cr $
Goodwill          45,000
Capital – Usman           18,000
Capital – Vania           18,000
Capital – Waleed           9,000
parts.working: Dr goodwill 45,000 (B1); Cr capitals in the old ratio 2:2:1 (M1): 18,000, 18,000, 9,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many businesses do not keep a goodwill account in the books after a change of partners.
parts.answer: Goodwill generated inside the business cannot be measured reliably, so IAS 38 does not allow internally generated goodwill to be recognised as an asset; it is written off to the partners' capital accounts.
parts.working: 1 mark: value is subjective / cannot be measured reliably / can change quickly. 1 mark: accounting standards (IAS 38) / prudence do not allow internally generated goodwill to be shown.

practice.stem: Kamran and Laila run a bakery in Islamabad, sharing profits equally. On 1 April 2026 Mehwish is admitted for a one-quarter share of profits; Kamran and Laila will share the remaining three-quarters equally. Goodwill is valued at $72,000 and is not to be recorded in the books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an adjustment for goodwill is needed when a new partner is admitted.
parts.answer: The old partners built up the goodwill; without an adjustment the new partner would share in the value they created, so the old partners must be compensated for the share they give up.
parts.working: 1 mark: goodwill was created by the existing partners. 1 mark: new partner gains a share of it / old partners lose part of their share and must be compensated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net amount credited or debited to each partner's capital account for goodwill.
parts.answer: Kamran credit $9,000; Laila credit $9,000; Mehwish debit $18,000.
parts.working: New ratio K:L:M = 3/8 : 3/8 : 2/8. Kamran: +36,000 created − 27,000 written off = +9,000 (B1). Laila: same, +9,000 (B1). Mehwish: −72,000 × 1/4 = −18,000 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare a single journal entry to record the net goodwill adjustment. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer:
Dr $   Cr $
Capital – Mehwish  18,000
Capital – Kamran           9,000
Capital – Laila            9,000
parts.working: Dr Mehwish 18,000 (1); Cr Kamran 9,000 and Laila 9,000 (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Mughal and Noor share profits 3:1. Sadia is admitted and the new profit-sharing ratio is Mughal 2 : Noor 1 : Sadia 1. Goodwill is valued at $36,000. A goodwill account is created and then written off, so that no goodwill account remains. What is the entry in Sadia's capital account?
A Debit $9,000
B Credit $9,000
C Debit $12,000
D Debit $18,000
parts.answer: A Debit $9,000
parts.working: When goodwill is written off it is debited to all partners in the new ratio: 36,000 × 1/4 = 9,000 debit for Sadia. She receives no credit because she was not a partner when the goodwill was created. C uses 1/3 and D uses 1/2, neither of which is her new share; B reverses the side.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Ali and Bilal share profits 3:2. Chand is admitted and the new ratio is Ali 2, Bilal 2, Chand 1. Goodwill is valued at $60,000 but no goodwill account is to remain in the books.
What is the net effect of the goodwill adjustment on Ali's capital account?
A credit $12,000
B debit $12,000
C credit $36,000
D no change
parts.answer: A credit $12,000
parts.working: Goodwill created in old ratio: Ali credited 3/5 × 60,000 = 36,000. Written off in new ratio: Ali debited 2/5 × 60,000 = 24,000. Net credit $12,000. D is Bilal's position (24,000 − 24,000 = 0), not Ali's.

practice.stem:
Sana and Tariq run a furniture business in Faisalabad, sharing profits and losses 3:2. Their capital account balances on 31 December 2025 were Sana $80,000 and Tariq $60,000.
On 1 January 2026 Umar was admitted as a partner and paid $50,000 into the business bank account as his capital. It was agreed that:
1 land would be revalued from $120,000 to $150,000
2 inventory would be written down by $4,000
3 goodwill would be valued at $45,000; no goodwill account would be kept in the books
4 the new profit sharing ratio would be Sana 2, Tariq 2, Umar 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the revaluation account.
parts.answer:
Revaluation account                      $
Dr
Inventory                            4,000
Profit on revaluation: Sana (3/5)   15,600
                       Tariq (2/5)  10,400
                                    30,000
Cr
Land                                30,000
                                    30,000
parts.working: Dr inventory 4,000 (1); Cr land 30,000 and profit 26,000 shared 3:2, Sana 15,600 and Tariq 10,400 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the partners' capital accounts in columnar form, showing the balances carried down on 1 January 2026.
parts.answer:
Capital accounts                 Sana   Tariq    Umar
Dr
Goodwill written off (2:2:1)   18,000  18,000   9,000
Balance c/d                   104,600  70,400  41,000
                              122,600  88,400  50,000
Cr
Balance b/d                    80,000  60,000
Bank                                           50,000
Revaluation profit             15,600  10,400
Goodwill created (3:2)         27,000  18,000
                              122,600  88,400  50,000
parts.working: B1 opening balances and bank; B1 revaluation profit 15,600/10,400; B1 goodwill created 27,000/18,000; B1 goodwill written off 18,000/18,000/9,000; B1 each correct closing balance (max 2): Sana 104,600, Tariq 70,400, Umar 41,000.

practice.stem: Rafay, Saad and Zoya are partners in a software firm in Lahore, sharing profits 4:3:3. Saad retires on 31 August 2026. Rafay and Zoya will continue, sharing profits equally. Goodwill is valued at $90,000. No goodwill account is to appear in the books; the adjustment is to be made through the capital accounts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net goodwill adjustment for each partner, stating whether it is a debit or a credit.
parts.answer: Rafay debit $9,000; Zoya debit $18,000; Saad credit $27,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the adjustment, including a narrative.
parts.answer:
Dr $    Cr $
Capital – Rafay   9,000
Capital – Zoya   18,000
Capital – Saad           27,000
Narrative: adjustment for Saad's share of goodwill on his retirement; no goodwill account kept.
parts.working: Debits (1); credit (1); narrative (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Xavier and Yusra share profits 3:2. Zain is admitted and the new ratio is Xavier 2, Yusra 1, Zain 1. On admission the building is revalued upwards by $40,000 and machinery downwards by $15,000.
What is the entry in Yusra's capital account for the revaluation?
A credit $6,250
B credit $10,000
C credit $16,000
D debit $6,000
parts.answer: B credit $10,000
parts.working: Net revaluation profit 25,000 belongs to the old partners in the old ratio: Yusra 2/5 × 25,000 = 10,000 credit. A wrongly uses the new ratio (1/4); C ignores the machinery loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A partnership has capital employed of $625,000. A normal return for this type of business is 8% a year. Average annual profit is $90,000. Goodwill is valued at three years' purchase of the super profit. What is the value of goodwill?
A $50,000
B $120,000
C $150,000
D $270,000
parts.working: Normal profit 8% × 625,000 = 50,000; super profit 90,000 − 50,000 = 40,000; × 3 = 120,000. D (270,000) uses total profit, not super profit; C multiplies the normal profit.

practice.stem:
Farah, Gul and Hina are partners in a travel agency in Karachi, sharing profits and losses 2:2:1. Hina retired on 31 December 2025. On that date the balances were:
Capital accounts: Farah $70,000; Gul $60,000; Hina $40,000
Current accounts: Farah $5,000 credit; Gul $3,000 debit; Hina $6,500 credit
It was agreed that:
1 premises would be revalued upwards by $25,000 and office equipment downwards by $5,000
2 goodwill was valued at $50,000; no goodwill account would remain in the books
3 Hina's current account would be transferred to her capital account
4 Hina would receive $20,000 in cash immediately and the rest of the amount due to her would be transferred to a loan account
5 Farah and Gul would share profits equally in future.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the capital accounts of Farah, Gul and Hina in columnar form on 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Capital accounts             Farah     Gul    Hina
Dr
Goodwill written off (1:1)  25,000  25,000
Bank                                        20,000
Hina loan account                           40,500
Balance c/d                 73,000  63,000
                            98,000  88,000  60,500
Cr
Balance b/d                 70,000  60,000  40,000
Current account                              6,500
Revaluation profit (2:2:1)   8,000   8,000   4,000
Goodwill created (2:2:1)    20,000  20,000  10,000
                            98,000  88,000  60,500
parts.working: Revaluation profit = 25,000 − 5,000 = 20,000 shared 2:2:1 (B1). Goodwill created 20,000/20,000/10,000 (B1); written off 25,000/25,000 (B1). Current account transfer 6,500 (B1). Bank 20,000 and loan 40,500 (B1). Closing balances Farah 73,000 and Gul 63,000 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the balance on Hina's loan account.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the partners agreed to transfer part of the amount due to Hina to a loan account.
parts.answer: Paying the full amount in cash at once would leave the business short of working capital.
parts.working: Any one: protects the bank balance / liquidity; avoids selling assets; gives time to raise finance.

practice.stem:
Nadia and Omar own a wholesale rice business in Hyderabad, sharing profits 3:1. Their capitals on 31 March 2026 were Nadia $90,000 and Omar $50,000.
On 1 April 2026 Pervez was admitted. He brought in $30,000 cash and a delivery vehicle valued at $18,000 as his capital. It was agreed that:
1 premises would be revalued from $160,000 to $200,000
2 inventory, shown at $42,000, would be reduced to its net realisable value of $38,500
3 a provision for doubtful debts of 5% would be created on trade receivables of $30,000
4 goodwill was valued at $64,000; it would not be kept in the books
5 the new profit sharing ratio would be Nadia 2, Omar 1, Pervez 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the revaluation account.
parts.answer:
Revaluation account                $
Dr
Inventory                      3,500
Provision for doubtful debts   1,500
Profit: Nadia (3/4)           26,250
        Omar (1/4)             8,750

parts.working: Dr inventory 3,500 and provision 1,500 (1); Cr premises 40,000 (1); profit 35,000 shared 3:1, Nadia 26,250, Omar 8,750 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the capital accounts of all three partners in columnar form on 1 April 2026.
parts.answer:
Capital accounts                Nadia    Omar  Pervez

Goodwill written off (2:1:1)   32,000  16,000  16,000

Balance b/d                    90,000  50,000
Bank                                           30,000
Vehicle                                        18,000
Revaluation profit             26,250   8,750
Goodwill created (3:1)         48,000  16,000
                              164,250  74,750  48,000
parts.working: B1 Pervez's cash and vehicle; B1 revaluation profit; B1 goodwill created 48,000/16,000; B1 goodwill written off 32,000/16,000/16,000; B1 closing balances Nadia 132,250, Omar 58,750, Pervez 32,000.

practice.stem:
Daud and Esha have shared profits equally in their pharmacy in Multan. From 1 July 2026 they agree to share profits Daud 3, Esha 2, because Daud will work full time. Capital balances on 30 June 2026: Daud $50,000; Esha $45,000.
It is agreed that goodwill is worth $80,000 (not to be kept in the books) and that the shop property is revalued upwards by $20,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a goodwill adjustment is needed even though no partner is joining or leaving.
parts.answer: Daud gains an extra 1/10 share of future profits, including profits from goodwill built up jointly; Esha gives up that share and must be compensated by Daud.
parts.working: 1 mark: change in ratio transfers a share of goodwill. 1 mark: the gaining partner compensates the losing partner.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance on each partner's capital account after the adjustments.

practice.stem: Imran retired from a partnership of engineers in Rawalpindi on 31 December 2025. The amount due to him was $84,000. He received $24,000 in cash on that date. The balance became a loan, repaid in three equal annual instalments starting on 31 December 2026. Interest at 8% per annum on the balance outstanding during each year is paid with each instalment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of each loan instalment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total amount (instalment plus interest) paid to Imran on 31 December 2026, 2027 and 2028.

parts.label: c

parts.label: a

Before any adjustments her capital account had a credit balance of $60,000 and her current account a debit balance of $4,500. Goodwill is valued at $90,000 and a revaluation of assets shows a net gain of $15,000. Both are credited to the old partners. How much is due to Rida on retirement?
A $80,500
B $90,500
C $95,000
D $99,500
parts.working: 60,000 − 4,500 (debit current account reduces amount due) + goodwill 30,000 + revaluation 5,000 = 90,500. D adds the debit balance instead of deducting it; C ignores the current account.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Jamil and Kiran share residual profits equally. Profit for the year was $96,000. Jamil receives a salary of $12,000. Interest on capital is 6% per annum; capitals are Jamil $50,000 and Kiran $70,000.
What is Kiran's total share of the profit?
A $38,400
B $42,600
C $48,000
D $48,600
parts.working: Interest on capital: Jamil 3,000, Kiran 4,200. Residual = 96,000 − 12,000 − 7,200 = 76,800; half = 38,400. Kiran's total = 4,200 + 38,400 = 42,600. A omits interest on capital; D forgets to deduct Jamil's salary.

• a salary for Yasmin of $9,000 a year

practice.stem:

parts.label: b

parts.working: 1 mark each for two points: discourages drawings / protects working capital; fairness between partners who draw different amounts or at different times.

parts.answer: The loan is not part of Hamid's capital; the business owes it as a lender would be owed, so the interest is an expense charged in the statement of profit or loss before profit is calculated.

parts.label: a

In a partnership, which change would reduce the residual profit shared between the partners?
A an increase in the rate of interest charged on drawings
B an increase in the salaries paid to partners
C repayment of a loan made to the business by a partner
D a decrease in the rate of interest allowed on capital
parts.answer: B an increase in the salaries paid to partners
parts.working: Salaries are deducted before residual profit, so higher salaries reduce it. A and D increase residual profit; C removes loan interest expense, raising profit.

parts.label: a

A interest on partners' capital
B interest on a loan made to the business by a partner
C salary paid to a partner
D interest charged on partners' drawings
parts.answer: B interest on a loan made to the business by a partner

parts.text:
There is no partnership agreement. On 1 July a partner lent the business $40,000. The year end is 31 December. What is the interest on the loan for the year and where is it shown?

B $1,000 in the appropriation account
C $2,000 in the statement of profit or loss
D No interest is due
parts.answer: A $1,000 in the statement of profit or loss
parts.working: The Partnership Act allows 5% a year on partners' loans: 40,000 × 5% × 6/12 = 1,000. It is an expense of the business (statement of profit or loss), not an appropriation of profit (B).
