practice.subtopic: Partnership statement of profit or loss
practice.stem:
Quratulain and Rashid run a printing and design studio in Karachi, sharing residual profits equally. Information for the year ended 31 December 2025:
                                                $
Fees from customers                       186,000
Inventory of materials 1 January 2025       3,200
Purchases of materials                     40,300
Inventory of materials 31 December 2025     2,500
Staff wages                                48,000
Rent paid                                  15,600
Electricity                                 7,400
Insurance paid                              3,600
Printers: carrying amount 1 January 2025   36,000
Loan from Rashid (since 1 January 2025)    20,000
Additional information:
1 rent of $1,300 is owing
2 insurance paid includes $900 for 2026
3 printers are depreciated at 25% per annum using the reducing balance method
4 Rashid's loan carries interest at 7% per annum; none has been paid
5 interest on capital is 5% per annum: capitals Quratulain $50,000, Rashid $30,000
6 Quratulain receives a salary of $12,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Statement of profit or loss                           $         $
Fees                                                      186,000
Cost of materials used (3,200 + 40,300 − 2,500)          (41,000)
                                                          145,000
Staff wages                                      48,000
Rent (15,600 + 1,300)                            16,900
Electricity                                       7,400
Insurance (3,600 − 900)                           2,700
Depreciation – printers                           9,000
Loan interest – Rashid                            1,400
Total expenses                                           (85,400)
Profit for the year                                        59,600
parts.working: B1 materials used 41,000; B1 rent 16,900 and insurance 2,700; B1 depreciation 9,000; B1 loan interest 1,400 as an expense; B1 profit 59,600.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the appropriation account for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Appropriation account                   $
Profit for the year                59,600
Interest on capital: Quratulain   (2,500)
                     Rashid       (1,500)
Salary: Quratulain               (12,000)
Residual profit                    43,600
Quratulain (1/2)                   21,800
Rashid (1/2)                       21,800
parts.working: B1 interest on capital; B1 salary; B1 residual 43,600 shared 21,800 each (own figure rule).

practice.subtopic: Partnership statement of profit or loss
practice.stem:
Rizwan and Qadir shared profits equally in a bookshop in Peshawar. On 1 May 2025 Sumbal was admitted; from then profits were shared Rizwan 2 : Qadir 2 : Sumbal 1. Data for the year ended 31 December 2025:
Revenue $420,000, earned evenly through the year; gross profit is 35% of revenue.
Rent $36,000 and depreciation $12,000 accrue evenly.
Wages were $9,000 for January–April and $15,000 for May–December (an extra assistant was hired).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the profit for each of the two periods of the year.
parts.answer:
1 Jan–30 Apr $  1 May–31 Dec $
Gross profit (35% of revenue)                 49,000          98,000
Rent and depreciation (time basis)            16,000          32,000
Wages (actual)                                 9,000          15,000
Profit                                        24,000          51,000
parts.working: B1 revenue split; B1 GP; B1 time-based expenses; B1 wages actual; A1 A1 profits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Rizwan's total share of profit for the year.
parts.answer: First period ½ × 24,000 = 12,000; second period ⅖ × 51,000 = 20,400; total $32,400
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the profit must be split at the date of admission.
parts.answer: Profits earned before 1 May belong only to the old partners in their old ratio; after admission profits are shared in the new ratio, including Sumbal.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Partnership statement of profit or loss
practice.stem:
Tahir and Usama run an electronics shop in Rawalpindi. Draft profit for the year is $118,000. Errors found:
1 Closing inventory includes phones at cost $9,200; they are outdated and will sell for $8,000 with selling costs of $600.
2 Tahir took goods costing $700 for his own use; no entry was made.
3 Insurance of $2,000 on Tahir's private car was charged to motor expenses.
4 Usama lent the firm $24,000 at the start of the year; no interest has been recorded and there is no agreement on interest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year.
parts.answer:
$
Draft profit                                         118,000
1 Inventory written down to NRV (9,200 − 7,400)      (1,800)
2 Goods taken by partner (purchases reduced)             700
3 Private car insurance removed from expenses (drawings)               2,000
4 Loan interest owing (5% × 24,000)                  (1,200)
Corrected profit                                     117,700
parts.working: 1 mark each adjustment; 1 mark final figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The partners share residual profit 3:1 and there are no other appropriations. Calculate the change in each partner's share caused by the corrections.
parts.answer: Change in profit (300): Tahir ¾ = (225); Usama ¼ = (75)
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the accounting concept applied in item 1.
parts.answer: Prudence (inventory at lower of cost and net realisable value).

practice.subtopic: Partnership statement of profit or loss
practice.stem: Vaqar and Wajiha run a printing works in Hyderabad. Profit before depreciation and before any disposal adjustment is $74,500, and rent received of $6,000 for sub-letting part of the premises has not yet been included. At 1 July 2025 machinery cost $90,000, accumulated depreciation $30,000. Machinery is depreciated at 25% per annum on the reducing balance, calculated monthly. On 1 January 2026 a machine that had cost $20,000 (accumulated depreciation at 1 July 2025 $16,000) was sold for $2,500. The year end is 30 June 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation on the machine sold, for the period up to the date of sale.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss on disposal.
parts.answer: Carrying amount at sale 4,000 − 500 = 3,500; proceeds 2,500 → loss $1,000
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation on the remaining machines for the year.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year.
parts.working: M1 A1 own figures.

practice.stem: Asma and Bushra started a partnership without a written partnership agreement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four provisions of the Partnership Act 1890 that will apply to their partnership.
parts.answer: Profits and losses are shared equally; no interest is allowed on capital; no interest is charged on drawings; no salaries are paid to partners; interest of 5% per annum is paid on partners' loans.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of the five provisions listed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the partners should draw up a written partnership agreement.
parts.answer: So that terms such as profit sharing, salaries and interest suit their different capital and work contributions, and to avoid disputes later.
parts.working: 1 mark: tailor terms to contributions (capital, time, skills). 1 mark: reduce disputes / clear rules for admission, retirement, dissolution.

practice.stem: Ayesha and Bilqees plan to open a tailoring business in Karachi together. A friend tells them they should 'get everything in writing'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four matters that should be covered in a written partnership agreement.
parts.answer: Any four of: capital each partner contributes; profit- and loss-sharing ratio; interest on capital (rate); interest on drawings; partners' salaries; limits on drawings; interest on partners' loans; how goodwill is valued on admission/retirement; procedure for admission, retirement or death; settling disputes; dissolution.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

practice.stem: Chaudhry and Dar run a transport business in Multan. Chaudhry invested most of the capital and Dar manages the day-to-day work.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a partnership agreement may give interest on capital.
parts.answer: To reward partners who invest more capital, compensating them for the return they could earn elsewhere; it is fairer than sharing all profit in a fixed ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark reward for capital; 1 mark fairness/opportunity cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a partnership agreement may give a salary to one partner.
parts.answer: To reward a partner who works more hours or has more responsibility in the business than the others.
parts.working: 1 mark reward for work; 1 mark unequal effort.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a partnership agreement may charge interest on drawings.
parts.answer: To discourage partners from taking out cash early or in large amounts, and to be fair to partners who leave their money in the business.
parts.working: 1 mark discourage; 1 mark fairness.

practice.stem: Ejaz, Farooq and Gohar run a carpet business in Lahore without a written agreement. Assume the rules of the Partnership Act 1890 apply where there is no agreement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the rule of the Partnership Act 1890 that applies to each of the following when there is no agreement: (i) sharing of profits and losses; (ii) interest on capital; (iii) partners' salaries; (iv) interest on drawings; (v) interest on loans made by a partner.
parts.answer: (i) Shared equally. (ii) No interest on capital. (iii) No salaries. (iv) No interest charged on drawings. (v) Interest at 5% per annum.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Hamza and Iqbal have run a grocery shop in Bahawalpur for three years with no partnership agreement. They are arguing about last year's profit. Assume the rules of the Partnership Act 1890 apply where there is no agreement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each statement, state whether the partner is correct and explain your answer.
1 Hamza: 'I put in twice as much capital as Iqbal, so I should get twice his share of profit.'
2 Iqbal: 'I work full time, so I am entitled to a salary.'
3 Hamza: 'The $10,000 I lent the firm last year should earn interest.'
4 Iqbal: 'Hamza should pay interest on all the cash he took out.'
parts.answer:
1 Incorrect – profits are shared equally regardless of capital.
2 Incorrect – no partner is entitled to a salary.
3 Correct – 5% a year on a partner's loan ($500 for a full year).
4 Incorrect – no interest is charged on drawings.
parts.working: 1 mark each with reason.

practice.stem: Bashir has run a mobile-phone repair shop in Quetta as a sole trader for five years. His friend Jalil, a trained technician, has offered to join him as a partner and invest $15,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of forming a partnership rather than continuing as a sole trader.
parts.answer: More capital available; shared workload and skills; losses and risk shared; more ideas/specialisation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of a partnership.
parts.answer: Unlimited liability (each partner liable for the firm's debts); profits must be shared; disagreements between partners; decisions slower; partner's actions bind the firm.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: Shoaib and Tahira formed a partnership without any agreement. Shoaib contributed capital of $60,000 and also lent the business $20,000 at the start of the year. Tahira contributed capital of $40,000 and works full time in the business; Shoaib works part time. The profit for the year before any interest on Shoaib's loan was $50,000. Shoaib claims profits should be shared in the ratio of capitals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's share of the profit as required by the Partnership Act 1890.
parts.answer: Shoaib $24,500; Tahira $24,500.
parts.working: Loan interest 5% × 20,000 = 1,000 is an expense (M1); profit 49,000 (A1) shared equally 24,500 each (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Shoaib's total income from the business for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether Shoaib's claim is valid.
parts.answer: No. Without an agreement the Act requires equal sharing of profits, whatever the capital contributed.
parts.working: 1 mark: claim not valid. 1 mark: the Act applies when there is no agreement – equal shares, no interest on capital.

practice.stem:
Komal, Laiba and Mehreen run a catering firm in Islamabad. Capitals: Komal $50,000, Laiba $30,000, Mehreen $20,000. Komal also lent the firm $30,000 at the start of the year. Profit for the year before any loan interest was $84,000. Assume the rules of the Partnership Act 1890 apply where there is no agreement.
The partners are considering an agreement that would give: interest on capital at 6%; a salary of $12,000 to Mehreen; residual profit shared Komal 3 : Laiba 2 : Mehreen 1; loan interest as under the Act.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's share of the profit if the Partnership Act applies.
parts.answer: Loan interest 5% × 30,000 = 1,500 is an expense: profit to share 82,500; equally $27,500 each.
parts.working: B1 loan interest deducted; M1 equal shares; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's total share of profit under the proposed agreement.
parts.answer:
Profit after loan interest 82,500; less Mehreen's salary 12,000; less interest on capital 6,000 → residual 64,500
Komal: 3,000 + 32,250 = $35,250
Laiba: 1,800 + 21,500 = $23,300
Mehreen: 12,000 + 1,200 + 10,750 = $23,950
parts.working: B1 residual; B1 B1 B1 each partner.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which partner gains most from the proposed agreement.
parts.answer: Komal: share rises from 27,500 to 35,250.
parts.working: B1 own figures.

practice.stem: Nasir and Omar run a pharmacy in Hyderabad and have no partnership agreement. On 1 August 2025 Nasir lent the business $45,000, to be repaid in 2028. The profit for the year ended 31 December 2025, before any interest on the loan, was $61,500. Assume the rules of the Partnership Act 1890 apply where there is no agreement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest on Nasir's loan for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.working: M1 time; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's share of the profit.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Nasir's $45,000 is treated as a loan and not as capital.
parts.answer: It was agreed as a loan, repayable separately; loans carry interest and rank before capital on dissolution, whereas capital is the permanent investment of the owners.
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

practice.stem: The agreement of a partnership running a gym in Karachi charges interest on drawings at 8% per annum from the date of withdrawal to the year end of 31 December 2025. Pervaiz drew $8,000 on 1 March and $8,000 on 1 September. Qamar drew $16,000 on 1 December.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest on drawings for each partner.
parts.working: M1 A1 Pervaiz; M1 A1 Qamar.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Both partners drew $16,000. Explain why their interest charges differ.
parts.answer: Interest depends on how long the money is out of the business: Pervaiz drew earlier, so the firm lost the use of his cash for longer.
parts.working: 1 mark timing; 1 mark use of funds.

practice.stem: The partnership agreement of an architects' practice in Lahore states that a retiring partner is paid the balance due in three equal annual instalments, with interest at 6% per annum on the balance outstanding at the start of each year. Rubab retired and was owed $72,000. The first instalment is paid one year after retirement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total amount paid to Rubab in each of the three years.
parts.working: 1 mark each year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage to the continuing partners of a clause allowing payment by instalments.
parts.answer: The business does not have to find a large sum of cash at once, so liquidity is protected and assets need not be sold or new finance raised.
parts.working: 1 mark cash/liquidity; 1 mark consequence.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the agreement provides for interest on the outstanding balance.
parts.answer: To compensate Rubab for waiting for her money (time value / she cannot invest it elsewhere).

practice.stem: Zeeshan and Areej run a tour company in Gilgit. Their agreement gives: interest on capital at 6% (capitals Zeeshan $80,000, Areej $50,000); a salary of $10,000 to Areej; residual profit shared 3:2. The agreement says nothing about loans. Zeeshan lent the firm $25,000 for the whole year. Profit for the year before loan interest was $70,000. Assume the rules of the Partnership Act 1890 apply where there is no agreement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the interest that should be allowed on Zeeshan's loan and explain why.
parts.answer: 5% × 25,000 = $1,250; the agreement is silent on loans, so the Act applies to this item.
parts.working: 1 mark figure; 1 mark reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the appropriation account for the year.
parts.answer:
$         $
Profit for the year (after loan interest)                 68,750
Salary – Areej                                          (10,000)
Interest on capital – Zeeshan                    4,800
                  – Areej                        3,000   (7,800)
Residual profit                                           50,950
Zeeshan (3/5)                                             30,570
Areej (2/5)                                               20,380
parts.working: B1 profit after loan interest; B1 salary and interest on capital; B1 residual; B1 shares.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate each partner's total share of profit.
parts.answer: Zeeshan $35,370; Areej $33,380
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Salman, Tariq and Uzma have no partnership agreement. Capitals: Salman $60,000, Tariq $40,000, Uzma $20,000. Tariq has also lent the firm $40,000 for the whole year. Uzma works full time; the others work part time. Profit before loan interest is $96,000. Assume the rules of the Partnership Act 1890 apply where there is no agreement.
Uzma proposes an agreement giving: a salary of $18,000 to herself; interest on capital at 5%; residual profit shared Salman 2 : Tariq 2 : Uzma 1; loan interest as under the Act.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's share of profit if the Partnership Act applies.
parts.working: B1 loan interest; M1; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's share under Uzma's proposal.
parts.working: B1 residual; B1 each partner ×3 (combined).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Uzma whether she should insist on the proposed agreement. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Under the Act she receives 31,333; under the proposal 33,000, a gain of 1,667. Her salary of 18,000 is paid before residual profit, so her income is better protected if profits fall, and a written agreement gives certainty and reduces disputes. Against: her residual share falls to one fifth, so if profits rise strongly she gains less than under equal sharing; Salman and Tariq must agree, and both are worse off (Salman $31,000, Tariq $30,000 v 31,333 each under the Act), so they may resist. Decision: she should press for the agreement, as it rewards her full-time work and reduces risk, but may need to compromise on the ratio
parts.working: 1 mark each figure-based comparison (2); 1 mark fairness/certainty point; 1 mark risk point; 1 mark reasoned decision.

practice.stem: Vikram (capital $90,000) and Waseem (capital $30,000) run an import business in Karachi without a written agreement. They have always shared profits equally. This year there is a loss of $24,000, and Waseem argues that he should bear only one quarter of it. Assume the rules of the Partnership Act 1890 apply where there is no agreement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the loss for the year will be shared if there is no partnership agreement.
parts.answer: Equally – the Partnership Act says profits and losses are shared equally, whatever the capital contributed, so each bears one half.
parts.working: 1 mark equal; 1 mark irrespective of capital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate Waseem's claim that the loss should be shared in the ratio of capital.
parts.answer: For: he contributed less capital (1/4 of total) and so has less invested; sharing by capital may be seen as fairer for a capital-intensive business. Against: without an agreement the law requires equal sharing; Vikram also bears more risk with his larger capital; a change requires both partners to agree; past profits were shared equally so it would be inconsistent to change only when there is a loss. Conclusion: the claim has no legal basis unless both agree to a new ratio for the future.
parts.working: 1 mark each relevant point (max 3); 1 mark conclusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Recommend two terms the partners should include in an agreement to avoid similar disputes.
parts.answer: A stated profit-and-loss-sharing ratio applying to both profits and losses; interest on capital to reward the larger investment; a salary for the partner who works more; a dispute-resolution clause.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Xenia, an investor in Dubai, will contribute $200,000 to a new restaurant partnership but will not work in it. Yasir, a qualified chef, will contribute $20,000 and will manage the restaurant full time. Xenia may lend a further $50,000 later. Expected profit before appropriations is about $90,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Recommend terms for a partnership agreement between Xenia and Yasir. Justify each term you recommend.
parts.answer:
Possible terms (credit any reasonable, justified set):
• Interest on capital (e.g. 8%) – rewards Xenia's $200,000, which could earn a return elsewhere.
• Salary for Yasir (e.g. $24,000) – rewards his full-time work and expertise.
• Residual ratio (e.g. equal, or 2:3 in Yasir's favour) – shares risk and incentive; Yasir's effort drives profit.
• Interest on drawings / limit on drawings – protects working capital.
• Clause stating whether Xenia's further $50,000 is a loan (with interest) or capital.
• Goodwill valuation and procedure on retirement/death, and a dispute clause.
Mark bands: 7–8 = at least four relevant terms each clearly justified from the case, balanced between both partners; 4–6 = three or four terms with some justification; 1–3 = terms listed with little justification.
parts.working: Levels-marked as shown.
