subtopics: Partnership statement of profit or loss

practice.stem: Ittehad Steel Fabricators, Lahore, makes gates, railings and window grilles in batches. It is introducing activity based costing (ABC).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a cost driver.
parts.answer: The factor that causes the cost of an activity to be incurred, so that the cost changes with the level of that factor.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Suggest a suitable cost driver for each of the following activities.
(i) setting up machines for a new batch
(ii) buying materials from suppliers
(iii) inspecting finished goods
(iv) despatching goods to customers
parts.answer: (i) number of set-ups (ii) number of purchase orders (iii) number of inspections (iv) number of despatches/deliveries
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Mehran Pharmaceuticals has identified the following activities for the coming year.
Activity                  Cost $  Expected driver volume
Machine set-ups           84,000             120 set-ups
Quality inspection        56,000       1,400 inspections
Material handling         37,500         2,500 movements

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Machine set-ups $700 per set-up; quality inspection $40 per inspection; material handling $15 per movement

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a cost pool.
parts.answer: The total of all the overhead costs caused by one activity, collected together before being charged to products using the cost driver rate.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A company uses these cost driver rates: $700 per set-up, $40 per inspection and $15 per material movement. Product K needs 18 set-ups, 260 inspections and 400 material movements to make 5,000 units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total overhead charged to product K using ABC.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of product K.

practice.stem: The purchasing department of Faisalabad Garments has annual costs of: staff salaries $38,000; stationery and postage $2,400; purchasing software $5,600. It expects to place 920 purchase orders in the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for the purchasing activity.
parts.answer: $50 per purchase order

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the purchasing cost charged to the hospital uniforms product line, which needed 140 purchase orders.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the number of purchase orders is a more suitable basis than direct labour hours for charging purchasing costs.
parts.answer: Purchasing cost is caused by the number of orders placed, not by how long workers spend making the products.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A commercial bank in Lahore wants to find the cost of each service it provides to customers.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Suggest a suitable cost driver for each of the following activities in the bank.
(i) processing loan applications
(ii) operating cash machines (ATMs)
(iii) handling customer complaints
parts.answer: (i) number of loan applications (ii) number of ATM transactions/withdrawals (iii) number of complaints received
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why activity based costing is useful to a service business such as a bank.
parts.answer: Most of its costs are overheads, so ABC gives a more accurate cost of each service or customer, helping to set fees.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Al-Rawdah Printing, Riyadh, is pricing a job for a customer. Direct costs are $2,400. The job needs 2 press set-ups (rate $180 per set-up), 6 hours of design (rate $45 per design hour) and 3 deliveries (rate $60 per delivery).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead charged to the job using activity based costing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the job and the price charged using a mark-up of 30%.
parts.answer: Total cost $3,210; price $4,173.00
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The owner of a spice-grinding and packing business in Hyderabad has heard about activity based costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of activity based costing.
parts.answer: Any two: overheads are collected in cost pools by activity; each pool has its own cost driver; costs are charged to products according to their use of each activity; recognises that some costs are driven by batches or complexity, not volume.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features of a business for which activity based costing is likely to be most useful.
parts.answer: Any two: overheads are a large part of total cost; many different products or services; products differ greatly in complexity, batch size or support needed; a competitive market where accurate prices matter.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Medicare Tablets makes a vitamin product in batches of 250 packs. Each batch needs one set-up (rate $500) and two inspections (rate $40 each). Each pack needs 0.2 machine hours (rate $30 per hour).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ABC overhead cost per unit.
parts.working: Batch costs (500 + 2 × 40) ÷ 250 = 2.32; machine 0.2 × 30 = 6.00; total 8.32. 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the batch-related overhead per unit would fall if batches of 500 units were made.
parts.answer: Set-up and inspection costs are incurred per batch, so they are spread over more units.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Sialkot Surgical Instruments makes stainless steel scalpel sets in batches. Its overheads for the coming year are analysed into three cost pools:
Activity             Cost $   Cost driver             Expected volume
Sterilisation        96,000   Sterilisation cycles    240 cycles
Packing              31,200   Packing hours           1,200 hours
Machine maintenance  54,000   Machine hours           4,500 hours

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Sterilisation $400 per cycle; packing $26 per hour; machine maintenance $12 per machine hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: One batch of 60 scalpel sets uses 3 sterilisation cycles, 12 packing hours and 85 machine hours. Calculate the overhead charged to this batch using activity based costing.
parts.working: 1 mark for the three activity charges; 1 mark for the total.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per scalpel set in this batch.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Kumasi Shea Products makes shea butter and shea soap. Before setting up activity based costing, the accountant lists five activities:
(i) cleaning the processing line after each production run
(ii) quality testing of each batch of butter
(iii) annual insurance on the factory building
(iv) packing each kilogram of shea butter into tubs
(v) registering and certifying a new soap product for sale

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each activity as unit-level, batch-level, product-sustaining or facility-level.
parts.answer: (i) batch-level; (ii) batch-level; (iii) facility-level; (iv) unit-level; (v) product-sustaining
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept reasonable alternatives only if the reason is given.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a suitable cost driver for activity (ii) and for activity (v).
parts.answer: (ii) number of batches tested; (v) number of new products certified (or number of product lines)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Any driver that varies with the activity is acceptable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the cost of insurance on the factory building should not be charged to products using a cost driver.
parts.answer: It is a facility-level cost that does not vary with the activity or output of any one product, so any driver would be an arbitrary allocation.
parts.working: 1 mark: the cost does not change with products or activities; 1 mark: any driver is arbitrary, so it is better shown as a general overhead or shared on a stated basis such as floor area.

practice.stem:
Karachi Sweets makes boxes of mithai (20,000 boxes a year) and celebration cakes (6,000 cakes a year). Its overheads have been analysed as follows.
Activity           Cost $  Cost driver           Mithai    Cakes
Batch set-ups      45,000  Number of set-ups         40      110
Quality checks     30,000  Number of checks         200      400
Packing            27,000  Packing hours          1,500    1,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Batch set-ups 45,000 ÷ 150 = $300 per set-up; Quality checks 30,000 ÷ 600 = $50 per check; Packing 27,000 ÷ 2,700 = $10 per packing hour
parts.working: 1 mark each rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per box of mithai and per cake.
parts.working: 1 mark each product total, 1 mark each cost per unit (to 2 decimal places).

practice.stem:
Chiniot Woodcraft makes 4,000 chairs and 1,000 tables a year. Direct costs per unit are: chair materials $22, labour $15; table materials $95, labour $48. Each chair takes 0.5 machine hours and each table 2 machine hours. Overheads are:
Activity              Cost $  Cost driver           Chairs   Tables
Machine operation     96,000  Machine hours          2,000    2,000
Machine set-ups       36,000  Number of set-ups         20       40
Order processing      18,000  Number of orders         100       50

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per chair and per table using activity based costing.
parts.answer:
Machine operation 96,000 ÷ 4,000 = $24 per machine hour; Machine set-ups 36,000 ÷ 60 = $600 per set-up; Order processing 18,000 ÷ 150 = $120 per order
Chairs: 2,000 × 24 + 20 × 600 + 100 × 120 = $72,000; ÷ 4,000 units = $18.00 per unit
Tables: 2,000 × 24 + 40 × 600 + 50 × 120 = $78,000; ÷ 1,000 units = $78.00 per unit
parts.working: 1 mark rates; 1 mark chairs total; 1 mark tables total; 1 mark per-unit figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost per chair and per table.
parts.answer: Chair $55; table $221
parts.working: Chair 22 + 15 + 18; table 95 + 48 + 78. 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of each product if the business adds a mark-up of 40% on total cost.
parts.answer: Chair $77.00; table $309.40
parts.working: Total cost × 1.4. 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Margalla Medical Centre, Islamabad, treats 6,000 outpatients and 1,200 day-surgery patients a year. It has analysed its support costs as follows.
Activity       Cost $  Cost driver             Outpatient  Day surgery
Admissions     72,000  Number of admissions         6,000        1,200
Theatre       240,000  Theatre hours                    0        1,600
Laboratory     54,000  Number of tests              4,500        1,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Admissions 72,000 ÷ 7,200 = $10 per admission; Theatre 240,000 ÷ 1,600 = $150 per theatre hour; Laboratory 54,000 ÷ 6,000 = $9 per test
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per patient for each type of patient.
parts.working: 1 mark each total, 1 mark each cost per patient.

practice.stem: Gulf Signs, Muscat, receives an order for 600 aluminium signs. Direct costs are $14.20 per sign. The order will need 3 set-ups, 12 inspections and 80 machine hours. ABC cost driver rates are $450 per set-up, $35 per inspection and $28 per machine hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost of the order using activity based costing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the order.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the price to quote for the order, in total and per unit, using a mark-up of 25% on cost. Give the price per unit to the nearest cent.
parts.answer: $15,662.50 in total; $26.10 per unit
parts.working: M1 × 1.25; A1 both figures.

practice.stem: The set-up cost pool of Bolan Plastics is $63,000 and the cost driver rate is $350 per set-up. Product P used 48 set-ups. The total ABC overhead charged to product P was $41,300, made up of set-up costs, inspection costs at $25 per inspection, and machine-related costs of $15,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of set-ups expected in the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the set-up cost charged to product P.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of inspections used by product P.

practice.stem:
Sunrise Distributors, Peshawar, supplies two customers. Customer A is a supermarket chain; customer B is a group of small shops. Activity costs are $40 per order processed, $85 per delivery and $25 per return handled.
                Customer A  Customer B
Revenue $           60,000      40,000
Gross margin           25%         40%
Orders                  50         120
Deliveries              50         100
Returns                 10          30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total activity cost of serving each customer.
parts.answer: Customer A $6,500; customer B $14,050

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit earned from each customer after activity costs.
parts.answer: Customer A $8,500; customer B $1,950

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions the business could take to improve the profit from customer B.
parts.answer: Any two: set a minimum order size; charge for deliveries or for small orders; combine orders into fewer deliveries; reduce returns (better quality/packing); encourage online ordering.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Nairobi Business College runs a full-time course (300 students) and a weekend course (600 students). Fees are $900 per full-time student and $260 per weekend student. Tutor costs are $280 and $110 per student respectively. Other costs are:
Activity       Cost $  Cost driver             Full-time  Weekend
Enrolment      36,000  Number of enrolments          300      600
Classrooms    180,000  Room hours                  8,000    4,000
Assessment     42,000  Scripts marked              2,400    1,800

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per student for each course using activity based costing.
parts.answer:
Enrolment 36,000 ÷ 900 = $40 per enrolment; Classrooms 180,000 ÷ 12,000 = $15 per room hour; Assessment 42,000 ÷ 4,200 = $10 per script
Full-time: 300 × 40 + 8,000 × 15 + 2,400 × 10 = $156,000; ÷ 300 students = $520.00 per student
Weekend: 600 × 40 + 4,000 × 15 + 1,800 × 10 = $102,000; ÷ 600 students = $170.00 per student
parts.working: 1 mark each rate (3); 1 mark each cost per student (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss per student for each course.
parts.answer: Full-time $100 profit; weekend $20 loss
parts.working: Full-time 900 − 280 − 520; weekend 260 − 110 − 170. 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Pine View Hotel, Murree, sold 9,000 standard room-nights and 2,000 suite room-nights last year. Its support costs were:
Activity         Cost $  Cost driver            Standard    Suite
Housekeeping     96,000  Cleaning hours            6,000    2,000
Laundry          28,000  Kilograms washed         20,000   15,000
Reception        18,000  Number of check-ins       2,800      800

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Housekeeping 96,000 ÷ 8,000 = $12 per cleaning hour; Laundry 28,000 ÷ 35,000 = $0.80 per kg; Reception 18,000 ÷ 3,600 = $5 per check-in
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per room-night for each type of room.
parts.working: 1 mark each total; 1 mark each cost per room-night.

practice.stem:
An online homeware retailer in Karachi has these activity cost rates: picking $0.40 per item, packing $1.20 per parcel, returns $3.50 per return, customer calls $2.00 per call. Monthly data:
                    Small orders  Large orders
Parcels (orders)          20,000         2,500
Items picked              20,000        20,000
Returns                      800           300
Customer calls             3,000         1,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total monthly activity cost of small orders and of large orders.
parts.answer: Small $40,800; large $15,050

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activity cost per order for each type.
parts.answer: Small $2.04; large $6.02
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The retailer currently adds a flat handling charge of $3 to every order. Explain why this is unfair.
parts.answer: Large orders cost about three times as much to handle as small orders, so small-order customers pay more than their cost and large-order customers pay less than their cost (cross-subsidy).
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

practice.stem:
Shahrah Motors, Lahore, assembles 10,000 City motorcycles (1.5 machine hours each, direct cost $410) and 3,000 Sport motorcycles (3 machine hours each, direct cost $690) a year. Overheads:
Activity                Cost $  Cost driver                     City    Sport
Purchasing             210,000  Number of purchase orders      1,200    1,800
Engineering changes     96,000  Number of changes                  8       24
Assembly line          480,000  Machine hours                 15,000    9,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ABC overhead cost per motorcycle for each model.
parts.answer:
Purchasing 210,000 ÷ 3,000 = $70 per order; Engineering changes 96,000 ÷ 32 = $3,000 per change; Assembly line 480,000 ÷ 24,000 = $20 per machine hour
City: 1,200 × 70 + 8 × 3,000 + 15,000 × 20 = $408,000; ÷ 10,000 units = $40.80 per unit
Sport: 1,800 × 70 + 24 × 3,000 + 9,000 × 20 = $378,000; ÷ 3,000 units = $126.00 per unit
parts.working: 1 mark each rate (3); 1 mark each per-unit figure (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of each model using a mark-up of 25% on total cost.

practice.stem: Lahore Engine Works uses activity based costing. Its engineering department has an annual overhead pool of $168,000 and the cost driver is the number of engineering change orders (ECOs) processed. The budgeted cost driver rate is $1,200 per ECO. During the year product P had 40 ECOs and product Q had 25 ECOs. The actual engineering overhead spent was $171,600 and the actual number of ECOs processed in the whole year was 152.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted number of ECOs for the year.
parts.working: 1 mark for the division; 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the engineering overhead charged to product P and to product Q.
parts.working: 1 mark each product.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the engineering overhead over-absorbed or under-absorbed for the year.
parts.answer: Absorbed 152 × 1,200 = $182,400; spent $171,600; over-absorbed by $10,800
parts.working: M1 absorbed amount; A1 over-absorbed by $10,800 (absorbed exceeds spent).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the number of ECOs is a more suitable cost driver than the number of units produced for engineering overhead.
parts.answer: Engineering work is caused by design changes, not by how many units are made; a product with many ECOs uses much more engineering time even if its output is small.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid explanation linking engineering effort to design changes rather than volume.

practice.stem:
Dhaka Dental Care uses ABC to find the cost of treating adult and child patients. Its support costs for the year, and the volumes used by each group, are:
Activity               Cost $   Cost driver          Total   Adults   Children
Instrument sterilising  54,000   Trays processed      6,000    4,500      1,500
Appointment booking    28,800   Appointments         4,800    3,600      1,200
X-ray room             36,000   X-ray sessions       1,500      900        600
The clinic treated 1,000 adult patients and 400 child patients in the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Sterilising $9 per tray; booking $6 per appointment; X-ray room $24 per session

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total overhead charged to adult patients and to child patients, and the overhead cost per patient in each group.
parts.working: 2 marks for the two totals (1 each group); 2 marks for the cost per patient in each group (1 each).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why child patients have a higher overhead cost per patient than adults, even though each child uses fewer trays and fewer appointments.
parts.answer: Children use X-ray sessions more often per patient (1.5 sessions each against 0.9 for adults), and an X-ray session is the most expensive driver at $24.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying the X-ray driver and the per-patient difference; 1 mark for the reason that the $24 rate is much higher than the others.

practice.stem:
Lahore Leather makes 8,000 standard bags and 1,500 designer bags a year. Direct costs are $24.45 per standard bag and $89.60 per designer bag. Overheads are:
Activity            Cost $  Cost driver              Standard  Designer
Design              60,000  Design hours                  100       400
Cutting set-ups     42,000  Number of set-ups              30        70
Inspection          33,000  Number of inspections         900       600

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each bag using activity based costing.
parts.answer:
Design 60,000 ÷ 500 = $120 per design hour; Cutting set-ups 42,000 ÷ 100 = $420 per set-up; Inspection 33,000 ÷ 1,500 = $22 per inspection
Standard: 100 × 120 + 30 × 420 + 900 × 22 = $44,400; ÷ 8,000 units = $5.55 per unit
Designer: 400 × 120 + 70 × 420 + 600 × 22 = $90,600; ÷ 1,500 units = $60.40 per unit
parts.working: 1 mark rates; 1 mark product totals; 1 mark per-unit figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of each bag needed to give a profit margin of 20% of selling price.
parts.answer: Standard $37.50; designer $187.50
parts.working: Total cost: standard 24.45 + 5.55 = 30.00; designer 89.60 + 60.40 = 150.00; divide by 0.8. 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A competitor sells a similar designer bag for $175. Advise Lahore Leather whether it should reduce the price of its designer bag to $175. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: At $175 the margin would fall to (175 − 150) ÷ 175 = 14.29%, still a profit of $25 per bag. For: keeps market share; ABC shows the true cost is $150, so the bag is still profitable. Against: lower margin; the brand may justify a higher price (quality, design); other customers may expect discounts. Decision e.g. match the price only if volumes rise, or keep $187.50 and stress quality.
parts.working: 1 mark revised margin/profit; 1 mark points for and against; 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem:
Penang Circuits makes three electronic modules. Annual data:
                                  X        Y        Z
Output (units)               10,000    5,000    2,000
Selling price per unit $         30       48      120
Direct costs per unit $          16       22       31
Overheads:
Activity               Cost $  Cost driver                 X        Y        Z
Set-ups               150,000  Number of set-ups          10       30       60
Component handling     90,000  Components handled      6,000    9,000   15,000
Testing               120,000  Test hours                500      700    1,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using activity based costing.
parts.working: 1 mark rates; 1 mark each product (3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss per unit of each product.
parts.working: Price − direct cost − ABC overhead. 2 marks all correct, 1 mark for two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors what action they should take on product Z. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Z makes a loss of $8.50 per unit because it uses a large share of set-ups and testing for low output. Options: raise the price above $128.50 (break-even cost), make Z in larger batches to cut set-ups, or redesign to reduce testing. Before dropping Z, check which overheads would actually be saved and whether customers buy Z with X and Y. Decision: e.g. raise price/reduce set-ups rather than drop at once.
parts.working: 1 mark use of figures and action(s); 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: Swift Filters, Gujranwala, makes 24,000 oil filters a year in batches of 400. Each batch needs one machine set-up costing $600 and four inspections costing $45 each. Each filter costs $40 to make, and inventory holding costs are 15% a year of the average value held.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the batch-related cost per unit with the current batch size of 400 units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the batch-related cost per unit if the batch size is increased to 1,000 units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net annual saving from the larger batch size, after allowing for higher inventory holding costs.
parts.working: Saving 46,800 − 18,720 = 28,080; extra holding cost: average inventory rises by (1,000 − 400) ÷ 2 = 300 units × $40 × 15% = 1,800; net 26,280. M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the managers whether to increase the batch size. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Yes on cost grounds: a large net saving. But larger batches mean more finished inventory, a risk of obsolescence, less flexibility to meet changing customer orders and more storage space. Decision: increase, perhaps to an intermediate size, if demand is steady.
parts.working: 1 mark point(s) using figures/qualitative; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Ravi Valves wants to win a contract to supply 3,000 valves a year at a market price of $64 each, with a profit margin of at least 10% of selling price. Direct costs are $41 per valve. Production uses 24 set-ups at $900 each, 300 inspections at $30 each and 1,500 machine hours at $20 per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current total cost per unit of the valve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum cost per unit that allows a 10% margin at a price of $64.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many set-ups must be eliminated if the cost reduction is to come entirely from set-ups.
parts.answer: 12 set-ups (from 24 to 12)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Discuss whether this reduction is realistic.
parts.answer: Halving set-ups means producing in batches twice as large, which increases inventory and holding costs and may not suit customer delivery schedules; set-up time might instead be cut by better tooling, or savings found in inspections.
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

practice.stem: Seaside Snacks, Gwadar, uses ABC. Product Z has annual revenue of $180,000 and direct costs of $102,000. ABC charges it with set-up costs $36,000, inspection costs $18,000 and facility costs $40,000 (factory rent and insurance, shared on floor area). If Z were discontinued, all its set-up and inspection costs would be saved, but the facility costs would not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss of product Z using activity based costing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect on the company's total profit if product Z is discontinued.
parts.answer: Profit falls by $24,000
parts.working: Lost revenue 180,000; saved direct costs 102,000, set-ups 36,000 and inspections 18,000; facility costs continue. 180,000 − 156,000 = 24,000 reduction. M1 avoidable costs; M1 facility cost excluded; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to discontinue product Z. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Do not discontinue on these figures: Z contributes $24,000 towards facility costs that would still be paid. Consider raising its price or reducing set-ups. Also consider whether the space could be used for a more profitable product and the effect on customers who buy other products.
parts.working: 1 mark use of the figure; 1 mark other factor; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Zamzam Bottling budgeted set-up costs of $120,000 for 200 set-ups and inspection costs of $60,000 for 1,500 inspections. Actual results were: 215 set-ups costing $126,500; 1,420 inspections costing $61,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Set-ups $600; inspections $40
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorbed and the amount over- or under-absorbed for each activity.
parts.answer: Set-ups: absorbed $129,000, over-absorbed $2,500. Inspections: absorbed $56,800, under-absorbed $4,200
parts.working: 215 × 600; 1,420 × 40. 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net effect on profit of the over- and under-absorption.
parts.answer: Net under-absorption $1,700, reducing profit

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason for the under-absorption of inspection costs.
parts.answer: Actual inspection costs were higher than budgeted (e.g. higher inspector wages) while fewer inspections were carried out than budgeted.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Kohinoor Paints sells 12,000 tins a year at $18 each to a hardware chain, delivered in 12 monthly deliveries. The chain now wants weekly deliveries (52 a year) with no change in total volume or price. ABC rates: delivery $140 per delivery; order processing $35 per order (one order per delivery); quality certificate $20 per delivery.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual activity cost of supplying the customer under the present arrangement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual activity cost if the customer's request is accepted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the increase in price per unit needed to keep the profit from this customer unchanged.
parts.answer: $0.65 per unit (price rises to $18.65)
parts.working: Extra cost 7,800 ÷ 12,000 units. M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the company how to respond to the customer's request.
parts.answer: Accept only if the price rises by about $0.65 a unit (or a delivery charge of $195 per extra delivery is made); otherwise profit falls by $7,800. Consider the value of keeping a large customer and whether deliveries can be combined with other customers' routes.
parts.working: 1 mark use of figures; 1 mark justified advice.

practice.stem:
Hyderabad Ceramic Tiles makes wall tiles (5,000 boxes a year) and floor tiles (2,500 boxes a year). Its overheads are analysed as:
Activity                         Cost $    Cost driver         Wall     Floor
Kiln firing                      240,000   Kiln hours          1,200       800
Glazing line set-ups              96,000   Set-ups               200       120
Factory rent and insurance        60,000   Floor area (m²)       180       120
The factory rent and insurance is shared by floor area, as shown. Direct costs are $14 per box of wall tiles and $22 per box of floor tiles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per box of wall tiles and per box of floor tiles using activity based costing.
parts.working: 1 mark for the three rates ($120 per kiln hour, $300 per set-up, $200 per m²); 1 mark for the wall total; 1 mark for the floor total; 1 mark for the two per-box figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the full cost per box of each product (direct cost plus ABC overhead).
parts.working: 1 mark each product.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The company wants a 20% margin on selling price for floor tiles. Calculate the minimum selling price per box of floor tiles. A customer offers $100 per box: state whether this is acceptable and give the margin it would earn.
parts.answer: $84.40 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = $105.50 per box. The offer of $100 is not acceptable; it gives a margin of (100 − 84.40) ÷ 100 = 15.6%.
parts.working: M1 selling price formula; A1 $105.50; A1 rejection with margin 15.6%.

practice.stem: Quetta Woollens absorbs all its production overheads using a single rate per direct labour hour. The finance director suggests changing to activity based costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages of activity based costing compared with traditional absorption costing.
parts.answer: Any two explained: more accurate product costs because overheads are charged according to what causes them; better pricing decisions, avoiding over-pricing high-volume and under-pricing low-volume products; identifies costly activities that can be controlled or reduced; better information for decisions about products and customers.
parts.working: 1 mark each advantage, 1 mark each explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one limitation of activity based costing.
parts.answer: Any one: expensive and time-consuming to set up and run; choice of cost drivers can be subjective; some costs (e.g. factory rent) have no clear driver and still have to be apportioned; still based on historical/budgeted data.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Dhaka Denim Works makes jeans and denim jackets. Overheads for the year are $192,000 and are absorbed on direct labour hours. Budgeted labour hours are 32,000. Jeans take 2 labour hours each and jackets take 3 labour hours each. The budgeted output is 10,000 pairs of jeans and 4,000 jackets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the absorption rate per direct labour hour.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of jeans and of jackets.
parts.answer: Jeans $12 (2 × 6); jackets $18 (3 × 6)
parts.working: 1 mark each product.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the total overhead absorbed by the budgeted output, and explain why this equals the overhead budget.
parts.answer: 10,000 × 12 + 4,000 × 18 = $192,000, the same as the budget, because the rate was calculated from the budgeted hours and output.
parts.working: 1 mark for the total absorbed; 1 mark for explaining that the rate recovers exactly the budget when actual activity equals budget.

practice.stem: Crescent Bakery, Peshawar, makes bread loaves and wedding cakes. All overheads, including oven running costs, cake decorating supplies and the bakery manager's salary, are absorbed into products using a single rate per oven hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'absorption costing'.
parts.answer: A method of costing that charges all production overheads to products using an overhead rate based on a volume measure such as labour hours or machine hours.
parts.working: 1 mark: all production overheads are charged to products; 1 mark: using a rate based on a volume-related measure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a single oven-hour rate could give misleading product costs for this bakery.
parts.answer: Wedding cakes need much decorating and special-order work but use few oven hours, so they are under-costed. The manager's salary and other costs unrelated to oven use are charged by oven hours, which is arbitrary.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: cakes use decorating time not oven time (under-costed); overheads unrelated to ovens are shared by oven hours; special orders cause set-up work not reflected in oven time; the allocation is arbitrary.

practice.stem: Ravi Pottery, Multan, makes ceramic pots. In the year it produced 5,000 pots and sold all 5,000. The selling price is $40 per pot and direct costs are $18 per pot. Production overheads are $60,000 for the year. There was no opening or closing inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year under absorption costing.
parts.answer: Revenue 5,000 × 40 = $200,000; less direct costs $90,000 and overheads $60,000 = profit $50,000
parts.working: 1 mark for revenue and costs; 1 mark for the profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the profit would be the same if the overheads were charged to pots using activity based costing.
parts.answer: All pots are sold, so all overheads are charged to cost of sales under either method; the total cost is the same, so the profit is the same even though the cost per pot differs.
parts.working: 1 mark: all production is sold so the total overhead expensed is $60,000 under both methods; 1 mark: the total is unchanged, only its allocation between pots differs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State when the two methods would give different profits for a year.
parts.answer: When the closing inventory value differs from the opening inventory value, so that different amounts of overhead are carried forward.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Lahore Print Solutions makes two products. Product A (3,000 units; 2 machine hours each) and product B (6,000 units; 1 machine hour each). Overheads are $120,000 a year and are absorbed on machine hours. An ABC analysis divides the overheads as follows:
Activity            Cost $   Cost driver          Product A   Product B
Set-ups             60,000   Number of set-ups          30          20
Machine running     60,000   Machine hours           6,000       6,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of product A and product B using the machine-hour absorption rate.
parts.answer: Product A $20 (2 × $10); product B $10 (1 × $10)
parts.working: Rate $120,000 ÷ 12,000 machine hours = $10 per hour. 1 mark each product.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of product A and product B using activity based costing.
parts.working: 1 mark for the two activity rates; 1 mark each product.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which product is under-costed by the machine-hour method, and explain why.
parts.answer: Product A is under-costed ($20 against $22) because it uses many set-ups per unit, which machine hours do not capture.
parts.working: 1 mark for product A with the reason.

practice.stem: Karachi Software House has 40 staff. It charges all its overheads (office rent, IT support, recruitment and client-project management) to client projects using a single rate per staff hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two activities in this business for which a single rate per staff hour is likely to be inaccurate, and give a suitable cost driver for each.
parts.answer: Recruitment: number of new staff hired. IT support: number of IT support tickets or IT hours used by each project. (Any two sensible pairs.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid activity with a suitable driver.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'cost pool' in activity based costing.
parts.answer: A cost pool is a group of overhead costs for one activity, collected together so that they can be charged to products using a single cost driver.
parts.working: 1 mark: a group of costs for one activity; 1 mark: charged to products using one driver.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why the business might still use the single staff-hour rate despite its weaknesses.
parts.answer: It is simple and cheap to operate, and the difference from ABC may be small for the business.
parts.working: 1 mark for a sensible reason (simplicity, low cost, small difference).

practice.stem:
Gulberg Gems, Lahore, sells two types of jewellery. The sales and cost figures per unit under ABC are:
                           Ring     Necklace
Selling price $            150          240
Direct costs $              60          110
ABC overhead $ per unit     30           75

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit per unit for each product.
parts.working: 1 mark each product.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit margin on selling price for each product, to the nearest whole percent.
parts.working: 1 mark each product.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The owner says the necklace should be promoted because it brings in more revenue per unit. Explain, using your answers, whether this is correct.
parts.answer: Not for profit: the necklace earns less profit per unit ($55 against $60) and a lower margin (23% against 40%), so the ring is more profitable per unit and per dollar of sales.
parts.working: 1 mark: profit per unit is lower for the necklace; 1 mark: lower margin, so higher revenue does not mean higher profit.

practice.stem: Lahore Biscuits absorbs overheads on the number of packets produced. Budgeted overheads are $240,000 and budgeted output is 80,000 packets. In the year, 60,000 packets were produced and actual overheads were $236,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the absorption rate per packet.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount of overhead over-absorbed or under-absorbed in the year.
parts.answer: Absorbed 60,000 × 3 = $180,000; spent $236,000; under-absorbed by $56,000
parts.working: M1 absorbed amount; A1 under-absorbed $56,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a per-packet rate may be unsuitable if the company makes both large packets and small packets.
parts.answer: A large packet uses more machine time and materials than a small one, but a per-packet rate charges both the same, so product costs are inaccurate. An activity driver such as machine hours would be more accurate.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate ignores the different resources used by each size; 1 mark: a more accurate driver (for example machine hours) would be better.

practice.stem: Ahmed Motors, Faisalabad, is considering activity based costing. Most of its overheads are the factory manager's salary, insurance on the factory building and the rent of the site. These costs do not change with the number of vehicles or batches produced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why activity based costing would not help much with these overheads.
parts.answer: These facility-level costs do not vary with any activity, so whatever cost driver is chosen is an arbitrary allocation and gives no better product cost.
parts.working: 1 mark: the costs do not vary with activities; 1 mark: any driver is arbitrary.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an approach for these overheads when making pricing decisions.
parts.answer: Treat them as period costs (not absorbed into product cost) and base pricing on contribution after variable and avoidable costs; or allocate on a stated basis such as floor area and say so.
parts.working: 1 mark for treating them as period or fixed costs; 1 mark for a stated, reasoned allocation basis if one is used.

practice.stem:
Sargodha Agro Tools makes Alpha (20,000 units, 1 direct labour hour each) and Beta (2,000 units, 2 direct labour hours each). Total overheads are $240,000, analysed as:
Activity           Cost $  Cost driver            Alpha     Beta
Set-ups           100,000  Number of set-ups         10       40
Order handling     60,000  Number of orders          50      100
Machining          80,000  Machine hours         15,000    5,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using a single absorption rate per direct labour hour.
parts.answer: Alpha $10.00; Beta $20.00
parts.working: 240,000 ÷ 24,000 hours = $10 per hour; Alpha 1 hour, Beta 2 hours. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using activity based costing.
parts.working: 1 mark set-up and order rates; 1 mark machining rate; 1 mark each per-unit figure (2).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two methods give such different results.
parts.answer: Beta is made in small batches with many set-ups and orders, but uses few labour hours. Absorption on labour hours ignores this, so Beta is under-costed and high-volume Alpha over-costed.
parts.working: 1 mark: low-volume/complex product uses more batch-level activities; 1 mark: labour hours do not reflect this.

practice.stem: Tulip Cosmetics produced 10,000 units of a face cream and sold 8,000 units in its first year. There was no opening inventory. Production overhead per unit is $12 under traditional absorption costing and $9 under activity based costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead included in the closing inventory under each method.
parts.answer: Absorption $24,000; ABC $18,000
parts.working: Closing inventory 10,000 − 8,000 = 2,000 units; × $12 and × $9. 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect on reported profit for the year of using ABC instead of absorption costing.
parts.answer: Profit is $6,000 lower under ABC, because $3 less overhead per unit is carried forward in closing inventory, so more of the year's overhead is charged against this year's profit.
parts.working: 1 mark amount; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State when the two methods would give the same profit.
parts.answer: When there is no change in the level of inventory (production equals sales), since total overhead charged is the same.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Peshawar Furniture Works makes 300 wooden chairs for a hotel order, in one batch. Direct costs are $68 per chair. Each chair uses 2.5 machine hours. The business currently absorbs overheads at $30 per machine hour. An ABC analysis of this batch shows: three machine set-ups costing $1,200 each, machine running costs of $10 per machine hour, and finishing costs of $6 per chair.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cost per chair under absorption costing.
parts.answer: $143 (direct $68 + absorbed overhead 2.5 × $30 = $75)
parts.working: 1 mark for absorbed overhead $75; 1 mark for total $143.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost per chair under activity based costing.
parts.answer: $111: direct $68 + set-ups 3 × 1,200 ÷ 300 = $12 + machine running 2.5 × 10 = $25 + finishing $6 = $43 overhead
parts.working: 1 mark for set-up cost per chair $12; 1 mark for machine running $25; 1 mark for total $111.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The business adds a mark-up of 25% on total cost. Calculate the total price for the 300 chairs under each method.
parts.working: 1 mark each method.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State which method gives the lower price, and one thing the business should check before quoting the lower price.
parts.answer: The ABC price is lower. The business should check its ABC rates are accurate, otherwise it may quote too low and lose money.
parts.working: 1 mark for both points.

practice.stem:
Kasur Textile Mills makes three products. Overheads are $300,000 a year and are absorbed on machine hours (20,000 hours in total, so $15 per hour). The data are:
Product    Units    Machine hours per unit   Set-ups per year   Selling price $   Direct cost $
Shirts     40,000             0.20                    40              6.00               2.00
Trousers   16,000             0.25                    60              9.00               3.00
Jackets    16,000             0.50                   100             13.00               5.00
Under ABC, set-up costs total $120,000 (200 set-ups, $600 each) and machine running costs total $180,000 ($9 per machine hour).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total profit for each product under absorption costing.
parts.working: 1 mark each product.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total profit for each product under activity based costing.
parts.working: 1 mark for the set-up rate and running rate; 1 mark for the unit costs; 1 mark for the profits or loss.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise whether the jackets should be discontinued. Give one reason for and one reason against.
parts.answer: Discontinue: under ABC they make a loss of $4,000, and if their set-up and machine costs are avoidable total profit would rise by $4,000. Against: some set-up and machine-time costs are shared and cannot be avoided, so profit may fall.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reason for; 1 mark for a reason against (unavoidable overhead).

practice.stem: Jhelum Steel Pipes makes 20,000 pipes a year in 40 production runs. Set-up costs are $90,000 a year and are the only ABC pool that changes. A quick-change tooling system would reduce the number of set-ups to 30 a year, but the set-up cost pool would rise to $96,000 because of the new tooling.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the set-up cost per set-up and the set-up cost per pipe before the change.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the set-up cost per set-up and the set-up cost per pipe after the change.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how much the set-up cost per pipe changes, and advise whether the new system should go ahead.
parts.answer: Cost per pipe rises by $0.30, so the overhead per pipe is higher. The change should only go ahead if the other benefits (for example faster delivery or fewer defects) are worth more than the extra $6,000 a year.
parts.working: 1 mark for the $0.30 increase; 1 mark for a reasoned recommendation with the $6,000 extra cost.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why a fall in the number of set-ups does not automatically reduce the set-up cost per pipe under ABC.
parts.answer: Under ABC the set-up cost pool depends on the cost of the activity itself. If that cost rises, the rate per set-up rises, so fewer set-ups may not reduce the cost per pipe.
parts.working: 1 mark: the pool or rate depends on the cost of the activity, not only the number of set-ups; 1 mark: the rise in pool cost can outweigh the fall in set-ups.

practice.stem:
Indus Bank, Karachi, uses ABC to cost its two main products. Its operating costs for the year, and the drivers used by each product, are:
Activity                 Cost $    Cost driver              Current accounts   Business loans
Account administration   192,000   Number of accounts              30,000            2,000
Transaction processing   240,000   Number of transactions         580,000           20,000
Loan appraisal           150,000   Number of applications               0            1,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: $6 per account; $0.40 per transaction; $100 per loan application

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total ABC cost of each product and the ABC cost per business loan.
parts.working: 1 mark for the current account total; 1 mark for the loan total; 1 mark for the cost per loan.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a single charge per account would give a different, and misleading, cost for the business loans.
parts.answer: A per-account rate ignores the heavy appraisal work each loan application needs, so business loans would be under-costed and their profitability overstated.
parts.working: 1 mark: loan appraisal is not related to number of accounts; 1 mark: loans would be under-costed.

practice.stem:
Pathway Laboratory, Karachi, runs two types of test. Blood count tests: 45,000 tests a year, 0.2 technician hours each. Culture tests: 9,000 tests a year, 1.0 technician hours each. Total laboratory overheads are $1,080,000. Under the current method they are absorbed on technician hours. An ABC analysis divides the overheads as follows:
Activity            Cost $    Cost driver           Blood count   Culture
Sample handling     432,000   Samples received         45,000     9,000
Incubator running   648,000   Incubator hours               0    36,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per test for each type using the technician-hour absorption method.
parts.answer: Blood count $12 (0.2 × $60); culture $60 (1.0 × $60). The rate is $1,080,000 ÷ 18,000 technician hours = $60 per hour
parts.working: 1 mark each test type; the rate is shown in the working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per test for each type using activity based costing.
parts.answer: Sample handling rate $432,000 ÷ 54,000 = $8 per sample; incubator rate $648,000 ÷ 36,000 = $18 per hour. Blood count $8 per test; culture (9,000 × 8 + 36,000 × 18) ÷ 9,000 = $80 per test
parts.working: 1 mark for the two rates; 1 mark for the blood count cost; 1 mark for the culture cost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit per test for each type under ABC if blood count tests are charged at $15 and culture tests at $85.
parts.answer: Blood count $7 per test (15 − 8); culture $5 per test (85 − 80)
parts.working: 1 mark each test type.

practice.stem: Quetta Blankets makes 12,000 blankets a year. Each batch needs one set-up costing $720 and two quality checks costing $45 each. Factory rent of $36,000 a year is a facility-level cost. Batches are currently 240 blankets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the batch-related overhead per blanket at the current batch size.
parts.working: 1 mark for 50 batches and $810 per batch; 1 mark for the per-blanket figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the batch-related overhead per blanket if the batch size is increased to 300 blankets.
parts.working: 1 mark for the total; 1 mark for the per-blanket figure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the saving per year from the larger batch size, ignoring inventory holding costs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for the two totals, or 1 mark for the saving.

practice.stem: Gujranwala Cables uses ABC. Its inspection cost pool is $90,000 a year and the cost driver rate is $50 per inspection. Product C was charged $27,500 for inspections and product D was charged $15,000. Actual inspections in the year were 1,850, and the actual inspection cost was $96,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of inspections expected in the year.
parts.answer: 1,800 inspections (90,000 ÷ 50)
parts.working: 1 mark for method; 1 mark for answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of inspections charged to product C and to product D.
parts.working: 1 mark each product.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the inspection cost charged to all other products, and the number of inspections this represents.
parts.answer: Other products: 90,000 − 27,500 − 15,000 = $47,500, which is 950 inspections at $50
parts.working: 1 mark for the $47,500; 1 mark for 950 inspections.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the amount of inspection overhead over-absorbed or under-absorbed for the year.
parts.answer: Absorbed 1,850 × 50 = $92,500; actual $96,000; under-absorbed by $3,500
parts.working: M1 absorbed amount; A1 under-absorbed $3,500.

practice.stem: Managers at Shalimar Engineering are reluctant to introduce activity based costing, and the finance director wants to persuade them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why managers might resist introducing ABC.
parts.answer: Collecting and maintaining activity data is costly and time-consuming; new cost figures may change the performance measures or bonuses managers are judged on.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid reason, for example cost and time of data collection, changes to performance measures or bonuses, unfamiliarity, loss of control.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways the business could introduce ABC at low cost.
parts.answer: Start with the largest overhead pools only; use existing records for drivers; pilot ABC on one product line; use ABC for pricing decisions and review it once a year.
parts.working: 1 mark for each sensible suggestion.

practice.stem:
Spice Route, Karachi, sells 50,000 packs of ground spices (direct cost $2.00 each, 0.1 machine hours each) and 4,000 gift hampers (direct cost $30.00 each, 0.25 machine hours each). Overheads of $180,000 are currently absorbed on machine hours. An ABC analysis shows:
Activity             Cost $  Cost driver            Packs  Hampers
Set-ups              72,000  Number of set-ups         12       36
Packaging design     48,000  Design hours              20       60
Machining            60,000  Machine hours          5,000    1,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using the current machine-hour rate.
parts.answer: Packs $3.00; hampers $7.50
parts.working: 180,000 ÷ 6,000 hours = $30; packs 0.1 hours, hampers 0.25 hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using activity based costing.
parts.answer:
Set-ups 72,000 ÷ 48 = $1,500 per set-up; Packaging design 48,000 ÷ 80 = $600 per design hour; Machining 60,000 ÷ 6,000 = $10 per machine hour
Packs: 12 × 1,500 + 20 × 600 + 5,000 × 10 = $80,000; ÷ 50,000 units = $1.60 per unit
Hampers: 36 × 1,500 + 60 × 600 + 1,000 × 10 = $100,000; ÷ 4,000 units = $25.00 per unit
parts.working: 1 mark rates; 1 mark each per-unit figure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of each product under each method, using a mark-up of 30% on total cost.
parts.answer: Machine-hour rate: packs $6.50, hampers $48.75. ABC: packs $4.68, hampers $71.50
parts.working: 1 mark each method.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Discuss the consequences for the business of continuing to price using the machine-hour rate.
parts.answer: Packs are over-priced ($6.50 against an ABC-based $4.68), so the business may lose sales of its main product to competitors. Hampers are under-priced ($48.75 against $71.50), so they may sell well but could be making a loss. Overall profit may fall and wrong products be promoted.
parts.working: 1 mark packs over-priced/lost sales; 1 mark hampers under-priced/possible losses.

practice.stem: Indus Packaging plc makes 40 product lines, from high-volume standard cartons to small custom orders that need special design and many machine set-ups. Overheads are 60% of total cost and are absorbed using a single direct labour hour rate. The company has recently lost two large contracts for standard cartons to competitors that charged lower prices, while custom orders have increased. A new ABC system would cost $45,000 to install.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should replace absorption costing with activity based costing. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For ABC: overheads are 60% of total cost, so how they are charged matters; the 40 product lines vary greatly in batch size and the custom orders need many set-ups and design hours, so labour-hour absorption is likely to distort costs; recent loss of high-volume contracts suggests these are over-priced; ABC would give better pricing and show which customers and products are profitable.
Against ABC: the $45,000 system cost and staff time; drivers must be chosen and data collected continually; some costs (rent) still have to be apportioned; staff may resist change; benefits are not certain.
Decision: introduce ABC (perhaps first in the custom-order area) because the potential to correct pricing outweighs the cost.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for; up to 2 marks for points against (in context); 1 mark use of case data; 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem:
Bolan Shoes makes one style of leather shoe. Selling price is $50 per pair and direct cost is $18 per pair. Production overheads are $120,000 a year and are absorbed at a budgeted rate of $10 per pair, based on 12,000 budgeted pairs. Inventory is valued on a FIFO basis and there is no opening inventory at the start of Year 1.
Year 1: produced 12,000 pairs, sold 10,000 pairs. Actual overheads were $120,000.
Year 2: produced 9,000 pairs, sold 11,000 pairs. Actual overheads were $120,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory at the end of Year 1 under absorption costing.
parts.working: 1 mark for the cost per pair $28; 1 mark for $56,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for Year 2 under absorption costing, showing the under-absorbed overhead.
parts.working: 1 mark for revenue; 1 mark for cost of sales; 1 mark for the under-absorbed $30,000; 1 mark for the profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the under-absorbed overhead is charged as an expense for Year 2 and is not added to the value of inventory.
parts.answer: The overhead spent exceeds the amount absorbed into production, so the excess is a cost of the period. It is not a cost of individual pairs and so cannot be carried forward in inventory values (IAS 2).
parts.working: 1 mark: the excess is not a cost of making the pairs; 1 mark: IAS 2 requires only production cost (absorbed at normal capacity) to be included in inventory.

practice.stem: Multan Packaging is considering introducing ABC. The one-off cost of setting up the system is $45,000. The annual running cost (staff time and software) would be $12,000. The directors expect that better pricing and withdrawal from two loss-making products would increase profit by $30,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net annual benefit of introducing ABC.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the payback period for the one-off cost, in years.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to introduce ABC. Give two reasons and one risk that depends on the $30,000 estimate.
parts.answer: Introduce it: payback within three years and it improves pricing decisions. Risk: the $30,000 benefit depends on managers acting on the results and on the activity data being accurate; if these fail, the benefit may not be achieved.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons (payback, better decisions, low running cost); 1 mark for a risk tied to the estimate.

practice.stem:
Peshawar Plastics makes three products. The table shows annual figures under ABC. The avoidable ABC overhead is the amount that would stop if the product were discontinued. The unavoidable overhead is shared factory costs that would continue.
Product    Revenue $   Direct costs $   Avoidable ABC overhead $   Unavoidable overhead $
Crates       300,000          180,000                    60,000                   30,000
Bottles      200,000          120,000                    40,000                   15,000
Caps         120,000           80,000                    30,000                   15,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss on product Caps after its unavoidable overhead.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for the loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect on total profit if product Caps is discontinued.
parts.answer: Total profit falls by $10,000: revenue lost $120,000, direct costs saved $80,000, avoidable overhead saved $30,000, so the avoidable contribution of $10,000 is lost. The unavoidable $15,000 continues.
parts.working: 1 mark for lost revenue and saved costs; 1 mark for the avoidable profit of $10,000; 1 mark for the reason the $15,000 is not saved.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to discontinue product Caps. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Keep Caps: it contributes $10,000 a year towards the unavoidable overhead, so discontinuing it would reduce total profit by $10,000. The reported loss comes from allocating overhead that would continue anyway.
parts.working: 1 mark for the recommendation; 1 mark for the avoidable profit reasoning; 1 mark for noting the unavoidable overhead continues.

practice.stem: Kashmir Woollen Mills absorbs overheads at $25 per machine hour. Product Q uses 1,200 machine hours and 60 set-ups a year. Under ABC, machine running costs are $15 per machine hour and each set-up costs $400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead charged to product Q under absorption costing.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead charged to product Q under ABC, using the actual 60 set-ups.
parts.working: 1 mark for the machine running charge; 1 mark for the total including set-ups.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of set-ups at which the ABC charge would equal the absorption charge, and explain what this means for product Q.
parts.answer: Remaining $30,000 − $18,000 = $12,000; 12,000 ÷ 400 = 30 set-ups. Product Q uses 60 set-ups, so it is under-costed by absorption by $12,000 (42,000 − 30,000).
parts.working: 1 mark for $12,000 left for set-ups; 1 mark for 30 set-ups; 1 mark for the explanation that Q is under-costed under absorption.

practice.stem: Shahbaz Furniture, Multan, has 12 staff. It makes 8 styles of furniture in small batches and charges overheads using a single rate per direct labour hour. The owner's son has recently studied ABC and wants to introduce it. The business has a few large orders and many small orders, and two activities (set-ups and quality checks) use much more overhead than labour hours suggest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a small family-owned business should adopt activity based costing, and recommend a course of action.
parts.answer: Content points: ABC gives more accurate product costs where small batches and set-ups drive overhead; it supports better pricing and product decisions. Against: data collection costs time and money in a small business where a few staff keep the records; the benefit depends on the overheads being large enough to matter; ABC may be too complex for the owner to use. A good answer recommends a limited pilot on set-up and quality costs, or simply refining the labour-hour rate into two or three pools, and reviewing the cost of doing so against the benefit.
parts.working: Band 1 (1–4): one-sided, generic points. Band 2 (5–8): clear benefits and costs of ABC linked to this business, with a reasoned view. Band 3 (9–12): balanced evaluation, a clear recommendation with a sensible scale of change, and reference to the cost of data collection against the expected benefit.

practice.stem: Lahore Spice Packers uses ABC for batch set-ups. The set-up pool is $64,000 a year. Before a change in batch sizes, the total number of batches was 160, of which product W had 40. After the change, batch sizes are larger, the total number of batches falls to 120, and product W's batches fall to 30. The set-up pool is unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the set-up cost rate per batch before and after the change.
parts.answer: Before $400 per batch (64,000 ÷ 160); after $533.33 per batch (64,000 ÷ 120)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the set-up cost charged to product W before and after the change, and the set-up cost per unit if W makes 5,000 units.
parts.answer: Before 40 × 400 = $16,000; after 30 × 533.33 = $16,000; per unit $3.20 in both cases
parts.working: 1 mark for each total; 1 mark for the $3.20 per unit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the set-up cost charged to product W does not change, and what this means for the managers' claim that the larger batch size saves money.
parts.answer: The fall in product W's batches is exactly offset by the higher rate per batch, because the pool is unchanged. Using ABC, the larger batches save nothing overall for W, so the saving claim is not supported unless the pool itself falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: the rate rises as the driver volume falls, so the charge is unchanged; 1 mark: the saving claim is not supported unless the pool falls.

practice.stem:
Sukkur Dairy absorbs overheads on machine hours, but its ABC analysis uses three cost pools. Budgeted figures and actual figures for the year are:
Activity              Budgeted cost $   Budgeted driver volume   Actual cost $   Actual driver volume
Set-ups                      180,000                 300 set-ups        175,000               280 set-ups
Quality tests                 90,000               1,800 tests          112,000              2,100 tests
Machine running              120,000              8,000 hours          114,000              7,600 hours

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Set-ups $600 per set-up; quality tests $50 per test; machine running $15 per hour
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorbed and the amount over- or under-absorbed for each activity.
parts.answer: Set-ups: absorbed 280 × 600 = $168,000, under-absorbed $7,000. Quality tests: absorbed 2,100 × 50 = $105,000, under-absorbed $7,000. Machine running: absorbed 7,600 × 15 = $114,000, no over- or under-absorption.
parts.working: 1 mark for each absorbed amount; 1 mark for the under-absorbed amounts (accept $7,000 for set-ups and tests, and nil for machine running).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the total net over- or under-absorbed overhead, and suggest one reason why the set-up costs were higher than the rate predicted.
parts.answer: Net under-absorbed $14,000. Set-up costs were higher than the rate predicted: $175,000 ÷ 280 set-ups = $625 per set-up against $600 budgeted, possibly because set-up labour or materials cost more than planned (for example overtime).
parts.working: 1 mark for $14,000 under-absorbed; 1 mark for a sensible reason (higher set-up cost per set-up, for example overtime or materials).

practice.stem: Chenab Textiles must supply 25,000 units to a buyer at $42 per unit. It needs a profit of 15% of selling price. Direct costs are $26 per unit. Overheads are charged by ABC: set-ups at $150 each (1,000 set-ups in the year for these units) and inspections at $8 each (25,000 inspections, one for each unit).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ABC overhead per unit and the profit per unit at a price of $42.
parts.answer: Overhead $14 per unit (350,000 ÷ 25,000: set-ups 150,000 + inspections 200,000); profit $2 per unit (42 − 26 − 14)
parts.working: 1 mark for overhead per unit; 1 mark for profit per unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum total cost per unit allowed by the 15% margin, and the maximum ABC overhead per unit that would allow it.
parts.answer: Profit $6.30 (15% of $42), so maximum total cost $35.70 per unit; maximum overhead $9.70 per unit (35.70 − 26)
parts.working: 1 mark for the $35.70 maximum total cost; 1 mark for the $9.70 overhead.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many inspections would have to be eliminated if the whole overhead reduction came from inspections at $8 each, and state whether this is realistic.
parts.answer: Reduction needed $14 − $9.70 = $4.30 per unit × 25,000 = $107,500; at $8 each this is 13,438 inspections (about 54% of the total). This is unlikely to be realistic without changing the process.
parts.working: 1 mark for the total reduction $107,500; 1 mark for inspections (13,438); 1 mark for a reasoned view on realism.

practice.stem: Faisalabad Denim makes two products. The machine time available is limited to 3,900 hours a year. The contribution per unit after direct costs and avoidable ABC overheads is $30 for product A (0.5 machine hours per unit) and $32 for product B (1.5 machine hours per unit). Demand is 3,000 units of product A and 2,000 units of product B.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per machine hour for each product.
parts.answer: Product A $60 per machine hour (30 ÷ 0.5); product B $21.33 per machine hour (32 ÷ 1.5)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the production plan that maximises total contribution, and the total contribution.
parts.answer: Make 3,000 units of A (1,500 hours); remaining 2,400 hours make 1,600 units of B. Contribution 3,000 × 30 + 1,600 × 32 = $141,200.
parts.working: 1 mark for A's full demand; 1 mark for the B units from remaining hours; 1 mark for the total.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why product B, which has the higher contribution per unit, is not the better product to prioritise.
parts.answer: Product B uses far more machine time per unit (1.5 hours against 0.5), so it earns less per machine hour; when machine time is the limiting factor, product A should be made first.
parts.working: 1 mark: B earns less per limiting resource; 1 mark: A is prioritised first.

practice.stem: Jade River Toys transfers completed goods from its factory to its warehouse at production cost plus 20%. The production cost of goods completed for the year was $300,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the transfer price of goods completed and the factory profit.
parts.answer: Transfer price $360,000; factory profit $60,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a manufacturer may transfer goods to its trading account at a price above production cost.
parts.answer: To compare the factory's cost with the price of buying the goods from outside, so the factory's efficiency (and the trading section's) can be judged separately; it can also be used to reward factory managers.
parts.working: 1 mark compare with market/outside price; 1 mark measure factory performance separately/manager bonus.

practice.stem: Falcon Paints transfers goods to its trading account at production cost plus 20%. Finished goods inventory at the year end, valued at transfer price, was $48,000. The provision for unrealised profit brought forward was $6,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the provision for unrealised profit at the year end.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the adjustment to the provision for the year and state its effect on profit.
parts.answer: Increase of $1,500, which reduces profit.
parts.working: 8,000 − 6,500 = 1,500 increase (M1); charged against profit (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the value of finished goods inventory in the statement of financial position.

practice.stem: Orchid Soaps, Ipoh, transfers its products from its factory to its shop at production cost plus a mark-up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'unrealised profit' in a manufacturing business.
parts.answer: The factory profit added to goods that are still in finished goods inventory at the year end; it has not been earned because the goods have not been sold to customers.
parts.working: 1 mark factory profit/mark-up in closing inventory; 1 mark not yet sold outside the business.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a provision for unrealised profit is needed.
parts.answer: Without it, inventory would be shown above cost and profit would include profit the business has made from 'selling to itself', so profit and assets would be overstated.
parts.working: 1 mark inventory must be at cost (not above); 1 mark profit/assets would be overstated (realisation/prudence).

practice.stem: Sundarbans Honey processes and bottles honey in its own factory and sells it from its own warehouse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define (i) production cost of goods completed and (ii) transfer price.
parts.answer: (i) The total factory cost (prime cost plus factory overheads, adjusted for work in progress) of goods finished in the period. (ii) The value at which finished goods are passed from the factory to the trading account (production cost plus factory profit, or market value).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where (i) the factory profit and (ii) the provision for unrealised profit are shown in the financial statements.
parts.answer: (i) Added to the gross profit in the statement of profit or loss (transferred from the manufacturing account). (ii) The change is charged/credited in the statement of profit or loss; the balance is deducted from finished goods inventory in the statement of financial position.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Tulip Bakeware transfers goods to its shop at production cost plus 25%. Finished goods at transfer price at the year end were $40,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the provision for unrealised profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the provision is shown in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Deducted from finished goods inventory (shown at $32,000).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the accounting concept that says inventory should not be valued above cost, and explain it.
parts.answer: Prudence: assets and profits should not be overstated, so inventory is shown at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
parts.working: 1 mark prudence (accept realisation: profit is not recognised until goods are sold); 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem: Sialkot Surgical makes surgical scissors in its factory and passes them to its sales division at the price an outside supplier would charge. In the year ended 30 June 2026 the factory completed 9,000 boxes of scissors at a production cost of $270,000. An outside supplier would have charged $36 per box.

parts.label: a

parts.answer: Transfer value $324,000; factory profit $54,000

parts.label: b

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one advantage of transferring goods at market value rather than at production cost.
parts.answer: It shows whether the factory makes goods more cheaply than buying them in, so the factory's efficiency (and the trading section's) can be judged separately; it can be used to reward the factory manager.
parts.working: 1 mark compares with outside price; 1 mark performance evaluation

practice.stem: Finished goods held by Galaxy Shoes at the year end are valued at a transfer price of $75,000.

parts.answer: A 25% margin on transfer price is the same as a 33⅓% mark-up on cost, so more of the transfer price is unrealised profit; in (a) profit is one-fifth of transfer price, in (b) one-quarter.
parts.working: 1 mark mark-up based on cost v margin based on transfer price; 1 mark fraction 25/125 v 25/100.

practice.stem: Crimson Textiles, Faisalabad, transfers goods from its factory to its trading account at production cost plus a factory profit.

parts.label: a

parts.answer: (i) Debit manufacturing account $64,000; credit statement of profit or loss (factory profit) $64,000. (ii) Debit statement of profit or loss $2,300; credit provision for unrealised profit account $2,300.

parts.label: b

practice.stem: Information for Sapphire Glass Ltd for the year: gross profit $212,000; factory profit $88,000; administration expenses $74,500; selling and distribution expenses $52,300; provision for unrealised profit at start $14,000 and at end $16,500.

practice.stem: Lyallpur Looms transfers finished cloth from its factory at production cost plus 20%. At 31 March 2026 finished goods at transfer price were $96,000. parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

parts.label: a
