practice.stem: Mosaic Tiles transfers goods from its factory at production cost plus 15% (the same rate as last year). For the year: production cost of goods completed $500,000; revenue $820,000; finished goods at transfer price $46,000 at the start and $69,000 at the end; administration and selling expenses $110,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year of the business as a whole, using transfer prices.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit if all goods were valued at production cost, with no factory profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two profit figures are the same.
parts.answer: Factory profit is only an internal transfer; the provision removes the part still in unsold inventory, so the only profit recognised is that realised by selling to customers.
parts.working: 1 mark internal transfer/not earned from outside; 1 mark PUP removes unrealised element so totals agree.

practice.stem: The factory manager of Nile Valley Juices receives a bonus of 5% of factory profit. Goods produced this year cost $450,000 and would have cost $540,000 to buy from another manufacturer. The manager proposes that goods should be transferred at production cost plus 30% instead of at market price.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the factory profit (i) using the market price, (ii) using the proposed 30% mark-up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a market-price transfer is a better measure of the factory's performance.
parts.answer: It shows what the business would have paid an outside supplier, so the factory profit shows how much the factory saves by making the goods; a fixed mark-up gives a profit even if the factory is inefficient.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison with buying in; 1 mark mark-up hides inefficiency/rewards cost increases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors which basis to use for the factory manager's bonus. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Market price: the 30% mark-up would raise the bonus by $2,250 (5% of $45,000) without any improvement, and rises automatically if costs rise; market price rewards real cost savings, though market prices can be hard to find and may change.
parts.working: For market price: fair, motivates cost control, comparable with outside. Against: market price may be hard to obtain/volatile; manager cannot control it. For mark-up: simple, certain; but rewards higher costs. 1 mark per point (max 3), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Kestrel Boats transfers goods to its showroom at production cost plus 30%. In the statement of financial position, finished goods are shown at their production cost of $52,000.

practice.stem: Ember Stoves transfers completed goods from its factory to its trading account at production cost plus a fixed mark-up. At the year end, finished goods inventory at transfer price was $57,500; in the statement of financial position it is shown at production cost of $50,000. The factory profit for the year was $72,000. practice.stem: Kohinoor Appliances transfers goods from its factory at production cost plus 25%. At 31 December 2026 finished goods at transfer price were $125,000. This included a batch of 200 fans at a transfer price of $50 each. Owing to a fault, these fans can be sold for only $36 each after repairs of $4 each. The provision for unrealised profit at 1 January 2026 was $21,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the factory profit under (i) the current policy and (ii) market value.

Conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark overall profit unchanged; up to 2 marks for points on each side; 1 mark conclusion

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

practice.stem: The company classifies interest paid and tax paid as operating cash flows, interest and dividends received as investing cash flows, and dividends paid as financing cash flows.

(ii) Purchase of machinery
(iii) Tax paid
(iv) Interest received
(v) Repayment of debentures
(vi) A bonus issue of shares
parts.answer:
(i) Financing activities

(iii) Operating activities
(iv) Investing activities
(v) Financing activities

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'cash equivalents'.
parts.answer: Short-term, highly liquid investments that are readily convertible to known amounts of cash and have an insignificant risk of change in value – usually with a maturity of three months or less from acquisition.

practice.stem: Kestrel Foods Ltd: at 1 January 2026 tax payable was $18,400 and interest accrued was $900. The statement of profit or loss for 2026 shows a tax charge of $23,900 and finance costs of $6,200. At 31 December 2026 tax payable was $21,700 and interest accrued was $1,300.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

parts.answer: Both are deducted from cash generated from operations to give net cash from operating activities.

practice.stem: Ravi Plastics Ltd has 400,000 ordinary shares. In April 2026 it paid a final dividend for 2025 of $0.05 per share. In September 2026 it paid an interim dividend for 2026 of $0.03 per share. In February 2027 the directors proposed a final dividend for 2026 of $0.06 per share.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the proposed final dividend for 2026 is not included.
parts.answer: It was proposed after the year end and not paid during 2026, so there was no cash outflow in the year; it is not even a liability at 31 December 2026 (IAS 10), and will appear as a cash flow in 2027 when paid.
parts.working: 1 mark: no cash paid in 2026; 1 mark: not a liability at year end / included in 2027.

practice.stem: Property, plant and equipment of Hilltop Ltd had a carrying amount of $340,000 at 1 April 2026 and $392,000 at 31 March 2027. Depreciation for the year was $46,000. During the year equipment with a carrying amount of $18,000 was sold for $15,500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a large net outflow from investing activities is not necessarily a bad sign.

practice.stem:

parts.text: Explain why dividends paid are not an investing activity.
parts.answer: Investing activities are the purchase and sale of long-term assets and investments. Dividends paid are a return of money to the owners, which is a financing transaction, not a payment for an investment.
parts.working: 1 mark for investing being about assets and investments; 1 mark for dividends being a payment to owners (a financing flow).

parts.text: Calculate the profit from operations.

parts.label: d

Quartz Minerals Ltd: extracts from the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2027
Statement of profit or loss: profit from operations $104,000; finance costs $9,600; tax $24,000; profit for the year $70,400.

practice.stem: Flint Ltd's profit before tax for 2026 was $61,000. This was after finance costs of $7,700 and after including investment income of $5,400 (interest receivable $3,600 and dividends received $1,800). Interest receivable accrued was $700 at the start of the year and $1,100 at the end. During the year the company bought property, plant and equipment for $70,000 and sold investments for $12,000 (their carrying amount). The company classifies interest paid and tax paid as operating cash flows, interest and dividends received as investing cash flows, and dividends paid as financing cash flows.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit from operations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the interest received.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare the investing activities section of the statement of cash flows.
parts.answer:
Cash flows from investing activities
                                                   $
Purchase of property, plant and equipment   (70,000)
Proceeds from sale of investments             12,000
Interest received                              3,200
Dividends received                             1,800
Net cash used in investing activities       (53,000)
parts.working: B1 purchase and sale; B1 interest 3,200 and dividends 1,800; B1 net (53,000).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why investment income is deducted when calculating profit from operations.
parts.answer: It is not an operating item; the cash actually received is shown under investing activities, so it would otherwise be counted twice.

practice.stem:
Summary statements of cash flows of Marble Furniture Ltd:
                                             2026       2025
                                                $          $
Net cash from operating activities         38,000     92,000
Net cash used in investing activities   (145,000)   (30,000)
Issue of debentures                       100,000          –
Dividends paid                           (40,000)   (40,000)
At 31 December 2026 the company had a bank overdraft of $21,000. Profit for the year rose by 15% in 2026. Inventories and trade receivables both rose sharply during 2026, and the investing outflow was for a new factory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net change in cash and cash equivalents for 2026 and the balance at 1 January 2026.
parts.answer: Decrease of $47,000; balance at 1 January 2026 $26,000 (in hand)
parts.working: B1 net decrease 47,000; B1 opening 26,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the shareholders whether they should be concerned about the company's cash position. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Concerns: operating cash flow fell from $92,000 to $38,000 although profit rose 15% – profit is tied up in inventories and receivables (poor working-capital control); cash moved from $26,000 in hand to a $21,000 overdraft; dividends of $40,000 were paid that exceed operating cash; the new debentures add interest costs and must be repaid.
Reassurance: the outflow was mainly a one-off investment in a new factory, financed largely by long-term debentures (matching long-term finance to long-term assets); the factory should raise future profits and cash; the company is still profitable.
Decision: some concern – the investment is sensible, but management must improve credit control and inventory levels and may need to cut the dividend until operating cash flow recovers.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for concerns using figures; up to 2 marks for reassuring points; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three uses of a statement of cash flows to the shareholders and managers of a company.
parts.answer: Any three: shows how cash was generated and used; shows whether operating activities generate enough cash to pay interest, tax and dividends; helps assess liquidity and the ability to pay debts; shows how investment was financed; helps forecast future cash flows; cash figures are hard to manipulate and easy to compare.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a statement of cash flows is useful in addition to a statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: Profit is based on the accruals concept and includes non-cash items such as depreciation and provisions, so a profitable business can still run out of cash. The statement of cash flows shows actual cash movements and liquidity.
parts.working: 1 mark: profit uses accruals/non-cash items; 1 mark: cash flows show liquidity/actual cash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a profitable company may still need to borrow money.
parts.answer: Any two: profit is not cash, so money can be tied up in receivables and inventory; cash is needed for non-current assets; tax, loan repayments or dividends may fall due before cash comes in from sales; growth needs working capital.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason, with an explanation of why profit and cash differ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three uses of a statement of cash flows to a supplier that is considering giving the company 60 days' credit.
parts.answer: Any three: shows whether operations generate enough cash to pay suppliers on time; shows the cash balance and short-term liquidity; shows how much cash is committed to investing or loan repayments; shows whether the company is likely to pay late.
parts.working: 1 mark for each use, stated in terms of paying suppliers, liquidity or commitments.

practice.stem: Heron Packaging Ltd, year ended 30 June 2026, also bought property, plant and equipment for $74,000 in the same year, and its net cash from operating activities was $168,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the free cash flow, defined as net cash from operating activities less purchase of property, plant and equipment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why free cash flow is useful to a shareholder when considering dividends.
parts.answer: It shows the cash left after the company has maintained and expanded its non-current assets, so it indicates how much could be paid to shareholders or used to repay debt.
parts.working: 1 mark for cash left after investment; 1 mark for the link to dividends or debt repayment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two limitations of using the statement of cash flows alone to judge a company's performance.
parts.answer: Any two: it is a historical record and does not forecast future cash; it shows nothing about the value of assets or the profit trend; year-end payments can be timed to flatter the figures; it omits obligations not yet paid, such as lease commitments.
parts.working: 1 mark for each limitation explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a shareholder may prefer a company with higher net cash from operating activities to one with higher reported profit.
parts.answer: Cash pays dividends, loans and investment; profit can include non-cash items such as depreciation or accrued income; cash is harder to manipulate through accounting policies, so it gives a clearer view of the company's ability to pay.
parts.working: 1 mark for cash paying dividends and debts; 1 mark for profit including non-cash or accrual items; 1 mark for cash being harder to manipulate or a clearer test of ability to pay.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by cash generated from operations, and why a lender finds this figure useful.
parts.answer: Cash generated from operations is the cash the business earns from its trading before interest and tax are paid. A lender finds it useful because it shows the cash available to pay interest and repay the loan.
parts.working: 1 mark for a clear definition (cash from trading before interest and tax); 1 mark for the lender's use (paying interest and repaying debt).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a bonus issue of shares does not appear in the statement of cash flows.
parts.answer: No cash is received or paid; a bonus issue only transfers amounts within equity from reserves to share capital. Only transactions involving cash appear in the statement.
parts.working: 1 mark for no cash movement; 1 mark for the transfer within equity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two items that make net cash from operating activities differ from profit from operations, and explain how each creates the difference.
parts.answer: Any two items, each with an explanation: depreciation (a non-cash expense, so cash is higher than profit); an increase in inventory (cash spent on stock, so cash is lower); an increase in trade receivables (sales not yet collected, so cash is lower); an increase in trade payables (cash not yet paid, so cash is higher); a profit on disposal (the sale proceeds appear under investing, so it is removed from operating cash).
parts.working: 1 mark for each item identified (2); 1 mark for each explanation of the direction of the difference (2).

practice.stem: Ivory Ltd made a profit from operations of $120,000 for 2026, but its bank balance fell sharply. Its statement of cash flows shows: depreciation $26,000; increase in inventories $48,000; increase in trade receivables $61,000; decrease in trade payables $19,000; net cash from operating activities $18,000; net cash used in investing activities $200,000; net cash from financing activities $50,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net change in cash and cash equivalents for 2026.
parts.answer: Decrease of $132,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the figures, explain three reasons why Ivory Ltd's cash fell although it was profitable.
parts.answer:
1 Working capital absorbed cash: inventories rose by $48,000 and receivables by $61,000, so much of the profit is tied up in unsold goods and unpaid customer balances.
2 Suppliers were paid faster: payables fell by $19,000, another outflow not shown in profit.
3 Heavy investment: $200,000 was spent on non-current assets, only $50,000 of which was financed by long-term financing; the rest came from existing cash.
(Depreciation of $26,000 reduced profit without any cash outflow, which partly offset these.)
parts.working: For each of three reasons: 1 mark for identifying it and 1 mark for supporting it with figures from the question.

practice.stem: Heron Packaging Ltd, year ended 30 June 2026: profit from operations $210,000; net cash from operating activities $168,000 (after interest and tax paid).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash conversion ratio: net cash from operating activities as a percentage of profit from operations, to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 168,000 ÷ 210,000 × 100 = 80.0%. 1 mark for the formula; 1 for the answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why this ratio could be below 100% in a growing company.
parts.answer: Any two: receivables increased, so sales have not yet become cash; inventory was built up; payables were paid down; non-cash income was included in profit.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason linked to a working capital change.

practice.stem: Company A and Company B both have a year ended 31 December 2026. Net cash from operating activities: A $120,000; B $40,000. Net cash used in investing activities: A $80,000; B $5,000. Net cash from (used in) financing activities: A an inflow of $5,000; B an outflow of $30,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net change in cash and cash equivalents for each company.
parts.answer: Company A: +$45,000; Company B: +$5,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which company has the stronger cash position, giving two reasons.
parts.answer: Company A generates strong operating cash and is investing for growth while still raising cash, so it is in a healthier position. Company B's operating cash is weak and it has used cash to repay debt, which limits its ability to invest. Any well-reasoned judgement with two supported reasons earns full marks.
parts.working: 1 mark for stating a judgement; 1 mark for each reason supported by the figures.

practice.stem: Lindon Textiles Ltd, year ended 31 December 2026: net cash from operating activities $152,000 (after interest paid and tax paid); interest paid $16,000; tax paid $22,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash interest cover, to 1 decimal place. Cash interest cover = (net cash from operating activities + interest paid + tax paid) ÷ interest paid.
parts.answer: 11.9 times
parts.working: (152,000 + 16,000 + 22,000) ÷ 16,000 = 190,000 ÷ 16,000 = 11.875, so 11.9 times. 1 mark for the operating cash before interest and tax; 1 for the ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what a high cash interest cover tells a lender.
parts.answer: The company generates many times the cash needed to pay its interest, so the loan is well protected and the risk of default is low.
parts.working: 1 mark for generating well above interest; 1 mark for the lower risk of default.

practice.stem: Cedar Mills Ltd, year ended 31 December 2026: net cash from operating activities $96,000; dividends paid $48,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash dividend cover, that is net cash from operating activities ÷ dividends paid.
parts.answer: 2.0 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a shareholder would look at cash dividend cover.
parts.answer: It shows how many times the dividend is covered by actual cash, so it indicates whether the dividend is affordable without borrowing.
parts.working: 1 mark for cover by actual cash; 1 mark for affordability without borrowing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why cash dividend cover might differ from profit-based dividend cover.
parts.answer: Profit includes non-cash items such as depreciation and accrued income, and cash is affected by timing of receipts and payments and by investment, so the two covers can differ.
parts.working: 1 mark for the non-cash or timing difference; 1 mark for a clear explanation.

practice.stem: Ardent Steel Ltd, year ended 31 December 2026: net cash from operating activities $300,000; purchase of property, plant and equipment $240,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capital expenditure ratio, that is net cash from operating activities ÷ purchase of PPE, to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 1.25 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what a ratio below 1 would indicate.
parts.answer: The company spends more on new non-current assets than it generates from operations, so it must rely on existing cash, new borrowing or share issues to finance expansion.
parts.working: 1 mark for capex exceeding operating cash; 1 mark for the need for other finance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one risk of a ratio that stays below 1 for several years.
parts.answer: Borrowing rises to fund the shortfall, so interest and repayments increase and the company may struggle to pay its debts.
parts.working: 1 mark for the risk; 1 mark for the link to borrowing or cash shortage.

practice.stem: Fernhill Stores Ltd, year ended 31 December 2026: inventory increased by $18,000; trade receivables increased by $6,500; trade payables increased by $9,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net effect of the working capital changes on cash.
parts.answer: A net outflow of $15,500
parts.working: Increase in inventory −18,000; increase in receivables −6,500; increase in payables +9,000; net = −15,500. 1 mark for the signs; 1 for the total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a growing business often has this effect on cash.
parts.answer: Growth means holding more stock and offering more credit to customers, which uses cash before it is collected; some extra cash is gained from suppliers' credit.
parts.working: 1 mark for stock and receivables tying up cash; 1 mark for the offsetting payables benefit or growth link.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why depreciation is added back to profit from operations when calculating cash generated from operations.
parts.answer: Depreciation is a non-cash expense deducted in arriving at profit; no cash left the business when it was charged, so it is added back to reach cash.
parts.working: 1 mark for depreciation being non-cash; 1 mark for adding it back to reach cash.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the purchase of a non-current asset still appears as a cash outflow.
parts.answer: The payment is real cash spent on acquiring long-term capacity, so it appears under investing activities. It is not an operating expense, so it does not reduce profit from operations.
parts.working: 1 mark for a real cash outflow in investing; 1 mark for not being an operating expense.

practice.stem: Mistral Office Supplies Ltd has credit sales of $730,000 a year (365 days). Its average trade receivables currently represent 60 days of credit sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash released if receivable days fall from 60 to 45, using 365 days.
parts.working: Receivables at 60 days = 730,000 × 60 ÷ 365 = 120,000; at 45 days = 730,000 × 45 ÷ 365 = 90,000; release = 30,000. 1 mark for the receivables; 1 for the difference.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one risk the company faces by pushing customers to pay sooner.
parts.answer: Customers may move to a competitor that offers longer credit, so sales could fall; discounts for early payment reduce income.
parts.working: 1 mark for the risk; 1 mark for the effect on sales or income.

practice.stem: Maplecourt Ltd has 500,000 ordinary shares in issue. Its net cash from operating activities for the year was $210,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash from operating activities per share.
parts.answer: $0.42 per share

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an investor might use this cash measure rather than earnings per share.
parts.answer: Earnings per share uses profit, which includes non-cash items, while this measure shows the actual cash the business generated for each share; this shows the shareholder the cash backing for dividends. A good answer compares the two measures and notes that they can differ.
parts.working: 1 mark for cash being less affected by non-cash items or accruals; 1 mark for showing cash available for dividends or investment; 1 mark for comparing with EPS.

practice.stem: Quayside Engineering Ltd had a bank overdraft of $12,000 at 1 January 2026. The net increase in cash and cash equivalents for the year was $27,400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the closing cash and cash equivalents.
parts.working: Opening bank overdraft −12,000 + net increase 27,400 = 15,400.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a bank overdraft repayable on demand is included within cash and cash equivalents.
parts.answer: It is part of the company's cash management, because the overdraft balance changes daily with the bank balance; under IAS 7 it is netted against cash and cash equivalents.
parts.working: 1 mark for the overdraft being part of cash management; 1 mark for IAS 7 netting it within cash and cash equivalents.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why shareholders should read the statement of cash flows together with the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: The statement of financial position shows the position at one date, while the cash flow statement explains the movements during the year. Together they show how the change in cash and debt came about, for example whether a rise in borrowing funded investment. Reading them together shows whether profit has turned into cash.
parts.working: 1 mark for position at a date versus movements; 1 mark for explaining how the change in debt or cash arose; 1 mark for linking profit to cash.

practice.stem: Terrace Pharmacies Ltd, year ended 31 December 2026: net cash from operating activities $84,000; current liabilities at the year end $120,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash flow ratio, net cash from operating activities ÷ current liabilities, to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what a result below 1 indicates about the pharmacies' short-term position.
parts.answer: Operating cash flow over the year is less than the bills due within a year, so the company would need to use existing cash, sell assets or borrow to pay its current liabilities.
parts.working: 1 mark for operating cash below short-term obligations; 1 mark for the need for other finance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one better comparison to make this ratio meaningful and explain why.
parts.answer: Compare with the same ratio for earlier years or for other pharmacies, since a single figure has no benchmark on its own.
parts.working: 1 mark for the comparison; 1 mark for explaining that a single figure has no benchmark.

practice.stem: Brightline Telecoms Ltd: borrowings $120,000 and cash $15,600 at 1 January 2026. During 2026: net cash from operating activities $96,000 (after interest and tax paid); purchase of property, plant and equipment $60,000; dividends paid $22,000; a new loan of $40,000 received; no loans repaid. Borrowings at 31 December 2026 were $160,000. Net debt is borrowings less cash and cash equivalents.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net change in cash and cash equivalents for 2026.
parts.answer: An increase of $54,000
parts.working: 96,000 − 60,000 − 22,000 + 40,000 = 54,000. 1 mark for the correct signs; 1 for the total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net debt at 1 January 2026 and at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer: Net debt of $104,400 at 1 January 2026 and $90,400 at 31 December 2026

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why net debt fell during 2026 even though borrowings rose.
parts.answer: The new loan increased borrowings by $40,000, but cash rose by $54,000, so the cash increase was larger than the rise in debt. Net debt measures debt after deducting cash, so it fell by $14,000, meaning the company is less reliant on borrowing.
parts.working: 1 mark for borrowings rising by 40,000; 1 mark for cash rising by more than that; 1 mark for net debt falling by 14,000 and the meaning of that for the company.

practice.stem: Solaris Foods Ltd at 31 December 2026: total equity $480,000; non-current liabilities $220,000. Net cash from operating activities for 2026 was $118,000. Cash return on capital employed is defined here as net cash from operating activities as a percentage of capital employed, where capital employed is total equity plus non-current liabilities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capital employed at 31 December 2026, defined as total equity plus non-current liabilities.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cash return on capital employed as a percentage, to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 118,000 ÷ 700,000 × 100 = 16.857%, so 16.9%. 1 mark for the formula; 1 for the answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how this measure differs from return on capital employed based on profit.
parts.answer: Return on capital employed uses profit, which includes non-cash items and accrual adjustments, while this measure uses cash from operations, so it shows how much cash the capital actually produces and is less affected by depreciation policy. Both use the same denominator, so they can be compared.
parts.working: 1 mark for profit including non-cash items; 1 mark for cash showing actual generation; 1 mark for the comparison or the effect of accounting policy.

practice.stem:
Tarn Ceramics Ltd, year ends 31 December. Profit from operations and net cash from operating activities were:
2024: profit $150,000; net cash from operating activities $162,000
2025: profit $175,000; net cash from operating activities $140,000
2026: profit $230,000; net cash from operating activities $120,000
Cash conversion = net cash from operating activities ÷ profit from operations × 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash conversion ratio for each year, to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the trend and suggest one possible cause of it.
parts.answer: The ratio has fallen sharply, from above 100% to about 52%, so profits are increasingly not turning into cash. A likely cause is rising receivables or inventory, or lower customer payments, which ties up cash even as reported profit grows. Any reasonable cause supported by the data earns credit.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying the falling trend; 1 mark for explaining that profit is not turning into cash; 1 mark for a plausible cause linked to working capital.

practice.stem: Northmere Print Ltd at 31 December 2026: current assets $240,000, of which inventory is $150,000; current liabilities $100,000. Its current ratio is 2.4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the acid test ratio (current assets less inventory, divided by current liabilities), to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: (240,000 − 150,000) ÷ 100,000 = 0.9. 1 mark for removing inventory; 1 for the answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a company with a current ratio of 2.4 may still struggle to pay its suppliers on time.
parts.answer: Most of the current assets are inventory, which cannot be turned into cash quickly, so the quick assets are only 0.9 times the current liabilities. Cash flows, not the ratio, decide whether bills can be paid on time. A company can have large stocks of slow-moving goods and still lack cash.
parts.working: 1 mark for inventory being a large part of current assets; 1 mark for the acid test being below 1; 1 mark for the timing of cash flows; 1 mark for the point that the ratio does not show cash.

practice.stem: Pinnacle Group bought 80% of the shares of Westbrook Ltd for $95,000 cash. Westbrook Ltd had cash of $12,000 at the date of acquisition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash outflow shown under investing activities for the acquisition.
parts.working: Cash paid 95,000 − cash acquired 12,000 = 83,000. 1 mark for the subtraction; 1 for the answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the cash acquired is deducted from the consideration paid.
parts.answer: The group's cash has really increased by the cash it acquired, so the net cash cost of the purchase is the consideration less the cash obtained. Showing the gross figure would overstate the cash spent on the investment.
parts.working: 1 mark for the net cost being the real cash spent; 1 mark for the gross figure overstating the outflow.

practice.stem: Greenhill Ltd, year ended 31 December 2026: net cash used in operating activities $30,000 (after interest and tax paid); proceeds from sale of land $190,000; purchase of property, plant and equipment $25,000; repayment of a bank loan $60,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net change in cash and cash equivalents for the year.
parts.answer: An increase of $75,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net change excluding the sale of land.
parts.answer: A decrease of $115,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the increase in cash is not a sign of financial health.
parts.answer: Operations used cash (an outflow of $30,000) and the cash increase came from a one-off sale of land. Without it cash would have fallen by $115,000, so the business is not generating cash from its trading. Once the land is sold it cannot be sold again, so the position is not sustainable.
parts.working: 1 mark for operations being a cash outflow; 1 mark for the one-off nature of the land sale; 1 mark for the sustainability or trend point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that the statement of cash flows gives a more reliable picture of a company's financial health than the statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: Content points: for: cash is harder to manipulate and less affected by accruals, depreciation policy and judgements; it shows liquidity and the ability to pay debts and dividends; it reveals working capital problems that profit hides. Against: it is historical and does not show future cash flows; timing of year-end payments can distort it; it does not show profitability or asset values, which the statement of profit or loss and statement of financial position reveal; a single year can be misleading. A strong answer weighs both sides and reaches a judgement that the two statements are complementary.
parts.working: Band 1 (1–3): describes one or two features. Band 2 (4–6): explains reliability points on both sides with some balance. Band 3 (7–8): evaluates the view with reference to context. Band 4 (9–10): reaches a supported judgement that integrates both statements.

practice.stem: Silverleaf Bakery reduced its inventory from $90,000 to $50,000 during the year by delaying purchases and selling stock.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the effect of the inventory reduction on net cash from operating activities.
parts.answer: An inflow of $40,000
parts.working: 90,000 − 50,000 = 40,000 released as cash.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two risks to the bakery of running down its inventory this far.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: running out of stock on popular lines means lost sales; reduced choice can drive customers to rivals; ingredients bought in small batches can cost more; the rapid reduction may signal problems with supplier payments or demand.
parts.working: 1 mark for each risk identified (2) and 1 mark for each explanation (2).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A delivery van was bought for $48,000. It is expected to be used for 6 years and then sold for $6,000. The straight-line method is used. What is the annual depreciation charge?
A $7,000
B $8,000
C $6,000
D $9,000
parts.working: (48,000 − 6,000) ÷ 6 = $7,000. $8,000 ignores the residual value; $9,000 wrongly adds the residual value to cost.

practice.stem: Hamza Printers, Lahore, bought a printing machine on 1 January 2024 for Rs 1,250,000. Installation cost Rs 50,000. The machine is expected to last 5 years and then be sold for Rs 100,000. The straight-line method is used and the financial year ends on 31 December.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual depreciation charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the machine at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the accounting concept applied when depreciation is charged, and explain how it is applied.
parts.answer: Matching (accruals) concept: the cost of the machine is spread over the years in which it helps to earn revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming matching/accruals; 1 mark for explaining that the cost is charged against the revenue of the periods that benefit from the asset.

practice.stem: Rukhsana runs a tailoring workshop in Peshawar and owns sewing machines and a delivery motorcycle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two causes of depreciation of non-current assets.
parts.answer: Wear and tear through use; obsolescence (also: passage of time, depletion).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: wear and tear; obsolescence (new technology/fashion); passage of time (e.g. lease); depletion (e.g. a quarry).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect on the financial statements if a business does not provide for depreciation.
parts.answer: Expenses are understated so profit is overstated, and non-current assets are overstated in the statement of financial position.
parts.working: 1 mark profit overstated (expenses too low); 1 mark non-current assets/capital overstated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State three figures needed to calculate a straight-line depreciation charge.
parts.answer: Cost of the asset, expected residual value, expected useful life.
parts.working: All three for 2 marks; two correct for 1 mark.

practice.stem: A freelance designer in Dhaka buys a laptop for $2,400 and depreciates it at 30% per annum using the reducing balance method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for each of the first two years.
parts.answer: Year 1 $720; year 2 $504

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount at the end of year 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the reducing balance method suits a laptop.
parts.answer: Laptops become obsolete quickly and lose most value in the first years, so a larger charge early matches the fall in value.
parts.working: 1 mark obsolescence/early loss of value; 1 mark matching charge with benefit/value.

practice.stem: Zainab Fashions, Faisalabad, bought shop fittings for Rs 360,000 on 1 July 2025. Its year ends on 31 December. Fittings are depreciated at 12.5% per annum on cost, calculated monthly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for the years ended 31 December 2025 and 31 December 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The owner says, 'Depreciation means I am saving money to replace the fittings.' Explain why this is not correct.
parts.answer: Depreciation is a non-cash expense: it reduces profit but no money is set aside, so cash is not saved unless the owner chooses to keep it in a separate fund.
parts.working: 1 mark non-cash/book entry; 1 mark no cash set aside/does not create a replacement fund.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A machine was bought at the start of year 1 for $80,000. It is depreciated at 25% per annum using the reducing balance method. What is the depreciation charge for year 3?
A $11,250
B $20,000
C $15,000
D $33,750
parts.working: Year 1: 25% × 80,000 = 20,000 (CA 60,000). Year 2: 25% × 60,000 = 15,000 (CA 45,000). Year 3: 25% × 45,000 = $11,250. $20,000 is the straight-line style charge on cost; $33,750 is the carrying amount at the end of year 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business with a year end of 31 December bought equipment for $36,000 on 1 April 2025. Depreciation is charged at 20% per annum on cost, calculated on a monthly basis. What is the depreciation charge for the year ended 31 December 2025?
A $5,400
B $7,200
C $1,800
D $6,000
parts.working: 20% × 36,000 = 7,200 per year; April to December = 9 months; 7,200 × 9/12 = $5,400. $7,200 charges a full year; $1,800 charges only 3 months.

practice.stem: SwiftDrop, a courier business in Nairobi, bought a delivery van for $40,000. It uses the reducing balance method at 40% per annum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for each of the four years using the reducing balance method.
parts.working: 40% × 40,000 = 16,000; 40% × 24,000 = 9,600; 40% × 14,400 = 5,760; 40% × 8,640 = 3,456. M1 for applying 40% to the carrying amount, A2 all four correct (A1 for two or three correct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The van will be worth $5,184 after four years. Calculate the annual charge if the straight-line method were used instead.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the reducing balance method may be more suitable for the van.
parts.answer: A van loses more of its value in its early years, and repair costs rise as it gets older, so a high early charge gives a more even total cost each year.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: van loses most value early; carrying amount closer to resale value; maintenance rises with age so depreciation + repairs is more even; van used most heavily when new.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the effect on profit for year 1 of using the reducing balance method instead of the straight-line method.
parts.answer: Profit is $7,296 lower.
parts.working: 16,000 − 8,704 = 7,296 (M1); profit lower/decreases (A1).

practice.stem: Oakfield Dental Clinic depreciates office equipment at 20% per annum on cost. A full year's depreciation is charged in the year of purchase and none in the year of disposal. On 1 January 2025 equipment at cost was $90,000; none of it was fully depreciated. On 3 March 2025 new equipment was bought for $14,000. On 30 November 2025 an item bought in 2022 for $8,000 was sold for $2,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for office equipment for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.working: Equipment held at year end at cost: 90,000 − 8,000 + 14,000 = 96,000 (M1 M1). 20% × 96,000 = $19,200 (A1). Full year on the new item, nothing on the item sold.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss on the disposal of the item sold.
parts.answer: Loss $700
parts.working: Depreciation charged 2022, 2023, 2024 = 3 × 1,600 = 4,800 (M1). Carrying amount = 8,000 − 4,800 = 3,200 (A1). Proceeds 2,500 → loss $700 (A1).

practice.stem: Lumière Bakery, in Montreal, bought an oven for $50,000 at the start of year 1. Its policy is to depreciate the oven at 20% per annum using the reducing balance method. Years 1 and 2 were correct, but in year 3 the bookkeeper charged 20% of the original cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the correct depreciation charge for year 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of the error on the profit for year 3.
parts.answer: Profit understated by $3,600
parts.working: Charged 10,000, should be 6,400; difference 3,600 (M1); profit understated (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of the error on the statement of financial position at the end of year 3.
parts.answer: Accumulated depreciation overstated by $3,600, so the carrying amount of non-current assets (and capital) is understated by the same amount.
parts.working: 1 mark non-current assets/carrying amount understated by the amount; 1 mark capital (retained profit) understated.

practice.stem:
Shalimar Traders depreciates buildings at 2% per annum on cost (straight-line) and fixtures and fittings at 15% per annum using the reducing balance method. Land is not depreciated. Balances at 1 January 2025:
                         Cost $   Accumulated depreciation $
Land                    200,000                            0
Buildings               350,000                       56,000
Fixtures and fittings    64,000                       25,000
There were no purchases or sales during 2025.

parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charges for the year and prepare a journal entry to record them. A narrative is not required.

Buildings $7,000; fixtures $5,850.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why land is not depreciated.
parts.answer: Land has an unlimited useful life (it does not wear out).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Al-Noor Motors, a garage in Karachi, uses the revaluation method for its loose tools. On 1 January 2025 the tools were valued at Rs 84,000. During the year tools costing Rs 37,500 were bought and paid by bank. On 31 December 2025 the tools were valued at Rs 96,300.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation of loose tools for the year.
parts.working: Opening valuation 84,000 + purchases 37,500 − closing valuation 96,300 (M1) = Rs 25,200 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the loose tools account for the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.working: B1 opening valuation debit; B1 purchases debit; B1 depreciation credit and closing valuation c/d.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the revaluation method is used for loose tools rather than the straight-line method.
parts.answer: Loose tools are many low-cost items, so keeping a record of each one is impractical; they are lost, broken or replaced often, so a yearly valuation reflects their real use.

practice.stem: Cloudline Data, a web-hosting company in Singapore, bought server equipment for $125,000. It expects to sell the equipment for $27,000 after three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual reducing balance rate that reduces the cost to the residual value in exactly three years. Give your answer as a whole-number percentage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for year 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount at the end of year 2.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the business chose the reducing balance method for this equipment.
parts.answer: The equipment (e.g. computer servers) becomes out of date quickly and loses most of its value early, so a higher charge in early years matches its fall in value and use.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying early loss of value/obsolescence; 1 mark for linking to matching cost with benefit.

practice.stem: Kestrel Tools has a financial year ending 31 December. Its draft profit for 2025 is $68,400. A machine was bought on 1 October 2025 for $40,000; delivery cost $1,200. Policy: 15% per annum straight-line on cost, calculated monthly. The bookkeeper charged a full year's depreciation of $6,000 on the $40,000 and debited the delivery cost to carriage inwards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the correct depreciation charge for the machine for the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year.
parts.answer:
$

Add delivery cost wrongly expensed     1,200
Less correct depreciation            (1,545)
Corrected profit                      74,055
parts.working: B1 add back 6,000; B1 add back 1,200; B1 deduct own correct depreciation; B1 corrected profit (own figure).

practice.stem: Farhan is opening a furniture workshop in Sialkot and will apply for a bank loan after his first year. He buys a CNC machine for $90,000, expected to last 5 years with a residual value of $10,000. He can use the straight-line method or the reducing balance method at 35% per annum. Profit before depreciation for year 1 is expected to be $60,000. He wants to choose the method that shows the higher profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for year 1 under each method.
parts.answer: Straight-line $44,000; reducing balance $28,500

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Farhan which method he should use. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Advice should favour the method that best reflects how the machine is used, applied consistently, rather than the one that flatters the loan application (e.g. reducing balance if the machine loses value fast).
parts.working: Points for SL: higher year-1 profit by $15,500; simple; suits even use. Points for RB: matches heavy early use/fall in value; more prudent; profits more even when repairs rise. Consistency concept: once chosen, the method must be kept, so a switch later to boost profit is not allowed; a bank will look at cash flow and security, not only profit; choosing a method only to impress the bank misleads users. Up to 4 marks for points (max 3 one side), 2 marks for a justified decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A machine cost $30,000. Accumulated depreciation on it was $18,000 when it was sold for $9,500 cash. What was the result of the disposal?
A Loss of $2,500
B Profit of $9,500
C Profit of $2,500
D Loss of $20,500
parts.answer: A Loss of $2,500
parts.working: Carrying amount = 30,000 − 18,000 = 12,000. Proceeds 9,500 < 12,000 → loss of $2,500. 'Profit of $2,500' reverses the comparison; 'Loss of $20,500' ignores the accumulated depreciation.

practice.stem: Greenleaf Accountants, Cape Town, sold an old office computer server for $7,200 cash. It had cost $18,000 and accumulated depreciation was $11,250.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the server at the date of sale.
parts.working: Cost 18,000 − accumulated depreciation 11,250 (M1) = $6,750 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss on disposal and state where it is shown in the financial statements.
parts.answer: Profit $450, shown as other income (added to gross profit) in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.working: 7,200 − 6,750 = 450 (M1) profit (A1); B1 statement of profit or loss as income (or deducted from expenses).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the double entry for the cash received.
parts.answer: Debit bank (cash); credit disposal account.
parts.working: 1 mark each side.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A machine which cost $52,000 was sold for $14,000 cash. The sale gave a profit on disposal of $3,500. What was the accumulated depreciation on the machine at the date of sale?
A $34,500
B $38,000
C $41,500
D $48,500
parts.working: Carrying amount = proceeds − profit = 14,000 − 3,500 = 10,500; accumulated depreciation = 52,000 − 10,500 = 41,500. B (38,000) uses 52,000 − 14,000 and ignores the profit; A adds the profit to the proceeds.

practice.stem:
Mei owns a catering business in Kuala Lumpur. Her old van has a carrying amount of $11,500. She needs a new van with a list price of $58,000.
Option 1: the dealer gives a trade-in allowance of $13,000 on the old van and Mei pays the balance.
Option 2: Mei sells the old van privately for $15,500 after paying $600 for advertising, and the dealer gives her a 4% trade discount on the new van because there is no trade-in.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash paid out under each option.
parts.answer: Option 1 $45,000; option 2 $40,780

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Mei which option to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Option 2 saves $4,220 in cash, but Mei must weigh the time, risk and delay of a private sale.
parts.working: For option 2: saves 4,220; higher profit on disposal (3,400 v 1,500). For option 1: quick and certain, no advertising effort, no risk the private buyer pulls out, no period without a van. 1 mark each for up to 3 points (both sides), 1 mark for a justified decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business buys a new van and the dealer accepts its old van in part-exchange, giving a trade-in allowance. Which entries record the trade-in allowance?
A Debit disposal account; credit vans account
B Debit vans account; credit disposal account
C Debit bank account; credit disposal account
D Debit disposal account; credit bank account
parts.answer: B Debit vans account; credit disposal account
parts.working: The allowance is part of the cost of the new van (debit vans) and acts as the 'proceeds' of the old van (credit disposal). C would mean cash was received, but no cash changes hands for the allowance; A reverses the entry.

practice.stem:
Fresh Basket Supermarket, Kandy, depreciates refrigeration equipment at 15% per annum on cost, with a full year's charge in the year of purchase and none in the year of disposal. The year end is 31 December.
At 1 January 2025 equipment at cost was $150,000. This included a refrigerator bought in March 2022 for $30,000, which was sold in October 2025 for $19,000. New equipment costing $45,000 was bought in June 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the accumulated depreciation on the refrigerator sold, at the date of sale.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss on disposal.
parts.answer: Carrying amount 30,000 − 13,500 = 16,500; proceeds 19,000 → profit $2,500
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why a profit on disposal does not mean the business has made a good investment.
parts.answer: It shows only that too much depreciation was charged in earlier years (the estimate of life/residual value was too cautious); it is an adjustment to past depreciation, not a trading gain.
parts.working: 1 mark over-depreciation; 1 mark estimate/not trading.
