                                  40,000  |                                    40,000
parts.working: B1 cost 40,000 debited; B1 depreciation 26,000 (3 years 24,000 + 3 months 2,000); B1 trade-in allowance credited (debit vehicles); B1 loss 5,000; B1 dates/narratives.

practice.stem: Takumi Textiles, Osaka, bought a machine on 1 January 2022 for $64,000. It is depreciated at 25% per annum using the reducing balance method, with a full year's charge in the year of purchase and none in the year of sale. The machine was sold on 1 January 2025 at a loss of $3,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the machine on 1 January 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sale proceeds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the loss on disposal shows about the depreciation charged on the machine.
parts.answer: The machine was under-depreciated: the charges in earlier years were too low, so its carrying amount was above its real market value. The loss is a correction of past profits.
parts.working: 1 mark under-depreciated/carrying amount too high; 1 mark earlier profits overstated or estimates (rate/life) wrong.

practice.stem:
The following information relates to the vehicles of a courier company in Lahore for the year ended 31 December 2025:
Vehicles at cost, 1 January 2025: $410,000
Accumulated depreciation, 1 January 2025: $145,000
Accumulated depreciation, 31 December 2025: $171,000
Depreciation charge for the year: $58,000
During the year one vehicle which had cost $75,000 was sold, giving a profit on disposal of $4,600. A new vehicle was bought for $90,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the accumulated depreciation transferred to the disposal account.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sale proceeds of the vehicle.
parts.answer: Carrying amount 75,000 − 32,000 = 43,000; proceeds = 43,000 + profit 4,600 = $47,600
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the cost of vehicles at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Prepare the disposal account.
parts.answer:
Disposal account
Dr                                $   Cr                                   $
Vehicles (cost)              75,000   Accumulated depreciation        32,000
Statement of profit or loss           Bank                            47,600
  (profit on disposal)        4,600
                             79,600                                   79,600
parts.working: B1 cost; B1 profit on debit side; B1 own figures.

practice.stem:
A school in Quetta depreciates minibuses at 20% per annum on cost, calculated monthly. Its year end is 31 December.
A minibus bought on 1 January 2022 for $48,000 was part-exchanged on 1 April 2025 for a new minibus with a price of $62,000. The dealer gave a trade-in allowance of $15,000 and the school paid the balance by bank transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation on the old minibus for the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss on disposal of the old minibus.
parts.answer: Accumulated depreciation 48,000 × 20% × 3¼ years = 31,200; carrying amount 16,800; trade-in 15,000 → loss $1,800
parts.working: B1 accumulated dep; B1 carrying amount; B1 result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare journal entries to record the part-exchange. Narratives are not required.
parts.answer:
Dr Disposal 48,000; Cr Minibuses 48,000
Dr Accumulated depreciation 31,200; Cr Disposal 31,200
Dr Minibuses 62,000; Cr Disposal 15,000; Cr Bank 47,000
Dr Statement of profit or loss (loss) 1,800; Cr Disposal 1,800
parts.working: B1 each line (new minibus at full price $62,000).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the total depreciation charge on minibuses for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.working: M1 A1.

practice.stem: Aster Ltd owns land bought for $180,000. A professional valuer now values it at $260,000. The directors decide to show the land at the new value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount credited to the revaluation reserve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the double entry to record the revaluation.
parts.answer: Debit land account $80,000; credit revaluation reserve $80,000.
parts.working: 1 mark each side.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the increase is not shown as income in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: Realisation concept: the gain is not realised until the land is sold, so it is a reserve, not profit; showing it as profit could lead to dividends paid out of an unrealised gain.
parts.working: 1 mark unrealised/realisation concept; 1 mark development (not available for dividends / would overstate profit).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A limited company revalues its land upwards for the first time. Where is the increase in value recorded?
A As revenue in the statement of profit or loss
B In a revaluation reserve within equity
C In retained earnings
D As a non-current liability
parts.answer: B In a revaluation reserve within equity
parts.working: An unrealised gain on revaluation is taken to a revaluation reserve (shown in equity and in other comprehensive income). It is not revenue (A) because it is not realised and does not arise from trading.

practice.stem: Noor Fabrics Limited, Faisalabad, owns a building that cost $300,000. Accumulated depreciation is $60,000. A professional valuer has valued the building at $420,000, and the directors have decided to record this value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revaluation surplus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the revaluation. A narrative is required.
parts.answer:
Dr Accumulated depreciation – buildings 60,000
Dr Buildings (420,000 − 300,000) 120,000
Cr Revaluation reserve 180,000
Narrative: revaluation of buildings to professional valuation of $420,000.
parts.working: B1 accumulated depreciation eliminated; B1 buildings increased by 120,000; B1 reserve with narrative.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the buildings will be shown in the statement of financial position immediately after the revaluation.
parts.answer: Non-current assets: buildings at valuation $420,000 (accumulated depreciation nil).

practice.stem: The directors of Sunrise Hotels Limited, Murree, are considering revaluing the company's hotel buildings, which were bought 25 years ago.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why the directors of a company may decide to revalue the company's property.
parts.answer: To show a true and fair (up-to-date) value in the SOFP; to support borrowing (higher security); to show a realistic figure before a sale/merger or to deter a cheap takeover; depreciation then reflects the current value.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which accounting concept is departed from when property is revalued.
parts.answer: Historical cost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the revaluation reserve cannot be used to pay a cash dividend.
parts.answer: The gain is unrealised – no cash or sale has occurred – so it is not part of distributable profits (retained earnings); paying it out could reduce capital and harm creditors.
parts.working: 1 mark unrealised; 1 mark not distributable/creditor protection.

practice.stem: Greenfield Nurseries Limited, Pretoria, bought land for $150,000 in 2019. The land was revalued at $210,000 on 31 December 2024 and at $240,000 on 31 December 2025. Each increase was recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance on the revaluation reserve at 31 December 2024.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance on the revaluation reserve at 31 December 2025 and the amount added during 2025.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the amount at which the land is shown in the statement of financial position at 31 December 2025, and explain why no depreciation is charged.
parts.answer: $240,000. Land normally has an unlimited useful life, so it is not depreciated.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A building cost $400,000 and has accumulated depreciation of $80,000. It is revalued to $500,000. What amount is credited to the revaluation reserve?
A $100,000
B $180,000
C $80,000
D $580,000
parts.working: Carrying amount = 400,000 − 80,000 = 320,000; 500,000 − 320,000 = $180,000. $100,000 compares with cost and ignores the accumulated depreciation.

practice.stem: Harbour View Ltd bought premises on 1 January 2016 for $600,000 and depreciates them at 2% per annum on cost. On 1 January 2026, when accumulated depreciation was $120,000, the premises were revalued at $900,000. The remaining useful life is 40 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the journal entries to record the revaluation. Narratives are not required.
parts.answer:
Debit $   Credit $
Provision for depreciation – premises   120,000
  Premises                                         120,000
Premises                                420,000
  Revaluation reserve                              420,000
parts.working: B1 B1 transfer of accumulated depreciation 120,000; M1 increase 900,000 − 480,000; A1 420,000 credited to revaluation reserve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for the year ended 31 December 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where the revaluation reserve is shown in the financial statements and why it is not included in profit.
parts.answer: In the equity section of the statement of financial position (and statement of changes in equity); the gain is not realised because the premises have not been sold.
parts.working: 1 mark equity/reserves; 1 mark unrealised (realisation concept).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A building was bought on 1 January 2016 for $500,000 and was being depreciated on the straight-line basis over 50 years. On 1 January 2026 it was revalued at $720,000. Its remaining useful life is unchanged. What is the depreciation charge for the year ended 31 December 2026?
A $10,000
B $14,400
C $18,000
D $22,000
parts.working: After 10 years the remaining life is 40 years: 720,000 ÷ 40 = 18,000. B divides by the original 50-year life; A is the old charge on cost.

practice.stem: Delta Distribution Limited, Chittagong, has a warehouse with a carrying amount of $380,000. It has never been revalued. The directors adopt the revaluation model and a valuer reports a fair value of $330,000. The draft profit for the year, before this adjustment, is $215,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the decrease in value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the decrease must be treated in the financial statements and why.
parts.answer: Charged as an expense in the statement of profit or loss (impairment/revaluation loss). There is no previous revaluation surplus on this asset to set it against, so it cannot go to the revaluation reserve; prudence requires the loss to be recognised.
parts.working: 1 mark expense in SOPL; 1 mark no surplus available; 1 mark prudence.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year after this adjustment.
parts.working: B1 own figure.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one effect of the adjustment on the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Property carrying amount reduced to $330,000; retained earnings (equity) reduced by $50,000.

practice.stem: Crescent Logistics Limited, Abu Dhabi, bought a building on 1 January 2010 for $800,000. It is depreciated at 2% per annum on cost (a 50-year life), calculated monthly. On 1 July 2025 the building was revalued at $1,100,000; the remaining useful life was unchanged. The year end is 31 December. (Depreciation for 1 January to 30 June 2025 was charged before the revaluation.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the accumulated depreciation on the building at 1 July 2025, before revaluation.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revaluation surplus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total depreciation on the building for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.working: B1 first half; M1 remaining life 34.5 years; A1 total.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the carrying amount of the building at 31 December 2025.

practice.stem: Lakeview Engineering Limited, Kampala, had a revaluation reserve of $90,000 at 1 July 2025, all relating to its office building ($30,000) and its factory ($60,000). During the year ended 30 June 2026: land with a carrying amount of $175,000 was revalued at $240,000; the office building was revalued downwards by $20,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the revaluation reserve column of the statement of changes in equity for the year ended 30 June 2026.
parts.answer:
Revaluation reserve                          $
Balance at 1 July 2025                  90,000
Revaluation of land                     65,000
Decrease on office building            (20,000)
Balance at 30 June 2026                135,000
parts.working: B1 land increase; B1 decrease set against reserve; B1 closing balance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the decrease on the office building is not charged to the statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: The office building already has a surplus of $30,000 in the reserve from an earlier revaluation; a later decrease is set against that surplus first, up to its amount. Only a fall greater than $30,000 would be an expense.
parts.working: 1 mark set against earlier surplus; 1 mark limit.

practice.stem: Daraz Storage Ltd bought land for $250,000 in 2020. In 2024 the land was revalued to $320,000 and the increase was credited to a revaluation reserve. In 2026 the land was revalued to $230,000. Land is not depreciated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how the decrease in value in 2026 is treated.
parts.answer: Decrease $90,000: $70,000 debited to the revaluation reserve; $20,000 charged as an expense in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.working: 320,000 − 230,000 = 90,000 (M1); 70,000 against reserve, remaining 20,000 to profit or loss (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry for the 2026 revaluation. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer:
Debit $   Credit $
Revaluation reserve                                          70,000
Statement of profit or loss (impairment/revaluation loss)    20,000
  Land                                                                  90,000
parts.working: B1 reserve 70,000; B1 profit or loss 20,000; B1 land credited 90,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the whole decrease is not taken to the revaluation reserve.
parts.answer: The reserve holds only the earlier gain of $70,000 on this asset; a fall below original cost is a real loss and, by prudence, must be recognised in profit.
parts.working: 1 mark reserve only contains the previous surplus on this asset; 1 mark fall below cost is a loss charged to profit (prudence).

practice.stem: Vista Healthcare Limited, Lahore, has a hospital building that cost $500,000 and has accumulated depreciation of $100,000 (10 years of a 50-year life, straight-line). On 1 January 2026 it was revalued at $640,000; remaining life 40 years. The company's policy is to transfer each year, from the revaluation reserve to retained earnings, the difference between depreciation on the revalued amount and depreciation on the original cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revaluation surplus on 1 January 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for the year ended 31 December 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amount transferred from the revaluation reserve to retained earnings for 2026, and the balance on the revaluation reserve at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer:
Excess depreciation = 16,000 − (500,000 ÷ 50 = 10,000) = 6,000, transferred
Reserve balance 240,000 − 6,000 = $234,000
parts.working: M1 old charge; A1 transfer; A1 balance.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain the purpose of this annual transfer.
parts.answer: As the building is used up, part of the surplus is realised through use; transferring the extra depreciation caused by the revaluation from the reserve to retained earnings keeps distributable profit as it would have been under historical cost. It is a transfer within equity and does not pass through profit.
parts.working: 1 mark realised through use; 1 mark equity transfer not profit.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Calculate the total effect of the revaluation on retained earnings for 2026.
parts.answer: Profit reduced by extra depreciation 6,000, offset by transfer in 6,000: net effect nil.

practice.stem:
Pak Steel Fabricators Limited carried out its first revaluation of non-current assets on 31 December 2025:
Asset                       Carrying amount $  Fair value $
Land                                  300,000       420,000
Head office building                  255,000       300,000
Machinery (whole class)               190,000       160,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount credited to the revaluation reserve.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount charged to the statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: Machinery decrease $30,000 (no earlier surplus on that class).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the overall change in total equity caused by the revaluations.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The finance director suggests offsetting the machinery decrease against the land surplus so that profit is not reduced. Evaluate this suggestion.
parts.answer: Not allowed: IAS 16 treats each class/asset separately; a decrease is charged to profit unless it reverses an earlier surplus on the same asset. Offsetting would overstate profit by $30,000 and mislead shareholders, breaching prudence/true and fair view; auditors would likely require correction. Total equity is the same either way, but the profit and EPS shown would be wrong.
parts.working: 1 mark rule; 1 mark profit overstated with figure; 1 mark concept/audit; 1 mark conclusion.

practice.stem: Horizon Foods Limited, Cairo, reported profit from operations of $180,000. Capital employed is $1,200,000 (equity $900,000 and 8% debentures $300,000). The directors propose to revalue property upwards by $400,000, which would increase the annual depreciation charge by $12,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed and the gearing ratio (long-term loans ÷ capital employed) before the revaluation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the two ratios after the revaluation, allowing for the extra depreciation.
parts.working: B1 profit 168,000; B1 capital employed 1,600,000; B1 both ratios.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether the revaluation makes the company's performance look better or worse to shareholders and lenders.
parts.answer: ROCE falls: the company appears less efficient, though nothing has changed in its trading. Gearing falls: lenders see more asset cover and lower risk, making borrowing easier. Ratios now compare less easily with earlier years or with companies using historical cost. Overall the SOFP is more realistic but users must adjust comparisons.
parts.working: 1 mark ROCE; 1 mark gearing; 1 mark comparability; 1 mark conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business bought a machine. The details were:
list price $120,000
trade discount 10%
delivery $3,500
installation $2,200
one-year maintenance contract $1,800
At what cost should the machine be recorded?
A $113,700
B $115,500
C $125,700
D $108,000
parts.working: 108,000 (after 10% discount) + 3,500 + 2,200 = $113,700. The maintenance contract is revenue expenditure ($115,500 wrongly includes it); $125,700 ignores the trade discount.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is revenue expenditure?
A Legal fees paid on the purchase of new premises
B The cost of installing a new machine
C Repainting the outside of the existing shop
D Adding an extra floor to the office building
parts.answer: C Repainting the outside of the existing shop
parts.working: Repainting maintains the existing asset and gives no new benefit, so it is an expense. A, B and D are part of acquiring or improving an asset (capital). D is the main distractor: an extension increases capacity, so it is capital.

practice.stem:
Malik Bakers, Gujranwala, bought a delivery van. The invoice and related payments were:
Item                                               $
Van (list price)                              28,000
Delivery to the bakery                           400
One-off registration and number plates           350
Sign-writing the bakery's logo on the van        900
Fitting a roof rack                              600
First tank of fuel                               120
Annual road tax                                  300
Insurance for the first year                   1,450

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount to be debited to the delivery vans account.
parts.answer: 28,000 + 400 + 350 + 600 = $29,350 (sign-writing excluded: it is advertising, not needed to bring the van into use)
parts.working: M1 correct items; A1 $29,350.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount to be treated as revenue expenditure.
parts.answer: Sign-writing 900 + fuel 120 + road tax 300 + insurance 1,450 = $2,770
parts.working: M1 identifies the revenue items; A1 $2,770.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the annual road tax is not part of the cost of the van.
parts.answer: It is a recurring running cost for one year's use, not a cost of acquiring or bringing the van into use.

practice.stem: The bookkeeper of a small textile workshop in Karachi is unsure how to classify spending on equipment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure.
parts.answer: Capital expenditure is spending on buying or improving non-current assets that give benefit for more than one year; revenue expenditure is spending on running the business/maintaining assets, used up within the year.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A repair costing $7,000 has been debited to the machinery account. State the effect of this error on (i) the profit for the year and (ii) non-current assets.
parts.answer: (i) Profit overstated by $7,000 (less any depreciation charged on it). (ii) Non-current assets overstated by $7,000.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one accounting concept that is breached by the error in (b).
parts.answer: Matching (accruals) – the expense is not matched with the year; also prudence/true and fair view.

practice.stem: A packaging company in Lahore imported a cutting machine. Costs were: list price $85,000 less 5% trade discount; import duty $6,200; sea freight $3,100; insurance during shipping $700; installation $2,400; materials used in test runs $500; sales tax $12,000 (recoverable from the tax authority); training of operators $1,800; a one-year maintenance contract $2,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost at which the machine should be recorded.
parts.answer: 85,000 × 95% = 80,750; + import duty 6,200 + freight 3,100 + insurance in transit 700 + installation 2,400 + test materials 500 = $93,650
parts.working: B1 trade discount; B1 costs to bring into use included; B1 total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the following items are not included: (i) the sales tax, (ii) the staff training, (iii) the maintenance contract.
parts.answer: (i) The sales tax is recoverable from the tax authority, so it is not a cost to the business. (ii) Training benefits staff, not the machine; it is an expense. (iii) Maintenance is a running cost of future periods, so it is an expense/prepayment.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Two businesses in Islamabad have each bought a plot of land.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term non-current asset.
parts.answer: An asset held for use in the business (not for resale) and expected to be used for more than one year.
parts.working: 1 mark use not resale; 1 mark more than one year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A property developer buys a plot of land to build and sell houses. A hospital buys a plot of land to build a new wing. Explain why the land is a non-current asset for only one of them.
parts.answer: The developer holds the land for resale, so it is inventory (current asset). The hospital will use the land in its business for many years, so it is a non-current asset.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Pine Crest Hotel, Murree, spent the following during the year:
                                                       Rs
New boiler                                        850,000
Installation of the boiler                         45,000
Repainting guest rooms                            120,000
Building a new dining extension                 2,400,000
Repairing roof after a storm                       75,000
Legal fees on buying an adjacent plot of land      60,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total capital expenditure.
parts.working: Capital: boiler 850,000, installation 45,000, extension 2,400,000, legal fees 60,000 (M1 identifying, M1 excluding repainting and repairs) = Rs 3,355,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The installation cost was debited to the repairs account. State the effect on profit and on non-current assets. Ignore depreciation.
parts.answer: Profit understated by Rs 45,000; non-current assets understated by Rs 45,000.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it is important to distinguish between capital and revenue expenditure.
parts.answer: Wrong classification misstates profit and asset values, so the financial statements would not give a true and fair view to users.
parts.working: 1 mark profit misstated; 1 mark assets misstated/true and fair view.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business bought a plot of land with an old shed on it and built a factory. Costs were: land $450,000; legal fees on the purchase $9,000; demolition of the shed to clear the site $12,000; architect's fees $25,000; construction $600,000; insurance for the first year after completion $4,000; opening ceremony $3,000. What is the total cost of land and buildings?
A $1,071,000
B $1,084,000
C $1,096,000
D $1,103,000
parts.working: All costs needed to get the site ready and build the factory are capital: 450,000 + 9,000 + 12,000 + 25,000 + 600,000 = 1,096,000. D wrongly adds insurance and the opening ceremony (running/promotional costs); B leaves out demolition.

practice.stem: Shaheen Builders' Merchants, Peshawar, used its own staff to build a storeroom. All costs have been debited to expense accounts: materials taken from inventory (recorded in purchases) $46,000; wages of staff working on the building $28,500; hire of a concrete mixer $5,200; architect's fees $7,000. The owner also wants to add $4,000 of general administration overheads.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the new storeroom.
parts.answer: 46,000 + 28,500 + 5,200 + 7,000 = $86,700 (general overheads excluded)
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to transfer the costs to the buildings account. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer:
Dr Buildings 86,700
Cr Purchases 46,000
Cr Wages 28,500
Cr Equipment hire 5,200
Cr Professional fees 7,000
parts.working: B1 debit; B1 materials and wages; B1 other credits.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the effect of your journal on the profit for the year, before depreciation.
parts.answer: Profit increases by $86,700.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the $4,000 of general administration overheads is not capitalised.
parts.answer: They would have been paid anyway and are not directly attributable to bringing the asset into use.
parts.working: 1 mark not incremental; 1 mark not directly attributable.

practice.stem: On 1 January 2025 a firm of architects in Riyadh bought computers for $24,000. The cost was debited to office expenses. Computers are depreciated at 25% per annum on cost. The draft profit for the year ended 31 December 2025 was $156,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: B1 add back 24,000; B1 depreciation; B1 answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the amount at which the computers will appear in the statement of financial position at 31 December 2025.
parts.answer: Cost 24,000 less accumulated depreciation 6,000 = carrying amount $18,000
parts.working: 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it is important to correct this error.
parts.answer: Profit is understated and assets understated, so the statements do not give a true and fair view; it breaches matching because the cost should be spread over the computers' useful life.
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

practice.stem:
During the year a food processor in Multan spent:
1 $120,000 building an extension to the factory
2 $3,800 replacing broken windows in the existing factory
3 $25,000 upgrading a packing machine so it can pack 40% more units an hour
4 $2,600 on the annual service of the delivery vehicles

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each item as capital or revenue expenditure, giving a reason.
parts.answer:
1 Capital – increases floor area/capacity.
2 Revenue – restores the asset to its original condition.
3 Capital – improves the machine beyond its original capacity.
4 Revenue – routine maintenance.
parts.working: 1 mark each with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total capital expenditure and the total revenue expenditure.
parts.answer: Capital $145,000; revenue $6,400
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: If item 3 had been treated as revenue expenditure, state the effect on profit for the year (ignore depreciation).
parts.answer: Profit understated by $25,000.

practice.stem: On 1 September 2025 a travel company in Abbottabad bought a minibus. The invoice showed: list price $92,000 less 5% trade discount; delivery $1,600; registration $900; annual road licence (1 September 2025 to 31 August 2026) $1,200; fuel $300. Minibuses are depreciated at 25% per annum using the reducing balance method, calculated monthly. The year end is 31 December.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the minibus.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation for the year ended 31 December 2025, to the nearest $.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the minibus at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the amount of the licence prepaid at 31 December 2025 and the total of the licence and fuel charged as expenses in 2025.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
The draft profit of Zenith Plastics, Sialkot, for the year ended 30 June 2026 is $212,000. Machinery is depreciated at 20% per annum on cost and buildings at 2% per annum on cost, with a full year's charge in the year of acquisition. The following were found:
1 A delivery charge of $2,000 on a new machine was debited to carriage inwards.
2 Roof repairs of $9,000 were debited to the buildings account and depreciation was charged on them.
3 Wages of $6,000 paid to the firm's staff for installing the new machine were debited to wages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year.
parts.answer:
$
Draft profit                               212,000
1 Delivery charge capitalised                2,000
  extra depreciation 20%                     (400)
2 Roof repair expensed                     (9,000)
  depreciation on repair reversed 2%           180
3 Installation wages capitalised             6,000
  extra depreciation 20%                   (1,200)
Corrected profit                           209,580
parts.working: 1 mark for each item (with depreciation) ×3; 1 mark depreciation adjustments; 1 mark final figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net change in the carrying amount of non-current assets as a result of the corrections.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the delivery charge should not be included in carriage inwards.
parts.answer: Carriage inwards is part of the cost of goods for resale; delivery of a machine is a cost of bringing a non-current asset into use, so it is capital.

practice.stem: A diagnostic centre in Nairobi bought an MRI scanner on 1 January 2025: purchase price $140,000; delivery $3,500; installation $6,000; repair of a wall damaged by careless installers $2,200; initial testing $1,300; three-year maintenance contract paid in advance $9,000; staff training $4,000. Medical equipment is depreciated at 10% per annum on cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the scanner to be capitalised.
parts.working: M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total amount charged to the statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 2025 in respect of the scanner.
parts.answer: Wall repair 2,200 + maintenance 9,000 ÷ 3 = 3,000 + training 4,000 + depreciation 15,080 = $24,280
parts.working: B1 wall repair expensed; B1 maintenance 3,000; B1 total.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the amount of the maintenance contract shown in the statement of financial position at 31 December 2025, and its classification.
parts.answer: $6,000, shown as a prepayment (current asset): $3,000 relates to 2026 and $3,000 to 2027.
parts.working: 1 mark amount $6,000; 1 mark prepayment (current asset).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the cost of repairing the wall is not part of the cost of the scanner.
parts.answer: It is an abnormal cost caused by careless installation; it was not necessary to bring the scanner into working condition, so it is an expense.
parts.working: 1 mark abnormal/avoidable; 1 mark not necessary.

practice.stem: Bright Path Education Limited runs schools in Karachi and Lahore.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two conditions that must be met before an item of property, plant and equipment is recognised as an asset.
parts.answer: It is probable that future economic benefits will flow to the business; its cost can be measured reliably.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The marketing director wants to capitalise a $60,000 advertising campaign for a new product, because 'it will bring in sales for three years'. Explain why this is not allowed.
parts.answer: Advertising does not create an identifiable asset that the business controls; future benefits are uncertain and cannot be measured reliably/linked to the cost, so it must be expensed (prudence). It is not property, plant or equipment.
parts.working: 1 mark no controllable asset; 1 mark uncertain/unreliable; 1 mark prudence/expense.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The company writes off all items of equipment costing less than $500 as an expense. Explain which concept justifies this policy.
parts.answer: Materiality: these amounts are too small to affect users' decisions, so the cost of tracking and depreciating them outweighs the benefit.
parts.working: 1 mark materiality; 1 mark explanation.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Rukhsana does not keep full accounting records. Her business net assets were $25,000 at the start of the year and $31,400 at the end. During the year she took drawings of $8,200 and paid $3,000 of her own savings into the business bank account. What was her profit for the year?
A $1,200
B $6,400
C $11,600
D $17,600
parts.working: Profit = closing capital − opening capital + drawings − capital introduced = 31,400 − 25,000 + 8,200 − 3,000 = $11,600. D adds the capital introduced instead of deducting it; the extra $3,000 came from Rukhsana's savings, not from trading.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An electronics wholesaler in Karachi keeps incomplete records. Trade receivables were $7,420 at the start of the year and $8,950 at the end. During the year it received $61,300 from credit customers, allowed cash discounts of $1,150 and wrote off irrecoverable debts of $480. What were the credit sales for the year?
A $59,770
B $62,830
C $64,460
D $61,400
parts.working: Credit sales = receipts + discounts allowed + irrecoverable debts + closing receivables − opening receivables = 61,300 + 1,150 + 480 + 8,950 − 7,420 = $64,460. B ignores discounts allowed and irrecoverable debts, which also reduce what customers owe.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem:
Zara runs a tailoring shop in Lahore and keeps only a bank statement file. At 1 January 2026 she gives this information:
Equipment: $18,500
Delivery van: $12,000
Inventory: $6,240
Trade receivables: $3,180
Cash at bank: $2,960
Cash in hand: $340
Trade payables: $4,710
Rent accrued: $600
Loan from brother (repayable 2030): $5,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a statement of affairs.
parts.answer: A statement listing the assets and liabilities of a business at a date, used to find the owner's capital (capital = assets − liabilities) when full records are not kept.
parts.working: 1 mark: list of assets and liabilities at a date to find capital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare Zara's statement of affairs at 1 January 2026 to find her capital.
parts.answer:
Zara: Statement of affairs at 1 January 2026

Assets

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem: Haider owns a stationery shop in Hyderabad. He does not keep double-entry records. His capital, found from statements of affairs, was $41,300 at 1 April 2025 and $47,850 at 31 March 2026. During the year he took $900 cash each month for personal use and took stationery costing $1,250 for his children. In January 2026 he paid $6,000 he had inherited into the business bank account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Haider's profit for the year ended 31 March 2026. Show your workings.
parts.answer:
$         $
Capital at 31 March 2026                    47,850
Less capital at 1 April 2025              (41,300)
Increase in capital                          6,550
Add drawings: cash                10,800
            goods                  1,250    12,050
                                            18,600
Less capital introduced                    (6,000)
Profit for the year                         12,600
parts.working: Increase in capital 6,550 (1); drawings 10,800 + 1,250 added (1); capital introduced deducted (1); profit $12,600 (1OF).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why the profit calculated in (a) may not be accurate.
parts.answer: Any one: asset values in the statements of affairs may be estimates; some drawings or capital introduced may have been forgotten; there is no double entry to check accuracy.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid reason.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem:
Mehwish runs a bakery in Quetta. During 2025 she paid rent of $14,300 and electricity of $5,180.
At 1 January 2025: rent prepaid $1,100; electricity accrued $420.
At 31 December 2025: rent accrued $1,300; electricity accrued $510.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rent expense for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.working: M1 add opening prepayment and closing accrual to the amount paid; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electricity expense for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.working: M1 deduct opening accrual, add closing accrual; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the rent and electricity balances at 31 December 2025 will appear in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Rent accrued $1,300 and electricity accrued $510: both shown as current liabilities (other payables).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem:
Ayesha owns a beauty salon in Lahore. For the year ended 31 December 2025:
- She took $650 cash from the business each month.
- The business bank paid for her family holiday, $2,300.
- She took salon products for her own use; they cost $480 and would have sold for $720.
- The business paid her son's school fees of $1,900.
- She paid the salon's insurance of $1,200 from her personal bank account.
Her capital at 1 January 2025 was $35,600 and the profit for the year was $16,050.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Ayesha's total drawings for the year.
parts.working: Cash drawings 12 × 650 = 7,800 (1); goods at cost 480, not selling price (1); total (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Ayesha's capital at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: Capital introduced (insurance paid privately) added (1); profit added and drawings deducted (1); A1 OF.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem:
Bushra runs a courier business in Rawalpindi. Her financial year ends on 31 March.
- On 1 October 2025 she borrowed $20,000 at 6% interest per year. Interest paid by 31 March 2026 was $450.
- At 1 April 2025 insurance of $640 was prepaid for April–June 2025. On 1 July 2025 she paid $2,880 for insurance for the year to 30 June 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the loan interest expense for the year and the amount owing at 31 March 2026.
parts.working: M1 six months only; A1; A1 accrual.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the insurance expense for the year and the prepayment at 31 March 2026.
parts.working: M1 include opening prepayment; A1 expense; A1 prepayment.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader's trade payables were $5,630 at the start of the year and $6,105 at the end. During the year she paid suppliers $48,270, received cash discounts of $940, returned goods costing $1,120 to suppliers and set off $350 against a customer who is also a supplier. What is the balancing figure for credit purchases in her total trade payables account?
A $50,035
B $50,215
C $50,805
D $51,155
parts.working: Debit side: bank 48,270 + discounts received 940 + returns 1,120 + contra 350 + balance c/d 6,105 = 56,785. Credit side: balance b/d 5,630 + purchases. Purchases = $51,155. A leaves out the returns; returns reduce the amount owed, so they must be added back to find the goods bought.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records

parts.label: a
parts.text:
All of a grocer's sales are for cash. In the year, cash sales were $38,600. From the takings he paid wages of $9,800 and cash purchases of $2,370, and paid $22,150 into the bank. He took the rest as drawings, apart from the cash in the till: $420 at the start of the year and $510 at the end. What were his cash drawings?
A $4,190
B $4,280
C $4,370
D $5,210
parts.working: Drawings = opening cash + takings − wages − bankings − cash purchases − closing cash = 420 + 38,600 − 9,800 − 22,150 − 2,370 − 510 = $4,190. C reverses the till balances: the opening cash is available to spend and the closing cash was not taken.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem:
Wanjiru owns a building-supplies shop in Nairobi. Her records for the year show:
Trade payables at start $9,240; at end $8,615
Paid to suppliers by bank transfer $71,580
Discounts received $1,460
Goods returned to suppliers $2,030
Amount owed by a customer set off against the amount owed to the same firm as supplier $780
Cash purchases $3,900

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the total trade payables account for the year, showing credit purchases as the balancing figure.
parts.answer:

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem:
Tomasz runs a printing shop in Gdańsk. His bank summary for the year is incomplete. Balance at start of year: $3,250 in the bank. Balance at end of year: overdrawn $1,180.
Payments: Paid to suppliers $46,900; Wages $12,600; Rent $7,200; Drawings $6,000; New equipment $4,500.
Receipts: Cash sales banked $31,400; Loan from bank $5,000; receipts from credit customers (not known).
Trade receivables were $4,100 at the start of the year and $3,640 at the end. Discounts allowed were $550.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount received from credit customers during the year.
parts.answer: Total payments 77,200. Opening balance 3,250 + cash sales 31,400 + loan 5,000 + receipts from customers − 77,200 = −1,180 (overdraft). Receipts from credit customers = 77,200 − 1,180 − 3,250 − 31,400 − 5,000 = $36,370
parts.working: M1 total payments; M1 treat closing overdraft as a negative balance; M1 balancing; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the credit sales for the year.
parts.working: M1 add discounts allowed; M1 adjust for receivables; A1 OF.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem: A furniture workshop in Chiniot keeps incomplete records. The carrying amount of its machinery was $42,000 at 1 January 2025 and $51,300 at 31 December 2025. Depreciation for the year was $8,900. During the year a machine was sold for $3,200, making a profit on disposal of $700. All other machinery bought was paid for by bank transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the machine sold.
parts.working: M1 proceeds less profit; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of machinery bought during the year.
parts.answer: Opening 42,000 − disposal 2,500 − depreciation 8,900 + additions = closing 51,300; additions = 51,300 − 42,000 + 8,900 + 2,500 = $20,700
parts.working: M1 add back depreciation; M1 add back carrying amount of disposal; A1 OF.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem:
A tyre dealer in Gujranwala keeps incomplete records. For the year:
Trade receivables: start $12,800; end $14,500
Cheques received from credit customers $96,500, including one of $300 that was later dishonoured
Irrecoverable debts written off $1,050; discounts allowed $1,700
The allowance for irrecoverable debts is kept at 3% of trade receivables at each year end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the credit sales for the year.
parts.working: M1 receipts, discounts and irrecoverable debts added; M1 closing less opening; M1 dishonoured cheque deducted (it increases the amount owed); A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in the allowance for irrecoverable debts and state its effect on profit.
parts.answer: Closing allowance 435 − opening 384 = increase of $51; profit is reduced by $51.
parts.working: 1 mark amount; 1 mark effect.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the figure for trade receivables in the statement of financial position.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem:
Nikhil runs a mobile food van in Colombo. His capital at 1 January 2025 was $27,400. For 2025 his profit was $18,250 and his drawings were $13,600. At 31 December 2025 his other balances were:
Furniture $9,800
Motor vehicle $17,500
Inventory $7,350
Trade receivables $4,120
Trade payables $5,930
Electricity owing $290
He has lost his bank statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Nikhil's capital at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the bank balance at 31 December 2025 and state whether it is an asset or a liability.
parts.answer: Capital = assets − liabilities. Assets other than bank 38,770; liabilities 6,220. Bank = 32,050 − 38,770 + 6,220 = −500: an overdraft of $500, a current liability.
parts.working: M1 use of accounting equation; A1 amount; 1 mark liability (overdraft).

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem:
Sana runs a gift shop in Kuala Lumpur and keeps no double-entry records.
At 1 July 2025: Shop fittings $11,000; Inventory $4,750; Trade receivables $1,960; Bank $2,380; Trade payables $2,640.
At 30 June 2026: Shop fittings $9,900; Van $8,000; Inventory $5,820; Trade receivables $2,410; Bank overdraft $1,150; Trade payables $3,090; Bank loan $6,000.
The van was bought during the year using the bank loan and $2,000 from the business bank account. Sana's drawings for the year were $9,600. She introduced no new capital.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Sana's capital at 1 July 2025.
parts.working: M1 assets − liabilities; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Sana's capital at 30 June 2026.
parts.answer: Assets 26,130 − liabilities 10,240 = $15,890
parts.working: Van and loan included (1); overdraft as liability (1); A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate Sana's profit or loss for the year ended 30 June 2026.
parts.working: M1 change in capital + drawings; A1 OF.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem: The inventory records of a pottery shop in Multan for last year were lost. Revenue was $45,000, purchases were $31,600 and closing inventory was $6,900. All goods are sold at a mark-up of 50%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the opening inventory.
parts.working: M1 cost of sales + closing − purchases; A1 OF.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inventory turnover, correct to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Average inventory = (5,300 + 6,900) ÷ 2 = 6,100; turnover = 30,000 ÷ 6,100 = 4.92 times
parts.working: M1 average inventory; A1.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Goods were stolen from a shoe shop in Peshawar shortly before the year end. Opening inventory was $14,200, purchases were $63,800 and revenue was $84,000. All goods are sold at a mark-up of 40% on cost. The inventory remaining at the year end cost $9,450. What was the cost of the goods stolen?
A $18,000
B $8,550
C $18,150
D $27,600
parts.working: Cost of sales = 84,000 × 100/140 = 60,000. Expected closing inventory = 14,200 + 63,800 − 60,000 = 18,000. Stolen = 18,000 − 9,450 = $8,550. C treats 40% as a margin (cost of sales 50,400), but a mark-up is a percentage of cost.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem:
Gulnaz owns a fabric shop in Sialkot. On 15 June 2026 a fire destroyed most of her inventory. Her records for 1 January to 15 June 2026 show:
Inventory at 1 January 2026 (at cost) $22,600
Purchases $48,350; purchases returns $1,150
Sales $72,500; sales returns $2,500
Her gross margin is always 30% of net sales. Goods saved from the fire cost $3,480.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

parts.answer: Claim 12,990; loss borne 17,320 − 12,990 = $4,330; shown as an expense (loss of inventory by fire).
parts.working: 1 mark amount; 1 mark treatment as an expense.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem:

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem:
Kamal repairs bicycles in Multan. He has no bank statements for the last month and wants his statement of financial position at 31 March 2026. He gives you:
Equipment at cost $30,000; accumulated depreciation at 1 April 2025 $9,000. Depreciation is 20% per year, reducing balance.
Inventory $5,620; trade receivables $2,840; rent prepaid $350
Trade payables $3,910; electricity owing $260
Bank loan $8,000, repayable in 2030
Capital at 1 April 2025 $18,400; profit for the year (after depreciation) $14,700; drawings $11,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for the year and the carrying amount of the equipment at 31 March 2026.
parts.answer: Depreciation = (30,000 − 9,000) × 20% = $4,200; carrying amount = $16,800
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem:
Ramón runs a sports shop in Buenos Aires. He did not count inventory at 30 September 2026. His gross margin is 35% on all sales. For the year to 30 September 2026:
Opening inventory $8,200; purchases $52,600; revenue $76,000
Wages paid $21,450. Wages owing: start of year $380; end of year $470.
The wages paid include $1,200 that Ramón paid to himself.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory at 30 September 2026.
parts.working: M1 cost of sales; M1 opening + purchases − cost of sales; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wages expense for the year.
parts.working: M1 accrual adjustments; M1 remove owner's amount (drawings, not wages); A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the closing inventory found in (a) may differ from the true figure.
parts.answer: The 35% margin is an average; if some goods were sold at a discount, damaged, stolen or sold at different margins, actual inventory will differ from the estimate.
parts.working: 1 mark reason; 1 mark development.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader adds a mark-up of 25% to the cost of all goods. What is his gross margin?
A 20%
B 25%
C 31.25%
D 33⅓%
parts.working: Cost 100, selling price 125, gross profit 25. Margin = 25 ÷ 125 = 20%. B confuses margin with mark-up: the mark-up is profit as a percentage of cost, but margin is profit as a percentage of selling price.

practice.stem: A craft shop in Jaipur buys hand-painted lamps for $64 each and sells them at a mark-up of 35%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of one lamp.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin on one lamp, correct to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the selling price needed to earn a gross margin of 30%, correct to two decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A wholesaler of school uniforms in Faisalabad earns a gross margin of 40% on all sales. What is the mark-up?
A 28.6%
B 40%
C 60%
D 66⅔%
parts.answer: D 66⅔%
parts.working: Margin 40% means gross profit 40 on revenue 100, so cost is 60. Mark-up = 40 ÷ 60 = 66⅔%. C (60%) is cost as a percentage of revenue, not the mark-up.

practice.stem: A shoe shop in Peshawar buys a pair of sandals for $48 and sells them for $60.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit on one pair of shoes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate (i) the mark-up and (ii) the gross margin, as percentages.

practice.stem: Farah runs a bookshop in Hyderabad. She adds a mark-up of 40% to the cost of all books. Her revenue for the year was $245,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales and the gross profit for the year.
parts.answer: Cost of sales $175,000; gross profit $70,000

practice.stem: A trainee in an accountant's office in Multan is confused by the terms 'mark-up' and 'margin'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between mark-up and gross margin.
parts.answer: Mark-up is gross profit as a percentage of cost of sales; gross margin is gross profit as a percentage of revenue (selling price).
parts.working: B1 mark-up on cost; B1 margin on revenue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why, for the same item, the margin percentage is always lower than the mark-up percentage.
parts.answer: Both use the same gross profit, but margin divides it by revenue, which is larger than cost (revenue = cost + profit).

practice.stem: A bakery in Gujranwala makes a celebration cake at a cost of $36. The owner wants a gross margin of 20% on the selling price.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of one cake.
parts.working: Cost is 80% of selling price; 36 ÷ 0.8 = 45 (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mark-up percentage.

practice.stem: Leila sells kitchenware in Dubai. Her gross margin is 37.5% and her cost of sales for the year was $55,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revenue and the gross profit for the year.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mark-up percentage that gives this margin.
parts.working: M1 gross profit ÷ cost of sales; A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader's revenue for the year was $180,000. She uses a mark-up of 50%. Opening inventory was $14,000 and closing inventory was $18,000. What were her purchases for the year?
A $94,000
B $116,000
C $120,000
D $124,000
parts.working: Cost of sales = 180,000 ÷ 1.5 = 120,000. Purchases = cost of sales + closing inventory − opening inventory = 120,000 + 18,000 − 14,000 = 124,000. B (116,000) adjusts for inventory the wrong way round.

practice.stem: On 18 May 2026 a fire destroyed most of the inventory of Kamran's electrical shop in Sukkur. Since 1 January 2026: inventory at 1 January was $26,000; purchases were $148,000; sales were $190,000. Goods costing $3,500 were saved from the fire. Kamran earns a gross margin of 30% on all sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the inventory destroyed by the fire.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why the actual loss may differ from your calculation.
parts.answer: E.g. the margin may not have been exactly 30% for all goods (some sold at discount); goods may have been stolen or damaged earlier; the owner may have taken goods.

practice.stem: Rashid owns a grocery in Abbottabad. All sales are for cash and he adds a mark-up of 25% to cost. He suspects that an assistant has been stealing cash. For the year: opening inventory $18,000; purchases $96,000; closing inventory $22,000. Cash banked from takings was $108,600 and $2,400 of expenses were paid out of takings before banking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected sales for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount of cash that may have been stolen.

practice.stem: Imran's inventory records for his clothing shop in Lahore were lost. For the year: revenue $300,000; gross margin 25%; opening inventory $30,000; purchases $236,000. During the year Imran took clothes costing $4,000 for his family; this has not been recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the closing inventory at cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the double entry for the goods taken by Imran for his own use.
parts.answer: Dr Drawings $4,000; Cr Purchases $4,000
parts.working: B1 debit drawings; B1 credit purchases.

practice.stem: A wholesaler of cooking oil in Karachi sets its list price at cost plus 60%. It gives a retailer a 15% trade discount on list price. One carton costs the wholesaler $250.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the selling price to the retailer, the gross profit and the gross margin on one carton. Give the margin to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Selling price $340; gross profit $90; margin 26.47%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the actual mark-up earned.

practice.stem: A shop in Karachi sells mobile phones at a mark-up of 20% and accessories at a mark-up of 60%. Last year it sold phones for $96,000 and accessories for $24,000. Opening inventory was $14,000 and purchases were $92,500. The inventory count at the year end found goods costing $10,300.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales for each product line.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overall gross margin, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 total gross profit; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the value of the inventory missing at the year end.
parts.working: M1 total cost of sales used; M1 expected inventory; A1.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

practice.stem: A mobile phone shop in Dubai sells phones at a mark-up of 20% and accessories at a mark-up of 50%. This year phone sales were $150,000 and accessory sales were $60,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit for each line and the overall gross margin for the year. Give the margin to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Phones $25,000; accessories $20,000; overall margin 21.43%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Next year the owner expects phone sales of $120,000 and accessory sales of $90,000, at the same mark-ups. Calculate the expected overall gross margin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the overall margin changes even though total revenue and each mark-up are unchanged.
parts.answer: The sales mix has moved towards accessories, which have the higher mark-up, so a larger share of revenue earns more gross profit.
parts.working: B1 sales mix; B1 higher-margin product forms a bigger share.

practice.stem: Zainab owns a fashion boutique in Lahore and normally uses a mark-up of 60%. In the year she sold all the goods she bought. Goods costing $40,000 were sold in an end-of-season sale at 15% below the normal selling price; the remaining goods costing $200,000 were sold at normal prices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revenue, gross profit and gross margin for the year. Give the margin to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Revenue $374,400; gross profit $134,400; margin 35.90%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit lost because of the sale.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin the business would have earned without the sale.
parts.working: Mark-up 60% → margin 60 ÷ 160 = 37.5%.

practice.stem: Sohail claims that he always adds 40% to cost when pricing goods in his hardware shop in Rawalpindi. His records for the year show: opening inventory $15,000; purchases $170,000; closing inventory $25,000; recorded revenue $210,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales and the revenue that would be expected if the 40% mark-up had been applied to all goods.
parts.answer: Cost of sales $160,000; expected revenue $224,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the actual mark-up and the actual gross margin. Give answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Mark-up 31.25%; margin 23.81%

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest three possible reasons for the shortfall of $14,000.
parts.answer: Any three of: cash takings stolen; goods stolen or damaged/out of date; owner took goods without recording them; selling prices reduced/discounts given; errors in the inventory count; some sales not recorded.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Ali sells fruit from a stall in Quetta. All sales are for cash at a mark-up of 30%. He pays his suppliers by bank transfer. From the takings he paid some expenses in cash, took drawings for himself, and banked the rest. For the year:
                                             $

Inventory at end                        11,500

Takings banked                          81,200
Expenses paid from takings               3,900
Cash float at start                        300
Cash float at end                          500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sales for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Ali's cash drawings taken from the takings.

practice.stem: Tariq sells second-hand books from a small shop in Lahore. He keeps a cash book and files his invoices, but has no ledgers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why a small trader might keep incomplete records rather than a full double-entry system.
parts.answer: Any two: lack of bookkeeping knowledge; saves time; saves the cost of a bookkeeper or software; the business is small with few transactions.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages to the trader of keeping incomplete records.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: (1) no trial balance, so arithmetical errors are hard to find; (2) no detailed statement of profit or loss, so the trader cannot see which expenses are rising; (3) theft or loss of cash or goods may go unnoticed; (4) harder to get a bank loan or satisfy tax authorities without reliable statements.
parts.working: 1 mark for each disadvantage and 1 mark for each explanation, max 2 disadvantages.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader keeps incomplete records. Her capital was $42,000 at the start of the year and $55,000 at the end. During the year she took drawings of $9,000 and paid an inheritance of $5,000 into the business. What was her profit for the year?
A $9,000
B $13,000
C $17,000
D $27,000
parts.working: Profit = closing capital − opening capital + drawings − capital introduced = 55,000 − 42,000 + 9,000 − 5,000 = 17,000. A (9,000) subtracts drawings and adds capital introduced – the wrong way round.

practice.stem: Saleem owns a sweet shop in Multan. He does not keep double-entry records. At 1 January 2026 his business had: premises $85,000; equipment $12,400; inventory $7,600; trade receivables $3,100; bank balance $2,250; cash $150; trade payables $4,800; a bank loan of $20,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement of affairs at 1 January 2026 to calculate Saleem's capital.
parts.answer:
Statement of affairs at 1 January 2026           $           $
Premises                                                85,000
Equipment                                               12,400
Inventory                                                7,600
Trade receivables                                        3,100
Bank                                                     2,250
Cash                                                       150
Total assets                                           110,500
Trade payables                               4,800
Loan                                        20,000    (24,800)
Capital                                                 85,700
parts.working: B1 total assets 110,500; B1 liabilities 24,800; B1 subtraction; B1 capital 85,700.

practice.stem: Shabnam runs a beauty salon in Islamabad. She keeps only a cash book and a file of bills.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two disadvantages to Shabnam of keeping incomplete records.
parts.answer: Any two of: no trial balance, so errors are hard to find; she cannot easily see how much individual customers owe/she owes suppliers; little information for control and decision-making (e.g. no detailed expenses); fraud/theft harder to detect; the accountant's fees to reconstruct the accounts may be higher; banks/tax authorities may not accept the figures.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Babar is a plumber in Karachi. He records receipts and payments in a cash book only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a trial balance cannot be extracted from Babar's records.
parts.answer: A trial balance lists the balances of the ledger accounts, which depend on every transaction being recorded twice (double entry). Babar records each transaction only once, in a cash book, so there are no ledger balances to list.
parts.working: B1 trial balance needs ledger balances from double entry; B1 single entry/cash book only.

practice.stem: Gul Khan sells carpets in Peshawar and keeps no ledgers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a statement of affairs.
parts.answer: A list of the assets and liabilities of a business at a particular date, prepared from incomplete records, used to calculate the owner's capital (assets − liabilities).
parts.working: B1 assets and liabilities at a date; B1 to find capital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which a statement of affairs differs from a statement of financial position.
parts.answer: A statement of affairs is prepared when there are no full double-entry records, and figures are often estimated/valued rather than taken from ledger balances; capital is the balancing figure rather than built up from the capital account.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Sara runs a home bakery in Karachi and keeps incomplete records.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two users who may need Sara's financial statements, and give one reason why each needs them.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. tax authorities – to calculate the tax on her profit; a bank – to decide on a loan or overdraft; suppliers – to decide whether to give credit; a possible partner/buyer – to value the business.
parts.working: B1 each user; B1 each reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader keeps no books. At the start and end of each year she simply lists her business assets and liabilities. Which can be found from these two lists alone, with no other details?
A the gross profit for the year
B the owner's capital at each year end
C the profit for the year
D the cost of goods stolen during the year
parts.answer: B the owner's capital at each year end
parts.working: Capital = assets − liabilities, so a statement of affairs at each date gives the capital. C is wrong because profit from the change in capital also needs the drawings and any capital introduced, which the lists of assets and liabilities do not show.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an advantage of keeping a full double-entry system rather than incomplete records?
A Inventory no longer needs to be counted at the year end
B A trial balance can be extracted to check arithmetical accuracy
C Errors cannot occur in the records
D Employees are prevented from committing fraud
parts.answer: B A trial balance can be extracted to check arithmetical accuracy
parts.working: Only double entry gives two equal sides that can be listed in a trial balance. D is wrong: double entry and controls make fraud easier to detect, but cannot prevent it; C is wrong because errors such as omission or commission do not show in a trial balance.

practice.stem: Hina runs a stationery shop in Sialkot and keeps incomplete records. At 1 April 2025 her business assets totalled $64,000 and liabilities $9,500. At 31 March 2026 assets totalled $81,200 and liabilities $12,700. During the year she took $600 a month in cash and goods costing $1,100 for her own use. She also paid a legacy of $10,000 into the business bank account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Hina's capital at 1 April 2025 and at 31 March 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year ended 31 March 2026.

practice.stem: The accountant of Usman, a tyre dealer in Gujrat, has so far calculated his profit by preparing a statement of affairs at the start and end of each year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one limitation of calculating profit only by comparing capital at the start and end of the year.
parts.answer: It gives only the total profit figure; it does not show revenue, cost of sales, gross profit or individual expenses, so the owner cannot see why profit changed or control costs.
parts.working: B1 only a single profit figure; B1 no detail for analysis/control.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State four items of information the accountant would need to prepare a statement of profit or loss for Usman instead.
parts.answer: Any four of: cash and bank receipts and payments analysed (cash book/bank statements); opening and closing trade receivables and payables; opening and closing inventory; accruals and prepayments of expenses; details of non-current assets for depreciation; discounts and irrecoverable debts; drawings (cash and goods).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Rubina makes and sells embroidered shawls in Hyderabad. She keeps only a cash book. She wants a bank loan of $40,000 to open a second shop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the bank is likely to ask for financial statements prepared from proper records.
parts.answer: The bank needs reliable evidence of profitability and cash flow to judge whether the loan and interest can be repaid, and of assets that could secure the loan.
parts.working: B1 judge ability to repay; B1 reliability/security.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Rubina on two benefits of moving to full double-entry records before applying for the loan.
parts.answer: 1 A trial balance and control accounts give arithmetical checks, so the figures are more reliable and credible to the bank. 2 Detailed records of receivables, payables and expenses allow management information (ratios, budgets) to support the application and to run the larger business. Also: easier to prepare up-to-date statements quickly.
parts.working: B1 + B1 each benefit stated and developed (2 × 2).

practice.stem: Tahir runs a delivery service in Lahore and keeps incomplete records. His capital at 1 July 2025 was $22,000. At 30 June 2026: van (at carrying amount) $14,000; inventory of packing materials $5,200; trade receivables $2,700; rent paid in advance $400; bank $1,100; trade payables $3,900; electricity owing $300. During the year he took drawings of $4,500 and paid $3,000 of his savings into the business.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Tahir's capital at 30 June 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss for the year ended 30 June 2026. State clearly whether it is a profit or a loss.
parts.answer: Loss $1,300

practice.stem: Amna's capital at 1 January 2025 was $40,000. Her accountant has reconstructed a statement of profit or loss showing a profit of $15,500 for 2025. During the year she took drawings of $11,000 and introduced additional capital of $2,500. At 31 December 2025 her assets, excluding the bank balance, were $52,300 and her liabilities, excluding the bank balance, were $4,100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Amna's capital at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the bank balance at 31 December 2025, stating whether it is an overdraft.
parts.answer: Overdraft $1,200
parts.working: Capital = assets − liabilities: 47,000 = 52,300 + bank − 4,100 (M1); bank = −1,200 (A1); overdraft (B1).

practice.stem: Idris owns a furniture workshop in Chiniot. Five years ago he had four customers who paid in cash; now he has 35 credit customers and six employees. He keeps a cash book only, and an accountant prepares his statements from statements of affairs each year. Last year cash differences of $1,800 could not be explained. Idris wants a bank loan of $40,000 to buy a new machine. A part-time bookkeeper would cost $3,000 per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise Idris whether he should change to a full double-entry bookkeeping system. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A reasoned recommendation, e.g. Idris should change to full double entry (or computerised accounts): the business has grown, a bank loan is wanted and the cost is small compared with the benefits. Either decision accepted if justified.
parts.working: For (max 4): bank needs reliable statements for the $40,000 loan; full detail of expenses lets him control costs; control accounts and trial balance help find errors and fraud (cash differences of $1,800 last year); detailed receivables records help chase the 35 credit customers; accounting software can automate entries. Against (max 4): cost of a bookkeeper ($3,000 per year) or software and training; time taken from running the workshop; incomplete records have produced a profit figure so far; an accountant could still prepare statements from his records at year end. Decision with justification linked to the figures (1). Max 7: at most 5 for one-sided answers.

practice.stem: Kashif sells vegetables from a market stall in Faisalabad. All sales and purchases are for cash, and he has no employees. He records receipts and payments in a cash book, and his cousin, an accountant, prepares his statements each year from a statement of affairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise Kashif whether he needs to change to a full double-entry system. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For staying with incomplete records: all sales and purchases are for cash, so there are no receivables or payables to control; the business is small and simple; a cash book and receipts are enough for an accountant to prepare annual statements; double entry would cost time/fees. For change: no arithmetical check, theft of cash harder to detect; little information for decisions (product profitability, cost control); a bank or tax authority may require better records if he expands. Conclusion: at present incomplete records (with a well-kept cash book, daily banking and regular inventory counts) are adequate; move to double entry/accounting software if he starts giving credit or opens more stalls.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): balanced, applied to Kashif's cash-only business, justified conclusion. Level 2 (3–4): points on both sides, limited application. Level 1 (1–2): simple statements.

practice.stem:
Nasreen owns a toy shop in Islamabad. Her capital at 1 January 2025 was $21,000 and her drawings for 2025 were $9,600. She has listed the following at 31 December 2025:
                                             $
Shop fittings (carrying amount)          9,000
Inventory at cost                       14,600
Trade receivables                        6,300
Bank                                     3,200
Her private car                         18,000
Trade payables                           5,400
Wages owing                                350
Mortgage on her private house           40,000
Inventory includes toys costing $1,800 that can be sold for only $700. A customer owing $450 has emigrated and will not pay.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Nasreen's business capital at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: Inventory 14,600 − (1,800 − 700) = 13,500 (B1); receivables 6,300 − 450 = 5,850 (B1); private car and home loan excluded (B1); assets 9,000 + 13,500 + 5,850 + 3,200 = 31,550 less liabilities 5,400 + 350 = 5,750 (M1); 25,800 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the accounting concept applied when the private car is left out.
parts.answer: Business entity.

practice.stem: Waqar owns a pharmacy in Bahawalpur with three employees. He keeps only a cash book and suspects one employee has been taking cash from sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a full double-entry system with control accounts and bank reconciliations would help Waqar detect the theft.
parts.answer: Sales ledger control account would show what customers should have paid; differences from cash received would be investigated. A bank reconciliation each month compares the cash book with the bank statement, so receipts not banked would show. Separation of duties (recording vs handling cash) is possible with full records. Regular trial balances reveal irregular balances.
parts.working: B1 each valid point explained (up to 4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how, without a full system, his accountant could still estimate the amount stolen.
parts.answer: Using the normal mark-up/margin: calculate cost of sales from opening inventory + purchases − closing inventory, apply the mark-up to find expected sales, and compare with takings recorded/banked; the difference estimates the loss.
parts.working: B1 margin/mark-up to estimate sales; B1 compare with recorded takings.

practice.stem: Fatima started the year with inventory of $4,000 and cash of $1,000; she had no other assets or liabilities. All her transactions are for cash. During the year: sales $30,000; purchases $21,000; expenses $3,500; drawings $4,000. Closing inventory was $5,500.

parts.text: Calculate Fatima's capital at the start and at the end of the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare a statement of profit or loss for the year.

$           $
Revenue                                   30,000
Opening inventory              4,000
Purchases                     21,000
Closing inventory            (5,500)    (19,500)
Gross profit                              10,500

practice.stem: Yasir runs an auto-repair workshop in Mardan and keeps incomplete records. His capital was $35,000 at the start of the year and $39,200 at the end. Yasir says he took only $600 a month in cash for himself.

parts.label: a

parts.working: Closing capital = opening capital + capital introduced + profit − drawings (M1); 39,200 = 35,000 + 6,000 + 18,600 − drawings (M1); drawings 20,400 (A1).

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

Investigation: examine bank statements for private payments; do a margin check on sales; recount/re-value inventory.
parts.working: B1 each explanation (×2); B2 a suitable investigation linked to an explanation.

(iv) Discount received
(v) Insurance paid in advance
(vi) Drawings

(iii) Non-current liability
