(vi) Deducted from capital in the statement of financial position

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between a current liability and a non-current liability.
parts.answer: A current liability is due for payment within 12 months of the date of the statement of financial position; a non-current liability is due after more than 12 months.
parts.working: 1 mark each side of the distinction (within 12 months / after 12 months).

parts.answer: Interest $2,400; accrued $600

parts.text:
At the year end a trader forgot to record electricity of $620 that had been used but not yet billed. What is the effect of this omission on the financial statements?
A profit overstated by $620 and current liabilities understated by $620
B profit understated by $620 and current liabilities overstated by $620
C profit overstated by $620 and current assets overstated by $620
D profit understated by $620 and current assets understated by $620
parts.answer: A profit overstated by $620 and current liabilities understated by $620
parts.working: The expense is too low, so profit is too high; the accrued expense (a current liability) is missing. C is wrong because an accrual affects liabilities, not current assets.

practice.stem: On 1 May 2026 Sadia, who owns a bakery in Hyderabad, borrowed $45,000 from a bank at 8% interest per annum. Interest is paid every six months, on 31 October and 30 April. The loan is repayable in 2031. Sadia's financial year ends on 31 December 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the loan interest expense for the year ended 31 December 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the loan interest accrued at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show how the loan and the accrued interest appear in the statement of financial position at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer: Non-current liabilities: bank loan $45,000; current liabilities: accrued loan interest (other payables) $600
parts.working: B1 loan as non-current liability (repayable after more than 12 months); B1 accrued interest as current liability

practice.stem:
Zeeshan's financial year ends on 31 December. He pays local business rates once a year, in advance, on 1 April.
Rates for the year ending 31 March 2026: $4,800 (paid 1 April 2025).
Rates for the year ending 31 March 2027: $5,400 (paid 1 April 2026).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rates expense for the year ended 31 December 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rates prepaid at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rates prepaid at 1 January 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the journal entries needed at 30 September 2026. Narratives are not required.
parts.answer:
1 Dr Prepayments (other receivables) 1,166.67; Cr Advertising 1,166.67.
2 Dr Accrued income (other receivables) 940; Cr Commission income 940.
3 Dr Security expenses 480; Cr Accruals (other payables) 480.
parts.working: 2 marks per entry: 1 for each correct debit and credit; prepaid advertising = 1,750 × 2/3 = $1,166.67

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overall effect of the three adjustments on the profit for the year.
parts.answer: Profit increases by $1,626.67

practice.stem:
Kareem's year ends on 31 March 2026.
Electricity: at 1 April 2025 $520 was owing. Payments during the year were $4,860. In May 2026 a bill of $1,080 was received for the three months ended 30 April 2026.
Stationery: at 1 April 2025 unused stationery cost $310. Stationery bought during the year cost $2,240. Unused stationery at 31 March 2026 cost $430.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electricity expense for the year ended 31 March 2026.
parts.working: B1 accrual 2/3 × 1,080 = 720 (February and March); M1 4,860 − 520 + 720; A1 5,060.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the stationery expense for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how electricity and stationery appear in the statement of financial position at 31 March 2026.
parts.answer: Electricity accrued $720 – current liability; unused stationery $430 – current asset (prepayment/other inventory).
parts.working: B1 each correct item and classification.

practice.stem:
Mariam runs an online tutoring business in Lahore; her year ends on 31 December. Her internet and telephone account has two parts:
• line rental of $210 per quarter, paid in advance on 1 March, 1 June, 1 September and 1 December, each payment covering the following three months;
• call and data charges, billed every quarter in arrears.
At 1 January 2026 line rental for January and February 2026 ($140) had been prepaid and call charges of $95 were owing.
Payments in 2026: line rental 4 × $210; call and data charges $1,180.
On 2 February 2027 she received a bill of $315 for call and data charges for November 2026 to January 2027.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the line rental prepaid at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: Payment on 1 December covers Dec–Feb; January and February = 2/3 × 210 = $140 B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the call and data charges accrued at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: November and December = 2/3 × 315 = $210 B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare the internet and telephone account for the year ended 31 December 2026, showing the balances brought down on 1 January 2027.
parts.answer:
Dr: balance b/d (prepaid) 140; bank (rental) 840; bank (calls) 1,180; balance c/d (accrued) 210 = 2,370.
Cr: balance b/d (accrued) 95; statement of profit or loss 2,135; balance c/d (prepaid) 140 = 2,370.
1 Jan 2027: Dr balance b/d 140; Cr balance b/d 210.
parts.working: B1 opening balances both sides; B1 payments; B1 closing prepayment c/d on credit; B1 closing accrual c/d on debit; B1 transfer to SOPL $2,135 (OF); B1 balances b/d on correct sides

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why two balances can be carried down on the same expense account.
parts.answer: Two different parts of the expense are at different stages: rental has been paid for a future period (asset) while calls have been used but not yet paid (liability). Each must be shown separately in the SOFP rather than netted off.
parts.working: 1 mark: one part is prepaid/asset and one accrued/liability; 1 mark: they are shown separately (current asset and current liability), not offset

practice.stem:
Leila runs a dental practice in Dubai. Her draft profit for the year ended 30 June 2026 is $62,450. Her draft statement of financial position shows current assets of $18,900 and current liabilities of $11,300. The following have not been taken into account:
1 Cleaning contract: $300 per month; the June 2026 invoice has not been paid or recorded.
2 Professional indemnity insurance of $2,880 was paid on 1 March 2026 for the twelve months to 28 February 2027 and was all charged as an expense.
3 A patient prepaid $1,500 on 25 June 2026 for treatment to be carried out in July 2026; it was included in fee income.
4 Rent receivable from a pharmacy sub-letting part of the building, $650 for June 2026, has not been received or recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement of corrected profit for the year ended 30 June 2026.
parts.answer: Draft 62,450 − cleaning 300 + insurance prepaid 1,920 − fees in advance 1,500 + rent receivable 650 = $63,220
parts.working: Insurance prepaid 2,880 × 8/12 = 1,920 B1; B1 each other adjustment with correct sign (3); corrected profit $63,220 B1 (OF)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected current assets and current liabilities at 30 June 2026.
parts.answer: Current assets $21,470; current liabilities $13,100

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the $1,500 received from the patient is a liability and not income.
parts.answer: The service has not yet been provided, so the income has not been earned (realisation concept); Leila owes the patient either the treatment or a refund.
parts.working: 1 mark: not earned/realised until treatment done in July; 1 mark: an obligation to the patient (deferred income)

practice.stem:
Bashir opened a fitness centre in Peshawar on 1 January 2026. Members pay a fee of $360 for twelve months' membership, in full, when they join. His year ends on 31 December. Memberships sold in 2026:
Joined          Members
1 January           90
1 April             40
1 July              60
1 October           30
In addition, 12 members paid their membership fee on 28 December 2026 for membership starting on 1 January 2027.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cash received from membership fees in 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the membership income for the year ended 31 December 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the membership fees received in advance at 31 December 2026 and state where this amount is shown in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: $26,820, shown as a current liability (income received in advance)
parts.working: $83,520 − $56,700 = $26,820 B1; current liability B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
At 31 December 2026 trade receivables were $48,000. A debt of $2,000 is to be written off. The provision for doubtful debts is to be 5% of the remaining receivables; at 1 January 2026 it was $2,500. By how much will these adjustments reduce profit for 2026?
A $1,900
B $1,800
C $4,300
D $200
parts.working: Irrecoverable debt 2,000; new provision 5% × 46,000 = 2,300, a decrease of 200 (income). Net reduction 2,000 − 200 = 1,800. A bases the provision on 48,000; C charges the full provision instead of the change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: On 14 March 2026 a customer, P. Mensah, who owed $840, was declared bankrupt. Nothing is expected to be received. Prepare the journal entry to record this. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer:
Dr Irrecoverable debts $840
Cr Trade receivables – P. Mensah $840
parts.working: B1 debit irrecoverable debts; B1 credit P. Mensah (trade receivables).

parts.label: b
parts.text: On 20 September 2026 a debt of $560 owed by S. Iqbal, written off in 2024, was received in full by cheque. Prepare the journal entries to record this. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer:
Dr Trade receivables – S. Iqbal $560; Cr Irrecoverable debts recovered $560
Dr Bank $560; Cr Trade receivables – S. Iqbal $560
parts.working: B1 reinstate debt (Dr S. Iqbal); B1 Cr irrecoverable debts recovered; B1 Dr Bank, Cr S. Iqbal. (Reinstating the debt keeps a record of the customer's payment history.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where irrecoverable debts recovered appears in the financial statements.
parts.answer: Statement of profit or loss, as other income (added to gross profit).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A debt of $380 owed by K. Mirza was written off as irrecoverable last year. This year Mirza unexpectedly paid the $380 by bank transfer. Which entries complete the recording of this receipt, after the debt has been reinstated in Mirza's account?
A Dr Bank, Cr K. Mirza
B Dr K. Mirza, Cr Bank
C Dr Bank, Cr Provision for doubtful debts
D Dr Irrecoverable debts, Cr Bank
parts.answer: A Dr Bank, Cr K. Mirza
parts.working: First the debt is reinstated (Dr Mirza, Cr Irrecoverable debts recovered); then the receipt is recorded Dr Bank, Cr Mirza. B reverses the receipt; C wrongly uses the provision, which only covers debts not yet written off.

practice.stem: Ayesha sells building materials on credit to contractors in Multan. Last year she wrote off debts of $6,800, which was 4% of her credit sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two credit control procedures Ayesha could use to reduce her irrecoverable debts.
parts.answer: e.g. check new customers' credit references/trade references before giving credit; set credit limits; send monthly statements and reminders promptly; stop further supplies to customers who exceed terms; offer cash discounts for prompt payment; ask for deposits on large orders.
parts.working: 1 mark for each procedure identified (×2) + 1 mark for each explanation of how it reduces irrecoverable debts (×2)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one disadvantage to Ayesha of tightening her credit terms.
parts.answer: Some contractors may buy from competitors offering easier credit, so sales and profit may fall.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: At 31 March 2026 the trade receivables of Ghulam Electricals, Quetta, were $58,300 before writing off two debts: S. Baloch $1,150 and R. Kakar $650. The provision for doubtful debts at 1 April 2025 was $1,520. The provision is to be 3% of the remaining trade receivables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the provision for doubtful debts required at 31 March 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the amounts shown in the statement of profit or loss for the year for (i) irrecoverable debts and (ii) the change in the provision for doubtful debts.
parts.answer: (i) $1,800 expense; (ii) increase $175 expense
parts.working: B1 1,800; B1 1,695 − 1,520 = 175 increase (expense)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net trade receivables shown in the statement of financial position at 31 March 2026.

practice.stem: Lucy keeps a provision for doubtful debts equal to 4% of trade receivables at the year end. At 1 January 2025 the provision was $1,200. Trade receivables were $36,000 at 31 December 2025 and $29,000 at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the provision for doubtful debts account for the years ended 31 December 2025 and 31 December 2026.
parts.working: B1 opening 1,200; B1 increase 240 credited from profit or loss in 2025; B1 balance 1,440; B1 decrease 280 debited in 2026; B1 closing 1,160.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the entries in the statement of profit or loss for each year.
parts.answer: 2025: increase in provision $240 – expense. 2026: decrease in provision $280 – other income.
parts.working: B1 each year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show the trade receivables in the statement of financial position at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer: Trade receivables 29,000 less provision for doubtful debts 1,160 = $27,840

practice.stem:
Ali Hardware analyses its trade receivables by age at 30 June 2026.
Age of debt                          $ Provision %
Not yet due                     24,000          1%
1–30 days overdue                9,500          3%
31–60 days overdue               4,200         10%
Over 60 days overdue             2,300         25%
The over-60-days figure includes $1,100 owed by a customer who has disappeared; this debt is to be written off before the provision is calculated. The provision for doubtful debts at 1 July 2025 was $1,520.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the provision for doubtful debts required at 30 June 2026.
parts.working: B1 over-60 balance reduced to 1,200; M1 240 + 285 + 420 + 300; A1 1,245.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the change in the provision and how it is treated in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: Decrease of $275; added to gross profit as other income.
parts.working: B1 decrease 275 (own figure); B1 shown as income.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two credit control measures Ali Hardware could use to reduce irrecoverable debts.
parts.answer: Any two: check credit references before giving credit; set credit limits; send statements and reminders promptly; offer cash discounts for early payment; stop supplying customers who are overdue; use an aged receivables report every month.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid measures.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
At the start of the year a business had a provision for doubtful debts of $2,600. At the end of the year trade receivables were $40,000 and the provision is to be 5% of trade receivables. How does the change in the provision affect the financial statements?
A profit increases by $600; net trade receivables $38,000
B profit decreases by $600; net trade receivables $38,000
C profit increases by $600; net trade receivables $37,400
D profit decreases by $2,000; net trade receivables $38,000
parts.answer: A profit increases by $600; net trade receivables $38,000
parts.working: New provision 40,000 × 5% = $2,000; decrease of $600 is added to profit (credited to the SOPL). SOFP shows 40,000 − 2,000 = $38,000. C deducts the old provision.

practice.stem:
Kamran sells office furniture in Rawalpindi and gives customers 30 days' credit. Information for two years:
                              2025 $     2026 $
Credit sales               438,000    471,500
Trade receivables at year end  42,000     61,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the trade receivables turnover (collection period) in days for each year. Use a 365-day year and give answers to the nearest whole day.
parts.working: Trade receivables ÷ credit sales × 365 M1; both correct A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the change in the collection period.
parts.answer: It has risen from 35 to 47 days, well above the 30-day terms: customers are paying more slowly, so cash is tied up and the risk of irrecoverable debts is greater.
parts.working: 1 mark: compares with 30-day terms / worse; 1 mark: consequence (cash flow, higher risk of irrecoverable debts)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions Kamran could take to bring the collection period back towards 30 days.
parts.answer: e.g. chase overdue accounts and send reminders; offer a cash discount for early payment; stop supplying customers over their limits; check credit status before giving credit; charge interest on overdue accounts.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any two

practice.stem: Naveed's year ends on 31 December. On 1 July 2026 a customer, Shine Traders, owed him $2,500. On 15 November 2026 Shine Traders was declared bankrupt and Naveed received a final payment of 30 cents for every dollar owed, by bank transfer. The rest was written off.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount received and the amount written off.
parts.answer: Received $750; written off $1,750
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare journal entries to record the receipt and the write-off. Narratives are not required.
parts.answer: Dr Bank 750, Cr Shine Traders 750; Dr Irrecoverable debts 1,750, Cr Shine Traders 1,750
parts.working: B1 each correct debit and credit (4)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of the write-off on Naveed's profit for the year.
parts.answer: Profit falls by $1,750
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: At 30 June 2026 Faiza's trade receivables, after writing off irrecoverable debts, totalled $84,600. These include two specific debts that are doubtful: Al-Noor Stores $3,200 (provision of 50% required) and Raza Traders $1,800 (provision of 100% required). A general provision of 2.5% is to be made on all other trade receivables. The provision at 1 July 2025 was $4,950.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total provision for doubtful debts required at 30 June 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in the provision and state whether it increases or decreases profit.
parts.answer: Increase of $440; profit decreases
parts.working: 5,390 − 4,950 = 440 B1; decreases profit B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a provision for doubtful debts is made even though the customers have not yet failed to pay.
parts.answer: Prudence: some receivables are unlikely to be collected, so assets and profit should not be overstated; matching: the expected loss belongs to the period in which the sales were made.
parts.working: 1 mark per point (prudence; matching / realistic receivables)

practice.stem:
At 31 December 2026 Ravi's trade receivables were $62,400 before the following adjustments.
1 K. Osei's debt of $1,400 is irrecoverable and is to be written off.
2 L. Tan owes $2,000. L. Tan is in financial difficulty, so a provision is to be made for the whole debt.
3 A general provision of 3% is to be made on the remaining receivables.
The provision for doubtful debts at 1 January 2026 was $2,950. During the year $300 was received from a customer whose debt had been written off in 2025; this had been correctly recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total provision for doubtful debts at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: B1 specific provision 2,000; B1 general 3% × (61,000 − 2,000) = 1,770; B1 total 3,770.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net effect of irrecoverable debts, debts recovered and the provision on the profit for the year.
parts.answer: Profit reduced by $1,920 (irrecoverable debts 1,400 + increase in provision 820 − debts recovered 300)
parts.working: B1 increase in provision 820; B1 irrecoverable debt 1,400 and recovery 300 included; B1 net reduction 1,920.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the trade receivables figure shown in the statement of financial position.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why L. Tan's debt is provided for but not written off.
parts.answer: It is doubtful, not certainly irrecoverable: the debt may still be paid, so prudence requires a provision while the debt remains on the ledger.

practice.stem:
Rashid keeps a provision for doubtful debts. Trade receivables at each year end, after writing off irrecoverable debts, and the provision rates were:
Year ended    Trade receivables $   Provision rate
31 Dec 2024          56,000               4%
31 Dec 2025          71,500               4%
31 Dec 2026          64,000               3%
Irrecoverable debts written off were: 2025 $2,140; 2026 $3,380. The provision at 1 January 2025 was $2,240 (4% of $56,000).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the provision for doubtful debts at 31 December 2025 and at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total effect on profit of irrecoverable debts and the provision for each of the years 2025 and 2026.
parts.answer: 2025: profit reduced by $2,760; 2026: profit reduced by $2,440

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare the trade receivables extract of the statement of financial position at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer: Trade receivables 64,000; less provision for doubtful debts 1,920; net 62,080
parts.working: B1 layout with provision deducted; B1 net figure

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why Rashid reduced the rate of provision in 2026.
parts.answer: e.g. better credit control / experience shows fewer customers fail to pay / customer base now more reliable
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual cost of the cash discounts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual savings in (i) overdraft interest and (ii) irrecoverable debts.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Usman whether he should offer the cash discount. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Net annual benefit $14,400: savings $25,200 exceed the discount cost $10,800, so the discount should be offered (subject to the points below).
parts.working: Calculation of net benefit (1). For: improves cash flow/liquidity; less risk of bad debts; reduced overdraft; may attract customers (max 2). Against: estimates uncertain—take-up may differ; some customers may take the discount but pay late; competitors' terms; discount reduces revenue on every early payment (max 2). Decision consistent with argument (1).

practice.stem:
Saima's draft profit for the year ended 31 December 2026 is $37,820. Her draft statement of financial position shows trade receivables of $46,500 less a provision for doubtful debts of $1,200 (the provision brought forward from 2025, unchanged). The following were then discovered:
1 A debt of $900 owed by T. Hussain is irrecoverable and has not been written off.
2 $420 received from J. Ahmed, whose debt was written off in 2024, was credited to sales.
3 A debt of $350 owed by P. Khan, written off in June 2026, was paid in full in December 2026; the receipt was credited to P. Khan's account and is included in trade receivables as a credit balance, reducing the total.
4 The provision for doubtful debts is to be 4% of trade receivables at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected trade receivables (before the provision) at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: 46,500 − 900 (write off) + 350 (remove credit balance: the amount is irrecoverable debt recovered, not a reduction of receivables) M1 = $45,950 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.working: − 900 B1; item 2: reclassify sales to irrecoverable debts recovered, no effect on profit B1; + 350 recovered income B1; provision 1,838 − 1,200 = 638 increase deducted; corrected $36,632 B1 (OF)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why item 2 does not change the profit for the year but should still be corrected.
parts.answer: The $420 is income either way, so profit is the same; but it is not revenue from sales, so gross profit and revenue are overstated and ratios such as gross margin are distorted.
parts.working: 1 mark: no effect on profit for the year; 1 mark: revenue/gross profit misstated

practice.stem:
Yasmin's draft profit for the year ended 31 October 2026 was $31,600. The following were then discovered.
(i) Depreciation of $2,400 on the delivery van had not been charged.
(ii) Commission receivable of $650 for October 2026 had not been recorded.
(iii) Wages of $900 owing at 31 October 2026 had not been recorded.
(iv) Goods costing $400 taken by Yasmin for her own use had not been recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement of corrected profit for the year ended 31 October 2026.
parts.answer:
Statement of corrected profit
                                                     $
Draft profit                                    31,600
(i) Depreciation of van                        (2,400)
(ii) Commission receivable                         650
(iii) Wages accrued                              (900)
(iv) Goods for own use (purchases reduced)         400
Corrected profit                                29,350
parts.working: 1 mark for each adjustment with the correct sign (4); 1 mark corrected profit 29,350.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of item (iii) on current liabilities.
parts.answer: Current liabilities increase by $900.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader's draft profit is $30,000. It is then found that goods costing $800 taken by the owner for her family have not been recorded. What is the corrected profit?
A $29,200
B $30,000
C $30,800
D $31,600
parts.working: Recording the drawings reduces purchases (Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases), so cost of sales falls by $800 and profit rises to $30,800. A deducts the goods as if they were an expense.

practice.stem:
Tahir owns a hardware shop in Sukkur. His draft profit for the year ended 31 August 2026 was $26,940. The following errors and omissions were found:
1 Rent of $1,200 paid for September 2026 was included in rent expense.
2 Commission of $310 earned in August 2026 has not been received or recorded.
3 Tahir's private mobile phone bill of $540 was paid from the business and charged to telephone expenses.
4 Goods returned by a customer, selling price $460, were not recorded. The goods were put back into inventory, which was counted correctly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement of corrected profit for the year ended 31 August 2026.
parts.working: Draft 26,940; + 1,200 B1; + 310 B1; + 540 B1; − 460 (sales returns reduce revenue) B1; corrected $28,530 B1 (OF)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the double entry to correct item 3.
parts.answer: Dr Drawings $540; Cr Telephone expenses $540
parts.working: B1 each

practice.stem:
Ruby runs a café in Kuala Lumpur. For each item below, state whether correcting it will increase, decrease or have no effect on (i) profit for the year and (ii) Ruby's capital at the year end.
1 Interest of $120 charged by the bank had not been recorded.
2 A cash sale of $95 was recorded twice.
3 Ruby paid $2,000 of her own savings into the business bank account, but it was recorded as sales.
4 A payment of $60 to a supplier was debited to the wrong supplier's account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copy and complete the effect of each correction on profit and on capital.
parts.answer: 1 profit decrease, capital decrease; 2 profit decrease, capital decrease; 3 profit decrease, capital no effect (capital introduced replaces profit); 4 profit no effect, capital no effect
parts.working: 1 mark per correct cell (8). Item 3: profit falls by 2,000 but capital introduced rises by 2,000, so closing capital is unchanged.

practice.stem: Before preparing final financial statements, a trader makes year-end adjustments to the figures in the trial balance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why year-end adjustments are needed.
parts.answer: The trial balance shows amounts recorded during the year, which may not match the income earned and expenses incurred in the period (accruals concept), or may overstate assets (prudence), e.g. inventory, depreciation, accruals, prepayments, irrecoverable debts.
parts.working: 1 mark: matching/accruals; 1 mark: prudence/true and fair view or an example

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each adjustment, state the effect on profit: (i) an increase in closing inventory; (ii) an accrued expense; (iii) depreciation; (iv) a prepaid expense at the year end.
parts.answer: (i) increases profit (reduces cost of sales); (ii) decreases; (iii) decreases; (iv) increases
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A draft profit of $42,000 has been calculated. It is then found that:
• closing inventory was overstated by $1,500
• electricity of $800 owing was not accrued
• insurance of $600 paid for next year was charged as an expense.
What is the corrected profit?
A $39,100
B $41,900
C $43,300
D $40,300
parts.working: Overstated closing inventory overstated profit (−1,500); the accrual adds an expense (−800); the prepayment removes an expense (+600). 42,000 − 1,500 − 800 + 600 = 40,300. A treats the prepayment as an extra expense.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which correction will increase the profit for the year but have no effect on net current assets?
A depreciation of $500 on equipment had been charged twice
B closing inventory had been understated by $500
C rent of $500 paid in advance had been treated as an expense
D electricity of $500 owing had been omitted
parts.answer: A depreciation of $500 on equipment had been charged twice
parts.working: Removing the duplicate depreciation increases profit and the carrying amount of a non-current asset, not current assets. B and C increase both profit and current assets; D reduces profit.

practice.stem:
Farhan's capital at 1 April 2025 was $84,500. His draft profit for the year ended 31 March 2026 was $31,250 and his drawings were recorded as $18,600. It was then found that:
1 Loan interest of $900 for March 2026 had not been accrued.
2 A computer bought for the business for $1,800 on 1 April 2025 had been debited to drawings. Computers are depreciated at 25% per annum on cost.
3 Farhan took cash of $750 from the till for personal use; this was not recorded anywhere and the cash book balance is overstated by the same amount.
4 Additional capital of $5,000 paid in on 1 October 2025 was recorded as a loan from Farhan's brother.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year ended 31 March 2026.
parts.working: 31,250 − 900 − 450 depreciation M1 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected drawings.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare the capital section of the statement of financial position at 31 March 2026.
parts.answer: Capital 1 April 2025 84,500; add capital introduced 5,000; add profit 29,900; less drawings 17,550; capital 31 March 2026 101,850
parts.working: B1 opening + capital introduced; B1 profit (OF); B1 drawings (OF); B1 closing $101,850

practice.stem: Nasreen's draft profit for the year ended 31 December 2026 is $44,600. On 1 October 2026 she bought a delivery van for $24,000 by cheque. The bookkeeper debited the payment to motor repairs. Nasreen depreciates vehicles at 20% per annum using the straight-line method, with a full month's charge in the month of purchase. No depreciation has been charged on the new van.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation on the van for the year ended 31 December 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the difference between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure, using this error as an example.
parts.answer: Capital expenditure buys or improves a non-current asset that benefits several years (the van) and goes to the SOFP; revenue expenditure is the day-to-day running cost consumed within the year (e.g. repairs) and goes to the SOPL. Treating the van as repairs understated profit and non-current assets.
parts.working: 1 mark capital definition; 1 mark revenue definition; 1 mark effect of the error

practice.stem:
Kofi sells household appliances in Kumasi. His draft figures for the year ended 30 April 2026 show revenue $312,000, closing inventory $27,400 and gross profit $93,600. The following items were found:
1 Appliances with a selling price of $3,600 were sent to a customer on sale or return on 26 April 2026 and recorded as a credit sale. The customer has not yet accepted them. Kofi sells at cost plus 50%. They were not included in closing inventory.
2 Goods costing $1,450 received on 30 April 2026 were included in closing inventory, but the supplier's invoice has not been recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected revenue and the corrected closing inventory.
parts.answer: Revenue $308,400; closing inventory $29,800
parts.working: Revenue 312,000 − 3,600 B1; cost of goods on sale or return 3,600 ÷ 1.5 = 2,400 M1; inventory 29,800 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected gross profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the accounting concept that explains why the goods on sale or return are not yet a sale.
parts.answer: Realisation concept
parts.working: B1

practice.stem:
Extract from Sumaira's draft statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 July 2026:
                                   $
Revenue                       186,400
Cost of sales                (121,200)
Gross profit                   65,200
Expenses                      (38,700)
Profit for the year            26,500
The following have not been recorded:
1 Carriage inwards of $860, paid in cash and included in expenses.
2 Closing inventory should be reduced by $1,140 for damaged goods.
3 Discount allowed of $520.
4 Sales of $2,300 on the last day of the year were omitted from revenue; the goods were correctly excluded from closing inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected gross profit.
parts.working: 65,200 − 860 (carriage inwards belongs in cost of sales) − 1,140 + 2,300 M1 M1 = $65,500 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: 26,500 − 1,140 − 520 + 2,300 (carriage inwards only moves within the statement) M1 M1 = $27,140 A1

practice.stem:
Ibrahim's draft financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2026 show a profit of $48,250 and net current assets of $18,600. The following have not yet been taken into account.
(i) Closing inventory includes damaged goods that cost $2,300. They can be sold for $1,500 after repairs costing $200.
(ii) A customer owing $700 has been declared bankrupt. The debt has not been written off. The provision for doubtful debts of 2% was calculated on receivables that included this debt.
(iii) Rent of $1,800 paid for January–March 2027 was charged as an expense of 2026.
(iv) Repairs to the premises costing $1,600 were debited to the premises (non-current asset) account. No depreciation is charged on premises in the year of expenditure.
(v) Loan interest of $450 owing at 31 December 2026 has not been recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement of corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.answer:
Statement of corrected profit
                                                             $
Draft profit                                            48,250
(i) Inventory written down to NRV (2,300 − 1,300)      (1,000)
(ii) Irrecoverable debt written off                      (700)
(ii) Reduction in provision (2% × 700)                      14
(iii) Rent prepaid                                       1,800
(iv) Repairs charged as expense                        (1,600)
(v) Loan interest accrued                                (450)
Corrected profit                                        46,314
parts.working: B1 NRV 1,300 and write-down 1,000; B1 debt 700 deducted; B1 provision reduced by 14 added; B1 prepayment +1,800; B1 repairs −1,600; B1 interest −450 and corrected profit 46,314.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected net current assets at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: M1 18,600 − 1,000 − 700 + 14 + 1,800 − 450 (item (iv) affects non-current assets only); A1 18,264.

practice.stem:
Draft statement of financial position of Zafar, a wholesaler in Gujranwala, at 31 March 2026:
                                         $
Non-current assets (carrying amount)  96,000
Inventory                              24,300
Trade receivables                      31,800
Other receivables                       1,100
Bank                                    6,700
Total assets                          159,900
Capital at 1 April 2025               104,000
Profit for the year                    33,400
Drawings                              (21,000)
Trade payables                         38,200
Other payables                          5,300
Total capital and liabilities         159,900
The following must be taken into account:
1 Depreciation of $4,800 on fixtures has not been charged.
2 An irrecoverable debt of $1,300 is to be written off.
3 Insurance of $780 paid for April–June 2026 was charged as an expense.
4 Zafar took goods costing $1,250 for his own use; this has not been recorded.
5 A supplier's invoice for $2,150 for goods included in closing inventory has not been recorded.
6 Bank charges of $190 shown on the bank statement have not been entered in the cash book.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the corrected statement of financial position at 31 March 2026.
parts.answer: Non-current assets 91,200; current assets: inventory 24,300, trade receivables 30,500, other receivables 1,880, bank 6,510 = 63,190; total assets 154,390. Capital 104,000 + profit 26,990 − drawings 22,250 = 108,740; current liabilities: trade payables 40,350, other payables 5,300 = 45,650; total 154,390.
parts.working: B1 NCA; B1 trade receivables; B1 other receivables; B1 bank; B1 profit (OF); B1 drawings; B1 trade payables; B1 totals agree

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why item 4 does not change closing inventory.
parts.answer: The goods taken had already left the shop before the count, so they were never in closing inventory; only purchases (cost of sales) and drawings need to be adjusted.
parts.working: 1 mark not in count; 1 mark adjustment is to purchases/drawings

practice.stem:
Hamid's draft financial statements for the year ended 30 September 2026 show profit of $52,700, current assets of $47,900 and current liabilities of $29,600 (including a bank overdraft of $8,400). The following adjustments are needed:
1 Closing inventory included goods costing $3,200 that can now be sold for only $2,000 after repairs costing $450.
2 A cheque for $1,700 received from a customer on 30 September 2026 was recorded in the cash book but not in the customer's account.
3 Wages of $2,600 owing at 30 September 2026 have not been recorded.
4 Rent receivable of $1,500 for October 2026 was received in September and included in income.
5 Loan interest of $1,350 paid on 30 September 2026 was debited to the loan account instead of loan interest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: Inventory write-down 3,200 − 1,550 = 1,650 M1; −2,600; −1,500; −1,350 (loan balance understated, expense missing) M1 M1; $45,600 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected net current assets (working capital).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how item 5 affects the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: The loan (non-current liability) is understated by $1,350 and must be increased.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem:
Lin Wei owns a print shop in Penang. Her draft profit for the year ended 31 December 2026 is $41,500. On reviewing the books the following were found:
1 A printer that cost $12,000 on 1 January 2024 was sold on 1 July 2026 for $5,200. The proceeds were credited to sales and nothing else has been recorded. Printers are depreciated at 20% per annum on cost, charged monthly; depreciation for 2026 has been charged on all printers held at 31 December 2026 but not on this one.
2 Depreciation of shop fittings has been calculated at 10% on cost ($30,000) instead of the business's usual 10% reducing balance. Accumulated depreciation on the fittings at 1 January 2026 was $5,700.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss on disposal of the printer.
parts.answer: Loss $800
parts.working: Accumulated depreciation 12,000 × 20% × 2.5 years = 6,000 M1; carrying amount 6,000 M1; 6,000 − 5,200 = loss $800 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the correct depreciation on shop fittings for 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.working: 41,500 − 5,200 (remove from sales) − 1,200 (depreciation Jan–Jun) − 800 (loss) + 570 (fittings depreciation overstated) M1 M1 M1 = $34,870 A1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader has a damaged bicycle helmet that cost $40. It can be sold for $55 if repaired at a cost of $10. The salesperson receives commission of 10% of the selling price. At what value should the helmet be included in closing inventory?
A $39.50
B $40.00
C $45.00
D $55.00
parts.working: NRV = 55 − 10 − 5.50 = $39.50, which is below cost $40, so the lower figure is used. B ignores the selling costs.

practice.stem: Hafsa runs a stationery shop in Islamabad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the rule in IAS 2 Inventories for valuing inventory.
parts.answer: At the lower of cost and net realisable value
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'net realisable value'.
parts.answer: The estimated selling price less the estimated costs of completion and the costs necessary to make the sale.
parts.working: 1 mark selling price; 1 mark less costs to complete/sell

parts.label: c
parts.text: A box of 200 calendars for 2026 cost $1.80 each. In January 2026 they can only be sold for $1.20 each. Calculate their value for closing inventory at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: 200 × 1.20 (NRV below cost) B1

practice.stem:
Arif sells sports goods in Sialkot. At 30 June 2026 his inventory included the following lines:
Line            Units   Cost per unit $   Selling price per unit $   Selling costs per unit $
Cricket bats       50         22                  38                       3
Footballs          80         15                  14                       1
Hockey sticks      30         18                  25                       9
Tennis rackets     40         30                  45                       4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of each line and the total value of closing inventory at 30 June 2026.
parts.answer: Bats 1,100 (cost); footballs 1,040 (NRV 13); hockey sticks 480 (NRV 16); rackets 1,200 (cost); total $3,820
parts.working: B1 footballs at NRV; B1 hockey sticks at NRV; B1 bats and rackets at cost; B1 total $3,820

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the accounting concept that requires inventory to be valued at the lower figure.
parts.answer: Prudence
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: Tariq sells mobile phone accessories. At his year end he has 300 phone cases that cost $4 each. A new phone model has made them less popular.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the inventory value of the phone cases if they can be sold for $6.50 each, with packaging of $0.50 each.
parts.working: NRV 6.00 > cost 4.00, so cost: 300 × 4 B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the inventory value if instead they can be sold for only $3.60 each, with packaging of $0.40 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect on gross profit of the valuation in (b) compared with valuing at cost.
parts.answer: Gross profit is $240 lower

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business has three lines of inventory at its year end.
Line              Cost $ Selling price $ Selling costs $
X                  4,000           5,200               0
Y                  3,500           2,900               0
Z                  6,100           6,400             500
At what value should the inventory be shown in the statement of financial position?
A $13,600
B $13,000
C $12,800
D $14,000
parts.working: Each line at the lower of cost and net realisable value: X 4,000; Y 2,900; Z NRV 6,400 − 500 = 5,900 (below cost 6,100). Total 12,800. B ignores the selling costs of Z; A uses cost throughout.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
At 31 December 2025 a trader valued a line of inventory at its cost of $6,000, although its net realisable value was only $4,500. The goods were sold in 2026 for $4,500. What is the effect of this error?
A profit for 2025 overstated by $1,500 and profit for 2026 understated by $1,500
B profit for 2025 understated by $1,500 and profit for 2026 overstated by $1,500
C profit for 2025 overstated by $1,500 and no effect on profit for 2026
D no effect on profit for 2025 and profit for 2026 understated by $1,500
parts.answer: A profit for 2025 overstated by $1,500 and profit for 2026 understated by $1,500
parts.working: Closing inventory 2025 too high → 2025 profit too high by $1,500. It becomes opening inventory 2026, so 2026 cost of sales is too high and 2026 profit too low. C forgets the effect carried into the next year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of inventory at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: 36,850 + 5,500 (sales at cost) − 3,140 − 400 (returns in at cost) + 260 − 380 (write-down) M1 for each correct adjustment (5), A1 $38,690

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why an inventory count should take place as close as possible to the year end.
parts.answer: Fewer adjustments are needed, so there is less risk of error in the year-end figure.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem:
A spice wholesaler in Karachi holds three lines of inventory at its year end:
Line        Cost $    Net realisable value $
Cumin      12,400          15,100
Saffron     8,800           6,900
Cardamom    9,600          10,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory if the lower of cost and NRV is applied to (i) each line separately and (ii) total inventory.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which value must be used and explain why.
parts.answer: $28,900: IAS 2 applies the rule item by item (line by line), so the loss on saffron is recognised and is not hidden by gains on other lines that are not yet realised.
parts.working: 1 mark correct value; 1 mark explanation (prudence/no offsetting of unrealised gains)

practice.stem:
Edward owns a bookshop in Nairobi. His inventory at 31 March 2026, valued at cost, was $41,750. The following facts were then discovered:
1 Books costing $1,600 were in transit from a supplier at 31 March. Edward had already received and recorded the invoice; the goods became his when they were shipped. They were not counted.
2 Books costing $2,300 were held by Edward on sale or return from a publisher and were included in the count.
3 Twenty atlases costing $35 each were included; a new edition means they will sell for $28 each, less a 10% discount to clear them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected value of inventory at 31 March 2026.
parts.working: +1,600 B1; −2,300 (belongs to the publisher) B1; atlases NRV 28 × 0.9 = 25.20, write-down 20 × 9.80 = 196.00 M1; $40,854 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the goods held on sale or return are excluded.
parts.answer: They still belong to the publisher until Edward accepts or sells them, so they are not his asset.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: Sana owns a gift shop in Lahore. Her assistant suggests that closing inventory should be valued at its selling price, 'because that is what the goods are worth'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why inventory is not normally valued at selling price.
parts.answer: Valuing at selling price would include profit before the goods are sold; profit is only recognised when it is realised (realisation concept), and prudence means assets should not be overstated.
parts.working: 1 mark: includes unrealised profit; 1 mark: realisation/prudence

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why inventory is reduced to net realisable value when this is below cost.
parts.answer: If goods will be sold for less than they cost, the loss is foreseeable; prudence requires the loss to be recognised now and the asset not to be overstated.
parts.working: 1 mark: foreseeable loss; 1 mark: prudence / asset not overstated

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two examples of situations in a gift shop when net realisable value may fall below cost.
parts.answer: e.g. seasonal items (Eid or New Year cards) left after the season; damaged or shop-soiled goods; items out of fashion; prices cut by competitors.
parts.working: 1 mark each

practice.stem:
Grace owns a fashion shop. Her inventory at 31 December 2026 was counted and valued at cost: $54,800. The following were then found.
1 Forty jackets costing $45 each are out of fashion. They can be sold through an agent for $38 each; the agent charges 10% commission on the selling price.
2 Goods that cost $900 are damaged. After repairs costing $150 they can be sold for $1,000.
3 One box of goods costing $1,650 was counted twice.
4 Goods costing $2,400 have a net realisable value of $3,100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected value of inventory at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer:
Inventory
                                                 $
Value at cost                               54,800
Jackets: 40 × (45 − 34.20)                   (432)
Damaged goods: 900 − 850                      (50)
Box counted twice                          (1,650)
Goods with NRV above cost – no change            0
Corrected inventory                         52,668
parts.working: B1 jacket NRV 38 × 90% = 34.20 and write-down 432; B1 damaged goods write-down 50; B1 double count removed; B1 no change for item 4 and total 52,668.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of the corrections on gross profit.
parts.answer: Gross profit decreases by $2,132.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
parts.answer: Prudence: losses are recognised as soon as they are foreseen, so assets and profit are not overstated. Unrealised profits (NRV above cost) are not recognised until goods are sold (realisation).
parts.working: 1 mark: prudence – avoid overstating assets/profit; 1 mark: profit not recognised until realised / IAS 2 requirement.

practice.stem:
Precision Tools, a trader in Gujrat, has 500 units of an obsolete drill in inventory, which cost $64 each. Two options are available:
Option 1: sell them as they are to a scrap dealer for $18 each, with the dealer paying for collection.
Option 2: convert them to a new specification at a cost of $25 each and sell them at $80 each, paying a sales commission of 10% of the selling price and delivery of $4 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net realisable value per unit under each option.
parts.answer: Option 1 $18; Option 2 $43
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value at which the drills should be shown in closing inventory, assuming the business will choose the better option.
parts.working: NRV is the higher net amount the business can realise, $43, which is below cost $64 M1; 500 × 43 = $21,500 A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the write-down that must be charged against profit.

practice.stem:
Horizon Imports Ltd buys electric scooters from China. For a consignment of 120 scooters the following costs were paid:
                                         $
Purchase price (120 × $310)          37,200
Import duty                           4,464
Shipping and insurance to warehouse   2,736
Storage in warehouse after arrival      960
Advertising for the scooters          1,800
Delivery to customers                 1,440
At the year end 45 scooters were unsold. A competitor has cut prices, and the company now expects to sell them for $370 each, after spending $12 on each to fit a safety upgrade, and paying selling commission of 5% of the selling price.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost per scooter in accordance with IAS 2.
parts.working: Include purchase price, import duty and shipping to bring to present location (M1); exclude storage after arrival, advertising and delivery to customers (M1); 44,400 ÷ 120 = $370 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net realisable value per scooter.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the value of the unsold scooters in the statement of financial position.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why storage costs after arrival are excluded from the cost of inventory.
parts.answer: They do not bring the goods to their present location and condition; they are incurred after that point and are expenses of the period.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: In preparing the financial statements of Dua's boutique for the year ended 31 December 2026, it was discovered that closing inventory at 31 December 2025 had been overvalued by $2,700 because damaged dresses had been included at cost instead of net realisable value. The dresses were sold in 2026. Closing inventory at 31 December 2026 included shoes costing $4,100 whose net realisable value is $2,950. The draft profits, before any corrections, were: 2025 $38,400; 2026 $41,250.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.working: 41,250 + 2,700 (opening inventory overstated, so cost of sales too high) M1 − 1,150 (write-down of shoes) M1 = $42,800 A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the overall effect of all the corrections on Dua's capital at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer: Decrease of $1,150

practice.stem:
Rafiq runs a furniture showroom in Hyderabad and sells at cost plus 25%. His inventory count at 30 June 2026 gave a figure of $73,500 at selling price, because the assistant recorded the price labels. Further information:
• Included in the count is a dining set with a price label of $4,000. It has a scratched table top and will be sold for $2,600 after a repair costing $300.
• A sofa with a price label of $1,500 was sold and paid for on 29 June 2026 but was still in the showroom waiting for delivery; it was included in the count. The sale was recorded.
• A wardrobe costing $1,200 was out on loan to a customer for approval (sale or return) and was not included in the count.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of inventory at cost before the dining set is considered, after removing the sofa and adding the wardrobe.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the final value of inventory at 30 June 2026.
parts.working: Dining set cost 4,000 ÷ 1.25 = 3,200; NRV 2,300 M1; write-down 900 M1; $57,900 A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the sofa is excluded although it is still in the showroom.
parts.answer: Ownership has passed to the customer and the sale has been recorded, so it is no longer Rafiq's inventory.
parts.working: B1
