parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature applies to a sole trader?
A The owner has limited liability.
B The business is a separate legal entity from its owner.
C The owner has unlimited liability for the business's debts.
D The business must publish audited financial statements.
parts.answer: C The owner has unlimited liability for the business's debts.
parts.working: A sole trader is not a separate legal person, so the owner is personally liable for all business debts (unlimited liability). A and B describe limited companies.

practice.stem: Areeba plans to open a small bakery in Multan as a sole trader.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of operating as a sole trader.
parts.answer: Any two: owner keeps all the profit; full control and quick decisions; easy and cheap to set up; financial affairs are private (no need to publish accounts).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of operating as a sole trader.
parts.answer: Any two: unlimited liability; limited capital (own savings and loans only); heavy workload / no one to share responsibility; business may end if the owner dies or is ill; harder to borrow.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term limited liability.
parts.answer: Shareholders can lose no more than the amount they have paid (or agreed to pay) for their shares; their personal assets cannot be used to pay the company's debts.
parts.working: 1 mark: loss limited to investment in shares; 1 mark: personal assets protected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by saying a limited company is a separate legal entity.
parts.answer: The company exists in law separately from its owners: it can own assets, enter contracts, sue and be sued in its own name, and it continues if shareholders change or die.
parts.working: 1 mark: separate person in law; 1 mark: example (contracts, own assets, continuity).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between ownership and control in a limited company.
parts.answer: Shareholders own the company, but the directors (who may not be shareholders) manage and control it on their behalf.
parts.working: 1 mark owners = shareholders; 1 mark control = directors/managers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why limited companies must publish annual financial statements.
parts.answer: Because shareholders do not run the company, they need information to judge the directors' performance (stewardship); creditors and lenders need information because their claims are limited to the company's assets (limited liability).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of business organisation can raise finance by offering its shares for sale to the general public?
A sole trader
B partnership
C private limited company
D public limited company
parts.answer: D public limited company
parts.working: Only a public limited company may offer shares to the general public (e.g. through a stock exchange). A private limited company can sell shares only privately, for example to family or invited investors.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about a public limited company are correct?
1 Its shares may be offered for sale to the general public.
2 Its shareholders have unlimited liability.
3 It is a separate legal entity from its shareholders.
4 It must have only one owner.
A 1 and 2
B 1 and 3
C 2 and 4
D 3 and 4
parts.answer: B 1 and 3
parts.working: A public limited company can offer shares to the public (1) and is a separate legal entity (3). Shareholders' liability is limited to the amount unpaid on their shares, so 2 is wrong; it can have many shareholders, so 4 is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between a private limited company and a public limited company.
parts.answer: Any two: a private company cannot offer its shares to the general public, a public company can (and may be listed on a stock exchange); private company shares are usually transferred only with the directors' agreement, public company shares are freely traded; a public company usually needs a minimum share capital and stricter disclosure; a private company name ends in 'Limited/(Private) Limited', a public one in 'plc' or equivalent.
parts.working: 2 marks per difference, comparing both types.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why a family business might prefer to remain a private limited company.
parts.answer: The family keeps control because shares cannot be sold to outsiders without approval, so there is no risk of takeover; also fewer disclosure requirements and lower costs.
parts.working: 1 mark reason, 1 mark development.

practice.stem: Usman has run a computer accessories shop in Hyderabad as a sole trader for six years. He wants to open a second branch and start selling online. His brother, who has IT skills, offers to invest $40,000 and become a partner.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise Usman whether he should form a partnership with his brother. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: extra capital ($40,000) to open the second branch; brother's IT and online-sales skills add expertise; workload and decision-making shared; cover during illness or holidays. Against: profits must be shared; unlimited liability continues — Usman becomes liable for his brother's business decisions; disagreements may arise, especially in a family; slower decisions; partnership may end on death or retirement. Decision: e.g. form the partnership with a written partnership agreement covering profit sharing, interest on capital and salaries, because the capital and skills are needed for the expansion.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for advantages and up to 2 for disadvantages, applied to the case; 1 mark recommendation of a written agreement or other safeguard; 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: Fahad, a sole trader, has closed his furniture business. It owes creditors $85,000. The business assets were sold for $52,000. Fahad has personal assets (savings and a car) worth $60,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount that Fahad must pay from his personal assets.
parts.working: Debts 85,000 − business assets realised 52,000 = 33,000. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fahad's friend Nasir owned 30,000 $1 shares, fully paid at $1.20 each, in a limited company that collapsed with debts larger than its assets. State the maximum Nasir could lose and explain why.
parts.answer: $36,000. Nasir has limited liability: his loss is limited to the amount paid for his shares (30,000 × $1.20); his personal assets cannot be claimed by the company's creditors.
parts.working: 1 mark amount, 1 mark limited liability, 1 mark personal assets protected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare how owners withdraw profits from (i) a sole trader business and (ii) a limited company.
parts.answer: (i) The sole trader takes drawings, recorded in the capital account. (ii) Shareholders receive dividends declared by the directors out of distributable profits; directors who work in the company also receive salaries treated as expenses.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare how the owners' capital is shown in the statement of financial position of a partnership and of a limited company.
parts.answer: Partnership: each partner has a capital account (often fixed) and a current account for profit shares, interest and drawings. Company: equity shows issued share capital and reserves (share premium, retained earnings and other reserves).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each organisation, state whether it is a sole trader, a partnership, a private limited company, a public limited company or a non-profit organisation.
(i) Three doctors share a clinic, profits and unlimited liability.
(ii) A cricket club funded by members' subscriptions.
(iii) A company whose shares are bought and sold on a stock exchange.
(iv) A family firm whose shares can only be transferred with the directors' permission.
parts.answer: (i) partnership; (ii) non-profit organisation (club); (iii) public limited company; (iv) private limited company.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Hamza holds 5,000 ordinary shares of $1 each in a limited company. The shares were issued at $1.60 each, of which $1.20 per share has been called and paid. The company is wound up with debts greater than its assets.
What is the maximum further amount Hamza can be required to pay?
A $0
B $2,000
C $3,000
D $8,000
parts.working: Limited liability limits a shareholder's loss to the amount unpaid on the shares: 5,000 × (1.60 − 1.20) = $2,000. $3,000 wrongly uses the share premium (1.60 − 1.00); $8,000 is the full issue price, already partly paid.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A hockey club in Sialkot is run for its members, not to make a profit. Which statement does it prepare instead of a statement of profit or loss, and what is the name of its equivalent of capital?
A income and expenditure account; accumulated fund
B receipts and payments account; retained earnings
C statement of changes in equity; accumulated fund
D income and expenditure account; current account
parts.answer: A income and expenditure account; accumulated fund
parts.working: Non-profit organisations prepare an income and expenditure account (accruals basis) and their capital is the accumulated fund. A receipts and payments account (B) is only a summary of cash and does not replace the statement of profit or loss.

practice.stem: Zainab and Kiran are partners in an interior design business in Karachi. Turnover has tripled in three years and they have just won a contract to design the interior of a 200-room hotel, which will need expensive materials bought in advance. A cousin is willing to invest money but does not want to take part in running the business or have unlimited liability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise Zainab and Kiran whether they should convert their partnership into a private limited company. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For conversion: limited liability protects their homes against claims (important given the large contract and its risks); the company is a separate legal entity, so it continues if a partner leaves; easier to raise finance — can issue shares to investors such as their cousin and use loan notes; may appear more credible to large clients. Against: set-up costs and legal formalities; must file accounts publicly (loss of privacy) and may require an audit; profits taxed as a company and owners paid through salaries and dividends; banks may still ask for personal guarantees, reducing the benefit of limited liability; shares in a private company cannot easily be sold. Decision: convert, because the growth in contract size and the need for outside capital make limited liability and access to share finance worth the extra cost.
parts.working: Level 3 (7–8): well-applied points on both sides and a justified decision. Level 2 (4–6): some applied points on both sides or one-sided with a decision. Level 1 (1–3): general features of partnerships/companies.

practice.stem: Hassan bought 40,000 ordinary shares of $1 each in a private limited company at $1.25 per share, fully paid. Salman is a general partner in a firm of architects with one other partner.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the maximum amount Hassan could lose as a shareholder, and the maximum Salman could lose as a partner. Explain the difference.
parts.answer: Hassan: $50,000 (40,000 × $1.25 paid). Salman: there is no limit — he could lose his capital and his personal assets, because partners have unlimited liability and are jointly liable for all the partnership's debts (including those caused by the other partner).
parts.working: 1 mark Hassan's 50,000; 1 mark Salman unlimited; 1 mark limited liability explained; 1 mark joint liability/personal assets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way in which the law allows a partner to have limited liability, and the condition that applies.
parts.answer: A limited partner (in a limited partnership / LLP structure) may have liability limited to their capital, provided there is at least one general partner with unlimited liability and the limited partner takes no part in managing the business (or the firm is registered as a limited liability partnership).
parts.working: 1 mark limited partner/LLP; 1 mark condition (no management role / at least one general partner / registration).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item is capital expenditure for a courier company?
A fuel for the delivery vans
B repainting the office
C purchase of a new delivery motorcycle
D insurance of the vans
parts.answer: C purchase of a new delivery motorcycle
parts.working: Buying a new motorcycle provides a non-current asset used for more than one year, so it is capital expenditure. Repainting (B) only maintains an existing asset, so it is revenue expenditure.

practice.stem: Bano Distributors bought and equipped a warehouse in Gujranwala.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each item as capital expenditure or revenue expenditure.
(i) Legal fees for buying a new warehouse
(ii) Wages of the warehouse staff
(iii) Installing air-conditioning in the warehouse for the first time
(iv) Replacing a broken window pane in the warehouse
parts.answer: (i) capital; (ii) revenue; (iii) capital; (iv) revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item is revenue expenditure for a hotel?
A new beds for the guest rooms
B the cost of building an extra wing
C wages of the reception staff
D legal fees paid when buying the hotel building
parts.answer: C wages of the reception staff
parts.working: Wages are a day-to-day running cost, used up within the year, so they are revenue expenditure. Beds, the new wing and legal fees on buying the building all add to non-current assets that benefit several years.

practice.stem:
Pindi School Transport runs buses for schools in Rawalpindi. During the year it paid for the following:
(i) a new bus
(ii) diesel for all buses
(iii) fitting seat belts to the new bus before it was first used
(iv) annual insurance of the buses
(v) replacement tyres for an old bus
(vi) a GPS tracking system installed in every bus, which will be used for several years

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define capital expenditure.
parts.answer: Spending on buying, or improving, non-current assets that will be used in the business for more than one year (including costs of getting them ready for use).
parts.working: B1 non-current assets bought or improved; B1 benefit more than one year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Classify each item (i)–(vi) as capital or revenue expenditure.
parts.answer: Capital: (i), (iii), (vi). Revenue: (ii), (iv), (v).
parts.working: 1 mark for each two correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why item (v) is revenue expenditure.
parts.answer: Replacing tyres maintains the bus in its existing condition; it does not improve it or extend its life.

practice.stem:
A trader received the following amounts during the year:
(i) proceeds from selling an old delivery van
(ii) rent received from sub-letting part of the shop
(iii) a bank loan
(iv) cash sales
(v) extra capital paid in by the owner
(vi) commission received

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each item as a capital receipt or a revenue receipt.
parts.answer: Capital receipts: (i), (iii), (v). Revenue receipts: (ii), (iv), (vi).
parts.working: 1 mark for each two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where revenue receipts are shown in the financial statements and where capital receipts (iii) and (v) are shown.
parts.answer: Revenue receipts are income in the statement of profit or loss. The loan is a liability and the capital introduced is added to the capital account, both in the statement of financial position.
parts.working: B1 revenue receipts; B1 capital receipts.

practice.stem: Nishat Weaving bought a weaving machine. The invoice and other costs were: price $86,000; delivery $2,400; installation $3,100; staff training on the machine $1,800; first-year maintenance contract $950; insurance for the first year $1,200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount to be capitalised as the cost of the machine.
parts.working: Price 86,000 + delivery 2,400 + installation 3,100 = 91,500. Training, maintenance and insurance are revenue. M1 A1 + 1 for excluding all revenue items.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revenue expenditure and state where it is shown.
parts.answer: $3,950; shown as expenses in the statement of profit or loss.

practice.stem: A school in Abbottabad built an extension to its building costing $40,000. The bookkeeper debited this to repairs and maintenance. Buildings are depreciated at 10% per year on cost, with a full year's charge in the year of acquisition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the effect of the error on profit for the year.
parts.answer: Profit is understated by $36,000.
parts.working: The 40,000 should be removed from expenses (+40,000) and depreciation of 10% × 40,000 = 4,000 charged; net +36,000. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of the error on the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Non-current assets are understated by $36,000 (cost 40,000 less depreciation 4,000), and capital (via profit) is understated by the same amount.
parts.working: 1 mark NCA; 1 mark capital/retained profit.

practice.stem:
Malik Couriers bought a new delivery van. The payments were:
                                              $
List price                               32,000
Less trade discount 5%
Registration fee (one-off)                  450
Number plates                               120
Racking fitted inside the van for deliveries   680
Insurance for the first year              1,400
First tank of fuel                          150
Annual road tax                             300

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount to be recorded as the cost of the van.
parts.working: B1 32,000 × 0.95 = 30,400; B1 registration, plates and racking added; A1 31,650.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revenue expenditure and state where it is shown.
parts.answer: $1,850, as expenses in the statement of profit or loss.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the racking is treated differently from the insurance.
parts.answer: The racking is needed to use the van for deliveries and lasts its whole life (capital); insurance covers only one year of running (revenue).
parts.working: B1 each.

practice.stem:
Khan Furnishings used its own employees to build a showroom extension. The extension was completed on the last day of the year; no depreciation is charged in the year of completion. These costs were recorded as follows:
Item                                      Amount ($)   Recorded in
Materials                                     18,600   Purchases
Wages of employees on the build               7,200   Wages
Architect's fees                              2,500   Professional fees
Hire of scaffolding                             900   General expenses
The draft profit for the year is $64,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the extension.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: M1 all four items added back; A1 93,200.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of the errors on the statement of financial position, and name the accounting concept that has not been applied.
parts.answer: Non-current assets (premises) understated by $29,200 and capital (profit) understated by $29,200. Accruals (matching): the cost benefits future years and should be spread over them through depreciation.
parts.working: B1 NCA understated; B1 capital understated; B1 accruals/matching.

practice.stem: A clinic in Multan spent $5,000 repainting its building. The bookkeeper debited the premises account. Premises are depreciated at 2% a year on cost, with a full year's charge in the year of any addition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the effect of the error on the profit for the year.
parts.answer: Profit overstated by $4,900
parts.working: M1 5,000 − 100 depreciation; A1 overstated 4,900.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect on the carrying amount of premises at the year end.
parts.answer: Overstated by $4,900

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why repainting is revenue expenditure.
parts.answer: It keeps the building in its existing condition (maintenance); it does not add to the building or increase its useful life.
parts.working: B1 maintenance; B1 no improvement/extension of life.

practice.stem:
Royal Pharmacy spent the following on its building during the year:
1 Replacing worn roof tiles: $6,800
2 Adding a second floor: $95,000
3 Repainting the shop front: $3,200
4 Installing a new lift (not there before): $28,500
5 Architect's fees for the second floor: $7,400
6 Cleaning after the building work: $1,100

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total capital expenditure and the total revenue expenditure.
parts.answer: Capital $130,900; revenue $11,100
parts.working: Capital: items 2, 4, 5 = 95,000 + 28,500 + 7,400 = 130,900. Revenue: items 1, 3, 6 = 6,800 + 3,200 + 1,100 = 11,100. 1 mark each correct classification group, 1 mark each total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why item 1 is revenue expenditure while item 2 is capital expenditure.
parts.answer: Replacing worn tiles restores the building to its original condition (maintenance), so it is an expense; adding a floor improves/enlarges the asset and increases its earning capacity for more than one year, so it is capital.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Distinguish between a capital receipt and a revenue receipt, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: Capital receipt: from sale of non-current assets, loans or capital introduced (e.g. proceeds of selling an old van). Revenue receipt: from normal trading (e.g. sales revenue, rent received, commission).
parts.working: 1 mark each with example.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader records the cost of servicing a delivery van as an addition to the van's cost. What is the effect on the financial statements for the year, ignoring depreciation?
A profit overstated; non-current assets overstated
B profit understated; non-current assets overstated
C profit overstated; non-current assets understated
D profit understated; non-current assets understated
parts.answer: A profit overstated; non-current assets overstated
parts.working: Revenue expenditure treated as capital means an expense is missing from the statement of profit or loss, so profit is overstated, and the van is shown at too high a cost. D is the effect of the opposite error (capital expenditure treated as revenue).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On 1 January a business bought a machine for $12,000 but debited the amount to the repairs account. Machinery is depreciated at 20% a year on cost, with a full year's charge in the year of purchase.
What is the effect of the error on the profit for the year ended 31 December?
A understated by $12,000
B understated by $9,600
C overstated by $9,600
D understated by $14,400
parts.answer: B understated by $9,600
parts.working: Repairs are overstated by 12,000 but depreciation of 12,000 × 20% = 2,400 was not charged; net, expenses are 9,600 too high, so profit is understated by $9,600. $12,000 ignores the depreciation that should have been charged.

practice.stem:
Sadiq's draft profit for the year ended 31 December 2026 was $48,750. Depreciation in the draft was calculated on year-end cost: machinery 10% and office equipment 20%. The following were then found:
1 Delivery charges of $600 on a new machine were debited to carriage outwards.
2 Repairs to machinery of $1,800 were debited to the machinery account.
3 An office computer costing $2,400 was debited to office expenses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the effect of each item on the profit, including any change in depreciation.
parts.answer: 1 increase $540; 2 decrease $1,620; 3 increase $1,920
parts.working: For each: B1 direct effect; B1 depreciation adjustment (60, 180, 480).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit.
parts.working: B1 (own figure).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net change in the carrying amount of non-current assets.
parts.answer: Increase of $840
parts.working: M1 machinery −1,080 net (600 − 1,800 less depreciation change −120); office equipment +1,920; A1 840.

practice.stem: Zaib Cosmetics spent $90,000 on a television advertising campaign this year. The marketing director expects it to increase sales for three years and wants to treat it as capital expenditure, writing it off equally over three years. Profit before charging any of the campaign is $150,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year if the campaign is treated as (i) revenue expenditure and (ii) as the director wishes.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the marketing director's proposal.
parts.answer: For: matching – the benefit (extra sales) arises over three years, so spreading the cost matches it with revenue. Against: the future benefit is uncertain and cannot be measured reliably, and the business does not control a separate asset, so it fails the definition of an asset; accounting standards (IAS 38) do not allow advertising to be capitalised; prudence – profit would be overstated by $60,000 this year; it could mislead users and investors. Conclusion: treat as revenue expenditure.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for; up to 3 marks for points against (incl. IAS 38/prudence/asset definition); 1 mark for justified conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the book of prime entry in which each transaction is first recorded.
(i) An invoice received for goods bought on credit for resale
(ii) A credit note sent to a customer for faulty goods returned
(iii) A cheque paid to a supplier
(iv) The purchase of office furniture on credit
parts.answer: (i) purchases journal (day book); (ii) sales returns journal; (iii) cash book; (iv) the journal (general journal).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business pays its monthly rent by bank transfer. Which entries record this?
A Dr bank, Cr rent
B Dr rent, Cr bank
C Dr rent, Cr cash
D Dr capital, Cr bank
parts.answer: B Dr rent, Cr bank
parts.working: Rent is an expense, so it is debited; money leaves the bank account, so bank is credited. Option A reverses the entries; option C uses cash, although payment was by bank transfer.

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry
practice.stem:
Rubina owns a gift shop. For each transaction, state the account to be debited and the account to be credited.
(i) Rubina took goods costing $300 for her own use.
(ii) The bank statement shows bank charges of $45.
(iii) An old display unit was sold for $120 cash.
(iv) Rubina paid Ahmed Traders, a credit supplier, $1,600 by bank transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the double entry for transactions (i)–(iv).
parts.answer: (i) Dr drawings, Cr purchases. (ii) Dr bank charges, Cr bank. (iii) Dr cash, Cr disposal account (display unit). (iv) Dr Ahmed Traders (trade payable), Cr bank.
parts.working: 1 mark for each transaction (both entries needed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the book of prime entry used for transaction (i).
parts.answer: The journal (general journal).

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry
practice.stem:
Faisal starts a printing business on 1 July 2027 with the following:
Premises $60,000; fixtures $8,500; inventory $6,200; bank $4,300; a bank loan of $20,000; amounts owing to suppliers $2,700.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Faisal's opening capital.
parts.working: M1 assets 79,000 − liabilities 22,700; A1 56,300.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the opening journal entry. A narrative is required.
parts.answer: Dr Premises 60,000; Dr Fixtures 8,500; Dr Inventory 6,200; Dr Bank 4,300; Cr Bank loan 20,000; Cr Trade payables 2,700; Cr Capital 56,300. Narrative: assets, liabilities and capital at the start of the business.
parts.working: B1 assets debited; B1 liabilities credited; B1 capital credited; B1 narrative and totals 79,000.

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry
practice.stem: Zara, a wholesaler, sells goods with a list price of $6,400 on credit to Bilal Stores, allowing 15% trade discount.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the amount at which the sale is recorded in Zara's books.
parts.working: Trade discount is deducted before recording: 6,400 × 85% = 5,440.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
For each transaction, state the account to be debited and the account to be credited in Zara's ledger.
(i) the credit sale to Bilal Stores
(ii) Bilal Stores returns goods with a net value of $340
(iii) Bilal Stores pays the balance by bank transfer
parts.answer: (i) Dr Bilal Stores (trade receivable), Cr Sales $5,440. (ii) Dr Sales returns, Cr Bilal Stores $340. (iii) Dr Bank, Cr Bilal Stores $5,100.
parts.working: 1 mark each double entry (amount in (iii) must be correct).

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business receives a credit note from a supplier for damaged goods it returned. In which book of prime entry is the credit note recorded?
A purchases journal
B purchases returns journal
C sales returns journal
D cash book
parts.answer: B purchases returns journal
parts.working: Goods returned to a supplier are returns outwards (purchases returns), recorded from the credit note received. C would be used for a credit note sent to a customer.

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why businesses use books of prime entry rather than posting every transaction straight to the ledger.
parts.answer: They group similar transactions (e.g. all credit sales) so that only totals need to be posted to the nominal ledger, saving time and reducing errors; they also provide a chronological record and audit trail back to source documents.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the source document used to write up (i) the sales journal and (ii) the purchases returns journal.
parts.answer: (i) copies of sales invoices sent; (ii) credit notes received from suppliers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A credit customer who owes $2,400 pays by bank transfer within the credit terms, deducting a 2.5% cash discount.
Which entries record this in the seller's books?
A Dr bank $2,400; Cr trade receivable $2,400
B Dr bank $2,340; Dr discount allowed $60; Cr trade receivable $2,400
C Dr bank $2,340; Cr trade receivable $2,340
D Dr bank $2,340; Cr discount allowed $60; Cr trade receivable $2,280
parts.answer: B Dr bank $2,340; Dr discount allowed $60; Cr trade receivable $2,400
parts.working: Discount = 2.5% × 2,400 = 60. Bank receives 2,340; the discount allowed is an expense (debit); the customer's whole debt of 2,400 is cleared (credit). Option C leaves $60 still owing by the customer.

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry
practice.stem:
Laila keeps a two-column cash book (cash and bank). On 1 June her cash balance was $380 and her bank balance was $5,200 (debit).
2 June Cash sales $940
3 June Paid wages in cash $410
4 June Paid cash into the bank $700
5 June Received a cheque from Sadia, a credit customer, $1,850, and paid it into the bank
6 June Paid electricity by bank transfer $620
7 June Withdrew $300 from the bank for office cash
7 June Paid Tariq, a supplier, $2,400 by bank transfer

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare Laila's cash book for the week and balance it on 7 June.
parts.answer: Cash column: Dr 380, 940, 300 (contra); Cr 410, 700 (contra); balance c/d $510. Bank column: Dr 5,200, 700 (contra), 1,850; Cr 620, 300 (contra), 2,400; balance c/d $4,430.
parts.working: B1 opening balances; B1 cash receipts; B1 cash payments; B1 bank entries; B1 contras both sides; B1 balances 510 and 4,430.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'contra entry' using the transaction on 4 June.
parts.answer: A transaction between cash and bank, so both entries are in the cash book: debit bank column and credit cash column with $700.
parts.working: B1 both sides in the cash book; B1 applied.

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry
practice.stem:
A wholesaler issued these sales invoices in March:
Customer           List price ($) Trade discount
Asma Stores                 2,400            10%
Babar Traders               1,850             0%
Chand Mart                  3,600            15%
Danish & Co                   980             5%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the sales journal for March.
parts.answer: Asma Stores $2,160; Babar Traders $1,850; Chand Mart $3,060; Danish & Co $931; total $8,001
parts.working: B1 Asma and Babar; B1 Chand; B1 Danish; B1 total 8,001.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the sales journal is posted to the ledgers.
parts.answer: Each invoice is debited to the customer's account in the sales ledger; the monthly total is credited to the sales account in the general (nominal) ledger.
parts.working: B1 individual debits; B1 total credit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why trade discount is not recorded in the ledger accounts.
parts.answer: It is a reduction in the list price given before the sale is made, so the sale is recorded at the net amount.

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry
practice.stem:
Imran buys goods on credit from Kohat Traders. On 1 March he owed them $1,240.
5 March Bought goods with a list price of $3,600, less 10% trade discount
9 March Returned goods with a list price of $400 (bought on 5 March)
20 March Paid the balance owing on 1 March by bank transfer, less 2.5% cash discount
28 March Bought goods for $1,500 (no trade discount)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the account of Kohat Traders in Imran's purchases ledger for March and balance it.

parts.text: Name the type of each error and calculate its effect on profit.
parts.answer: 1 Compensating errors: profit overstated by $500 (sales) and understated by $500 (wages), so no net effect on profit, but both accounts are wrong. 2 Error of principle: profit overstated by $2,000 (before any depreciation effect) and non-current assets overstated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the assistant's statement.

parts.working: B1 what a TB proves; B1 errors not revealed; B1 other checks; B1 conclusion.

practice.stem: The accounting equation is: assets = liabilities + capital.
