parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an increase in capital is not the same as profit.
parts.answer: Capital also changes because of drawings (which reduce it) and extra capital introduced (which increases it); these are owner transactions, not business performance.
parts.working: 1 mark drawings; 1 mark capital introduced.

practice.stem: After several loss-making years, a sole trader's furniture shop in Peshawar has assets of $42,700 and liabilities of $51,900.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capital and explain what it means.
parts.answer: −$9,200: the business owes more than it owns; the owner's investment has been wiped out (net liabilities).
parts.working: B1 −9,200; B1 meaning.

parts.label: b
parts.text: If the business closes and the assets are sold for only 80% of their book value, calculate how much the owner must pay from private resources to settle all the liabilities.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the owner must pay this amount, and how the position would differ if the business were a limited company.
parts.answer: A sole trader has unlimited liability: business debts are the owner's personal debts. Shareholders of a limited company lose at most the amount unpaid on their shares; the creditors would bear the shortfall.
parts.working: B1 unlimited liability; B1 personal assets at risk; B1 limited company contrast.

practice.stem:
Iqra does not keep full records. At 1 April 2026 her business assets were $58,000 and liabilities $21,400. At 31 March 2027 assets were $73,600 and liabilities $18,900. During the year:
• she transferred her private car, valued at $9,000, into the business
• she paid a $4,000 instalment on the business loan from her private bank account
• she took goods costing $1,700 for her family
• she drew $1,500 cash each month

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opening and closing capital.
parts.answer: Opening $36,600; closing $54,700
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year.
parts.working: B1 increase 18,100; B1 less capital introduced 9,000 + 4,000; B1 add drawings 1,700 + 18,000; A1 24,800.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the loan instalment paid privately is treated as capital introduced.
parts.answer: Private money was used to pay a business liability, increasing the owner's investment in the business.

practice.stem:
Information about Usman's business:
• At 31 December 2025, assets were $112,000 and liabilities were $37,000.
• In 2025: profit $22,000; drawings $14,000; capital introduced $5,000.
• In 2026: loss $6,500; drawings $11,000; no capital introduced.
• At 31 December 2026, liabilities were $41,300.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capital at 1 January 2025.
parts.working: B1 closing 2025 capital 75,000; M1 reverse profit, drawings and capital introduced; A1 62,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the capital and the total assets at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer: Capital $57,500; assets $98,800

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the change in Usman's capital during 2026.
parts.answer: Capital fell by $17,500 because he made a loss and still withdrew $11,000; continued drawings above profit will erode the business's resources.
parts.working: B1 causes; B1 consequence.

practice.stem: A student says: 'If a business's total assets increase during a year, it must have made a profit.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate this statement, using numerical examples.
parts.answer: Assets can rise without profit: a $20,000 bank loan raises assets and liabilities by $20,000; buying $5,000 of goods on credit raises assets and liabilities; capital introduced of $10,000 raises assets and capital but is not profit. Equally, a business can make a profit while assets fall, e.g. profit $8,000 but $15,000 used to repay a loan. Profit is shown only by an increase in capital after adjusting for capital introduced and drawings. Conclusion: the statement is incorrect.
parts.working: B1 each of up to three correct numerical examples; B1 example where profit made but assets fall or link to change in capital; B1 profit = change in capital adjusted; B1 conclusion.

subtopics.name: Double entry and books of prime entry

subtopics: Double entry and books of prime entry
Double entry and books of prime entry
Double entry and books of prime entry
Double entry and books of prime entry
Double entry and books of prime entry

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Bilal owns a mobile phone repair shop in Rawalpindi. He pays the electricity bill for his family home from his own savings account, and it is not recorded anywhere in the shop's books. Which accounting concept is being applied?
A business entity
B duality
C going concern
D money measurement
parts.answer: A business entity
parts.working: Business entity: the owner's private transactions are kept separate from the business's records. Money measurement (D) is wrong because the bill can be measured in money; it is left out because it is private, not because it cannot be valued.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bookshop values a box of last year's diaries at their expected selling price of $140 less selling costs of $20, because this is lower than their cost of $310. Which concept requires this?
A consistency
B matching
C prudence
D realisation
parts.answer: C prudence
parts.working: Prudence: assets must not be overstated and expected losses are recognised as soon as they are foreseen, so inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value ($120). Realisation (D) concerns when revenue is recognised, not the value of unsold goods.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item would NOT be recorded in the books of a software company because of the money measurement concept?
A a laptop bought on credit from a supplier
B the loyalty and good morale of its programmers
C a loan received from a bank
D an amount owed by a customer who is unlikely to pay
parts.answer: B the loyalty and good morale of its programmers
parts.working: Morale and loyalty cannot be measured objectively in money, so they are not recorded. D is recorded (it is measurable; an irrecoverable debt or allowance would be used).

practice.stem: Nadia runs a printing business in Karachi. She has owned a large printing press for three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the going concern concept.
parts.answer: The assumption that the business will continue to trade for the foreseeable future and has no intention or need to close down or greatly reduce its operations.
parts.working: 1 mark: continue trading; 1 mark: for the foreseeable future / no intention to liquidate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the going concern concept affects the value of non-current assets in a statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Non-current assets are shown at cost less accumulated depreciation (carrying amount), spread over their useful lives, rather than at what they would fetch if sold immediately (break-up value).
parts.working: 1 mark: cost less depreciation over useful life; 1 mark: not at break-up / forced-sale value because the business is not expected to sell them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the money measurement concept.
parts.answer: Only transactions and events that can be measured objectively in monetary terms are recorded in the accounting records.
parts.working: 1 mark: only items measurable in money; 1 mark: measured objectively/reliably are recorded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items of value to a business that are not recorded because of this concept.
parts.answer: Any two of: skill/experience of the workforce; staff morale; good relations with customers or suppliers; a good location (unless purchased); quality of management.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid non-monetary items.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the duality concept.
parts.answer: Every transaction has two equal and opposite effects on the business, so for every debit entry there is a credit entry of the same amount.
parts.working: 1 mark: two aspects/effects; 1 mark: equal debit and credit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Kamran buys a delivery van costing $14,500 on credit from Pak Motors. State the two effects of this transaction on the accounting equation.
parts.answer: Non-current assets (van) increase by $14,500; liabilities (other payable, Pak Motors) increase by $14,500.
parts.working: 1 mark: assets +14,500; 1 mark: liabilities +14,500. Capital unchanged.

practice.stem: Farah's bakery has a year end of 30 June. On 1 July 2026 electricity of $780 was owing for June 2026. During the year to 30 June 2027 she paid electricity bills of $9,640. On 30 June 2027 electricity of $1,120 was owing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the accounting concept that requires the electricity expense to include amounts not yet paid.
parts.answer: Accruals (matching) concept.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electricity expense to be shown in the statement of profit or loss for the year ended 30 June 2027.
parts.working: Paid 9,640 − opening accrual 780 (belongs to last year) + closing accrual 1,120 = 9,980. M1 deduct opening accrual, M1 add closing accrual, A1.

practice.stem: Ali Traders bought land in 2004 for $85,000. A valuer says it is worth $410,000 today. The business has never revalued the land.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the historical cost concept.
parts.answer: Assets are recorded at their original cost (the price paid to acquire them).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of using historical cost for the land bought by Ali Traders.
parts.answer: Advantage: the cost is objective and can be checked against the purchase documents. Disadvantage: the figure is out of date and understates the land's current value, so the SOFP may mislead users.
parts.working: 1 mark advantage (objective/verifiable); 1 mark disadvantage (out of date/understates value).

practice.stem: Saima runs a dental clinic in Peshawar. Her year ends on 31 December. On 1 January 2026 insurance of $2,400 had been prepaid for January to September 2026. On 1 October 2026 she paid $3,600 for twelve months' insurance to 30 September 2027.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the insurance expense for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.working: Opening prepayment 2,400 (Jan–Sep 2026) + 3/12 × 3,600 = 900 (Oct–Dec) = 3,300. M1, M1, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the amount of the prepayment at 31 December 2026 and where it appears in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: $2,700, shown as a current asset (other receivables).
parts.working: 9/12 × 3,600 = 2,700 B1; current asset B1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the realisation concept.
parts.answer: Revenue (and profit) is recognised when it is earned — when goods or services have been transferred to the customer — not when cash is received.
parts.working: 1 mark: recognised when earned / control passes; 1 mark: not when cash received.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A customer orders goods on 3 March, receives them on 9 March and pays on 20 April. State the date on which the revenue is recognised.
parts.answer: 9 March (when the goods are delivered to the customer).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader charges the cost of a machine to the statement of profit or loss over its five-year useful life instead of in the year it was bought. Which accounting concept is being applied?
A business entity
B matching (accruals)
C money measurement
D realisation
parts.answer: B matching (accruals)
parts.working: B: depreciation spreads the cost over the periods that benefit, matching expense with the revenue it helps earn. A (main distractor) concerns separating owner and business, not timing of expenses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the accounting concept that requires income to be recorded in the period in which it is earned, whether or not it has been received.
parts.answer: The accruals (matching) concept.
parts.working: B1 accruals / matching.

parts.label: b
parts.text: On 1 October 2026 Zara Enterprises placed $60,000 on a fixed deposit at 7.5% interest per year. Interest is paid by the bank every 12 months, the first payment being on 30 September 2027. Calculate the interest receivable to be included in the statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.working: 60,000 × 7.5% × 3/12 = 1,125 (M1 time apportionment, A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where the interest not yet received appears in the statement of financial position at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer: As a current asset (other receivables / accrued income).
parts.working: B1 current asset.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each of the following, name the accounting concept that is being applied.
(i) The owner's private holiday paid from the business bank account is recorded as drawings.
(ii) Closing inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
(iii) A business continues to use the reducing balance method for its vehicles every year.
(iv) A loyal and skilled workforce is not shown as an asset.
(v) Every transaction is recorded with a debit entry and an equal credit entry.
parts.answer: (i) business entity (ii) prudence (iii) consistency (iv) money measurement (v) duality
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hassan owns a courier business in Multan. He uses his private car for business deliveries about 40% of the time. During the year he paid all of the car's fuel, $3,600, from the business bank account. Calculate the amount of fuel that should be charged as an expense of the business.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the remaining fuel cost should be recorded, and name the concept that requires this.
parts.answer: $2,160 is debited to drawings; the business entity concept.
parts.working: B1 drawings $2,160; B1 business entity concept.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a business that expects to win a legal claim of $12,000 next year does not include it in its profit for the current year.
parts.answer: Under prudence (and realisation) gains are not recognised until they are reasonably certain/realised; the outcome is not yet certain, so including it would overstate profit and assets.
parts.working: 1 mark: names prudence/realisation; 1 mark: gain not certain so profit would be overstated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The business also expects to lose a separate claim brought by a customer and estimates it will pay $5,000. Explain how prudence affects the treatment of this expected loss.
parts.answer: Prudence requires the expected loss to be recognised now: an expense of $5,000 is charged against profit and a liability (provision) is shown.
parts.working: 1 mark: loss recognised as soon as foreseen; 1 mark: expense and liability/provision of $5,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the historical cost concept.
parts.answer: Assets are recorded at their original cost price (the amount paid when acquired), not at current value.
parts.working: 1 mark recorded at cost; 1 mark at the date of acquisition / not market value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a period of high inflation, explain two limitations of using historical cost in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Assets bought long ago are shown at values far below their current worth, so the SOFP understates the business's resources; depreciation based on old costs is too low so profit is overstated compared with the cost of replacing assets; figures from different years are not comparable because money has changed in value.
parts.working: 2 marks each for any two developed points: undervalued assets; depreciation too low / profit overstated; poor comparability between years; does not show replacement cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the matching concept justifies charging depreciation on a delivery van.
parts.answer: The van helps earn revenue over several years, so its cost is spread over those years and matched against the revenue it helps to earn, rather than all charged in the year of purchase.
parts.working: 1 mark cost spread over useful life; 1 mark matched with revenue of each period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A café owner buys a coffee machine for $2,400 with an expected life of 4 years and no residual value, using the straight-line method. Calculate the depreciation charge for each year and the carrying amount after two years.
parts.answer: $600 per year; carrying amount $1,200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the business entity concept for a sole trader and the separate legal personality of a limited company.
parts.answer: For a sole trader, business entity is only an accounting rule: the books treat the business separately, but in law the owner and business are the same person and the owner has unlimited liability. A limited company is a separate legal person in law: it owns its assets, can sue and be sued, and shareholders' liability is limited.
parts.working: 1 mark sole trader: accounting separation only; 1 mark not separate in law / unlimited liability; 1 mark company separate legal person / limited liability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A director of Ravi Foods Limited pays her personal income tax from the company's bank account. State how this should be treated in the company's books.
parts.answer: It is not a company expense; it is debited to an amount owed by the director (a receivable from the director) or treated as part of her remuneration, not charged as a company tax expense.
parts.working: B1 not a company expense – recorded as amount due from director / director's remuneration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mobile phone shop sells a phone on 28 June. The customer collects it the same day, promising to pay on 15 July. The shop's year ends on 30 June. State, with a reason, the year in which the revenue should be recognised.
parts.answer: Year ending 30 June (this year): the phone has passed to the customer and a legal debt exists, so the revenue is realised even though cash comes later.
parts.working: 1 mark correct year; 1 mark goods transferred / customer obliged to pay (realisation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sales commission of 2% is paid to staff one month after the sales are made. June sales were $84,000. Calculate the commission to be accrued at 30 June and name the concept applied.
parts.answer: $1,680; accruals (matching) concept.
parts.working: 84,000 × 2% = 1,680 (B1); accruals/matching (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why accounting concepts are needed when financial statements are prepared.
parts.answer: They give a common framework so that statements are prepared in the same way, making them reliable and comparable between periods and businesses, and reducing personal bias.
parts.working: 1 mark consistency/comparability; 1 mark reliability / reduces bias / users can trust the figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two groups of users who rely on financial statements being prepared using the same concepts each year, and give one decision each group makes.
parts.answer: e.g. bank/lender – whether to grant or continue a loan; investor/shareholder – whether to buy or keep shares; supplier – whether to give credit; tax authority – tax payable.
parts.working: 1 mark per user, 1 mark per matching decision (two users).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A large hotel company buys a waste-paper bin for $18. It is expected to last five years, but the cost is charged in full to the statement of profit or loss as general expenses. Which concept justifies this treatment?
A historical cost
B materiality
C going concern
D prudence
parts.answer: B materiality
parts.working: Materiality: the amount is too small to affect users' decisions, so the cost of depreciating it over five years is not worth the effort. Prudence (D) is not the reason, because the bin is not being undervalued out of caution; it is simply insignificant.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A furniture maker's year ends on 31 December 2026. A customer ordered a table on 10 December 2026 and paid in full on 2 January 2027. The table was delivered to and accepted by the customer on 29 December 2026. In which year should the sale be recognised, and which concept applies?
A year ended 31 December 2026; realisation
B year ended 31 December 2027; realisation
C year ended 31 December 2026; going concern
D year ended 31 December 2027; matching
parts.answer: A year ended 31 December 2026; realisation
parts.working: Realisation: revenue is recognised when control of the goods passes to the customer (delivery and acceptance on 29 December 2026), not when cash is received. B wrongly uses the date of payment.

practice.stem: Omar sells solar lamps. On the last day of his financial year he sent lamps to a retailer on sale or return. The retailer had not accepted them by the year end. Omar included the lamps in revenue at their selling price of $4,800, which is cost plus 20%. They were not included in closing inventory. His draft profit for the year was $41,350.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the treatment of these goods breaks the realisation concept.
parts.answer: Revenue should only be recognised when control passes to the customer, i.e. when the customer accepts the goods. The goods sent on sale or return have not been accepted, so no sale has taken place.
parts.working: 1 mark: revenue recognised when goods accepted / control passes; 1 mark: applied — not yet accepted, so not revenue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: Cost = 4,800 × 100/120 = 4,000. Revenue reduced by 4,800; closing inventory increased by 4,000. 41,350 − 4,800 + 4,000 = 40,550. B1 cost, M1 both adjustments, A1.

practice.stem:
At the end of her financial year, Hina, a clothing retailer in Lahore, has the following inventory.
Item                      Cost $       NRV $
Cotton shirts              6,200       9,100
Silk scarves               3,450       2,800
Leather belts              1,980       1,650
Denim jackets              7,400      11,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory.
parts.working: Each line at the lower of cost and NRV: 6,200 + 2,800 + 1,650 + 7,400 = 18,050. M1 lower of cost/NRV line by line, M1 at least two lines correct, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the accounting concept you have applied and explain why it is applied item by item rather than to the total.
parts.answer: Prudence. If the totals were compared, gains on some items would hide losses on others, so inventory (and profit) would be overstated.
parts.working: 1 mark: prudence; 1 mark: totals would offset expected losses against unrealised gains.

practice.stem: Zubair Engineering bought a machine two years ago for $48,000. It has been depreciated at 10% per year on cost (straight-line). For year 3 the accountant proposes to use 20% per year on the reducing balance instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the consistency concept.
parts.answer: Once a business has chosen an accounting method (e.g. a depreciation method), it should use the same method from year to year, so that results can be compared over time.
parts.working: 1 mark: same methods each year; 1 mark: allows comparison between periods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation for year 3 under the existing method and under the proposed method.
parts.answer: Straight-line: $4,800. Reducing balance: $7,680.
parts.working: SL = 10% × 48,000 = 4,800. Carrying amount after 2 years = 48,000 − 2 × 4,800 = 38,400; RB = 20% × 38,400 = 7,680. B1 SL, M1 carrying amount, A1 RB.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect on profit for year 3 if the method is changed, and state one condition under which a change of method is acceptable.
parts.answer: Profit would fall by $2,880. A change is acceptable if the new method gives a fairer (truer) view of the asset's use, and the change and its effect are disclosed.
parts.working: 1 mark: decrease 2,880 (own figure); 1 mark: fairer presentation/disclosed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the materiality concept.
parts.answer: An item is material if leaving it out or misstating it could influence the decisions of users of the financial statements. Immaterial items need not be treated strictly (e.g. small tools may be expensed).
parts.working: 1 mark: could influence users' decisions; 1 mark: immaterial items can be treated in the simplest way.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A stapler costing $25 is material to a small corner shop but not to a multinational bank. Explain this statement.
parts.answer: Materiality is relative to the size of the business: $25 is a large proportion of the shop's profit or assets, but an insignificant fraction of the bank's.
parts.working: 1 mark: relative to size/scale; 1 mark: compared with profit or total assets.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two items, other than small value equipment, for which materiality affects the accounting treatment.
parts.answer: Any two: separate disclosure of large unusual items; whether to record small accruals or prepayments; grouping small expenses into 'sundry expenses'; whether to correct a small error.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Rashid owns a grocery shop. During the year he took goods costing $650 from the shop for his family's use, and paid his home electricity bill of $420 from the business bank account. Both amounts were recorded as business expenses: the goods remained in purchases and the bill was debited to the shop's electricity account. His draft profit for the year was $38,200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: Goods taken: reduce purchases (cost of sales) by 650 → profit +650. Home electricity removed from expenses → +420. 38,200 + 650 + 420 = 39,270. M1 M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how each item should be recorded, and name the concept that has been broken.
parts.answer: Goods taken: Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases $650. Home electricity: Dr Drawings, Cr Electricity (expense) $420. Concept: business entity.
parts.working: 1 mark each double entry; 1 mark business entity.

practice.stem: Crescent Textiles Limited has made losses for three years and its bank has warned it may withdraw the overdraft.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two indicators that a company may not be a going concern.
parts.answer: Any two: repeated large losses; net current liabilities / unable to pay debts as they fall due; loss of a major customer or supplier; bank refusing to renew loans; loan repayments in default; key licence withdrawn.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects on the financial statements if a company is no longer a going concern.
parts.answer: Assets are revalued to realisable (break-up) values, often much lower, e.g. specialised machinery and inventory. Non-current liabilities may become current because they must be repaid on closure. Extra liabilities (e.g. closure costs, redundancy) may need to be recognised. Depreciation over useful life no longer applies.
parts.working: 2 marks each effect: identification + explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each situation, name the accounting concept that is applied or broken.
(i) A taxi company changes from straight-line to reducing balance depreciation each year, choosing whichever gives the higher profit.
(ii) The owner records the business's van at the price paid, not its current market value.
(iii) A wholesaler makes an allowance for a customer who has entered liquidation.
(iv) Commission earned in the final week of the year is included in income although it will be received next month.
parts.answer: (i) consistency (broken); (ii) historical cost (applied); (iii) prudence (applied); (iv) accruals/matching or realisation (applied).
parts.working: 1 mark each. (iv) accept accruals, matching or realisation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the treatment in (i) could mislead users of the financial statements.
parts.answer: Changes in profit would be caused by the switch in method rather than real performance, so year-to-year comparisons are unreliable and profit may be manipulated upwards.
parts.working: 1 mark: not comparable; 1 mark: profit manipulated / not a fair view.

practice.stem: A wholesaler in Faisalabad has trade receivables of $64,000 at the year end. It keeps an allowance for irrecoverable debts of 2.5% of trade receivables. The allowance brought forward is $1,250.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount to be charged to the statement of profit or loss for the allowance for irrecoverable debts.
parts.answer: $350 (increase)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the net figure for trade receivables in the statement of financial position.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the concept that requires an allowance for irrecoverable debts and explain why.
parts.answer: Prudence: receivables should not be overstated, so the expected loss on debts that may not be collected is recognised now. (Accept matching: the expected loss is matched to the year of the sale.)
parts.working: 1 mark concept; 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem: Kareem is thinking of lending money to a small manufacturing business and is studying its financial statements for the last four years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the consistency concept is important to users of financial statements.
parts.answer: 1 It allows a business's results to be compared from year to year, so trends in profit and performance are real and not caused by changes in method. 2 It prevents managers or owners from manipulating profit by switching methods (e.g. inventory valuation or depreciation) to show the result they want. Also accept: helps comparison with other businesses using similar policies.
parts.working: 2 marks per reason: 1 identification + 1 development.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which treatment is an application of the prudence concept?
A recording a gain from a court case the business expects to win next year
B valuing closing inventory at selling price because it is certain to be sold
C recognising an expected loss on inventory that can only be sold below cost
D increasing the value of premises to their market value each year
parts.answer: C recognising an expected loss on inventory that can only be sold below cost
parts.working: C: prudence requires expected losses to be recognised as soon as they are foreseen (inventory at lower of cost and NRV). A is wrong because prudence does not allow gains to be recognised before they are realised.

practice.stem: Mehwish lets part of her warehouse in Sialkot to a tenant. At 1 April 2026 the tenant owed $650 rent. During the year ended 31 March 2027 she received $14,200 rent. At 31 March 2027 the tenant had paid $1,100 rent in advance for April 2027.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the rent receivable account for the year ended 31 March 2027, showing clearly the amount transferred to the statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: Rent receivable to SOPL $12,450; balance c/d (rent received in advance) $1,100 credit.
parts.working: Dr: balance b/d (arrears) 650; Income statement 12,450; balance c/d (in advance) 1,100 = 14,200. Cr: bank 14,200. B1 opening arrears debit, B1 bank credit, B1 c/d in advance on debit side, B1 transfer 12,450.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the accruals concept has been applied in your answer.
parts.answer: Only the rent earned for the 12 months is income of the year: rent relating to last year (arrears) is excluded and rent received in advance for next year is carried forward as a liability.
parts.working: 1 mark income = amount earned for the period; 1 mark arrears/advance adjusted.

practice.stem:
At the start of a month Kiran's stationery business had total assets of $52,000 and total liabilities of $14,000. During the month:
1 She bought inventory on credit for $3,500.
2 She paid a trade payable $2,200 by bank transfer.
3 She sold goods costing $1,800 for $2,700 cash.
4 The owner took $600 cash for private use.
5 She borrowed $5,000 from a bank, received by bank transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capital at the start.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each transaction state its effect (increase, decrease or no change, with the amount) on total assets, total liabilities and capital.
parts.answer: 1: assets +3,500, liabilities +3,500, capital no change. 2: assets −2,200, liabilities −2,200, capital no change. 3: assets +900 (cash +2,700, inventory −1,800), liabilities no change, capital +900 (profit). 4: assets −600, liabilities no change, capital −600. 5: assets +5,000, liabilities +5,000, capital no change.
parts.working: 1 mark per transaction fully correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate total assets, total liabilities and capital after the five transactions, and show that the accounting equation still balances.
parts.working: M1 totals, A1 equation shown.

practice.stem: Owais runs a hardware shop in Gujranwala. He has always valued inventory using FIFO. This year closing inventory is $38,400 under FIFO and $35,900 under AVCO. He wants to change to AVCO 'just for this year' to reduce his tax bill.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in gross profit for the year if the closing inventory is valued at $35,900 (AVCO) instead of $38,400 (FIFO), and state whether profit rises or falls.
parts.answer: Gross profit falls by $2,500.
parts.working: Lower closing inventory → higher cost of sales: 38,400 − 35,900 = 2,500 decrease (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the consistency concept makes it difficult for the owner to change methods every year.
parts.answer: Consistency requires the same method to be used each year so results are comparable; switching to whichever method gives the desired profit would allow profit to be manipulated and mislead users.
parts.working: 1 mark same method each period / comparability; 1 mark changing could manipulate profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two conditions under which a change of inventory valuation method would be acceptable.
parts.answer: If the new method gives a truer and fairer view (more reliable/relevant information); if required by a new accounting standard or law; the change and its effect should be disclosed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Kohinoor Logistics Limited has a policy that any single item of equipment costing less than $500 is treated as an expense. During the year it bought:
• office chairs, 6 at $95 each, $570
• a server rack, $4,800
• a desk lamp, $65
• a delivery trolley, $1,250
• a set of kitchen kettles, $140

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total amount that should be (i) charged as an expense and (ii) capitalised as non-current assets.
parts.working: Policy is per item: each chair costs $95, which is less than $500, so chairs (570), lamp (65) and kettles (140) are expensed = 775 (M1 A1); server rack and trolley capitalised = 6,050 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the company does not depreciate the chairs even though they will last several years.
parts.answer: The amounts are immaterial to the company's results; the cost of recording and depreciating them is greater than the benefit, and treating them as an expense will not mislead users (materiality).
parts.working: 1 mark immaterial; 1 mark cost/effort outweighs benefit / no effect on users' decisions.

practice.stem: Science Today, a monthly magazine published in Lahore, sold 1,800 annual subscriptions at $48 each in August 2026, all paid in cash. Each subscription is for 12 monthly issues starting with the September 2026 issue. The publisher's year ends on 31 December.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revenue to be recognised for the year ended 31 December 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the amount to be shown as a liability at 31 December 2026 and explain why, with reference to the realisation concept.
parts.answer: $57,600 as a current liability (income received in advance / deferred income). Revenue is realised only when the magazines are delivered; the publisher still owes 8 issues.
parts.working: B1 amount, B1 current liability, B1 explanation.

practice.stem: Sabir Wholesale has trade receivables of $92,000 at its year end. The allowance for irrecoverable debts brought forward is $1,600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge to the statement of profit or loss for the allowance for irrecoverable debts under (i) the usual 2% policy and (ii) the proposed 5% policy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The accountant says that the change is acceptable because several large customers are now in financial difficulty. Discuss whether the change conflicts with the consistency concept.
parts.answer: Consistency means using the same policy unless there is a good reason to change. Here the risk of non-payment has genuinely increased, so a higher allowance gives a truer and fairer view and applies prudence; it is acceptable provided it is based on evidence and not used to reduce profit for other reasons, and the effect is disclosed.
parts.working: 1 mark consistency explained; 1 mark change justified by new circumstances / prudence; 1 mark conclusion with condition (evidence / disclosure).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A company with a profit of $2.4 million finds that $350 of stationery was posted to the repairs account instead of the stationery account. Explain whether this error is material.
parts.answer: No – it is tiny compared with profit, and it does not affect profit at all because both are expenses; it would not change any user's decision.
parts.working: 1 mark size relative to profit; 1 mark no effect on users' decisions / profit unchanged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the materiality concept might affect the amount of detail shown in a company's published statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: Small items are combined into totals (e.g. administrative expenses) rather than shown separately, because separate disclosure would not help users; only material items are shown separately.
parts.working: 1 mark grouping of small items; 1 mark only material items disclosed separately.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of an item that might be material because of its nature rather than its size.
parts.answer: e.g. a payment to a director, a fine for breaking the law, a related-party transaction, an item that turns a profit into a loss.
parts.working: B1 any valid example.

practice.stem: Askari Pharmaceuticals Limited owns a building bought 10 years ago for $360,000. It was being depreciated over 40 years with no residual value. The directors are considering revaluing it to $540,000, with its remaining useful life of 30 years unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual depreciation of the building based on (i) historical cost and (ii) the revalued amount.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect on the company's annual profit if it revalues the building.
parts.answer: Profit falls by $9,000 a year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one advantage of revaluation to users of the statements, and why the historical cost concept is still widely used.
parts.answer: Revaluation shows a more relevant, up-to-date value of the asset and a more realistic depreciation charge; historical cost is objective and verifiable (based on an invoice), cheaper and not open to opinion.
parts.working: 1 mark advantage; 1 mark reason historical cost still used.

practice.stem: Nadeem's shop pays business rates quarterly in advance. The rate was $1,500 per quarter until 31 March 2026 and $1,740 per quarter from 1 April 2026. On 1 January 2026 the quarter January–March 2026 had already been paid. During 2026 he paid $6,960, covering the four quarters from April 2026 to March 2027.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the business rates expense for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.working: Jan–Mar at old rate 1,500 + three quarters at new rate 3 × 1,740 = 6,720 (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the prepayment at 31 December 2026, and show that your answers agree with the cash paid during 2026.
parts.working: B1 prepayment; B1 reconciliation shown.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader's financial year ends on 31 March 2027. Rent of $1,850 per month is payable for a shop. During the year she paid $20,350, which covered April 2026 to February 2027. What rent expense should appear in the statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 March 2027?
A $18,500
B $20,350
C $22,200
D $24,050
parts.working: Matching (accruals): the expense is the rent for the 12 months used, 12 × $1,850 = $22,200, whether paid or not; March's $1,850 is accrued. B is the cash paid, which ignores the accrual.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about accounting concepts are correct?
1 The consistency concept means that a business can never change its depreciation method.
2 The going concern concept supports valuing non-current assets at cost less depreciation rather than at their forced-sale value.
3 The duality concept means that every transaction has two equal and opposite effects.
4 The money measurement concept means that the skill of a business's workforce is shown as an asset.
A 1 and 2
B 1 and 4
C 2 and 3
D 3 and 4
parts.answer: C 2 and 3
parts.working: 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is wrong: a method may be changed if the new method gives a fairer view, with the change disclosed. Statement 4 is wrong: the skill of workers cannot be measured reliably in money, so it is not recorded.

practice.stem:
Tariq has decided to close his electronics shop next month. His draft statement of financial position shows: inventory $26,000; equipment (carrying amount) $40,000; trade receivables $15,000; cash $3,800; trade payables $21,400.
If the shop closes: the inventory can be sold for $17,500; the equipment for $22,000; and 10% of the trade receivables will not be collected. Cash and payables are unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Tariq's capital (net assets) on the going concern basis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Tariq's capital if the business is no longer a going concern, and the decrease in capital.
parts.answer: Capital $35,400; decrease $28,000.
parts.working: Inventory 17,500 + equipment 22,000 + receivables 90% × 15,000 = 13,500 + cash 3,800 − payables 21,400 = 35,400. Decrease 63,400 − 35,400 = 28,000. M1 break-up values, M1 receivables 90%, A1 capital, A1 decrease.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the going concern concept no longer applies to Tariq's business.
parts.answer: Tariq intends to close the business within weeks, so it will not continue to trade for the foreseeable future; assets must be valued at what they will realise on sale.
parts.working: 1 mark: closure planned / not foreseeable future; 1 mark: so realisable (break-up) values used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the prudence concept and the realisation concept work together when a business values its closing inventory.
parts.answer: Inventory is valued at cost (not selling price) because the profit on it is not realised until it is sold — realisation. If the net realisable value falls below cost, the expected loss is recognised now — prudence. So gains wait until realised, losses are recognised when foreseen.
parts.working: 1 mark: cost not selling price; 1 mark: profit only recognised when realised (sold); 1 mark: losses recognised at once / lower of cost and NRV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether too much prudence can conflict with the aim of giving a true and fair view.
parts.answer: Excessive prudence (e.g. very large allowances for doubtful debts or undervalued assets) understates profit and assets, so statements are no longer neutral or faithful. Profit is moved to later years, breaking matching and making comparison misleading. Some caution is needed so owners do not withdraw unrealised profits. Conclusion: prudence should mean caution, not deliberate understatement.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 4 developed points: understatement of profit/assets; not neutral/faithful; shifts profit between periods/affects matching; caution still useful to protect capital; a balanced conclusion.

practice.stem: Jamal Kitchens' year ends on 30 June. On 20 June 2027 a customer ordered an industrial oven for $8,000 and paid a deposit of $2,000. The oven, which cost Jamal $5,000, was still in the warehouse on 30 June and was delivered on 5 July 2027. The bookkeeper recorded the full $8,000 as revenue, set up a trade receivable for $6,000, and left the oven out of closing inventory. Draft profit was $63,400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, with reference to the realisation concept, why this sale should not be included in revenue for the year ended 30 June 2027.
parts.answer: Revenue is recognised when control of the goods passes to the customer. The oven was delivered after the year end (5 July), so the sale belongs to the next year. Receiving the order and deposit does not realise the revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark: control passes on delivery; 1 mark: delivered after year end, so next year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the deposit of $2,000 should be shown in the statement of financial position at 30 June 2027, and state the other correction needed to that statement.
parts.answer: The deposit is a current liability (amount received in advance / contract liability) of $2,000, because the business still owes the customer the oven. The trade receivable of $6,000 recorded for the balance must be removed, and inventory increased by $5,000.
parts.working: 1 mark current liability; 1 mark reason; 1 mark remove receivable / add inventory.

practice.stem: The conceptual framework used for international financial reporting sets out the qualitative characteristics that make financial information useful to investors, lenders and other creditors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the two fundamental qualitative characteristics of useful financial information.
parts.answer: Relevance: information can make a difference to users' decisions because it has predictive value, confirmatory value, or both (and is material). Faithful representation: information depicts what it claims to — it is complete, neutral and free from error.
parts.working: 1 mark each characteristic named, 1 mark each correct explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two enhancing qualitative characteristics and explain how one of them helps an investor comparing two companies.
parts.answer: Any two of: comparability, verifiability, timeliness, understandability. E.g. comparability: if both companies use similar policies consistently and disclose them, the investor can identify real differences in performance rather than differences caused by accounting methods.
parts.working: 1 mark each name (max 2); 1 mark explanation applied to comparing companies.

practice.stem:
Sofia's draft profit for the year is $54,300. The following have been discovered:
1 Revenue includes goods with a selling price of $3,000 sent on sale or return and not yet accepted. They cost $2,250 and are not in closing inventory.
2 Closing inventory includes goods at cost $1,800 which can only be sold for $1,100.
3 Rent expense includes $1,500 paid for the first month of next year.
4 The school fees of Sofia's daughter, $2,400, were paid from the business bank account and charged to general expenses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each item, name the accounting concept that has not been applied.
parts.answer: 1 realisation; 2 prudence; 3 accruals (matching); 4 business entity.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year.
parts.answer:
Corrected profit $56,750
Draft profit                            54,300
1 Remove sale or return goods          (3,000)
1 Add them to closing inventory          2,250
2 Reduce inventory to NRV                (700)
3 Rent prepaid for next year             1,500
4 Owner's private school fees            2,400
Corrected profit                        56,750
parts.working: 1 mark per correct adjustment line (max 4, item 1 needs both lines); 1 mark corrected profit (own figure).

practice.stem: Indus Agro Limited revalued its land upwards by $30,000 during the year. The land was not sold. The accountant included the gain in the statement of profit or loss, giving a draft profit for the year of $72,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, with reference to accounting concepts, why the revaluation gain should not be included in the profit for the year.
parts.answer: The gain is unrealised: the land has not been sold, so no revenue has been earned (realisation). Prudence means unrealised gains are not reported as profit that could be withdrawn or distributed. The gain is credited to a revaluation reserve in equity (other comprehensive income) instead.
parts.working: 1 mark realisation/unrealised; 1 mark prudence/not available for distribution; 1 mark revaluation reserve.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The managing director argues that showing the land at $30,000 more makes the statements more useful. Evaluate this argument.
parts.answer: For: an up-to-date value is more relevant to users assessing the company's worth and security for loans. Against: valuations are subjective and less verifiable than historical cost; future depreciation charges rise. Conclusion: revaluation in the SOFP is acceptable if done for the whole class and by an independent valuer, but the gain must not go through profit.
parts.working: 1 mark for, 1 mark against, 1 mark reasoned conclusion.

practice.stem: Leila owns a shoe shop in Islamabad. At her year end she has 1,200 pairs of shoes that cost $14 each and normally sell for $22 each. She wants to apply for a bank loan and proposes to value her closing inventory at selling price to show a higher profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount by which profit would be overstated if Leila used her proposed valuation.
parts.working: At selling price 1,200 × $22 = 26,400; at cost 1,200 × $14 = 16,800; overstatement 9,600. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Leila whether she should value her closing inventory at selling price. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: the profit on unsold goods has not been realised (realisation); prudence says gains are not anticipated, so inventory should be at the lower of cost and NRV; overstated profit could lead her to withdraw cash the business has not earned; the bank would be misled about her performance; next year's profit would be understated when the goods are sold. For: selling price shows what she expects to receive and may impress the bank. Decision: she should not; she should value at cost ($16,800) unless NRV is lower, and explain her expected margin to the bank separately.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for points (at least one on each side for full marks), 1 mark for a clear justified decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sole trader's draft profit is $46,800. She has not recorded wages owing of $1,350 at the year end, and rent received includes $900 relating to the next year. What is the corrected profit?
A $46,350
B $44,550
C $47,250
D $49,050
parts.working: B: wages owing is an extra expense (−1,350); rent received in advance is not income of this year (−900). 46,800 − 1,350 − 900 = 44,550. A wrongly adds the income received in advance.

practice.stem: Sana's kitchen-equipment business has a year end of 31 May 2027. Goods costing $5,200 were delivered to and accepted by a customer on 29 May 2027. The invoice for $7,800 was not sent until 4 June 2027 and the sale was recorded in June. The goods were not included in the closing inventory count. Draft profit for the year is $61,400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the sale should be included in the year ended 31 May 2027 even though the invoice was raised in June.
parts.answer: Realisation: the goods passed to the customer, who accepted them and became liable to pay, on 29 May; the date of the invoice does not decide when revenue is earned.
parts.working: 1 mark goods delivered/accepted = point of sale; 1 mark invoice date irrelevant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: Revenue +7,800. The goods were (correctly) left out of closing inventory as they had been delivered, so cost of sales is already right: 61,400 + 7,800 = 69,200 (M1 A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the two changes needed to the statement of financial position at 31 May 2027.
parts.answer: Trade receivables increase by $7,800; capital (profit / retained earnings) increases by $7,800.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Gul Ahmed Bookshop sold gift vouchers for $12,000 cash during 2026. By 31 December 2026, vouchers worth $7,500 had been exchanged for books. The vouchers are valid for 12 months.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revenue that should be recognised from gift vouchers for the year ended 31 December 2026, and the liability at that date.
parts.answer: Revenue $7,500; liability $4,500.
parts.working: Revenue is earned only when vouchers are exchanged for goods: 7,500 (B1). Unredeemed 12,000 − 7,500 = 4,500 (M1) is a current liability – the shop owes goods to holders (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The owner recorded all the voucher sales as revenue when the cash was received. Calculate the effect of correcting this on the profit for the year.
parts.answer: Profit decreases by $4,500.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Some vouchers are never used. Discuss whether the shop should recognise revenue for vouchers that are expected not to be used before they expire.
parts.answer: Prudence/realisation suggest waiting until the vouchers expire, when it is certain no goods will be given; however, if past experience gives a reliable estimate of unused vouchers, recognising part earlier gives a fairer matching of revenue. A sound conclusion: recognise only when reliable evidence exists, otherwise at expiry.
parts.working: 1 mark argument for waiting (prudence/certainty); 1 mark argument for estimate (matching/reliable experience); 1 mark justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Indus Auto Parts Limited makes brake parts for car assemblers. In the last year: its largest customer, which bought 70% of its output, moved production abroad; the company made a loss for the second year running; its bank has refused to renew the overdraft; and a $2 million loan is repayable in four months. Several senior engineers have resigned.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three pieces of evidence that Indus Auto Parts Limited may not be a going concern.
parts.answer: Loss of its main customer (70% of sales); bank refusing to renew the overdraft; loan repayable in 4 months that it cannot refinance; continuing losses / negative cash flow; key staff leaving.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three items taken from the case.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the statement of financial position would change if the going concern basis were no longer appropriate.
parts.answer: Assets would be valued at their realisable (break-up/forced sale) values, which are usually lower – especially specialised machinery and inventory; all liabilities would become current, as long-term loans become immediately repayable; extra liabilities such as closure costs/redundancy might be recognised.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three developed points.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The directors want to continue to prepare the statements on a going concern basis without mentioning the problems. Evaluate this decision.
parts.answer: For: if a new customer or finance is likely, the company may survive and the going concern basis remains valid; break-up values could cause panic. Against: users (bank, suppliers, shareholders) need to know of material uncertainty to make decisions; hiding it misleads and is not a true and fair view; directors have a stewardship duty. Conclusion: going concern may still be used if survival is likely, but the uncertainty must be disclosed.
parts.working: 2 marks for arguments on each side, max 3; 1 mark justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the prudence concept and the consistency concept can conflict. Use examples in your answer.
parts.answer: Points: prudence requires recognising expected losses and not overstating assets; consistency requires the same methods each year. Conflict arises when circumstances change so that the existing method overstates assets (e.g. depreciation method too slow for technology assets, allowance for irrecoverable debts too low in a recession, inventory method giving values above NRV) – prudence argues for a change, consistency for keeping the method. Also excessive prudence (creating large hidden reserves then releasing them) undermines comparability. Resolution: change only with good reason and disclose the effect; the overriding aim is a true and fair view.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): explains both concepts, at least two relevant examples of conflict, balanced discussion and a reasoned conclusion. Level 2 (3–4): both concepts explained, one example, some discussion. Level 1 (1–2): simple descriptions of the concepts.

practice.stem:
Ayesha owns a boutique in Hyderabad. Her capital at 1 January 2026 was $84,500. Draft profit for 2026 is $37,200 and she withdrew $18,000 in cash, correctly recorded as drawings. It is found that:
1 She took clothes costing $1,400 for her own use; nothing was recorded.
2 The rent of her flat, $3,600, was paid by the business and charged to rent expense.
3 In July she gave her private car, valued at $10,000, to the business; it was recorded as a non-current asset but no other entry was made.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: Draft 37,200 + home rent wrongly charged 3,600 (B1) + goods taken credited to purchases 1,400 (B1) = 42,200 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the owner's capital at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: Opening 84,500 + car introduced 10,000 + profit 42,200 − drawings (18,000 + 1,400 + 3,600 = 23,000) = 113,700 (M1 drawings, M1 capital introduced, A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the concept that requires each of the corrections and explain why the goods taken increase profit.
parts.answer: Business entity concept – private items are drawings, not business expenses. The goods were included in purchases (cost of sales) but not sold by the business; removing them from purchases reduces cost of sales, so profit rises.
parts.working: 1 mark concept; 1 mark explanation of goods adjustment.

practice.stem:
Draft profit of Jahangir Tiles for the year ended 30 June 2027 is $128,600. The following have been found:
1 A sale of $6,000 was recorded on 30 June 2027 for goods that the customer will collect and pay for in August 2027. The goods (cost $4,200) were excluded from closing inventory.
2 Insurance of $2,880 paid on 1 April 2027 covers twelve months from that date and was all charged as an expense.
3 Closing inventory includes goods at cost $5,400 that can now be sold for only $3,100 after spending $300 on repairs.
4 Office furniture costing $9,000 bought on 1 July 2026 has been charged in full to administrative expenses. It should be depreciated at 10% straight-line per year, a full year in the year of purchase.
5 Interest of $1,250 on a loan for June 2027 has not been paid or recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 30 June 2027.
parts.working: Draft 128,600; less revenue not realised (6,000) add back inventory at cost 4,200; add prepaid insurance 2,160 (2,880 × 9/12); less inventory write-down 2,600 (5,400 − 2,800); add furniture 9,000 less depreciation 900 = +8,100; less interest accrued 1,250. Corrected profit 133,210. 1 mark per item, 1 mark final figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the accounting concept applied in each of items 1, 3 and 5.
parts.answer: 1 realisation; 3 prudence; 5 accruals (matching).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A business owner says: 'My best asset is my shop's reputation and my 20 years of customer loyalty, but my statement of financial position ignores it. The accounts are useless.' Explain why the reputation is not recorded, and evaluate the owner's view.
parts.answer: Not recorded because of money measurement – it cannot be measured reliably in money – and because internally generated goodwill has no cost (historical cost). Evaluation: statements do omit important non-financial factors, so they are incomplete for judging the value of the business; but they still reliably show resources, obligations and performance, which banks, tax authorities and the owner need; the value of reputation is reflected indirectly in profits; it would be recognised as purchased goodwill if the business were sold. Conclusion: accounts are not useless but must be read alongside non-financial information.
parts.working: 1 mark money measurement; 1 mark no cost / internally generated goodwill not recognised; up to 3 marks for evaluation points (both sides); 1 mark justified conclusion.

practice.stem:
Karakoram Bottling Limited's directors are considering closing the business. Values at 30 June 2027:
                                       Going concern $   Break-up $
Inventory                                       42,000       25,200
Bottling machinery (carrying amount)           156,000       48,000
Trade receivables                               31,000       27,900
Cash                                             8,500        8,500
Trade payables                                  39,000       39,000
Bank loan                                       90,000       90,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net assets of Karakoram Bottling Limited on (i) a going concern basis and (ii) a break-up basis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the specialised bottling machinery shows the largest fall in value.
parts.answer: It is designed for one purpose, so few buyers would want it; under the going concern basis it is shown at carrying amount (cost less accumulated depreciation), which assumes it stays in use; on a forced sale only a low scrap or second-hand price is available.
parts.working: 1 mark specialised, few buyers; 1 mark carrying amount (cost less depreciation) vs low forced-sale value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the result in (a)(ii) means for the shareholders if the company closes.
parts.answer: Net assets are negative/very low, so after paying creditors the shareholders would receive nothing (they lose their investment; liability limited to unpaid share capital).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A company's financial statements for two years are being compared by an investor. In year 1 the company charged all advertising costs when paid; in year 2 it matched them to the period of the campaign. Year 2 included $18,000 paid in advance for a campaign running in year 3. Explain the effect of the change on the comparability of the two years' profits, and how the company should deal with it.
parts.answer: Year 2 profit is $18,000 higher than it would have been under the old policy, so profit growth is partly due to the change in method, not better performance – years are not comparable (consistency). The company should disclose the change and its effect, and restate year 1 on the new basis so both years use the same policy; the new policy is better because it applies matching.
parts.working: 1 mark effect on profit (+18,000); 1 mark not comparable / consistency; 1 mark disclose / restate prior year; 1 mark new policy applies matching.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the accruals concept and the prudence concept would both apply to a business that has received a supplier's estimate of $4,000 for repairs completed on 28 December, with the invoice not expected until February. The year ends on 31 December.
parts.answer: Accruals: the repairs were carried out in this year so the cost belongs to this year and must be accrued even though not invoiced. Prudence: the best estimate of the liability ($4,000) is provided rather than leaving it out, so profit is not overstated.
parts.working: 1 mark each concept correctly applied.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which cost is a direct cost for a business that makes wooden tables?
A timber used to make the tables
B rent of the factory
C salary of the factory supervisor
D depreciation of the cutting machines
parts.answer: A timber used to make the tables
parts.working: Timber can be traced directly to each table. Factory rent, supervision and depreciation (B, C, D) are production overheads: they are incurred for the factory as a whole and cannot be traced to a single table.

practice.stem: Mehran Bakery, Lahore, had the following costs in June 2026: flour $18,400; packaging for each loaf $2,300; wages of bakers $26,500; depreciation of ovens $1,900; bakery rent $3,200; wages of the delivery van driver $2,750.

(i) flour
(ii) wages of bakers
(iii) depreciation of ovens
(iv) wages of the delivery van driver
parts.answer: (i) direct materials (ii) direct labour (iii) production overhead (iv) non-production (distribution) overhead

parts.label: b

practice.stem: Shoaib Shoes, Sialkot, values its inventory of finished shoes at production cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between product costs and period costs. Give one example of each for a shoe manufacturer.
parts.answer: Product costs are the costs of making the goods (direct materials, direct labour, production overheads); they are included in the value of inventory and charged as cost of sales when the goods are sold, e.g. leather. Period costs are not part of production (administration, selling and distribution); they are charged in full against profit in the period in which they are incurred, e.g. sales staff salaries.
parts.working: 1 mark each definition, 1 mark each valid example.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business increases its output from 1,000 units to 2,000 units in a month. Which statement is correct, assuming there is no change in capacity?
A total fixed cost doubles
B variable cost per unit halves
C fixed cost per unit halves
D total variable cost stays the same
parts.answer: C fixed cost per unit halves
parts.working: Total fixed cost is unchanged, so it is spread over twice as many units and fixed cost per unit halves. B is wrong: variable cost per unit stays constant; it is total variable cost that doubles.

practice.stem:
Kibet runs a printing business in Nairobi. Some of his costs are:
1 paper used for print jobs
2 rent of the print shop

4 insurance of the printing machines
5 packaging for each customer order
6 telephone: line rental plus a charge for each call

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each cost as fixed, variable or semi-variable.
parts.answer: 1 variable; 2 fixed; 3 semi-variable; 4 fixed; 5 variable; 6 semi-variable
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a semi-variable cost.
parts.answer: A cost with a fixed element that is paid whatever the output and a variable element that changes with the level of activity.
parts.working: 1 mark fixed element; 1 mark variable element

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A semi-variable cost is $13,000 when 2,000 units are made and $22,000 when 5,000 units are made. What will the cost be when 6,500 units are made?
A $19,500
B $26,500
C $28,600
D $42,250
parts.working: Variable cost per unit = 9,000 ÷ 3,000 = $3; fixed element = 13,000 − 2,000 × 3 = 7,000. At 6,500 units: 7,000 + 6,500 × 3 = 26,500. C treats the whole cost as variable (22,000 ÷ 5,000 × 6,500).

practice.stem:

Month          Units  Total cost $

parts.answer: It uses only two observations, which may not be typical; the forecast for 7,000 units is outside the range of the data and assumes cost behaviour stays the same.

practice.stem:
A food processing company in Nairobi records three costs at two levels of output.

X                 6,000          6,000
Y                 4,500         13,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each cost X, Y and Z by its behaviour. Give a reason for each.
parts.answer: X is fixed (total unchanged when output changes); Y is variable (total rises in proportion: $4.50 per unit at both outputs); Z is semi-variable (rises with output but not in proportion: it has a fixed element).

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

practice.stem: Taj Ceramics, Gujrat, makes tiles. Variable cost is $7.50 per unit. General fixed costs are $18,000 per month. One quality supervisor, paid $3,600 per month, is needed for every 2,500 units (or part of 2,500 units) produced each month.

parts.text: Explain why the cost per unit falls by much less between 5,000 and 6,000 units than between 4,000 and 5,000 units.
parts.answer: The supervisors' cost is a stepped fixed cost. Above 5,000 units a third supervisor is needed, so fixed costs rise by $3,600 and the benefit of spreading fixed costs over more units is partly lost.

practice.stem: Bengal Shirts, Dhaka, recorded total overheads of $186,000 in a month with 12,000 machine hours and $221,000 in a month with 15,500 machine hours. parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the variable overhead per machine hour and the fixed overhead per month.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the company whether it should accept the order. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Accept, subject to the points below. Revenue 22,000 − variable cost 21,200 = contribution $800; fixed overhead does not change, so profit rises by $800. However the margin is very small; check there is spare machine capacity, that regular customers will not demand the same low price, and whether the order may lead to future work.
parts.working: 1 mark contribution calculated; 1 mark relevant non-financial point(s); 1 mark clear decision consistent with the analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Total costs of a business were $52,000 when 4,000 units were made and $79,000 when 7,000 units were made. Fixed costs increase by $6,000 when output exceeds 5,000 units. What is the total cost of making 6,000 units?
A $66,000
B $70,000
C $72,000
D $76,000
parts.working: Remove the step: (79,000 − 6,000 − 52,000) ÷ 3,000 = $7 variable cost per unit; fixed cost below 5,000 units = 52,000 − 28,000 = 24,000. At 6,000 units: 24,000 + 6,000 + 42,000 = $72,000. B ($70,000) uses a high–low rate of $9 that ignores the step in fixed cost.

practice.stem:

parts.answer: Uses only two observations, which may be unusual; assumes a straight-line cost relationship; ignores step changes in fixed cost; the relationship may not hold outside the observed range.
parts.working: 1 mark each

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prices of raw materials have risen steadily during the year. Compared with AVCO, what is the effect of using FIFO?
A higher closing inventory and higher gross profit
B higher closing inventory and lower gross profit
C lower closing inventory and higher gross profit
D lower closing inventory and lower gross profit
parts.answer: A higher closing inventory and higher gross profit
parts.working: Under FIFO the oldest (cheapest) units are issued first, so closing inventory is valued at the latest, higher prices. Cost of sales is lower, so gross profit is higher. B forgets that a higher closing inventory reduces cost of sales.

practice.stem: Rania is choosing a method of valuing the inventory of spare parts for her motorcycle repair business in Amman.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of the FIFO method of inventory valuation.
parts.answer: Any two: follows the usual physical flow of goods; closing inventory is valued at recent prices; easy to understand; no averages need to be recalculated; acceptable under IAS 2.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of the AVCO method.
parts.answer: Any one: it smooths out price changes so that issue prices and profits fluctuate less; all units of the same item are given the same value.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why a company preparing financial statements under international standards may not use LIFO.
parts.answer: IAS 2 Inventories does not allow LIFO.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:

B $4.40

parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory on 30 April using AVCO (perpetual). Give your answer to the nearest cent.

parts.label: a
parts.text:

parts.answer: B AVCO gives a higher closing inventory value than FIFO
parts.working: With falling prices FIFO leaves the newest (cheapest) items in closing inventory, while AVCO includes some older, dearer costs, so AVCO's closing inventory is higher and its profit is higher. A is the result when prices are rising, not falling.

practice.stem: Darzi Uniforms, Karachi, prices each job at total cost plus 25%. Job J47, 120 school blazers, needs 250 metres of fabric. parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of fabric charged to Job J47 using (i) FIFO and (ii) AVCO.

parts.label: c

parts.answer: Material cost is part of total cost and price is cost plus a mark-up; with rising prices AVCO charges a higher cost than FIFO, so the price is higher.
parts.working: 1 mark: cost-plus link; 1 mark: rising prices → AVCO higher

practice.stem:
Falcon Pharma Distributors uses AVCO. Its profits and closing inventory values were:
                                Year 1 $  Year 2 $
Profit for the year (AVCO)        71,200    84,000
Closing inventory: AVCO           45,900    50,100
Closing inventory: FIFO           48,600    52,300
Opening inventory for year 1 was the same under both methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for year 1 if FIFO had been used.
parts.working: Higher closing inventory raises profit: 71,200 + (48,600 − 45,900) = 73,900. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for year 2 if FIFO had been used.
parts.working: Opening inventory is also higher under FIFO, which reduces profit: 84,000 + (52,300 − 50,100) − (48,600 − 45,900) = 83,500. M1 closing adjustment; M1 opening adjustment; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The directors receive a bonus based on profit and want to change from AVCO to FIFO. Advise them whether they should make this change. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Points for: FIFO is allowed by IAS 2; inventory in the statement of financial position is closer to current prices; profit would have been higher in year 1.
Points against: the consistency concept means a method should be changed only if the new one gives a fairer view, and the change must be disclosed; over time total profit is the same (year 2 would be lower); changing to raise bonuses is unethical and misleading to users.
Decision: do not change merely to increase the bonus.
parts.working: 1 mark points for/against using figures; 1 mark consistency/IAS 2; 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem:
Gulf Tyres, a trader in Muscat, is deciding whether to use FIFO or perpetual AVCO for one type of tyre. January 2026:
Date     Details

3 Jan    Bought 600 tyres at $22.00

practice.stem:
Kandy Tea Packers records the following for packaging film in June 2026:
