parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a feature of a just-in-time (JIT) system of inventory management?
A raw materials are delivered in small quantities as they are needed
B large buffer inventories are held in case of supplier delays
C materials are bought in bulk to obtain trade discounts
D suppliers are chosen only on the basis of the lowest price
parts.answer: A raw materials are delivered in small quantities as they are needed
parts.working: JIT aims to hold little or no inventory, so deliveries arrive in small batches just before they are used. B and C describe the opposite approach; under JIT suppliers are chosen for reliability and quality, not only price (D).

practice.stem: Indus Auto Parts, Karachi, assembles brake units for car manufacturers. It currently keeps three months' inventory of components in a rented warehouse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages to the business of adopting a just-in-time system.
parts.answer: Any two explained: lower holding costs (storage space, insurance, security); less working capital tied up in inventory, improving cash flow; less risk of obsolescence, damage or theft; storage space can be used for production; close links with suppliers can improve quality.
parts.working: 1 mark each advantage, 1 mark each explanation in context.

practice.stem: Pearl Electronics, Penang, holds average inventory of $300,000. Under JIT this would fall to $60,000. The warehouse no longer needed could be rented out for $2,500 per month. Insurance is 1.5% of average inventory. Annual losses from obsolete inventory would fall from $9,000 to $1,500. A supplier liaison officer would be employed at a salary of $22,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net annual benefit of introducing JIT.
parts.answer:
Rent from warehouse: 12 × $2,500                       30,000
Insurance saved: 1.5% × (300,000 − 60,000)              3,600
Obsolescence losses saved: 9,000 − 1,500                7,500
Less salary of supplier liaison officer              (22,000)
Net annual benefit                                     19,100
parts.working: 1 mark each item; total own figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two risks of introducing JIT for this business.
parts.answer: Any two: late or failed deliveries stopping production; loss of bulk discounts; supplier price rises once the firm depends on them; sudden increases in demand cannot be met; quality problems.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a disadvantage of a just-in-time inventory system?
A production may stop if a supplier delivers late
B more warehouse space is needed
C more working capital is tied up in inventory
D inventory is more likely to become obsolete
parts.answer: A production may stop if a supplier delivers late
parts.working: With little or no buffer inventory, any late or faulty delivery can halt production. B, C and D are disadvantages of holding large inventories, which JIT reduces.

practice.stem: Amna Pharma Distributors, Lahore, keeps a large buffer inventory of every product so that it never runs out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three costs of holding inventory.
parts.answer: e.g. storage/warehouse rent; insurance; security; interest on capital tied up (opportunity cost); deterioration, expiry and obsolescence; handling staff.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a just-in-time system differs from holding a buffer inventory.
parts.answer: Under JIT materials or goods are delivered only when they are needed, in small frequent deliveries, so little or no inventory is held; a buffer inventory is a safety stock kept in case of delays or high demand.
parts.working: 1 mark JIT description; 1 mark buffer contrast

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about just-in-time inventory management are correct?
1 It reduces the cost of storing inventory.
2 It increases the risk that production will stop.
3 It makes it easier to obtain bulk-purchase discounts.
4 It depends on reliable suppliers.
A 1, 2 and 4
B 1 and 3 only
C 2, 3 and 4
D 3 and 4 only
parts.answer: A 1, 2 and 4
parts.working: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: JIT orders are small and frequent, so bulk-purchase discounts are usually lost.

practice.stem: Green Valley Foods, Mardan, holds average inventory of raw materials of $240,000. Annual holding costs are 18% of average inventory. Under a proposed JIT system average inventory would fall to $40,000. There would be 500 extra deliveries a year costing $12 each, and suppliers would increase prices by 1% on annual purchases of $1,200,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected net annual saving from introducing JIT.
parts.answer:
Holding cost saved: (240,000 − 40,000) × 18%       36,000
Less extra delivery costs: 500 × $12              (6,000)
Less price increase: 1% × 1,200,000              (12,000)
Net annual saving                                  18,000
parts.working: M1 A1 holding cost saving; B1 delivery costs; B1 price increase; A1 net saving.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the managers whether to introduce JIT. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The saving of $18,000 supports JIT. But the company must be confident of its suppliers' reliability, since a late delivery would stop production; demand must be steady; and the 1% price rise may grow. Decision: introduce JIT if suppliers can guarantee delivery, perhaps keeping a small buffer at first.
parts.working: 1 mark use of the figure; 1 mark non-financial factor(s); 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: A furniture manufacturer in Chiang Mai, Thailand, is thinking of changing to JIT for its supplies of timber and fittings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two conditions that must exist for a just-in-time system to work successfully.
parts.answer: Any two explained: reliable suppliers that can deliver at short notice; suppliers located close by or good transport links; high and consistent quality of materials (no time to replace faulty items); stable, predictable demand and production schedules; good communication/IT links with suppliers; a flexible, well-trained workforce.
parts.working: 1 mark each condition, 1 mark each explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one effect of JIT on the working capital of a business.
parts.answer: Less money is tied up in inventory, so cash is released (current assets fall).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company's average inventory is expected to fall from $250,000 to $70,000 if it adopts JIT. Holding costs are 14% of average inventory each year. More frequent deliveries will cost an extra $9,500 a year. What is the net annual saving?
A $15,700
B $25,200
C $25,500
D $34,700
parts.working: (250,000 − 70,000) × 14% = 25,200; less 9,500 = $15,700. B ignores the extra delivery cost; D adds it instead of deducting it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net annual financial effect of adopting JIT.
parts.answer: Net saving $10,500
parts.working: Interest saved 13,500 B1; rent 14,000 B1; obsolescence 9,000 B1; extra component cost 18,000 B1; delivery admin 8,000 and net $10,500 B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to adopt JIT. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Financial benefit of $10,500 a year. Against: reliance on one supplier; risk of stoppages from late deliveries or road disruption; price premium may rise; quality must be right first time. For: less space, less obsolescence, better cash flow, supplier relationship. Decision.
parts.working: 1 mark uses figure; up to 2 marks non-financial points for, up to 2 against (max 4 points); 1 mark justified decision (max 5)

practice.stem: Coastal Furniture, Mombasa, is introducing a just-in-time system for timber.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the effect of JIT on the working capital of the business.
parts.answer: Less inventory is held, so less cash is tied up in current assets; working capital needs fall and cash can be used elsewhere (e.g. to repay overdraft).
parts.working: 1 mark lower inventory; 1 mark effect on cash/working capital

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the choice between FIFO and AVCO has less effect on profit after JIT is introduced.
parts.answer: With very little closing inventory, almost all materials bought are used in the period, so cost of sales is close to purchases whichever method is used; the methods only differ in how closing inventory is valued.
parts.working: 1 mark small inventory; 1 mark difference lies in inventory valuation

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two requirements of suppliers if JIT is to succeed.
parts.answer: Reliable, punctual deliveries; consistent quality; located close by / able to make small frequent deliveries; willing to agree long-term contracts.
parts.working: 1 mark each

practice.stem: Atlas Bicycles, Lahore, is considering JIT for its components. Average inventory would fall from $380,000 to $120,000; holding costs are 20% a year of average inventory. The number of orders would rise from 12 to 150 a year, each costing $85 to process. The production manager expects JIT to cause 4 days of production stoppage a year, losing contribution of $6,500 per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected net annual financial effect of adopting JIT.
parts.answer:
Holding cost saved: (380,000 − 120,000) × 20%          52,000
Less extra ordering costs: (150 − 12) × $85          (11,730)
Less expected lost contribution: 4 × $6,500          (26,000)
Net annual saving                                      14,270
parts.working: 1 mark holding cost; 1 mark ordering cost (138 extra orders); 1 mark stoppage cost; 1 mark net saving.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of days of stoppage per year at which JIT would no longer be worthwhile.
parts.answer: More than 6.20 days, i.e. 7 or more whole days

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to adopt JIT. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: a net saving is expected; less cash tied up in inventory. Against: the saving depends heavily on the stoppage estimate; only about two more days of stoppage would remove it; supplier reliability and transport links must be checked. Decision consistent with these points, e.g. adopt only with a supplier guarantee or penalty clause.
parts.working: 1 mark for points for and against; 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: Sindhri Juices, Multan, makes mango juice. Fresh mangoes are available locally only from June to August; the company freezes pulp in a large cold store so that it can make juice all year. Bottles and cartons are bought from a nearby supplier who can deliver daily. The directors have read that JIT reduces costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether Sindhri Juices should adopt just-in-time purchasing for fresh mangoes. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For JIT: less fresh fruit wasted through spoilage; lower cold-storage costs; less cash tied up; fruit used fresher, improving quality.
Against JIT: mangoes are available only in a short season, so supply cannot be called off all year; prices rise sharply out of season; weather can disrupt harvests and transport; juice production must run at full capacity during the season.
Possible compromise: JIT for packaging and bottles, which can be supplied all year, but bulk buying and pulp storage for mangoes.
Decision: do not adopt JIT for mangoes.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for; up to 2 marks for points against (in context); 1 mark for a compromise or further analysis; 1 mark justified decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected net annual saving from JIT.
parts.working: Holding saving 45,000 B1; expiry saving 22,000 B1; stock-out cost 21,000 B1; net $46,000 B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the hospital's managers whether to adopt JIT for its pharmacy. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: saving of $46,000; less expired medicine; space freed for clinical use; capital released. Against: a stock-out of a critical medicine could put patients' lives at risk, which is not captured by $3,500; emergencies and outbreaks cause sudden demand; dependence on one wholesaler and on Karachi traffic; reputation and legal risk. Possible compromise: JIT for routine items while keeping safety stocks of critical/life-saving medicines. Clear decision.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for points in favour, up to 3 against (non-financial points needed for full marks), 1 mark for a justified decision

practice.stem:
Extract from the statement of financial position of Faran Foods, Lahore, before a proposed change to JIT:
                         $
Inventory           180,000
Trade receivables    90,000
Cash at bank         30,000
Trade payables      210,000
Under JIT, inventory would fall to $40,000. All the cash released would be used immediately to pay trade payables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and the liquid (acid test) ratio before the change. Give answers to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Current 1.43 : 1; liquid 0.57 : 1
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and the liquid ratio after the change.
parts.answer: Current 2.29 : 1; liquid 1.71 : 1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether the change to JIT will improve the business's ability to pay its debts.
parts.answer: Both ratios rise; the liquid ratio moves from well below 1 to well above 1, so short-term solvency improves and supplier relationships may improve. But no new cash is created: cash stays the same; the improvement comes from repaying payables; any production stoppage under JIT could cut sales and cash inflows; suppliers may demand faster payment.
parts.working: 1 mark each for relevant points on both sides, max 3; 1 mark conclusion

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A worker is paid $12 per hour for a basic week of 40 hours. Overtime is paid at time-and-a-half. In one week she works 44 hours. What is her gross pay?
A $528
B $552
C $576
D $792
parts.working: 40 × 12 + 4 × 18 = 480 + 72 = 552. A pays all hours at the basic rate; C pays the overtime at double time.

practice.stem: Hassan runs a repair workshop for air-conditioning units in Doha and is deciding how to pay his technicians.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to the employer of paying workers a time rate rather than a piece rate.
parts.answer: Advantage (any one explained): quality is not sacrificed for speed; pay is simple to calculate; suitable where output cannot be measured. Disadvantage (any one explained): no incentive to work faster, so supervision is needed; labour cost per unit rises when output falls.
parts.working: 1 mark advantage, 1 mark explanation; 1 mark disadvantage, 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A factory pays a differential piece rate: $0.50 per unit for the first 400 units a week and $0.60 for each unit above 400. A worker produced 520 units in a week. What is her gross pay?
A $252
B $260
C $272
D $312
parts.working: 400 × 0.50 + 120 × 0.60 = $272. D ($312) wrongly pays the higher rate on all 520 units.

practice.stem:
Haris works in a bottling plant in Hyderabad. He is paid $9 per hour for a basic day of 8 hours, Monday to Friday. Extra hours on weekdays are paid at time-and-a-half and all hours on Sunday at double time. Hours worked in one week:
Mon 10   Tue 9   Wed 8   Thu 11   Fri 8   Sun 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Haris's gross pay for the week.
parts.working: Basic 40 × 9 = 360 B1; weekday overtime 6 × 13.50 = 81 B1; Sunday 5 × 18 = 90 B1; total $531

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overtime premium included in his pay.

practice.stem: Fatima manages a bakery in Rawalpindi employing bakers, packers, cleaners and a delivery driver.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between direct labour and indirect labour, giving one example of each from the bakery.
parts.answer: Direct labour is the cost of workers who work directly on making the product and can be traced to units, e.g. bakers or packers. Indirect labour cannot be traced to particular products, e.g. cleaners, supervisors, maintenance staff.
parts.working: 1 mark each definition; 1 mark each example

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by idle time and how it is treated in the cost accounts.
parts.answer: Time paid for but in which no production takes place (e.g. oven breakdown, waiting for flour); its cost is treated as a production overhead (or written off if abnormal), not as direct labour.
parts.working: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark treatment

practice.stem: A garment workshop in Karachi pays machinists $0.85 per garment with a guaranteed minimum of $360 per week. Output in one week was: Asif 520 garments, Bilal 390 garments, Chen 465 garments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross pay of each worker for the week.
parts.working: Asif 520 × 0.85 = 442.00; Bilal 390 × 0.85 = 331.50, below the minimum so paid 360.00; Chen 465 × 0.85 = 395.25. 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total labour cost and the labour cost per unit produced. Give the cost per unit to the nearest cent.
parts.working: Total 1,197.25 ÷ 1,375 units = 0.87. 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason for paying a guaranteed minimum wage.
parts.answer: Gives workers security of income when output is low for reasons outside their control (machine breakdown, shortage of materials); may be required by law.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Twelve production workers at Margalla Furniture each worked 45 hours last week. The basic week is 40 hours at $10 per hour, and overtime is paid at time-and-a-half. The overtime was needed because of a general increase in orders, not for any particular job.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total gross wages for the week.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much of the gross wages should be treated as direct labour and how much as production overhead.
parts.answer: Direct labour $5,400; production overhead $300
parts.working: All hours at basic rate are direct: 12 × 45 × $10 = 5,400. The overtime premium 12 × 5 × $5 = 300 is overhead because the overtime was due to the general level of work. 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain when the overtime premium would be treated as a direct cost.
parts.answer: When the overtime is worked at the specific request of a customer or for a particular job, the premium can be traced to that job and is charged to it as direct labour.
parts.working: 1 mark specific job/customer; 1 mark charged directly to that job.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Twenty production workers each worked 46 hours in a week. The basic week is 40 hours at $11 per hour, and overtime is paid at time-and-a-half. The overtime was caused by a general increase in orders. What is the direct labour cost for the week?
A $8,800
B $10,120
C $10,780
D $660
parts.working: All hours at the basic rate are direct labour: 20 × 46 × 11 = $10,120. The overtime premium (20 × 6 × 5.50 = $660) is a production overhead because no particular job caused it, so C is wrong.

practice.stem: A team of four workers at a football factory in Sialkot is paid $8 per hour for all hours worked. The team also earns a group bonus of $0.40 for each ball made above a weekly target of 2,000 balls. The bonus is shared in proportion to hours worked. In one week the team made 2,600 balls. Hours worked: Adeel 40, Bushra 45, Chaudhry 35, Danish 40.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total group bonus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gross pay of each worker.
parts.answer: Adeel $380.00; Bushra $427.50; Chaudhry $332.50; Danish $380.00
parts.working: Bonus per hour 240 ÷ 160 = 1.50 M1; A1 for each pair of workers (lose 1 per error)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the labour cost per ball, to two decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of a group bonus scheme compared with an individual bonus.
parts.answer: Advantage: encourages teamwork / suits work where individual output cannot be measured. Disadvantage: hard-working members subsidise slower ones, which may cause resentment.
parts.working: 1 mark each

practice.stem: Shabana packs dates in Khairpur. She is paid $10 per hour for a 40-hour week plus a bonus of $1.50 for each carton packed above 320 cartons in the week. Her output in three weeks was: week 1 300 cartons; week 2 380 cartons; week 3 410 cartons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Shabana's gross pay for each week.
parts.answer: Week 1 $400; week 2 $490; week 3 $535
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour cost per carton for each week, to two decimal places.
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the labour cost per carton is lower in week 2 than in week 1.
parts.answer: The fixed time wage of $400 is spread over more cartons, while the bonus of $1.50 per extra carton is less than the time-wage cost per carton, so the average falls.
parts.working: 1 mark spreading of fixed wage; 1 mark bonus rate below average cost

practice.stem: A tailoring unit in Lahore pays its three machinists $12 per hour for a 40-hour week. Last week Ejaz made 160 shirts, Farid 200 shirts and Ghazala 240 shirts. The manager is considering a piece rate of $2.50 per shirt instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour cost per shirt for each machinist under the time rate.
parts.answer: Ejaz $3.00; Farid $2.40; Ghazala $2.00
parts.working: 480 ÷ output, B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total weekly wages under (i) the time rate and (ii) the piece rate, assuming output is unchanged.
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to the business of changing to the piece rate.
parts.answer: Advantage: labour cost per shirt fixed at $2.50 and faster workers are rewarded, which may raise output. Disadvantage: workers may rush and quality may fall / slower workers' pay falls so they may leave / more checking needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each

practice.stem: Workers at Rose Valley Packaging, Swat, are paid $14 per hour plus a bonus of 50% of the time saved, valued at the hourly rate. The standard time is 0.4 hours per unit. In one week both Farida and Gul worked 38 hours. Farida produced 110 units and Gul produced 92 units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross pay of each worker for the week.
parts.answer: Farida $574; Gul $532
parts.working: Farida: standard time 110 × 0.4 = 44 hours, time saved 6 hours, bonus 50% × 6 × 14 = 42; pay 532 + 42 = 574. Gul: standard time 92 × 0.4 = 36.8 hours, no time saved, pay 38 × 14 = 532. 2 marks each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour cost per unit for each worker. Give your answers to the nearest cent.
parts.answer: Farida $5.22; Gul $5.78
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether the bonus scheme benefits the company.
parts.answer: Benefit: the faster worker's cost per unit is lower even after the bonus, because time saved is shared 50:50. Drawback: workers may rush and quality may fall; slow workers still receive full time-rate pay, so there is no penalty.
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the weekly profit under the present time rate.
parts.working: Output 12,000 units B1; contribution before labour 72,000 less wages 20,000 M1; less 36,000 = $16,000 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the weekly profit under the proposed piece rate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the labour cost per unit under each scheme, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Time rate $1.67; piece rate $1.80

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to introduce the piece rate. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Profit rises by $3,960 a week if output really rises 15%. Against: labour cost per unit rises; quality risk; output forecast uncertain; extra inspection; workers may resist or the union object; slower workers earn less. For: motivation, higher output, more contribution. Decision.
parts.working: 1 mark using the comparison; up to 2 marks for, up to 2 against; 1 mark justified decision (max 5)

practice.stem: A machine operator at Indus Steel Fabricators is paid $15 per hour for a 40-hour week and is paid for 52 weeks a year, including 6 weeks of paid holiday. The employer also pays social security contributions of 12% of gross pay. Of the hours the operator attends work, 8% are idle time (machine set-up and waiting for materials).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total annual cost to the employer of the operator.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of productive hours a year.
parts.answer: 1,692.8 hours

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the cost per productive hour, to the nearest cent.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why this rate, rather than $15 per hour, should be used when costing jobs.
parts.answer: Jobs must bear all labour costs, including holiday pay, employer's contributions and unavoidable idle time; using $15 would understate job costs and prices may not cover costs.
parts.working: 1 mark all costs recovered; 1 mark consequence of under-costing

practice.stem: Workers at a garment factory in Korangi are paid $0.80 for each garment, plus $9 per hour for idle time caused by machine breakdowns. Each worker is guaranteed at least $420 per week in total. In one week a breakdown caused 6 hours of idle time for each of three workers. Output that week: Kiran 420 garments, Lubna 600 garments, Maryam 560 garments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross pay of each worker.
parts.answer: Kiran $420; Lubna $534; Maryam $502
parts.working: Kiran 336 + 54 = 390, raised to guarantee 420 B1; Lubna 480 + 54 B1; Maryam 448 + 54 B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much of the total wages is direct labour and how much is a production overhead.
parts.answer: Direct labour $1,264; overhead $192
parts.working: Piece earnings 336 + 480 + 448 = 1,264 direct B1; idle time 3 × 54 = 162 B1; guarantee top-up 30, both overhead, total 192 B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the guarantee top-up is not charged as direct labour.
parts.answer: It is not caused by producing particular garments; it relates to low output in general, so it is an indirect cost spread over all production through the overhead rate.
parts.working: 1 mark not traceable to units; 1 mark overhead

practice.stem: Two traders in Karachi, one selling dried fruit and one with a shop in Dubai, agree to work together for one shipment only and share the profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'joint venture'.
parts.answer: A short-term business arrangement in which two or more parties combine resources for a single, specific project and share the resulting profit or loss in an agreed ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: two or more parties for a specific/single project. 1 mark: temporary, sharing profit or loss in agreed ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two differences between a joint venture and a partnership.
parts.answer: A joint venture ends when the project is completed, whereas a partnership continues indefinitely; joint venturers usually carry on their own separate businesses and there is usually no firm name or separate continuing set of books.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: duration (temporary vs continuing); scope (one project vs ongoing business); venturers keep own businesses; no firm name / records often kept in venturers' own books.

practice.stem: A Pakistani rice mill is considering a joint venture with a packaging company in Malaysia to supply a large supermarket order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why the rice mill might enter into the joint venture.
parts.answer: To share the cost and risk of the order; to use the partner's skills, contacts and packaging facilities.
parts.working: 1 mark each: share risk/finance; access to expertise, contacts or market; complete an order too large alone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two risks for the rice mill of entering into the joint venture.
parts.answer: Disagreements over how profit and costs are shared; the other venturer may fail to meet its obligations or may mishandle the money received.
parts.working: 1 mark each: disputes; dependence on partner's performance; loss of control; unlimited liability for shared losses; delays in settlement.

practice.stem: Ikram keeps a 'Joint venture with Salma' account in his own books. The venture has made a profit and Ikram's share is $4,600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the double entry in Ikram's books to record his share of the profit.
parts.answer: Debit Joint venture with Salma account $4,600; credit statement of profit or loss (profit on joint venture) $4,600.
parts.working: 1 mark debit; 1 mark credit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After his share of profit is recorded, Ikram's 'Joint venture with Salma' account has a debit balance of $9,300. Explain what this balance shows and how it will be cleared.
parts.answer: Salma owes Ikram $9,300 (she has received more from the venture than her costs plus her share of profit); it is cleared when Salma pays Ikram $9,300 (debit bank, credit the joint venture account).
parts.working: 1 mark: Salma owes Ikram / receivable. 1 mark: cleared by cash received from Salma.

practice.stem: Sialkot Leather sends handbags to an agent in Doha. The agent sells them for a commission and returns the money. A competitor instead works with a Doha trader who shares the profit on the goods equally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which arrangement is a consignment and which is a joint venture.
parts.answer: Sialkot Leather and its agent: consignment. The competitor and the Doha trader: joint venture.
parts.working: B1 both correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two differences between a consignment and a joint venture.
parts.answer: In a consignment the consignor owns the goods until they are sold and bears all the profit or loss; the agent earns only commission. In a joint venture the venturers are co-owners for the project and share profit or loss in an agreed ratio. Also, a consignee acts for the consignor as agent, whereas joint venturers are like temporary partners with equal standing.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per difference: ownership of goods; who bears profit/loss (commission vs share of profit); relationship (principal–agent vs co-venturers).

practice.stem: Asif (Lahore) and Bano (Karachi) agree a joint venture to sell 2,000 cricket bats, sharing profits equally. Asif bought the bats for $36,000 and paid carriage of $1,500. Bano paid advertising of $2,800 and sold all the bats for $52,000, keeping the cash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State each venturer's share of the profit.
parts.answer: $5,850 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amount that must be paid in settlement, and state who pays whom.
parts.answer: Bano pays Asif $43,350.
parts.working: Asif: 37,500 + 5,850 = 43,350 due to him (M1); Bano pays Asif 43,350 (A1).

practice.stem:
Chaudhry and Daniyal entered a joint venture to trade in basmati rice, sharing profits and losses 3:2. Each recorded his own transactions.
Chaudhry: bought rice $64,000; paid transport $3,200; sold rice for $30,000.
Daniyal: paid storage $2,400; paid packing $1,900; sold rice for $52,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer:

Transport (Chaudhry)               3,200
Storage (Daniyal)                  2,400
Packing (Daniyal)                  1,900
Share of profit – Chaudhry         6,300
Share of profit – Daniyal          4,200
                                  82,000

                                  82,000
parts.working: B1 purchases and transport; B1 storage and packing; B1 sales 82,000; B1 profit 10,500; B1 shares Chaudhry 6,300, Daniyal 4,200.

practice.stem:
Kashif and Lubna share joint venture profits 2:3. A summary of their joint venture records:
                         Kashif $  Lubna $
Costs paid                 21,500    4,700
Sales proceeds received     9,000   30,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the joint venture profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's share of the profit.
parts.answer: Kashif $5,200; Lubna $7,800.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the settlement payment and state who pays whom.
parts.answer: Lubna pays Kashif $17,700.

practice.stem: Usama and Wardah contributed $30,000 and $50,000 respectively to a joint venture importing tiles. They agreed to share the profit in the ratio of their contributions. The profit was $48,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's share of the profit.
parts.answer: Usama $18,000; Wardah $30,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why venturers might agree to share profit in the ratio of the money contributed rather than equally.
parts.answer: The venturer who puts in more money takes more risk and gives up the use of more funds, so a larger share rewards that contribution fairly.
parts.working: 1 mark: reflects risk/finance provided. 1 mark: fairness / equal sharing would favour the smaller contributor.

practice.stem:
Waseem and Yumna are in a joint venture. In Waseem's books the following took place:
1 Waseem paid $15,000 by bank for goods for the venture
2 Waseem received $9,000 by bank from sales of venture goods
3 Waseem's share of the venture profit was $2,750
4 Yumna paid Waseem the amount due to settle the venture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare journal entries in Waseem's books for items 1 to 4. Narratives are not required.
parts.answer:
Dr $    Cr $
1 Joint venture with Yumna                 15,000
  Bank                                             15,000
2 Bank                                      9,000
  Joint venture with Yumna                          9,000
3 Joint venture with Yumna                  2,750
  Statement of profit or loss (JV profit)           2,750
4 Bank                                      8,750
  Joint venture with Yumna                          8,750
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct entry; settlement 15,000 − 9,000 + 2,750 = 8,750.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the balance on the 'Joint venture with Yumna' account would appear in Waseem's statement of financial position if Yumna had not yet paid.
parts.answer: As a current asset (receivable: amount due from Yumna).

practice.stem: Arif and Bina share joint venture profits equally. Arif paid costs of $12,000. Bina paid costs of $3,000 and received all the sales proceeds of $20,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the joint venture profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the settlement payment and state who pays whom.
parts.answer: Bina pays Arif $14,500.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Before settlement, state whether the 'Joint venture with Bina' account in Arif's books has a debit or a credit balance, and what it represents.
parts.answer: A debit balance of $14,500, representing the amount Bina owes Arif (an asset/receivable).
parts.working: 1 mark: debit. 1 mark: amount owed by Bina.

practice.stem: Tariq and Omar form a joint venture to run a food and craft stall at a three-day Eid bazaar in Multan. They share profits and losses equally. Tariq bought stock for the stall for $18,500 and paid the stall fee of $1,200 from his own money. Omar received all cash takings of $27,300 and paid transport and generator hire of $900 out of those takings. There was no unsold stock.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.
parts.working: Total costs 18,500 + 1,200 + 900 = 20,600; sales 27,300 − 20,600 = 6,700. 1 mark for costs, 1 mark for profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State each venturer's share of the profit.
parts.answer: $3,350 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amount Omar must pay Tariq to settle the venture.
parts.working: Tariq is repaid what he paid (18,500 + 1,200 = 19,700) plus his profit share 3,350. Omar holds 26,400 after transport, so he keeps 3,350 (his own share). 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for 23,050.

practice.stem: Hamid and Kiran agree a joint venture to buy and sell 150 hand-carved chairs from Sialkot. Each venturer keeps his or her own books and records his or her own transactions. Hamid sends chairs from his own inventory, costing $9,000, to the venture. He then pays Kiran an advance of $2,000 by bank transfer to cover local costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the double entry in Hamid's books to record the chairs he sends from his own inventory to the venture.
parts.answer: Debit: Joint venture with Kiran account $9,000. Credit: Inventory (goods at cost) $9,000.
parts.working: 1 mark for the debit to the joint venture account, 1 mark for the credit to inventory at cost. The goods are a cost to the venture, not a sale.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the double entry in Hamid's books to record the $2,000 advance paid to Kiran by bank transfer.
parts.answer: Debit: Joint venture with Kiran account $2,000. Credit: Bank $2,000.
parts.working: 1 mark each side. An advance to a venturer is a transfer, not a cost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the $2,000 advance is not shown as an expense in the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer: It is cash handed over to another venturer, not a cost of the venture. The costs are recorded in the memorandum account when Kiran actually incurs them.
parts.working: 1 mark: the advance is a transfer between venturers, not a cost. 1 mark: costs appear only when they are incurred and paid for the venture.

practice.stem: Waleed (Peshawar) and Zarina (Lahore) run a joint venture to sell 400 bales of wool. They share profit equally. Waleed paid $31,000 for the wool. Zarina sold the wool for $40,000 in cash. At the end, 20 bales that cost $2,400 were unsold. Waleed took them over for his own use at an agreed value of $2,400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.
parts.answer: $11,400 (sales 40,000 + goods taken over 2,400 − costs 31,000)
parts.working: 1 mark for adding the goods taken over at their agreed value to the income side, 1 mark for total costs of 31,000, 1 mark for the profit of 11,400.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the goods taken over are credited to the memorandum joint venture account at their agreed value.
parts.answer: The goods leave the venture at the agreed value, so the venture receives this amount for them. Crediting it to the account reduces the costs of the venture that must be recovered, giving the correct profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: the agreed value is the amount the venture receives for the goods. 1 mark: crediting it keeps the memorandum account complete and gives the correct profit.

practice.stem: Asma and Bilal enter a joint venture to sell imported lamps at a school fair. Profits and losses are shared equally. Asma paid $6,800 for the lamps and $1,500 of other costs from her own money. Bilal sold all the lamps for $6,100 and paid nothing towards the costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the loss on the joint venture.
parts.working: Sales 6,100 less costs 8,300 (6,800 + 1,500) = loss of 2,200. 1 mark for the costs, 1 mark for the loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State each venturer's share of the loss.
parts.answer: $1,100 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amount Bilal must pay Asma to settle the venture, and state where the money comes from.
parts.answer: $7,200: Asma's costs 8,300 less her share of the loss 1,100. Bilal pays the $6,100 cash he holds and adds $1,100 from his own money.
parts.working: 1 mark for 8,300 − 1,100 = 7,200. 1 mark for 6,100 sales cash held by Bilal. 1 mark for the 1,100 that Bilal must provide himself because he holds less cash than the amount due.

practice.stem: Yusra and Zafar share joint venture profits in the ratio 3:2. They imported Kashmiri shawls to sell at a winter exhibition in London. At the end of the venture, Zafar's share of the profit was $4,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total profit on the joint venture.
parts.working: Zafar's 2 parts = 4,800, so 1 part = 2,400 and the total of 5 parts = 12,000. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for 12,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Yusra's share of the profit.

practice.stem: Nida and Jabir run a one-season venture to sell 1,200 pairs of school shoes in Quetta. Sales were $96,000. The costs were: shoes $68,400, and transport and stall rental $6,000. Profit is shared equally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture and express it as a percentage of sales.
parts.working: 1 mark for total costs of 74,400, 1 mark for profit 21,600, 1 mark for 22.5%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's share of the profit.

practice.stem: Ruth and Liam share joint venture profits equally. Ruth keeps a 'Joint venture with Liam' account in her own books. The venture has made a profit of $3,900 in total.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the double entry in Ruth's books to record her share of the profit.
parts.answer: Debit: Joint venture with Liam account $1,950. Credit: Profit and loss (or Ruth's capital account) $1,950.
parts.working: 1 mark for debiting the joint venture account, 1 mark for crediting profit and loss or capital. The share is 3,900 ÷ 2 = 1,950.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the amount in part (a) is debited to the joint venture account rather than credited.
parts.answer: Ruth's joint venture account is a debit balance (the amount the venture owes her). Her share of profit increases what she is owed, so the account is debited; the matching credit goes to profit and loss.
parts.working: 1 mark for the reason linking the credit balance to the transfer.

practice.stem: Hafiz (Lahore) and Rubab (Dubai) run a joint venture to sell 1,500 pairs of sunglasses. Rubab is the sales agent. She is paid commission of 5% of sales, deducted before profit is shared. Sales were $60,000. Hafiz paid the purchase costs of $42,500. Rubab paid shipping of $1,000. The profit after commission is shared equally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the commission Rubab earns on sales.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture after commission and shipping.
parts.working: 1 mark for deducting commission and shipping, 1 mark for profit 13,500.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's share of the profit.
parts.answer: $6,750 each

practice.stem: Ruqayya and Samina run a joint venture to sell handmade leather bags at a trade fair. Ruqayya is entitled to 45% of the profit and Samina to the remaining 55%. Total sales were $52,000 and total costs were $37,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.
parts.working: Sales 52,000 less costs 37,000 = 15,000. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Ruqayya's share of the profit, given that she is entitled to 45%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate Samina's share of the profit.

practice.stem: Sami (Karachi) and Ruhi (Muscat) run a joint venture to sell imported dates. Profits are shared 2:1 (Sami : Ruhi). Sami supplied dates costing $27,600. Ruhi sold all the dates for $33,000 and paid $2,100 of transport from the sales money.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.
parts.working: Sales 33,000 less goods 27,600 and expenses 2,100 = 3,300.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Sami's share of the profit.
parts.working: Sami has 2 of 3 parts: 3,300 × 2 ÷ 3 = 2,200.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the amount that Ruhi must pay Sami to settle the venture.
parts.answer: $29,800 (Sami's goods 27,600 + his share 2,200). Ruhi keeps 1,100, which is her own share.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method (27,600 + 2,200), 1 mark for 29,800.

practice.stem: Two venturers each record their own joint venture transactions in their own books. At the end of the venture a memorandum joint venture account is prepared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer: It brings together the transactions of all venturers to calculate the profit or loss of the whole venture, so that it can be shared in the agreed ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: combines all venturers' transactions. 1 mark: to find total profit/loss to be shared.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the memorandum joint venture account is not part of the double-entry system.
parts.answer: Each transaction has already been recorded in a venturer's own 'Joint venture with …' account; the memorandum account is a working statement prepared from copies of those records, so no entries are posted from it.
parts.working: 1 mark: transactions already recorded in venturers' own books. 1 mark: it is only a statement/memorandum, no double entry.

practice.stem: Joint venture transactions may be recorded either in a separate set of books with a joint bank account, or in each venturer's own books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of keeping a separate set of books with a joint bank account.
parts.answer: Advantage: all receipts and payments pass through one account, so the venture's records are complete and transparent and the profit is easy to calculate. Disadvantage: it costs more time and money to open an account and keep extra books, which may not be worthwhile for a small, short venture.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for an advantage (identify + explain) and up to 2 marks for a disadvantage (identify + explain).

practice.stem: At 31 December 2025, Amjad's joint venture with Bushra had been completed, but Bushra had not yet paid Amjad the $12,400 owed to him. Amjad's share of the venture profit was $5,100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how the $5,100 should be shown in Amjad's statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer: As income: 'share of profit on joint venture' $5,100.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the $12,400 should be shown in Amjad's statement of financial position at 31 December 2025, and explain why.
parts.answer: As a current asset (other receivable – amount due from Bushra), because it is money owed to Amjad that he expects to receive within a year.
parts.working: 1 mark: current asset/receivable. 1 mark: reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the accounting concept that requires the profit to be recognised in 2025 even though the cash has not been received.
parts.answer: Accruals (matching) concept.
parts.working: B1 accruals (also accept realisation).

practice.stem: Ejaz and Fatima share joint venture profits equally. Ejaz sent goods from his own inventory costing $24,000 and paid freight of $1,100. He sold some of the goods for $18,000. Fatima paid selling expenses of $2,500 and sold the rest of the goods for $22,000. The venture was then completed and settled in cash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the 'Joint venture with Fatima' account in Ejaz's books, including the settlement.
parts.answer:
Joint venture with Fatima (Ejaz's books)       $

                                          31,300

                                          31,300

practice.stem: Ghulam and Hassan bought and resold used cars in Rawalpindi as a joint venture, sharing profits 2:1. Ghulam bought the cars for $45,000 and paid repairs of $3,600. Hassan paid advertising of $1,200 and registration fees of $900, and sold all the cars for $58,500. The venture made a profit of $7,800 and was settled in cash.

                                            53,800

                                            53,800

practice.stem: Mehdi and Nida ran a summer camp in Murree as a joint venture, sharing profits equally. They opened a joint bank account: Mehdi paid in $25,000 and Nida $15,000. From the joint bank account they paid: venue hire $18,000; food $12,500; staff $7,300; transport $4,200. Camp fees of $52,000 were paid into the account. At the end, the venturers were paid what was due to them and the account was closed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the joint bank account.
parts.answer:
Joint bank account          $
Dr
Mehdi – capital        25,000
Nida – capital         15,000
Camp fees              52,000
                       92,000

Transport               4,200
Mehdi – final payment  30,000
Nida – final payment   20,000
                       92,000
parts.working: B1 capital paid in; B1 fees and payments; B1 final payments 30,000 and 20,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the amounts paid to Mehdi and Nida at the end are different although they share profit equally.
parts.answer: Each receives his or her own capital back plus a $5,000 share of profit; Mehdi contributed $10,000 more capital, so he receives $30,000 and Nida $20,000.
parts.working: 1 mark: capital returned plus share. 1 mark: figures.

practice.stem: Usman and Vikram organised a one-night music concert in Dubai as a joint venture, sharing profits 3:2. Usman paid venue hire of $28,000 and sound equipment hire of $6,500, and received all ticket sales of $92,000. Vikram paid the artist's fee of $40,000 and advertising of $5,500, and received sponsorship of $8,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer:
Memorandum joint venture account        $
Dr
Venue hire (Usman)                 28,000
Sound equipment hire (Usman)        6,500
Artist fee (Vikram)                40,000
Advertising (Vikram)                5,500
Share of profit – Usman            12,000
Share of profit – Vikram            8,000
                                  100,000
Cr
Ticket sales (Usman)               92,000
Sponsorship (Vikram)                8,000
                                  100,000
parts.working: B1 costs 80,000; B1 income 100,000; B1 profit 20,000; B1 shares 12,000 / 8,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the 'Joint venture with Vikram' account in Usman's books, including the settlement.
parts.answer:
Joint venture with Vikram (Usman's books)       $
Dr
Venue hire (Usman)                         28,000
Sound equipment hire (Usman)                6,500

parts.working: B1 costs and share of profit debited; B1 ticket sales credited; B1 cash paid to Vikram 45,500.

practice.stem: Xenia (Dubai) and Yasir (Karachi) imported a consignment of dates as a joint venture, sharing profits and losses equally. Xenia bought the dates for $32,000 and paid shipping of $4,400. Yasir paid customs duty of $2,100 and warehousing of $1,500. Part of the shipment was damaged and Yasir sold all the dates for only $36,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer:
Memorandum joint venture account       $
Dr
Purchase of dates (Xenia)         32,000
Shipping (Xenia)                   4,400
Customs duty (Yasir)               2,100
Warehousing (Yasir)                1,500
                                  40,000
Cr
Sales (Yasir)                     36,800
Loss – Xenia                       1,600
Loss – Yasir                       1,600
                                  40,000
parts.working: B1 costs 40,000; B1 sales; B1 loss 3,200 shown on credit side; B1 shared 1,600 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the 'Joint venture with Xenia' account in Yasir's books, including the settlement.
parts.answer:
Joint venture with Xenia (Yasir's books)       $
Dr
Customs duty (Yasir)                       2,100
Warehousing (Yasir)                        1,500

                                          38,400
parts.working: B1 customs and warehousing debited; B1 sales and share of loss 1,600 credited; B1 cash paid to Xenia 34,800.

practice.stem: Daud and Eman share joint venture profits 3:2. Daud supplied goods from his own inventory at cost, $30,000. Eman paid delivery costs of $1,700 and sold all the goods on credit for $45,000. She allowed cash discounts of $600, and one customer owing $1,500 became bankrupt and paid nothing. Eman collected the rest of the money.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer:
Memorandum joint venture account       $
Dr
Goods supplied (Daud)             30,000
Delivery (Eman)                    1,700
Discounts allowed (Eman)             600
Irrecoverable debt (Eman)          1,500
Share of profit – Daud             6,720
Share of profit – Eman             4,480
                                  45,000
Cr
Sales (Eman)                      45,000
                                  45,000
parts.working: B1 goods and delivery; B1 discount and irrecoverable debt debited; B1 profit 11,200; B1 shares 6,720 / 4,480.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount Eman must pay Daud in settlement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the irrecoverable debt is charged to the joint venture rather than borne by Eman alone.
parts.answer: The sale was made on behalf of the venture, so the risk of non-payment is a cost of the venture shared by both venturers, unless the agreement makes Eman responsible (e.g. through a del credere commission).
parts.working: 1 mark: sale made for the joint venture. 1 mark: losses shared in agreed ratio unless agreement says otherwise.

practice.stem: Jamal and Kinza share joint venture profits 2:1. Jamal bought goods for $33,000 and sent Kinza a cash advance of $8,000 to help her pay the venture's expenses. Kinza paid expenses of $6,700 and sold all the goods for $52,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the 'Joint venture with Kinza' account in Jamal's books, including the settlement.
parts.answer:
Joint venture with Kinza (Jamal's books)       $
Dr
Goods                                     33,000
Bank – advance to Kinza                    8,000
Share of profit                            8,200
                                          49,200
Cr
Bank – received from Kinza                49,200
                                          49,200
parts.working: B1 goods and advance debited; B1 share of profit 8,200; B1 cash received from Kinza 49,200.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the $8,000 advance does not appear in the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer: The advance is only a transfer of cash between the two venturers; it is not income or a cost of the venture, so it does not affect the profit. It is cancelled out in the settlement.
parts.working: 1 mark: transfer between venturers. 1 mark: no effect on profit.

practice.stem: Naveed (Peshawar) and Lubna (Dubai) agree a joint venture to import perfume. Profits are shared 3:2 (Naveed : Lubna). Naveed paid $48,000 for the perfume and $1,500 for shipping. Lubna sold all the perfume for $62,000 and paid $2,700 customs duty out of the sales money.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer: Debit side: goods 48,000; shipping 1,500; customs duty 2,700; profit share Naveed 5,880; profit share Lubna 3,920 (total 62,000). Credit side: sales 62,000.
parts.working: 1 mark each for the costs, 1 mark for the profit shares, 1 mark for totals agreeing at 62,000, 1 mark for sales on the credit side. Profit 9,800 = 62,000 − 48,000 − 1,500 − 2,700.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount Lubna must pay Naveed to settle the venture, and state how much cash Lubna keeps.
parts.answer: Lubna pays Naveed $55,380 (his costs 49,500 + profit share 5,880). Lubna keeps $3,920, her own profit share.
parts.working: 1 mark for profit 9,800 and shares (5,880 and 3,920), 1 mark for 55,380, 1 mark for 3,920 kept (62,000 − 2,700 − 55,380).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the customs duty is charged to the joint venture rather than to Lubna's own account.
parts.answer: Customs duty is a cost of carrying out this venture, so it reduces the profit both venturers share. Charging it to Lubna alone would give her an unfair advantage or disadvantage.
parts.working: 1 mark for it being a venture cost, 1 mark for it reducing the shared profit.

practice.stem: Maryam (Karachi) and Kashan (Dubai) agree a joint venture to sell 2,000 boxes of Eid chocolates. Maryam supplied the chocolates, costing $52,000, and paid freight of $1,450. Kashan sold all the boxes for $85,000 cash. He keeps 4% of sales as his commission, deducted before profit is shared. The rest of the profit is shared 3:2 (Maryam : Kashan).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the commission, the profit after commission, and each venturer's share of the profit.
parts.working: 1 mark for commission 3,400, 1 mark for profit 28,150, 1 mark for the two shares 16,890 and 11,260.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount Kashan must pay Maryam, and the total cash Kashan keeps for himself.
parts.answer: Kashan pays Maryam $70,340 (goods 52,000 + freight 1,450 + share 16,890). Kashan keeps $14,660 (commission 3,400 + his share 11,260).
parts.working: 1 mark for 53,450 + 16,890, 1 mark for 70,340, 1 mark for 85,000 − 70,340 = 14,660 which equals commission plus share.

practice.stem: Farooq and Hina run a joint venture through a joint bank account, with a separate set of books. Farooq paid $30,000 into the account and Hina paid $18,000. Goods costing $36,000 were paid from the bank account. Hina sold all the goods for $52,000, which was paid into the bank account. Expenses of $4,250 were paid from the bank account. Profits are shared 3:2 (Farooq : Hina).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance on the joint bank account at the end of the venture.
parts.working: 1 mark for the receipts (30,000 + 18,000 + 52,000), 1 mark for 59,750 after payments of 36,000 and 4,250.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit and each venturer's share of it.
parts.working: 1 mark for profit, 1 mark for Farooq's share, 1 mark for Hina's share.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amount each venturer takes out of the joint bank account at the end.
parts.working: 1 mark for each: capital paid in plus profit share. The totals add to the balance in part (a).

practice.stem: Imtiaz manages a joint venture that sells garden furniture from Faisalabad. Before profit is shared, the venture pays Imtiaz a fixed management fee of $5,000. Sales were $74,000 and other costs were $46,800. The profit after the fee is shared equally between Imtiaz and Shabana.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit after the management fee.
parts.working: 1 mark for deducting the fee and other costs, 1 mark for 22,200.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Shabana's share of the profit and Imtiaz's total return from the venture.
parts.answer: Shabana $11,100. Imtiaz receives $16,100 in total (fee 5,000 + share 11,100).
parts.working: 1 mark for each share, 1 mark for the total including the fee.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the fixed fee is charged before the profit is shared.
parts.answer: The fee is a cost of running the venture, so it is deducted to find the profit. It is not a share of profit, so it is paid whatever the profit is.
parts.working: 1 mark: it is a cost of the venture. 1 mark: it is paid regardless of profit, so it is not a profit share.

practice.stem: Three venturers, Nadia, Oscar and Rehan, share profits in the ratio 4:3:3. Oscar paid for goods costing $70,000. Rehan paid expenses of $6,000 from his own money. Nadia collected all sales of $120,000 and paid none of the costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.
parts.working: Sales 120,000 less costs 76,000 = 44,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's share of the profit.
parts.working: 1 mark for the ratio total of 10 parts, 1 mark for the three shares.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amounts Nadia must pay Oscar and Rehan, and the cash Nadia keeps.
parts.working: 1 mark for Oscar's amount, 1 mark for Rehan's amount, 1 mark for the 17,600 retained (120,000 − 83,200 − 19,200).

practice.stem: Hafsa lends her joint venture $40,000 for nine months at interest of 6% a year. The interest is an expense of the venture. Profit before interest is $20,000. After the interest is charged, the remaining profit is shared equally by Hafsa and Ibrahim. Hafsa's advance is repaid in full at the end of the venture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest charged to the venture.
parts.working: Interest for nine months is 40,000 × 6% × 9 ÷ 12 = 1,800. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for 1,800.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit after interest and each venturer's share of it.
parts.answer: Profit after interest $18,200; each venturer's share $9,100.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total Hafsa receives from the venture in interest and profit share, excluding repayment of her advance.
parts.answer: $10,900 (interest 1,800 + profit share 9,100).
parts.working: 1 mark for adding interest and share, 1 mark for 10,900. The advance of $40,000 is repaid separately and is not income.

practice.stem: In a joint venture to sell mobile phone accessories, Mahnoor receives 40% of the profit and Adeel receives 60%. Mahnoor's share of the profit is $4,160. Total sales were $58,000. Assume there were no other income items.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total profit on the joint venture.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for 10,400.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total costs of the venture.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the costs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate Adeel's share of the profit.

practice.stem: Sara and Idris plan to make a short documentary film in Karachi. The project will last four months and needs about $60,000 of funds, which they will put in equally. They have worked together before and trust each other, but they are worried about personal liability if the film makes a loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise two entrepreneurs, Sara and Idris, whether they should run a four-month film shoot in Karachi as a joint venture or through a new limited company. Justify your advice.
parts.answer: Recommend a joint venture if the project is short, the partners trust each other, and the risk is small. Content points: a joint venture has no separate legal identity and the venturers share profits and losses (and liability) directly; it ends with the project and needs no company registration or annual filing; accounts are kept as a memorandum account and each partner's books. A company has its own legal identity and limited liability for shareholders; it needs registration, filing and annual accounts, which cost money and time; it suits long or large projects. Conclude with a clear recommendation linked to the facts given.
parts.working: 1 mark for each relevant point up to 5 for the comparison (joint venture: no separate entity, shared liability, short life and low admin; company: separate entity, limited liability, cost and filing). 2 marks for a clear recommendation supported by the facts of the project.

practice.stem: Ramsha and Hassan run a joint venture importing table lamps and share profits equally. Ramsha bought goods for $35,000. She returned goods costing $1,800 to the supplier for a full refund. Hassan sold the remaining goods for $44,000 and paid $2,700 of expenses from the sales money.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture and each venturer's share of it.
parts.working: 1 mark for the purchases net of return (33,200), 1 mark for profit 8,100, 1 mark for 4,050 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the goods returned to the supplier are treated in the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer: The returned goods reduce the cost of the venture, because they are no longer a cost once returned for a refund. They are deducted from the costs in the memorandum account, so profit is higher than if they had been kept as costs.
parts.working: 1 mark for reducing the cost of goods; 1 mark for the effect on profit or the logic of the refund.

practice.stem: Nafees supplied goods costing $42,000 to a joint venture with Tabassum. Nafees sold the goods in Karachi and collected $38,000. Tabassum sold the goods in Lahore and collected $27,500. From these takings she paid $1,400 of stall costs and sent the remaining $26,100 to Nafees. Profits are shared equally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.
parts.working: 1 mark for total sales of 65,500 less costs of 43,400, 1 mark for profit 22,100.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount Nafees must pay Tabassum in settlement.
parts.answer: Nafees pays Tabassum $11,050, her share of profit. Nafees keeps $53,050 (his costs 42,000 + his share 11,050).
parts.working: 1 mark for each venturer's share of 11,050. 1 mark for Nafees holding 64,100 (38,000 + 26,100). 1 mark for the settlement of 11,050, calculated as 64,100 − 53,050.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Tabassum's $1,400 of expenses is not added to the amount Nafees pays her.
parts.answer: Tabassum paid the $1,400 from the Lahore sales money before remitting the balance. Her expenses have already been deducted from the cash she sent, so only her share of profit is still due to her.
parts.working: 1 mark for the expenses already being deducted from the cash remitted, 1 mark for only the profit share remaining due.

practice.stem:
Haider Builders, Lahore, wants to bid for a bridge contract worth $2,400,000.
Option 1: bid alone. Haider would have to hire specialist equipment and engineers; total costs are estimated at $2,280,000.
Option 2: form a joint venture with a foreign engineering company. Total costs of the venture are estimated at $1,950,000 and Haider would receive 40% of the profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Haider's expected profit under each option.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Haider Builders which option to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For the joint venture: higher expected profit ($60,000 more); the foreign partner's expertise lowers the risk of cost overruns and delays; Haider gains experience for future bridge contracts; less finance needed. Against: Haider loses control over decisions; profit depends on the partner's performance; disputes over sharing; Haider builds less of its own reputation. Bidding alone keeps all profit but the margin is only 5% of contract value, so a small overrun would cause a loss. Decision: choose the joint venture, provided a clear written agreement sets out duties, profit sharing and settlement.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for the joint venture; up to 2 marks for points against / for bidding alone; 1 mark for use of the calculated figures (e.g. 60,000 difference, 5% margin); 1 mark for a justified decision.

practice.stem: Rashid and Tahir share joint venture profits equally. At the end of their venture in garden furniture, unsold goods that cost $6,000 are taken over by Rashid at an agreed value of $4,000, their net realisable value. Before this item, the memorandum joint venture account showed a profit of $15,000 (all goods counted as sold or taken over at cost).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revised joint venture profit.
parts.working: Taking over at 4,000 rather than cost 6,000 reduces the credit by 2,000 (M1); 15,000 − 2,000 = 13,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's share of the revised profit.
parts.answer: $6,500 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether the goods should be taken over at net realisable value rather than cost.
parts.answer: Prudence: goods should not be valued above what they can be sold for, so $4,000 is appropriate if NRV is reliable. However, Rashid benefits if he later sells them for more, so the value must be agreed fairly and independently; Tahir bears half the $2,000 reduction. Conclusion: NRV is acceptable if it is agreed by both venturers or set by an independent valuation.
parts.working: 1 mark: prudence / IAS 2 lower of cost and NRV. 1 mark: conflict of interest – taker benefits from low value. 1 mark: conclusion/agreement needed.

practice.stem:
Iqbal and Javeria entered a joint venture to make and sell embroidered garments in Faisalabad. Profits after commission are shared Iqbal 3, Javeria 1.
Iqbal bought fabric for $40,000 and paid dyeing costs of $6,000.
Javeria paid stitching costs of $9,000 and sold garments for $68,000. She is entitled to a commission of 5% on her sales.
At the end of the venture Iqbal took over the unsold garments at an agreed value of $4,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer:
Memorandum joint venture account         $
Dr
Fabric (Iqbal)                      40,000
Dyeing (Iqbal)                       6,000
Stitching (Javeria)                  9,000
Commission – Javeria (5% × 68,000)   3,400
Share of profit – Iqbal             10,575
Share of profit – Javeria            3,525
                                    72,500
Cr
Sales (Javeria)                     68,000
Unsold garments taken over (Iqbal)   4,500
                                    72,500
parts.working: B1 costs; B1 commission 3,400 debited; B1 sales and goods taken over credited; B1 profit 14,100; B1 shares 10,575 / 3,525.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount paid in settlement and state who pays whom.
parts.answer: Javeria pays Iqbal $52,075.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Javeria's commission is charged before the profit is shared.
parts.answer: The commission rewards Javeria for the extra work of selling; it is a cost of the venture, so it is deducted to find the profit that both share.

practice.stem:
Omer and Parveen set up a joint venture to sell solar panels in rural Sindh, sharing profits 3:2. They opened a joint bank account into which Omer paid $30,000 and Parveen $20,000.
From the joint bank account: a generator for the venture was bought for $12,000; solar panels were bought for $48,000; wages of $6,000 were paid. Sales of $70,000 were banked.
At the end of the venture Omer took over the generator at an agreed value of $9,000 and Parveen took over the unsold panels at $5,500. The bank balance was then paid out to the venturers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the joint venture account (in the separate set of books) showing the profit and its division.
parts.answer:
Joint venture account             $
Dr
Generator                    12,000
Solar panels                 48,000
Wages                         6,000
Profit – Omer (3/5)          11,100
Profit – Parveen (2/5)        7,400
                             84,500
Cr
Sales                        70,000
Generator taken over – Omer   9,000
Panels taken over – Parveen   5,500
                             84,500
parts.working: B1 costs debited; B1 sales and items taken over credited; B1 profit 18,500; B1 shares 11,100 / 7,400.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount paid from the joint bank account to each venturer at the end.
parts.answer: Omer $32,100; Parveen $21,900.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the generator was taken over at less than its cost.
parts.answer: It had been used during the venture and had lost value (depreciation/wear).

practice.stem:
Qadir and Rizwan built a block of flats in Islamabad as a joint venture. They agreed that each venturer would receive interest at 10% per annum on money he contributed, from the date of payment until the venture ended on 31 December 2025, and that the remaining profit would be shared equally.
Qadir paid $120,000 for the land on 1 January 2025. Rizwan paid $180,000 for construction on 1 April 2025. On 31 December 2025 all the flats were sold and Qadir received the proceeds of $360,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest due to each venturer.
parts.answer: Qadir $12,000; Rizwan $13,500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit to be shared and each venturer's share.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the settlement payment and state who pays whom.
parts.answer: Qadir pays Rizwan $210,750.
parts.working: Rizwan is due 180,000 + 13,500 + 17,250 = 210,750 (M1); Qadir holds the proceeds and pays him (A1).

practice.stem: Sohail and Tania share joint venture profits equally. Sohail's 'Joint venture with Tania' account showed: goods supplied $26,000; expenses paid by Sohail $3,400; sales made by Sohail $15,000; his share of the profit (figure missing); cash received from Tania in settlement $22,600. Tania paid expenses of $4,800 and made all the other sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Sohail's share of the profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total joint venture profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the value of the sales made by Tania.

practice.stem:
Zahid, Amna and Basit traded in carved wooden furniture from Chiniot as a joint venture, sharing profits 2:2:1.
Zahid bought furniture for $50,000.
Amna paid polishing costs of $6,000 and showroom rent of $4,500, and sold furniture for $46,000.
Basit paid advertising of $3,500 and sold furniture for $34,000.
Zahid took over the remaining furniture at an agreed value of $2,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer:
Memorandum joint venture account          $
Dr
Furniture (Zahid)                    50,000
Polishing (Amna)                      6,000
Showroom rent (Amna)                  4,500

parts.label: b

parts.answer:

practice.stem: Farhan and Ghazal ran wedding catering for one season in Lahore as a joint venture, sharing profits equally. Farhan bought catering equipment for the venture for $24,000 and received all catering fees of $96,000. Ghazal paid for food, $38,000, and staff wages, $15,000. At the end of the season Ghazal took over the equipment at an agreed value of $17,500.

parts.text: Prepare the memorandum joint venture account.

practice.stem: Hamza and Irum entered a joint venture to trade in surgical instruments from Sialkot, sharing the profit after commissions equally. Irum arranged and paid for purchases of $50,000 and receives 4% commission on purchases. Hamza paid shipping and insurance of $3,000, sold all the instruments for $72,000 and receives 6% commission on sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the commission due to each venturer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit to be shared and each venturer's share.
parts.answer: Profit $12,680; $6,340 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's total return from the venture.
parts.working: Commission + share (B1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the settlement payment and state who pays whom.
parts.answer: Hamza pays Irum $58,340.
parts.working: Irum due 50,000 + 2,000 + 6,340 = 58,340 (M1); Hamza holds the sales proceeds and pays her (A1).

practice.stem:
Latif, a football maker in Sialkot, and Mason, a sports retailer in Manchester, agreed a joint venture for one shipment of match footballs. Profits after commission are shared Latif 3, Mason 2.

Mason paid import duty of $3,800 and warehouse charges of $1,600. He sold two-thirds of the footballs for $54,000, on which he receives a commission of 5%. He took over the remaining footballs at an agreed value of $18,500.

parts.answer: He provided most of the finance/goods ($43,200 of costs) and so bore more risk.

practice.stem: Sherwani and Rafay agree a joint venture to run a wedding decoration service in Peshawar for one season. Sherwani manages the venture and receives a bonus equal to 10% of the profit before bonus. The remaining profit is shared equally. Profit before bonus is $50,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the bonus paid to Sherwani.
parts.working: Bonus is 10% of profit before bonus: 50,000 × 10% = 5,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's total return from the venture.
parts.working: 1 mark for the remaining profit 45,000, 1 mark for Sherwani's total 27,500, 1 mark for Rafay's 22,500.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the bonus is calculated on profit before the bonus, rather than on profit after it.
parts.answer: Calculating on profit after bonus would be circular, since the bonus itself reduces that profit. Using profit before bonus gives a clear figure that is fixed before the profit is shared.
parts.working: 1 mark for avoiding circularity (the bonus would reduce its own base). 1 mark for a clear, fixed figure.

practice.stem: Shehzad paid $62,000 for all the goods in a joint venture with Ghazal, and paid no other costs. Ghazal sold goods for cash of $30,000 and on credit for $50,000. Of the credit sales, $5,000 proved irrecoverable and the rest was collected in cash. Ghazal paid the venture's expenses of $4,400 out of cash collected. At the end, Ghazal took over unsold goods that cost $5,000 at an agreed value of $3,000. Profit is shared equally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.
parts.answer: $11,600 (sales 80,000 − irrecoverable 5,000 + goods taken over 3,000 − costs 62,000 − expenses 4,400)
parts.working: 1 mark for sales net of irrecoverable debts (75,000), 1 mark for adding the goods taken over at agreed value (78,000), 1 mark for total costs of 66,400, 1 mark for the profit of 11,600.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cash Ghazal must pay Shehzad, and the cash Ghazal keeps for herself.
parts.answer: Ghazal pays Shehzad $67,800 (costs 62,000 + share 5,800). Ghazal keeps $2,800 cash, which together with the goods (3,000) gives her share of 5,800.
parts.working: 1 mark for each venturer's share of 5,800, 1 mark for the 67,800 payment, 1 mark for cash of 70,600 (75,000 − 4,400) less 67,800 = 2,800.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the unsold goods are credited at their agreed value of $3,000 and not at their cost of $5,000.
parts.answer: The agreed value is the amount the venturer takes the goods over at, and it is the value received by the venture. The goods have lost value, so cost would overstate what the venture receives.
parts.working: 1 mark for the agreed value being what is received. 1 mark for the reason, linked to net realisable value or the reduction in value.

practice.stem: Gul and Noor run a joint venture to trade in rugs for two seasons. They agreed that profits are shared 3:1 (Gul : Noor), but that losses are shared equally. In season 1 the venture made a profit of $28,000. In season 2 it made a loss of $9,600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Gul's and Noor's shares of the season 1 profit.
parts.working: 1 mark for the ratio total of 4 parts, 1 mark for both shares.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's share of the season 2 loss.
parts.working: 1 mark for the knowledge that losses are shared equally, 1 mark for 4,800 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the overall net amount each venturer has gained or lost over the two seasons.
parts.working: 1 mark for the net figures; 1 mark for the total of 18,400 matching profit less loss (28,000 − 9,600).

practice.stem: Zaheer supplied goods costing $44,000 to a joint venture with Thuraya. Thuraya sold all the goods for $70,000. At the year end she had collected $42,000 in cash, and $28,000 was still owed by customers. She had paid expenses of $3,000 from the cash she collected. Profits are shared equally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.
parts.working: 1 mark for the sales less goods and expenses, 1 mark for 23,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cash Thuraya can pay Zaheer immediately.
parts.working: 1 mark for the cash collected, 1 mark for deducting the expenses paid from cash.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amount Thuraya still owes Zaheer after this payment.
