parts.answer: $16,500 (Zaheer's goods 44,000 + share 11,500 − 39,000 paid)
parts.working: 1 mark for Zaheer's total entitlement 55,500, 1 mark for the balance 16,500.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the full $70,000 of sales is included in the memorandum account even though $28,000 is still owed by customers.
parts.answer: The sales were made in the venture, so they are part of its result. The amounts owed are an asset of the venture and are settled when collected; any bad debts would be charged later.
parts.working: 1 mark for the sales being made in the venture, 1 mark for the outstanding debtors being a venture asset that may later be partly irrecoverable.

practice.stem: Irfan supplied goods costing $36,000 to a joint venture with Rafiq. Rafiq sold all the goods, paid expenses of $2,900 from the sales money, and then paid Irfan $41,600 in full settlement. Profits are shared 60% to Rafiq and 40% to Irfan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.
parts.working: 1 mark for the 5,600 share of profit to Irfan, 1 mark for profit 14,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total sales of the joint venture.
parts.answer: $52,900 (profit 14,000 + goods 36,000 + expenses 2,900)
parts.working: 1 mark for adding costs and profit, 1 mark for 52,900.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit share retained by Rafiq, and the cash he holds at the end before paying Irfan.
parts.answer: Rafiq's share is $8,400 (60% of 14,000). His cash before settlement is $52,900 − 2,900 = $50,000, of which he keeps $8,400.
parts.working: 1 mark for 8,400, 1 mark for the 8,400 retained (50,000 − 41,600).

practice.stem: A joint venture will cost $88,000 to make 500 handmade hampers. All the hampers will be sold through a commission agent who is paid 5% of sales, deducted before profit is shared. The venturers want a profit of exactly 15% of sales. Profit is shared 2:1 between Imtiaz and Lubna.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sales value needed for the venture to achieve a profit of 15% of sales.
parts.answer: $110,000. Profit is sales − commission (5% of sales) − costs 88,000 = 15% of sales, so 0.80 × sales = 88,000.
parts.working: 1 mark for setting up the equation with commission, 1 mark for 0.80 × sales = 88,000, 1 mark for sales of 110,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the commission and the profit at this level of sales.
parts.working: 1 mark for commission, 1 mark for profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate Imtiaz's and Lubna's shares of the profit, which are shared 2:1.
parts.answer: Imtiaz $11,000; Lubna $5,500.
parts.working: 1 mark for Imtiaz's 2/3, 1 mark for Lubna's 1/3.

practice.stem: Hina contributed $40,000 to a joint venture for 6 months. Shahid contributed $30,000 for the full 12-month venture. The profit of $38,000 is to be shared in the ratio of money contributed multiplied by the number of months.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio in which profit should be shared, using money contributed multiplied by months.
parts.answer: Hina 240,000 : Shahid 360,000, which simplifies to 2:3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's share of the profit of $38,000.
parts.working: 1 mark for Hina's 2/5 share, 1 mark for Shahid's 3/5 share.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this method is fairer to Shahid than sharing profit in the ratio of the money contributed alone.
parts.answer: Shahid's capital was at risk for twice as long. Sharing by money alone would give Hina 40/70 (about 57%) of the profit, which ignores that her money was in the venture for half the time.
parts.working: 1 mark for the time element rewarding longer investment. 1 mark for the comparison (money alone would give Hina about 57%).

practice.stem: Ahsan and Chaudhry run a joint venture to import school bags. Chaudhry supplied bags costing $52,000 and paid no other costs. Ahsan sold all the bags for $96,000 and paid other expenses of $4,000 out of the sales money. Before profit is shared, Ahsan receives a commission equal to 20% of the profit before commission. The rest is shared equally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the commission Ahsan receives.
parts.answer: $8,000 (20% of profit before commission 40,000).
parts.working: 1 mark for profit before commission 40,000 (96,000 − 52,000 − 4,000), 1 mark for 8,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount Ahsan pays Chaudhry in settlement, and the total cash Ahsan keeps.
parts.answer: Ahsan pays Chaudhry $68,000 (goods 52,000 + share 16,000). Ahsan keeps $24,000 (commission 8,000 + share 16,000).
parts.working: 1 mark for the remaining profit 32,000 and each share 16,000, 1 mark for 68,000, 1 mark for 92,000 − 68,000 = 24,000 kept.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why a venturer might prefer commission on profit to commission on sales.
parts.answer: Commission on profit rewards the venturer only if the venture earns a profit, so the incentive is linked to results. Commission on sales can be paid even when the venture makes a loss.
parts.working: 1 mark for the link to profit, 1 mark for the contrast with sales commission.

practice.stem: A joint venture takes over unsold goods at an agreed value of $12,000. Their net realisable value is $7,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether the memorandum joint venture account gives a fair view of the profit when unsold goods are taken over at an agreed value above their net realisable value.
parts.answer: Not a fair view. Goods taken over at 12,000 but worth 7,500 overstate profit by 4,500, and the overstatement is shared between the venturers. Prudence and the fair view point to net realisable value (7,500). However, the agreed value is a genuine agreement between venturers, and it may be accepted if documented and the recipient pays the agreed price. Balanced conclusion: profit should be reported at the lower value unless the agreement is clear and the valuation is reasonable.
parts.working: 1–2 marks: identifies the valuation issue. 3–4 marks: explains the effect (profit overstated by 4,500, shared unfairly). 5–6 marks: evaluates both sides and reaches a supported conclusion, referring to prudence or net realisable value.

practice.stem: Ayaz and Dania have two separate joint ventures with the same people. In JV1, Ayaz owes Dania $6,400 for goods she supplied. In JV2, Dania owes Ayaz $4,150 from the sale of imported rugs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net amount and state who pays whom.
parts.working: 1 mark for the net figure, 1 mark for the direction of payment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each joint venture must be recorded and settled separately, even though the same people are involved.
parts.answer: Each venture has its own profit or loss and its own memorandum account, so the results cannot be combined. Each venture's share of profit must be calculated from its own transactions.
parts.working: 1 mark for each venture having its own profit or loss. 1 mark for the need to calculate each venture's results separately.

practice.stem: Karakoram Foods Limited has 4,000 shareholders. The company is run by a board of five directors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term stewardship in the context of a limited company.
parts.answer: Stewardship is the responsibility of the directors to look after the company's resources (assets) properly on behalf of the shareholders who own it, and to account to them for how those resources have been used.
parts.working: 1 mark: directors manage/safeguard resources for shareholders; 1 mark: accountability/reporting to owners.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which directors demonstrate good stewardship.
parts.answer: Any two: keeping proper accounting records; preparing annual financial statements that give a true and fair view; safeguarding assets and preventing fraud through internal controls; having the statements audited and presenting them at the annual general meeting; using resources efficiently in shareholders' interests.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between an internal auditor and an external auditor.
parts.answer: Any two: appointment — internal auditor is an employee appointed by management, external auditor is independent and appointed by the shareholders; reporting — internal auditor reports to the directors/audit committee, external auditor reports to the shareholders; purpose — internal audit reviews systems, controls and efficiency for management, external audit gives an opinion on whether the statements give a true and fair view; legal requirement — external audit is required by law for most companies, internal audit is optional; qualification/independence — external auditor must be a registered, independent accountant.
parts.working: 2 marks per difference (both sides compared).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three statutory rights of a company's external auditor.
parts.answer: Any three: right of access at all times to the company's books, records and vouchers; right to require information and explanations from directors and officers; right to receive notice of and attend general meetings; right to speak at general meetings on matters concerning them as auditor; right to make written representations if they are to be removed or not reappointed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the meaning of the phrase 'a true and fair view'.
parts.answer: The financial statements are free from material misstatement and fairly present the company's financial performance and position, prepared in accordance with accounting standards and the law. It does not mean that every figure is exactly correct.
parts.working: 1 mark: free from material misstatement / faithfully presented; 1 mark: in accordance with standards / not absolute accuracy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State who is responsible for preparing a company's financial statements.
parts.answer: The directors (not the auditors).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State who appoints the external auditors of a limited company, and to whom they report.
parts.answer: They are appointed by the shareholders (usually at the annual general meeting) and report to the shareholders.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important that the external auditor is independent of the directors.
parts.answer: The auditor checks the statements prepared by the directors; if not independent they might be influenced to accept misstatements, so shareholders could not rely on the opinion.
parts.working: 1 mark: checking directors' work / objective opinion; 1 mark: shareholders' reliance/confidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four items normally included in an external auditor's report.
parts.answer: Any four: title and addressee (the shareholders); the auditor's opinion; basis for opinion (statement that the audit was done under auditing standards and the auditor is independent); key audit matters (for listed companies); material uncertainty related to going concern, if any; responsibilities of the directors for the financial statements; responsibilities of the auditor; auditor's name, signature, address and date.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two threats to the independence of an external auditor.
parts.answer: Self-interest: e.g. the auditor owns shares in the client or depends heavily on its fees, so may avoid a qualified opinion. Self-review: the audit firm also prepares the accounts it audits. Familiarity: a long relationship or family ties with directors. Intimidation: directors threaten to remove the auditor. Advocacy: the auditor promotes the client's interests.
parts.working: 2 marks each: threat named + example/explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Other than shareholders, name two groups who rely on a company's audited financial statements, and explain why each relies on the audit.
parts.answer: Any two: banks/lenders — deciding whether to lend and checking loan covenants, need assurance figures are reliable; suppliers — deciding whether to give credit; tax authorities — assessing tax payable; potential investors — deciding whether to buy shares; employees/trade unions — job security and pay negotiations; government/regulators.
parts.working: 1 mark each group; 1 mark each reason linked to reliability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how publishing an audited annual report helps the directors carry out their stewardship responsibility.
parts.answer: The annual report shows shareholders how the directors have used the company's resources and what results they achieved; the audit gives independent assurance that this account is true and fair; shareholders can then question directors and vote on their reappointment at the AGM, so the directors are held accountable.
parts.working: 1 mark: reports use of resources/results; 1 mark: independent assurance; 1 mark: accountability (AGM/votes).

practice.stem:
During the audit of Chitral Tea Limited, the auditor identified the following errors in the draft statement of financial position, which shows net assets of $2,460,000:
• Damaged inventory not yet written down to net realisable value: effect on net assets −$36,000
• Accrued audit fee not recorded: effect on net assets −$18,000
• Prepaid rent omitted: effect on net assets +$12,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected net assets of the company.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The directors agree to make all the corrections. State the type of audit opinion that is likely to be given and explain why.
parts.answer: An unmodified opinion: once the misstatements have been corrected, the statements give a true and fair view in all material respects, so there is no reason to modify the opinion.
parts.working: 1 mark unmodified; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'materiality' in an audit.
parts.answer: A misstatement is material if its omission or misstatement could influence the economic decisions of users of the financial statements.
parts.working: 1 mark for the idea that users' decisions could be influenced; 1 mark for stating that the auditor judges size or nature against a threshold.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benchmark an auditor might use to set a materiality threshold.
parts.answer: Profit before tax (or revenue, total assets, net assets).
parts.working: 1 mark for any one benchmark.

practice.stem: Mahnoor Traders Limited has trade receivables of $264,000 at its year end, owed by 180 customer accounts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three audit procedures the external auditor could use to obtain evidence that trade receivables exist and can be recovered.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g. direct confirmation of balances with customers; inspection of cash received after the year end; inspection of sales invoices and despatch records; review of the receivables ageing analysis; review of credit notes issued after the year end; discussion of recoverability with management.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correctly named procedure, maximum 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of these procedures gives the most reliable evidence of existence, and give one reason.
parts.answer: Direct confirmation with customers (circularisation).
parts.working: 1 mark for the procedure; 1 mark for the reason: the evidence comes directly from an independent third party.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the audit expectation gap and give two causes of it.
parts.answer: The expectation gap is the difference between what users expect an audit to achieve (for example, a guarantee that the company is free of fraud and will not fail) and what an audit provides (reasonable assurance, based on sample testing, that the accounts give a true and fair view). Two causes: users misunderstand the auditor's role; the audit is sample-based and cannot detect everything, for example collusive fraud.
parts.working: 1 mark for the definition; 1 mark each for any two causes: users misunderstand the auditor's role; the audit is sample-based; the standard wording of the report is not understood; company failures are blamed on auditors; collusive fraud is hard to detect. Maximum 4.

practice.stem: Shahzad Plastics Limited owes its bank $900,000 under a loan due for repayment in eight months. The bank has said it will not renew the loan. The directors believe the company can continue trading and have not mentioned the loan problem in the notes to the financial statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the auditor must consider about whether the company can continue as a going concern.
parts.answer: Whether the directors' assumption that the company is a going concern (able to continue operating for the foreseeable future) is appropriate, given the loan repayment and the bank's refusal to renew.
parts.working: 1 mark for assessing the going concern assumption; 1 mark for relating it to the loan repayment and the bank's decision.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the directors should disclose, and what happens to the audit opinion if this disclosure is not made.
parts.answer: The directors should disclose the material uncertainty and their plans to deal with it (for example, negotiating a new loan). If they do not, the auditor is likely to give a qualified or adverse opinion.
parts.working: 1 mark for disclosure of the material uncertainty; 1 mark for a qualified or adverse opinion.

practice.stem: Hamza Logistics Limited employs three internal auditors. The internal audit department reports to the finance director, who is responsible for preparing the company's financial statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one reason why this reporting line may reduce the objectivity of the internal auditors.
parts.answer: The finance director is responsible for the figures the internal auditors review, so they may be reluctant to criticise work that reports to their own line manager.
parts.working: 1 mark for stating the threat (objectivity or self-review); 1 mark for explaining it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one change that would improve their independence.
parts.answer: Internal audit should report directly to the audit committee (or to the board) rather than to the finance director.
parts.working: 1 mark for the change; 1 mark for explaining that it removes the finance director's influence over audit findings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define sampling in audit testing and state two reasons why an auditor uses it rather than testing every transaction.
parts.answer: Sampling is testing a selected subset of items from a population and using the results to form a conclusion about the whole population. Reasons: testing every item would cost too much and take too long; a well-chosen sample gives sufficient appropriate evidence at a reasonable cost.
parts.working: 1 mark for the definition; 1 mark each for two reasons (cost; time or practicality).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the responsibilities of the directors and of the external auditor for the financial statements of a limited company.
parts.answer: The directors prepare the financial statements, keep proper accounting records and maintain internal control. The external auditor forms and expresses an independent opinion on whether the statements give a true and fair view.
parts.working: 1 mark for the directors' preparation of the statements and records; 1 mark for the directors' internal control; 1 mark for the auditor's independent opinion.

practice.stem: Bahawalpur Pharmacy Limited uses four controls: (i) a password is required before a user can post sales to the ledger; (ii) the bank statement is compared with the cash book every month; (iii) cash is kept in a safe that only the owner can open; (iv) a count of stock is compared with the stock records at the year end and differences are investigated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each control (i) to (iv), state whether it is a preventive or a detective control.
parts.answer: (i) preventive; (ii) detective; (iii) preventive; (iv) detective.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct classification. A preventive control stops an error or fraud happening; a detective control finds one after it has happened.

practice.stem: The sales manager and the warehouse supervisor of Dadu Sugar Mills Limited agree to record false despatches, so that $52,000 of stock appears to have been sold to a customer they control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why internal control is less effective against this type of fraud.
parts.answer: Collusion between two people in different roles defeats segregation of duties, because each can cover for the other. The despatch documents look genuine and the records agree with each other, so routine checks do not reveal the fraud.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: collusion defeats segregation of duties; falsified documents look genuine; both people can override controls; routine checks compare records that have been falsified together; a sample may not select the items.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one control that would reduce the risk of this fraud.
parts.answer: Independent confirmation of customer balances directly with customers.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one sensible control, e.g. confirming balances with customers, rotating duties, or surprise checks by someone outside sales and warehousing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an unmodified audit opinion does not mean that a company will remain profitable in future years.
parts.answer: The audit opinion only states whether past financial statements give a true and fair view. It does not assess future profits, the company's strategy or its future cash flows.
parts.working: 1 mark for stating the opinion relates to past statements; 1 mark for true and fair view being about historical reporting; 1 mark for stating that future profitability is not covered.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between an unmodified (unqualified) audit opinion and a qualified audit opinion.
parts.answer: Unmodified: the auditor concludes that the financial statements give a true and fair view in all material respects. Qualified: the auditor concludes that the statements give a true and fair view except for the effects of a specific matter, which is material but not pervasive (a material misstatement, or an inability to obtain enough evidence about one area).
parts.working: 2 marks each: meaning + key words ('true and fair', 'except for', material but not pervasive).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the three types of modified audit opinion and state when each is given.
parts.answer: Qualified opinion ('except for'): a misstatement or lack of evidence that is material but not pervasive. Adverse opinion: misstatements are material and pervasive, so the statements do not give a true and fair view. Disclaimer of opinion: the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and the possible effects are material and pervasive, so no opinion is expressed.
parts.working: 1 mark each type named; 1 mark each correct circumstance.

practice.stem: The auditors of Ravi Garments Limited found that closing inventory was overstated by $48,000 because obsolete stock had been valued at cost. The directors refuse to adjust it. Profit before tax was $620,000. The audit firm treats any misstatement above 5% of profit before tax as material. No other problems were found.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the misstatement as a percentage of profit before tax, correct to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the type of audit opinion the auditor is likely to give. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A qualified ('except for') opinion. The overstatement of inventory is material (well above the 5% threshold the firm uses) but it affects only one area of the statements, so it is not pervasive; the rest of the statements give a true and fair view.
parts.working: 1 mark qualified; 1 mark material (with reference to the figure); 1 mark not pervasive / limited to inventory.

practice.stem: Mehran Retail Limited runs 45 supermarkets across Pakistan and has set up an internal audit department.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three functions of an internal audit department.
parts.answer: Reviewing and testing internal controls (e.g. authorisation of purchases, segregation of duties) to see that they work; checking the accuracy and reliability of accounting records and reports to management; detecting and preventing fraud and error; reviewing the efficiency and value for money of operations; checking compliance with laws, regulations and company policies; helping the external auditor, who may rely on its work.
parts.working: 2 marks each: function identified (1) + explanation (1), max 3 functions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two limitations of an external audit.
parts.answer: Auditors test samples of transactions, not every one, so some errors may go undetected; many figures rely on judgement and estimates (e.g. depreciation, allowances, provisions), so the opinion is reasonable not absolute assurance; auditors rely on information and explanations from management, which may be incomplete or deliberately misleading (collusion/fraud); the audit is of past information and is out of date when published; time and cost limits.
parts.working: 2 marks each: limitation + explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why shareholders of a large company need an external audit.
parts.answer: Ownership is separated from control: shareholders do not run the company and cannot check the records themselves. The directors prepare the statements and could present results favourably to protect bonuses or reputation. An independent expert's opinion that the statements are true and fair gives shareholders confidence when assessing directors' stewardship and making decisions (buy/sell/vote). It also helps deter fraud and error.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four points, or 2 marks each for two developed points.

practice.stem: After a cashier at Sadiq Motors Limited was found to have stolen $18,000 over two years, a shareholder complained at the annual general meeting that the auditors 'should have found the fraud'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the responsibility of (i) the directors and (ii) the external auditor in relation to fraud.
parts.answer: (i) The directors are primarily responsible for preventing and detecting fraud, by setting up and monitoring internal controls and a culture of honesty. (ii) The auditor must plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance that the statements are free from material misstatement whether caused by fraud or error; they are not required to find all fraud, but must report material fraud they discover to the appropriate level of management/shareholders.
parts.working: 2 marks each part.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four responsibilities of the directors of a limited company relating to its financial records and statements.
parts.answer: Any four: keep adequate accounting records; prepare annual financial statements that give a true and fair view and follow accounting standards; select suitable accounting policies and apply them consistently; make reasonable judgements and estimates; safeguard the company's assets; take reasonable steps to prevent and detect fraud; assess whether the company is a going concern; file the statements as required by law.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The internal auditor of Indus Hardware Limited attended the year-end inventory count. The inventory records show a book value of $145,600. The physical count, valued at cost, is $138,950.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the inventory shortage and express it as a percentage of the book value, correct to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three possible causes of the shortage.
parts.answer: Any three: theft by staff or customers; goods sent out without being invoiced; recording errors (e.g. purchases recorded twice); damaged goods thrown away and not recorded; count errors; goods returned to suppliers not recorded.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one internal control that would reduce the risk of this happening again.
parts.answer: E.g. regular surprise inventory counts by staff independent of the storekeeper; restricted access to the store; goods-out notes authorised for every dispatch.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term segregation of duties.
parts.answer: Dividing the stages of a transaction between different people so that no one person controls it from start to finish; this makes fraud harder because it would need collusion, and errors are more likely to be spotted.
parts.working: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark benefit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of segregation of duties in the purchases system of a company.
parts.answer: Any two: the person who orders goods is not the person who receives them; the person who records invoices is not the person who authorises payment; the person who signs payments is not the person who keeps the purchases ledger; a different person reconciles supplier statements.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Swat Marble Limited has 2,500 shareholders, none of whom work in the business. This year its external auditor gave a qualified audit opinion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the external auditor's report is addressed to the shareholders rather than to the directors.
parts.answer: The auditor is appointed by, and acts for, the shareholders, who own the company but do not manage it. The report gives them an independent opinion on the statements the directors have prepared, so it is a check on the directors' stewardship.
parts.working: 1 mark appointed by / acts for shareholders; 1 mark checks directors' stewardship for owners who do not run the company.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three possible consequences for Swat Marble Limited of receiving a qualified audit opinion.
parts.answer: Any three: shareholders lose confidence in the directors and may vote against their reappointment; the share price may fall; banks may refuse loans or charge higher interest; suppliers may reduce credit; potential investors may be put off; the company's reputation may suffer.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The honorary auditor of the Peshawar Squash Club checks the treasurer's records for the year. Cash in hand at the start was $3,850. Receipts recorded were: subscriptions $46,200; event ticket sales $18,750; donations $9,500. All recorded payments, supported by receipts, totalled $61,400. The cash counted at the year end was $11,280.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of cash that should be held at the year end, and the amount missing.
parts.answer: Should hold $16,900; missing $5,620

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two controls the club committee could introduce to improve the stewardship of its funds.
parts.answer: Any two developed: all receipts banked intact and promptly, with numbered receipts issued; two signatories required for payments; regular bank reconciliations reviewed by someone other than the treasurer; an independent honorary auditor checks the accounts annually; monthly reports to the committee comparing receipts with members' list.
parts.working: 2 marks each: control + how it protects funds.

practice.stem: Taj Hotels Limited reports profit before tax of $2,400,000. The auditor sets materiality at 5% of profit before tax. During the audit, the auditor finds an unrecorded accrual of $135,500 for utilities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the materiality threshold.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether this misstatement is material.
parts.answer: It is material, because $135,500 is greater than the threshold of $120,000, so the directors should correct it.
parts.working: 1 mark for comparing the misstatement with the threshold; 1 mark for the conclusion and the need to correct it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the misstatement as a percentage of profit before tax, correct to one decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an adverse opinion and a disclaimer of opinion, and give one circumstance in which each would be given.
parts.answer: Adverse opinion: the auditor concludes the financial statements do not give a true and fair view because the misstatements are both material and pervasive. Disclaimer: the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and the possible effects are so material and pervasive that no opinion can be expressed. Example of an adverse opinion: directors refuse to correct errors that affect most of the statements. Example of a disclaimer: the records for the whole year were destroyed and cannot be reconstructed.
parts.working: 1 mark for the adverse opinion explained; 1 mark for the disclaimer explained; 1 mark for a valid adverse example; 1 mark for a valid disclaimer example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three audit procedures used to test whether trade payables are complete, and state the evidence that each procedure provides.
parts.answer: Any three, with description and evidence: review of invoices and payments made after the year end to find liabilities relating to the year (evidence of unrecorded liabilities); review of goods received notes and cut-off around the year end (evidence that goods received are recorded in the correct period); obtaining supplier statements and reconciling them to the ledger (evidence of balances owed); analytical review of purchases against the prior year (evidence of unusual gaps).
parts.working: 2 marks per procedure: 1 for a clearly described procedure; 1 for the evidence it provides. Maximum 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of an audit committee in supporting the external auditor and in strengthening the directors' stewardship.
parts.answer: Any points explained, e.g.: recommends the appointment and fees of the external auditor to shareholders; agrees the scope of the audit; meets the external auditor without executive directors present to discuss findings; reviews significant accounting judgements; oversees the internal audit function; monitors internal controls and follows up audit recommendations; reviews the auditor's independence; reports to the board and shareholders.
parts.working: 2 marks for each clearly described role that also explains how it supports the audit or stewardship; maximum 3 roles, maximum 6 marks.

practice.stem: The internal auditor of Multan Packaging Limited tests a random sample of 40 sales invoices from a total of 1,200 invoices issued in the year. Three of the sampled invoices contain errors, and the total error in the sample is $4,350.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of invoices in the population that are expected to contain errors.
parts.answer: 90 invoices
parts.working: 1 mark for 3 ÷ 40 × 1,200; 1 mark for 90.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the projected total error in the population of invoices.
parts.working: 1 mark for the average error per sampled invoice: $4,350 ÷ 40 = $108.75; 1 mark for × 1,200 = $130,500.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why the internal auditor should still examine the three erroneous invoices in more detail.
parts.answer: The errors may indicate fraud or a systematic weakness in invoicing controls, and a projection from a small sample may be inaccurate.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid reason; 1 mark for an explanation.

practice.stem: At Quetta Fruit Exports Limited, the same cashier receives customer payments, records them in the receivables ledger and prepares the daily bank deposit slip. The owner rarely reviews the ledger or the deposit slips.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the internal control weakness shown in this case.
parts.answer: Lack of segregation of duties: one person handles the cash, records the receipt and prepares the deposit.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming the weakness with the duties involved.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend two controls that would reduce the risk of cash being stolen without detection.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g.: separate the handling of cash from the recording of receipts; independent comparison of deposit slips with the bank statement by someone else; regular review of the receivables ledger by the owner; sequential numbered receipts; surprise cash counts.
parts.working: 2 marks for each control: 1 for naming it; 1 for explaining how it reduces the risk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the external auditor may give a qualified opinion if the directors refuse to disclose a material uncertainty about the company's ability to continue as a going concern.
parts.answer: Inadequate disclosure of a material uncertainty means the financial statements are materially misstated. The auditor therefore concludes that they do not fully comply with the reporting framework and gives a qualified ('except for') opinion, or an adverse opinion if the effect is pervasive.
parts.working: 1 mark for stating that the disclosure failure is a misstatement; 1 mark for a qualified 'except for' opinion; 1 mark for the materiality judgement; 1 mark for an adverse opinion if the effect is pervasive.

practice.stem: The directors of Bahawal Dairy Limited receive a bonus of 3% of profit before tax. Reported profit before tax is $1,500,000. The auditor finds an unrecorded expense of $80,000 for staff training that relates to this year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the bonus based on the reported profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected bonus and the amount overpaid to the directors.
parts.answer: Corrected profit before tax is $1,420,000; corrected bonus $42,600; overpayment $2,400.
parts.working: 1 mark for the corrected bonus: 3% × $1,420,000 = $42,600; 1 mark for the overpayment: $45,000 − $42,600 = $2,400.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this bonus arrangement may encourage the directors to misstate profit.
parts.answer: The bonus rises with reported profit, so the directors gain personally from overstating profit or understating expenses, which conflicts with their duty to shareholders.
parts.working: 1 mark for explaining the incentive; 1 mark for linking it to the conflict between directors and shareholders.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the external auditor asks management to sign a written representation letter at the end of the audit. State one limitation of relying on this letter.
parts.answer: The letter confirms management's responsibility for the financial statements and that all information and records have been provided; it gives the auditor written evidence to use. Limitation: it is a statement by management, who may be biased or may be responsible for the misstatement, so it is not independent evidence and cannot replace other procedures.
parts.working: 1 mark for the purpose; 1 mark for confirmation that records were provided; 1 mark for a valid limitation; 1 mark for explaining why it is not independent.

practice.stem: Sukkur Hospital Trust buys a new X-ray machine for $210,000 at the start of the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two audit procedures the external auditor could use to verify the existence and ownership of the machine, and the evidence each provides.
parts.answer: Any two: physical inspection of the machine (evidence that it exists and is in use); inspection of the supplier invoice and payment record (evidence of cost and purchase); inspection of ownership documents or the warranty registered in the trust's name (evidence of ownership); review of the asset register and its reconciliation to the ledger.
parts.working: 2 marks per procedure: 1 for a named procedure; 1 for the evidence it provides.

practice.stem: Pak Agro Exports Limited has no internal audit department. Last year losses from undetected errors and staff fraud were estimated at $140,000. The finance director proposes an internal audit department costing $95,000 a year, which is expected to reduce such losses by 60%. The external auditor has said it may be able to rely on some of the internal auditors' work.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected annual saving in losses and the net annual cost or benefit of the internal audit department.
parts.answer: Saving $84,000; net annual cost $11,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should set up the internal audit department. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: on these figures it costs $11,000 a year more than it saves; the saving is only an estimate; internal auditors are employees, so they are less independent than the external auditor and cannot replace the external audit. For: it reviews and tests internal controls continuously, deterring fraud as well as detecting it; it can improve the efficiency of operations and the reliability of records for management; the external auditor may rely on its work, which could reduce the external audit fee and close the $11,000 gap; it helps the directors show good stewardship of shareholders' assets. Decision: e.g. set it up, because the net cost is small and the non-financial benefits (stronger controls, possible lower audit fee) are likely to outweigh it.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points against (using the $11,000 figure), up to 3 marks for points in favour applied to the company, 1 mark for a justified decision.

practice.stem: During the year, the directors of Lahore Builders Limited: (1) bought land for $1.3 million from a company owned by the managing director's brother; an independent valuer had valued it at $1.0 million, and the transaction was not disclosed in the annual report; (2) increased their own bonuses by 40% while reducing the dividend per share from 12 cents to 8 cents; (3) published the annual report four months later than usual. The company's profit for the year rose by 12% and the directors set up an internal audit department.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the directors of Lahore Builders Limited have carried out their stewardship responsibilities properly. Conclude with a judgement.
parts.answer: Against good stewardship: buying land from a company owned by the managing director's brother at 30% above valuation is a conflict of interest and may waste shareholders' funds; failure to disclose the related party transaction; directors' bonuses increased while dividends cut — possible self-interest; the delay in publishing accounts reduces accountability. For: profits rose by 12%; they set up an internal audit department and kept proper records; the land may have strategic value. Judgement: overall the directors have not fully discharged their stewardship duty because of the undisclosed related-party purchase and the bonus/dividend issue, although operational performance improved.
parts.working: Level 3 (7–8): balanced discussion applied to the case with a justified judgement. Level 2 (4–6): some applied points, may be one-sided, some judgement. Level 1 (1–3): general statements about stewardship.

practice.stem: A flood destroyed the head office of Sindh Rice Mills Limited, including most sales and inventory records for the year. Revenue, trade receivables and closing inventory together make up most of the figures in the financial statements. The directors have estimated these figures, but there is no supporting evidence for the auditor to test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of audit opinion the auditor should give. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A disclaimer of opinion. The auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence for revenue, receivables and inventory, which affect most of the statements, so the possible effects are both material and pervasive. The auditor therefore does not express an opinion. A qualified opinion would only be suitable if the lack of evidence affected a limited area, and an adverse opinion needs evidence that the statements are actually misstated.
parts.working: 1 mark disclaimer; 1 mark inability to obtain evidence; 1 mark material; 1 mark pervasive; 1 mark distinguishing from qualified/adverse.

practice.stem: The bank has withdrawn all loans from Margalla Shoes Limited and the directors have decided to put the company into liquidation shortly after the year end. However, they have prepared the financial statements on a going concern basis and refuse to change them or to disclose the planned liquidation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of audit opinion the auditor should give. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: An adverse opinion. The company is not a going concern (bank has withdrawn finance, directors intend to liquidate), but the statements are prepared on a going concern basis, so assets are at cost less depreciation rather than realisable values and liabilities may be misclassified. This misstatement is material and affects the statements as a whole (pervasive), so they do not give a true and fair view. It is not a disclaimer because the auditor has sufficient evidence.
parts.working: 1 mark adverse; 1 mark basis of preparation wrong; 1 mark material; 1 mark pervasive; 1 mark sufficient evidence/not a disclaimer.

practice.stem: Thar Coal Services Limited reports profit before tax of $1,150,000. Its mining equipment cost $3,600,000 and has a useful life of 12 years with no residual value, but the directors have decided not to charge any depreciation on it this year. The external auditor disagrees. The directors tell shareholders that "the auditor is responsible for getting the figures right".

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the straight-line depreciation for the year, the corrected profit before tax, and the misstatement as a percentage of the reported profit before tax, correct to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Depreciation $300,000; corrected profit before tax $850,000; misstatement 26.09%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the directors' statement is wrong, and state with reasons the audit opinion likely to be given if the directors refuse to charge depreciation.
parts.answer: The directors are responsible for preparing financial statements that give a true and fair view; the auditor only examines them and gives an independent opinion on them. The misstatement (26.09% of profit) is material, but it is confined to one item (depreciation, carrying amount of equipment and retained earnings) rather than the statements as a whole, so it is not pervasive. The auditor is therefore likely to give a qualified ('except for') opinion.
parts.working: 1 mark directors prepare; 1 mark auditor gives opinion only; 1 mark material with reference to figure; 1 mark qualified because not pervasive.

practice.stem: At the annual general meeting of Kohat Cement Limited, shareholders must vote on reappointing Khan & Co as external auditors. Khan & Co received an audit fee of $85,000 and a further $240,000 for consultancy, including designing the company's new computerised accounting system. The same audit partner has led the audit for 11 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate non-audit fees as a percentage of the total fees received from the company, correct to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the shareholders whether they should vote to reappoint Khan & Co as auditors. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: non-audit fees are almost three times the audit fee (about 74% of total), creating a self-interest threat — the firm may be reluctant to qualify its opinion and risk losing lucrative consultancy work; the firm designed the new accounting system, so it would be auditing its own work (self-review threat); the audit partner has been in charge for 11 years (familiarity threat). For: the firm knows the business well, which may make the audit efficient and cheaper; no evidence of any wrongdoing; changing auditors has costs. Decision: shareholders should not reappoint unless safeguards are put in place (e.g. rotate the audit partner, stop providing system design/consultancy, or have a separate team); otherwise appoint a new independent firm.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for independence threats applied, up to 2 marks for points in favour, 1 mark for safeguards, 1 mark for a justified decision.

practice.stem: The directors of Faisal Textiles Limited each receive a bonus equal to 2% of the year's profit before tax. This year the directors postponed essential machine maintenance and changed the estimated useful life of machinery from 8 to 15 years, increasing profit by $1.2 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the conflict of interest between the directors and the shareholders of Faisal Textiles Limited, and suggest how the shareholders could reduce the risk that the directors act in their own interest.
parts.answer: Conflict: the directors' bonus depends on annual profit, so they have an incentive to boost short-term profit (e.g. by delaying maintenance, cutting training, or choosing accounting estimates that increase profit), while shareholders want long-term growth in value and reliable statements; directors also control the information shareholders receive. Ways to reduce it: link part of pay to long-term targets or share price over several years (or pay part in shares); appoint independent non-executive directors and an audit committee; keep a strong independent external audit; require clear disclosure of directors' remuneration and related-party transactions; vote on remuneration at the AGM.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for explaining the conflict with reference to the case, up to 3 marks for suitable safeguards explained.

practice.stem: The directors of Hala Ceramics Limited propose that the company's internal audit department, which reports to the finance director, should take over the work of the external auditor. This would save the external audit fee of $120,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the directors' proposal.
parts.answer: Against: internal auditors are employees who report to the finance director, so they are not independent of the people whose statements they would check; shareholders, lenders and other users need an independent opinion that the statements give a true and fair view; an external audit is normally a legal requirement for a limited company, so it cannot simply be replaced; the external auditor is appointed by and reports to the shareholders, whereas internal audit serves management. For: the saving of $120,000 a year; internal auditors know the business well. Conclusion: reject the proposal; keep both, and instead let the external auditor rely on the internal auditors' work where appropriate, which may reduce the fee.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for points (at least one in favour for full marks) applied to the company, 1 mark for using the $120,000 or the reporting line, 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Lahore Paints Limited reports profit before tax of $3,000,000 and revenue of $45,000,000. The auditor sets materiality at 5% of profit before tax. The auditor finds three errors: (1) closing inventory is overstated by $210,000 because damaged paints were valued at cost; (2) a trade receivable of $95,000 from a customer in liquidation has not been written off; (3) an electricity bill of $80,000 for the year has not been accrued.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit before tax.
parts.working: 1 mark for recognising that all three errors overstate profit; 1 mark for $3,000,000 − $210,000 − $95,000 − $80,000 = $2,615,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total misstatement as a percentage of reported profit before tax, correct to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State, with reasons, whether the auditor should expect to modify the opinion.
parts.answer: Yes. Materiality is $150,000 (5% of $3,000,000). The inventory error alone ($210,000) exceeds it, and the total misstatement of $385,000 is well above it. If the directors do not correct the errors, the auditor should give a qualified ('except for') opinion, or an adverse opinion if the errors are pervasive.
parts.working: 1 mark for the threshold of $150,000; 1 mark for comparing the errors with it; 1 mark for the conclusion that the opinion may be modified; 1 mark for saying the directors should correct the errors first. Maximum 4.

practice.stem: Iqbal & Partners is the external auditor of Rahim Steel Limited. The firm also prepares the company's tax returns and has offered to design its new payroll system. Fees from Rahim Steel are 38% of the firm's total fees. The audit engagement partner's brother is the company's finance director.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two threats to the auditor's independence from these facts, naming each threat and explaining it.
parts.answer: Self-review threat: the firm would audit tax returns and a payroll system it prepared or designed. Self-interest threat: 38% of the firm's fees depend on one client, so the firm may be reluctant to report problems. Familiarity threat: the partner's family link to the finance director may make the partner too sympathetic. Any two.
parts.working: 2 marks for each threat: 1 for naming it; 1 for explaining the link to these facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate two safeguards the firm could apply, and state whether they would be sufficient in this case.
parts.answer: Safeguards: a separate audit partner and team with no role in the tax or payroll work; an independent second partner review; the audit committee approves all non-audit work. Evaluation: separation and independent review reduce the self-review and familiarity threats, but the fee-dependence threat remains, and a close family link is hard to safeguard. The firm should probably decline the payroll work and rotate the engagement partner, or the company should appoint a different auditor.
parts.working: 2 marks for two suitable safeguards; 2 marks for evaluation of their effectiveness with a reasoned conclusion.

practice.stem: Discuss whether a company should change its external auditor every five years, rather than keep the same firm for many years. Reach a reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the question.
parts.answer: A discussion covering: benefits of rotation (fresh perspective and scepticism; reduced familiarity and self-interest threats; shareholder confidence). Costs (the new auditor needs time to understand the business; higher initial costs; risk of weaker audit quality in early years; disruption to management; limited choice of firms for large companies). Evaluation linked to the company's size, complexity and the quality of the existing audit, and whether rotation is required by law or chosen. A justified conclusion.
parts.working: Band 1 (1–2): one or two points with little explanation. Band 2 (3–5): several points, some explained, limited evaluation. Band 3 (6–8): balanced discussion of benefits and costs, evaluation linked to the company's circumstances, and a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Sanjan Ceramic Works Limited reports profit before tax of $40,000 this year, compared with $1,200,000 last year. Revenue this year is $8,000,000. The auditor is deciding which materiality benchmark to use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the materiality threshold using 5% of profit before tax.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the materiality threshold using 0.5% of revenue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which benchmark the auditor should prefer, and explain why.
parts.answer: Revenue (0.5%, giving $40,000) is more appropriate because profit has fallen sharply and is unusually small. A threshold based on profit would be too low, so the audit would be disproportionately detailed; revenue is a more stable measure of the company's size.
parts.working: 1 mark for choosing revenue; 1 mark for profit being unusually low or volatile; 1 mark for the consequence (threshold too low, excessive testing).

parts.label: d
parts.text: A misstatement of $25,000 has been found. State whether it is material under each benchmark.
parts.answer: Under the profit benchmark ($2,000) it is material; under the revenue benchmark ($40,000) it is not material.
parts.working: 1 mark for each benchmark correctly applied.

practice.stem: A fire destroyed 60% of the sales records of Gulberg Hotels Limited for the first six months of the year. The directors have prepared revenue of $3,200,000 for the year from bank statements and surviving records. The auditor cannot verify revenue for those six months but is satisfied with all other items.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a qualified ('except for') opinion and a disclaimer of opinion.
parts.answer: A qualified 'except for' opinion states that the statements are fair except for the effect of a material but not pervasive matter the auditor could not verify. A disclaimer means no opinion is expressed, because the possible effects of the limitation are both material and pervasive.
parts.working: 1 mark for the qualified opinion (material but not pervasive, 'except for'); 1 mark for the disclaimer (no opinion expressed); 1 mark for the disclaimer requiring pervasive effects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which opinion is most appropriate here, and justify your answer with reference to how far the limitation affects the financial statements.
parts.answer: A qualified 'except for' opinion is most likely: the limitation is material because it covers revenue for six months, but it is confined to revenue and related items, and the other items were verified satisfactorily. A disclaimer would follow only if the limitation affected most of the statements.
parts.working: 1 mark for the opinion; 1 mark for the limitation being material; 1 mark for it being limited (not pervasive); 1 mark for justifying with the items that were verified.

practice.stem: Over three years, the accounts clerk at Pindi Pharma Stores Limited made 52 unauthorised payments to a fictitious supplier, totalling $186,400. The fraud was found by the internal auditor when a genuine supplier's statement did not agree with the ledger.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average value of each unauthorised payment, to the nearest dollar.
parts.working: 1 mark: $186,400 ÷ 52 = $3,584.62, so $3,585 to the nearest dollar.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two weaknesses in internal control that allowed the fraud.
parts.answer: Any two: the same clerk could create supplier records and authorise payments (no segregation of duties); no independent approval of payments to new or unfamiliar suppliers; the supplier master file was not reviewed; supplier statements were not reconciled to the ledger.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid weakness.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the external auditor's sample may not have detected these payments, and what the internal auditor did that was more effective.
parts.answer: External audit uses a sample, and 52 small payments spread over three years could easily fall outside it. The fictitious supplier's documents looked genuine, so vouching a sample would not reveal the problem. The internal auditor reconciled a supplier statement, which is evidence from outside the company, to the ledger; this independent comparison exposed the fraud.
parts.working: 1 mark for the sampling point; 1 mark for payments being small and documents looking genuine; 1 mark for the internal auditor using independent evidence; 1 mark for explaining the reconciliation as an independent check.

practice.stem: On 30 December, the finance director of Hyderabad Textile Mills Limited instructs the accounts team to record $350,000 of sales for goods that have not yet been despatched. The finance director says the goods will be despatched in January and the sales are 'virtually certain'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this instruction is an example of management override of controls, and why auditors treat such a risk as significant.
parts.answer: Management override is a senior manager using their authority to bypass normal controls to misstate results; here revenue is overstated by recording sales before they occur (a cut-off error). Auditors treat it as significant because management can override controls, the intention is to misstate results, and the entries can look ordinary, so they are hard to detect.
parts.working: 1 mark for defining override; 1 mark for a senior manager bypassing normal controls; 1 mark for revenue being overstated (cut-off); 1 mark for explaining why the risk is significant and hard to detect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two audit procedures the external auditor should perform on this revenue.
parts.answer: Any two: cut-off testing, examining despatch documents and invoices dated before and after 31 December; review of journal entries made near the year end and the authority for them; direct confirmation of the sale with the customer; review of post year-end returns or credit notes.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid procedure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how an audit committee could reduce the risk of this type of misstatement.
parts.answer: The audit committee can require management to justify significant year-end adjustments and can meet the external auditor privately to discuss management's judgements and the cut-off findings.
parts.working: 1 mark for a stated action; 1 mark for explaining how it reduces the risk.

practice.stem: The auditor counts five of the 12 inventory locations of a company at the year end and compares each count with the stock records. The differences (count minus book) are: +$1,200; −$3,400; −$560; +$90; −$2,150.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net difference and the gross difference (the sum of the differences ignoring their signs).
parts.answer: Net difference: −$4,820. Gross difference: $7,400.
parts.working: 1 mark for the net difference: 1,200 − 3,400 − 560 + 90 − 2,150 = −4,820; 1 mark for the gross difference: 7,400.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the auditor should extend the count to more locations, even though the net difference is only −$4,820.
parts.answer: The gross difference is much larger than the net difference, so overages and shortages offset each other and the net figure hides several significant errors. This points to weak recording or counting controls across the locations. Extending the count provides enough evidence to decide whether the inventory total is materially misstated.
parts.working: 1 mark for explaining the offsetting errors; 1 mark for the control weakness; 1 mark for the extra evidence needed to conclude on materiality.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the steps an external auditor should take when the directors refuse to correct a material misstatement the auditor has found, and explain how the audit opinion may be affected.
parts.answer: Steps: communicate the misstatement to the directors and the audit committee and request correction; assess whether it is material and whether it is pervasive; if the directors still refuse, consider a qualified or adverse opinion and give the reasons in the audit report; consider whether to resign in a serious case and communicate with those charged with governance; report to the appropriate regulator where the law requires. Effects: shareholders rely on the report, so a modified opinion must be clear; the choice between qualified and adverse depends on pervasiveness. Conclusion on the appropriate action.
parts.working: Band 1 (1–3): one or two steps described with little explanation. Band 2 (4–6): several steps with reasons and some reference to materiality and opinion types. Band 3 (7–8): a clear sequence of steps, use of materiality and pervasiveness to decide the opinion, consideration of resignation and reporting duties, and a justified judgement.

practice.stem: The auditor of Mirpur Textiles Limited uses analytical procedures. The prior year gross profit margin was 30%. This year revenue is $6,400,000 and cost of sales is $4,640,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate this year's gross profit margin as a percentage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected gross profit and the difference between expected and actual gross profit.
parts.answer: Expected gross profit $1,920,000; actual gross profit $1,760,000; difference $160,000.
parts.working: 1 mark for the expected figure: 30% × $6,400,000 = $1,920,000; 1 mark for the difference: $1,920,000 − $1,760,000 = $160,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two business reasons (not errors) that could explain the lower margin, and state what the auditor should do next.
parts.answer: Any two: a change in sales mix towards lower-margin products; price cuts to win customers; a rise in supplier prices or freight costs not passed on; losses from theft or wastage of stock. Next, the auditor should ask management for explanations and corroborate them with evidence (purchase invoices, price lists, stock records), extending testing if the explanations are not supported.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid reason (maximum 2); 1 mark for asking management for explanations; 1 mark for corroborating them with evidence or extending testing.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a physical security measure for a computerised accounting system?
A a password on each user account
B encryption of the data files
C a locked room for the server
D a firewall on the network
parts.answer: C a locked room for the server
parts.working: A locked room physically prevents access to the hardware. A, B and D are software (logical) controls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the main purpose of making regular backup copies of accounting data?
A to stop hackers from reading the data
B to allow the data to be restored if it is lost or corrupted
C to check that entries have been input correctly
D to reduce the storage space needed
parts.answer: B to allow the data to be restored if it is lost or corrupted
parts.working: A backup is a copy kept so that lost or damaged data can be recovered. It does not stop unauthorised reading (A, which needs encryption/passwords) or check accuracy (C).

practice.stem: Fatima owns a clothes shop in Hyderabad and keeps her accounts by hand. She is thinking of buying accounting software.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages to Fatima of using a computerised accounting system.
parts.answer: Records and reports (e.g. trial balance, statements to customers) are produced quickly; arithmetic is accurate and ledgers update automatically.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: speed; accuracy of calculations; automatic posting to ledgers; up-to-date information; easy reports; less storage space.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages to Fatima of using a computerised accounting system.
parts.answer: Cost of hardware, software and training; risk of data loss through system failure, viruses or hacking.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: cost; training time; risk of breakdown/data loss; security threats; input errors processed unnoticed.

practice.stem: Ravi Motors, Karachi, keeps its customer and supplier records on a computerised accounting system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two methods the business could use to prevent unauthorised access to its accounting data.
parts.answer: Passwords: each user must enter a secret password, so only authorised staff can log in. Access levels: staff can see or change only the parts of the system they need, e.g. a sales clerk cannot open the payroll. (Also: encryption, biometric log-in, automatic log-out, firewalls.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per method (1 identify, 1 explain).

practice.stem: A trading business in Lahore saves all its accounting data on one office computer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways the business could reduce the risk of losing its accounting data.
parts.answer: Make regular backups; store a backup copy off-site or in the cloud.
parts.working: 1 mark each: regular backups; off-site/cloud storage; antivirus software; uninterruptible power supply; fire-proof storage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a backup copy should be stored away from the office.
parts.answer: If the office suffers a fire, flood or theft, both the computer and an on-site backup could be destroyed; an off-site copy can still be used to restore the records.
parts.working: 1 mark: risk of physical disaster/theft at the office. 1 mark: off-site copy allows restoration.

practice.stem: The finance manager of a school in Islamabad prepares the annual budget on a spreadsheet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways a spreadsheet helps in preparing budgets.
parts.answer: Formulas recalculate totals automatically when any figure is changed, saving time and avoiding arithmetic errors. 'What-if' analysis lets the manager test different fee levels or salary increases and see the effect on the budget straight away. (Also: easy charts, copying layouts for each month, sharing.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per way (1 identify, 1 explain).

practice.stem: The external auditor of Indus Foods Ltd asks whether its accounting software keeps an audit trail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'audit trail'.
parts.answer: A record kept by the system of every transaction and change, showing who made it and when, so that each entry can be traced from the source document to the financial statements.
parts.working: 1 mark: record of transactions/changes with user and time. 1 mark: allows tracing source to final accounts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an audit trail is useful to the auditor.
parts.answer: The auditor can check that recorded figures are supported by source documents and can identify unauthorised or suspicious changes, which helps detect errors and fraud.
parts.working: 1 mark: verify figures to evidence. 1 mark: detect unauthorised changes/fraud.

practice.stem: A computerised accounting system needs both hardware and software.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between hardware and software, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: Hardware is the physical equipment, e.g. a computer or printer; software is the programs that run on it, e.g. an accounting package.
parts.working: 1 mark each, with example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two reports that accounting software can produce automatically.
parts.answer: Trial balance; aged trade receivables report (also: statement of profit or loss, customer statements, VAT/tax return, inventory report).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Sunrise Bakery, Peshawar, is introducing a computerised accounting system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why staff should be trained before the system is used.
parts.answer: So that they enter transactions correctly and avoid input errors that would make the accounts wrong. So that they can use the system efficiently and obtain the reports needed, getting the expected time savings. (Also: understand security procedures such as passwords and backups; reduce resistance to change.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per reason (1 identify, 1 explain).

practice.stem: The accounts department of a hospital has a payroll clerk, a purchases clerk and an accountant, all using one computerised system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'access levels'.
parts.answer: Each user is allowed to view or change only the parts of the system that their job needs.
parts.working: 1 mark: restricted rights per user. 1 mark: related to job role/view vs edit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of how access levels could be used in this department.
parts.answer: The purchases clerk cannot open or change payroll records.
parts.working: B1 any sensible example.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one physical control that would protect the accounting system.
parts.answer: Lock the server room (also: CCTV, lockable cabinets for backups, fire protection).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which input control checks that a compulsory field, such as a customer code, has been filled in?
A Range check
B Presence check
C Hash total
D Check digit
parts.answer: B Presence check
parts.working: A presence check rejects a record when a required field is blank. A range check tests that a value lies between set limits, a hash total adds up codes that have no money value, and a check digit detects keying errors in a code.

practice.stem: A sales system numbers invoices consecutively from 1001 to 1500. In one month, invoice 1222 and invoice 1223 are followed by invoice 1225. No invoice 1224 appears in the records.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the control that would find the missing invoice number, and explain what it does.
parts.answer: A sequence check. It checks that each new number follows on from the last one, and reports any gap (here 1224) so that it can be investigated.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming the sequence check; 1 mark for explaining that it reports gaps or out-of-order numbers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why a missing invoice number matters to the business.
parts.answer: The sale may have been made but not recorded, so sales and receivables could be understated, or the gap may hide an error or fraud.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid reason.

practice.stem: Ruby Books, a bookshop in Hyderabad, lets its staff log on to the accounting system with a password. The owner wants a second check before anyone can log on.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by two-factor authentication.
parts.answer: A login that needs two different kinds of proof, such as something the user knows (a password) and something the user has (a one-time code sent to a phone or a security token).
parts.working: 1 mark for two separate factors; 1 mark for the factors being of different types, with an example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one way the bookshop could set this up for its staff.
parts.answer: Each member of staff must enter a one-time code sent to their own phone, in addition to the password, before the accounting system opens.
parts.working: 1 mark for any sensible method.

practice.stem: A small trading business keeps its accounting data on a server in its office. The server is connected to the internet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a firewall.
parts.answer: A firewall is a security system (hardware or software) that monitors network traffic and blocks connections that are not allowed by its rules.
parts.working: 1 mark for monitoring and blocking traffic according to rules.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a firewall protects the business's accounting system from attack from outside the business.
parts.answer: It stops outside computers from connecting to the accounting server unless the traffic is allowed, so hackers cannot easily reach the data over the internet.
parts.working: 1 mark for blocking unauthorised outside connections; 1 mark for explaining the protection of data from hackers.

practice.stem: A business backs up its accounting data every night.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between a full backup and an incremental backup.
parts.answer: A full backup copies all the data each time. An incremental backup copies only the data that has changed since the last backup (of any type).
parts.working: 1 mark for full backup copying everything; 1 mark for incremental copying only changes since the last backup.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of each type of backup.
parts.answer: Full backup: restoring the data needs only one set of copies, so it is quicker and simpler. Incremental backup: it takes less time and storage to make each day.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid advantage of full backups; 1 mark for a valid advantage of incremental backups.

practice.stem: A business backs up 3.6 GB of accounting data each night. It keeps the last 14 nightly backups before overwriting them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the storage needed for these backups, in GB.
parts.working: 1 mark for multiplying 3.6 by 14; 1 mark for 50.4 GB.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why at least one copy of the backup should be stored away from the office.
parts.answer: A fire, flood, theft or ransomware attack at the office could destroy both the computer and the copies kept there. A copy stored elsewhere lets the business restore its data.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming a risk to the office; 1 mark for explaining that an off-site copy allows recovery.

practice.stem: A retail shop's computerised sales system is down for 4.5 hours. Average sales are $2,800 an hour, and gross profit is 35% of sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sales lost during the outage.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for 12,600.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit lost during the outage.
parts.working: 1 mark for applying 35% to the sales lost; 1 mark for 4,410.

practice.stem: A clerk keys in four customer account numbers from a batch: 2071, 2185, 2254 and 2319. Account numbers have no monetary meaning, so the batch uses a hash total of the account numbers as a control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the hash total of the four account numbers.
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the hash total checks, and what happens if the clerk keys one account number wrongly.
parts.answer: It checks that every record in the batch was entered, and that no record was missed or altered. If one account number is mis-keyed, the total computed by the system will differ from the hash total prepared beforehand, so the error is detected.
parts.working: 1 mark for what the hash total checks (completeness or accuracy); 1 mark for explaining that a wrong number changes the total; 1 mark for the comparison with the pre-prepared total.

practice.stem: A small firm's accounting server could lose power during its month-end processing run.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) does.
parts.answer: It supplies battery power automatically when the mains supply fails, so the computer keeps running briefly or shuts down safely without losing data.
parts.working: 1 mark for automatic battery power when mains fails; 1 mark for keeping the data safe.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one control, other than a UPS, that protects the data if the power fails.
parts.answer: Saving data regularly (auto-save) or keeping up-to-date backups.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid control.

practice.stem: A business prints a payroll report every month from its computerised accounting system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two output controls for a printed monthly payroll report.
parts.answer: Check the total on the report with the control total from the input batch; check the number of employees on the report with the staff list; limit distribution of the report to authorised staff.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid control (any two).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the payroll report should be checked before the payments are made.
parts.answer: Errors in the input or processing would otherwise be paid to employees and could be hard to recover. A check catches any incorrect pay before money leaves the business.
parts.working: 1 mark for the risk of wrong payments; 1 mark for the check preventing the error being paid.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business's purchase system will not accept a single invoice above $10,000. A clerk keys in an invoice for $85,000 instead of $8,500.
Which validation check will reject the entry?
A format check
B range (limit) check
C presence check
D check digit
parts.answer: B range (limit) check
