parts.working: A range or limit check tests that a value lies within set limits. A format check only tests the pattern of characters, which 85,000 still matches; a presence check only tests that a value has been entered.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a disadvantage of a computerised accounting system compared with a manual system?
A ledger balances are updated automatically
B reports such as the trial balance can be produced quickly
C an input error may be repeated in every record that uses that data
D arithmetic errors in totalling the ledgers are eliminated
parts.answer: C an input error may be repeated in every record that uses that data
parts.working: If wrong data is input, the system processes it faithfully and the error flows through all linked records ('garbage in, garbage out'). A, B and D are advantages.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the purpose of an audit trail in a computerised accounting system?
A to prevent staff from changing their passwords
B to allow each transaction to be traced from its source document through to the financial statements
C to make a copy of all files at the end of each day
D to stop viruses from entering the system
parts.answer: B to allow each transaction to be traced from its source document through to the financial statements
parts.working: An audit trail records who entered or changed each transaction and when, so it can be traced. C describes a backup; D describes antivirus software.

practice.stem: A wholesaler's clerks key in customer account codes (format: two letters followed by four digits, e.g. KH2041) and invoice amounts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name and describe three validation checks that would be suitable for this data.
parts.answer: Format check: tests that the account code is two letters followed by four digits. Existence (lookup) check: tests that the account code matches an existing customer. Range check: tests that the invoice amount is within set limits, e.g. above $0 and below the customer's credit limit. (Also: presence check that no field is left blank.)
parts.working: For each of three checks: 1 mark name, 1 mark description applied to the data.

practice.stem: Zaitoon Traders uses an integrated accounting package in which the sales, purchases, inventory and nominal ledgers are linked.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what happens in the system when a credit sales invoice is entered.
parts.answer: The customer's account in the sales ledger is debited; the sales account in the nominal ledger is credited and the sales ledger control (trade receivables) account is updated; the inventory records are reduced by the quantity sold.
parts.working: 1 mark each: customer account debited; sales/control accounts updated in nominal ledger; inventory updated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit of the ledgers being integrated.
parts.answer: Each transaction is entered only once, so all records agree and are up to date.
parts.working: B1 (single entry, consistency, saves time, fewer posting errors).

practice.stem: A garment exporter in Sialkot has received emails that appear to come from its bank, asking staff to confirm the company's online banking log-in details. Last month another firm in the city had its accounting files locked by ransomware.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'phishing' and suggest one way to protect the business against it.
parts.answer: Phishing is a fraudulent message pretending to be from a trusted organisation to trick staff into revealing passwords or bank details. Protection: train staff never to give log-in details by email and to check messages with the bank directly.
parts.working: 1 mark explanation; 1 mark protection (training, spam filters, two-factor authentication).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'ransomware' and suggest one way to protect the business against it.
parts.answer: Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts or locks files and demands payment to release them. Protection: keep regular backups stored separately so files can be restored without paying, and keep antivirus software and updates current.
parts.working: 1 mark explanation; 1 mark protection (separate backups, antivirus, updates, not opening unknown attachments).

practice.stem: An online retailer in Karachi stores customers' names, addresses, phone numbers and payment records in its accounting system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two responsibilities the business has when holding this personal data.
parts.answer: Keep the data secure: use passwords, encryption and access controls so it cannot be stolen or misused. Use the data only for the purpose it was collected and keep it accurate and up to date, deleting it when no longer needed. (Also: obey data protection law, do not share without consent.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per responsibility (1 identify, 1 explain).

practice.stem: The owner of a computerised business says, 'The computer never makes mistakes, so our accounts must be correct.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify and explain two types of error that can still occur in a computerised accounting system.
parts.answer: Error of original entry: a wrong amount is keyed in from the invoice, and the system posts the wrong figure to both accounts. Error of commission: a payment is posted to the wrong supplier's account; debits still equal credits so the system does not detect it. (Also: error of omission, error of principle, compensating errors.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per error (1 identify, 1 explain why the system does not detect it).

practice.stem: A pharmacy in Rawalpindi uses its accounting software to keep a running record of inventory. The software automatically produces a purchase order when inventory of an item falls to its reorder level. For one medicine, maximum daily usage is 120 packs and the maximum time for delivery is 5 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the reorder level for this medicine, using maximum usage × maximum lead time.
parts.answer: 600 packs

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit and one risk of the software producing purchase orders automatically.
parts.answer: Benefit: the pharmacy will not run out of medicines because orders are made on time without staff having to check shelves. Risk: if the recorded inventory is wrong (e.g. theft or input error), orders may be wrong, so physical counts are still needed.
parts.working: 1 mark benefit; 1 mark risk.

practice.stem:
Ravi Builders spent the following when introducing a computerised accounting system:
                                             $
Computers and printers                   9,000
Accounting software (permanent licence)  3,000
Installation of the network                600
Staff training course                    1,200
Annual maintenance contract                800
Temporary staff to key in old records      700

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total capital expenditure and the total revenue expenditure.
parts.answer: Capital $12,600; revenue $2,700.
parts.working: Capital: hardware 9,000, software 3,000, installation 600 (B1 B1) = 12,600. Revenue: training 1,200, maintenance 800, temporary staff 700 (B1) = 2,700 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect on the profit for the year if the training course were treated as capital expenditure.
parts.answer: Profit would be overstated by $1,200 this year (less any depreciation charged), and non-current assets would also be overstated.
parts.working: 1 mark: profit overstated by 1,200. 1 mark: assets overstated / breaks the rule that training is revenue expenditure.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sales module updates the nominal ledger and the receivables ledger automatically when an invoice is posted. This is an example of:
A batch processing
B integration
C parallel running
D data encryption
parts.answer: B integration
parts.working: In an integrated system, one posting updates several ledgers at once. Batch processing groups transactions for later processing; parallel running is a changeover method; encryption protects data from being read.

practice.stem: Ocean Textiles, Karachi, stores its customers' bank account details in its accounting database.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by encryption.
parts.answer: Converting data into a coded form using a key, so that it can only be read by someone who has the correct key.
parts.working: 1 mark for converting into a coded form; 1 mark for the key being needed to read it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the business should encrypt the bank details, and state one situation in which the encrypted data could still be at risk.
parts.answer: If a thief copies the database, the bank details are unreadable without the key. Risk: the key is stored with the data, or an authorised user's logged-in account is hacked or misused so the data can be read or copied.
parts.working: 1 mark for protection if the data is stolen; 1 mark for explaining why encryption works; 1 mark for a valid risk (key stored with the data, or a hacked logged-in account).

practice.stem: A hospital accounts department keeps its accounting system on a server in a locked room. Staff log in to the system with their own user IDs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between physical access controls and logical access controls. Give one example of each.
parts.answer: Physical controls restrict entry to equipment and rooms, for example a locked server room opened by a key card. Logical controls restrict the use of software and data, for example user IDs and passwords that give each member of staff different levels of access.
parts.working: 1 mark: physical controls defined; 1 mark: logical controls defined; 1 mark: physical example; 1 mark: logical example.

practice.stem: A computerised purchase system costs $540 a month, including licence and support. It processes 1,800 supplier invoices a month. Manual processing of the same invoices would cost $0.65 per invoice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the system's cost per invoice.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for $0.30.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the monthly saving compared with manual processing.
parts.working: 1 mark for the saving per invoice (0.35); 1 mark for 630 per month.

practice.stem: A shop's stock system records every sale and purchase as it happens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between real-time processing and batch processing.
parts.answer: Real-time processing updates the records immediately as each transaction occurs. Batch processing collects transactions and processes them together at a set time.
parts.working: 1 mark for real-time updating each transaction; 1 mark for batch grouping transactions to process together.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of real-time processing for a stock control system.
parts.answer: Stock levels are always up to date, so the business does not sell items it does not have and can reorder promptly.
parts.working: 1 mark for the advantage; 1 mark for linking it to stock information being current.

practice.stem: A consultancy firm's accounting server could be destroyed by fire. The firm wants to be able to resume work within a few days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two components of a disaster recovery plan for a computerised accounting system.
parts.answer: Regular off-site backups, with a tested procedure for restoring them. A priority list of which systems and records must be restored first, with named staff responsible. Other valid components include an alternative computer or site to continue work, and a list of supplier contacts.
parts.working: 2 marks for each component: 1 mark for naming it, 1 mark for explaining what it does (any two).

practice.stem: A business has delayed installing the latest security update for its accounting software for four months, to avoid disruption at month-end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why security updates to the accounting software and operating system should be installed promptly.
parts.answer: Updates fix security weaknesses that hackers and malware can exploit. Delaying the update leaves the system open to attack for longer.
parts.working: 1 mark for updates fixing known weaknesses; 1 mark for the longer the delay the greater the exposure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one risk of delaying the updates.
parts.answer: Malware, ransomware or unauthorised access could damage or expose the business's data.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid risk.

practice.stem: On 1 January 2026, a business buys a server computer for $48,000. It is expected to be used for four years and to have no residual value. The business uses straight-line depreciation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for each year.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for 12,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net book value of the server at 31 December 2027.
parts.working: 1 mark for deducting two years' depreciation; 1 mark for 24,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where the depreciation charge appears in the financial statements.
parts.answer: In the statement of profit or loss as an expense; the net book value appears among the non-current assets in the statement of financial position.
parts.working: 1 mark for profit or loss expense (the net book value in the statement of financial position is also acceptable).

practice.stem: A clerk in a school office often leaves the accounting system open on a shared computer when she goes to the staff room.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why staff should log out of the accounting system, or lock their screen, when they leave their desk.
parts.answer: If an unattended computer is left logged in, another person can read, change or delete data under the first person's user ID, which breaks the audit trail.
parts.working: 1 mark for the risk of unauthorised use; 1 mark for the effect on the audit trail or accountability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two risks of this practice.
parts.answer: Unauthorised change to records; data copied or viewed by visitors; a fraud that cannot be traced to the person who was logged in.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid risk (any two).

practice.stem: A business's payment system requires two different staff members to authorise any payment above $5,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a business would require two authorisers for payments above $5,000.
parts.answer: A second person reviews the payment, reducing the risk of fraud or error by one person. Two separate people must agree before the money moves.
parts.working: 1 mark for reducing the risk of one person acting alone; 1 mark for a second person reviewing the payment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways the accounting software can enforce this rule.
parts.answer: The software can hold any payment above $5,000 until a second user with approval rights approves it, so the same user cannot enter and approve it. It can also set user roles so that the person who creates a payment cannot authorise it.
parts.working: 2 marks for each method, with 1 mark for describing it and 1 mark for explaining how it applies the rule (any two).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business uses an integrated computerised accounting system in which every entry must have equal debits and credits.
Which error could still occur?
A a sales ledger total that is added up incorrectly
B a debit entry with no corresponding credit entry
C a trial balance that does not agree
D a sales invoice posted to the account of the wrong customer
parts.answer: D a sales invoice posted to the account of the wrong customer
parts.working: Posting to the wrong customer is an error of commission: debits still equal credits, so the system cannot detect it. The software performs the arithmetic and enforces double entry, so A, B and C cannot occur.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A batch of supplier invoices has a manually calculated batch total of $23,640. After the invoices were keyed in, the computer total was $23,910.
Which single error would explain the difference?
A an invoice for $4,580 was keyed in as $4,850
B an invoice for $270 was not keyed in
C an invoice for $4,850 was keyed in as $4,580
D a credit note for $270 was keyed in as an invoice
parts.answer: A an invoice for $4,580 was keyed in as $4,850
parts.working: The computer total is 270 too high (23,910 − 23,640). Keying 4,850 for 4,580 adds 270. B and C would make the total 270 too low; D would make it 540 too high.

practice.stem:
Noor Pharmacy, Quetta, is considering a computerised accounting system. Estimated costs and savings:
                                                   $
Software (one-off)                             4,800
Hardware (one-off)                             7,200
Staff training (one-off)                       1,500
Annual software licence                          900
Annual saving in part-time bookkeeper's wages  6,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total initial cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net annual saving.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the payback period in years, correct to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 2.65 years

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the owner whether to introduce the system. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: the cost is recovered in under three years, after which $5,100 a year is saved; faster, more accurate records and up-to-date inventory and receivables information. Against: hardware may need replacing in about three to five years; staff must learn the system; risks of breakdown and data loss; savings are estimates. Decision: introduce the system, as payback is short compared with the system's likely life, but plan backups and training.
parts.working: 1 mark: financial point using figures. 1 mark: non-financial benefit. 1 mark: drawback/risk. 1 mark: justified decision.

practice.stem: Kaghan Supplies gives every customer a four-digit account number followed by a check digit. The check digit is calculated as follows: multiply the four digits by the weights 5, 4, 3 and 2 in order; add the results; divide by 11; the check digit is 11 minus the remainder. When an account number is entered, the computer multiplies the five digits by 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 and accepts the number only if the total is exactly divisible by 11.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the check digit for account number 3725.
parts.answer: 7 (full number 37257)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A clerk keys in 37527 instead of 37257. Show that the computer will reject it.
parts.answer: Weighted total = 69, which is not divisible by 11, so the number is rejected.
parts.working: 3×5 + 7×4 + 5×3 + 2×2 + 7×1 = 69 (M1); 69 ÷ 11 leaves remainder 3, so rejected (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of input error this check is designed to detect.
parts.answer: Transposition errors (digits swapped) and single-digit keying errors.

practice.stem: Margalla Engineering Ltd is replacing its old accounting software with a new system. The finance director must choose between direct changeover (switching completely on one day) and parallel running (running both systems together for three months).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'parallel running'.
parts.answer: Operating the old and new systems at the same time, with the same data, so their results can be compared before the old system is dropped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the finance director which method to use. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Parallel running: results from the new system can be checked against the old, and if the new system fails the old one is still available, so the risk of losing accounting records is low; but staff must enter everything twice, which is costly, slow and may cause mistakes. Direct changeover: cheap and quick, and staff concentrate on one system; but if the new system fails there is no fallback and records, payments to suppliers or payroll could be disrupted. Decision: for a company's main accounting records, use parallel running (perhaps for one month-end close only) because the cost of failure is greater than the extra staff time.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points on parallel running; up to 2 marks for points on direct changeover; 1 mark for applying to the company (size, importance of records, staff time); 1 mark for a justified decision.

practice.stem: Bolan Distributors issues 2,400 sales invoices a month. Preparing an invoice by hand takes 6 minutes; with the proposed system it would take 1.5 minutes. Invoicing clerks are paid $9 an hour. The new system would cost $12,000 a year to rent and maintain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of clerk hours saved each month.
parts.answer: 180 hours

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual saving in clerks' wages.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net annual saving after the cost of the system.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Discuss non-financial factors the directors should consider before introducing the system.
parts.answer: Staff may resist the change or fear job losses, affecting morale; staff need training and there may be early errors; faster, more accurate invoices may improve customer service and cash collection; dependence on the system creates risks of breakdown and data loss.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to three relevant factors, developed (staff morale/redundancy; training; customer service; security/reliability).

practice.stem:
The accounting software of Chenab Wholesalers produced this aged trade receivables report at 31 March 2026:
Age of debt        $
0–30 days     45,200
31–60 days    21,000
61–90 days    10,500
Over 90 days   7,300
Total         84,000
The business creates a provision for doubtful debts of 2% on debts up to 30 days, 5% on 31–60 days, 10% on 61–90 days and 40% on debts over 90 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of trade receivables that are more than 60 days old. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the provision for doubtful debts at 31 March 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the computerised aged receivables report helps credit control.
parts.answer: It is produced instantly and accurately at any time, so the credit controller can quickly see which customers are overdue and by how long, and chase them or stop further credit before debts become irrecoverable.
parts.working: 1 mark: quick/accurate/up to date. 1 mark: identifies overdue customers for action.

practice.stem: At Khyber Steel Ltd one purchases clerk can set up new suppliers in the computerised purchase ledger, record invoices and authorise payments. Last year the clerk created a false supplier account and paid $18,000 into his own bank account before the fraud was discovered.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two weaknesses in the control system that allowed the fraud.
parts.answer: There was no segregation of duties: one person could create suppliers, record invoices and approve payments. Access levels were too wide and no one else reviewed new supplier accounts or payments.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend controls to prevent such a fraud happening again. Justify your recommendations.
parts.answer: Separate duties so that different staff create suppliers, record invoices and authorise payments, so fraud needs collusion. Set access levels so the clerk cannot add suppliers; new suppliers approved by a manager with checks on bank details. Review the audit trail and exception reports of new suppliers and payments regularly. Require two authorisations for payments above a set limit.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per developed recommendation (control + why it works), max 4.

practice.stem: Sadia & Co. Ltd introduced a computerised accounting system last year. A director says: 'Now that the software does all the double entry, we no longer need to prepare bank reconciliations or check control accounts.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the director's statement.
parts.answer: Partly true: the software keeps debits equal to credits, posts to ledgers and control accounts automatically and removes arithmetic errors, so some manual checks are no longer needed. However, the bank reconciliation compares the business's records with an independent source (the bank statement); it still finds unpresented cheques, bank charges, direct debits not entered, keying errors and fraud. Errors of commission, omission and original entry are not detected by the software. Control accounts and reconciliations are also internal controls that auditors expect. Conclusion: the statement is not justified; reconciliations should continue, although the software makes them quicker.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points supporting the statement; up to 3 marks for points against (independent check, errors not detected, fraud, audit expectations); 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Rehman Electricals, a small business in Multan, is thinking of moving from accounting software on one office computer to a cloud-based accounting package paid for by monthly subscription.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the business should move to cloud-based accounting.
parts.answer: For: data can be reached from anywhere, e.g. by the owner at home or the accountant; the provider makes automatic backups and updates; no large up-front cost; can link to online banking for automatic bank feeds. Against: depends on a reliable internet connection, which may be a problem in some areas; monthly fees continue for ever; data held by a third party raises security and confidentiality concerns; staff need retraining. Conclusion: move to the cloud if the internet is reliable and the provider has strong security, because backup and access benefits outweigh the subscription cost.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for advantages and up to 2 marks for disadvantages applied to the business; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An employee changes a supplier's bank details in the purchase ledger, then the next payment goes to the new account. Which control would most effectively DETECT this kind of fraud after it happens?
A Encryption of the supplier file
B A password change every 30 days
C A supervisor's regular review of a log of all changes to supplier bank details
D A firewall between the office and the internet
parts.answer: C A supervisor's regular review of a log of all changes to supplier bank details
parts.working: A review of the change log reveals unauthorised or unusual changes once they have been made, so it detects them. Encryption and a firewall mainly protect data from outsiders, and password changes reduce guessing but do not show a change made by an authorised user.

practice.stem: Bazaar Foods is comparing two accounting software options over three years. Option A is cloud-based: a set-up fee of $1,200 and a monthly subscription of $180. Option B is installed on the business's own server: a one-off licence of $9,000 and maintenance of $1,000 a year. Ignore interest and inflation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of Option A over three years.
parts.working: 1 mark for 36 monthly payments; 1 mark for 7,680.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of Option B over three years.
parts.working: 1 mark for maintenance over three years; 1 mark for 12,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which option is cheaper, by how much, and one non-financial factor the business should consider before choosing.
parts.answer: Option A is cheaper by $4,320. Non-financial factor (any one): data is stored on the supplier's servers and access depends on the internet; the business depends on the supplier's continued service; the supplier may increase its charges.
parts.working: 1 mark for option A; 1 mark for 4,320; 1 mark for one valid non-financial factor with a reason.

practice.stem: A business keeps backup copies of its accounting data each day, each week and each month. Each copy is 2.4 GB. Daily copies are kept for 7 days, weekly copies for 4 weeks and monthly copies for 12 months.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of backup copies kept at any one time.
parts.answer: 23 copies (7 daily + 4 weekly + 12 monthly).
parts.working: 1 mark for each type of copy counted; 1 mark for 23.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total storage needed, in GB.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for 55.2 GB.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the business should test restoring from a backup at least once a year.
parts.answer: A backup that cannot be restored is useless, and the test shows whether the copies, the media and the procedure actually work when needed.
parts.working: 1 mark for a backup that may be faulty; 1 mark for the test confirming recovery will work.

practice.stem: A business estimates the expected annual loss from a ransomware attack as: probability of attack in a year × cost of the attack. The cost of an attack would be $60,000. Without extra security the probability is 8% a year. A security service costing $3,000 a year reduces the probability to 2% a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected annual loss without the security service.
parts.working: 1 mark for 4,800.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected annual loss with the security service.
parts.working: 1 mark for 1,200.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net annual benefit of the service, and state whether the business should buy it. Give one reason.
parts.answer: The reduction in expected loss is 3,600 a year; the service costs 3,000, so the net benefit is $600 a year. The business should buy it on this estimate, because the benefit is positive, but the probabilities are only estimates and should be reviewed.
parts.working: 1 mark for the reduction of 3,600; 1 mark for net benefit of 600; 1 mark for a decision with a reason (for example that the estimates are uncertain).

practice.stem: A clerk keys in a batch of account numbers, and a hash total of the account numbers is used as the control total. Account numbers in this batch include 2071 and 2185.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, with an example, why a hash total can fail to detect two keying errors that cancel each other out.
parts.answer: Account 2071 is keyed as 2081 (+10) and account 2185 is keyed as 2175 (−10). The total is still 4,256 for both, so the hash total agrees even though both numbers are wrong.
parts.working: 1 mark for the two errors offsetting; 1 mark for a correct example in which the total is unchanged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one further check that would help detect such errors.
parts.answer: A check digit on each account number, which detects a mis-keyed number individually; or a separate record count or a second control total on a different field.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid check; 1 mark for explaining how it would catch the error.

practice.stem: A purchase department uses a computerised system for all purchases from suppliers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a computerised purchase system uses three-way matching to prevent payment for goods that were not received. Give one limitation of this control.
parts.answer: The system compares the purchase order, the goods received note and the supplier's invoice for quantity and price. Payment is released only when the three agree within set tolerances. Limitation: the match does not check the quality of the goods, and it cannot detect false goods-received notes created by staff who are in collusion with the supplier.
parts.working: 3 marks for explaining the three-way comparison, with 1 mark for each of: the three documents compared; the matching of quantity and price; release of payment only when they agree. 1 mark for a valid limitation.

practice.stem: A wholesaler processes 6,000 sales invoices a year. Manual processing takes 9 minutes per invoice. The new computerised system takes 2.5 minutes per invoice. One clerk works 1,800 paid hours a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the hours saved each year.
parts.answer: 650 hours (manual 900 hours − new system 250 hours).
parts.working: 1 mark for the time of each method (900 and 250 hours); 1 mark for 650.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of full-time clerks the change releases, using 1,800 paid hours a year for each clerk.
parts.working: 1 mark for dividing the hours saved by 1,800; 1 mark for 0.36.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss two non-financial effects of the change that the owner should consider.
parts.answer: Staff may need training and may resist the change, or the remaining staff may take on new roles. The system may reduce keying errors and speed up invoicing, but the business becomes dependent on the software and needs contingency plans if it fails.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of up to three valid effects, each with a brief reason (any two discussed fully).

practice.stem: Lotus Pharmacy Ltd, Lahore, keeps customer records and its accounting data on its own server. The owner is considering moving the data to a cloud provider whose servers are located in another country, to reduce IT costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether the company should store its data with a cloud provider whose servers are in another country. Consider security, legal and operational factors, and reach a recommendation.
parts.answer: Security: encryption of data in transit and at rest, strong access controls, the provider's certifications and tested backups. Legal: which data protection law applies, whether the company can access, audit and delete its data, and where disputes would be heard. Operational: dependence on the internet and on the provider's service levels, downtime, and how the company would get its data back if the provider failed. Recommendation: a clear decision, for example to proceed only if the contract guarantees encryption, audit rights, data return and a service level, or to choose a provider with a local data centre.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for security points, 2 for legal points, 2 for operational points, and 1 mark for a reasoned recommendation linked to the facts (for example the sensitivity of customer data at a pharmacy). Maximum 8.

practice.stem: A medium-sized trading business in Karachi wants accounts staff to work from home on some days. The accounting system is hosted on the office server and can be reached over the internet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the business should allow its accounts staff to log in to the accounting system from home, using their own laptops.
parts.answer: Benefits: flexibility and continuity of work. Risks: unsecured home networks and shared devices; malware on personal laptops; data stored locally and lost if the device is stolen; little supervision of who sees the data. Controls: a secure connection (such as a VPN), two-factor authentication, business-managed devices, no local storage of data, and logging of remote access. Conclude with a justified view of whether the risk is acceptable given the controls available.
parts.working: 1–2 marks: identifies benefits and risks. 3–4 marks: explains the risks and the controls that reduce them. 5–6 marks: a balanced discussion that reaches a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: The payroll clerk's hand-prepared control total for the net pay of 22 employees is $412,380. After processing, the computer's payroll report shows a total of $412,830.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the two payroll totals.
parts.working: 1 mark for 450.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the most likely type of input error and explain your reasoning.
parts.answer: A transposition error: the difference of 450 is exactly divisible by 9 (450 ÷ 9 = 50), which is typical of two digits swapped. In 412,380 the digits 3 and 8 in the hundreds and tens places have been swapped to give 412,830.
parts.working: 1 mark for transposition error; 1 mark for the divisibility by 9 (450 ÷ 9 = 50); 1 mark for identifying the swapped digits.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one control that would catch this error before payments are released.
parts.answer: An independent re-check of keyed amounts, or a comparison of the payroll report total with the hand-prepared control total before release.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid control.
